# About the Book

A man comes to himself on a sunlit street of an eastern port city, not remembering who he is, nor how he came to be here, nor why this city seems strangely familiar to him.

And then the impossible begins.

Drawn into the world of an aristocratic house, he meets a mysterious stranger, an abandoned castle, and two ancient stones that seem to answer to the borders between worlds. Fragments of another life surface in visions of Ancient Egypt. A note in an unknown language points him the way to Sultanahmet. And somewhere in the shadows a grey figure watches him.

The deeper the mystery, the faster the borders between past and present blur. The man discovers that he is bound to a Pharaoh in the Valley of the Nile, to the Ottoman Empire, and to a forgotten history in which, perhaps, lies the key to his own identity.

Inspired by the author's travels through 62 countries of the world, "The Appearance" is a sweeping adventure-mystery novel that joins historical prose, mysticism and the enchantment of far wandering. From the ancient world to the streets of Constantinople, each discovery poses a more unsettling question:

What if the past has never gone away?

And what if someone - or something - is waiting for him to finally remember?

"The Appearance" is the first book in the "Terra Incognita" series: a journey through lost stories, mysterious worlds and secrets hidden beyond the borders of time.

# Part One. The Appearance

## Chapter I. The Appearance

A step. Then another. Soft velvet boots the colour of burgundy trod the sun-warmed cobbles so confidently that it seemed my feet remembered this road better than I did. The day was warm and languid, one of those days that thicken toward noon with the heat and with the smell of the sea drifting somewhere beyond the tiled roofs.

Who am I? Where am I? And - a far stranger question - where am I going?

I stopped for a moment, as though a body held motionless might compel memory to yield an answer. It did not. All around me, here and there, stood houses that might have stepped from the pages of an Eastern fairy tale: the ground floor of stone, pale, with a faint coffee tint, the upper floor of wood, jutting slightly forward, as if the house were bowing to the street. The roofs were crowned with dark-red undulating tiles, and from the chimneys, unhurriedly, without any fuss, rose a light bluish-grey smoke, dissolving into a sky gone white with heat.

A warm, damp wind, smelling of salt and spices and of something else - distant, indefinable - swayed the weathervane on the roof of the house opposite, as it did on all the other houses along the street. Between the windows of the upper storeys, ropes had been strung, and on them, rinsing in the breeze, hung coverlets of the most unimaginable colours: scarlet, ochre, turquoise - as though someone had hung the very rainbow out to dry, cut into ragged strips. Some windows had no glass at all - they were curtained with carpets or thick cloth; others stood flung wide open, and from their half-darkness came smells that, against my will, set my stomach aching. Roast meat. Fresh bread. Something spiced and tantalising whose name I did not know.

So, it was midday. And I was hungry - though, curse it, I could not remember whether I had ever eaten at all in my life, or whether this hunger was as unfamiliar to me as my own name.

Children raced along the street - shouting, laughing, with no visible purpose, as children run everywhere and always, in every age and every country. Two boys drove a wooden hoop ahead of them with a stick, and the hoop, bouncing over the uneven stones, rattled as if a tiny chariot were rolling down the road. A girl of about six, with braids tied up in red thread, sat on a doorstep feeding something from her palm to a mangy ginger cat, which accepted the treat with the air of a queen condescending to her subjects. The grown-ups strolled at a stately pace, greeting one another with a brief nod and a hand laid to the chest; someone older had settled in the shade of a cornice and was playing a game faintly resembling draughts - or perhaps backgammon, I was not sure, my memory refused to supply even so small a thing. The occasional passer-by smiled at me warmly and said something in a language of which I did not understand a single syllable - but from the warmth of their glances I guessed that the words were kind.

Who am I and where am I - again, more insistently now, I asked myself. I do not remember… I do not know… or do I not wish to remember? Neither my name, nor the city, nor the purpose of my journey. And why, devil take it, was I dressed so strangely?

I looked myself over - as if seeing myself for the first time. Soft suede boots of burgundy colour, with a dainty bow. A dark-red turban with a tassel. Trousers of an indigo so deep, so nearly black, that they seemed a starless night sky, for some reason pulled over the middle of a sunlit day. A white shirt. A leather belt. And over it all, a light travelling cloak on a soft silk lining, too elegant, perhaps, for a walk on foot through a port town.

The clothes told me absolutely nothing. They merely doubled the number of questions without giving a single answer.

Perhaps my pockets would prove more talkative? I thrust my hand into the right pocket of my trousers and felt two stones there - smooth, almost polished, a little larger than a big bean. One black, one white. I drew them out into the light and turned them between my fingers. There was a strange heaviness in them - not physical, something else, hard to explain, as though the stones knew far more about me than I knew about myself.

What did they mean? Who had given them to me - or where had I picked them up?

In the left pocket I found a sheet of paper, neatly folded in four - perfectly blank, without a single letter or mark - and several coins bearing strange symbols such as I had never seen before. And deeper still, in a hidden pocket of the cloak, I discovered a small scrap of paper with an inscription in a language resembling Arabic or Farsi, which I could not have read had my life depended on it.

These finds shed not a drop of light on my situation - they only thickened the darkness. Strange money. Two stones. A blank sheet. A mysterious note. I was not even certain whether I could read this language at all - or whether someone else had slipped the note into a pocket that was foreign to me while I was not looking.

And yet, turning the white stone between my fingers, I caught myself in a feeling for which it was hard to find any word other than recognition. As though I had already held this stone - not today, not here, but somewhere, sometime, in a hand that was mine and at the same time belonged, it seemed, to quite another man. The sensation flickered and vanished, leaving only a vague aftertaste, like waking from a dream whose contents are forgotten faster than you can open your eyes.

I shook my head to drive off the delusion, put the stones back in my pocket, and slowly moved on along the winding, narrow, yet in its own way cosy little street.

* * *
"Simit! Taze simit! Sıcak simit!"

A ringing boy's voice rang out behind me so unexpectedly that I started. Turning, I saw a lad of about twelve - barefoot, in a faded shirt, trousers rolled to the knee, and a tiny round cap that by some miracle stayed on the crown of his head. On his head, right on top of the cap, rested an enormous wooden tray laden with golden-brown rings of bread generously sprinkled with sesame. The boy carried it with that careless, almost acrobatic dexterity with which one carries things that have long since become part of one's own body: the tray never once swayed, even when the lad leapt over a puddle by the gutter.

The smell of fresh bread, toasted sesame and something sweetish, treacly, struck my nose with such force that my stomach, until then merely grumbling quietly, let out a full-throated howl.

The boy, evidently, heard it. At any rate, he stopped right in front of me, looked over my turban, my cloak, my velvet boots with open interest - and broke into the broad, gap-toothed grin of a man who has scented a profitable customer.

"Buyurun, efendi! Simit?" He deftly lifted one ring from the tray and waved it under my nose as if luring a cat.

"I would gladly," I said, "but I am afraid I do not understand a word."

The boy tilted his head to one side, listening to my speech with the same expression with which one listens to the song of an unfamiliar bird. Then he repeated, louder and slower, as people speak to the deaf or to foreigners - in all the countries of the world, it seems, the same:

"Si-mit. Simit!"

And, for good measure, he took a bite of the ring himself, demonstratively, closing his eyes with exaggerated delight - after which he held the bitten ring out to me.

I could not help laughing. The pantomime was so expressive that no translation was needed.

"I see," I said. "This is eaten. This is delicious. And you want me to pay for it."

I thrust my hand into my left pocket and fished out one of the strange coins - small, yellowish, with an incomprehensible sign on one side and something like interlaced lines on the other. I held it out to the boy.

He took the coin between two fingers, brought it right up to his nose, turned it over, held it up to the light, and then, to my astonishment, briskly bit it with his teeth - and frowned thoughtfully. He said something - questioningly, jabbing a finger at the sign on the coin. I spread my hands. He said something more, now with a note of suspicion, and called to someone over his shoulder, loudly, for the whole street to hear:

"Hasan Amca! Bak şuna!"

From the shop opposite - tiny, two paces wide, crammed with sacks and baskets of something colourful and fragrant - a man looked out. Heavy-set, in a long robe girdled with a sash, with a full beard dyed with henna a deep russet. He wiped his hands on his robe, unhurriedly crossed the street, took the coin from the boy, looked at it, then at me, then at the coin again.

The shopkeeper began to speak - unhurriedly, resonantly - and I caught surprise in his speech, but not hostility. He showed the coin to the boy, shook his head, explained something, tapping his forehead with a finger - a gesture which, it seemed to me, meant not "this man is mad" but rather "never seen the like, but he must be from far away." Then he returned the coin to me - carefully, with both hands, as though returning something precious - and pointed to the ring in the boy's hand, then to me, and waved his hand. The gesture was unmistakable: take it, no charge.

"No, no," I protested, "I cannot…"

But the shopkeeper had already laid a heavy palm on my shoulder and said something at which the boy, shrugging, pressed into my hands not one but two rings at once - one bitten, the other whole.

"Misafir," said the shopkeeper, poking a finger at me and smiling into his russet beard. "Misafir."

I did not know the word. But by the way he said it - warmly, with a slight solemnity - I guessed that it meant something like "guest." And that a guest here is not expected to pay for bread.

"Thank you," I said, laying my palm on my chest as the passers-by did. "Thank you very much."

The shopkeeper, hearing the unfamiliar sounds, nodded as though he had understood every word, and unhurriedly returned to his sacks. The boy walked beside me a little longer, studying me with undisguised curiosity and murmuring something from time to time - and then, evidently deciding that nothing more could be got out of the oddity in velvet boots, he whistled, adjusted his tray, and dashed off up the street, singing out his ringing "Simit! Taze simit!"

I bit into the whole ring. A crisp crust, a soft, faintly sweet crumb, sesame tickling the palate. The taste was so simple and so perfect that for a moment I closed my eyes. If I had ever eaten anything better, my memory had mercifully spared me the necessity of comparing.

* * *
The red-bearded man's shop, as I saw in passing, dealt in spices - and looked as though all the colours of the world had been carted here and poured into sacks. Blood-red pepper in a heap, fiery orange turmeric, dark, almost black cinnamon rolled into little tubes, green cardamom pods, golden saffron in tiny glass vials which the shopkeeper kept on a separate shelf, out of reach of strangers' hands. Over the sacks hung bunches of dried peppers and garlic, and at the very entrance stood a wicker basket filled to the brim with dried figs - dark, wrinkled, with a whitish sugary bloom on their sides.

The red-bearded man, noticing my glance, at once fished the largest fig from the basket and held it out to me. I tried to refuse - I had not even paid for the bread - but he merely shook his hand impatiently, and I gave in. The fig proved soft, honey-sweet, with a thousand tiny seeds crunching between my teeth.

"İncir," said the shopkeeper with pride, as though he had grown it himself.

"Fig," I repeated, and he burst into satisfied laughter, slapping himself on the belly.

At that moment I felt a light, almost weightless touch at my right side.

I lowered my eyes - and saw a small swarthy hand, carefully, with two fingers, creeping into the pocket of my trousers. Where the stones lay.

Without thinking, I seized the slender wrist. Its owner - a grubby boy of about nine, with a shaven head and eyes in which there was not a drop of remorse, only the vexation of a professional caught over a trifle - jerked, trying to break free. A second boy, who had been standing a little way off and was evidently distracting my attention while the first worked, at once took to his heels.

"Oh no," I said, not releasing the wrist. "That is mine. It seems to be the only thing I have at all."

The boy shouted something - judging by the tone, by no means an apology. But before I could decide what to do with him, the red-bearded shopkeeper popped up from behind his sacks with a nimbleness unexpected for his build and brought down upon the thief a whole torrent of words - loud, rolling, at which all the lad's insolence vanished at once. The boy shrank, lowered his head. The shopkeeper finished his tirade, dealt him a ringing cuff on the back of the head, and nodded to me: let go.

I loosened my fingers. The thief sprang back a pace, rubbed his wrist, shot me a quick glance - and suddenly, to my surprise, awkwardly laid his hand to his chest and muttered something short. Then he turned and vanished into the crowd.

The shopkeeper turned to me and began to speak - now apologetically, shaking his head and spreading his hands. I did not understand the words, but the sense was clear: he was ashamed of his street before a guest.

"It is nothing," I said, patting my pocket, where the stones lay still in their place. "Nothing is missing. All is well."

He understood, it seems, only the intonation - and that proved enough. He nodded, smiled again into his russet beard, and pressed another fig into my hand - evidently as compensation for the ordeal.

I walked on, chewing the honeyed fruit, and thought that of all the things lying in my pockets - the strange coins, the blank sheet, the mysterious note - the thief had reached precisely for the stones. Chance? Most likely. The boy had simply felt something heavy in the pocket and hoped it was gold. And yet I caught myself keeping my right hand in my pocket all the way to the end of the street, clutching both stones in my palm as though they might run away of their own accord.

* * *
The lane swerved, and before me opened a small square with a stone fountain in the middle - cracked, mossy, but still faithfully letting fall a thin thread of water into a rounded basin. Above the basin, on a marble slab, an inscription was carved - the same script, graceful, flowing, like that on my note, though not quite: the letters here were larger, bolder, chiselled by the hand of a master who knew no haste. I looked at it for a long time, trying to find even one familiar stroke - and found none. The inscription was as stubbornly silent as my memory.

Several women were drawing water into clay pitchers, conversing among themselves in low, sing-song voices. At my approach they fell silent and stepped back, lowering their heads - and I, not knowing why, stepped back too, letting them finish, as one does, presumably, everywhere that others' customs are respected.

One of them, however, did not move away. An old woman - judging by her bent back and the thin, root-like fingers holding the pitcher - a very ancient old woman, muffled in dark cloth from head to foot so that only her eyes could be seen. Those eyes, faded, watery, looked straight at me - long, intently, unblinking.

I smiled awkwardly and nodded to her. She did not return the nod. Instead she set the pitcher on the edge of the fountain, slowly raised her hand, and folded her fingers into a strange sign - spreading them like a fan, palm toward me. Then she muttered a few words, spat over her shoulder - three times, distinctly - and, picking up the pitcher, hobbled away, glancing back again and again.

The other women exchanged looks. One of them, younger, said something quietly, reproachfully, after the old woman, then cast me a quick apologetic glance and lowered her eyes again.

I stood at the fountain, not knowing what to think. The gesture was too eloquent to be mistaken: this is how one wards off the evil eye. This is how one defends oneself against what seems incomprehensible and therefore dangerous. What had this old woman seen in me? A stranger in an overly costly cloak? A foreigner whose speech grates on the ear? Or - an absurd thought, but it came of itself, uninvited - something else, which the others did not see? Something that I myself did not yet see?

I drove the thought away. Old women in all countries must be alike: they fancy the evil eye everywhere.

When the women had gone, I at last scooped up some water in my palm and raised it to my lips. The water was cool and strangely sweetish, as though something had been dissolved in it for which there is no name in any language.

"Su! Buz gibi su!"

From around the corner, clinking like a walking belfry, came a water-seller - a dry, sinewy old man with an enormous copper vessel on his back, its curved neck thrown over his shoulder. At his belt hung tin cups polished to a shine, and at every step they chimed out something like a simple tune. Seeing that I was drinking from the fountain, he stopped, shook his head reproachfully and said something - judging by his gestures, to the effect that drinking from the fountain was the way of the poor, and a respectable gentleman ought to drink from his vessel, where the water was both colder and sweeter and, one must suppose, dearer.

I showed him my empty palms - no money - and he, shrugging, without any offence moved on, jingling his cups and calling out across the whole square: "Su! Buz gibi su!" It seemed that on this street no one knew how to take real offence.

Somewhere far off, beyond the roofs, a steamer's whistle bellowed, long, with a deep, lingering echo. Water somewhere near - not only in the fountain. A sea? A strait? A navigable bay? For a moment, shreds of something - memories or merely sensations - stirred in me, connected with ships, with the salt wind, with a deck underfoot - bright as a flash of rainbow, and as fleeting. Before I could seize them, they melted without a trace, leaving only the vexation of a man who has not been allowed to finish reading a letter.

Another sensation flickered after the first - no longer about ships. Someone's face, blurred, as though seen through a depth of water or through the years. I had no time to make out its features - neither the line of the cheekbones nor the colour of the eyes - but along with this vague image came a feeling to which I could not have given a name: not quite warmth, not quite alarm, perhaps both at once, twisted into one tight knot somewhere beneath my ribs. I froze, tried to hold the image, to look closer - but it slipped away as swiftly as the steamer's whistle had dissolved in the scorched air of the square, leaving behind only the echo of something for which I could find neither cause nor name.

Strange, I thought, moving away from the fountain. Not to remember one's own name is cruel enough in itself. But never to understand what troubles you in a face you scarcely had time to glimpse - that is cruelty of another, quieter kind.

* * *
Beyond the square the street plunged steeply downward, and between the houses, through a gap, water suddenly opened up.

I stopped, astonished. There below lay a sea - or not a sea but a wide strait, deep blue, almost violet in the noon light, flecked with the white triangles of sails and the dark spots of boats. Over the water, lazily, aslant, trailed a black tail of smoke - the very steamer whose whistle I had heard - and on the opposite shore, in a bluish haze, another city rose: hills thickly covered with houses, and above them - domes. Huge, heavy, leaden-grey domes, surrounded by towers thin as needles. One, another, a third - I lost count. They pierced the whitish sky with such imperturbable assurance, as though they had stood here since the creation of the world and meant to stand until its end.

I did not know what city it was. I did not know what this water was called. I did not know whose domes those were, or to whom they prayed beneath them. But looking at it all - at the blue, the sails, the needles of the towers - I suddenly felt something that took my breath away: not even recognition, but something greater and at the same time less definite. As if this city, which I did not know, knew me. As if it were looking at me from across the strait - patiently, without surprise, as one looks at a traveller who has at last returned after a long absence.

Beside me, on a low stone wall, sat an old man in a worn robe, leisurely smoking a long pipe. Noticing how I had frozen, he followed my gaze, then looked at me - and smiled understandingly.

"Güzel, değil mi?" he said, pointing with his pipe at the strait.

I did not understand the words. But I understood the meaning - it was in his voice, in his smile, in the way he looked at the water.

"Beautiful," I answered. "Very beautiful."

The old man nodded as though we had understood each other perfectly, and drew on his pipe again. We looked at the water together in silence - two strangers without a single word in common - and it seemed to me for a moment that this was the most meaningful conversation I had had all that morning.

* * *
I moved forward again, trying to distract myself from thoughts too heavy for so sunny a day. The passers-by continued to nod and smile at me; I tried to reply in kind, with a broad, open smile which, judging by the reaction of those I met, made the most favourable impression on them - perhaps the only thing of which I could now be certain.

I was definitely missing something in my hands - perhaps a walking stick. Not that I needed it physically: my legs carried me lightly and freely. But some forgotten feeling suggested that a cane was an integral part of my everyday appearance, a detail without which the costume seemed incomplete, like a sentence without its last word.

As for the appearance of the other passers-by - the men were dressed almost as I was, differing only in the colour and quality of the cloth. The same burgundy turbans with tassels, trousers of every shade, white shirts girded with plain cloth belts of black or red. Their footwear, however, differed markedly from mine - leather coarse to look at, stiff, uncomfortable - though neat and well kept.

No one wore a cloak. Still, I thought, who would muffle himself in a travelling cloak while strolling by his own doorstep?

Women were seen rarely and were covered from head to foot in dark garments, remotely resembling the Indian sari - with the difference that here not only the hair was hidden, but the face as well, and the hands, absolutely everything that could be hidden from strangers' eyes.

At the open door of a barber's shop - I guessed its purpose from the copper basin hanging over the entrance - sat a man with lathered cheeks, his head thrown back against the back of a low chair, while the barber, slight and deft, drew a long gleaming razor along his throat and at the same time told some tale at which the customer kept trying to burst out laughing - and each time the barber snatched the razor away with a reproachful exclamation. Seeing me, the barber broke off his work for a moment, ran a professional eye over my chin - evidently assessing the stubble - and beckoned with his razor toward a vacant chair. I hastily shook my head. The barber shrugged with the air of one watching me commit the great mistake of my life, and returned to his customer.

I stopped in the middle of the street. It was time to admit the obvious: I was in one of the port cities of the Near East - where seas, caravan routes and continents meet, where merchants of every tongue and faith come together. In a city where boys sell bread from trays on their heads, where shopkeepers treat strangers to sweets, where thieves apologise with a hand pressed to the heart, and where old women ward off the evil eye from foreigners.

In a city that, it seemed, knew me better than I knew myself.

* * *
Of all the houses along the street, my eye singled out one - with bright-red tiles, evidently recently re-laid, with the wooden cladding of the upper floor covered in glossy lacquer, and a ground floor of pale, faintly coffee-coloured stone. Something about this house - perhaps the neatness with which it was built, or perhaps something less explicable - disposed me toward it for no visible reason that I could put into words.

Right by the entrance, a little to one side of the road, on the lush green grass, a magnificent carpet runner had been spread - an old one, judging by the intricate pattern depicting flowers and plants such as I had never seen before even in my boldest (though entirely forgotten) dreams. A company had settled on the carpet: two elderly men with grey beards, in warm robes and skullcaps, and three young men bustling around them, receiving from time to time brief, good-natured remarks from the elders. Between the old men stood a large wooden box carved with patterns - looking closer, I recognised in it a backgammon set: those very dice and counters which, it seemed, I had already seen twice that morning, though I could not once have explained how I knew the word at all.

One of the old men clicked the dice, dropped a phrase - quiet but commanding - and the young men bustled obediently, pouring something steaming from a tall copper kettle into small glass tumblers.

I moved toward them, feeling resolve strengthening in me - or perhaps merely the despair of a man left with no option but to trust the first benevolent faces he meets. This street had already proved to me twice that benevolence here was not a rarity but a custom. As I walked I took out of my pocket once more the scrap of paper with the incomprehensible inscription, hoping - without much reason - that someone here would be able to help me.

And then, at the very edge of vision, where the narrow lane turned around the corner of a house with blue shutters, a figure flickered.

Grey - not in the colour of its clothes, but as though wholly, from head to foot, moulded of ash and mist - it stood motionless in the shadow of an arch, and it seemed to me that it was looking straight at me, intently, with no friendliness in its gaze, which I, however, scarcely made out - too quickly, too far.

I blinked. The figure was gone. Only the shadow of the cornice and a light shimmer of noonday heat trembling above the scorching paving stones - the most ordinary optical illusion, of which any man must surely suffer who has spent too long in the heat with not a single thought in his head about who he is.

"It only seemed so," I told myself as confidently as I could.

And yet I could not help recalling the old woman at the fountain, her splayed fingers and the three spits over her shoulder. Perhaps, I thought, she had seen not me. Perhaps she had seen what stood behind my back.

The inner voice - the very one that two minutes earlier had refused to console me with any explanation regarding the stones - did not trouble to answer at all. Which was, perhaps, more eloquent than any reply.

Shaking my head for the second time that mad morning, I banished the ominous shadow to the farthest corner of my mind - to the same place where the nameless face, the vague yearning and the shreds of ship memories already lay - and resolutely made my way toward the old men seated on the carpet in the shade of the hospitable house, to obtain at last some answer, however modest, to the question that had tormented me from the very moment I had found myself in the middle of this strange, warm street that smelled of the sea and of spices.

## Vision I. Luxor

We were walking - this I remember with perfect clarity, though everything else about that day grows hazier each time I try to recall it, as if my memory had agreed to keep one single detail in exchange for the whole. We were walking.

But before that - before that, there was the river.

I remember it the way one remembers the face of a dying man: not whole, but feature by feature, each more painful than the last. The Nile, which at this season ought to have been full and heavy, turbid with the silt that brings life to the fields, flowed in a narrow, weary ribbon down the middle of its immeasurably wide bed. Its banks lay bare and cracked on either side, like old ribs - grey shoals strewn with abandoned boats bleached by the sun, and herons standing knee-deep in the mud, too emaciated to take wing at our approach.

And down this dying river sailed a god.

A golden barque, shining so brightly that it hurt to look at it, glided ahead, drawn on ropes by two dozen oarsmen in the smaller boats. On the barque, beneath a canopy of the finest linen, in a closed shrine like a carved ark, stood a statue - I did not see it, no one saw it but the initiated - yet I knew it was there, as one knows of a heart one cannot see. After it came the barque of the queen of the gods, and after hers the barque of their son, and only then, a little apart, as is fitting for a mortal, though a living god - mine.

A festival. I remember that it was a festival. I remember the music - it drifted from the banks, from somewhere behind the palms, where crowds, in spite of the hunger, in spite of the drought, had gathered to watch the god sail to his southern home. Tambourines. The rattle of sistra, jingling like scattered silver. Flutes spinning out something high and thin, almost plaintive. And above it all, the singing of women, long and drawn out, now merging into a single voice, now breaking apart into hundreds.

"My Pharaoh," said the helmsman of my barque, an old man with a face like sycamore bark, leaning toward me so that the rowers should not hear. "Allow me to speak a word that, perhaps, ought not to be spoken."

"Speak," I answered. I remember that I answered precisely so. I remember my own voice - even, calm, as a Pharaoh's voice should be at a festival.

"I have steered barques on this river since the day my beard began to grow," said the helmsman. "And never once have I seen a god travel south on water so shallow. Twice this morning the god's barque ran aground on a shoal. Twice the rowers hauled it free with their hands, waist-deep in the silt." He fell silent for a moment, looking at the golden radiance ahead. "The old men among us say: if the god does not wish to go, he should not be dragged."

"And if the god wishes it, but the river will not let him?" I asked.

The helmsman looked at me for a long time, and in his faded eyes there flickered something I did not then understand, and which now, years and lives later, I understand all too well: pity.

"Then, my Pharaoh," he said quietly, "one must ask oneself whose will it is - the god's, or that of those who hold the ropes."

He did not say another word until we reached Luxor.

* * *
I remember the landing. I remember how the barque nosed against the stone steps that led down to the water - steps which in good years went almost entirely under, and which now stood exposed to their very foundations, covered in green slime and dried shells. I remember the crowd on the bank - thousands of faces turned toward me, thousands of hands reaching upward. Hungry faces. Wasted hands. People cried out, threw themselves on their faces, held out their children to me - so that the Pharaoh's shadow might fall on them and bring good fortune.

I remember that I walked through that crowd along a living corridor cleared before me by the guard - and that this guard was not the usual one. The faces were strangers'. The shields were the same, the spears the same, but the faces were strangers'. I remember that I noticed this and paid it no heed - or paid it heed, but decided that in the bustle of the festival the detachments had got mixed up, as everything gets mixed up at a festival.

From the landing to the temple ran an avenue of sphinxes - long and straight as a drawn bowstring, receding into the distance between two endless rows of stone beasts with the bodies of lions and the heads of rams. They lay on their plinths with their paws drawn in, and gazed at one another across the road - for thousands of years they had gazed, unblinking, as sentinels gaze who need neither sleep nor food nor to ask questions. Between the forepaws of each stood a small figure - a king, guarded by the beast - and in the slanting evening light it seemed that the beasts were pressing those small kings to their breasts, as mothers press their children.

The crowd pressed in on both sides of the avenue, behind the backs of the sphinxes, and at one moment a woman broke through the guard. Thin, in a sun-faded dress, with a child in her arms - a boy of about three, motionless, with closed eyes and dry, cracked lips. A guardsman swung the shaft of his spear at her, but I raised my hand, and he froze.

"My Pharaoh," the woman whispered, falling to her knees directly on the scorching flagstones. "He has not opened his eyes for three days. The healer said that only a god could help. Or you."

I remember how I looked at the child. I remember his lashes - long, still - and the thin vein in his neck, beating so faintly that it was barely visible. I knew that I was not a god. I knew it as clearly as I knew that I must do what was expected of me. I bent down and touched his forehead with my palm.

The forehead was hot. The child did not open his eyes.

"Take him to the priests of the House of Life," I said to the woman. "Tell them the Pharaoh commanded that he be treated as the children of the palace are treated. Tell them I shall ask after him tomorrow."

Tomorrow. I remember how I spoke that word - and I remember that even then, at that very instant, something within me said, quietly and distinctly: there will be no tomorrow. I drove the thought away. The woman crawled back into the crowd, pressing the child to her breast and repeating my name like a prayer. I never learned what became of the boy.

Somewhere in the crowd, at the foot of one of the sphinxes, sat a blind singer with a small harp on his knees. He plucked the strings and sang, in an aged, cracked, yet strangely pure voice, a song that seemed to be known to everyone around, for people took up individual lines:

"They came down from the Heavens when the earth was empty,
They kindled fire, and the water burst into flame,
They left us bread, and the Nile, and death -
And promised to return, that they might wipe all away."

I remember how I stopped for a moment upon hearing the last line. I remember how the singer, as if sensing my gaze, turned his sightless face toward me and smiled - toothlessly, serenely, as old men smile who have long ceased to be afraid. I remember that I wanted to ask him where the song came from. And I remember that the guard swept me onward, and the question remained unasked.

Beside me walked a man I knew. An old warrior, stocky, his face scored with scars - the commander of my army. His name in this dream slips away from me like a fish from the hand, though I know that I knew it, that I spoke it hundreds of times, that I trusted him more than anyone at court. He walked at my right hand, and his palm lay on the hilt of his sword - not on the belt, as is proper at a festival, but on the very hilt.

"I do not like this guard, my Pharaoh," he said under his breath, without turning his head. "Two of the commanders I do not know at all. Their detachments were supposed to have remained in the capital."

"A festival," I answered. "At a festival everything gets muddled."

"At a festival," he said, "men muddle what they wish to muddle."

I remember those words. I remember how they settled over me like cold - and how I drove that cold away, because a Pharaoh cannot be afraid in the sight of thousands.

At the temple gates we were met. The enormous pylons, two stone wings, rose before us into the sky, painted with scenes of the victories of long-dead kings, and before them, on either side of the entrance, sat stone giants - my predecessors, or ancestors, or those who were called ancestors - gazing over our heads at the river with that expression of eternal, unruffled calm which belongs only to stone. Before the pylons rose an obelisk - slender, sharp, covered with signs from top to bottom - and its shadow, long as a spear, lay across the square, its point aimed directly at the gates.

At the gates stood priests. Many priests. White robes, shaven heads gleaming in the sunset light, incense smoking in bronze bowls on long handles. And at their head - small, rotund, with a head smooth as polished stone - a priest whose face I remember better than I would wish. He bowed before me lower than all the others had bowed - so low that it resembled mockery.

"Peace be upon you, my Pharaoh," he said, in a voice soft and oily as wax. "The High Priest awaits you in the inner court. The god has arrived at his southern home, and the hour has come when the Pharaoh must appear before him - alone, as the First Ones appeared."

"Alone?" repeated the commander of the army, and steel rang in his voice.

"Only the initiated, honoured sir," replied the rotund priest, without so much as glancing at him. "Such is the custom. For thousands of years. Warriors have no place in the inner court of the god - neither armed nor unarmed."

"My Pharaoh…" The commander turned to me, and for the first time I saw in his face what I had never seen there before: fear. Not for himself. For me. "Allow me to go with you. At least as far as the colonnade. At least as far as the first court."

I remember how long I looked at him. I remember that I wanted to say "yes." I remember that behind him, in the crowd, someone was watching me - an old man leaning on a staff, grey-haired, heavy-set - and shaking his head, slowly, from side to side, as though trying to tell me something without words. I do not know who he was. In this dream I do not remember his name. But I remember his eyes, and I remember that they held the same thing as the eyes of the commander of the army.

"Wait for me here," I said. "At the gates. If I do not come out before moonrise…"

I did not finish. I do not remember why I did not finish. I remember only that the commander of the army clenched the hilt of his sword until his knuckles whitened, and bowed his head - heavily, slowly, as one bows one's head before a sentence.

"I shall be here, my Pharaoh," he said. "Until moonrise. And after."

* * *
Beyond the gates lay the first court, and in it were people whose faces I remember only in snatches, like flashes of lightning above a night river.

I remember a young man in costly garments, with bracelets on both arms, standing by a column with the air of one who does not belong here and knows it. As I passed, his bracelets chimed - he hastily pressed his arm to his side to muffle the sound, and looked away. He did not bow. Or he bowed, but too late. I remember only the chime - thin, melodious, out of place, like laughter at a funeral.

I remember a girl in the robes of a junior priestess - very young, with enormous dark eyes ringed in black paint. She stood among the singers who held the sistra, and she was not singing. She was looking at me. When our eyes met, she shook her head almost imperceptibly - once, twice - and her lips soundlessly formed a single word. I did not catch it. But I knew what word it was. I knew it as one knows in dreams things that cannot possibly be known.

"Do not go."

The senior priestess beside her, noticing this, jerked her sharply by the arm, and the girl was led away somewhere into the depths, behind the columns, before I could stop. I remember that I wanted to stop. I remember that I did not.

And I remember a young man. Young, slender, dark-eyed, in the plain linen dress of a scribe. He was trying to make his way to me through the crowd of priests - squeezing between the white robes, working his elbows, and his face was twisted with the despair known only to those who are late, and know they are late. He was shouting something - I saw his lips moving - but in the din of sistra, tambourines and singing I could make out no sound. Two priests intercepted him, took him by the arms and drew him back, gently, almost tenderly, as one draws a child away from a fire. He turned to me once more - and tears stood in his eyes.

I remember that look. Of everything that happened that day, I think I remember it most clearly of all. I do not know why. I do not even know who he was. But somehow, recalling that court, I feel neither fear nor cold - but a sharp, almost unbearable sorrow, as though in that moment something had been taken from me that I had never had time to call my own.

* * *
The High Priest awaited me in the inner court, by the altar, where incense smoked in bronze bowls - thick, sweet, enough to make the head spin.

He was tall, straight as the obelisk at the gates, and no longer young, though age seemed to have no power over his bearing. His robe was whiter than all the others, and on his chest hung a broad collar bearing the image of the sacred Eye, which seemed to look at me together with his own eyes.

"My Pharaoh," he said, and bowed exactly as far as custom required - not a finger's breadth lower. "The god has arrived at his southern home. I thank you for having escorted him."

"I escort the god every year," I answered. "As my predecessors did."

"As the First Ones did," he corrected gently. "Yes. But this year everything is different. This year the river did not wish to let the god go south. You saw it yourself, my Pharaoh. Twice the barque ran aground."

"I saw."

"The gods speak to us in signs," continued the High Priest, slowly circling the altar, the incense smoke curling about him as if alive. "Drought is a sign. A shallow river is a sign. Famine is a sign. The drought will not relent, my Pharaoh, until the scales are set right anew. For too long one pan has outweighed the other."

"And whose pan, in your opinion, has outweighed?" I asked, though the answer was clear to me in advance, as the answer is clear to a question asked not for the sake of an answer, but to hear whether the other will dare to utter it aloud.

He did not dare. Instead of answering he smiled - with that indulgent, patient smile known only to those who are certain that time works for them and not for you.

"The First Ones, who descended from the Heavens," he said instead, "left us not only the Epic. They left us something else. That which the Pharaoh holds in his hand when he stands before the god in his southern home. That which no Pharaoh has held in his hands for many generations - for none of them was worthy."

He made a sign, and from behind a column came a priest - the same one, rotund and oily - bearing before him a casket of black wood, bound at the corners with gold. He set the casket on the edge of the altar and withdrew.

The High Priest lifted the lid.

Inside, on a cushion of faded red linen, lay two stones. One black, one white. Smooth as river pebbles, yet perfect - so perfect that they seemed polished not by human hands but by time itself, for hundreds upon hundreds of years. They did not gleam. They seemed to drink in the light of the torches without reflecting it.

"Take them, my Pharaoh," said the High Priest. "So the First Ones did. Take them - and the gods will see who you are."

I remember how I stretched out my hand. I remember how I touched them - and how something passed through my fingers, from fingertips to wrist, that I can call neither warmth nor cold nor pain - something like recognition, as though I had held them before, long ago, in a hand that was mine and yet was not. I remember that I closed my palm around them and did not wish to let them go.

And I remember the High Priest's face at that moment - no, at that instant, for in those days they knew no minutes, but my memory, it seems, muddles the times. He was looking at my palm clenched around the stones, and on his face was an expression I had never seen before in all the years: not triumph, not gloating, but hunger. A naked, ancient hunger, such as belongs to one who has waited too long.

"Come, my Pharaoh," he said. "There is something you must see with your own eyes before we continue this conversation."

And we went.

* * *
I do not remember how long that journey lasted - an instant, an eternity - but I remember distinctly the gigantic columns of Luxor rising before us one after another like a petrified forest, each trunk broader than the arms of ten men could encircle. Their capitals, open like papyrus buds frozen in the eternal blossoming of stone, were lost somewhere in the darkening heights, from which not a single ray of sunset light fell upon us any longer - up there, only night held sway, having descended sooner than it should have descended upon the earth beneath our feet.

Evening had already fallen on Luxor, but in the west the sky still held a narrow band of dull copper light - that peculiar shade seen only here, above the Nile, when the day does not die at once but reluctantly, clinging to the horizon with its last glimmers, as though even the sun were loath to leave this land.

I was the Pharaoh. I knew it as firmly as I knew the weight of the double crown upon my head - and yet in that knowledge there was not a drop of what might be called power. I was surrounded on all sides: priests walked to the left, to the right, behind me, and only ahead, where we were heading, was it empty - frighteningly, deliberately empty, as it is empty before the place to which you are led without being asked for your consent.

The music had been left behind. Sistra, tambourines, flutes, the singing of women - all of it had fallen silent, cut off by the walls as a thread is cut with a knife. Here, between the columns, it was quiet. So quiet that I could hear the shuffle of the priests' bare feet on the stone flags, the crackle of the torches, and my own breathing - uneven, alien, as though it were not I who breathed, but someone within me.

Between the columns the air was different - thicker, heavier, smelling of torch resin and of something else for which I could not then find a name, and which now, in remembering, I do not dare to name again.

"Tell me, High Priest," I said, and my voice sounded unexpectedly loud in that silence, rebounding from the columns and returning to me as an echo. "What is it that I must see?"

"The truth, my Pharaoh," he answered, without turning. He walked ahead, a little to one side, and the torch in the hand of the priest beside him cast trembling russet glints on his white robe. "The truth that the First Ones knew and their descendants forgot. That the Pharaoh is only a vessel. That the power he holds in his hand never belonged to him. That he merely keeps it - until the appointed time."

Until the appointed time. I remember how those words answered within me with a strange, inexplicable echo - as though I had heard them before, as though I should hear them again, in another place, at another time, in another tongue.

"And when the appointed time runs out?" I asked.

The High Priest at last turned. His face in the torchlight was calm - frighteningly calm.

"Then the power returns to the place from which it came, my Pharaoh. To those who are worthy to keep it."

The priests' steps, until then resounding and confident, grew shorter. I did not understand why at once - and when I understood, it was already too late to understand anything at all: they were not walking beside me, they were encircling me, closing in tighter with every ten paces, as water closes behind the stern of a boat which that same water will in the end swallow up.

I remember that I looked back. I remember the gates far behind, beyond the forest of columns - a tiny rectangle of sunset sky in which, it seemed to me, stood a stocky silhouette with a sword at its belt. He was waiting. He had promised to wait until moonrise. The moon had not yet risen.

The High Priest was the first to halt - between two columns so enormous that in their shade vanished not only my shadow but, it seemed, all that remained of the evening light which had still been clinging to the horizon a moment before.

"Here," he said quietly, almost tenderly.

I wanted to ask - what is here, why here - but I did not manage to utter a word. Whether someone behind my back turned too sharply for a man in a peaceful procession, or the flame of a torch held by one of the priests on my right wavered, casting upon the column's stone a shadow all too like a raised hand, or whether it merely seemed so to me - I cannot say for certain even now, years and, it seems, lives later.

I remember cold. Not the evening cold that descends upon the Valley with the darkness, but another - sharp, concentrated somewhere on the left, beneath the ribs - and the two stones, black and white, suddenly grown heavier in my palm, as if they had absorbed all this cold at once, to keep it from reaching my heart.

I remember that they glowed. Very faintly. Like embers beneath ash.

I do not remember whether anyone struck me. I do not remember whether I cried out. I do not even remember whether I fell - or whether it simply grew dark faster than it should have grown dark even here, among the gigantic columns that so securely hide the sky from the earth.

I remember only one thing - the last, before everything vanished. Far away, beyond the columns, at the gates, someone cried out. A deep, hoarse, desperate cry of a warrior who has realised he is too late. I recognised that voice. I knew that voice. I could not recall the name of the one to whom it belonged - but I knew that he was crying out mine.

And then - darkness. Complete, soundless, without edge or bottom - a darkness into which not even the echo of footsteps reaches, footsteps that only a moment before had seemed to me the most important sound in the world.

* * *
I opened my eyes - and found that I was standing in the middle of a sunlit street, with a scrap of paper in my hand, two paces from old men playing backgammon on a motley carpet.

My heart pounded as though I had truly just been running - or had just died. I raised my free hand to my left side. No wound, no pain. Nothing but the memory of cold, too distinct to be merely a dream - and a question to which I had no answer: had what happened between those columns already happened to me, or had I just seen how it would happen?

I opened my other hand - the one that had been clenched in a fist, I know not since when. Two stones, black and white, lay in it - cool, smooth, silent. Perfectly ordinary. The same as I had found them in my pocket that morning.

I did not know where they had come from. But looking at them, for the first time in all that long, strange morning, I was afraid not that I did not remember the answer - but that somewhere deep within myself, it seemed, I already knew it.

## Chapter II. The Castle of Artemia Aristarkhovna

"You are late, sir," said Ignatiy Savvich, in the tone in which one announces the death of a distant relative: with sorrow, but without superfluous detail.

The old butler stood at the tall double doors of the dining hall as he had stood, no doubt, all his life: erect, grey-haired, in a dark tailcoat with polished buttons, white gloves on his dry hands, and the expression of a man who has seen so many dinner parties in his time that nothing short of the end of the world could surprise him, and even that only if it occurred before the hot course was served.

"Has the turkey been served already?" I asked.

"It has, sir. Madam was pleased to observe that the turkey, unlike certain persons, arrives on time."

"Auntie said that?"

"Madam expressed herself more briefly, sir. I permitted myself to translate it into language fit for repetition."

I could not help laughing. Ignatiy Savvich allowed himself a barely perceptible twitch at the corner of his lips - the highest degree of merriment he permitted himself on duty - and, straightening the knot of my neckcloth with a movement that held not a drop of servility but only the same calm, long-standing care with which he had, no doubt, straightened everything in this house, he threw open the doors before me.

* * *
The great stone hall received guests as it had received them for more than one decade: with towering vaults drowned in half-darkness, with gigantic chandeliers that rang with crystal at the slightest draught, and with a fireplace that crackled and spat somewhere at the far end of the hall, filling the air with the resinous, cosy scent of a pine log.

Above the fireplace, in the most prominent place, was displayed the family coat of arms: a predatory bird with wings spread wide, whether an eagle or something more ancient and less heraldically definite, framed by green, feathery branches. The walls were hung with pelts and antlers, interspersed with guns of the most various eras - from flintlocks to quite modern pieces - and the whole collection gave the hall the look not so much of a dining room as of a museum of trophies in which, through some misunderstanding, a supper had been laid.

The table - gigantic, oval, covered with a cloth of such flawless whiteness that it cut the eye no less than the midday sun - stood exactly in the middle, and around it, in the subdued light of the candles, sat a respectable company: the men mostly in military uniform, the ladies in light evening gowns, crowned with hats of feathers and bows that might have stepped straight from the pages of a metropolitan fashion journal. At the side, in a special floor stand, gleamed the set-aside sabres and firearms of the military guests - an object no less refined than the table service itself.

Not counting the servants, who stood frozen along the walls in respectful expectation, I counted eleven persons engaged in unhurried, low-voiced conversation. The table groaned with delicacies: a whole roast turkey on a silver tray of artful chasing, jellied sturgeon trembling under the lamps like amber, pies with vesiga and with mushrooms, mounds of soaked apples, salted saffron milk caps in a crystal vase, vegetables of every sort, bread - white and black, that very black bread which I, for some reason, loved best of all, though I could not have explained this fondness even under torture - and, of course, an enormous, steaming samovar surrounded by dry rings and bagels.

The maid Dunyasha, rosy, round-faced, with a thick flaxen braid coiled around her head, glided between the chairs with a tray, handing round the cordial, and, passing me, managed to whisper without moving her lips: "Master, I've saved you a pie with vesiga, the last one, under the napkin," - and vanished at once, before I could thank her.

My attire that evening was, as usual, predominantly white: beige, slightly snug trousers, a snow-white shirt, a light-grey frock coat of the softest cloth, and my favourite red-and-blue neckerchief, tied at the throat in an intricate knot - the one liberty I allowed myself in this realm of impeccable etiquette.

"You are late again, mon cher," came a familiar voice from the right, and in the next instant a hand settled familiarly on my shoulder.

Lieutenant Konstantin - in brand-new uniform, fresh from the needle, still retaining that peculiar stiffness of cloth found only in a uniform that has never been caught in the rain - looked at me with the broad, slightly insolent smile that had been his calling card almost from birth.

"I am not late," I objected, sitting down beside him. "I arrived precisely when the turkey was ready to arrive for me."

"A philosopher," he snorted approvingly. "Your aunt has been entertaining Alyosha all evening with tales of your unbearable seclusion. Any moment now she will tell him you live on moonlight alone."

"And what did you answer her?"

"That you live on moonlight only on fast days," said Konstantin imperturbably, piling a slice of turkey onto my plate as if it were his direct duty. "And on the others, on my company. Eat, or you really will turn transparent. I should have no one to travel to the capital with."

I glanced toward the opposite end of the table. Artemia Aristarkhovna, my aunt, sat there in all the splendour of her evening gown - a dark-lilac dress whose only ornament was a string of pearls - and was conducting a lively conversation with the young Lieutenant Alexei, whom she invariably addressed affectionately: Alyosha. He listened to her with that rapt attention usually reserved for very beautiful women or very influential persons - and my aunt, it must be admitted, was both at once.

The grey-haired General Pavel Nikolaevich, who sat at her left hand, listened to this conversation with far less rapture. He kept sipping his tea nervously and snorting into his magnificent, carefully groomed moustache - without once, however, permitting himself a single remark aloud. Lieutenant Alexei, absorbed in the conversation beyond all measure, simply failed to notice the General's reproachful glances, which in my opinion was either the height of innocence or the height of recklessness - depending on what actually bound the General and my aunt, a matter about which no one in the whole house spoke aloud, but which, it seemed, absolutely everyone suspected.

"What do you think," Konstantin whispered to me, leaning so that his words were meant for me alone, "will the General shoot him before dessert is served, or after?"

"After," I said gravely. "He is too well bred to spoil the turkey with bloodshed."

Konstantin snorted into his napkin so unluckily that for a moment the whole table looked in our direction, and I vainly tried to compose my face into the most well-behaved expression of which I was capable.

* * *
To the left of the General sat a lady of venerable years in a lavish white gown and a hat adorned with feathers and emeralds of such size that I could not help wondering whether the hat weighed more than its owner. Evdokia Gerasimovna - Konstantin's aunt, a frequent guest of ours and, by rumour, the object of the General's secret and unrequited (or perhaps requited, but carefully concealed) adoration - sighed at the table no less often than her neighbour, though the reason for her sighs, I suspect, was precisely the same.

Opposite her, on the other side of the General, sat two guests whom I had seen in our house only once before - Nadezhda Porfirievna Kutasova, widow of a provincial marshal of the nobility, a decisive, stout lady with a lorgnette on a chain and a voice capable of drowning out a regimental band, and her daughter Lizonka, a girl of some eighteen years, slight, fair-haired, in a pink dress with so many frills that she resembled a pastry mistakenly seated at table with the guests.

There was no need to guess the purpose of their visit. Nadezhda Porfirievna did not take her lorgnette off the General with the persistence with which a gunner does not take his eyes off an enemy redoubt.

"Pavel Nikolaevich," she sang out, as soon as the General set down his cup, "my Lizonka was embroidering a tobacco pouch for you the other day. With roses! She heard that you are a great admirer of roses."

"Exceedingly touched, madam," replied the General in a voice in which there was exactly as much courtesy as etiquette demanded and not a grain more. "Although, I confess, I have not smoked for twelve years."

"But one need not smoke!" said Nadezhda Porfirievna, not in the least abashed. "The pouch can be for... for something else. For seeds! For rose seeds. Lizonka, tell Pavel Nikolaevich which roses you embroidered."

"T-tea roses, Mamma," faltered Lizonka, blushing to the very frills.

"Tea roses!" Nadezhda Porfirievna announced triumphantly. "Did you hear, Pavel Nikolaevich? Tea roses!"

"I heard, madam," said the General. "Tea roses do not set seed. They are propagated by cuttings."

A silence fell in which one could hear the fire crackling. Evdokia Gerasimovna raised her fan to her face, and it seemed to me that behind the fan she was smiling. Konstantin stepped on my foot under the table with such force that I nearly cried out.

"I cannot bear this," he whispered in my ear, shaking with silent laughter. "That is the third time this evening he has buried her. One more salvo and the pouch of tea roses will go into the fireplace together with Mamma."

"Hush," I hissed, barely restraining myself. "She will hear."

"She hears nothing but the word 'general.' Her ears are tuned to that rank like a hunting dog's to game."

Nadezhda Porfirievna, however, did not know how to retreat. Having suffered defeat on the rose front, she immediately shifted her fire - and, to my horror, onto me.

"And you, young man," she addressed me, levelling her lorgnette, "you, I hear, are a great lover of books? Lizonka adores reading too! Lizonka, say what you are reading now."

"A Nest of Gentlefolk, Mamma," whispered Lizonka, looking at her plate.

"A splendid book," I said, turning to the girl with the most amiable smile I could muster, "though, I admit, its ending is sad. I hope you have not finished it yet, Elizaveta..." I faltered.

The patronymic. I had just heard it - or had I not? Nadezhda Porfirievna was the widow of the marshal, but what was the marshal's own name? I had been told. I had known it for certain a moment ago - known it as firmly as I knew the name of my own aunt - and now in the place of that knowledge yawned an even, smooth emptiness, as though someone had carefully drawn a single thread out of my memory without disturbing the rest.

The pause dragged on. Lizonka lifted her eyes to me - bewildered, frightened.

"Elizaveta Andreevna," Konstantin prompted calmly, as though it were the most natural thing in the world. "My friend, madam, became so absorbed in A Nest of Gentlefolk that he forgot which nest he himself is in."

Everyone laughed. Nadezhda Porfirievna nodded graciously, Lizonka turned pink again, and the conversation rolled on. And I sat looking at my plate and felt a slow chill creeping down my spine. It was a trifle - a forgotten patronymic of a scarcely known young lady, it happens to everyone. And yet in the way it had been forgotten - not faded gradually, as unimportant names fade, but vanished all at once, instantly, as though it had been plucked out - there was something I did not like.

"Thank you," I whispered to Konstantin.

"Don't mention it," he answered, just as quietly, without looking at me. "You are not yourself tonight, mon cher. All evening it is as if you were not here." And, after a pause, he added in his former, mocking tone: "However, if you take it into your head to forget someone's name again, I shall be sitting beside you. That is what friends are for: to remember for you when you cannot do it yourself."

I looked at him. He had already turned away, helping himself to jellied sturgeon, and his face wore its usual carefree expression, as though he had said nothing out of the ordinary. But something in those words - "remember for you" - echoed in me with a strange, warm and at the same time disquieting resonance that I could not have explained.

* * *
"Permit me, permit me, young man," came a creaking voice with a slight German accent from the other end of the table. "I have been observing you for a quarter of an hour. You are pale as lime, you are rubbing your temple, and you have just forgotten the patronymic of a young lady that was given to you no later than the soup. Is it a headache?"

Doctor Karl Fyodorovich Strauch - an old friend of the house, my aunt's physician and, in addition, the only man capable of declining a second slice of pie in her presence - looked at me over his gold spectacles with the professional interest with which an entomologist looks at a rare beetle.

"A trifle, Karl Fyodorovich," I said. "It has ached a little since morning."

"Since morning," repeated the doctor, as though writing it down in an invisible notebook. "And yesterday? And the day before? Have you not had of late... how shall I put it... lapses? Moments when you cannot recall how you came to be in this or that room? Or what you were doing an hour ago?"

It grew quieter at the table. My aunt, breaking off her conversation with Alexei, turned her head in our direction - quickly, too quickly.

"Karl Fyodorovich," she said evenly, "this is a dinner party, not an infirmary reception."

"I beg your pardon, Artemia Aristarkhovna," the doctor bowed slightly but did not take his eyes from me. "Professional habit. Memory is a most peculiar organ, gentlemen. I have treated people for thirty years and still do not understand how it is made. One man remembers what the sky looked like on the day of his christening, yet cannot recall what he ate for breakfast. And another time..." - he paused - "another time a man remembers what never happened to him at all."

"How do you mean, what never happened?" Alexei grew interested.

"Just so, young man. I had patients who described with perfect clarity cities in which they had never been. Streets, smells, faces. One retired major swore that he remembered standing on the deck of a ship bound for shores that are on no map. He described the rigging, the colour of the water, the voices of the sailors. And yet he had never in his life travelled farther than Tula."

I felt the tips of my fingers go cold. The deck of a ship. The salt wind. The shreds that had flickered through my head all that day and which I could neither hold nor explain.

"And how did you treat him?" asked the General with an interest unexpected in him.

"With cold rubdowns and readings of Karamzin, Your Excellency," replied the doctor. "The rubdowns did not help. Neither did Karamzin."

The table laughed, and the awkwardness dispersed. But I noticed that my aunt did not laugh. She looked at Doctor Strauch with a long, heavy look, which he, it seems, understood perfectly, for he did not once speak of memory again all evening.

* * *
Farther down the table, Colonel Mikhail Ivanovich - husband of the quiet, affable Vera Anatolievna - was just finishing another tale of his martial exploits, twirling his very long, longest of moustaches with the same methodicalness with which some people click the beads on a counting-house abacus.

"...and then," he thundered, addressing himself chiefly to his own plate, "the Turkish battery fired a salvo, and we, imagine, were standing in an open position, without any cover whatever..."

"Misha," Vera Anatolievna interrupted him gently, "might we perhaps let the guests finish their turkey before the battery opens fire?"

The Colonel laughed good-naturedly at his own lack of restraint, and I, taking advantage of the pause, at last turned to the plate I had hardly touched so far - too busy was I observing this small, familiar theatre played out at my aunt's table nearly every other evening. Under the napkin, as promised, I found the pie with vesiga, still warm. I caught Dunyasha's eye by the wall and nodded to her almost imperceptibly; she beamed.

It was at that moment that I noticed Vera Anatolievna's gaze turned upon me.

That gaze lingered on my face a fraction of an instant longer than simple politeness requires - one looks thus not at an acquaintance, but at something vaguely recognisable that one cannot quite recall: perhaps a portrait once seen, perhaps a face from an old, half-forgotten dream. Then she blinked, smiled at me with the most ordinary, social smile, and said:

"You look very pensive today, my friend. Is your aunt not making you read too much of an evening?"

"A little," I answered, trying to make my voice sound light, though that first look of hers had somehow lodged in me like an unpleasant splinter. "I fear I shall soon have to ask her for my wages to buy a new pair of eyes."

She smiled again, this time quite ordinarily, and the conversation flowed safely on, to some fashionable new novels brought from Paris or perhaps London - but for some time I kept stealing glances in her direction, trying to understand what exactly I had fancied in that first, overlong look. No explanation presented itself. The list of my inexplicable things today, however, had already swollen to indecent proportions, so I decided to set this riddle aside for the time being in the same place where all the others already rested - until better, clearer times.

The General, taking advantage of the fact that the conversation had turned away from Alexei, thought it possible to put in a remark of his own - as always, terse and to the point.

"The Porte is troubled again," he said, addressing no one in particular, though it was evident that the phrase was directed first of all at the Colonel, the only one at the table capable of appreciating its weight. "The Sultan again asks for assistance. I fear that before a year is out I shall have to pack for Constantinople once more."

At that word - Constantinople - something strange stirred in me: not a memory, no, rather the echo of a memory, a distant reverberation of a narrow lane smelling of the sea and spices, of a carpet with a strange pattern, of two grey-bearded old men at a game of backgammon. I blinked, driving off the delusion - it too closely resembled the earlier feeling at the fountain for me to wish its repetition - and tried to concentrate on the turkey.

"You travel too often to those parts, Pavel Nikolaevich," my aunt intervened, and a shade of real, unfeigned anxiety flickered in her voice. "One day I shall cease to be surprised if you announce to me that you have decided to settle there altogether."

"Duty, Artemia Aristarkhovna," replied the General with dignity, "seldom asks our consent as to the route."

"As does life in general," Konstantin put in with feigned philosophical air, for which he promptly earned from his aunt Evdokia Gerasimovna a ringing slap of the fan on the hand.

"Constantinople!" Nadezhda Porfirievna clasped her hands, scenting a new breach in the defences. "Ah, Pavel Nikolaevich, how I should dream of seeing Constantinople! Lizonka, would you like to see Constantinople?"

"It is said to be very hot there, Mamma," whispered Lizonka.

"Hot, madam," confirmed the General. "And dusty. And dogs everywhere. And, I venture to assure you, absolutely no tea roses."

Evdokia Gerasimovna, behind her fan, emitted a sound which, with a certain indulgence, might be taken for a cough.

* * *
When dessert was served - blancmange trembling on its dish, cranberry kissel, and pastila brought, as my aunt announced with pride, from Kolomna itself - Evdokia Gerasimovna suddenly snapped her fan shut and declared to the whole table:

"Lizonka, my dear, you play charmingly, they say! Will you not delight us?"

Nadezhda Porfirievna beamed as though she had been awarded a decoration. Lizonka flushed, protested, was persuaded, escorted to the piano standing in the corner of the hall beneath the portrait of some stern-eyed ancestor in a powdered wig - and, after hesitating, touched the keys.

She played a romance. I did not know its name - or I knew it, but this evening, evidently, my memory had decided to give me nothing for free. The melody was simple, a little sad, and Lizonka, forgetting her shyness, played it unexpectedly well - with the sincerity of those people to whom it is easier to speak in music than in words. The hall fell quiet. Even Nadezhda Porfirievna lowered her lorgnette. The General, leaning back in his chair, gazed somewhere into the fire of the hearth, and his face, usually so impenetrable, became for a moment strangely young and defenceless. I noticed that Evdokia Gerasimovna was looking not at Lizonka, but at him.

And suddenly, in the midst of that melody, I smelled a scent.

Salt. Spices. Sun-warmed stone. It came from nowhere - not from an open window, the windows were closed, not from the kitchen, where nothing of the kind was being cooked - it simply arose, filled for an instant my whole being and at once vanished, leaving in my mouth the aftertaste of something sweet, honeyed, like a dried fig. The music went on playing. No one around noticed anything.

I raised my palm to my temple. The headache that had plagued me all evening grew sharper.

"You are going away again," Konstantin said softly, without turning his head. "I see how you go away. Where do you go, mon cher?"

"Nowhere," I answered. "Just my head."

He said nothing. But I felt his shoulder - in the stiff, new cloth of his uniform - touch mine for a moment and linger a little longer than chance required. As though he were checking whether I was still here.

Lizonka finished. The hall applauded - sincerely, even the General. Nadezhda Porfirievna wiped away a tear with a lace handkerchief and repeated: "My Lizonka! My little dove!" Doctor Strauch, clapping, watched me closely over his spectacles.

* * *
The evening flowed on in its customary course - laughter, the clink of dishes, snatches of conversation about new books, about the prospects of the harvest, about which of the capital's young ladies had made the better marriage this season. I listened with half an ear, now and then putting in a remark when I felt that my silence was becoming too noticeable - and when Konstantin, inspired, began to question me about some book on heraldry that I had been leafing through in the library the other day, I caught myself talking for almost a quarter of an hour on end, unable to stop, until I noticed that the whole company had long since moved on to another subject, while I was still enthusiastically telling Konstantin the history of family coats of arms, which no one but him, it seemed, had any intention of listening to.

"You are sometimes perfectly insufferable," he remarked with undisguised pleasure, "one moment you cannot be drawn out with pincers, the next you cannot be silenced."

"Then I am unpredictable," I answered. "That is far more interesting than being predictable."

"More interesting," agreed Konstantin. "But more tiring. Especially for those who try to guess what you will be like tomorrow."

"And do you try?"

He looked at me - for a moment seriously, without his usual smirk - and at once looked away, reaching for a bagel.

"Hardly," he said. "As if I had nothing better to do."

The supper, which had apparently been going on for more than an hour, began at last to incline toward its natural end. The headache that had plagued me almost from the very beginning of the evening had grown so much that I thought it best to take my leave before it turned into something more serious.

"Auntie," I said, rising and approaching Artemia Aristarkhovna, "forgive me, but my head today flatly refuses to serve me any longer. Allow me to wish you good night."

She held out her hand for me to kiss - a gesture which over the long years had become almost a ritual between us - and I touched my lips to the thin, ring-laden fingers.

"Go and rest, my friend," she said with that warmth that was meant for me alone and for no one else at that table. "You are too pale today. Karl Fyodorovich is right, though I shall not allow him to say so at dinner."

Then, lowering her voice so much that only I and, perhaps, the General, who sat closer than the rest, could hear, she added - half in jest, half in earnest, with that strange, fleeting sadness which occasionally, against her will, showed in her face whenever the conversation touched, even by its edge, upon the past:

"Do not wander too far along the corridors tonight, do you hear? This castle is older than it seems, and it has, believe me, places that are better left in peace."

"Places?" I asked, involuntarily smiling at so unexpected a warning. "Are you frightening me with family ghosts, Auntie?"

She looked at me for a long moment - and in that look flashed something I had never before noticed in her: not fear, but something neighbouring on fear, the memory of something she would have preferred never to recall.

The General, sitting beside her, slowly lowered his cup onto its saucer. The sound was very quiet - but in the pause that fell between us it rang out like the click of a cocking hammer. I noticed that the General was looking not at me but at my aunt, and that in his look was a question to which she, almost imperceptibly, shook her head.

"Let us leave it," she said at last, restoring lightness to her voice. "It is late, my friend. Go to sleep."

Already on my way to the door, I caught myself in a thought that seemed to me almost sacrilegious: I knew, in essence, nothing of our kinship but the very word "aunt," by which I had called her since I could remember. Never once had she told me whose sister she was - my mother's or my father's. Never once had she shown me a portrait or a letter that would confirm this relationship by anything other than her love for me and my faith in her words. The thought, scarcely arisen, seemed to me absurd and ungrateful, and I hastened to be rid of it - but to be rid of it entirely, it seems, I did not quite succeed.

I bowed to the esteemed company, received parting wishes of good night from the General, the Colonel, Doctor Strauch and Konstantin - the last of whom, however, contrived to shout after me something remarkably spiteful, which I had no time to make out - and left the hall for the dimly lit corridor.

Ignatiy Savvich, standing at the doors just as erect, as though in all those hours he had not moved an inch, handed me a lighted candle in a copper candlestick.

"Shall I see you to your room, sir?"

"There is no need, Ignatiy Savvich. I know the way."

The old man paused. Then he said - evenly, without changing the expression of his face, as though reporting the weather:

"Madam bade me give her regards and remind you: the left wing is locked for the night. Draughts, sir. An old house."

"Draughts," I repeated.

"Precisely so, sir," said Ignatiy Savvich, and looked at me as one looks at a man to whom something has been said and who, regrettably, will most likely not obey. "Good night."

I took the candle and went along the corridor, carrying with me not only the heaviness in my temples but also the strange, itching aftertaste of my aunt's words, lodged somewhere on the very border of consciousness, in the same place where all my inexplicable anxieties of that day had settled.

This castle is older than it seems.

I could not know that evening how soon I should be convinced of the truth of those words - and how bitterly I should regret it.

## Chapter III. Pharaoh Menes
