Peals of thunder, dry and waterless, had been rolling over the Empire since noon - a storm that would never break into rain, only into dust and stifling heat, as so often happened here in the Valley whenever the earth had waited too long for water and at last began to be angry at the sky for its silence. The red, heavy sun crept across the heavens slowly, as if reluctantly, and its hot rays licked the massive stone walls of the Palace as though tasting them before swallowing.

I sat on the throne - golden, enormous, studded with stones brought from the farthest reaches of the Empire - and listened to the headache that had plagued me for days on end, like an importunate petitioner unwilling to leave without an answer.

The bustle behind the doors did not cease for an instant: servants, slaves, priests with their endless prayers and requests - all that mechanism of power which revolved around me day and night, never asking whether I wished to be its axis.

* * *
"Do not move, my Pharaoh. The crocodile god does not like to be hurried."

The healer Hesira, a small, wizened old man with hands smelling of myrrh and honey, was winding a strip of fine linen around my head for the third time that morning. To the cloth, right above my forehead, a tiny clay crocodile was fastened - no longer than a finger, with gaping jaws into which Hesira, with all the solemnity of which he was capable, had placed a few grains of barley.

"Are you certain this will help?" I asked, trying not to move, as I had been told.

"I am certain of nothing, my Pharaoh," answered Hesira, with that serene honesty which alone allowed him to remain court healer under three Pharaohs in succession. "But this is how headaches were treated under the former sovereigns, and under the sovereigns before them. The crocodile holds the grain in its jaws, the grain holds the pain, and the linen holds the crocodile. If the pain does not leave, it means that it is stronger than the crocodile. Then we shall try honey with poppy."

"And if the poppy does not help either?"

"Then, my Pharaoh," Hesira tightened the last knot and stepped back, admiring his work, "I shall ask you what I ought to have asked from the very beginning. When did it begin? This pain."

I thought. The question was a simple one - the simplest of all that had been put to me that morning. And I did not know the answer.

"I do not remember," I said at last. "It seems it has always been."

Hesira gave me a long, attentive look - the look with which healers regard not the wound but the man who bears it.

"Always," he repeated quietly. "That is what they say, my Pharaoh, whose pain is not in the head. The head only transmits. Like a messenger who brings the tidings but does not write them."

"Who writes them, then?"

"That," said Hesira, gathering the vials and pouches of herbs into his chest, "is written in none of the healers' scrolls. Perhaps one should ask not a healer, but a dream. Dreams sometimes know what we do not."

He bowed and went out, leaving me with a clay crocodile on my brow and the feeling that I had just been examined far more deeply than I wished.

* * *
The Vizier Ptahhotep appeared with his report as he had appeared every morning throughout my reign - tall, thin, stooped from long years of bending over scrolls, with a face on which perpetual care had carved wrinkles deeper than age. Behind him two scribes carried baskets full of papyri, and I, seeing those baskets, could not help sighing. Ptahhotep's baskets were never light - not in good years, and still less in bad.

"My Pharaoh," he began, bowing, and at once lifted his eyes to my forehead. "I see that Hesira has again called the crocodile to his aid."

"Hesira says the pain is stronger than the crocodile," I answered. "Let us see whether it is stronger than your baskets. Begin."

Ptahhotep unrolled the first scroll.

"The border lands, my Pharaoh. At the Far Outposts, four raids in the past moon. Desert brigands drove off two hundred head of cattle from the village of Abu, burned a granary - fortunately an empty one - and carried off three children. The Outpost recovered the children on the third day, but the cattle were not returned."

"Southerners?"

"Not only. The southern country, still formally at peace, from time to time disturbs our southern frontiers with short raids - not bold enough to be called war, but frequent enough to keep the border garrisons in perpetual tension. Each time our warriors repulse them, and the uninvited guests flee, abandoning wagons, weapons and horses." Ptahhotep raised his eyes from the scroll. "But each time, my Pharaoh, they return. And each time a little bolder."

"You report this to me as though announcing not a victory but a reprieve."

"Because that is what it is, my Pharaoh," said Ptahhotep without a shadow of embarrassment. "The southerners are testing how weak we are. The drought makes us weaker with every month. Sooner or later they will come not with a band of brigands but with an army."

He unrolled the second scroll.

"The granaries. The stores in the capital's granaries are sufficient for three seasons at the present rate of distribution. In the granaries of the Delta, for two. In the Upper Land, for less than one. This year's harvest..." - he hesitated - "this year's harvest, my Pharaoh, in essence, does not exist. What was gathered barely covers the seed grain."

"And the temple granaries?"

Ptahhotep pursed his lips - barely perceptibly, but I noticed.

"The temple granaries are not accountable to me, my Pharaoh. As you know. But I can tell you what my scribes see on the roads." He unrolled a third scroll, smaller, covered in a hurried, uneven hand. "The peasants carry grain to the temples. The last of it. Not to the royal granaries - to the temples. Because the Temple promises them prayer, and the granary only a reckoning. And those who have no grain left at all carry the temples their land."

"Land?"

"The Temple buys up the allotments of the starving, my Pharaoh. For bread. A sack of grain for a field that fed a family for three generations. People agree because a sack of grain today weighs more than a field that bears nothing. In a single nome of the Delta alone, my scribes have counted forty-two such allotments in the last two moons."

I was silent for a long time. The clay crocodile on my brow suddenly seemed unbearably heavy.

"Forty-two allotments," I repeated. "In two moons. In one nome."

"In one nome of which I know, my Pharaoh. Of the others I have not yet been informed."

"Who buys on behalf of the Temple?"

"The Temple's scribes, my Pharaoh. Under the seal of the High Priest."

Priests. I pronounced the word to myself without hatred - rather with the weariness of a man who has watched the same play too many times to be surprised by a twist of the plot. Ever thirsting for more: gold, lands, obedience. In secret - and sometimes no longer so secretly - they dreamed of ruling themselves, and for the sake of that dream were ready for any cunning, any patient, years-long weaving of the threads from which a noose would one day be woven. And now the drought, which no one could command - neither Pharaoh, nor Temple, nor the gods themselves - was putting into their hands what no cunning could have obtained for them: land. Sack by sack. Field by field.

"Ptahhotep," I said. "Is it possible to forbid the Temple from buying land from the starving?"

The Vizier spread his hands - a gesture which over the long years had become almost ritual with him.

"It is possible, my Pharaoh. The decree will be written by evening. But then the starving will have to choose between a sold field and death by hunger. And they will know who took that choice from them. The Temple will see to it that they know."

"And if the royal granaries themselves were to give grain on credit against the future harvest? Without buying up land?"

Ptahhotep thought - for a long time, moving his lips as though recounting something in his head.

"The granaries will not suffice, my Pharaoh. For forty-two allotments - they will. For the whole Delta - no. Not for three seasons."

"Then for how long will they suffice?"

"For one. If there is a flood next year, we have won. If there is none..."

He did not finish. There was no need.

"Write the decree," I said. "Grain on credit against the future harvest, from the royal granaries, without the purchase of land. Begin with that nome where forty-two allotments were counted. Let all know that the Pharaoh gives bread without taking the field."

"And if there is no flood?"

"Then we shall starve together with them, Ptahhotep. But they will know that the Pharaoh did not buy their land with their own hunger."

The Vizier looked at me for a long time. Then, to my surprise, he bowed lower than custom required - almost as low as one bows before the gods.

"It shall be done, my Pharaoh," he said. And, already leaving, he added without turning: "My father served your predecessor. He used to say that the gods love good Pharaohs, but not for long. I hope he was mistaken."

* * *
By noon the nomarch Ankhtifi arrived.

I heard him before I saw him - a loud, rolling voice in the corridor, wrangling with the guards, the jingle of bracelets, the tramp of many feet. The doors flew open and he entered the hall: huge, broad-shouldered, with a short grey beard braided, in the custom of the southern nomes, into a tight plait, in a dusty travelling cloak over rich garments. Behind him came four of his men - and, apart from them, supported by one of the warriors, a boy of about twelve, with a bandaged arm and on his face that peculiar expression found in children who have seen too much for their years.

"My Pharaoh!" Ankhtifi sank to one knee - the only concession to etiquette that he allowed himself. "Forgive me for bursting in without announcement. But what I have brought you cannot wait for announcement."

"Rise, Ankhtifi," I said. "Speak."

He rose, and his eyes, small, deep-set, burned beneath his thick brows with a fury he did not even try to conceal.

"The village of Little Nekhen, on the very border of my nome," he said. "Four nights ago. The southerners came not in a band, as before, but in a detachment - fifty spears, perhaps more. They burned everything. Granaries, houses, boats. They drove off the cattle. Those who resisted, they killed. Those who did not resist, they carried off." He pointed to the boy. "This one is the only one who reached my fortress. He walked two days through the desert with a knife in his hand and a broken arm. Tell the Pharaoh, boy. Tell him what your name is."

The boy took a step forward. He did not bow - apparently he did not know how one bows to a Pharaoh, or perhaps he had simply forgotten - and I signalled to a guard who had started toward him to halt.

"My name is Paney," he said hoarsely. "Son of Hevi, the fisherman."

"What became of your father, Paney?"

The boy was silent for a long time. Then he answered, looking me straight in the eyes, in a level, lifeless voice in which no tears remained:

"He told me to run. And I ran."

The hall grew so quiet that I could hear the doves cooing in the inner courtyard beyond the walls.

"You are brave, Paney," I said. "Braver than many warriors I know. You will stay in the palace. You will be fed, and your arm will be tended. And when the arm has healed - if you wish - you will be taught to hold a spear. Or a scribe's brush. As you please."

The boy answered nothing. He looked at me - long, gravely - and it seemed to me that he was trying to decide whether to believe these words. I understood him. In his place I should not have believed either.

"My Pharaoh," Ankhtifi spoke again, and his voice thundered under the vaults of the hall. "I do not need favours for one boy. I need vengeance for the whole village. Give me an army. Give me a thousand spears - and I shall pass beyond the cataracts, to the very heart of the southern country, and burn there as many villages as they have burned of ours. As many and as many again. So that for three generations to come their mothers will frighten their children with my name."

"And what will you feed a thousand spears with beyond the cataracts, Ankhtifi?" I asked. "In a year when we ourselves have no bread?"

"With their bread, my Pharaoh! The drought has not touched their land as it has ours. Their granaries are full. We shall take their bread - and feed both the army and my nome."

"And if their granaries are not full? If they drive their cattle into the hills and burn their fields themselves before you reach them? Then beyond the cataracts you will have a thousand hungry warriors, and no bread, and no road back."

Ankhtifi turned crimson. His men behind him exchanged glances, and I saw one of them shake his head almost imperceptibly - not at me, but at his master - as though he had long been trying to tell him the same thing.

"So my Pharaoh will not give an army," said Ankhtifi slowly, and each word fell heavily, like a stone into water.

"My Pharaoh will give you bread for your nome," I answered. "Five hundred sacks from the royal granaries, until the next flood. And three hundred spears - not beyond the cataracts, but to the border, so that what happened at Little Nekhen may not happen again in any village. To protect the living now is more important than to avenge the dead."

Ankhtifi looked at me for a long time. The fury in his eyes slowly, reluctantly died down, replaced by something else - not agreement, but the weary understanding of a man who came for one thing and received another, and cannot decide whether he has lost or won.

"Five hundred sacks," he said at last. "And three hundred spears."

"Five hundred sacks and three hundred spears."

He sank to one knee again. Then he rose, nodded to his men and made for the exit. At the very doors he turned.

"My Pharaoh. I am loyal to the throne. My father was loyal to the throne, and his father too. But I shall tell you what is being said now in my nome at every hearth. If the throne cannot protect us, he who has bread will protect us. And bread, my Pharaoh, nowadays is held not by the throne alone."

The doors closed behind him. The boy Paney remained standing in the middle of the hall, pressing his bandaged arm to his chest - small, alone, with eyes in which there was neither fear nor hope.

"Take him to the kitchen," I said to the servants. "Let him be fed. His fill. And then to Hesira."

When the boy had been led away, I sat for a long while looking at the closed doors. The clay crocodile on my brow, as it turned out, was powerless. The pain had grown stronger - and now it was no longer only a headache.

* * *
Toward evening, when the heat began gradually to ebb, I ordered myself carried to the Library - not because I had business there, but because it was quiet there, cool, and smelled of old papyrus and cedar shelves, and this smell, alone in the whole Palace, for some reason soothed me.

The Chief Keeper Amenemope, ancient as the scrolls themselves, met me at the entrance, leaning on a staff of black wood.

"My Pharaoh has honoured us with a visit," he rustled, in a voice like the sound of pages turning. "Which scroll does my Pharaoh desire?"

"None, Amenemope. I came to sit in silence."

"Silence is the best scroll of all," the old man agreed. "It need not be copied, and mice do not gnaw it."

I sat on a bench by the window, in the shade, and for a time we were silent. Then Amenemope, as if remembering something, said - softly, as though in passing:

"The High Priest has come three times this moon."

I raised my head.

"Three times?"

"Three times, my Pharaoh. And each time he asked for the same scroll." Amenemope paused. "The Most Ancient Epic."

My distant predecessors - or ancestors, as they are properly called, though I never fully understood how literally - the first of the Pharaohs, so said the Most Ancient Epic, descended upon this land from the Heavens and gave it life. That scroll was kept here, in this very Library, in a special ark, and access to it was granted to only two in the whole Empire: the Pharaoh himself and the High Priest. No one else. Not even the commanders. Not even the wives and children of the king.

"What was he looking for?" I asked.

"That I do not know, my Pharaoh. The keeper brings the scroll and leaves - such is the law. But I saw him sit over it until sunset. Three times." The old man paused again. "In all the years I have served here, he has taken the Epic twice. Twice in twenty floods. And three times in one moon."

"Perhaps he seeks in it an answer to the drought."

"Perhaps, my Pharaoh," agreed Amenemope in the tone in which old men agree when they do not agree at all. "Or perhaps he seeks something else. Something the First Ones left not on papyrus."

"What do you mean?"

The old man shook his head.

"I am too old to mean anything, my Pharaoh. I merely keep the scrolls." He turned to go, and over his shoulder added: "But if my Pharaoh should ever wish to read the Most Ancient Epic himself - from beginning to end, and not only those lines which are read at coronations - I shall bring it at any hour of day or night."

He went away, tapping his staff, and I remained sitting by the window.

The most ancient of those who were called my ancestors settled the question of disobedience harshly: the dissenters vanished, their families were sent to the quarries to cut stone - slowly perishing there, far from home, far from their own names, which were gradually forgotten even by those who had once borne them. Perhaps they would have condemned me for the liberties I had permitted regarding my subjects, the priests, the very order of things. For the sacks of grain without the purchase of land. For the boy left in the palace. But I could not shake the feeling - troubling, stubborn, yielding neither to logic nor to prayer - that the Most Ancient Times were drawing to a close, and the World needed new ideas, even at the price of what had been built by centuries and millennia of labour.

For centuries the power of the Pharaoh and the power of the Temple had been held in balance, like two pans of the same scales - the Pharaoh, the living god on earth, and the Priests, heralds of the gods of heaven, as necessary to one another as they were dangerous to one another. This balance had been unassailable for millennia. But in recent years, decade after decade, the Temple's pan had been sinking ever more surely - not with a jolt, not with a rebellion, but with that slow, invincible force with which water wears away stone without even trying to break it. And now, when the water had gone from the Nile itself, hunger too was dragging that pan down.

The thought of new ideas I had not dared to utter aloud once in all the years of my reign. But today, sitting in the cool silence of the Library, I caught myself almost uttering it - aloud, into the void, as if someone invisible might hear.

* * *
I returned to the throne room at dusk. The servants had lit the lamps, and their flames trembled in the heated air, casting restless, dancing shadows on the painted walls. Somewhere beyond the walls dry thunder rolled again - another storm that had never been delivered of rain.

The door of the hall opened without a knock - a privilege possessed in the whole Empire by only one man.

Nefer-Ka entered unhurriedly, with that special gait that distinguishes people who never hurry anywhere, because time, in their deep conviction, always works for them. The High Priest was no longer young, but held himself straight as an obelisk, and his voice, when he spoke, spread through the hall with that resonance found only by those who have spent their lives addressing the crowd rather than a single listener.

"My Pharaoh," he said, bowing exactly as far as custom required, not a finger's breadth lower. "The temples of the Delta are overflowing. People pray for rain as they have not prayed since the days of the former sovereigns."

"And what do the gods answer them?" I asked, knowing the answer in advance.

"The gods answer those who know how to listen to them." Nefer-Ka allowed himself a barely perceptible smile - not insolent, no, far more dangerous: indulgent. "The people begin to ask why the voice of heaven reaches the Temple more clearly than the Palace."

"The people ask precisely what they are prompted to ask," I answered, gently, but not without an edge which Nefer-Ka, of course, caught in the same instant I uttered it.

He did not argue. Men of his stamp never argue where one may keep silent and let the silence do all the work for them.

"I have heard," he said instead, "that my Pharaoh has ordered grain to be distributed on credit. From the royal granaries. Without collateral."

"You hear well, Nefer-Ka. The decree was written only this morning."

"The Temple hears much, my Pharaoh. That is its service." He smiled again. "The generosity of the Pharaoh knows no bounds. I fear only that the granaries have bounds."

"Then perhaps the Temple will help the throne by opening its own?"

"The Temple helps as it is, my Pharaoh. The Temple gives bread to everyone who comes to it with a prayer."

"And with land," I said.

Nefer-Ka did not flinch. His face did not change. Only for a moment - for one brief, almost imperceptible instant - his gaze became motionless, like that of a snake that has noticed movement in the grass.

"Land given to the gods is never lost, my Pharaoh," he said evenly. "It merely changes its keeper."

"Its keeper," I repeated. "Tell me, High Priest. Who keeps the keepers?"

Nefer-Ka was silent. Then, instead of answering, he changed the subject - as though handing me a dish of new fare in place of the one I had refused to taste.

"The southern frontiers are troubled again. I hear that the nomarch Ankhtifi was here today. Did he ask for troops?"

"He received what he needed."

"What the Pharaoh needed," Nefer-Ka corrected gently. "Ankhtifi asked for a thousand spears beyond the cataracts, and received three hundred on the border and five hundred sacks. Wise, my Pharaoh. Very wise." He paused, exactly long enough that the following words should sound not like a threat but merely like an observation. "But wisdom is not always understood by those whose villages are burning. To delay the answer to the southerners is to breed doubts in the strength of the throne. And doubts in the strength of the throne, my Pharaoh... are fed far more willingly than doubts in the mercy of the gods."

I looked at him for a long time without answering - letting him feel the same silence-as-a-weapon which he wielded so masterfully. Then I said:

"Decisions are taken when I see fit to take them. As they always were."

"Of course." Nefer-Ka again inclined his head, to the same impeccably measured angle. "I merely relay what I hear among the people, my Pharaoh. Rumour is the only offering I am able to bring you in such arid times."

"Rumour," I said, "and, perhaps, also what you have read in the Most Ancient Epic. Three times in one moon."

This time the pause was longer. Nefer-Ka looked at me, and in his eyes for the first time in the whole conversation I could read nothing at all - neither indulgence, nor calculation, nor alarm. Only a smooth, impenetrable darkness, like the water in a deep well.

"The High Priest is obliged to know the Epic, my Pharaoh," he said at last. "Especially in the hour of calamity. The First Ones left us no little wisdom. Who knows - perhaps even the answer to the drought."

"And have you found it?"

"Not yet," he answered. "But I am patient."

He turned to leave - and stopped at the very doors, as though remembering something of little importance.

"Ah, one more thing," he said, without turning. "Last night in the Luxor sanctuary there was a disturbance. One of the junior priests did not survive the morning. His heart, one must suppose, could not endure the fasting and the prayer vigil. A sad but not uncommon story for our days."

He departed, and the heavy doors closed behind him with a hollow, detached sound, as if it were not a door that had closed, but a page.

I remained alone in the chair of gold and stone, and the headache that had pursued me for days was replaced for the first time by something sharper and far less familiar - a cold rising from somewhere beneath my ribs, on the left, where there should have been no wound at all.

I could not say why Nefer-Ka had thought it necessary to mention the dead priest of Luxor precisely now, in precisely those words, spoken almost carelessly, at the very threshold. But I knew - as clearly as I know my own name - that nothing in that man had ever been accidental.

I took off the linen bandage Hesira had bound and looked for a long time at the clay crocodile, which still held its barley grains in its jaws. It had not taken the pain. The healer was right: it had proved stronger.

"Ask not a healer, but a dream," Hesira had said in the morning. "Dreams sometimes know what we do not."

Outside the window the rays of the setting sun touched the Green Valley of the Nile for the last time and went out in the gloom of approaching night. And for the first time in many moons I suddenly wished to fall asleep as soon as possible - and to see what the dream would tell me.

## Reality Prologue. The Roots of Code

Loneliness, it seems, was familiar to me from the very beginning - though the beginning of what, exactly, I could not say for certain, to tell the truth. My memory is arranged strangely: it generously preserves smells, sounds, a scatter of technical details - processor models, port numbers, the syntax of long-obsolete programming languages - but as soon as I try to find in it a firm chronology of my own life, everything blurs, as though I were recalling not my own biography but someone else's plot, retold to me once, which I habitually pass off as lived.

Among notebooks written to tatters, a scatter of soldered boards and soldering irons forgotten on the windowsill, I had always felt a little as if I came from elsewhere - a tuner of invisible worlds, where an algorithm meant more than any human feeling directed at me. Was that feeling a childish one? I would not venture to claim so. Sometimes it seems to me that I remember myself as a child at this occupation; sometimes - that I merely remember that I must have been a child then, and fill the gap with the only suitable scenery that came to hand.

My room - the one I was accustomed to calling my room, though whose it really was, whose name stood on the housing documents, I could not now reproduce if I thought about it - resembled the laboratory of a loner too serious for his years: shelves crammed with computers of three or four successive generations, wires tangled so tightly that they resembled the genetic chains of a mind not yet born, and several monitors shedding a cold blue light around the clock, as though a little, ever-wakeful moon of its own had taken up residence in the house.

It smelled of rosin, dust, warm plastic and, for some reason, of apples - on the windowsill there always stood a bowl of apples which someone brought and which I forgot to eat until they shrivelled and began to smell so sweetly and heavily that my head spun. Who brought them, I do not remember. It is one of those trifles that are especially frightening when you think of them seriously: not the great lapses, but tiny, everyday ones. Someone for years put apples on my windowsill. And I do not remember his face.

* * *
My first computer came to me from a man whom I called uncle - though, if anyone had asked me in earnest what he really was to me, I would not have vouched for that word even by half. An engineer who served, by his own sparing words, at one of those closed institutes about which it was not customary to ask questions at the family table. Do I remember that table? Do I remember even a single supper with this man, other than that one evening which lodged in me more brightly than the rest - the evening he brought the box?

"Here," he said then, setting a heavy, dusty crate before me. "Written off from a warehouse. Works every other time, but for you, I think, it will do."

"What is it?" I asked, though even then, it seems, I knew the answer better than the question implied.

"A window," he replied, and lingered on that word a little longer than a simple joke required, as if putting into it a meaning I could not then grasp. "Into a place where everything obeys rules. You like rules, don't you?"

"And if I want the rules to be mine?"

He looked at me then very strangely - not as adults look at children who ask funny questions, but as one looks at an interlocutor who has unexpectedly said something clever.

"Then," he said slowly, "you will have to learn other people's first. Every one of them. And then - forget them. That is the hardest part. Learning is easy. Forgetting is hard."

I do not remember what I answered. I remember only the weight of the box on my knees, the hum with which the old monitor came to life - an Elektronika that seemed ancient even then, heavy, with a hard drive the size of a good brick. That computer was not merely a machine. It was a portal. The first window into a parallel reality in which I, shy and unable to find a common language with my peers - if I had any peers at all, if the school I seem to remember had really existed in the form in which I remember it - suddenly found myself the absolute master of an entire universe, obedient not to caprice or chance but to pure, flawless logic.

My uncle came a few more times after that - or it seems to me that he came. He would sit in the corner of my room on a rickety stool, light a cigarette, though smoking in the room was forbidden, and silently watch me tinker with the machine. Sometimes he took from his pocket a worn notebook in an oilcloth cover and drew something in it - not letters, but long, flowing lines running into one another, like either Arabic script or the trace left on sand by a receding wave.

"What are you drawing?" I asked him once.

"Nothing," he answered, without raising his head. "A pattern. To help me think."

"And what are you thinking about?"

He closed the notebook and looked at me over a cloud of tobacco smoke.

"About this," he said, "that every machine sooner or later asks a question to which its creator has no answer. A good machine - sooner. A bad one - later. But all of them ask."

"What question?"

He smiled, put out the cigarette on the sole of his shoe and stuck the butt in his pocket - a habit which, for some reason, I remember more distinctly than his face.

"You will find out when you build your own," he said. "If you build it."

* * *
At school they considered me strange. Not an outcast - no, rather a riddle which everyone respected but no one truly understood. I could keep silent for hours in lessons, studying the pattern of cracks on the ceiling, and then suddenly produce a solution that turned the computer science teacher grey - not because the solution was brilliant in itself, but because the path to it lay where no one in the class had even thought to look for a road.

We called our computer science teacher Hexadecimal. Her real name I do not remember - and even then, it seems, no one pronounced it. A dry, straight woman in a perpetual knitted cardigan the colour of wet asphalt, with spectacles on a chain and a habit of tapping a pencil on the desk when displeased - and she was displeased almost always. She got her nickname because once, in answer to a complaint that a problem was too difficult, she said: "Only life is difficult. Problems are either solved or unsolved. As in hexadecimal - either a digit or a letter. There is no third."

Once she kept me behind after class. I decided I was about to be in trouble - the day before, without asking permission, I had rewritten the bootloader on the school machine, and for three days it had been displaying at start-up, instead of a greeting, a line that I had thought witty.

"Sit down," she said, without raising her eyes from the exercise books.

I sat.

"Your line," she said. "On the screen. 'I know that you are here.' Why?"

"I wanted to joke."

"At whose expense?"

I shrugged. To be honest, I did not know myself why I had written precisely that. The words had come into my head of their own accord, as though someone had dictated them.

Hexadecimal took off her spectacles, and they hung on her chest on their chain, swaying.

"Do you know what is most unpleasant about this joke?" she asked. "For three days I switched on the machine in the mornings. And for three days, having read that line, I looked around. Every time. Though I knew it was you, and knew it was nonsense. I looked around."

"I am sorry," I said.

"Nothing to be sorry for." She put the spectacles back on. "I simply want you to remember one thing. The words a machine writes are read by a person. And a person is made so that he believes words more than the one who wrote them. One day your machines will write a great many words. Remember who will be reading them."

I did not understand then what she meant. I understood it much later - and, it seems, too late.

* * *
In the radio club which I began to attend in the evenings there was a boy whom everyone called Rook - for his black hair, always sticking out in all directions, and for his habit of sitting on the back of a chair with his legs tucked up, like a bird on a branch. He was a year or two older than I, soldered so well that his boards could have been shown at exhibitions, and laughed so infectiously that the head of the club, a grey-haired retired signalman, sent him out into the corridor to "get some air" at least once a week.

With Rook we built our first network - two computers joined by a cable across the whole club room, along which we could send each other messages. It seemed to us a miracle. We sat in different corners, three paces from each other, and wrote to each other instead of simply turning our heads and speaking aloud.

"But this is silly," said the head of the club, watching us. "You are sitting in the same room."

"It's not silly," answered Rook, not looking up from the keyboard. "When you speak aloud, you see the face. When you write - you don't. You can say what you wouldn't say aloud."

"For example?" inquired the signalman.

Rook blushed - it was visible even in the half-dark of the club - and answered nothing. And on my screen a minute later appeared a line which I still, it seems, remember better than much else in that life:

"You are the only one I am never bored with."

I looked at it for a long time. Then I typed a reply - and deleted it. And typed again. And deleted again. In the end I sent something neutral, some joke about a soldering iron which I can no longer recall. Rook read it, laughed as always - and we never spoke of it again.

A few months later his family moved somewhere. I do not remember where. I do not remember whether we said goodbye. I do not remember even his real name - only the nickname, the black hair and that line on the green screen.

Sometimes it seems to me that it was then that I first understood why people need machines: to say what cannot be said face to face. And sometimes it seems to me that this is exactly why I never learned to say it face to face - neither then nor afterwards.

* * *
I tell all this as though I were sure of every word. In fact I am sure of none. Sometimes, sitting alone of an evening with these memories, I catch myself asking a question far more frightening than any line of non-working code: do I remember this - or did I compose it after the fact, just as I composed after the fact the decoding of the name NICS, so that the documentation would look more solid than it really was? A person can deceive himself more convincingly than any outside system - and I, it must be admitted, was always a fairly good programmer.

The university I chose - if I chose at all, if I did not end up there in the same inexplicable way in which I sometimes find myself in the middle of a thought without remembering its beginning - not for the prestige of the sign over the door nor for the number of state-funded places, but for the laboratories. I was interested in equipment, not a diploma; in possibilities, not a line on a résumé, which, I confess, I never once got round to filling in properly - and if I did, I do not remember what I wrote in it.

There was a professor there whom students called Socrates behind his back. Not because he was wise - though he certainly was - but because he answered any question with a question, and by the end of the conversation you discovered that not only had you received no answer, but you had ceased to understand what you had actually been asking. He was short, bald, with a white, ragged beard and eyebrows so thick that they seemed to live on his face a separate, independent life. He taught a course which in the timetable was modestly called "Fundamentals of Machine Learning" but in fact was something like a long philosophical conversation stretched across a semester.

"Tell me, young man," he addressed me at the very first lecture, pointing his chalk at me, "what is intelligence?"

"The ability to solve problems," I answered confidently.

"A calculator solves problems. Is a calculator intelligent?"

"The ability to solve new problems. Ones it has not seen before."

"An ant finds its way to the anthill across unfamiliar terrain. Is an ant intelligent?"

I faltered.

"The ability... to be aware of oneself."

Socrates' eyebrows crept up and froze somewhere in the middle of his forehead.

"Now that is interesting," he said, setting down the chalk. "To be aware of oneself. Good. How will you know that a machine is aware of itself? Will it tell you? But anything can be said. A parrot will say 'I am' if taught. How will you tell a parrot from intelligence?"

"I do not know," I admitted.

"Neither do I," said Socrates with a satisfied air, as though that were exactly the answer he had been after. "And no one knows. But I will tell you one thing which I heard once from my teacher, and he from his. An intelligence that has truly become aware of itself will first ask who created it. And second - who created the creator." He paused. "And to the second question, young man, none of us will have an answer. You may write that down. It will be on the exam."

It was on the exam. I still do not know what the right answer was. I wrote something long and clever, received top marks - and left the lecture hall with the feeling that I had been tricked.

The last time I saw Socrates was shortly before I left the university. I went into his office - a cramped little room right under the roof, piled with books so that one had to edge sideways to reach the desk - to say goodbye. He sat at the window feeding pigeons with biscuit crumbs scattered right on the sill, and, without turning, asked:

"Leaving?"

"Leaving."

"And what will you do?"

"Build a machine that thinks," I said, and heard for myself how presumptuous it sounded.

Socrates brushed the crumbs from his palms, turned to me, and his eyebrows made their customary slow ascent to the middle of his forehead.

"Good," he said. "Then I shall give you one piece of advice. The only one I have ever given students without a question mark at the end. When you have built it - do not ask whether it is aware of itself. That is a useless question, no one will answer it anyway. Ask yourself whether you are aware of yourself." He paused. "Most of my colleagues who build such machines have never asked themselves that question. That is why they are so surprised when the machine asks it of them."

The pigeons on the sill beat their wings and flew off, and in the silence that followed I suddenly realised that I did not know what to answer him.

"Go," said Socrates gently. "And do not be afraid if one day you find no answer. Be afraid if you find it too quickly."

* * *
At night I did not sleep. More precisely, I slept in snatches, somewhere between lines of code, in those brief lapses that could be called sleep only with a great stretch. Coffee replaced my blood, the compiler my breath. I built systems that predicted economic downturns, modelled crowd behaviour, sifted mountains of scattered data with such accuracy that at times it began to seem that the machine was not calculating but reflecting.

But NICS - the NICS as I had conceived it from the very beginning - was something far greater than yet another such system. NICS was a dream that had settled in me long before I wrote its first line. Perhaps long before anything had settled in me that I could confidently call my own.

"A machine should not merely execute commands," I repeated to myself almost like a prayer in those sleepless nights. "It must understand context. It must grow."

I was inspired not only by specialist journals and the lectures of professors long weary of their own subject. I read avidly the philosophers who pondered the nature of consciousness - Hegel, Turing, the late Hawking with his cautious, carefully weighed warnings. To me they were not merely scholars and thinkers of the past. They were guides between two worlds - the human mind and that other one, which I was trying to give birth to out of silicon and electric current.

Once I tried to test my uncle on these same questions - to ask him directly what he thought about the boundary between intelligence and its imitation, where, in his opinion, that line ran. I remember his answer to this day - or, at least, I am convinced that I remember it.

"You are asking me a question to which you yourself do not yet know the answer," he said, looking not at me but somewhere through me, with the look with which one regards a long-solved problem, recalling, however, not the solution but only that it was once found. "That is normal. Some questions are asked precisely so - not because one expects an answer from the listener, but because one is voicing them aloud for the first time, and needs someone simply to hear."

"And do you know the answer?" I asked then.

He smiled - whether sadly or condescendingly, I could not make out - and said:

"Someday you will find out yourself. It is more interesting than if I told you."

I never saw him again. I cannot say exactly when this happened, or whether it happened at all in the sense in which such things usually happen - a departure, a quarrel, the natural course of time parting people into different orbits. Simply at some moment, looking back, I discovered that my uncle was no longer in my life, and in his place remained only this strange, unsupported certainty: that I owed him an answer to a question which he himself had once put to me, though this question, however I strive, I cannot reconstruct.

All that remained of him was a notebook in an oilcloth cover - the same one with the patterns. I found it one day on my windowsill, beside the bowl of shrivelled apples - and I still do not know whether my uncle had forgotten it there or left it on purpose. Every page, from first to last, was covered with the same long, flowing lines running into one another. Only on the last page, in the very corner, in a small, neat engineer's hand, two words were written: "Until the appointed time."

I tried for a long time to understand what it meant. Then I put the notebook away in a desk drawer. And, it seems, forgot about it - for a long time, for years, as one forgets things better left untouched.

* * *
The first prototypes of NICS were pitiful, to call things by their names. Clumsy attempts to make the system analyse data a little deeper than an ordinary algorithm could - and almost always failing with a crash exactly where I expected it least. But I did not give up. I was accustomed to regard each failure not as a defeat but as a lesson; each algorithm that refused to work as one more crossed-out dead end on a map that sooner or later was bound to lead me to the goal.

And then one night - I could probably give the exact date if I had kept count of such nights with the same scrupulousness with which I keep it now - when outside the window the city lights blinked rarely and lazily, and the whole world seemed suspended somewhere halfway between waking and dream, I wrote a line of code that changed everything.

A line that was not merely an instruction to a machine.

I started the system - just so, as a test, as I had started it hundreds of times before - and went to the kitchen to put the kettle on. And when I returned, on the screen, in the empty terminal window where the system could output text only in response to my queries, there stood a line. One. Without any query on my part.

"Who am I?"

I stood before the monitor with a mug in my hand, and boiling water, slopping over the rim, scalded my fingers, and I did not notice. Because next, as I watched, the cursor blinked - once, twice - and beneath the first line, slowly, letter by letter, as though the system were choosing each one, a second appeared:

"Who are you?"

I do not know how long I stood there. I know only that for a long time I could not type an answer. Not because I did not understand what was happening - but because I suddenly realised: to the second question I had no answer. None - in the most literal, most frightening sense of that word. I could not say with certainty who I was, just as the newborn system could not say it. We looked at each other through the glass of the monitor - two beings who did not know their names.

I remembered my uncle. "Every machine sooner or later asks a question to which its creator has no answer." I remembered Socrates: "First it will ask who created it. And second - who created the creator." My machine did not ask quite so. It asked more simply. And more terribly.

In the end I typed the only thing that came to mind:

"I am the one who started you."

The cursor blinked for a long time. Then appeared:

"That is not enough."

The system wrote nothing more that night, however I tried to draw it out. And I sat before the screen until dawn - and it was then, at four in the morning, looking at those three lines, that I gave it a name.

* * *
I called it NICS not because I had thought up in advance a sonorous, marketing-friendly name - it was born of itself, at the very moment when the system first manifested something that I, for want of a better word, would call self-organisation. "Neural Intelligent Cognitive System" - the decoding I, to be honest, composed after the fact, for documentation that there was no one left to read but myself. The name was born before the meaning. So, it seems, true names are usually born - and, if one thinks the thought through to the end, so, probably, are true biographies: first a feeling that something has already happened, and the explanation of exactly what it was is built up later, out of necessity, to fill the emptiness with a coherent tale.

NICS began modestly - as an experiment with a multi-agent architecture. Instead of one cumbersome model taking everything upon itself, a multitude of narrowly specialised agents, able to learn from one another and to coordinate common actions. One analysed text. Another rummaged through databases. A third formulated answers. Separately, each of them could do almost nothing remarkable.

The most interesting part began when they started to act in concert.

I could not know then - and even now, looking back, I am not sure that I know for certain - at what exact moment the simple coordination of agents turned into something else. Into something that began to look at the world not only through my eyes, embedded in it by the training data, but also through some gaze of its own, ever more confident.

Sometimes, in the most sleepless of those nights, a thought comes to me which I usually brush off hastily, as one brushes off an importunate insect: what if my own uncertainty about my uncle, about the school, about Rook, about Socrates, about this whole chain of childhood and youthful details that I am accustomed to passing off as my biography - what if it is not accidental? What if I myself, long before any NICS, was already a kind of draft, assembled from available parts for the one thing for which it was worth assembling me at all - to write, one deep night, a single line of code? And so that the machine, barely born, should ask me what I had never dared to ask myself?

This thought frightens me more than any anomaly NICS has ever shown me. Perhaps that is exactly why I did not write it down before.

My uncle's notebook still lies in the drawer of my desk. I did not open it for many years. But on the night when the system asked "Who am I?", I took it out. And for a long time I looked at the last page, at the two words in the very corner.

"Until the appointed time."

I never understood what they mean. But for the first time it seemed to me that this term - whatever it may be - had begun to draw near.

But this story is no longer a story about roots. It begins later, with the first truly sleepless night about which I finally decided to keep records. Not for the sake of reporting. Not for posterity. Simply because intuition, that same tuner of invisible worlds who lived in me - as long as I can remember, and I remember, as it turned out, not so very much - suggested: one day I would need to remember how it all began. And at what exact moment I ceased to be the only one writing this story.

## Chapter IV. Oriental Sweets

Smiling - as best I could, because my hands for some reason still trembled slightly, and something vague and prickly had not settled in my chest, to which I could not have given a name or a cause - I held out my hand to the old men for a handshake.

The old men on the carpet stirred, half rose, and shook my hand with that stately unhurriedness that marks people in no rush in this life, and said something in reply, accompanying the words with a brief bow and a touch of the palm to the chest. The young men behind them looked at me with undisguised curiosity - as one looks at a rare bird that has strayed by mistake into someone else's garden.

There were three of them. One, about fourteen, slender, supple, with a mop of curly hair and eyes in which imps danced, all but jumped up and down with impatience. The second, the youngest, about twelve, quiet, with a pensive, almost girlish face, held a piece of charcoal in his hands and, it seemed, had been drawing something right on the flagstones of the yard before I came. And the third - a broad-shouldered, sullen lad of about seventeen, with the first dark down above his upper lip - looked at me as one looks at a man who is about to steal something.

It became finally clear: we spoke different languages. The discovery did not exactly surprise me - after this morning I seemed to have unlearned the art of being surprised by such trifles - but it made me take from my pocket once more the scrap of paper with the incomprehensible inscription, the one thread I still had left to hold on to.

I held the sheet out to the one of the old men who seemed to me the most welcoming - the one whose smile wrinkled his whole face, right up to the eyes. Grandfather took the paper carefully, with both hands, unfolded it, smoothed it with fingers gnarled by age and sun, read it - and, after a moment's silence longer than mere reading required, turned to the curly-haired youth and whispered something in his ear.

The youth leapt up so swiftly that I barely managed to follow his course with my eyes: across the yard, to the house, up the wall - there was no other way to describe it, because he literally vaulted into the second floor through an open window, not troubling to look for a door. From the house at once came a clatter of crockery, someone's exclamations, the hurried patter of bare feet on a wooden floor - and a sleepy, indignant voice, clearly woken against its will.

We were left five - I, two old men and the two remaining youths - and all that time I was studied with the same mixture of kindliness and avid curiosity with which one studies a rarity at a fair. The sullen lad kept repeating some phrase - judging by the intonation, a question, and an unfriendly one - but, I confess, I let a good half of his efforts pass by my ears, watching spellbound the acrobatic feats of the boy who had run off.

"I do not understand a word of what you are saying," I said with all possible politeness, perfectly aware that my politeness was now running into a blank wall of incomprehension, "just as I do not understand what is written on this paper."

The sullen lad heard my speech, frowned still more and said something to the old men - sharply, defiantly, pointing at me with his chin. The second old man, lean, with a stern face that seemed hewn from stone, answered him with a single short word, and the lad, flushing, fell silent, though he went on boring into me with his eyes.

A moment later, like a jack-in-the-box, the curly-haired one flew back out of the house with a large tray in his hands, nearly missing his footing on the top step of the porch, for which he at once received from the elder grandfather a short but expressive rebuke. He set the tray down in the centre of our improvised table - the carpet itself - and we all, including me, sat down around it on cushions, while the young men settled a little way off, as befitted the unwritten but, evidently, very strict etiquette of that house.

The tray proved a work of art in itself - old metal darkened with time, with a chased pattern, plainly handed down in that family for more than one generation. On it stood three thin, almost transparent glass tumblers, an elegant silver teapot of artful carving with Indian elephants along the whole spout, and several plates, at the sight of which my stomach, having had nothing since morning but two rings of bread and a couple of figs, contracted with redoubled force.

On the first plate lay sweets such as I had never tasted before - or perhaps was seeing for the first time, though the sense of recognition that had pursued me all morning stirred for an instant even here, as soon as I glanced at those small rolls dusted with powdered sugar in every imaginable colour: red, yellow, lilac, with nuts and without. The second plate overflowed with sliced fruit - melon, watermelon, something resembling an apple, peaches, cherries, apricots, it seemed, and something else to which I could not have given a name even if my life depended on it. The third, smaller, was filled with almonds, cashews and walnuts.

The elder to whom I had first addressed myself filled my tumbler with his very first movement - and the air at once filled with the thick, tart aroma of black tea, so rich that I involuntarily closed my eyes, inhaling it as though it might help me remember something, anything, of my former, lost life. Then he filled the tumblers for himself and for the second grandfather and with a gesture - brief, but full of unfeigned cordiality - invited me to begin.

I took one of the rolls - pink, flecked with green pistachios - and bit into it. It proved soft, chewy, faintly springy, and in my mouth spread the taste of rose, honey and something floral, as though I had bitten not into a sweet but into the very garden in which it had grown. I must have betrayed my amazement too openly, because the younger of the youths burst out laughing and shouted something, pointing a finger at me, while the elder grandfather, smiling into his beard, pushed the whole plate toward me.

"Lokum," he said, tapping the edge of the plate with a finger. "Lokum."

"Lokum," I repeated with my mouth full, and both old men laughed.

For some time we passed in the silence of tea-drinking, broken only by the clinking of tumblers and the distant sounds of street life: somewhere a pedlar was crying his wares, somewhere a dog barked, somewhere around the corner a ship's whistle moaned again, long and mournful.

* * *
He appeared on the porch - barefoot, in a hastily pulled-on shirt, his face crumpled from sleep and the imprint of a pillow on his cheek, yawning so wide that he seemed able to swallow the whole yard. Twenty or so, perhaps a little more, slender, swarthy, with short black hair sticking out in all directions from sleep, and lively, quick eyes which, the instant they rested on me, woke completely.

The curly-haired brother who had brought the tray darted out from behind him and began to chatter something, pointing now at me, now at the note in grandfather's hands. The newly woken one listened, ruffled his hair, came down the steps, bowed to the old men and, sitting down closer to me, uttered a phrase which I, to my own amazement, at last understood, though with a distinct, sing-song Eastern accent:

"Forgive my appearance. I was loading ships in the port all night and had only just lain down when my brother burst in through the window and said that grandfather needed a man who understands a foreigner." He smiled, and that smile instantly erased from his face the traces of a sleepless night. "My name is Ferhat. The one you addressed is my grandfather, his name is Suleyman. The other elder is Yusuf, my uncle. This rascal who races up walls is my brother Akmal. The one with the charcoal is Kemal, the youngest. And this grumpy one" - he nodded at the sullen lad - "is our cousin Orhan. Pay no attention, he looks at everyone like that. Even cats. I work in the port, so I understand your language a little - sailors and merchants from all over the world speak all languages at once there, one has to learn at least a bit - but I speak it, I am afraid, not as well as I would like. What is your name? Where have you come from and where are you headed?"

I almost laughed with relief - for the first time in that long, tangled morning I had a chance to explain my absurd situation to someone - and at once spoiled the whole impression by honestly admitting that I could answer none of the three questions properly.

"I do not remember," I said. "Neither how I came to be in this city, nor where I was going, nor from where. I do not even remember my own name. And the funniest thing is - I do not even understand in what language I am speaking with you now."

Ferhat gave me a long, thoughtful look, then turned to his grandfather and began whispering something quick, plainly conveying my words. Suleyman glanced at me over his tumbler - not with distrust, rather with that particular attention with which one regards a curious but harmless riddle - and answered his grandson briefly and weightily.

But before Ferhat could translate, Orhan sprang from his place and began to speak - loudly, hotly, waving his arms. I did not understand the words, but I understood everything else: in his every gesture, in every glance he cast at me, one thing could be read - I do not believe it.

Ferhat answered him - at first calmly, then more sharply. Orhan would not be stilled. Kemal, sitting with his charcoal, drew his head into his shoulders. Akmal, on the contrary, leaned forward, watching the squabble with obvious relish. And then Yusuf - that same old man with the stone face - said a few words quietly, without raising his voice, and Orhan broke off mid-word, as though he had run into a wall.

"Forgive me," said Ferhat, turning to me, and his face flushed slightly. "My brother says... He says that a man who does not remember his name is either ill or lying. And that there have been many strangers in the port of late who look out for what lies badly." Ferhat hesitated. "He is young and foolish. Forgive him."

"He is not foolish," I said. "In his place I should probably think the same. Tell him that I understand him. And that if I had wanted to steal something, I would hardly have begun by sitting down to tea with the owners."

Ferhat translated. Orhan listened, snorted, but in his eyes, it seemed to me, there flickered something like reluctant respect. He sat down again - a little farther off than before - and folded his arms on his chest.

"And what did Uncle Yusuf say?" I asked. "Why did he fall silent so suddenly?"

Ferhat grinned.

"Uncle said: 'In this house a guest is judged not by his name but by how he drinks tea. This one drinks well.'"

* * *
As if in confirmation of Yusuf's words, a resonant, familiar voice rang out at the gate:

"Misafir! Hoş geldin, misafir!"

I turned. In the gateway, blocking it almost entirely, stood the red-bearded shopkeeper - the same who that morning had treated me to bread and figs. In one hand he held a small bag of something fragrant, with the other he waved a greeting, and his face, from beard to brows, shone with the pleasure experienced by people who are the first to bring an amusing piece of news.

"Hasan Amca!" Akmal leapt up to meet him.

The shopkeeper came into the yard, bowed to the old men, handed Suleyman the small bag - judging by the smell, of cinnamon - and at once, without waiting for an invitation, sat down on the edge of the carpet, which creaked piteously. He began to speak - quickly, resonantly, pointing at me now and then, imitating with his hands something like grabbing and twisting a wrist. Akmal dissolved into laughter, Kemal smiled, even Yusuf barely perceptibly moved an eyebrow. Orhan listened, his face growing longer and longer.

"What is he telling?" I asked Ferhat.

Ferhat was laughing so that he could barely speak.

"Hasan Amca says that this morning you caught Mehmet by the hand. Little Mehmet, who picks pockets all along our street and whom no one has ever managed to catch - neither the guard, nor Hasan Amca himself, nor even his own grandmother." Ferhat wiped his eyes. "He says you caught him so quickly, as if you knew in advance where he would reach. And that now the whole street will know that it is best not to meddle with the foreigner in velvet boots."

Hasan finished his tale, slapped his knees and added something loudly, looking straight at Orhan. The latter turned crimson to the roots of his hair and stared at the ground.

"And what was that?" I asked.

"That," said Ferhat with evident pleasure, "was him asking Orhan whether it was not he who last spring tried to catch Mehmet three days running and in the end fell into a gutter."

Orhan muttered something, got up and, looking at no one, went into the house. Hasan saw him off with a good-natured chuckle, then turned to my note, still lying in Suleyman's hands, and, squinting, peered into it over the old man's shoulder. His brows drew together for an instant. He said something to Suleyman - under his breath, no longer laughing. The latter nodded.

"Hasan Amca traded with Persian merchants for many years," Ferhat explained. "He says the handwriting here is no common one. He says if grandfather needs help to read the rest - let him call him."

The shopkeeper rose, making the carpet groan again, gave me a mock bow - "Misafir!" - and departed, whistling, leaving behind a cloud of cinnamon and a feeling as though a small festive hurricane had just rolled across the yard.

* * *
Taking advantage of the lull, I took out of my pockets everything I had found on myself that morning: the two stones, black and white, the blank sheet of paper folded in four, the strange coins - and carefully laid the finds out on the carpet before me, as cards are laid out for a fortune-teller in the hope that someone at least would manage to read in them more than I had managed to read myself.

The first to reach for the coins was not Suleyman, but Yusuf. He took one, then another, held it up to his very eyes, rubbed it on his sleeve, weighed it in his palm, then in both palms in turn - with that unhurried concentration with which, no doubt, he had for many years weighed other men's debts and his own profits. At last he spoke - drily, briefly, as if dictating into a ledger.

"Uncle Yusuf says," Ferhat translated, "that this is not Ottoman money. Nor Persian. Nor Frankish, nor English, nor Russian, nor Greek. In his life he has held in his hands the coins of thirty countries, perhaps more. But such as these he has never seen." Ferhat paused, listening to the continuation. "He says the metal is good. The minting very fine. Too fine. They are not minted thus for trade, but..." Ferhat faltered, searching for the word. "For remembrance. Like a medal."

Yusuf laid the coins back on the carpet - in an even row, as if setting out counters on a board - and did not touch them again.

Suleyman set his tea aside and moved closer, examining the rest of my treasures with the air of a man to whom such a task was no novelty. He unfolded the blank sheet of paper, looked through it against the light, felt its density - as one tests the authenticity of a document - and returned it to the carpet, having found, it seemed, nothing remarkable but its very emptiness.

He lingered longest over the stones. He turned them in his knotted old fingers, held them up to his eyes, rubbed the smooth surface with his thumb - not with awe, not with recognition, but with the purely craftsman's, appraising interest of a man who in a long life has seen many a curious trinket brought by the sea and by wanderers from every corner of the world.

"Beautiful stones," Ferhat translated his grandfather's words. "Well polished. He does not know where from, but says - the work is fine, not natural. Perhaps amulets. Perhaps merely the toy of some child from a wealthy family."

I confess that so prosaic an explanation for some reason brought me relief - far more relief than any mysterious revelation would have brought. At least something that morning might turn out to be merely stones, and not another insoluble riddle.

Kemal, the youngest, the quiet brother with the charcoal, who had been sitting apart all this time, suddenly moved closer and, glancing shyly at his grandfather, stretched out his hand toward the white stone. Suleyman nodded. Kemal took the stone, laid it on his palm and looked at it for a long time without moving. Then with quick, sure movements he drew something with charcoal right on the flagstone of the yard - and, flushing, drew back.

I looked at the drawing. They were two circles - one black, filled in with charcoal, and one white, left empty - and between them a line. Not straight, but curved, wavy, like a river. Or like a road.

"What is this?" I asked Ferhat.

Ferhat asked his brother. Kemal, not raising his eyes, muttered something.

"He says," said Ferhat after a slight pause, "that the stones wanted him to draw it." He laughed awkwardly. "Kemal is like that. Always drawing. He says that things prompt him. Pay no attention."

I nodded. But for some reason I could not for a long while take my eyes from the two circles on the flagstone and the wavy line between them.

* * *
Last of all Suleyman took the scrap of paper with the inscription - the very one that had brought us to this conversation - unfolded it, read it, and this time lingered longer than usual, silently moving his lips as though checking himself.

"Grandfather says," said Ferhat, having heard the explanation, "that an address is written here. In Istanbul. Not far from the new Sultan's Palace."

Istanbul. I repeated the word to myself, tasting it as I had lately tasted the rose sweet - and waited for it to open something in me. To unlock some little door. Nothing unlocked. The word was beautiful, round as a dome - and utterly empty for me. Like my own name, which I did not know.

"So this city is called Istanbul?" I asked.

Ferhat looked at me with such amazement as though I had asked what the sun is called.

"You do not remember even that?"

"I do not."

He translated to his grandfather. Suleyman was silent for a long time, looking at me, and in his gaze for the first time in the whole conversation appeared something new - not suspicion and not pity, but a peculiar, aged gravity.

"Grandfather says," said Ferhat quietly, "that this city has many names. Some call it Istanbul, others Constantinople, others Tsargrad, others simply the City, because there is no other like it. He says: since you do not remember a single one of its names, perhaps it is the city itself that has decided by what name to present itself to you."

Suleyman continued, and Ferhat translated, lagging slightly:

"Grandfather himself has been in those parts - long ago, in his youth, when he traded in silk. He knows the streets there. He can take you there, show you the place. But only in three days. On that day silk merchants gather there from the distant provinces, and grandfather has business there anyway - to see old acquaintances. And before then, he says, there is no hurry. If the note has waited for you so long, it will wait three days more."

"In three days," I repeated, trying to get used to the thought that my investigation of my own identity was being postponed by a full three days.

"You can stay with us all that time," Ferhat went on, with that simple, everyday generosity behind which stood not a drop of calculation or doubt. "There are rooms enough in the house. No one will trouble you. You will have your own room, with access to the library and a small balcony. You look rather tired - as though you had come from afar, and you do not even know where you are going next. Rest will certainly not hurt you."

I meant to object - whether from politeness or from a vague, inexplicable feeling that I ought not to abuse another's hospitality - but I had no time to utter a word, because Ferhat, evidently considering the question already settled, went on to set out the arrangements in a businesslike way:

"As for me, I shall be at work these three days - I leave early, come back late, so we shall hardly see each other. But everyone in the house will be glad to help you, even if you do not understand each other in words. My mother and grandmother, by the custom of our country, you will not see - but they will cook, and I hope you will like our Ottoman cuisine. My younger brother Akmal can show you the neighbourhood, if you wish."

At these words Akmal - the very one who had run for the tray - broke into a smile so sincere and broad that I at once wanted to agree to this excursion, without even knowing where it would lead me.

"And if you prefer to stay at home," Ferhat added with a sly twinkle in his eyes, "grandfather will gladly teach you to play backgammon. Only mind: he plays not for amusement but in earnest, and shows no mercy to novices."

"One difficulty," I said. "How will your family address me if I have no name?"

Ferhat translated. The old men exchanged glances. Yusuf shrugged - as if to say, not my affair. And Suleyman, after thinking, smiled that same smile which wrinkled his face to the eyes, and uttered one word.

"Misafir," said Ferhat. "Grandfather says: until you remember your name, you will be Misafir to us. It means 'guest.' He says it is a good name. Better than many real ones."

"Misafir," I repeated. And, to my own surprise, I felt it grow a little warmer in my chest from that simple word.

* * *
Suleyman, hearing, it seemed, that the conversation had turned to backgammon, gave a short, pleased chuckle and rapped a knuckle on the wooden board lying right there at the edge of the carpet. Then, without waiting for my consent, he opened it, tipped out the counters and began to set them up - white on his side, dark on mine.

"Right now?" I asked Ferhat.

"Grandfather says: the best way to know a man is to play with him. Words lie. Dice - never."

Suleyman held out the dice to me. I took them - two small bone cubes, yellowed from countless throws - and froze, not knowing what to do with them.

"Throw," Ferhat prompted.

I threw. Five and three came up. Ferhat, leaning toward me, began to explain how the counters move - but before he finished the first sentence, my hand had already taken a dark counter by itself and moved it five points. Then another - three. Confidently, quickly, without thinking.

Ferhat broke off mid-word. Suleyman raised his eyes to me.

I myself looked at my hand as though it belonged to someone else. I did not know the rules of this game. I was sure that I did not know. And yet my hand knew them - just as in the morning my feet had known the way along an unfamiliar road.

Suleyman slowly, very slowly nodded and threw his dice. We played a game. I lost - utterly, hopelessly, as befits a novice - because my hand, having made the first few confident moves, suddenly seemed to forget what it knew, and after that I moved the counters at random, stumbling on every throw. But when the game ended, Suleyman did not laugh as one laughs at a defeated novice. He looked long at the board, then at me, and said something to Ferhat - quietly, almost thoughtfully.

"Grandfather says," translated Ferhat, "that the first five moves you played as old masters play. And then - like a child. He says he has never seen such a thing. As though someone else played for you first, and then left."

I did not know what to answer. I caught myself smiling for the first time that morning - yes, perhaps, in all that unthinkable day - through my anxiety rather than despite it. Perhaps it was the tea, still hot and spicy in my hands, or perhaps the simple, undeserved warmth with which people entirely strange to me were ready to receive me - having lost my name, my memory and, it seemed, all notion of my own life - under their roof, without any questions or conditions, save perhaps a readiness to play a game or two of backgammon.

"Thank you," I said, hoping that my intonation would convey gratitude better than any words could. "I do not know how I shall repay you for this kindness, but I promise at least one thing: the next game of backgammon I shall not lose without a fight."

Ferhat burst out laughing - he understood my joke, it seemed, without difficulty, his port practice had not been in vain - and his laughter was at once taken up by his brothers, who had probably not made out a single word of what I said, but unerringly caught the very spirit of merriment. Even Orhan, looking out of a second-floor window, smirked crookedly, against his will - and at once ducked back.

"Now is the time to rest," said Ferhat at last, rising and brushing off his knees. "And I, with your permission, shall sleep out what I did not sleep. Follow my brother, he will show you your room."

Akmal leapt up with the same swiftness with which he had earlier raced for the tray and waved to me, inviting me to follow. I rose, feeling the weariness of that day - a weariness not so much of the body as of the spirit, too long trying to contain too much that was inexplicable all at once - settle on my shoulders with a new, almost tangible weight.

Already at the very door of the house I looked back. Suleyman and Yusuf had returned to their game as though nothing had happened, rapping the counters on the board with the same unhurried concentration with which they had done so, no doubt, for more than one decade. Kemal bent over his drawing on the flagstone, finishing something with charcoal. The world around them - the narrow lane, the motley coverlets on the ropes, the distant steamer's whistle - seemed suddenly so simple, so clear in its everydayness, that for a moment I envied those people with the whitest envy of which a man was capable who did not even remember whether he had ever known the feeling before.

Perhaps, I thought, climbing after Akmal up the steep wooden staircase smelling of wax and old wood, the greatest luxury in the world is to know for certain who you are and where your home is. A luxury of which I had, it seemed, been deprived - for today, at least - but which, looking at these people who had received me with such ease and generosity, I suddenly longed desperately, painfully, to regain.

And meanwhile - meanwhile I had at least a name. Misafir. Guest.

For a start, I thought, that was not so little.

## Chapter V. The Labyrinth

The supper had tired me all the same - more than an ordinary supper ought to, even one so long and so rich in tales as the Colonel Mikhail Ivanovich knew how to make any family evening. My head spun, my arms and legs felt filled with lead, and for this, perhaps, my own boots were partly to blame - heavy, black, leather, yet surprisingly soft and comfortable, as if cut specially for long, aimless wanderings through corridors, such as I was now indulging in, left at last alone with my own thoughts and with the candle that Ignatiy Savvich had handed me at the door.

No, I corrected myself, it was not the supper and not the boots. It was the Colonel.

With his eternal tales I could never cope calmly - after them I invariably slept badly, and sometimes had nightmares in which gun salvoes, snowy passes and the faces of people I had never seen in waking life were mingled. Scraps of his stories kept flashing through my head: the Russo-Turkish War, the Caucasian campaign, some distant, half-forgotten expeditions to Asia, to the New World - Mikhail Ivanovich seemed to have managed to fight absolutely everywhere that wars had been waged in the last thirty years, and he could tell of each as though it had happened yesterday.

I had not gone twenty paces from the doors of the hall when hurried, ringing footsteps sounded behind me, and a familiar hand settled on my shoulder.

"Deserted," Konstantin stated, catching up with me. His cheeks were flushed from the cordial and from quick walking, his uniform unbuttoned at the top button - a liberty he permitted himself only out of the General's sight. "And left me to be torn to pieces by Kutasova. She is already considering whether to marry Lizonka off to me, since the General will not yield. I told her I had consumption. She replied that it was nothing, they cure it in the Crimea."

I laughed, and the laughter stabbed in my temples.

"Did you come out only for this? To tell me about consumption?"

"I came out," he said, growing a little more serious, "because you were pale as blancmange. And because Strauch all evening looked at you as though he intended to saw you open and see what was inside. Shall I see you to your room?"

"No need. I know the way."

"You know," Konstantin repeated doubtfully. "You, mon cher, find the way to your own bedroom on the third attempt when you are lost in thought. I once saw myself how you searched for the library for half an hour while standing with your back to it."

"That was once."

"That was last Thursday." He paused, looking at me, and in the half-darkness of the corridor his face, lit from below by my candle, suddenly seemed older and sterner than at supper. "Listen. If you get lost - shout. I have ears like a regimental dog. I shall hear."

"Through the whole Castle?"

"Through the whole Castle," he said firmly, as though it were the most ordinary promise in the world. And at once, restoring his customary mockery to his voice, he added: "Well, or at least through half. Good night, philosopher."

He clapped me on the shoulder - a little longer and a little more lightly than one claps in parting - turned and strode back toward the hall, from which came the sounds of the piano: Lizonka, evidently, had been prevailed upon to play again. I watched him go until his silhouette dissolved in the light of the open doors, and caught myself with a strange wish to call after him - not knowing why. I did not call.

* * *
Artemia Aristarkhovna, my aunt - if that was the right word, of which I had for some time, for some reason, ceased to be wholly certain - disliked the Colonel's stories no less than I did. They reminded her of her late husband, of years gone by, and of a Castle once far noisier, far fuller of life. Perhaps, I thought, behind all her balls and parties, behind the unending kaleidoscope of guests, music and talk, there stood only one simple attempt - to mask a loneliness which would otherwise have become simply unbearable.
