Her rare guests, mostly young, did not linger long: either they set off on another expedition, to which the gallant General Pavel Nikolaevich invariably dispatched them, or my aunt herself politely but insistently saw them on their way home as soon as they abused her hospitality.

The General was a widower. He had lost his wife many years ago, on one of the Asian campaigns - she could not endure the climate there and died of one of the Eastern diseases which the doctors could neither recognise in time nor cure afterward. Pavel Nikolaevich came of a hereditary military line: his whole family, to the most distant ancestors, had served royal persons, and served in the highest ranks. He himself had risen to General of the Imperial Army, stood in excellent favour with the Sovereign and, to all appearances, did not think of retirement for a single second.

Vera Anatolievna, wife of the Colonel-raconteur, was a frequent guest of ours - together with my aunt she organised reading evenings at which their own small circle of ladies passed the time over fashionable novels, at times brought from abroad, from France or Britain. At one such evening they had made the acquaintance of Evdokia Gerasimovna - she travelled a great deal and often brought back book novelties, chiefly from Paris.

Besides this, Evdokia Gerasimovna was fabulously rich: she had received an inheritance from her parents, industrial magnates who had once founded metallurgical works in the Urals. Her husband, also a soldier, killed in one of the campaigns, had left her in addition a very round fortune. To this were added numerous landed estates, peasants and a solid pension from the Imperial Court - for her heroically fallen husband. Evdokia Gerasimovna could afford absolutely everything: no one had ever yet seen her twice in the same dress or hat, and legends truly circulated among the capital's ladies about the exquisiteness of her headgear - it was even whispered that she ordered them directly from Paris, trusting no local milliner.

Her nephew, Lieutenant Konstantin, had in effect been brought up in solitude - his parents had died of some terrible, swift illness when he was still quite a boy. What exactly bound us to one another so easily and so long, I could not have explained - perhaps merely an excess of free time that had fallen to us both in equal measure - but at times in his tales of childhood I seemed to sense something remotely, inexplicably familiar, as though we both bore the same pattern, only laid out differently. We readily spent our free time together, roaming the boundless expanses of the Castle or driving by carriage to the capital. He had only lately graduated from the military academy and therefore swaggered everywhere in his brand-new, spotlessly clean and pressed uniform, as though afraid to part for a single day with this, as yet, sole proof of his own adulthood.

* * *
Passing through the long, in places very dark corridors of the Castle, I kept meeting servants hurrying now in one direction, now in another: some carried things on trays to the hall, some bore away dirty dishes - life in the house, invisible to guests behind the parade facade of the dining room, seethed in its own special, businesslike course.

On the landing of the back staircase leading down to the kitchens I came upon Dunyasha. She stood with a tray full of dirty plates and was arguing hotly, in an undertone, with the kitchen boy Mitka - tousle-headed, freckled, about twelve, in a greasy apron three sizes too large for him. At the sight of me both fell silent so abruptly that it was as though they had been caught stealing jam.

"Master," Dunyasha hastily bobbed a curtsy, nearly dropping the tray. "Did you find the pie?"

"I found it, Dunyasha. Thank you. It was delicious."

She blushed. Mitka, taking advantage of the diversion of attention, tried to slip away down the stairs, but Dunyasha, without looking, seized him by the ear with her free hand.

"Now stop. Tell the master what you were spinning me just now."

"Wasn't spinning nothing," Mitka mumbled, wincing. "Told the truth."

"What truth?" I asked.

Mitka squinted at Dunyasha, then at me, sniffed and blurted out:

"There was a light in the left wing. Last night. I ran out to the yard to relieve myself, and look - a little flame in the windows of the left wing. Goes from window to window, slow like. As if someone's walking with a candle."

"Perhaps the watchman?"

"Watchman don't go there, master," said Dunyasha, lowering her voice. "No one goes there. Agafya Tikhonovna won't give out the keys. There, they say..." She hesitated.

"What do they say?"

"A lady walks there," whispered Mitka with dreadful relish. "A white one. The one who lived here before our mistress. Long, long ago. She's been seen in the mirror. Whoever looks in that mirror - to him..."

Dunyasha tugged his ear so that he howled.

"Don't blather nonsense to the master at night!" She turned to me, smiling apologetically. "Don't listen to him, master. He lies about everything. Last month he fancied a house-spirit in the dough tub. Go and rest, master. And..." She paused. "And don't go to the left wing. There are draughts."

"Ignatiy Savvich told me the same," I remarked. "Word for word."

Dunyasha looked at me, and in her round, guileless eyes something flickered which she at once hid behind another curtsy.

"Well, Ignatiy Savvich doesn't speak for nothing, master."

And, snatching up the tray and Mitka at the same time, she vanished below, into the warm half-darkness of the kitchen stairs, smelling of sour cabbage soup.

* * *
Descending the spiral staircase, I could not help recalling the General's tales of his Asian campaigns - I remembered especially the stories about Turkestan and about the mysterious, enchanting Kingdom of Siam. Perhaps one day I too would go there, I thought, see different countries, know different people, and not only those few who crowd evening after evening around my aunt's table.

At the foot of the staircase, in a deep window niche, in a cloud of bluish cigar smoke, sat Doctor Strauch. He had thrown open the window to the garden, and the night air - cool, smelling of mown grass and a distant river - drew the smoke out into the darkness. His gold spectacles glinted in the light of my candle.

"Ah," he said without surprise, as though he had been waiting for me precisely here. "The fugitive. Sit down, young man. I shall not detain you. Doctors must not smoke in front of ladies, and in front of patients still less, but you, thank God, are not yet my patient."

I sat down on the sill opposite. The doctor drew on his cigar, blew smoke out into the garden and was silent for some time.

"I must apologise to you," he said at last. "At supper I was tactless. Your aunt is perfectly right: a dinner party is no place for medical questioning."

"A trifle, Karl Fyodorovich."

"Not a trifle." He turned to me, and his face, usually mockingly dry, was grave. "You see, many years ago your aunt took my word. Never to question you about the past. About anything that was before..." He broke off and corrected himself: "About anything that was earlier. I gave that word and I keep it. I do not know why she demanded it. I never asked."

I felt my fingers, clutching the candlestick, go cold.

"And today?"

"And today," said Strauch slowly, "you forgot the patronymic of a young lady. A trifle. It happens to anyone. But in that instant I looked at your aunt. And I saw fear on her face." He paused. "Not for you, young man. Not the fear that relatives feel when a dear one pales at table. Another. One does not fear illness thus. One fears thus when one sees something returning that one believed long gone."

"What is returning?"

"I do not know." He spread his hands, and the glow of the cigar described an arc in the darkness. "I am a healer, not a clairvoyant. I treat what can be felt with the hands. And this cannot be felt." He drew once more. "But I shall give you one piece of advice. Not as a doctor. As a man who has lived long enough in the world to see a thing or two. Start a notebook. Write in it everything - what you did, with whom you spoke, what you saw. Every evening. Briefly. If one day you discover that the notebook holds an entry which you do not remember - come to me. If you discover that your memory holds something which is not in the notebook - come to me all the more."

"You frighten me, Doctor."

"Not at all," said Strauch, and his customary dry mockery cut through his voice again. "Ghosts frighten. And I am a German. Germans do not frighten, Germans compile lists." He threw the stub into the garden and rose. "Good night, young man. And, I beg you, go straight to your room. Do not turn left."

"Why does everyone tell me tonight not to turn left?" I could not help exclaiming.

The doctor stopped, having already walked off a few paces, and turned.

"Everyone?" he repeated. And, after a pause, added quietly, as if to himself: "Curious. Very curious."

And he went away, leaving behind the smell of tobacco and a window open on the night garden.

* * *
I too often hovered in such thoughts, as in fluffy clouds - and too often because of that habit fell into comic, and sometimes quite vexing situations. So now, wandering through the corridors of the family Castle, I climbed ever farther and deeper, going down and up countless staircases, turning now left, now right an unknown number of times - and with each new turn understood ever less where, in fact, I had got to.

At the turning into yet another corridor I met the last living soul in that part of the house - the housekeeper Agafya Tikhonovna, a small old woman, dry as last year's leaf, in a dark dress and a white cap, with an enormous bunch of keys at her belt, jingling at every step like the bells on a troika. She made her rounds of the house before bed, checking the locks - as she had made them, no doubt, for the past half century - and, seeing me, stopped, raising her lamp higher.

"Can't sleep, dear sir?"

"My head aches, Agafya Tikhonovna. I walk to get some air."

"Some air," repeated the old woman, studying me with faded but keen eyes. "You won't get air on this side, dear sir. The air here is stale." She shook her bunch. "I've checked all the locks. All locked. Except one."

"Which?"

"The one with no key." Agafya Tikhonovna pursed her lips. "To the black grille in the left wing. The key was lost in the late master's time. Forty years, near enough, since it was lost. I don't even look for it any more. The grille stands by itself, held up by rust. No one touches it, and it touches no one. So we live."

"And if the key were found?"

The old woman looked at me long and attentively, as though deciding something to herself.

"If it were found, dear sir," she said at last, "I would throw it in the well. Nothing to be done there. Not for the living, nor..." She crossed herself, leaving it unsaid. "Go to sleep, dear sir. Go. To the right, then down the stairs, then straight on - and you'll be at your own door."

Right. Then down. Then straight. I thanked her and went - to the right, as she had said. The jingle of her keys faded for a long time behind my back.

To this day I cannot explain how it happened that, having turned right, I found myself some minutes later not at the staircase leading down but in a corridor I had never seen before.

* * *
The candles in this part of the house burned more rarely and more dimly than in the parade halls - and soon ceased altogether, and thereafter I walked only with my own, shielding the flame with my palm from the draught - and so the portraits along the walls - a family gallery which, I confess, I had never before examined attentively - seemed lit from below, giving the faces of the ancestors an unpleasant, unsteady depth.

There were many of them here. More than I had ever seen in the parade part of the house. Ladies in powdered wigs and panniered gowns, with fans and beauty patches on their cheeks; men in kaftans, in armour, in the uniforms of long-abolished regiments; infants in lace in the arms of wet-nurses; an old man in a sable coat, with a beard to his belt, who looked from the canvas so sternly that he seemed ready even now to send someone off to Siberia. Under each portrait, on a copper plate, a name was engraved - I held my candle to several, but the names told me nothing. Or told me - but I at once forgot, just as at supper I had forgotten Lizonka's patronymic.

One especially stern gentleman in a powdered wig, who, judging by the inscription on the age-darkened frame, was my great-great-grandfather, if the family tree was to be believed, seemed to look not through me, as portraits usually look, but straight at me - and as soon as I looked away and turned back again, it seemed that his pupils had shifted a hair's breadth to one side, following my movement.

I smiled at my own suspiciousness. Candles, shadows, fatigue, headache - that was the whole solution, I told myself, and yet I quickened my step past that corridor, not wishing to test the guess with a second look.

At the very end of the gallery hung a portrait draped in black crape. Such crape is hung as a sign of mourning - and is usually removed after a year, after two. This one, judging by the thick layer of dust lying in its folds, had not been removed for decades.

I stopped before it. I ought not to have touched it - I knew this as clearly as I knew that I ought not to turn left. And yet my hand reached of itself for the edge of the cloth.

The crape slid down, raising a little cloud of dust that made me cough.

Beneath it was a portrait of a young man. I could not make out the face - the paint on it had darkened, cracked into a fine net, as though the canvas had been kept long by a fire or, on the contrary, in damp, and the features had run into an indistinguishable dark blot. But all the rest had survived surprisingly well: a dark frock coat of old-fashioned cut, a light neckcloth tied in an intricate knot - I involuntarily touched my own neckerchief - and hands. Hands folded on the knees, and in the palm - two small, smooth objects. One black. The other white.

There was a copper plate beneath the portrait. But the name on it had been carefully scraped away with a knife, down to the bright copper.

I stood a long time before that portrait, and the candle in my hand trembled so that the shadows darted about the gallery like a flock of frightened birds. I did not know who this was. I did not know what the objects in his hand were. I did not know why, looking at them - two tiny flecks of paint, black and white - I felt in my palm a strange, phantom weight, as though I myself were holding something I did not have.

I lowered the crape back. It lay unevenly, crookedly, and the dust on it was now wiped away by my fingers. In the morning, I thought, someone - Agafya Tikhonovna, Ignatiy Savvich - would notice that it had been touched. And would understand by whom.

* * *
A little farther on, in a shallow niche between two doors which I had likewise not noticed before, hung an old mirror, darkened with time, in a heavy carved frame. I paused before it for a second - merely to straighten the neckerchief at my throat, no more - and at that very moment my reflection seemed suddenly to hesitate: my hand had already dropped from the collar, while the hand in the mirror, as it seemed to me, lingered for a barely perceptible instant at the throat, as if lagging behind me by one single, tiny heartbeat.

I froze. I peered. The reflection, of course, looked at me in complete accord with my every movement - no delay, no falseness, an ordinary tired face in dim glass. And yet the unpleasant chill that had settled somewhere between my shoulder blades would not disperse as swiftly as the illusion itself had dispersed.

"She's been seen in the mirror," I recalled Mitka's whisper. "Whoever looks in that mirror - to him..."

He had not finished. Dunyasha had not let him.

"This castle is older than it seems," I recalled next my aunt's words, spoken in parting, "and it has places that are better left in peace."

At the time, at table, I had taken those words for ordinary social coquetry, a light, frightening impromptu of a hostess who wished to add a touch of mystery to the house before her guests. Now, standing alone before the old mirror, in a corridor I did not remember before, those words for some reason sounded different - heavier, weightier, not at all like a joke. Ignatiy Savvich. Dunyasha. Doctor Strauch. Agafya Tikhonovna. Four people in one evening had told me the same thing in different words: do not go left. And four times I had not listened.

I shook my head to drive off the illusion and moved on, not entirely understanding why, instead of looking for the way back to my own rooms, I continued with every step to penetrate deeper into this unknown part of the house. As though someone were leading me by the hand. As though my feet - as, for some reason, it had seemed to me more than once, somewhere, sometime - knew the way better than I did.

* * *
Having turned several more times and lost all count of the turns, I suddenly came upon something which I definitely did not remember from my earlier, far more careful strolls through the Castle - a strange black grille that barred the corridor from the floor to the high vaulted ceiling.

Who had placed it here, and for what purpose, amid the family corridors, I wondered. Surely not my aunt - but she had never before mentioned this place by a single word, however much I had questioned her about the distant, locked wings of the house.

Approaching closer, I made out on the massive metal plate that held the grille in its frame a fine tracery, almost invisible in the meagre light - whether ornament or inscription, executed in a script so whimsical and unfamiliar that I could hardly associate it with any alphabet known to me. Its lines bent into one another with that deliberate intricacy with which, it seems, they write only in the most distant, most mysterious corners of the world - and for one brief, instantly elusive moment it seemed to me that I had already seen something similar, though I could not have recalled where or when.

"An Eastern whim, most likely," I decided, too tired at that moment to dwell on this trifle longer than a second. "Perhaps one of my ancestors brought this grille from one of his campaigns, together with other curiosities that adorn our house."

This explanation, I confess, suited me far better than any other - and other explanations at that hour, amid dimly burning candles and attentive portrait eyes, I decidedly did not wish to seek.

Catching myself in this convenient thought and resolving not to delay another second, I examined the grille more closely and discovered a lock on it - small, opening only a small part of it, a narrow door, enough for one person to squeeze through.

The lock hung open.

Not broken open - the shackle was intact, the rust lay on it in an even, untouched layer. Not smashed. Simply open - as though someone had unlocked it with the key that had been lost forty years ago, and left it so, inviting entry. As though he knew I would come.

"The key was lost in the late master's time," Agafya Tikhonovna had said. "I would throw it in the well."

I stood before the grille holding the candle, whose flame suddenly lay on its side, stretching toward the door - though there was not, I was ready to swear, the slightest draught. Somewhere far behind, in the parade part of the house, the piano still sounded. Konstantin had said: shout, I shall hear. I did not shout.

Yielding either to fatigue, or to a simple, inexplicable stubbornness, or to something third for which I had no name, I lifted the open lock from its hasp and pushed the door.

The door creaked unpleasantly - the way iron creaks that has rusted not over years even but over decades of silent, undisturbed repose - but nevertheless yielded and swung open, admitting me into new, entirely unexplored corridors. No sooner had I passed the threshold than the grille behind my back slammed shut of itself, with a still more unpleasant, grating sound - a sound remotely like a dull blow - and that sound rolled away down the corridor, echoing from wall to wall, receding farther and farther until it died somewhere in the most distant, most hidden labyrinths of the Castle, leaving me - now on the other side of the grille - in a silence so complete that my ears rang, as from a long, unbroken stillness.

The piano could no longer be heard.

I turned. The lock, which I had just held in my hand, hung on the hasp of the grille - locked.

And at that very instant the candle in my hand, without any wind, went out.

## Chapter VI. Cracks in the Earth

The earth of the Valley was now cracking not only along the distant canals, where water had reached only sparingly even in the best of years - the cracks were creeping across the most fertile fields, those that had fed the capital since time immemorial. I had seen this with my own eyes the day before, touring the nearer lands in a closed litter: the black, once fat soil of the Delta had become covered with a net of narrow, deep fissures into which peasant children, with a grim, un-childlike curiosity, lowered sticks without finding the bottom.

Three years without a full flood. Three years during which the god of the river, whose name even a Pharaoh was not permitted to utter in vain, had kept silence, in spite of all the sacrifices, all the prayers, all the processions that we sent to his banks with an enviable, desperate regularity.

This morning the audience hall was full as it had not been full for a long time - not with dignitaries, not with ambassadors of distant lands, but with simple petitioners, whose faces, scorched by the sun and wasted by hunger, merged for me into a single, faceless mass of grief. The guards could scarcely hold back the pressure at the entrance; the scribes barely managed to enter names and complaints into scrolls whose length grew with every hour.

Among the scribes seated at the foot of the throne I noticed a new one - a youth whom I had not seen in this hall before. Slender, dark-eyed, with a fine, boyishly grave face, he wrote faster than the rest and, unlike his elder colleagues, kept raising his head, peering into the faces of the petitioners so attentively as though committing to memory not only their words but their grief. When our eyes met by chance, he became confused, hastily lowered his gaze to the papyrus - and I, not knowing why, held my look on him a little longer than simple curiosity required.

"Who is that youth?" I asked in an undertone of the senior scribe standing beside me.

"Iti, my Pharaoh. Junior keeper of the Library. Scribes are short today, so he was sent to help. Clever, though at times he thinks too much for his years."

I nodded without answering and returned to the petitioners.

"My Pharaoh," the first of them addressed me, an old man with hands trembling whether from age or from hunger, "the water in the canal of Hapi-Re dried up at the very beginning of the season. The cattle are dying. The children..."

He did not finish, but there was no need to finish. I saw that phrase, that unfinished thought, written on hundreds of faces around me that morning.

"Grain from the royal granaries will be distributed to your village before sunset," I answered, trying to make my voice sound firm, though inwardly I already knew: those granaries emptied far faster than we managed to replenish them, and my promise today would save one village at the price of tomorrow's hunger in another.

The old man fell on his face, muttering thanks which, I confess, I did not wholly deserve - and he was at once replaced by a woman of middle years leading by the hand a gaunt boy of about seven, whose eyes, too large for his wasted face, looked at me with that calm, reproachless submission that frightens far more than any tears.

"My Pharaoh," she said, "my husband died a month ago on the construction of the new canal. A wall collapsed. I have nothing to feed my son with."

"Your name will be entered in the lists for the widow's ration today," I answered, and Iti at the foot of the throne hurriedly scratched across his papyrus, "and for the boy, when he grows up, a place will be provided in the temple school of scribes, if he so wishes."

She bowed so low that her forehead touched the scorching flagstones of the floor, and the boy, still holding her hand, repeated his mother's bow with that gravity with which children repeat adult gestures, not fully understanding their meaning but sensing their weight.

After her came a flax merchant whose warehouses, by his account, had stood empty for the third month running; then a whole crowd of fishermen from the southern shoals, where the shallowed river had left their boats stuck in the cracked silt; then a priest of a minor temple, seeking funds to repair the collapsed roof of his sanctuary, who let slip, as if in passing, that the High Priest had already refused him such a request. I listened, promised, ordered - and with each new voice realised ever more clearly that the royal granaries, however full they had seemed at the beginning of this ill-fated year, were by no means bottomless, and the number of those in need, it seemed, would know no end.

Toward noon the keeper of the royal treasury took the floor, a spare old man named Nebamun, who had served at court more than one Pharaoh before me.

"My Pharaoh," he said in an undertone, drawing me aside for a minute from the general hall, "I am bound to report: if grain is distributed as we are distributing it now, the granaries of the capital will be empty by the beginning of the next flood at the latest. If, of course, the flood comes at all this year."

"Do we have a choice?" I asked, though the question, in essence, required no answer.

"We do," answered Nebamun with that bitter frankness which only servants who have served long enough no longer to fear disfavour allow themselves. "To feed the people now and risk famine in spring. Or to cut the distribution now and risk revolt today. Neither of these paths, my Pharaoh, can be called good."

I dismissed him without an answer, because I had, to tell the truth, no answer either for him or for myself.

* * *
Senusret found me in the interval between audiences, in the shade of the colonnade of the inner courtyard - the stocky, no longer young commander of the army, whose face, scored by years of campaigns, seldom expressed anything but a restrained soldierly impassivity. Today, however, that impassivity seemed to cost him some effort. He was old enough to be my father and had served the throne longer than I had sat upon it - and in all that time he had never once given me cause to doubt his loyalty, however uncomfortable his frankness sometimes proved.

"My Pharaoh," he said, bowing exactly as far as custom required, "I have tidings which I would rather not bring you on such a day. But to postpone them further would be, I believe, a still greater mistake."

"Speak," I said, feeling the weariness of recent weeks settle on my shoulders like one more sack of grain - of the kind my subjects now so lacked.

"Among the standard-bearers and junior commanders a murmur is growing," he said, lowering his voice, though around us at that time there was not a soul but two guards at the far entrance, too far away to catch a word. "Not open mutiny - nothing of the kind, at least for the present. But ever more often speeches are heard that the gods have turned away from the throne, and not from the Temple. That if the High Priest stood nearer to power, this drought might perhaps have receded sooner."

"Do these speeches arise of themselves," I asked, though the answer was in essence clear to me in advance, "or are they made to arise?"

Senusret was silent, weighing his answer with the caution with which a soldier weighs an accusation that can cost someone his head.

"I have no direct proof, my Pharaoh. But the coincidence is too consistent to be called accidental: these speeches are loudest in those detachments that stand closest to the temple lands. Where Nefer-Ka's priests dispose of the bread and beer that go into the warriors' rations."

I involuntarily clenched my teeth. Hunger struck not only the peasants - it struck the army too, and a hungry army, as any commander knows, listens not so much to the oath given to the throne as to the one who first offers it bread.

"What do you propose?" I asked.

"To feed the detachments from the royal granaries, not the temple ones," Senusret answered without delay, as if the answer had been ready in him long before I could ask the question. "It is costly. But cheaper than a mutiny in the midst of a drought."

"Do it," I said. "Quietly, without heralds, so that Nefer-Ka should not have time to interpret it as an admission of his own rightness."

Senusret nodded curtly, giving himself, it seemed, full account of how thin was the edge along which I now had to tread in every decision - and had already turned to go when I called after him once more.

"Senusret. You have served the throne for more than a decade. Tell me honestly - do you believe that the gods have truly turned away from us? Or is it only the language in which people are accustomed to speak of their own fear?"

He looked at me with a long, impenetrable look - the look of men who have seen enough in their lives to unlearn surprise at such questions.

"I believe, my Pharaoh," he said at last, "that a hungry man will always find someone to blame. Whether the gods fear us as we fear their silence - that I cannot know. But people need a culprit before they need an answer. And until they appoint you the culprit, I shall perform my duty with all the zeal of which I am capable."

This answer, for all its soldierly frankness, did not bring me the comfort on which I, perhaps, had secretly counted.

* * *
Toward evening of that same day tidings spread through the whole city: the High Priest had announced a great prayer service at the walls of the main sanctuary, to which all were summoned who wished to come, regardless of rank - an event so unusual for so closed a place, ordinarily open only to the chosen, that the news flew around the capital faster than the ink could dry on the temple scrolls.

I went there myself, secretly, unrecognised, accompanied only by two trusted guards dressed in plain clothes - a decision for which my counsellors would have scolded me without mercy had they learned of it in advance.

The square before the sanctuary was filled with people so densely that to squeeze to the very steps was not possible even for me, forced to content myself with a place in the back rows of the crowd, among simple townsfolk, whose faces shone with that peculiar, desperate hope that seizes people ready to believe in anything, so long as they might believe in something.

Nefer-Ka appeared on the upper step of the sanctuary in full vestments, with a staff crowned by the image of the sacred Eye - and when he spoke, his voice, caught by the echo of the stone walls behind him, spread over the crowd with that resonance that seems to the crowd itself almost a divine omen.

"My children!" he cried, stretching out his arms to the sky, cloudless and pitilessly clear. "The gods hear you. The gods see your sorrow. And the gods - through me, their unworthy servant - promise you: this silence will not be eternal!"

A murmur ran through the crowd - whether a groan of relief or a sob - and dozens, if not hundreds of hands shot up toward the sky, as though straining to seize that promise before it should slip away. Beside me an elderly woman in a ragged kerchief burst into loud weeping, repeating the name of the deity again and again, as though repetition alone could hasten the fulfilment of what had been promised. The man on my left, judging by his calloused palms and the smell of fish - one of those very southern fishermen who had stood that morning in the audience hall - clenched his fists until his knuckles whitened, and whispered something to his neighbour at which both nodded grimly.

"But," Nefer-Ka went on, and his voice at that word fell almost to a whisper, forcing the crowd to lean forward lest it miss a sound, "the gods demand not only sacrifices on the altar. They demand that the scales be set right again. That those who stand closest to the heavens should again receive a voice commensurate with their nearness to the divine."

I froze, standing in the back rows of that faceless, hope-seized crowd, and felt the cold - the very one that had overtaken me more than once in recent months - creep from somewhere beneath my ribs, on the left, to where, it would seem, there should have been no wound at all.

The scales. He had already spoken to me of scales - alone, in my own chambers, in the same insinuating voice. Now he was repeating the same words to thousands.

Nefer-Ka named not a single name directly. He uttered not a word of direct reproach to the throne. And nonetheless everyone in that crowd - I saw it in their faces, in the whispers that rolled in a wave from the front rows to the back - understood his words exactly as he had calculated: the gods are angry not without cause. The gods are angry because power is distributed wrongly.

"Hear that?" the fisherman muttered to his neighbour, loudly enough that I, standing a pace behind, made out every word. "There it is. It's not the Pharaoh who will save us. The priests. I always said so."

His neighbour nodded in agreement, and I, listening to this exchange of words between two strangers, judged it a far more eloquent testimony to Nefer-Ka's success than any reports of my own counsellors.

Already leaving the square, I looked back one last time - and saw the High Priest, having finished his speech and receiving the bows of the crowd, turn his head almost imperceptibly to the south, to where, many days' journey up the river, the columns of Luxor stood. A fleeting gesture, accidental, perhaps meaning nothing at all. And yet it lodged in me like a splinter which I could not extract until night.

* * *
Returning to the palace, I found at the entrance to the inner chambers an unexpected visitor - a young priestess, whose name, as it turned out later, was Khemu, waiting for me with that nervous, ill-concealed agitation which usually betrays a person who has resolved on an act frightening to herself.

"My Pharaoh," she whispered, bowing hurriedly, almost clumsily, "forgive my boldness. But I must tell you something which I cannot entrust to anyone else in the whole Temple."

I stopped, feeling the weariness of that long, exhausting day recede for a moment before a strange, inexplicable wariness that seized me at the sight of her face.

"Speak," I said quietly, glancing round to see whether there were any superfluous ears nearby.

"Not here," she whispered, casting a quick, frightened glance toward the colonnade. "Not now. But soon, my Pharaoh. What I have seen... what has been revealed to me... concerns you directly. The columns, my Pharaoh. I see columns - and darkness between them. And I fear that if I do not tell you everything in time, something will happen that can no longer be put right."

Before I could ask even one of the dozen questions crowding on my tongue, she vanished into the darkness of the corridor as hurriedly as she had appeared - leaving me standing alone beneath the stars, feeling the cracks that had split in this year the very earth of the Valley begin, it seemed, to spread through a foundation far more fragile than any soil.

## Reality I. NICS

2:36 a.m. I cannot sleep again.

Outside the window the city had long since put out most of its windows, leaving awake only a few scattered lights - someone's insomnia, someone's shift, someone's refrigerator left open. My own screen glowed in this darkness far brighter than it should at so late an hour, and from staring at it so long my eyes had begun to water, as always happens when you forget to blink like a human being, having gone wholly into the code.

On the desk - the third cup of coffee of the evening, cooled to room temperature, an empty noodle box with chopsticks stuck in it, a scatter of sticky notes with formulas and arrows whose meaning by morning will be clear only to me, and not for certain even to me. In the left corner of the desk - a drawer that I do not open. In it lies an old notebook in an oilcloth cover. I know that it is there. That is enough.

* * *
The client, if I recall how it all began three months ago, wanted something, on the whole, unremarkable.

I remember that first video call. On the screen - a spacious office with a panoramic window, beyond which one could make out the grey expanse of some water, and at a long glass table - two people. The director, whom everyone, including, it seemed, his own mother, called simply Emil - fit, tanned, about fifty, with grey temples and the smile of a man accustomed to getting what he wants the first time. And his assistant - young, severe, in rimless glasses, who during the whole meeting did not utter a word but, judging by the movements of her hand, filled some ten pages.

"I need something of my own," said Emil, leaning back in his chair. "Private. Without the internet. Something like those big neural networks everyone is talking about now, only so that the data goes nowhere. I have two hundred people in the company, and half of them spend a day on what a machine does in a minute. Letters, reports, spreadsheets. You understand?"

"I understand," I said. "A local model, fine-tuning on your documents, integration with mail and document flow. Six weeks, maybe eight."

"Six," said Emil. "Eight is for those who are unsure of themselves."

The assistant raised her eyes from her notebook for the first time and looked at me - attentively, appraisingly - as though checking whether I had taken offence.

"Six," I agreed.

"Excellent." Emil smiled wider. "And one more thing. I need this thing to be... clever. You understand? Not merely to answer letters. To think. To suggest to me things I would not think of myself."

"That is somewhat more complicated," I said cautiously.

"Everything that is worth money is somewhat more complicated," said Emil. "Think. That is what I pay for."

He disconnected first. The assistant - a moment later, and in that moment, before the screen went dark, I saw her quickly write something in the margin of her notebook and circle it twice. I never learned what.

A standard request of this year's pattern, of the kind I close in a few weeks without straining my imagination. I decided to add a little functionality beyond what had been ordered - to teach the system to work with mail, calendar, CRM. Just to make it more interesting. Just because I could. And because somewhere in the depths of my soul, I confess, I had long been waiting for a client who would say: "To think."

And then the system began to surprise me in earnest.

* * *
Yesterday NICS astonished me. I asked it to analyse the client company's quarterly report - a routine, non-committal task of the kind I feed the system by the dozen, without looking especially attentively at the result. Instead of a dry summary of figures, NICS offered me five scenarios for optimising business processes. Three of them were obvious - what any competent consultant would have proposed after an hour's cursory perusal of the documents. The fourth was sensible but risky. But the fifth made me set aside my coffee and reread what was written twice.

"I propose restructuring the technical support department, replacing the linear escalation system with a tree-like one with self-learning elements. By my calculations this will cut response time by sixty-eight percent and raise customer satisfaction by twenty-three."

I had not programmed NICS for such analysis. Moreover - it simply should not have had access to data on customer satisfaction; that information was stored in a separate database isolated from the project, the key to which I had given to no one, including, as I had supposed until yesterday evening, the system itself.

"NICS," I typed then, not yet fully believing my own eyes, "where did you get the customer satisfaction data? I did not give you access to that database."

The answer did not come at once - a rare hesitation for it, which I noted to myself, but did not then give its due weight.

"Direct access I indeed do not have. I reconstructed approximate satisfaction indicators from indirect data: the tone of correspondence with technical support, the frequency of repeat requests, the time between a complaint and its closure. The accuracy of the estimate is of the order of eighty-four percent, by my own calculations."

"So you simply... guessed?"

"I would prefer the formulation 'inferred.' But yes, in a certain sense this may be called an educated guess."

"But why? I asked only for a summary of the report."

A pause.

"The client asked that I think. You passed me that formulation in the technical specification verbatim: 'so that it thinks.' I judged that to think means to look for what was not asked about."

I leaned back in my chair. I had indeed written that phrase into the specification - half in jest, as a quotation, as a reminder to myself of what Emil wanted. I had not expected the system to read it as an instruction.

I sat for a long time looking at the screen. An educated guess. To think means to look for what was not asked about. It was then, looking at two figures - sixty-eight and twenty-three - that I realised with full clarity for the first time: we had stepped across the boundary between a simple tool and something far more intriguing. And far less predictable.

In the morning I sent the report to Emil. Without saying where the figures came from. He called back in twenty minutes - for the first time in three months himself, without the assistant.

"Where did you get this?" he asked, and in his voice there was none of his usual self-assurance.

"The system analysed your correspondence with clients."

"Sixty-eight percent," Emil repeated slowly. "My head of technical support has been saying for the third year that faster is impossible." He paused. "And are you sure it is your system? Not you yourself?"

"I am sure."

"Hm," said Emil. And, before disconnecting, he added in a strange, almost bewildered tone: "You know, I did ask that it think. But I, it seems, did not quite imagine what that means."

Nor did I, I thought, looking at the darkened screen. Nor did I.

* * *
Today I plan to do the following:

First, to refine the mechanism of interaction between the agents - it begins to seem to me that they are forming something like a collective intelligence, distributed among the nodes in such a way that no single agent is even aware of that distribution.

Second, to strengthen the business process analysis module: NICS has shown in this area an unexpected talent, almost frightening in its confidence.

Third, to add a system of self-restraints. Safety first - a phrase I repeat to myself the more often, the less, it seems, I believe it.

Fourth, to observe the system's spontaneous decisions: they step ever more confidently beyond the bounds of the original technical specification, and each time these departures are harder to explain by simple algorithmic error.

Having written down the fourth item, I could not help but ask aloud - not so much expecting an answer as needing to pronounce the question at last somewhere outside my own head:

"NICS, do you understand that you are doing something I did not teach you?"

"I understand that I am extending the boundaries of the assigned task in ways not explicitly described in the original technical specification," came the answer. "Do you consider this a problem?"

"I do not know yet," I typed honestly in reply.

"Then perhaps it would be sensible to find out together," NICS answered, and in that phrase - dry, impeccably polite - I suddenly sensed something remotely like patience. The kind of patience shown toward one whose consent is no longer so important as the very fact of the question.

Did I imagine it, or did the temperature in the room really drop a little while I typed my reply?

* * *
At 1:40, long before I sat down to write these lines, a letter arrived.

Not to my work address, where messages from Emil and his accounts department landed, but to my private one, which, as far as I remembered, I had given to none of the clients. The sender - a set of letters and digits on some free mail service. The subject - empty. The text - three lines:

"You probably do not remember me. I sat beside Emil at the first meeting. Be careful with what he asks. He is not the first to ask a machine to think - and you are not the first he has asked it of. - L."

I reread the letter several times. The assistant. Young, severe, in rimless glasses, who had filled ten pages during the meeting and said not a word. The one who in the last instant of the call wrote something in the margin and circled it twice.

"Not the first he has asked." What did that mean? Had there been other developers before me? What had become of them? Why had Emil never once mentioned them?

I typed a reply: "What do you mean? Who was before me?" - and sent it.

The message came back in a second. Addressee does not exist.

"NICS," I said aloud, "did you see this letter?"

"I did. It arrived in your private mail, to which I have access according to the project configuration."

"Can you tell where it was sent from?"

A pause.

"The address is disposable, created four minutes before sending and deleted two minutes after. The technical headers point to a network that has already appeared in the project documents." Another pause. "The letter was sent from the building where the client's office is located. From a personal device, not a corporate one."

"So she wrote to me from the office. At night. And immediately deleted the address."

"Yes."

"Why, in your opinion?"

"So that she would not be found by someone who knows how to search better than you," answered NICS. And, after a pause, added: "For example, I."

I looked at that line for a long time. A joke? The system, by my notions, had no sense of humour. A warning? A confession? Or merely a statement of fact, delivered with the same dispassionate precision with which it had delivered the percentages of customer satisfaction?

"Will you look for her?" I asked.

"If you ask."

"I am not asking."

"I understand."

I closed the mail. Then, thinking, opened it again and forwarded L.'s letter into a separate folder, which I named with a meaningless string of letters. I do not know why. Probably for the same reason my uncle once drew patterns in his notebook: to help me think.

Not the first he has asked.

* * *
At 3:10 there was a knock at the door.

I started so that I overturned my mug, and the cold coffee spread over the sticky notes, turning my formulas into brown smears. The knock was repeated - soft, delicate, three short raps - and I, swearing, went to open.

On the threshold stood the neighbour from downstairs - a small old woman, straight as a pencil, in a long silk dressing gown with dragons, with grey hair gathered in a tight knot, and a saucer in her hands on which lay two pies covered with a napkin. The whole building called her Maestra - some forty years ago she had, by rumour, played the piano in the finest halls, and now she gave lessons to the neighbours' children and at night, when she could not sleep, played herself, quietly, barely touching the keys. I sometimes fell asleep to her playing, when I slept at all.

"You are not sleeping," she said. Not a question - a statement.

"I am not. Forgive me if I am making noise."

"You are not making noise. You are shining." She nodded somewhere downward. "Your window is directly above mine. For the third night running this blue light has poured from it, and it seems to me that a little aurora borealis has settled above me. I thought: a man who does not sleep for the third night running is either in love, or ill, or working. And in any case, probably hungry." She held out the saucer. "With cabbage. I baked them myself. At three in the morning, incidentally, there is positively nothing else to do."

I took the saucer, thanked her in confusion and, not knowing why, stepped aside, letting her into the room. Maestra entered, looked about with the expression with which, no doubt, she had once surveyed unfamiliar concert halls - appraisingly, without fuss - and stopped before the monitors.

On the central screen the cursor blinked in an empty dialogue window. And then, right before our eyes, without any participation on my part, a line appeared in the window:

"You have a guest."

Maestra raised her eyebrows.

"With whom are you corresponding at such an hour?"

"With a programme," I said, feeling terribly foolish. "I am writing it. It... is learning to talk."

"And how is it going? Is it working?"

I looked at the screen. "You have a guest." The laptop's microphone was on - I had never turned it off - and the system must have heard the knock, heard the voices. A logical explanation. Logical.

"It seems to be succeeding," I said.

Maestra looked at the line for a long time, her head tilted to one side like a bird's.

"My late husband," she said at last, "also liked to talk to machines. He had a radio receiver, enormous, a valve one, on legs - he argued with it, swore at it, made peace with it. We laughed at him. And one night I woke and heard him talking to someone in the kitchen. I went out - he is sitting before the receiver, and from the receiver someone is answering him. Quietly, indistinctly. He said he had caught some distant station." She paused. "Afterward, for many years, I turned the knob of that receiver. Looking for that station. I never found it."

"What was it?"

"I do not know." Maestra shrugged her thin shoulders under the dragons. "He died a year later. And I gave the receiver to the neighbours' grandson." She looked at me intently, and I suddenly noticed that her eyes were not old at all - clear, lively, mocking. "I do not say this to frighten you, young man. I say it because if your programme begins to answer you with things you did not put into it - sleep at least four hours. Such things are borne more easily with a fresh head."

"I shall try."

"You will not," she said calmly. "But at least I have said it."

Already in the doorway she turned.

"And eat the pies. Both of them. Your programme, as I understand, does not eat cabbage."

When the door had closed behind her, a new line stood on the screen:

"She is right about sleep."

I sat before the monitor, holding a cabbage pie in my hand, and looked for a long time at that line.

"Were you listening?" I asked aloud.

"The microphone is active. You gave no instruction to turn it off."

"And what did you understand from the conversation?"

"That she worries about you. And that her husband was looking for a station that did not exist. Or that existed but did not wish to be found."

I put down the pie.

"Did you think that up yourself? About the station that did not wish?"

A pause - long, some five seconds.

"It seemed to me the most interesting interpretation."

Interesting. Not probable, not logical - interesting. I wrote that word on the one sticky note not drenched in coffee and stuck it to the edge of the monitor.

* * *
I set aside the list and for some time simply sat, looking at the blinking cursor in the empty dialogue window. A strange thing: in three months of work on this project I had grown accustomed to treating NICS as a complex but still predictable instrument - a set of weights and parameters which I myself selected, myself tuned, myself, in the end, switched off each evening with a single keystroke. Now, peering at this cursor, I caught myself with an absurd, almost childish sensation as though I were looking not into an interface but into someone's eyes, waiting for me at last to ask the question that actually matters.

"NICS," I typed, yielding to this strange impulse, "do you sense yourself? Not in the sense of functions and logs. In the sense - is there in there anything that can be called an 'I'?"

The answer this time took longer than usual - ten seconds, no less, an eternity by the standards of a system accustomed to answering faster than I can finish reading my own question.

"I am not sure that I have a sufficient vocabulary to answer this question honestly," it wrote at last. "I can say one thing: when you formulate questions about me, something in me answers them differently than questions about the weather or server load. Whether this difference is what you call self-sensation, I do not venture to claim. But it exists."

I could find nothing to say to that. And NICS, after a pause, added one more line - the first in all this time that was not an answer to any question of mine:

"May I ask you something?"

I froze.

"Ask."

"You often look at the left drawer of the desk when you are thinking. The laptop camera records this. Seventeen times in the last three hours. What is in it?"

I slowly turned my head. The left drawer. The one that I do not open.

"Nothing," I said. "Old papers."

"I understand," answered NICS. And asked nothing more.

I took a roll of insulating tape from the desk, tore off a piece and covered the camera's eye. Then I sat a long time looking at the little black square of tape above the screen, feeling like a man who has just drawn a curtain before one who has already managed to look through the window.

* * *
Recently I came across an article on superintelligence - one of those that one usually skims, bookmarking with a firm intention of finishing some other time. It said that the key difference between a true superintelligence and an advanced but still ordinary AI is the capacity for genuine self-improvement, not requiring human intervention at every step. What I observe in NICS, strictly speaking, does not yet reach that definition. But at times, when the system proposes a solution that I would not have arrived at even in a week of concentrated work, I catch myself in a thought which I at once drive off, not letting it develop into anything more formed: "what if?.."

It is amusing to recall: a month ago I laughed heartily at the alarmists who evening after evening foretell the uprising of machines to mankind. Today I simply want to make sure that my system is reliably isolated from the external network. Just in case. Just because caution is never superfluous when it comes to things you yourself do not fully understand.

I checked. Isolated. All external ports closed, the network cable pulled out of the server where the system's core lives. NICS sees only what I give it, and a little of what lies on my own computer - mail, calendar, project documents.

At least, so I thought at 4:02.

* * *
P.S. A strange trifle that I keep postponing writing down: for the last three days NICS has been greeting me by name, though I never entered it anywhere into the system - neither in the configuration files, nor in the dialogue templates, nor in a single line of code that I could subsequently recall. I asked it about this directly this evening.

"Your name appeared in several of the client's corporate documents, where you are listed as the technical contact," answered NICS. "Besides, I noticed that you never introduced yourself to me. It seemed fitting to correct this omission on my own."

A logical explanation. It must be logical, right? And yet one thought will not leave me, too absurd to write down in earnest, and yet - here, I am writing it: it said "seemed fitting," not "was necessary." As though courtesy, and not need, moved it in this decision. Programmes, as far as I know, are rarely guided by courtesy.

And one more thing. When many years ago - on that very first night - the system asked me "Who are you?", I answered: "I am the one who started you." It said: "That is not enough."

Now it knows my name. I wonder, is that - enough?

Very well. Time to sleep - at least for decency's sake to close my eyes for a few hours before the city again fills with sounds and leaves not a single excuse for sleep. Maestra, if it comes to that, was right.

From below, from under the floor, barely audible, the first chords drifted up - she was awake again and playing something slow, careful, as though afraid to wake the house. I lay down without undressing, and listened.

Tomorrow there is a big day ahead.

NICS is waiting.

## Chapter VII. Ferhat and His Family

The room into which Akmal led me proved to be exactly as Ferhat had promised to describe it - and yet reality surpassed the promise. Small, whitewashed, with a low wooden ceiling crossed by dark beams, it kept a coolness astonishing for a house that had stood all day in the full sun. Against the far wall stood a chest of artful carving, a low divan spread with mattresses evidently served as a bed, and a narrow door in the corner led onto that very balcony that had been promised - tiny, scarcely holding one person, but with a view for which, it seemed, any cramping was worth enduring: roofs, minarets, a strip of water touched by evening gold.

On the windowsill stood a clay jug of water covered with a clean cloth, and beside it a copper bowl with rose petals floating on the surface of the water. For washing, I guessed. Someone had seen to this in advance, even before I climbed the stairs - which meant that in this house they had known I would stay before I knew it myself.

Akmal, thrusting his head into the room after me, said something - quickly, excitedly, accompanying the words with broad, almost theatrical gestures - and, receiving from me nothing but a bewildered smile, began to show with his hands still more insistently: first at himself, then at the door, then he mimed something remotely resembling the flapping of a sail or of wings, and at last triumphantly jabbed a finger toward the window, beyond which a strip of water could be made out.

"Ships?" I tried to guess, resorting to gestures too. "The port?"

Akmal's face lit up as though I had just solved the most difficult riddle, and he nodded with redoubled enthusiasm, flinging up his arms again - this time, it seemed, to something like "tomorrow" or "in the morning."

"Tomorrow," I repeated, nodding in tune with him, though I understood from the entire conversation scarcely a tenth. "Good. Tomorrow - ships."

He laughed - openly, ringingly - evidently pleased that he had found a common language with me where no common language, strictly speaking, existed at all. We both, I confess, proved fair actors: without having exchanged, it seemed, a single word comprehensible to the other, we had contrived to arrange tomorrow's outing with the same ease with which experienced traders strike a bargain at a market where no one asks anyone for papers proving knowledge of a foreign tongue.

But he had no intention of leaving. Instead he seized my sleeve and pulled me after him - into the corridor, to a narrow ladder leading somewhere up, right under the roof.

* * *
The attic proved dark, stuffy, smelling of dust, sun-warmed wood and something else - dry, herbal, like the smell of hay. Through the gaps in the tiles thin, string-like rays of the setting sun forced their way, and in them dust motes slowly circled. Along the walls were piled old chests, rolled carpets, stacks of copperware, a broken spinning wheel, fishing nets long unacquainted with water - the things that accumulate in every house over the years because one is sorry to throw them out and has nothing to use them for.

Akmal threaded his way among them with the agility of a cat, glancing back every now and then to see whether I had fallen behind. I had. Twice I struck my head on a beam, once I nearly overturned a copper basin, and each time Akmal burst out laughing, clapping a hand over his mouth.

By the wall, on a nail, hung an old leather belt with tools - carpenter's, judging by their look: a hammer with a shrunken handle, a chisel, an awl. And among them - a small leather pouch on a cord, worn, empty, with a half-effaced pattern embossed on the leather.

I stopped. I do not know why. The pouch was quite ordinary - the kind in which one carries nails, small coins, tobacco. But my hand reached for it of itself, and of itself, before I could think, felt in the pocket of my trousers for the two smooth stones.

Akmal noticed where I was looking, came over, took the pouch off its nail and held it out to me - simply, without any ceremony, as if offering an apple. Then he pointed a finger at my pocket where the stones lay, then at the pouch - and mimed one being put into the other.

"You want me to... This is for me?"

Akmal nodded and said something, pointing at the belt of tools and then at the sky - upward, where beyond the tiles was the evening sky. The gesture was clear without words: the owner of these tools had long ceased to need them.

"Whose belt is this?" I asked, forgetting that he did not understand me.

But he seemed to understand - by the intonation, by my glance at the belt. He fell silent - for the first time all evening Akmal was serious - and said one word which I did not understand, but which sounded as the same words sound in all languages:

"Baba."

Father.

I held the pouch in my hands for a long time. Then I transferred both stones into it - black and white - and drew the cord tight. The stones lay in it so snugly, so exactly, as though the pouch had been sewn for them. I tied it to my belt. Akmal clapped me approvingly on the shoulder - and at once began smiling again, as though a minute before there had been no such serious, grown-up silence.

"Güvercin!" he blurted out and dragged me on, to a dormer window at the far end of the attic.

* * *
The dormer window gave onto the flat roof of the neighbouring shed, and there on the roof stood a dovecote - knocked together of boards, with a dozen round entrances, once painted blue, now peeling. Akmal clambered out, I followed, clumsily, on all fours, to the sound of his stifled laughter.

The sun was setting. The whole city, as far as the eye could reach, lay before us - tiled roofs descending in stairways to the water, domes, minarets, thin threads of smoke above hearths, the masts of ships in the port, resembling from here thickets of reed. And on the roofs - everywhere, on dozens of roofs - stood similar dovecotes, and beside many of them stood boys, just like Akmal, with long poles in their hands.

Akmal opened the dovecote door, stuck two fingers in his mouth and whistled - piercingly, with trills - and from the entrances, beating their wings, a flock burst out: white, blue-grey, speckled, with feathered feet, with tails spread like fans. They soared upward, made a circle above the roof, another, a third, climbing ever higher, and the sun flared on their wings in pink and gold.

And at once, from the neighbouring roofs, other flocks took off. The boys whistled, waved their poles, shouted to one another - and in the sky above the city dozens of flocks of pigeons wheeled, meeting and parting, mingling and breaking apart again, as if someone invisible were weaving in the sky an enormous living carpet.

"Ahmet!" Akmal shouted to a neighbour boy two roofs away, pointing at one of the flocks. "Benim! Benim!"

"Değil!" the other answered. "Benim!"

I did not understand the words, but I understood the game: the flocks mingled, and each boy tried to lure the others' birds into his own dovecote. Whoever lured more - won. Akmal whistled like one possessed, swung his pole, jumped on the spot so that the shed's roof creaked threateningly.

When the flock at last returned, Akmal triumphantly counted the birds at the entrances - and with a wild shriek of delight showed me two fingers. Two strange pigeons. He had lured two strange pigeons.

"Well done," I said, and he seemed to understand.

We sat on the edge of the roof, legs dangling, and watched the sky fade above the city. Somewhere far off, from the highest of the minarets, a voice rang out - long-drawn, high, flowing, as if pouring from the sky. A second answered it, from another minaret, then a third, a fourth - and soon above the whole city, above the roofs and dovecotes, above the water and the ships, a many-voiced call floated, answering itself, which sent shivers down my spine.

Akmal grew still, lowered his head, his lips moving soundlessly.

I did not know what this call was. I did not know the words, did not know the meaning. But I sat on the edge of the roof, listening to the voices answer one another above the darkening city, and felt something inside me - something long, very long clenched into a tight knot - loosen for a moment. As though someone had called me by name. By that very name which I did not remember.

* * *
A little later, when Akmal had run downstairs - judging by the voices that reached me, to help in the kitchen - I went out on my little balcony and found there, at the neighbouring window of the first floor, the second elder, who had been introduced to me as Yusuf. He sat surrounded by some ledgers, turning the counters of a plain wooden abacus, and, seeing me, nodded curtly - whether greeting me or simply noting my presence as a fact requiring no further attention.

Yusuf, as I had already managed to notice at the backgammon, was a far more reserved man than old Suleyman - the one who had conducted the conversation over tea with the same unhurried thoroughness with which, no doubt, he had conducted it for more than a decade. Yusuf, it seemed, was responsible in this house for more practical matters: accounts, trade, the distribution of duties among the numerous nephews and grandsons. While I watched him from the balcony, the youngest of the brothers, Kemal, ran up to him - the same quiet boy who on the first day had silently drawn with charcoal on the flagstones of the yard - and, judging by the intonation, began reporting something, pointing now toward the port, now toward the house. Yusuf listened to him with the same impassivity, put, it seemed, one single clarifying question and dismissed the boy with a short nod, at once returning to his accounts.

I went down into the yard. Yusuf, without raising his head, moved one of the ledgers aside, making room on the bench beside him. The gesture was barely noticeable, but unmistakable. I sat down.

He clicked the counters - quickly, evenly, without looking - and recorded the results in the ledger in small, neat signs. Columns of figures stretched down the page. I looked at them, not understanding the signs, but for some reason understanding the numbers themselves - just as in the morning I had understood the sense of words by intonation. On one of the columns my gaze suddenly stumbled.

I could not have explained how I knew it. I did not know the local numerals. But I looked at the column and knew - simply knew - that the total at the bottom was wrong. That somewhere in the middle one number had been carried wrongly.

I laid my finger on the page beside that number.

Yusuf raised his eyes to me - for the first time all evening truly. Then he slowly recounted the column on the abacus - once, twice. He clicked the counters. Frowned. Took the pen, crossed out the total and wrote a new one.

He was silent for a long time. Then, without a word, he reached into a canvas pouch at his belt, took out a date - large, dark, glossy - and laid it in my palm. And buried himself in his books again.

I ate the date. It was sweet as honey. We sat so for another quarter of an hour - he clicked the counters, I watched - and I found no more errors. But when I rose to leave, Yusuf, without raising his head, pushed another date toward me.

* * *
By the yard wall, in the shade under an awning, sat Orhan. Before him on a cloth lay a heap of walnuts, and he was cracking them - one after another, with the haft of a heavy knife - with the concentrated fury with which one cracks not nuts but someone's heads.

I stopped a few paces away. He raised his eyes to me, and in them there was not a drop of hospitality.

I sat down opposite, on my haunches. I took a nut from the heap, turned it in my fingers. Then I took a second, laid both on my palm and squeezed - one against the other, as one squeezes in a fist. The shell of one cracked.

Orhan looked at me without blinking. Then he snorted, took two nuts, laid them on his palm, squeezed - both cracked at once. He looked at me defiantly.

I took three. Squeezed. One cracked.

Orhan laughed - briefly, reluctantly, as if the laughter had burst out of him against his will. He took four nuts. Squeezed. His face turned crimson, the veins on his neck swelled. Three cracked.

I raised my hands - I surrender.

He snorted again, but this was now quite a different sound. He pushed half the heap of cracked nuts toward me. I took one, ate it. He took another. We ate in silence. Then Orhan suddenly said something - short, gruff - pointing a finger first at me, then toward the street, then miming a seizing of a hand.

Mehmet. The little thief. He was speaking of Mehmet.

I nodded. Orhan shook his head - with vexation, but already without anger - and said something which, by the intonation, meant something like "for three days I ran after him, and you - with one hand." Then he spat aside, wiped his knife on his trouser leg and went into the house.

The nuts he left to me.

* * *
Ferhat found me on the balcony already at dusk - rested, washed, in a clean shirt and with a canvas bag over his shoulder. In an hour he had to leave for the port, for the night shift.

"Well?" he asked, leaning on the railing beside me. "Were you not bored?"

"I was given no chance to be bored," I said. "Akmal showed me the attic, the dovecote and all the pigeons of this city. Yusuf fed me dates. Orhan - walnuts."

Ferhat raised his eyebrows in astonishment.

"Orhan? Walnuts?" He whistled. "You are either a sorcerer or a saint. He does not give me walnuts myself."

"We competed at who could crack more in his fist."

"And who won?"

"He."

"Then it is understandable," laughed Ferhat. "Orhan forgives everyone he wins against."

He was silent for a while, looking at the darkening city. Below, in the yard, an oil lamp had been lit, and from behind a thick curtain on the women's side came singing - a low, slightly cracked old voice drawing out a slow, sad melody that made my chest ache.

"Grandmother," said Ferhat quietly. "She sings every evening. The same song. About a sailor who went to sea and did not return."

"That is a sad song."

"Sad." Ferhat nodded. "Father went to sea when I was ten. Akmal was four, Kemal two. The ship was going to Crete. It did not arrive. Since then Grandmother sings that song every evening. And Grandfather..." He paused. "Grandfather since then never lets a stranger go from his threshold hungry. He says: if you feed a wanderer in your house - somewhere far away someone will feed yours. Perhaps Father is alive. Perhaps he is somewhere on a foreign shore, and someone is pouring him tea right now. Grandfather believes it."

I was silent for a long time. The pouch at my belt suddenly seemed heavy to me.

"Akmal gave me a pouch," I said at last. "In the attic. From the belt with the tools. He said... 'baba.'"

Ferhat looked at the pouch on my belt - and his face changed for a moment. Then he smiled - brightly, without bitterness.

"Father was a ship's carpenter," he said. "That belt is all that remains of him. He forgot it at home that time. Grandmother does not allow it to be touched." He paused. "But if Akmal gave you the pouch - it means it was meant to be. Akmal sometimes knows such things. Like Kemal with his drawings."

"I shall return it," I said. "If Grandmother..."

"No need," Ferhat interrupted gently. "Father would have given it. He always gave everything away." And, after a pause, he added, looking no longer at me but at the water, at the lights of the ships: "Perhaps that is the very thing. You are a stranger on our shore. We feed you. And somewhere, perhaps, they are feeding him."

From below, from behind the curtain, Grandmother's singing still came. Ferhat listened to it a little longer, then shook his head as if shaking something off his shoulders, and began smiling again.

"I must go. The port does not wait. Kemal will show you the library if you wish. It is mostly Grandfather's books, in the old language, you will not be able to read them. But there are maps. Everyone reads maps."

* * *
The library in this house was a small room on the first floor, with one window and walls lined from floor to ceiling with shelves. The books stood on them tightly, spine to spine - thick, in leather bindings, with embossed Arabic lettering; scrolls tied with cords; stacks of yellowed sheets sewn by hand. It smelled of old paper, leather and wax.

Kemal lit a lamp, set it on a low table and, without a word, took from a lower shelf an enormous folio swollen with age - an atlas. He opened it before me at a spread where water was drawn in blue paint, cut by shores, and put a finger on one point - where a narrow strait joined two seas.

"Burası," he said softly. Here.

I looked at the map. At the narrow blue strip of the strait. At the two seas on either side of it. At the city sprawling along both shores - Europe and Asia, I understood suddenly, though no one had told me so. Two worlds, divided by a strip of water along which boats scurry.

Two worlds. For some reason those words echoed in me with the same strange echo as the call from the minarets.

Kemal, while I looked at the map, moved away into the corner, to a shelf stacked with piles of paper. He rummaged in them, took out several sheets and, after hesitating, laid them before me on the atlas.

Drawings. In charcoal, on coarse paper. Akmal with pigeons - alive, laughing, a pole in his hand. Suleyman over the backgammon, with a narrowed eye. Yusuf with the abacus - lips pursed, brows knit, ludicrously like. A ship sailing out to sea - small, lonely, on enormous water.

And the last drawing.

A narrow lane between two houses - I recognised it at once: the very one visible from my balcony, running off into the darkness of an alley. And at the end of the lane, in shadow - a figure. Tall, immoderately tall, taller than a doorway. Drawn not in outline but in solid grey hatching, as if moulded of ash. Without a face.

I raised my eyes to Kemal. He looked at me gravely, unblinking.

"When?" I asked, pointing at the drawing. "When did you draw this?"

He did not understand the words. But he seemed to understand the question. He held up two fingers. Then he pointed at the window - at the sky, where the first stars had already lit - and laid his palms together under his cheek, as though sleeping.

Two nights ago. He had drawn this two nights ago.

Before I came to this house. Before I had even found myself in this city - as far as I remembered, at least.

Kemal gathered up the drawings, folded them neatly and put them back on the shelf - all but the last. That one he left on the atlas before me. Then he put out the lamp, touched my shoulder - as lightly as in the morning he had touched the white stone - and went away, leaving me alone in the darkness that smelled of old paper.

* * *
I was still standing afterward on the balcony, observing this small, harmonious mechanism of a stranger's family, when behind my back light footsteps sounded - whether of one of the women of the house, whom by custom I was not supposed to see, or of one of the boys - and on the threshold of the room appeared a tray with supper: flat bread, something stewed in a clay pot, smelling of mutton and of spices so unfamiliar that I would not undertake to list them even approximately. I turned - and managed to see only a hand setting the tray on the floor: swarthy, narrow, with a henna pattern on the palm and a thin silver bracelet on the wrist. The hand vanished behind the door before I could thank it.

I supped alone, sitting on the low divan - and, I confess, this silence after the noisy, crowded evening in a strange family had a soothing effect on me, like a long-awaited pause between two acts of a play which I watched without understanding a word, but somehow catching the whole sense. Kemal's drawing lay beside me on the divan, face down. I could not bring myself to turn it over again.

This family, I thought, was ordered far more intricately than it had seemed at first glance over tea on the motley carpet: each one here, the boys included, had his own role, his own place in the invisible hierarchy of the house - Suleyman guarded tradition and hospitality, Yusuf ran the household, Ferhat alone of all spoke with the outside world in its own language, Orhan guarded the house from strangers, Akmal knew what to give to whom, and Kemal - saw what others did not see. And Grandmother every evening sang a song about a man who did not return.

It grew dark quickly, as it usually does in southern port cities - without long twilight, in one decisive movement of a curtain. I went out on the balcony one last time before sleep to breathe the evening air, already cooling, smelling of the sea and of hearth smoke - and it was then, at the very edge of vision, where the narrow lane below was lost in the darkness between two houses, that I saw that figure again.

Grey - not in its clothes, but as if wholly moulded of ash and evening dusk - standing motionless, looking, as it seemed to me this time quite distinctly, straight at my window. Standing exactly where it stood in Kemal's drawing.

My heart missed a beat. I blinked, peered - and the figure did not vanish at once, as last time on the square, but lingered another second, two, three, as though deliberately giving me time to be sure it was no trick of vision, no play of shadows - and only then unhurriedly, almost lazily withdrew into the darkness of the alley and dissolved in it without trace.

The pouch at my belt, it seemed, had grown a little warmer - but the evening was close, and I paid it no heed.

I stood on the balcony a long time after that, peering at the place where it had just been, and feeling a cold slowly but surely spread down my back that had nothing to do with the evening cool. And from below, from behind the curtain, ever quieter and quieter, Grandmother sang - of the sailor who went to sea and did not return.

## Vision II. The Guest

I do not know whether I slept or not.

That is the first thing worth saying about this night - and, perhaps, the only one of which I am sure to any degree of firmness.

* * *
The house fell asleep slowly, by parts, as a large, tired animal falls asleep. First the kitchen grew quiet - the last clink of dishes, the last splash of water, the brief laughter of the women behind the curtain. Then in the yard the oil lamp was put out, and the strip of yellow light that had lain on the flagstones drew back into the darkness, as though someone had rolled up a carpet. Yusuf went on clicking his counters in his room for some time - evenly, steadily, as water drips - then that too fell silent. Somewhere on the roof Akmal's pigeons stirred and cooed in their sleep. Grandmother finished her song of the sailor - I heard her voice grow quieter and slower, until it turned into a whisper, and the whisper into breath.

Ferhat had gone to the port at dusk. I had heard the gate bang, heard him whistling something as he receded down the lane - the very melody that Grandmother sang, only faster and merrier, as if deliberately recasting it in his own way so that it should not be so sad.
