Before I lay down, I heard heavy, shuffling steps on the stairs - and Suleyman appeared in the doorway. In one hand he held an oil lamp, in the other something small that glinted blue. He nodded to me, laid his palm on his chest - "do not get up" - and, rising on tiptoe, hung over the doorway, on a nail driven into the doorpost, a glass bead on a red thread. Blue, round, with a white ring and a black dot in the middle. An eye.

He tapped the bead with a finger, then his own eyelid, then pointed at me and shook his head - slowly, sternly, as one shakes one's head to drive off something unseen. Then he uttered one word which I did not understand - "nazar" - and, after a pause, added something long, under his breath, looking not at me but into the dark corner of the room behind my headboard. As though he were speaking not to me but to someone standing there.

I remembered the old woman at the fountain. Her splayed fingers. Three spits over the shoulder.

Suleyman finished his quiet speech, wished me, judging by the intonation, a good night and went away, carrying the lamp with him. The blue eye above the door glimmered for a long time in the darkness, catching the last reflections from the corridor - until they too went out.

I lay on the low divan, covered with a light woollen blanket smelling of something herbal and unfamiliar - mint, perhaps, or wormwood - and looked at the ceiling, at the dark beams crossing it like the ribs of an enormous fish. Beside me, on the edge of the divan, lay Kemal's drawing. Face down. I had still not ventured to turn it over again.

The leather pouch with the stones I had not untied from my belt. I do not know why. I simply lay down without undressing and laid my palm on it, as one lays a palm on the head of a sleeping dog - to feel that it is near.

Outside the window, on the balcony, a cat appeared noiselessly - ginger, mangy, with a torn ear, the same or another that in the morning had eaten from the hand of the girl with braids. It settled on the railing, wrapped its tail around its paws and fixed me with yellow, unblinking eyes. I looked at it. It looked at me. Then suddenly it flattened its ears, bristled the fur on its neck, hissed soundlessly - not at me, but at something behind my back, in the depth of the room - and in one leap vanished from the railing.

I turned. The room was empty.

The moon was rising above the roofs, and the strip of its light falling from the window onto the floor was creeping slowly, slowly toward me across the boards.

My eyelids were either closed or not - that boundary, usually so obvious, had that night worn thin almost to total disappearance.

* * *
The room around me was now present - I could make out the dark rectangle of the doorway, the strip of moonlight on the floor - now blurred, losing its outlines, as if someone with a generous hand had mixed it with a dream without asking my consent.

I felt him before I saw him.

Not a sound - there were no footsteps, no creak of floorboards, no rustle of cloth - but a change in the very air of the room, that particular heaviness which arises when in an enclosed space someone else suddenly appears, occupying far more room than an ordinary man could occupy. This heaviness settled on my chest before I could turn - not pain, not suffocation, but simply weight, enormous and imperturbable, like the weight of a mountain that does not care what happens at its foot.

I tried to turn my head. I could not.

I tried to raise a hand - at least a finger, at least an eyelid - and discovered with that peculiar, icy horror that comes only in a dream or at its very border that my body no longer belonged to me in the slightest. It lay obedient to some alien, unknown will, while my consciousness thrashed inside that motionless shell like a bird that has suddenly discovered that its cage has no door.

Only my palm - the one that lay on the pouch at my belt - still felt. Felt how the stones beneath the skin of the pouch grew warm. Then hot. Then so hot that had I been able to move, I would have snatched my hand away. But I could not. And that heat, strangely, did not burn but held me - like the one thread tying me to this room, to this divan, to this house, while everything else drifted away into the dark.

He stood to the side, a little behind, where I could not see him without turning my head - and yet I knew what he was like, with that inexplicable certainty with which one knows things not with the eyes but with something far more ancient and far less subject to reason. Tall. Immoderately, impossibly tall - so that had he straightened to his full height, the crown of his head, it seemed, would have passed the lintel of the low door without stooping. Grey, or perhaps black - the colour could not be determined, because it seemed to change depending on where the scanty moonlight fell, now absorbing it wholly, now reflecting it in dull, metallic ripples.

Exactly as Kemal had drawn him. Two nights ago. In charcoal, in solid grey hatching, without a face.

No menace came from him. That was, perhaps, the strangest thing in all that was happening: neither hatred, nor hunger, nor that special, recognisable sinister intent with which ordinary night terrors are filled. Only attention - intent, unblinking, scrutinising - turned on me as one scrutinises a rare specimen under a magnifying glass: wishing it no harm, but also not reckoning in the least with its own wishes in the matter.

I tried to cry out. The cry stuck somewhere in the depth of my throat, finding no outlet, as though someone with an invisible palm had clamped my mouth from within before the sound could be born.

Then he spoke.

* * *
His voice - if it was a voice at all in the usual sense of the word - did not so much sound as make itself felt: a low, resonant vibration which passed through me whole, from crown to heels, as though the surface of my body had for a brief moment become the resonating soundboard of some unthinkable instrument. The words - if they were words - were composed in a language unlike any I had happened to hear in that long, tangled day: neither the sing-song speech of Ferhat and his brothers, nor the drawn-out call from the minarets, nor even the language which, as it turned out, I myself spoke, not knowing from where. These sounds slid into one another without pauses, without stresses, like water pouring over stone - and in them, for all their complete, absolute incomprehensibility, one heard something like patient, almost condescending expectation. Thus one speaks to a child who has not yet learned the language of adults - not angry at his incomprehension, but not thinking it necessary to spare him.

And as he spoke, the walls of the room began to thin.

I do not know how else to describe it. The whitewashed wall opposite me, the one by which the carved chest stood, suddenly became transparent - not all at once, but in patches, as frost melts on glass under someone's breath. And through these patches I saw the same place. The same hillside, the same strip of water in the distance. But - different.

I saw night, and in it - bells. Enormous, resonant, bronze, swinging somewhere very near, beyond the wall, as if that wall had never been. And singing - male voices, low, harmonious, drawing out something slow and solemn in a language I did not know, but at which my throat tightened. Candles - hundreds, thousands of candles, flickering in darkness under a dome of such height that it seemed as if the sky had been taken from the sky and hung beneath a roof. People in dark garments, with beards, with bowed heads, with crosses in their hands.

Then the bells fell silent - all at once, as if cut with a knife - and in their place there was thunder. Dull, heavy, again and again, so that the earth shook and dust fell from the ceiling beams. Cannons, I understood. Enormous cannons pounding the walls. Cries. Smoke. Fire on the water - ships burning in the gulf, and the glow of the flames dancing on the surface like fish. And through the smoke - banners, red, with a white crescent, and drums - not bells, but drums, measured, triumphant, and trumpets, shrill as the cry of a bird of prey.

Then all fell still. And in the same place, on the same hillside, I saw morning. Peaceful, quiet. A boy with pigeons on a roof. An old man with a pipe on a stone wall. A boy with a tray of bread rings on his head. And above it all - the same dome as before, only now beside it stood towers thin as needles, and from them, answering each other, a call floated.

A city, I thought - or someone thought in me. One and the same city. Many names. Many lives. One land.

"This city has many names," Suleyman had told me over tea. "Perhaps it has itself decided by what name to present itself to you."

* * *
But the walls went on melting - and beyond them was no longer this city.

I saw a river. Broad, slow, turbid with silt, flowing between two strips of palms, behind which the desert began. A golden barque on the river. Columns - huge as the trees of a petrified forest, with capitals open like papyrus buds. And I knew those columns. I had already seen them - that very morning, in the street, before the old men with their backgammon, when for a moment, for just one moment, it had seemed to me that I stood between them, and someone beside me raised a hand.

Through the columns came a cry - a deep, hoarse, desperate cry of a warrior calling out someone's name. My name. I could not make it out. I knew that it was my name, but could not make out a single sound.

Then - a hall. High, vaulted, with heavy chandeliers ringing with crystal, with a fireplace in which logs crackled. A long table covered with a white cloth. A woman in a dark-lilac dress, with a string of pearls at her neck, turns her face to me - beautiful, stern, with eyes full of anxiety - and says something. I do not hear the words. I see only how her lips move. And beside her - a young man in a brand-new uniform, with a broad, insolent smile, who looks at me as though he knows me better than I know myself. He waves a hand to me. He calls me. I want to go to him - and cannot move.

I do not know these people. I had never seen them. But at the sight of that young man something quivered inside me - the same thing that had quivered in the morning at the fountain, at the thought of a face I had not had time to make out. Not he. Someone else. But - similar. As similar to one another as all those one misses.

And then - the last. The strangest of all.

A small room, dark, lit only by a cold blue light - not a candle, not a lamp, not the moon, but some even, dead glow emanating from a flat window, like a mirror, on a table. In this window, against a dark background, letters shone. Two lines. I did not know these letters. But I read them - read them as in the morning I had read the error in Yusuf's column, not understanding the signs, but understanding the meaning:

"Who am I?"

"Who are you?"

I do not know what this was. I do not know where this room is, or when, or whose. But I know that on that night, on the divan in Ferhat's house, bound hand and foot, I looked at those two lines - and felt that they were written to me. Or by me. Or - this was the most terrifying - that between these two possibilities there is no difference at all.

* * *
I did not understand a single syllable of his speech. And yet somewhere at the very bottom of consciousness, where neither fear nor the paralysis binding my body hand and foot could reach, there stirred a vague, disquieting feeling that I - if only I remembered how - might perfectly well understand this language.

And then - at the very end, in the last instant before the vibration broke off - from that fluid, incomprehensible stream of sounds one word suddenly stood out. One single word. In the language in which I thought. Clear, distinct, uttered so close as though someone had bent to my very ear:

"Remember."

The phrase broke off as suddenly as it had begun. The walls of the room became walls again - whitewashed, solid, with the carved chest by the far one. The weight on my chest eased - did not vanish at once, but precisely eased, as though someone were slowly, carefully lifting from me one layer of invisible load after another - and with each such layer a grain of power over my own body returned: first the fingers of my right hand, lying on the pouch, then the eyelids, then, at last, the neck, allowing me to turn my head to where he had just stood.

No one was there. Only a strip of moonlight on the floor, the same dark rectangle of the doorway - and my own laboured breathing, the single sound disturbing the silence of the room.

I sat up on the divan, feeling my chest with my palm, as though checking whether any imprint of that impossible weight remained on it. Nothing. No trace, no bruise, not the slightest proof that what had happened was anything more than an especially bad dream, born of the fatigue of a long day full of discoveries.

The pouch at my belt was hot. I felt its heat through cloth, through skin - even, calm, like the warmth of a hearth in a cooling house. I did not dare untie it. Not then.

* * *
Something stirred in the doorway.

I started so that the divan creaked. But it was not the grey figure. It was Kemal - small, barefoot, in a long nightshirt, with a clay lamp in his hand, its flame trembling and ducking in the draught. He stood on the threshold, not entering, and looked at me.

For a long time. In silence. With the same grave, unblinking look with which he had looked in the library when he laid his drawing before me.

Then he raised his free hand and pointed - not at me, but at the corner of the room, where by the wall, behind my headboard, the one I had not seen had just stood. He pointed - and raised his eyebrows questioningly.

I nodded.

Kemal was not surprised. Was not frightened. He simply sighed - quite un-childishly, heavily, as old men sigh - came into the room, set the lamp on the floor by the door, took the jug of water from the windowsill, poured it into a clay cup and held it out to me.

I drank. The water was cool, faintly sweetish - like the water from the fountain on the square, in the morning, a lifetime ago.

Kemal took the cup, set it back on the windowsill. Then he sat down on the floor by the door, leaning his back against the doorpost, drew his knees up to his chest, clasped them with his arms - and stayed so. Without a word. Not intending, apparently, to leave.

"Go to sleep," I said to him in a whisper, forgetting that he did not understand me. "I am all right. Go."

He understood - by the intonation, probably. He shook his head. He pointed a finger at himself, then at the threshold where he sat. Then - at the window, at the sky, where the moon was already sinking toward the roofs, and drew his palm through the air - slowly, from left to right, as the sun passes across the sky.

Until morning. He would sit here until morning.

I wanted to object - and did not. I lay back down on the divan, facing the door, and looked at the little figure on the threshold, lit by the trembling flame of the lamp. Kemal sat motionless, his chin on his knees, and looked not at me but at the corner behind my headboard. Guarding. As, no doubt, he would have guarded a younger brother against night terrors, had he had a younger brother.

I do not know how this twelve-year-old boy knew what to do. I do not know how many such nights he had himself lived through before he learned not to be afraid. I know only that that night, in a strange house, in a strange city, without a name and without memory, I felt for the first time that I was not alone.

When the sky outside the window began to turn grey, Kemal quietly rose, took his lamp, long since gone out, and, already at the threshold, stopped and raised his eyes to the doorpost, where Suleyman's blue bead hung on its red thread.

I followed his gaze.

The bead was cracked. Exactly in half - the crack ran precisely through the black pupil, through the white ring, from edge to edge - and one half hung on the thread, while the other lay on the floor at the threshold, glinting in the grey light of dawn.

Kemal bent down, picked up the fragment, looked at it for a long time on his palm. Then he put it in the pocket of his nightshirt - carefully, as one hides something precious - and as silently as he had come, vanished into the dark corridor. He did not look back once.

And yet, however many times I repeated to myself that simple, convenient explanation that all this had been merely a bad dream, I did not manage to sleep again - not for an instant, until the very dawn, which timidly and cautiously turned grey beyond the narrow window of my room.

Remember, he had said.

But what - and how?

## Chapter VIII. The Abandoned Castle

The darkness after the extinguished candle was so complete that for several moments I ceased to understand where my body ended and the corridor began. I stood with my back pressed against the grille, clutching in my hand a useless candlestick with a still-warm stub, and listened to my heart pounding - the only sound in the whole world.

"Konstantin," I said aloud. Quietly. Then louder: "Konstantin!"

The echo carried his name somewhere into the depth of the corridor, broke it into pieces, returned it to me in scraps - "...tin... tin..." - and died away. No one answered. The piano did not sound. The Castle behind my back was silent as houses are silent in which no one has lived for a long time.

I have ears like a regimental dog, he had said. I shall hear through the whole Castle.

He had not heard. Or - the thought came of itself, uninvited, and I hastily drove it off - here, on this side of the grille, was no longer the sort of place to which sound reaches from the parade hall.

And then warmth struck my face - before I could take even one step forward - a sudden, almost hot gust of air, so alien to the cold stone walls of our Castle that for a moment I doubted whether I was still beneath its roof. My aunt had always loved the coolness of these walls, was proud of it before guests as a special, family merit of the house - here, however, beyond the grille, the air was different: thick, warm, as if borrowed from a quite different climate, a different season, and perhaps a different latitude altogether.

And with the warmth came light - not at once, but gradually, as dawn comes: first I made out my own hand, then the edge of a wall, then the floor, stretching ahead in a long grey strip. The light came from somewhere far away, from the depth of the corridor, even and pale, unlike a candle or a lamp.

I froze on the threshold, listening to myself in search of some explanation - and, not finding one, moved forward, because to stand still in the ringing silence seemed to me a far more frightening occupation than to walk.

* * *
The corridor here proved narrower than before, and the dust that covered the floor in an even, undisturbed layer rose at every step in light, slow little clouds, then settled as unhurriedly, as though it too had nowhere to hurry in this forgotten corner of the house. The tapestries on the walls - the few that still held to their hooks - had rotted so that to recognise the subject once depicted on them was quite impossible: there remained only brown, faded patches where, no doubt, horsemen had once galloped or a stag been hunted. In one place the plaster had fallen away in large flakes, exposing beneath it masonry far more ancient than that of the parade halls familiar to me - stone dark, cracked, as though remembering not decades but centuries.

On the floor, in the dust, I noticed tracks. Not mine - mine stretched behind, deep, distinct. These were different: narrow, light, barely pressing the dust, as though someone weightless had passed along the corridor. The tracks came toward me - and broke off in the middle of the corridor, two paces from me, as though whoever had left them had stopped here, stood - and vanished. No tracks returning, none to the side.

"The White Lady," I recalled Mitka's whisper. "The one who lived here before our mistress."

I skirted the breaking-off tracks, trying not to step on them, and went on, feeling at the back of my head something like a draught, though the air around was motionless and warm.

I passed a niche in which, it seemed, a statue had once stood - the pedestal remained, but the figure itself had vanished without trace, leaving only two pale, inexplicably clean marks where its stone feet had once rested. For some reason it was precisely this detail - not the tapestries, not the dust, but precisely these two empty marks on the pedestal - that for the first time made me seriously doubt that I was still in the house I was accustomed to consider my own.

A little farther on, on the wall, hung a frame. Empty. The canvas had been cut out of it - neatly, evenly, with a sharp knife, along the very edge. Beneath the frame, on a copper plate, as in the gallery where the portrait under crape hung, the name had been scraped away.

I stopped. In the gallery. A portrait under crape, with little stones in his hand. Here - an empty frame. The same plate. The same knife.

I did not know what it meant. I did not want to know. I quickened my step.

* * *
At the end of this endlessly long corridor, the longest in the whole labyrinth that I had been through that evening, I made out a door of imposing size, ajar, with small square windows on either side of the leaf. In one of these windows burned that same faint, even light - not of a candle, not of a torch, but of something else, pale, lacking any tremor of living flame.

Coming closer, I discovered a small room, whose door likewise stood ajar. Inside, with his back to me, someone was arranging something on shelves - methodically, unhurriedly, shelf after shelf. I managed to make out rows of some flat volumes bound in dark leather, several vessels of cloudy glass, boxes with neat labels and something remotely resembling a plan or a map pinned to the far wall - a setting that seemed to me rather an archive or a laboratory than a dwelling. The man himself was clothed in garments of such strange, inexplicable cut that I would not have undertaken to assign them to any epoch or to any social estate known to me: whether uniform, or working smock, or something third whose name I did not know at all, sewn of cloth that glimmered dully and unfamiliarly in that even, incorporeal light. On his hands were thin white gloves, like a butler's - but what he held in them was not a tray but an old book, so carefully as though it might crumble from one careless breath.

I wanted to pass by. But a floorboard creaked under my foot.

The man turned.

He was no longer young - about fifty, with a neat greying beard, in spectacles with a thin metal frame of a kind I had never seen before - and he looked at me with the expression with which a host looks at a guest who has wandered into the wrong room: without alarm, but with slight annoyance.

"Are you from the group?" he asked.

I understood every word. He spoke my language - clearly, without any accent - but pronounced the words somehow differently: faster, more drily, swallowing the endings, as no one spoke among us. And the sense of his question eluded me completely.

"From what group?"

"Well, from the one in the garden." He waved a hand somewhere to the side. "Outsiders are not allowed in here, this is a depository. All your people are in the yard. The exit is there, up the stairs and to the right."

"A depository of what?" I asked.

He looked at me more attentively, over his spectacles. His glance slid over my frock coat, my trousers, lingered on the neckerchief - and in his eyes suddenly flared a lively, almost professional interest.

"Well, well," he said. "What a costume. Are you from the reenactment? They told us there would be people in costume, but I did not think so..." He came closer, squinting. "The cloth is real. And the cut. And the neckerchief is tied..." He broke off. "Who made it for you?"

"My aunt's tailor," I answered, and felt myself how absurd it sounded.

He laughed - briefly, good-naturedly - evidently taking my answer for a joke, for part of that very game in which, by his reckoning, I was a participant.

"Your aunt's. Of course." He shook his head. "Splendid work. Just like in our portraits. You know, in our gallery there is one..." He faltered, as though he had changed his mind about speaking. "Never mind, however. Go to your people, young man, before you are missed. And do not touch anything on the way, I beg you. Everything here holds on its word of honour."

He turned back to the shelves, but before turning away entirely he cast another quick glance at me over his shoulder - and in that glance, as it seemed to me, flickered something like what I had seen that evening at supper in the eyes of Vera Anatolievna: an attempt to recall a face that one cannot quite recognise.

I did not question him. I walked past the half-open door, passed the massive leaves at the end of the corridor and went out into the warm air, saturated with the fragrance of flowering plants.

* * *
Descending the few steps that separated this grandiose door from the ground, I saw a scene that took my breath away.

It was day. Not evening, not the night from which I had just come - a clear, sunny day, at the very height of summer, with a high pale-blue sky and heavy white clouds hanging motionless above the trees. I looked at my watch - and saw that its hands had stopped. Exactly at the minute when I had pushed the door of the grille.

A fairly large crowd of people - I would have counted some twenty, perhaps more - were doing something in the garden of our ancestral Castle. They were dressed in clothing no less strange than that of the man left in the depository behind me - but the strangeness was of another, more disquieting kind, because not one of my comparisons, hurriedly and vainly sorted through, would fit what I saw even approximately.

On some was a cut remotely resembling the military, but in colours such as I had not met in any army known to me - neither grey nor brown, devoid of any hint of parade or distinction. Others wore something like travelling dress, cut, however, in so alien a manner that I would have been at a loss to determine not only the country it came from but even the century in which such a cut could be considered fitting: now too short, now immoderately wide, lacking buttons where they should have been and furnished with fastenings where I had never in my life seen any. The women - I did not at once realise they were women - wore trousers, like men, with bare arms and uncovered heads, and no one around seemed to find anything strange in it.

Some held small, dark, glinting objects in their hands, which from time to time they raised to their eyes or to their ear - the purpose of these objects I decidedly did not understand, as I did not understand a good half of what was in general happening before me on that lawn. One of them held such an object up to the face of another - whether in jest or for some other reason unknown to me - and both afterward laughed with a short, abrupt laugh quite unlike the laughter to which my ear was accustomed.

In the middle of the lawn, on the very spot where my aunt every summer ordered the tent for tea to be pitched, stood an elderly lady in spectacles and some preposterous sun hat, with an umbrella raised above her head - not for shade but, apparently, as a banner which the crowd followed. She spoke loudly, in a sing-song, in that special voice with which people speak who repeat the same thing many times a day.

"...and here, ladies and gentlemen, the famous rose garden was laid out. They say the roses were brought here from the Balkans. The last mistress of the estate, a widow, was very fond of receiving guests - balls were given here, to which the whole province drove..."

I froze. Roses from the Balkans. A widow. Balls. She was speaking of my aunt - of our house, of our garden - speaking as one speaks of people long lying in the earth.

"...and then," the lady went on, lowering her voice for greater effect, and the crowd drew closer to her, "there happened that very story because of which the left wing was closed with a grille. They say that one night a man vanished in the house. Some tell it was a young master, others a servant, others that it was even a guest. He went into the left wing - and..."

At that moment someone in the crowd laughed loudly, someone shouted, calling the stragglers, somewhere some shrill trill rang out - from that same dark object in someone's hand - and the end of the phrase drowned in the general din. When the noise subsided, the lady was already leading her crowd on, toward the pond, telling something about crucian carp.

He went into the left wing - and.

I stood on the steps, and my knees trembled.

* * *
What is happening, I thought in the first, most bewildered instant. Can it be a masquerade - one of those mad balls that my aunt gave for the whole capital public?

But no: however wilful my aunt might be with her entertainments, she would certainly have mentioned such a spectacle to me beforehand, if only to laugh at my inevitable unwillingness to take part. Moreover, these guests behaved decidedly not as one should behave at a social function - they spoke too loudly, almost shouted, laughed without any occasion, ran about the lawn with a looseness I had never met at any reception in our house. One of them had even lain down right on the grass, his head thrown back toward the sky, as though it were the most natural occupation in the world for a guest of a respectable house.

Surely this is another prank of Konstantin's, the eternal jester, I decided, though even this thought, scarcely born, seemed to me unconvincing: the jest would have been too grand, he would have had to hire too many people for it, and Konstantin himself - the only man capable of explaining this madness to me in an intelligible tongue - was nowhere to be seen nearby.

"Mister!"

I started and lowered my eyes. Before me stood a girl of about seven - in a short, above-the-knee frock of bright yellow, with two sticking-out ponytails tied with something shiny, and in strange footwear of white, soft-looking material, with multicoloured laces. In her hand was that same dark, glinting object - flat, the size of a palm.

"Mister, are you real?"

"What?" was all I could manage.

"You look like from a picture," she said, studying me from head to foot. "May I remember you?"

Before I could understand what she meant, the girl turned her back to me, raised the plate before her at arm's length - and I suddenly saw on its dark surface, as in a tiny mirror, her own face, and behind it, over her shoulder, mine. My face. Bewildered, pale, in a dark frock coat and a red-and-blue neckerchief. Moving - repeating my every movement, like a reflection in water. Only reflections, as far as I knew, are never so bright.

Something clicked softly. The plate went dark.

"Thank you!" The girl turned round, beaming, and pressed the plate to her chest as one presses an expensive toy. "Now you will stay with me."

"Katya!" came a sharp woman's voice. "Katya, how many times must I say - do not pester people!"

A woman was hurrying toward us - young, in those same trousers, with a bag over her shoulder. She seized the girl by the hand and smiled at me apologetically.

"Forgive us, for God's sake. She pesters everyone." She ran her eyes over me and likewise lingered on the neckerchief. "What a costume you have... Are you one of the restorers? Or from those who are in historical clubs?"

"I..." I began, and understood that I did not know what to say next.

"Mum, he is real!" the girl broke in. "He does not even know what I have in my hand!"

"Katya!" The woman flushed, tugged her daughter's hand and dragged her away, throwing me over her shoulder: "Sorry again. Have a good day!"

"Now you will stay with me." I looked after them and thought that somewhere in this girl's hands, in a small dark plate, my face now remained - frightened, pale, in a neckerchief. And that I did not know in what year she would look at it.

* * *
I took a step in the direction of the nearest group - two men who were discussing something animatedly right by the flower bed, once, as I recalled, planted with my aunt's roses - intending after all to demand explanations directly, regardless of the whole absurdity of such an undertaking. But before I had come within ten paces, one of them turned his head in my direction - whether at the sound of my steps or for some other reason unknown to me - and his glance, which slid over me, seemed to me so empty, so devoid of any recognition of a living being, that I froze on the spot, unable to force myself to utter a word. He looked not at me - through me, as one looks through glass or through mist. He at once turned back to his interlocutor, as though he had not noticed me at all - but that single second proved enough for me to abandon any thought of seeking explanations from this noisy, alien crowd.

The girl had seen me. Her mother had seen me. The man in the depository - had seen. And this one - had not. As though some people in this garden were here truly, and others - only reflections, shadows, echoes of something long past. Or as though some saw me, and others could not. I did not know which of these was more terrible.

After standing so for a minute in utter stupefaction, feeling cold, clammy fear slowly rise from the very soles of my feet, I noticed in the far part of the garden a bright, orange figure moving unhurriedly in my direction - the only thing in all this unthinkable picture that seemed even remotely commensurate with my understanding of the world. Ignoring the bustle and hubbub around, I made my way toward it, as toward the one island of the recognisable in this sea of oddities suddenly flooding over me.

* * *
Drawing near, I discovered with amazement a monk - clad in bright burgundy robes, remotely recalling the General's tales of distant, hot Asia, of the monasteries of Siam, where he had travelled with the Imperial family. One of the monk's shoulders was bare, his head shaved clean, on his feet were plain sandals, and in his hand he held a rosary of dark wooden beads, which he told with his fingers, without looking, evenly and unhurriedly. His face, weathered but calm, seemed to me a surprisingly timely sight - the first in the last few minutes that did not arouse in me a desire at once to close my eyes tight and hope that all I had seen would prove merely the consequence of overstrain.

He did not belong to the crowd - that was visible at once. He walked by himself, to one side, looking neither at the lady with the umbrella nor at the people with the dark plates. And, unlike them, he looked straight at me. He was walking toward me. As though he had known I was here even before I came out of the doors.

Never before had I happened to meet monks, still less from such distant lands, so invisible to me, and so, obeying habit rather than sober calculation, I greeted him in French - supposing that on that language it would be easier for us to come to terms than on my own, which was native to me but hardly familiar to a visiting wanderer.

To my no small joy, the monk understood me.

"I greet you too," he answered calmly in good, slightly old-fashioned French, with a barely perceptible but unmistakably distinct friendliness in his gaze. "I was waiting for you. Although, I confess, I did not know on which day you would come."

"Waiting? For me?"

"For someone like you," he corrected gently. "For one who would come out of those doors. They are opened rarely."

An inexplicable, almost involuntary feeling of trust stirred in me at that same instant - trust which I did not that evening feel for a single other being around, myself included, perhaps.

"Forgive my bewilderment, Holy Father," I began, trying to make my voice sound steadier than my heart was pounding, "but I seem to have lost my way in the labyrinths of our Castle. I was returning in the evening from supper, chanced upon a part of the house unknown to me - and here I am on this lawn, among people whom I have never before seen and whose garments I decidedly do not understand. Tell me, what is happening here? Who are these people?"

The monk was silent, looking at me a little longer than a simple question required - and in that silence there was a special, calm sadness, such as, no doubt, doctors feel who have guessed the diagnosis before the patient himself.

"They come to look at the house," he said at last. "As one looks at old things, at graves, at what remains of other lives. They do not know who lived here. Legends are told to them. They photograph themselves and leave." He smiled slightly. "People love other people's past. Their own - less."

"But this is our house. My aunt, the guests, supper - all that was an hour ago..."

"Tell me," he interrupted gently. "Where you came from and where, in your understanding, you were going before you found yourself here."

I repeated my story - about the supper, the headache, the long, tangled corridors, the four people who had told me that evening not to go left, the portrait under crape and the black grille whose lock hung open, though the key to it had been lost forty years ago. The monk listened attentively, without interrupting, only his fingers still evenly told the beads of the rosary - and from time to time cast a quick, almost imperceptible glance toward the noisy crowd behind my back, as though checking my words against something known to him alone.

"My aunt, Artemia Aristarkhovna," I added, clutching at that name as one clutches at the banister of a rickety staircase, "remarked this evening at supper that in the Castle there are places better left in peace. I took it then for a hostess's ordinary jest. Now, however..."

"Now, however," the monk gently picked up, "you begin to suspect that she was not joking."

I nodded, unable to force out a word.

"Tell me one thing," said the monk, and his fingers on the rosary froze. "What year is it now? In your opinion."

"What do you mean, what year?" I even smiled at the absurdity of the question. "It is now..."

And fell silent.

I knew the answer. I ought to have known it. I had known it even at supper, when the General spoke of the Porte, when Kutasova spoke of Constantinople - the year was somewhere there, in every word, in every conversation, perfectly obvious, not requiring pronouncement. And now, when I was asked directly, in its place was that same even, smooth emptiness as in the place of Lizonka's patronymic. As though someone had pulled out that thread too.

"I... cannot remember," I said. And heard my voice tremble.

The monk nodded - slowly, without surprise, as though he had received precisely the answer he expected.

"It is nothing," he said quietly. "It happens here. Here years lie upon one another like leaves in a book. It is hard to say which page you are reading now."

As I spoke, his face - until then benevolent and open - slowly but inexorably changed: whether with anxiety, or pity, or that special expression with which one looks at a man not yet informed of the misfortune that has befallen him. He sighed - briefly, almost inaudibly - and for a short instant looked aside into the garden, as though gathering his courage or, perhaps, checking one last time whether there was not another, less cruel way to say what he was about to say.

It occurred to me in that second - absurdly, irrelevantly - of the old mirror in the niche, of the hand that had lagged behind me by a heartbeat, of the great-great-grandfather's gaze that had seemingly shifted after my movement, of the portrait under crape with two little stones in his hand, of the tracks in the dust breaking off in the middle of the corridor. All these trifles, each of which taken singly was no more than a play of shadows and a tired imagination, suddenly lined up in my head into a single, inexplicable line leading straight to this moment.

"Brother," he said at last, softly, almost tenderly, as though softening by that tone the very essence of what he was about to say, "this castle has been abandoned and empty for more than a hundred years."

The earth swayed beneath me before I could grasp even a word of that phrase. My head spun swiftly, ruthlessly; thoughts that a second ago were trying to arrange themselves into the semblance of a question scattered in a disorderly, dazzling whirl; my eyes darkened, as if someone with one movement had drawn a thick black curtain before me - and I fell, without even feeling the pain of striking the grass.

The last thing my memory retained of that night - or that day, I no longer knew - was the monk's concentrated but by no means frightened face, rushing swiftly toward me, and his outstretched hand, frozen halfway between us, like the last bridge connecting me with the world which, it seemed, I had just managed to lose irretrievably. And somewhere very far away, barely distinguishable, as though from behind a thick wall - a voice, calling out my name.

It seemed to me it was Konstantin's voice.

## Chapter IX. His Excellency, General Pavel Nikolaevich

The darkness beneath me was not dense - rather viscous, undulating, like water in a deep well, to the bottom of which I was slowly sinking, unable either to hasten or to slow the descent. From somewhere above, from that part of consciousness that still clung to the surface, scraps of sounds reached me - whether the voice of the monk, or the rustle of grass under someone's hurrying steps, or a distant, muffled cry calling out my name - but to make out anything coherent in them was impossible, as it is impossible to make out words spoken through a depth of water.

My thoughts, torn away from my own body, limply sprawled somewhere on the grass - in a garden which, if the monk was to be believed, no one had trimmed for more than a hundred years - drifted off in a direction wholly unconnected with the dreadful phrase I had just heard - as though reason, unable to bear its weight, had hastened to take shelter behind the first, safest thought it could find in its storerooms.

That thought, for a reason unknown even to me, turned out to be General Pavel Nikolaevich.

Perhaps because of all the people I knew he alone seemed to me a man who could not be lost. He was like the stone wall of an old house: however the wallpaper and the guests might change, the wall stayed in place. If the Castle has been empty for a hundred years - then where is the General? The thought was absurd, childish - and yet I seized on it as a drowning man seizes a plank.

I knew a great deal about him - far more, perhaps, than a mere family acquaintance ought to know - not because he himself was talkative about his own affairs (on the contrary, Pavel Nikolaevich was extremely sparing in speaking of himself), but because over the long years spent in my aunt's house scraps of his biography had accumulated in me of themselves - from table talk, from the Colonel's hints, from rare, chance-dropped phrases of my aunt herself, usually pronounced with that special, respectful intonation with which one honours only those whose past weighs far more than their present ranks.

* * *
He was an acting aide-de-camp general at the court of Alexander the Second - a rank granted not for mere length of service but for the particular trust with which the Sovereign honoured a bare few. He headed, besides, the Cabinet of Ministers of the Russian Empire, and in all questions concerning the policy of the Near and Far East his word weighed almost more than the word of certain ambassadors who had sat for years in distant missions.

About his part in the Russo-Turkish War of 'twenty-eight and 'twenty-nine they composed at court if not legends then something very close to them: then a young officer, he had managed to distinguish himself in such a way that his career afterward shot forward with a swiftness that falls to few. The Colonel, perhaps the only one who allowed himself to recall those years aloud in my presence, told how it was precisely then, under fire, that Pavel Nikolaevich first showed that special, icy calculation which later made him indispensable at negotiating tables far more peaceful but no less dangerous.

The experience of armed clashes on the distant frontiers of the Empire and in foreign lands made of him a man without whose opinion afterward no question of any importance touching relations with the Porte was decided.

The Ottoman Empire, as far as I remembered from table talk, was coming apart at the seams: torn by petty ethnic feuds, weakened by wars and uprisings for independence on its outskirts, it had long ceased to be the formidable neighbour it had been reputed a century earlier. And yet on the southern borders of our own Empire the Porte remained a rival serious enough that each of its internal crises echoed in our corridors of power as well.

Not long ago - by historical measure, of course, not by the measure of a single human life - the Egyptian viceroy, Pasha Muhammad Ali, had pursued his own policy, ever more independent of Istanbul, and, taking advantage of the Porte's weakness, undertaken a military campaign that came near to crowning itself with the capture of Constantinople itself. Only the timely help of the Russian Empire - and, by general admission, the personal participation of Pavel Nikolaevich in the negotiations - kept the Sultan on his throne at that critical hour. Since then, it was whispered, the Sultan had felt toward the General a gratitude rarely accorded any foreign subject, and Pavel Nikolaevich's influence extended not only at the court of Alexander the Second but in the Porte itself and, perhaps, at other royal courts of Europe and Asia.

He alone - and no one else of the entire suite - invariably accompanied the Imperial family on its journeys to the summer residence of the Kingdom of Siam; he alone was present at all the negotiations and trade agreements which the Sovereign so loved to conclude in his beloved Siamese palace.

* * *
But all this was information that any capital gossip could relate. I knew something else - what the General told himself, on rare evenings when guests were few, the fire burned hot, and my aunt, leaning back in her chair, asked: "Pavel Nikolaevich, do tell us something. Only not about the war."

He never refused her. Anyone else - he refused. Her - never.

One such story I remember so clearly it is as though I had heard it yesterday.

"About Sitka?" he asked that evening, setting his cup on the saucer. "As you wish, Artemia Aristarkhovna. Though it is not a cheerful story."

"Where is it, Sitka?" Konstantin at once put in, sitting on the carpet by the fireplace because all the armchairs were taken.

"At the edge of the world, Lieutenant. At that edge to which the sun goes to spend the night. An island in America, by the coldest sea. Novo-Arkhangelsk - the capital of Russian America. Was."

"Was?" Evdokia Gerasimovna repeated, raising her eyebrows above her fan.

"Was, madam. Until that October day when I stood on the hill above the harbour and watched them lower our flag."

He was silent. The fire crackled. My aunt looked at him without taking her eyes away.

"The Sovereign sold Alaska to the Americans," said the General evenly, as one reports an accomplished fact. "For a sum about which they argue in the capital to this day, whether it was cheap or dear. I was sent to be present at the handover. As a man who knows the East - though, God sees, I had seen nothing more eastern than Sitka in my life. The journey there took more than half a year. Across all Siberia, across the Sea of Okhotsk, where a storm battered us for three days, and then across the ocean, where the fogs are such that from the stern you cannot see the bow of your own ship."

"And what is it like, this Sitka?" my aunt asked softly.

The General looked into the fire, and his face, usually so impenetrable, suddenly became almost dreamy.

"Mountains, Artemia Aristarkhovna. Mountains covered with forest to the very summits, and above them - snow, even in summer. The water in the harbour is dark as ink, and in it stand islands - dozens of islands, green, shaggy, like the backs of sleeping bears. It rains almost every day - not hard, but fine, as if the sky were weeping but shy of it. On the hill - the governor's house, wooden, large, which we called Baranov's Castle. Below - a church with a green dome, warehouses, a shipyard, little houses. And everywhere - Indians."

"Indians!" Konstantin leaned forward, his eyes lit like a boy's. "With feathers? With tomahawks?"

"Without feathers, Lieutenant," the General smiled into his moustache. "Koloshi. They call themselves Tlingit. A proud, warlike, intelligent people. Their boats are hollowed from a single cedar, so long that thirty oarsmen sit in one. And in front of their houses they set up poles - enormous, taller than this ceiling - and on the poles they carve their ancestors. Raven, eagle, bear, whale. One above another, to the very top."

"And what did they say when the flag was lowered?"

The General did not answer for a long time.

"There was one old man," he said at last. "A chief. His name, as I remember, was Kashket - though perhaps I garble it. Grey-haired, in a cloak of mountain-goat wool, woven in a pattern that dazzled the eyes. He stood beside me on the hill while the American soldiers raised their flag and our sailors lowered ours. Our flag, incidentally, got tangled in the ropes at the very top of the mast and would not come down. A sailor had to climb after it. The ladies wept. And old Kashket turned to me and said through an interpreter - through the Creole Ivan Koshkin, son of a Russian trader and an Indian woman, who served at the office and knew all the languages on that coast:

"'You have sold what did not belong to you. The land was here before you. It will be here after them. People come and go from this hill as salmon come and go from the river. Only the salmon, at least, return.'"

The silence in the drawing room became so deep that one could hear the clock ticking on the mantelpiece.

"And what did you answer him, Pavel Nikolaevich?" my aunt asked almost in a whisper.

"Nothing, Artemia Aristarkhovna." The General took his cup, discovered that it was empty, and set it back. "What can one answer a man who is right? I took off my hat and bowed to him. He nodded to me. And went off down the hill, to his boats. I never saw him again."

"And the Creole? This Koshkin?" asked Konstantin.

The General suddenly smiled - for the first time in the whole tale.

"Koshkin saw me off all the way to the ship. And at parting he gave me this."

He reached into the inner pocket of his uniform and took out something small and dark - and laid it on his palm, holding it out to the firelight. It was a wooden figurine the size of a finger: a bird with an enormous curved beak, in which it held something round and shining - whether a pebble or the sun.

"Raven," said the General. "The Koloshi have a tale: the world was dark until Raven stole the sun from an old man who kept it in a box, and released it into the sky. Koshkin said: wear it, Your Excellency. Raven is a thief, but a thief who brings light. Perhaps it will come in handy."

He put the figurine back in his pocket - and I noticed how his fingers, before releasing it, lingered for a moment, as if checking that it was in place. Since then I had more than once seen the General, lost in thought at table, touch that very pocket. As though something far more important than a wooden bird lay there.

* * *
But Alaska was not the only region to which his service carried him.

Of the Asian lands he valued most of all Turkestan, with its ancient cities steeped in centuries of history - Tashkent, Bukhara, Khiva, Samarkand - where for centuries the trading and spiritual roads of almost all mankind had crossed.

"Have you been to Samarkand, Pavel Nikolaevich?" Vera Anatolievna once asked.

"I have, madam. Right after the city was taken by our troops." The General paused. "There is a square there which they call the Registan. A sandy place. Three enormous madrasas look at one another across the square, like three old men who have been quarrelling for four hundred years and cannot come to an agreement. Their portals are faced with tiles - blue, turquoise, azure - and when the setting sun falls on them it seems that the walls are made not of clay but of sky. On one portal tigers are painted, chasing deer, and above the tigers - a sun with a human face. I was told that it is against their faith to depict living things. And yet it was depicted. And it has stood for more than two hundred years."

"And what else is there?" asked Konstantin.

"The tomb of Tamerlane, Lieutenant. Beneath a dome like a melon. The stone on the grave is dark green, almost black, jade - the largest piece of jade I have seen in my life. The old watchman told me that a curse is written on the tomb: whoever opens the grave will unleash a war more terrible than Tamerlane himself." The General shrugged. "I asked whether anyone had opened it. He laughed and said: 'Not yet, sir. But you Russians have restless hands.'"

Colonel Mikhail Ivanovich burst into loud laughter, slapping his knee. The General did not laugh.

"I remembered that watchman," he said quietly. "For some reason it seems to me that he was right."

The General and the Colonel were bound by an old friendship, dating from the Turkestan days - that special, taciturn fondness of two men who have seen enough together to cease forever to need superfluous words between them. It was enough to see them exchange a brief, almost imperceptible glance over their glasses to understand: behind that glance stood something inaccessible to anyone else at the table - to me, or even to my aunt herself.

The Colonel, once only in my memory departing from his usual loquacity, told me - in an undertone, late one evening, when the other guests had already gone - how near Khiva their small detachment found itself cut off from the main forces at the end of a three-day waterless march, and how it was precisely Pavel Nikolaevich, then not yet a general at all, who took upon himself a decision for which another would have paid with his head, but which in the end saved if not all then the majority.

"What decision?" I asked then.

The Colonel looked long into his glass.

"He went to the Turkmen," he said at last. "Alone. Without weapons, without an interpreter. Straight into the camp of those who for three days had been driving us across the sands. We thought we should not see him again. And he returned at dawn - with a guide and with skins of water. How he came to terms with them, in what language, what he promised them - he did not say, neither then nor afterward. Neither to me nor in his report."

"Perhaps he knew their language?"

"Pavel?" The Colonel shook his head. "He then did not know a word of Turkmen. But here is what I shall tell you, boy. When he returned, he had a scroll inside his coat. Leather, old, with writing - with such squiggles, you know. I saw it out of the corner of my eye. He never showed it to anyone afterward." The Colonel finished his wine. "I asked him once. He said: 'It is payment for the water, Misha. Not my payment - theirs. They said that this thing had long awaited the man who would come for it. And that I was not that man. But I must pass it on.'"

"To whom?"

"He did not say." The Colonel rose, making it plain that the conversation was over. "And you do not ask him. He looked at me then in such a way that I never asked again."

The General himself, when I once let slip a mention of this conversation in his presence, only remarked coldly that the Colonel, as always, exaggerated, and at once changed the subject to something far less entertaining. But I saw that at that moment his hand of itself lay on that pocket of his uniform where the wooden raven lay.

* * *
Then there was China.

"Peking?" my aunt once laughed. "Pavel Nikolaevich, do not tell me you were in Peking too. I shall not believe you."

"You will not believe me - and rightly so, Artemia Aristarkhovna," the General answered imperturbably. "Into Peking itself I rode twice. But I lived there half a year. So you are right: to be in Peking is not at all the same as to live in it."

He told of Kyakhta - a little town on the very border, where in enormous merchants' courts caravans were exchanged: our furs, broadcloth and leathers for Chinese tea, silk and porcelain; where tea was such a chief commodity that it was used to pay in place of money, pressed into bricks hard as masonry. Of the endless road through Mongolia - through steppes where the sky is so huge that a man feels like an ant on a plate, and through the Gobi desert, where at night the sand sings. Of the Great Wall, running like a snake along the ridges of the mountains as far as the eye can see.

"And the city itself, Pavel Nikolaevich?"

"A city in a city in a city, madam. Like a matryoshka. Outside - walls. Behind them - other walls. Behind them - a third. And in the very middle - the Forbidden City, where the foot of no European has trod, save perhaps prisoners. The roofs there are yellow, golden, like ripe wheat - yellow can be worn only by the emperor. And on the ridges of the roofs sit little clay beasts - dragons, lions, phoenixes - lined up one behind another, as if guarding the roof from evil spirits."

"And did you see the emperor?"

"No, madam. No one sees the emperor." The General paused. "But I saw Mandarin Liu."

He recalled this mandarin with a particular, almost tender respect. A dignitary of the ministry of foreign relations, a small, wizened old man with long, polished nails enclosed in silver tips, and a round cap crowned with a ball of blue stone - the sign of high rank. With him the General had spent more than a hundred hours negotiating the border along the Amur - and had not lost a single argument to him, and had not won a single one.

"He never said 'no,'" the General related. "Not once in half a year. He said: 'That is a very interesting thought, it must be carefully considered.' And he considered. A month. Two. Three. Until your patience ran out, and his - never." The General smiled. "When I was leaving, he came to see me off at the gates. And gave me a fan. Paper, painted. On it was written a single poem, his own. I asked the interpreter - Hieromonk Nifont of our spiritual mission - to read what was there."

"And what was there?"

The General closed his eyes, recalling.

"'Two rivers flow from one mountain. One - to the east, the other - to the west. They will never meet. But in each is reflected the same moon.'"

My aunt was silent for a long time.

"Beautiful," she said at last. "But sad."

"Mandarin Liu told me that it is not sad," the General objected. "He said: 'You northern people think that if rivers do not meet, that is parting. But we think that if there is one moon in them, they have not parted.'"

Two rivers. One moon. I do not know why this fan, which I had never seen, came to my mind now, in the darkness, beneath a depth of black water where I was drowning. But it came - and for some reason comforted me.

* * *
And then he told of America - not of cold Sitka, but of another, hot, noisy, enormous one.

In 'sixty-three, when the North American States were in the throes of their terrible civil war - North against South - the Sovereign, to the amazement of all Europe, sent two squadrons to their shores: one to New York, the other to San Francisco. And Pavel Nikolaevich, on some secret commission of which he never told in detail, set out with the first.

"When our frigates entered the harbour," he told, "the Americans decided that we had come to save them. The whole city poured out onto the quays. They shouted 'hurrah' to us, threw flowers, orchestras played. We were driven through the streets in open carriages, balls were given in our honour - such that yours, Artemia Aristarkhovna, forgive me, are as far from them as the moon."

"Oh, come now," my aunt snorted.

"A thousand guests, madam. A ballroom the size of St Isaac's Square. Forty thousand candles. And the ladies - ladies in crinolines of such width that they went through doors sideways."

"And did we really come to save them?" asked Konstantin.

The General looked at him with an impenetrable face.

"We came, Lieutenant, because the English and the French were preparing to fight us over Poland. And a fleet locked in Kronstadt is useless. And a fleet standing in American harbours can strike English ships anywhere." He paused. "But to the Americans we did not say this. It pleased them to think that they were loved. And it pleased us that we were fed for nothing."

The Colonel roared with laughter again. The General permitted himself a barely noticeable smile.

"There was a captain of theirs," he continued, "Ebenezer Hall, from a steamer that ran from New York to the West Indies. Red-haired, huge, with a beard like Chernomor's, and a voice that made the windowpanes rattle. He made friends with our officers and once took me with him on a voyage - to Cuba and the islands. So I found myself in Havana."

* * *
"Havana," repeated Evdokia Gerasimovna, dreamily closing her eyes. "Is that where the cigars are?"

"There, madam. And sugar. And rum. And a heat that makes the air tremble, as above a samovar."

He described the white walls of the fortress above the entrance to the harbour and the lighthouse on its rock. Motley houses with wrought-iron balconies, painted pink, blue, yellow - like pastries in a confectioner's. Narrow streets where overhead, from house to house, washing hung - "just as in Constantinople, Artemia Aristarkhovna, only louder." Music that sounded from everywhere - from windows, from taverns, from squares - drums and guitars so fast that one's feet began to move of themselves. Women with high combs in their hair and fans. Black slaves on the sugar plantations - at this memory his face turned to stone, and he spoke of it little and dully.

"In Havana," he said, "I went into a tobacco factory. An enormous, bright hall where at long tables hundreds of people sat rolling cigars. And on a dais in the middle of the hall sat a man and read aloud to them. A book. Loudly, with expression, for the whole hall. I was explained that such was the custom: the work is long and dull, and the workers themselves pay the reader to read to them while they roll the leaves. Do you know what he was reading?"

"What?"

"The Count of Monte Cristo," said the General. "About a man whom everyone thought dead, and who returned under another name. Hundreds of people rolled cigars and listened, holding their breath. One old man beside me wept."

I remember that at that moment I raised my eyes to my aunt. And saw that she was looking not at the General but at me.

From Cuba Captain Hall took him to St Thomas - a little Danish island, where in the harbour stood ships under the flags of half the world, where in the market they spoke at once English, Danish, Spanish, French and some other sing-song dialect which no one understood but the locals - and from there, a month later, by steamer bound for Rio de Janeiro.

* * *
"Brazil," said the General once, when my aunt for the umpteenth time asked for "something not about war." "There, Artemia Aristarkhovna, there is nothing about war at all. There is only sun, mountains and sea."

He told of the bay of Rio - so enormous and beautiful that sailors, entering it for the first time, take off their caps as though entering a temple. Of a mountain like a sugarloaf, rising straight from the water. Of the forest which began immediately beyond the city - not even a forest, but a green wall, where creepers thick as an arm hung from trees tall as a belfry, where butterflies the size of a palm fluttered, blue as azure, and parrots - red, yellow, green - shrieked as if arguing about politics.

"And their emperor," added the General, "is the quietest of men. A scholar. Speaks a dozen languages, corresponds with the learned of all Europe, studies the stars. I was presented to him at a reception. He asked me about our Academy of Sciences - and listened as attentively as no minister in Petersburg has ever listened to me."

"And the Amazon?" Konstantin suddenly asked. "Did you see the Amazon?"

"I saw it, Lieutenant. The mouth." The General paused. "A river so wide that at the mouth the other bank cannot be seen. The water in it remains fresh for many miles out in the sea - one can scoop it up and drink, standing on deck in the middle of the ocean. A Portuguese pilot told me this. I did not believe it. I scooped up a bucketful. Tasted it. Fresh."

"It cannot be!"

"It can, Lieutenant. In this world almost anything can be." The General looked into the fire. "I have not seen anything impossible in my life. I have seen only what at first I did not believe."

It seems that it was then, that evening, that I first heard from him what he afterward repeated more than once, in different words, but with one and the same meaning:

"The world is bigger than it seems to you, young people. Much bigger. And much older. When you travel - and you will, I know - do not look at palaces. Look at faces. Sometimes in the farthest corner of the earth you will meet a face that seems familiar to you. Do not be frightened. It happens."

"Has it happened to you, Pavel Nikolaevich?" asked my aunt.

The General was silent for a long time.

"It has, Artemia Aristarkhovna," he said at last. And told nothing more that evening.

* * *
The General's family life, however, had turned out far sadder than his service life. He had lost his wife many years ago, on one of the Asian campaigns - she could not endure the climate there and died of an illness before which the doctors proved powerless. Since then Pavel Nikolaevich, it seemed, had abandoned all hope of his own family happiness, entirely absorbed in service to the state, and paid not the slightest attention to the young ladies who from time to time tried, with varying success, to secure as a husband so enviable, though no longer youthful, a match.

Scarcely an evening of my aunt's passed, it seemed, without one of her newly-minted friends making persistent attempts to become better acquainted with him. I myself more than once observed this simple comedy - no further back than today, with Lizonka Kutasova's pouch and the tea roses: the young lady would, as if by chance, find herself beside his armchair; the General would meet all her civilities with that impeccable, icy courtesy that disconcerts more surely than any direct rudeness - and within a quarter of an hour the luckless aspirant would retreat, carrying away with her wounded vanity and a firm intention henceforth not to waste effort in vain.

It was also whispered that the General himself, in spite of all his stern imperturbability, was not wholly indifferent to a certain person - but who exactly this mysterious lady was remained at court a secret which Pavel Nikolaevich kept with the same impenetrability with which, no doubt, he kept far more important state secrets. I, I confess, more than once caught myself thinking that the answer might lie far closer to home than idle capital gossip supposed - but I took care not to think this thought through to the end even alone with myself.

Once, however, I happened to become the involuntary witness of a scene which strengthened these suspicions of mine far more firmly than any gossip. It was at one of my aunt's evenings, near midnight, when most of the guests had already left; I, having lingered in the library over a book, chanced to see through a half-open door how Evdokia Gerasimovna, supposing, no doubt, that no one saw her, straightened in passing the disarranged collar of the General's uniform - with a gesture so natural, so devoid of any social, showy timidity, that it could belong only to a woman accustomed to doing it more than once. The General did not draw away. He only closed his eyes for a moment - briefly, almost unnoticeably - and at once put on again that impenetrable mask of courteous indifference with which he appeared before the rest of the world.

And then he said to her - so quietly that I barely heard:

"Dunya. If I go away again - you will wait, won't you?"

And she answered - also quietly, without a shadow of coquetry:

"I have been waiting for you since you were twenty, Pavel. What are another five years to me?"

I never discussed that subject again, with anyone, myself included.

* * *
He had no children - perhaps precisely for that reason he extended such boundless patronage to Lieutenant Alexei, in whom, as they whispered behind his back, he saw some reflection of a non-existent son. However much this frivolous, ever-enthusiastic young man sometimes vexed him, the General never once permitted himself a harsh word against him - except in those rare cases when the Lieutenant's flippancy touched Artemia Aristarkhovna, whom Pavel Nikolaevich respected and protected with an almost chivalrous scrupulousness. Once, I remember, I came upon him reprimanding Alexei - under his breath, at the very doors of the hall - for some innocuous, in essence, quip about my aunt's age; the General's face at that moment was so impenetrably severe that the poor Lieutenant did not lift his eyes to my aunt for the rest of the evening after that conversation.

"Why do you defend her so, Pavel Nikolaevich?" I asked him once, having screwed up my courage.

The General gave me a long, strange look.

"Because she once defended something that was very dear to me," he said. "And paid for it more than you can imagine."

"What exactly?"

"Someday," said the General, "she will tell you herself. Or will not tell. That is her right." And, after a pause, he added so quietly that I was not sure I heard rightly: "You are like him, you know. Sometimes - very."

"Like whom?"

But he had already turned away, and that evening I never ventured to ask again.

* * *
On his ancestral estate, which the General visited seldom, a truly luxurious garden had been laid out - with a snow-white arbour in the very centre of a living labyrinth of bushes and flowering plants. This arbour was entwined by a rose bush of astonishing beauty, brought from the Bulgarian Tsardom and presented to Pavel Nikolaevich in memory of his visit to that country; it was said that in spring the scent of this bush spread almost through the whole garden, drowning all other flowers at once. Roses in general were the General's true passion - it was hard to imagine, looking at his stern, at times almost coarse face, that behind this exterior hid so ardent a lover of flowers. On one of his numerous visits to the Balkan peninsula he had collected a whole collection of roses - white, pink, of the tea-tree shade and, of course, scarlet, dearest to his heart - and, by rumour, personally supervised their transplanting whenever some gardener dared to show initiative of his own without his approval.

To tend this garden the General had hired several men directly in the Balkans, reasoning rightly that no one understands roses as they are understood where roses bloom almost all year round. Stefan, his favourite gardener, was from Veliko Tarnovo - a glorious Bulgarian city, then part of the Ottoman Porte - and in the several years spent on the General's estate he had managed to turn the already blooming garden into a truly stunning park which, by general opinion, had no equal in the whole Russian Empire. Silent, taciturn, he appeared at the common table very rarely, preferring the company of his roses to the company of people - and the General, it seemed, valued in him precisely this reserve no less than his gardening talent.

Once, walking with Konstantin in the General's garden, I came upon Stefan at work: he was tying a scarlet rose to a trellis and quietly singing something in his own language. Seeing me, he fell silent, straightened - and looked at me so long that Konstantin had to cough. Then Stefan said - slowly, with a strong accent, as though with difficulty choosing foreign words:

"Roses remember. People forget - roses remember. Who planted, who watered, who picked. They remember everything." And turned back to the trellis.

"What was that?" asked Konstantin when we had walked away.

"I do not know," I said. And it was true.

Of all the corners of the world where Pavel Nikolaevich had happened to be, the Balkan peninsula remained, perhaps, his favourite place on earth: the warm waters of the Adriatic, the hot springs and healing muds of the Bulgarian Tsardom, the strong red wine from the western shore of the Black Sea, the winding streets of Constantinople, the strongest black tea which only the Turks knew how to brew, and, of course, the Greek principality - with its transparent waters and remarkably hospitable people.

But the true attachment of the General's heart was stolen, if one believed his own scanty admissions, by the Kingdom of Siam: its people, kindest and radiant, its marvellous nature, its ever-warm weather, in spite of the rainy season so characteristic of those latitudes.

From his Asian wanderings he had brought many curious trinkets, but he prized most of all a statue of the seated Buddha - white, visually almost weightless stone, so wonderfully harmonising with his garden of fragrant roses. By one version circulating among the servants, this statue had been presented to him personally by one of the Siamese monks in gratitude for some service about which the General never spoke to anyone; by another - he had bought it himself, at one of the distant markets, paying a price which he afterward preferred not to recall. Which of these versions was true I would not undertake to affirm - but the very existence of several mutually contradictory legends spoke better than any words of how dense a veil the General drew around absolutely everything touching his personal attachments.

Monks. Siamese monks in burgundy robes. The thought surfaced from the depths - and I suddenly remembered the face bent over me only a few moments ago, there, in the sunlit garden. Burgundy robes. A bare shoulder. A calm voice. Was he not from there? Not from those monasteries to which the General travelled with the Imperial family?

Pavel Nikolaevich did not consider himself a religious man, but he invariably respected the religious convictions of others, and of all the teachings known to him it was precisely the ideas of Buddhism that seemed to him closest to his own cast of mind. In his travels through Far Asia he had managed to visit, it seemed, a good half of the monasteries of the Kingdom of Siam and the Malay Sultanate; during visits to Siam itself he was invariably received in the royal palace, where the most ancient relics were kept, inaccessible to the ordinary mortal - but for Pavel Nikolaevich, to all appearances, there existed in all Asia no doors that would not open before him at the first necessity.

Sitka. Samarkand. Peking. New York. Havana. Rio. Bangkok. This man had seen more of the world than anyone I knew. And yet, remembering him now, in the darkness, I for some reason thought not of palaces and not of harbours, but of his hand laid on the pocket of his uniform. Of the wooden raven that stole the sun. Of the leather scroll with squiggles that the Turkmen gave him - "not to the right man, but that he pass it on." And of the words spoken under his breath by the fireplace: "Sometimes in the farthest corner of the earth you will meet a face that seems familiar to you. Do not be frightened. It happens."

* * *
...Somewhere at the very border of this strange, half-connected stream of thoughts I again felt the darkness surge beneath me, like the surface of that same deep well - and felt hands, insistent and careful at once, take me under the shoulders, drawing me back toward that unsteady, not yet quite distinguishable boundary separating oblivion from waking.

There were now several voices around - but whose exactly I never managed to make out, however I tried to catch with my consciousness even one of them. It smelled for some reason not of grass nor of a summer garden, but of candle wax, dust and old wood. One voice - if it was a voice at all and not the play of a tormented mind - seemed to me for a moment familiar, far more familiar than the meagre crumbs of memory still at my disposal allowed me to hope.

"I told you - shout," said this voice, quite close, angry and frightened at once. "I told you..."

A second voice, low, dry, accustomed to command, answered him something brief - and it seemed to me that somewhere right by my face, by someone's uniform, the button of a pocket creaked, that very pocket where the wooden raven lay.

But before I could hold on to this thought, the darkness closed over me again, this time finally, leaving not a single support to which I might cling.

## Chapter X. The Council of Commanders

Even before the sun had risen above the eastern hills, I went out into the inner courtyard - alone, without a retinue, as I went out more and more often in the last days, when sleep refused to come and my bed began to seem a cage.

The courtyard was empty. Almost. At its far end, by the colonnade, where in the shade lay the rolled-up mats of the guard, two men were practising with spears.

More precisely, one was practising - the boy Paney, the very one who had survived the burned Little Nekhen. His arm, still bandaged at the elbow with clean linen, held a short training spear without a point - simply a smooth stick of acacia - and opposite him, crouching, stood Bata, the young guardsman who had accompanied me unrecognised to the prayer service. Bata made a thrust - slowly, deliberately slowly - and Paney parried it, biting his lip, with such a concentrated, furious face as though before him were not a cheerful fellow with dimples in his cheeks but that very southerner who had set fire to his home.

"Not like that," said Bata, stopping. "You look at the spear. Do not look at the spear. Look here." He tapped himself on the chest with a finger. "The spear lies. The shoulder does not lie. Where the shoulder goes - there the blow goes."

"And if he is left-handed?" Paney asked hoarsely.

"Then look at the other shoulder," Bata laughed. "Come, again."

They did not see me. I stood in the shade of a column and watched the boy parry slow, ungrudging blows time after time, and how with each time his movements became a little surer, a little more exact - and his face, at first stone, thawed little by little, until, on the seventh or eighth thrust, Paney suddenly parried Bata's spear so deftly that it flew out of the guardsman's hand and rolled clattering across the flagstones.

Bata stared at his empty palm. Paney stared at Bata. And then the boy - for the first time since the day I had seen him in the throne room - laughed. Briefly, uncertainly, as though he had unlearned it in these days and was now recalling how it is done.

"Did you see?" said Bata, picking up the spear and not in the least offended. "Senusret himself will come to learn from you in a year."

"He will not come," objected a low voice behind me, and I started. Inu, the senior guardsman, stood two paces behind my back - so quietly that I had not heard him come. "Senusret learns from no one. But he will come to watch."

He bowed to me - briefly, in the soldier's way - and, after a pause, added in an undertone:

"The boy comes here every morning, my Pharaoh. Before dawn. Bata volunteered himself to teach him. Says he had a younger brother just like him. Died in the last famine."
