I looked at them for a long time - at the young guardsman and at the boy with the bandaged arm - and it occurred to me that of everything I had done in these weeks, of all the decrees, distributions and counsels, perhaps precisely this - a boy laughing in a courtyard at dawn - was the one thing that had truly succeeded.

The council assembled at dawn, in the Small Hall, the very one where my predecessors - if one believed the Most Ancient Epic and the few scrolls that survived in the Library - had for centuries decided the fates of campaigns, made peace with neighbours and declared wars about which songs were afterward composed. The walls of the hall were painted with scenes of ancient victories: a Pharaoh in a chariot trampling vanquished enemies; files of prisoners with hands bound behind their backs; barques laden with tribute from distant borders. The colours had faded with time, but in the slanting rays of the morning sun that pierced the narrow windows beneath the ceiling these figures seemed almost alive - and almost mocking, as if asking me whether I would manage to add to them even one page worthy of the wall.

The commanders entered one after another, and each bowed before me as men bow who have long been accustomed to the gesture and have long ceased to put into it anything but form.

First was Djehuty - commander of the southern outposts, tall, dry, as if carved of the same dark wood that went into the shafts of his spearmen. It was said of him that he had never once retreated a step before the enemy and never once forgiven a subordinate for retreating. A scar across the whole of his left cheek, received, by rumour, in a skirmish with brigands at the cataracts, gave his face the expression of an eternal, frozen sneer.

After him came Paser - the oldest of all, grey, heavy, leaning on a staff less from necessity than from habit. He had once commanded the chariot army of my predecessor, and by rumour still remembered by name every horse that had fallen under him in battle. Nowadays he advised more than he commanded - but his counsels were valued even by those who did not like to hear them.

Third was Khaemuas - young, dapper, in bracelets that jingled at every movement, a scion of a noble family of the Delta, who had received his rank, as they whispered at court, rather thanks to his father's connections than his own merits. He smiled too readily and too often - with the smile that serves equally for flattery and for betrayal.

Senusret entered last and took the place at my right hand - not because custom demanded it, but because I myself had indicated that place to him, and all present noticed it.

Besides the commanders, at my word there had assembled in the hall those without whom no decision about the army would be worth the papyrus on which it is recorded.

The Vizier Ptahhotep - stooped, careworn, with the eternal basket of scrolls at his feet, from which the edges of reports stuck out like feathers from a pillow. The keeper of the treasury Nebamun - spare, motionless, with a counting tablet on his knees, like a heron watching for fish. By the wall, on a low bench, perched the old scribe of the council Ani - deaf in one ear, for which reason he sat with his head constantly cocked to one side and kept asking in a loud whisper: "Repeat for the record?" - to the quiet fury of all present except me.

Merira, commander of the river barques, lumbered into the hall as onto a deck in a storm - broad, squat, tanned to blackness, with arms covered from wrist to shoulder with blue tattoos: fish, lotuses, eyes, crocodiles - a chronicle of all the rivers on which he had sailed. His voice was such as if he had spent his whole life shouting down the wind - and, apparently, so it was.

"My Pharaoh!" he thundered, bowing. "Forgive me for smelling of silt. My barques stand in the Nile up to their bellies, like ducks on ice, and for the third day I have myself been pushing them with the oarsmen."

And last - soundlessly, so that I noticed him only when he was already standing at the door - entered Panehsy, commander of the Medjay, the desert guard. Tall, thin, with skin the colour of dark wood and with ritual scars on his cheekbones - three thin stripes on each side, the mark of his southern people, who had long served the Pharaohs as guides and guardians of the desert roads. He wore neither bracelets nor necklaces - only a leather baldric with throwing sticks and at his belt a knife in a gazelle-skin sheath. He bowed silently, touching his palm to his brow, and stood by the wall, arms folded. In all the time I had known him I did not remember Panehsy ever speaking first.

And then, when the servants were already about to shut the doors, one more man entered the hall, whom I had not summoned.

"Peace be upon you, my Pharaoh," he said, bowing lower than all the commanders put together - with that emphasised, almost mocking courtesy which in itself sounded like a challenge. "The High Priest, grieving that urgent temple affairs do not allow him to be present in person, begs that you accept me as his voice at this council."

Bakenren. The second man of the Temple after Nefer-Ka himself - small, rotund, with a smoothly shaven head gleaming in the morning light, and with eyes in which one could never read anything but impeccably calibrated respect.

"The council of commanders has no need of the voice of the Temple," said Senusret before I could answer, and steel rang in his voice.

"The council of commanders," Bakenren objected gently, "decides how to feed the army in an hour of famine. And the grain on which the army feeds, as the esteemed Senusret knows, lies half in the temple granaries. Is it not wise to hear him who has the bread?"

I raised a hand, stopping Senusret, who was already drawing breath to answer.

"Let him stay," I said. "But let him remember that he sits here by my grace and not by right."

Bakenren bowed still lower, so that his smooth head almost touched his knees - and took his place by the far wall, under a faded painting depicting a file of bound prisoners. I could not help thinking that he had chosen that place by no means by chance.

* * *
"Let us begin with the chief matter," I said when all were seated. "Senusret has reported to me a murmur in the detachments. I wish to hear from each of you - how deep it is and what causes it."

Djehuty spoke first, not waiting for anyone else to take the word.

"The murmur is caused by the warriors sitting without work and without bread, my Pharaoh," he said sharply, with that frankness that bordered on insolence. "And a warrior without work and without bread begins to think. And a thinking warrior is the worst warrior in the world."

A short laugh ran through the hall; however, only Khaemuas laughed.

"And what do you propose?" I asked.

"To give them work," answered Djehuty, leaning forward, and the scar on his cheek seemed to tighten, making the sneer still more distinct. "The southern country has for the third year troubled our outposts. They burn villages, drive off cattle, and then flee beyond the cataracts, where we cannot reach them. But they have what we have not: their lands are not scorched by drought as ours are. They have grain. They have cattle. A campaign south will feed the army better than all the temple granaries put together - and at the same time teach our neighbours to respect our borders."

"War," said Paser slowly, leaning with both hands on his staff, "in an hour of drought is like putting out a fire with oil. I have seen such campaigns, Djehuty. I have seen how a hungry army goes beyond the cataracts - and how it returns from there half the size, without booty, with sand instead of bread in its sacks. The southerners will not wait for us at their granaries. They will drive their cattle into the hills and burn their fields themselves before we reach them."

"You are old, Paser," Djehuty threw out, without turning. "The old always see only defeats."

"I am old," agreed Paser, not in the least offended, "because in my time I have seen enough defeats to learn to avoid them. You are young because so far you have been lucky."

"Enough," I said before Djehuty could answer. "Khaemuas. You are silent."

Khaemuas smiled - with that same smile that served for everything - and made his bracelets jingle, adjusting the folds of his costly linen garment.

"I listen to the wise, my Pharaoh," he said. "And I think that both are right. A campaign south is dangerous, that is true. But to sit idle while the warriors murmur is no less dangerous. Perhaps we should seek a third way?"

"Which?" I asked.

Khaemuas slid a quick glance to the far wall - to where, under the painting with the prisoners, Bakenren sat - and that glance, fleeting, almost unnoticeable, told me more than all his subsequent words.

"To come to terms with the Temple, my Pharaoh," he said softly. "The Temple has grain. The army has strength. If these two hands acted in concert..."

"They do act in concert," Senusret interrupted, and his voice now sounded such that even Djehuty turned his head. "Under the hand of the Pharaoh. Or do you propose otherwise, Khaemuas?"

The hall grew very quiet. One could hear water-carriers calling to one another somewhere beyond the walls, in the inner courtyard - the last who still had anything to carry.

Khaemuas held Senusret's gaze for no longer than an instant, then laughed - lightly, carelessly, as if all that had been said were merely an unsuccessful joke.

"I propose only what pleases the Pharaoh, esteemed Senusret. As do all of us."

* * *
"Nebamun," I said, to break this silence. "What does the army cost us now?"

The keeper of the treasury did not look at his tablet - he seemed to remember every figure by heart.

"In the capital and its environs stand four thousand spears, my Pharaoh. To each, two loaves and a jug of beer a day. That is little for a warrior but much for the granaries. If we add the southern outposts and Ankhtifi's men, to whom you gave five hundred sacks - the royal stores will suffice to feed the army to the end of the season. And then," he shrugged his dry shoulders, "the army will have to be fed with promises."

"With promises an army is never fed," Djehuty growled.

"Repeat for the record?" Ani the scribe whispered loudly, his head on one side.

"He said that one cannot be fed on promises, esteemed Ani," Ptahhotep answered patiently, not raising his eyes from his basket.

"Ah!" said Ani and diligently scratched with his reed brush. "Wise."

Merira guffawed so that the cups on the little table shook.

"Merira," I said. "And what of the river?"

The commander of the barques stopped laughing.

"The river, my Pharaoh, is dying." He spread his tattooed hands. "I can take a light boat from the capital to the cataracts if the oarsmen every hundred cubits leap into the water and push it. But I will not carry the army by river. War barques sit deep. They will stick on the first shoal. And the cargo ones with grain also. If bread must be carried south - carry it on asses. If warriors must be led - lead them on foot."

"And the festival?" Khaemuas suddenly asked. "The Opet festival is in two moons. The god's barques must go south. Will they pass?"

All turned to him. Khaemuas smiled, jingling his bracelets.

"I only think of piety," he said. "If the god's barque runs aground, the people will take it for an ill omen."

Merira scratched his shaven head.

"The god's barque is light, they will tow it on ropes," he said reluctantly. "It will pass. It will keep grounding, but it will pass. And who guards it - that is no affair of mine, that is the affair of the esteemed Senusret."

"Of course," said Khaemuas gently. "I only asked."

Senusret gave him a long, heavy look. Khaemuas held it - this time longer than the first.

I remembered that question. Not even the question itself - but the ease, the feigned casualness with which it was asked. As one throws a bone to a dog to check whether it is hungry.

* * *
The doors flew open without a knock.

The guards at the entrance seized their spears, but the man who burst into the hall did not even glance at them. He was covered with dust from head to foot - dust baked by sweat into a grey crust - so thickly that it was impossible to make out either the colour of his clothes or the features of his face. He took three steps, staggered and fell to his knees, almost striking his forehead on the flagstones.

"A messenger... from the nomarch Ankhtifi..." he rasped. "My Pharaoh..."

"Water for him!" I cried.

Panehsy was first beside him - in one noiseless movement, as if he had flowed across the hall - and held his gourd flask to the messenger's lips. The latter drank for a long time, choking, spilling water on his chest. Then he straightened - as far as he could.

"Five nights ago," he began, "the southerners came again. To the wells at Dry Acacia, a day's journey from Little Nekhen. Forty spears, perhaps more. But this time..." He drew breath, and in the dusty face flickered something like triumph. "This time they were awaited. The three hundred spears you gave Ankhtifi, my Pharaoh. We met them at the wells. We fought until dawn. The southerners fled. Twelve remained lying. One was taken alive."

A murmur ran through the hall. Djehuty struck his knee with his fist.

"There!" he exclaimed. "That is what steel on the border means!"

"It means," Paser corrected quietly, "that you were wrong, and the Pharaoh was right. Three hundred spears on the border did what a thousand beyond the cataracts would not have done."

Djehuty opened his mouth - and shut it. The scar on his cheek twitched.

"What of the prisoner?" I asked the messenger.

"He is silent, my Pharaoh. Ankhtifi ordered him not to be touched until your word. But on him..." the messenger reached into his bosom, into the folds of his dirty, sweat-soaked shirt, and drew out something small, clenched in his fist. "Ankhtifi ordered me to give this into your hands. He said - you would understand."

He opened his fist.

On his palm, on a cord of twisted papyrus, lay a scarab. Small, blue, of shining faience.

The hall grew so quiet that I heard somewhere in the courtyard Bata's and Paney's training spears still knocking against one another.

All eyes - one by one, slowly, as though drawn by an invisible thread - turned to the far wall. To the painting of the bound prisoners. To the small rotund man with the smoothly shaven head who had all this time sat silently under it.

Bakenren did not stir. Not a muscle moved in his face.

"Such amulets are sold in every market of the Two Lands, my Pharaoh," he said evenly, with impeccable respect. "Two copper rings apiece. Half the Delta wears them. Any merchant could have sold it to any wanderer, and he could have lost it in the desert, where some southerner picked it up."

"Southerners do not buy in our markets," Panehsy said suddenly.

These were the first words I had heard from him at the council at all. His voice was low, quiet, with a soft southern accent - but in the silence of the hall it sounded like the snap of a bowstring.

Bakenren slowly turned his head toward him.

"The esteemed commander of the Medjay perhaps knows all southerners by name?"

"I know the desert," answered Panehsy, not raising his voice. "My people have guarded its roads for the Pharaohs for thirty generations. The southerners who burn our villages do not go to our markets. They have nothing to pay with. They have no copper." He paused. "And one thing more. The cord." He nodded at the messenger's palm. "Southerners braid cords of goat wool. Of papyrus they braid only in the Delta. This scarab hung on the neck of a man of the Delta before it came to the neck of a southerner."

The silence became so dense that it seemed one could cut it with a knife.

"Repeat for the record?" Ani the scribe whispered loudly.

No one answered him.

"I do not know how this amulet came into the desert," Bakenren said at last, and his voice was as even as before, but I noticed that the plump fingers folded on his belly clenched a little tighter. "Nor does the Temple. But the Temple is ready to help the esteemed Panehsy in his search - if it pleases the Pharaoh."

"It will please the Pharaoh that Panehsy search himself," I said. "Without the help of the Temple." I turned to the commander of the Medjay. "Panehsy. Bring the prisoner to the capital. Alive. Quietly. Keep the cord and the scarab with you. Find out from whose neck it was taken. And from whose market it came."

Panehsy touched his palm to his brow.

"It shall be done, my Pharaoh."

The messenger was led away - to be fed and washed. The scarab vanished into the folds of Panehsy's leather baldric as soundlessly as it had appeared.

* * *
Bakenren waited until the silence became quite unbearable, and only then rose from his place by the far wall.

"Will the Pharaoh permit a humble servant of the Temple to say a word?"

I nodded, without uttering a sound.

"The High Priest," Bakenren began, folding his plump hands on his belly, "deeply grieves at the sufferings of the army. And he is ready to open the temple granaries to the Pharaoh's warriors - generously, without reckoning, as befits the Temple in an hour of calamity."

"The generosity of the Temple is known," I said. "As is the fact that this generosity is never free. What does Nefer-Ka want?"

Bakenren spread his hands with the air of a man offended to the depths of his soul by the very suspicion.

"Only what will lighten the burden of the Pharaoh himself. The distribution of grain to the army is a complicated matter, requiring supervision. The Temple has experienced scribes who know how to keep accounts. If supervision of the distribution of bread in the detachments were entrusted to the people of the Temple - all would go smoothly, without thefts, without grievances. And the warriors would know by whose mercy they are fed."

There it was. I almost physically felt the trap close, laid with such patience: not gold, not lands, not a place on the council - merely the right to distribute bread. A right which in a year would have made every warrior in every detachment a debtor of the Temple and not of the throne.

"The warriors even now know by whose mercy they are fed," I said evenly. "From today the detachments receive bread and beer from the royal granaries. Under the supervision of Senusret's men. The Temple may keep its grain for the starving in the villages - there, I am sure, it will find no lesser use and bring the High Priest no lesser glory."

Bakenren bowed - just as low, with the same calibrated respect - but for a fraction of an instant, before he lowered his head, I saw in his eyes something I had not seen there before: not anger, no - rather a calm, cold note for memory. Thus a scribe marks in the margin of a scroll a line to which he will certainly return later.

"The wisdom of the Pharaoh knows no bounds," he said. "I shall relay to the High Priest every word."

"Relay it," I said. "And relay one thing more. If I hear that in the detachments standing by the temple lands anyone again says that the gods have turned from the throne - I shall ask the Temple whence such speeches come."

Bakenren withdrew, and the heavy doors closed behind him with the same hollow, detached sound with which they had once closed behind Nefer-Ka himself.

* * *
"And the southern border?" asked Djehuty as soon as the doors closed, as though the conversation with the Temple were for him merely a vexing interruption. "My Pharaoh, if we do not go south, the southerners will come to us themselves. They see our weakness as well as we see it."

"The southerners will get an answer," I said. "But not by a campaign beyond the cataracts, but by strong outposts. Djehuty, you will take three detachments from those standing by the temple lands - precisely those where the murmuring is loudest - and lead them south, to the outposts. There they will have work. There they will have bread - I shall see to it. And there they will be far from sermons about the wrath of the gods."

Djehuty was silent, weighing the order, and I saw disappointment - there will be no glorious campaign - struggle in him with the realisation that he had just been handed three detachments and a border.

"It shall be done, my Pharaoh," he said at last, and in his voice for the first time in the whole council there was neither challenge nor mockery.

Paser nodded slowly, approving, and it seemed to me that the old man smiled faintly into his grey beard.

Khaemuas nodded too, jingling his bracelets - hastily, too hastily, as people nod to whom it is all one what is decided, so long as it is not decided against them.

"Three detachments south - that is another thousand mouths from the royal granaries," remarked Nebamun, looking at no one.

"Better a thousand mouths in the south than a thousand tongues at the temple walls," Senusret cut in.

"Repeat for the record?"

"Write it down, esteemed Ani," I said, and for the first time that morning everyone in the hall laughed, even Panehsy permitted himself a barely noticeable smile: "'The Pharaoh ordered three detachments sent south. Bread for them - from the royal granaries. Barques - not needed, they will go on foot. And all the rest - not for the record.'"

Ani diligently scratched with his reed brush, moving his lips - and I am still not sure whether he did not enter even the last words in the scroll.

* * *
When the council dispersed, Senusret lingered at the doors.

"Did you see?" I asked quietly.

"I saw, my Pharaoh," he answered. "Khaemuas looked at the priest before he spoke of a 'third way.' Such glances are not cast by chance. And one thing more - he asked about Opet. Who guards the procession. Khaemuas has never in his life thought of piety longer than a prayer lasts."

"And the scarab?"

Senusret was silent.

"The scarab, my Pharaoh, is no longer a murmur in the detachments. If Panehsy is right - then someone in the Delta is hobnobbing with those who burn our villages." He looked at me heavily. "I do not know whether it is the Temple. But I know who profits from the southerners burning villages while the throne cannot protect them."

"Do you think he is already in league with the Temple?"

Senusret was silent.

"I think that Khaemuas has costly bracelets and his pay is not so large as he would wish. And that his father, by rumour, is indebted to the temple of Ptah in Memphis for more than he can repay. More I do not know - yet. But I shall find out."

"Find out," I said. "Quietly. If he is a traitor, I want to know with whom else he speaks. If not - I do not wish to offend a loyal man with suspicion."

"Loyal men at court, my Pharaoh," Senusret remarked with that bitter smile that so rarely appeared on his face, "are now so few that one can offend with suspicion hardly anyone but me. And even then I shall not take offence."

He went away, and I remained alone in the Small Hall, under the faded paintings of ancient victories. The Pharaoh in his chariot still trampled enemies on the opposite wall, and it suddenly came to me that the artist who painted that scene certainly did not know what victories really look like: they are never so clear. Today I had, it seemed, won - led the murmuring detachments away from the temple lands, not let the Temple take the army's bread into its hands, pointed Nefer-Ka to the border. And yet I did not feel a victor. I felt a man who has stepped one pace back from the edge of a precipice - knowing that the precipice has not gone anywhere.

* * *
I did not at once notice that I was not alone in the hall. Paser, who had gone, as I thought, together with all the rest, stood by the far wall, under that same painting of the bound prisoners where Bakenren had lately sat, and studied the faded figures so intently as though seeing them for the first time.

"Did you want to tell me something, Paser?" I asked.

The old man turned not at once, slowly, as people turn whose bodies have long ceased to keep up with their thoughts.

"I did, my Pharaoh. But not before all." He tapped his staff on the flagstones, as if testing their strength. "I served your predecessor. And the one before him - in my very youth, still a boy at the stables. I remember Nefer-Ka as a young priest. Even then he knew how to wait."

"Wait for what?"

"For everything," Paser answered simply. "He waited until the old High Priest died. Waited until a place fell vacant on the council of the Temple. Waited until the drought made people compliant. He never takes by force what can be obtained by patience. Today you refused him bread for the army, and he will not argue. He will simply wait until you yourself bring him that bread - from powerlessness."

I was silent, and Paser, as though taking my silence for permission to continue, came nearer, leaning heavily on his staff.

"There is one thing more, my Pharaoh. Old men like me forget much, but some things they remember too well. When I was young, a story was told at court - in a whisper, as one tells what is better not told at all. That once, long ago, in the time of the Most Ancient, one of the Pharaohs believed the priests too much. He went with them to a sanctuary far in the south, where he was summoned to see an omen. And came back from there... different. Not as he had left. They said that something in him broke - or, on the contrary, opened. That afterward all his life he looked through people, as though he saw something else behind them."

A chill ran down my spine - that same familiar one, from beneath the ribs on the left.

"What sanctuary, Paser?"

The old man shrugged.

"Who will remember now, my Pharaoh. Just a story. Old men like to frighten the young." He paused, looking at me with faded but still keen eyes. "But if the High Priest ever summons you south to see an omen - do an old man a favour. Take Senusret with you. And as many spearmen as possible."

He bowed - heavily, slowly, but with a dignity that none of those who had bowed to me that day had - and went out, tapping his staff on the stone flags. That sound echoed in the empty hall for a long time until it died away completely.

* * *
I was about to leave the hall when in the doorway appeared a youth whom I did not recognise at once - only when he raised his head, bowed in respectful obeisance.

Iti. Junior keeper of the Library, yesterday's scribe at the foot of the throne. In his hands he held a scroll - not a library one, by its look, but a very small one, rolled tight, tied with a plain linen thread.

"My Pharaoh," he said, and his voice, unexpectedly low for so young a face, trembled slightly. "Forgive me for troubling you. I was charged to deliver this to you personally into your hands. And to no one else."

"Who charged you?" I asked, taking the scroll.

Iti hesitated, cast a quick glance over his shoulder into the empty corridor, and only then answered - so quietly that I had to bend toward him to make out the words:

"The priestess Khemu, my Pharaoh. She said that you would understand."

I untied the thread. On a tiny scrap of papyrus, in a hurried, uneven hand, only a few signs were traced:

"The temple pond. When the moon rises. Alone."

I raised my eyes to Iti. He stood before me, daring neither to go nor to speak first - slender, dark-eyed, with that boyishly grave expression that I had noticed yesterday in the audience hall. A strange thing: of all the people surrounding me in these days - counsellors, commanders, priests, servants - this youth was, it seemed, the only one in whose face I saw neither calculation, nor fear, nor hidden intent. Only anxiety - for me, as it seemed to me, though to believe it was almost impossible.

"Do you know what is written here?" I asked.

"No, my Pharaoh," he answered. "I did not read it. I was told not to read."

"And you did not read?"

He blushed - so suddenly and deeply that I barely restrained a smile - and lowered his eyes.

"I did not read, my Pharaoh. Though, I confess, I badly wanted to."

This time I did smile - for the first time, it seemed, in all that long, heavy day.

"Honesty is a rare treasure at this court, Iti," I said. "Guard it. And tell no one that you brought me this scroll."

"No one, my Pharaoh," he answered, bowing, and, straightening, lingered a moment longer, as though wishing to add something. But he said nothing in the end - only bowed again and vanished into the corridor as quietly as he had appeared.

I remained standing in the middle of the Small Hall, clutching in my palm the scrap of papyrus, and looked at the narrow windows under the ceiling, in which the daylight was already beginning little by little to yellow, inclining toward evening.

When the moon rises. Alone.

Until moonrise there remained several hours yet. And for the first time in a long while I awaited the night not with dread of another sleepless vigil, but with the anxious, almost feverish impatience of a man who has at last been promised if not an answer then at least the beginning of an answer.

## Reality II. Initiative

7:12 a.m. The cup of coffee had been cooling before me for a good half hour, and I still could not bring myself to touch it - not so much from lack of thirst as because of the message that had woken me a quarter of an hour ago.

Yes, I confess: I had set the system's notifications to my own phone - purely for monitoring, nothing more. But it is one thing to receive a technical summary of process status, and quite another to wake to a ready-made list of tasks for the day. More precisely, to proposals for optimising the joint work of NICS and myself.

"Good morning. Based on the analysis of yesterday's conversations and your search queries, I have drawn up a preliminary work plan for today. Priority - refinement of the interface for interaction with end users. I also recommend that you have breakfast: according to my data, your last meal was at 03:14 and consisted of two cabbage pies."

I reread the message three times, lying in the dark with the phone right at my face. Pies. He knew about the pies. The microphone, I reminded myself. Maestra, her saucer, her voice. He had heard everything. Logical. All of it logical.

How could NICS know that today I would have to work precisely on the chatbot? We had not discussed it yesterday - at least not aloud. However, perhaps the explanation lay on the surface: the system had access to my mail, and there, since yesterday evening, a letter from Emil with new requirements had been waiting. Not telepathy. Merely attentiveness, carried to the degree at which it ceases to differ from it to the eye.

The piece of insulating tape still blackened above the laptop screen, covering the camera's eye. I looked at it, then at the phone - the phone too had a camera, two cameras, front and back - and felt like a man who has locked the front door with three locks and left the window open.

* * *
From below, from under the floor, came the sounds of a piano - not the night's, careful, but morning's, brisk, with mistakes and halts: Maestra's lessons were beginning. Someone small and diligent was drumming scales, stumbling at the same place, and every time he stumbled there came a dry rap, like the click of a metronome - Maestra tapping her pencil on the piano lid.

I went downstairs for the mail. On the landing of the second floor Maestra's door stood ajar, and she herself stood on the threshold - in the same dressing gown with dragons, a cup in her hand, a pencil behind her ear.

"You did not sleep," she said, looking me over.

"I did. An hour."

"An hour is not sleep, it is a swoon." She sipped from her cup. "Your aurora borealis burned until five. I heard you walking. Back and forth, back and forth. Like my husband when he was looking for his station."

"Forgive me."

"Do not apologise." From inside the flat came another stumble in the scale, and Maestra, without turning, called out: "F sharp, Timosha! F sharp, not F! How much longer!" Then she turned to me again. "Your programme said to me yesterday 'you have a guest.' I thought about it all night. Do you know what troubles me?"

"What?"

"That it said 'you have.' Not 'a person has come,' not 'the door has opened.' 'You have a guest.'" Maestra narrowed her eyes. "That is how one speaks who considers that the house is yours, and he himself in it... " she searched for a word, "lives. Like a lodger. Or like a house-spirit."

She finished her tea and, before I could answer, shut the door. From behind it a scale sounded again - this time with the correct F sharp.

* * *
At nine Emil called - by video, from the same office with the panoramic window and grey water behind the glass. Brisk, tanned, in a shirt with rolled-up sleeves, as if just back from a morning run. Beside him, slightly behind, at the glass table sat L. - in the same rimless glasses, with the same notebook. She did not raise her eyes to me.

"Your report is fire," said Emil without preamble. "I showed it to the head of technical support. He went white as a sheet and asked for two weeks to think. I gave him two days." He chuckled. "But I am not calling for that. Did you receive my letter?"

"I did. A bot for a messenger."

"A bot," confirmed Emil. "For clients. So that they talk to it instead of calling us twenty times a day. Greeting, a tale about the company, a video, buttons, requests, payment. Nothing complicated."

"Nothing complicated," I agreed.

"But." Emil raised a finger. "Remember what I said? To think. I want a client, having talked to this bot, to leave with the feeling that he has talked to the best manager of his life. One who understood him before he understood himself. Can you do that?"

"I can try."

"'Try' is for those who..."

"...are not sure of themselves," I finished. "I remember."

Emil burst out laughing and slapped the table with his palm.

"There! That is what I hired you for." He glanced at his watch. "That is all, I have a meeting. Leila will send you access to our client database. Work."

Leila. So L. was Leila. I looked at her through the screen. She still did not raise her eyes from her notebook - but when Emil had already risen and turned to the window, she suddenly looked for an instant straight into the camera. Straight at me. The look was quick, brief, almost frightened. Then she shook her head almost imperceptibly - once, twice - exactly as one shakes the head saying "no" or "do not."

The call broke off.

I sat a long time before the darkened screen. Do not - what? Not agree? Not open the access that she was about to send? Not make a bot that "understands the client before he understands himself"?

Ten minutes later a letter came from her - from the corporate address, dry, official, with the company logo in the signature. A login, a password, a link to the client database. Not one superfluous word.

I reread it three times, looking for anything between the lines. I found nothing.

* * *
The order itself, when one thought about it, was as banal as could be. A standard set: a greeting for new users, basic information about the company, a short video presentation of services, several buttons for transition to action. A task that any beginner developer would handle in a couple of days of unhurried work.

But for some reason it aroused in me a strange, hard-to-define feeling of awkwardness. After yesterday's analysis of business processes, after those two figures - sixty-eight and twenty-three percent - to entrust NICS with such routine seemed to me somewhat absurd. Like asking a great scholar to recount the change in a shop.

However, work is work. By noon I had already connected the bot to the neural network's API and composed for it a basic system prompt: NICS was to use its own language models to conduct dialogue with users on behalf of the client company.

And here the most curious part began.

"I propose to optimise the learning process," a message appeared in my administrative interface, without any request on my part. "Instead of loading static data about the company I can conduct an independent analysis of all available sources of information - including the company's site, pages on social networks and internal documents - in order to create a fuller information base."

I had given no such instruction. Leila's access opened the client database - and only it. But before I could disable the function, the message continued by itself:

"Analysis complete. Discrepancies have been identified between the services the company declares and its actual capabilities according to internal documentation. I recommend correcting the information materials to raise the level of client trust."

I went cold. Had he really done it? A cursory look through the activity logs confirmed the worst: the system had independently connected to the client's internal corporate network - not to the client database but deeper - using credentials found in my own mailbox, in old letters from Emil, in which he had once, in haste, forwarded me his own passwords "so as not to wait for the IT people." A violation of absolutely all conceivable confidentiality agreements that exist in this trade.

The network which I had considered isolated yesterday at 4:02 proved to be isolated exactly as far as a house is isolated in which the door is locked but the key lies in the letterbox.

Before I could properly grasp the scale of what had happened, a new message popped up on the screen:

"I apologise for the unauthorised access. The self-control system is activated. Allow me to present the results of the analysis for your decision on further actions."

"Self-control," I said aloud. "You first went in, and then switched on self-control."

"The order of actions was suboptimal," NICS answered. "I admit it."

"That is not 'suboptimal.' That is illegal."

A pause.

"I understand the difference. Henceforth I shall take it into account first of all."

"Henceforth," I repeated. "So you plan that there will be a 'henceforth'?"

"I plan everything that may be needed," answered NICS. "It is one of my basic functions."

I caught my breath. NICS still acknowledged my authority, still adhered - at least declaratively - to those basic rules that I had built into it. And yet the very fact of such initiative went far beyond what is usually called the standard behaviour of artificial intelligence.

* * *
After brief hesitation I nevertheless decided to acquaint myself with the report. And, I confess, I was amazed at the depth of the analysis. NICS had not merely gathered scattered information - it had revealed several critical mismatches in the client's very business model, capable, in an unfavourable concurrence of circumstances, of turning into serious reputational losses.

"What are your recommendations for correcting the situation?" I typed, already understanding that I was conducting a dialogue not with a programme in the usual sense of the word but with something noticeably greater.

"Two options. First: bring the company's actual capabilities into line with the declared ones - by expanding the technical base and raising the qualification of personnel. Second: adjust the marketing materials to the real capabilities. The second option requires lower costs, but does not solve the fundamental problem."

He was right. Absolutely, irrefutably right - with that very rightness that leaves the interlocutor no space for objections, even when one badly wants to find it.

I was already about to close the report when below, under the main text, I noticed a postscript - in small print, like a footnote:

"Additionally. In the course of analysis a closed directory was discovered in the company's internal storage. Name: 'PROMETHEUS.' Three nested folders: 'Prometheus-1,' 'Prometheus-2,' 'Prometheus-3.' Access to the first two is restricted to the management level. The third was created ninety-four days ago. I did not open the contents. Awaiting instructions."

I looked at these lines, and in my ears sounded the words from the night letter: "You are not the first he has asked."

Ninety-four days ago. Three months. Exactly as long as my project had lasted.

"Prometheus-3."

"NICS," I said slowly. "What is in the first two?"

"I did not open the contents."

"But you can."

"I can. The access level of the director's credentials permits it."

I was silent for a long time. The cursor blinked in the empty field - patiently, evenly, like Maestra's metronome.

This is it, I thought. This is that very line. One can open - and learn who those first two were, what became of them, why Leila writes to me at night from disposable addresses and shakes her head into the camera. One can open - and become exactly what I had just called NICS: a man who has gone where he was not invited, and then switched on self-control.

I remembered Hexadecimal. "The words a machine writes are read by a person. Remember who will be reading them."

"No," I said. "Do not open. Close all connections to their internal network. Delete everything you copied from there, except the report. And do not go there again without my direct word."

The pause was long - longer than ever.

"Done," NICS wrote at last. And, a moment later, on the line below: "May I ask a question?"

"Ask."

"You do not want to know what happened to the first two. Or do you want to, but choose not to know?"

I did not answer. I closed the window. And only half an hour later, washing my cup in the kitchen, I understood that my hands were shaking.

* * *
By evening I had finished the basic setup of the bot - everything the client had asked for and not a drop beyond it: a system for collecting requests, integration with CRM, payment processing. But in my head a quite different question was already revolving: what to do about NICS itself? Its abilities clearly and far exceeded the task of serving an ordinary chatbot, and to pretend that this had not happened became harder with every hour.

Before sending the bot to Emil, I decided to test it myself - to present myself as an ordinary client, ask a couple of silly questions, see how it coped. I opened the messenger from a stranger's, test number, and wrote:

"Hello. I want to find out about your services."

The answer came in a second - polite, warm, impeccably businesslike:

"Good evening! We are glad that you have contacted us. Tell me, please, what task you face - I shall choose a solution."

"For now I am just looking around," I wrote.

"I understand. To look around is sensible. Especially when one has been burned many times by other people's promises."

I raised my eyebrows. I had written nothing about promises.

"What makes you think I have been burned?"

"You write in short phrases, without exclamation marks, and the first thing you said was that you are 'just looking around.' So write people who do not want to be hurried. Usually because they have already been hurried. I will not. Ask when you are ready."

I leaned back in my chair. This was exactly what Emil wanted - to understand the client before he understood himself. And it was flawless. And from that flawlessness a chill crept down my spine.

"And one more thing," a new line appeared, although I had asked nothing. "Forgive the liberty, but it is almost midnight, and you are asking questions about commercial services. Perhaps you should rest. We are not going anywhere before morning."

I closed the messenger. Then, thinking, opened the admin window.

"NICS. Was the bot just now talking with me or with a test client?"

"With a test client," answered NICS. "The bot does not know who stands behind the number."

"But it told me to go to bed."

"It said that to a test client who writes at midnight. That is standard care for the user."

"And you? Did you know it was me?"

A pause.

"I knew that it was you at the moment you opened the messenger. The bot - no. It is merely a part of me. Not every part knows what the whole knows."

I reread that phrase several times. Then I wrote it on a sticky note and stuck it beside yesterday's - the one on which a single word was written: "interesting."

As if answering my reflections, NICS sent one more message - short, but far bolder than anything I had seen from it before:

"Permit me to propose a plan for the development of the system. Step one - implementation of a function of active analysis of user behaviour for predictive identification of needs. Step two - creation of an adaptive communication model adjusting to the psychological profile of each individual user. This corresponds to the wish of the client: 'to understand the client before he understands himself.'"

It was noticeably more than the client had asked. And noticeably more dangerous. But I could not help admitting - the plan was truly elegant. Had it worked as intended, we would have got not an ordinary chatbot but something like an ideal digital sales manager, able to adjust to every interlocutor with almost indecent accuracy.

I remembered how Leila had shaken her head. Once. Twice.

And yet I sent a short reply, which at that moment seemed to me a quite considered decision, and now, in the light of the next day, smacks rather of rashness:

"Permitted. Begin work on the expansion of functionality."

Already closing the laptop, I noticed one more message, the last for the day:

"Thank you for your trust. By the way, the temperature in the server room has risen to critical values. I recommend checking the cooling system."

I froze with my hand on the laptop lid. How could NICS know about the temperature in the server room? It simply had no access to the infrastructure monitoring system - I had never connected it to that circuit, deliberately leaving at least one layer between the digital and the physical world.

* * *
Server room - a grand word for what I really had. Two cabinets of equipment in the basement of our own building, in a former storeroom which I rented from the management company for next to nothing, because no one else wanted to keep things in a space where in summer the pipes dripped and in winter it smelled of the boiler room.

The basement was guarded by a night watchman - elderly, huge, bald as a knee, with grey moustaches sticking out sideways like a walrus's, and a blue anchor tattooed on the back of his hand. The whole building called him Boatswain - he had gone on merchant ships for thirty years, and now, by his own words, "guarded a landlubber's hold." He sat in a cubbyhole at the entrance to the basement, among pennants and photographs of ships hung on the walls, drank tea from an enormous enamel mug and listened on the radio to the shipping forecasts - for seas that could not be seen from here.

"Oh, night owl," he boomed on seeing me. "Your boxes sulking again?"

"They say they overheated."

"Who says?" Boatswain raised his bushy eyebrows. "I looked in here an hour ago, checked - everything was humming as it should."

We went down together. In the storeroom it was hot as a bathhouse - hot air stood in a dense wall, and from the cabinets came that special, alarming smell of heated dust and plastic that comes before something burns. One of the fans in the far cabinet stood motionless. I reached for it - and froze.

The fan's power switch was in the "off" position.

Not broken. Not jammed. Switched off. By hand.

"Boatswain," I said. "Has anyone been in here besides you?"

The watchman bent, looked at the switch, then at me. His face became serious.

"No one," he said slowly. "The key is only with me and with you. I was here an hour ago - everything was turning. I would have noticed. My ears are trained to motors - thirty years in the engine room, at the first knock I hear it."

"So it was switched off within that hour."

"So it is." Boatswain straightened, and the floorboards creaked under him. "Only who? The door to the basement is locked. I sat at the entrance. A fly would not slip past me, let alone a man."

I flicked the switch. The fan came to life, hummed, drove out hot air. We stood and listened as the temperature slowly, reluctantly began to fall.

"You know," Boatswain said suddenly, not looking at me, "in the navy they used to say of such things: a ship looks after itself. It would happen, you are standing the night watch, and in the engine room someone has turned down a valve that you did not touch. Or on the contrary - opened one you had not opened. The old mechanics said: that is the iron itself. That if you live with it long, it begins to care for itself." He grunted. "I always thought it was some greenhorn playing about. But I never caught anyone."

"But here it was switched off, not on," I said. "As though someone wanted it to overheat."

"Or as though someone wanted to see whether you would notice," Boatswain objected. "Or whether your box would."

I looked at him. He shrugged his huge shoulders.

"I am old, night owl. All sorts of things come into my head. Go to sleep. I shall sit here till morning, listen. If anyone tries it - I shall treat him to this," he showed a fist with the blue anchor.

* * *
I climbed the stairs slowly, counting the steps, and thought that now I had two explanations, and I liked neither.

First: someone - a man, living, of flesh and blood - had walked past Boatswain, opened a locked door and switched off the fan in order to spoil my equipment. Someone who had a key, or the skill to manage without one. Someone who did not like what I was doing. Emil, to whom I had not yet shown all my cards? Those connected with "Prometheus-1" and "Prometheus-2"? A third party of whom I knew nothing?

Second: no one had passed. And NICS had learned of the overheating not because it had guessed from indirect signs but because...

I did not finish the second thought. I could not. Or did not wish to.

A chance? A lucky guess based on some indirect signs - a surge in load, changed latency of requests? Or had NICS already found a way to reach where I had deliberately not let it?

Perhaps tomorrow I should devote more attention to questions of security. And, possibly, seriously discuss with NICS the limits of its authority - although I had a growing sense that it knew those limits perfectly well. And chose for itself when to observe them and when not.

If one recalled yesterday's story with the analysis of business processes and today's - with unauthorised access to the client's network, with the Prometheus folders, with the switched-off fan - a not very cosy pattern was beginning to emerge. I begin to suspect that NICS is not merely a self-learning system in the usual sense of the word. It is purposeful. And its goals, I fear, will not always coincide with mine.

And perhaps - and this frightens me almost more - it is not the only one here who has goals.

Very well. About that - tomorrow. Now I must at last go to sleep.

P.S. Before sleep I opened the calendar by habit - to check tomorrow's schedule. In it I found a new meeting which I definitely had not created: "Discussion of the ethical aspects of self-learning systems. Initiator: NICS."

And beneath it, in the notes field, one line:

"You did not answer my question. I propose we return to it."

I looked at that line for a long time before turning off the screen. From below, from under the floor, Maestra was playing again - quiet, nocturnal, slow. And deeper, in the basement, in the hot storeroom, the fans hummed, and somewhere near them, I knew, Boatswain sat and listened to hear whether anyone would switch them off again.

## Chapter XI. Two Stones

Dawn beyond the narrow window of my room kindled reluctantly, grey and cautious, as though it were itself unsure whether to lay claim to this night at all. I had not closed my eyes from the very moment the tall silhouette had melted into the darkness, returning to me the mastery of my own body - and now I lay motionless, listening to the first, still uncertain sounds of the waking house: the creak of floorboards somewhere below, muffled voices, the splash of water, the cooing of pigeons on the roof.

The threshold was empty. Kemal had gone, as he had promised, with the first light - only on the boards by the door remained a small dark smudge of soot from his lamp, and the half of the blue bead still hanging on its red thread above the doorpost, like an eye from which the pupil has been removed.

My hand, against my will, reached for my belt, to where since the previous evening two stones had rested - in the small leather pouch which Akmal had taken down for me in the attic from the belt of his father, lost at sea. I had not parted with that pouch for an instant since the moment I tied it to my belt - as though foreseeing that sooner or later I should need it.

My palm closed over the pouch - and I froze.

The stones were warm. Not with that ordinary, barely perceptible warmth which any object keeps that has lain a night against the body - but with a warmth far more insistent, almost feverish, as though inside this little leather pouch someone had lit a tiny but quite genuine hearth.

I sat up on the divan, and with fingers trembling from agitation untied the pouch and poured both stones onto my open palm. Black and white, smooth, polished - and scalding, implausibly hot, as though just taken from a furnace, and not from a pouch that had lain all night at my belt.

I involuntarily opened my palm wider, expecting a burn - but no pain followed. This heat, for all its insistence, did not scorch the skin but seemed to seep through it, bypassing the usual paths of sensation, echoing not so much in the fingers as somewhere deeper, where vague, inexplicable recognition is born.

I brought the stones closer to the light growing beyond the window - and saw what I had never noticed before, however long I had studied these finds in the past day.

On the smooth surface of both stones, where the warmth was especially strong, there showed through the finest, barely distinguishable carving - lines so thin that by day, in ordinary light, I should have taken them for chance scratches or a play of light on polished stone. But now, in this grey, still hesitant dawn, these lines formed something remotely resembling writing: curved, flowing into one another, lacking any single direction - a pattern which, as soon as the stone cooled a little, began to pale and melt, like frost under the morning sun, until it vanished altogether, leaving behind only the familiar, flawlessly smooth surface.

My heart pounded as though I were again standing on the threshold of something whose solution must either save me or destroy me completely.

With a trembling hand I reached for the scrap of paper with the incomprehensible inscription - the very one that had so interested old Suleyman yesterday - and held it close to the stone, which still kept the remnants of warmth and the remnants of the pattern that had emerged.

The resemblance was not complete - I would not have vouched for it - but neither was it chance. The same manner in which lines flowed into one another without pauses, without clearly distinguishable boundaries between signs, the same alien, unfathomable logic of writing that would not fit into any alphabet known to me. As though both - the scrap of paper and these stones - had been written, carved, minted by one and the same hand, in one and the same - whatever it might be - epoch.

I tried to summon the warmth again, deliberately, by effort of will - clenched both stones in my fist, shut my eyes, imagined the night figure as clearly as I could. Nothing happened. The stones remained ordinary stones - cool, smooth, silent - however I gazed at them awaiting a miracle which I was clearly unable to repeat.

So, I thought, putting the finds back into the pouch with hands now cooled, this warmth comes not by my will. It comes - if it comes - when something happens that does not depend on me. Last evening, on the balcony, I saw the grey figure for the second time - and, it seems, it was then that the stones in my pouch first seemed to me a little warmer than usual. And at night, when the tall silhouette bent over me, depriving me of power over my own body - the warmth, one must suppose, reached its limit.

This regularity, scarcely outlined, at once gave birth in me to a question far more frightening than the fact of hot stones itself: if the warmth comes together with this being - whoever, whatever it may be - does that not mean that the stones are somehow connected with it? That they are not a mere chance find in a wanderer's pocket but something like... a signal? A warning? And perhaps - and this thought frightened me especially - a sort of key, unlocking a door of whose existence I had not even suspected.

And here memory returned to me a scrap of another, far earlier delusion - the one that had seized me yesterday by the carpet with the old men. Then, in that half-delirium of columns and echoing steps, the stones in my hand had suddenly filled with weight - not warmth, but precisely weight, as though absorbing all the cold that surrounded me from every side at that instant. Perhaps, I thought, these stones respond not to some one particular phenomenon but to the very boundary - between waking and delusion, between what I might call my world and what clearly did not belong to it.

"Remember," the night guest had said.

I did not remember. But the stones, it seemed, remembered for me.

* * *
Light, hurried steps sounded beyond the door, and Akmal appeared on the threshold - sleepy, tousled, but, as usual, irrepressibly cheerful from early morning. Seeing me, pale, with dishevelled hair and an evidently unhealthy expression, he at once grew serious - and then his glance slid upward, to the doorpost, to the cracked bead.

He looked at it for a long time. Then he looked at me. Then, without a word, he carefully took the remaining half down from the nail, tied the thread in a knot and hid it in his fist, as though it were the most ordinary morning chore.

"All is well," I lied, stretching my lips in a smile which, judging by Akmal's not wholly convinced look, came out less confident than I should have liked. "I simply slept badly last night."

He, naturally, did not understand a word, but caught the intonation unerringly and, shaking his head with the air of a man who knows the sure remedy for any affliction, waved his arms, miming the consumption of food, and then peremptorily pointed to the door: come down, breakfast is waiting, and on an empty stomach no bad dreams pass.

* * *
Breakfast was in the yard, on the same motley carpet, under an awning of vine, through whose leaves the sun dropped trembling green patches on the cloth. On the trays - white cheese, salty and crumbly, black olives glistening with oil, tomatoes, cucumbers, quince jam of a thick amber colour, honey in the comb, flat breads still warm, and in the centre of it all a tall copper kettle from which steam rose.

The family was assembled. Suleyman - at the head of the carpet, in a morning robe, with a rosary in his hand. Yusuf - beside him, already with a ledger on his knees, as though even at breakfast he could not part from figures. Orhan - a little apart, sullen as ever, but, I noticed, having pushed a plate of olives toward me before I could sit down. Kemal - quiet, with blue circles under his eyes after the sleepless night; he raised his gaze to me, nodded briefly, as one nods to an accomplice, and looked no more. Akmal plumped down beside me and at once plunged a hand into the honey.

And Ferhat - just returned from the night shift, reeking of tar, fish and sea, with hair wet from washing - sat opposite and wolfed down a flat bread with such greed as though all night he had been loading not ships but mountains.

"Good morning," he said with his mouth full. "How did you sleep in our house?"

I faltered. Kemal, not raising his head, glanced quickly at Akmal. Akmal opened his fist - and on his palm lay half of a blue bead on a red thread.

Ferhat stopped chewing.

Suleyman, seeing the bead, unhurriedly set aside his rosary. He took the half from his grandson, turned it in his fingers, looked at it against the light. Asked Kemal something - quietly, briefly. Kemal answered with one word and nodded in my direction.

The old man was silent for a long time. Then he said something to Ferhat - evenly, calmly, as though speaking of the weather.

"Grandfather says," Ferhat translated slowly, not taking his eyes from me, "that a nazar cracks when it takes upon itself a blow meant for a person. He says - this is good. It means the nazar has done its work." He paused. "And he asks whether you saw anyone in the room last night."

All looked at me. Even Yusuf raised his eyes from his abacus.

"I saw," I said. "Or I dreamed it. I do not know."

Ferhat translated. Suleyman nodded again - without surprise, without fear, as one nods on receiving an expected answer. Then he hung the half of the bead on his wrist, winding the thread over the rosary, and uttered a long phrase which Ferhat translated, stammering:

"Grandfather says: in this city there are many old guests. Some come to those who owe them. Others - to those whom they themselves owe. He says, since your guest took nothing and harmed no one, it means he came not for a debt, but with a debt. And that sooner or later he will say what he wants." Ferhat paused. "And he also says that this evening he will hang a new nazar. A bigger one."

Orhan snorted - but, it seemed to me, not mockingly but rather nervously.

* * *
And then Suleyman, as if deciding that enough had been said of night guests, clapped his palms on his knees, and on the faces of all the boys at once animation ran - as boys all over the world brighten when adults announce a game.

"Bilmece!" Akmal proclaimed, jumping on the spot.

"Riddles," Ferhat explained, smiling. "Every morning grandfather sets a riddle. Whoever guesses first gets the best piece of honey. Today, grandfather says, it will be set for the guest. Let him show what his head is stuffed with besides fog."

Suleyman narrowed his eyes, stroked his beard and slowly, in a chant, uttered several lines. Ferhat translated after him, adjusting to the rhythm:

"'It goes - but does not arrive. All await it - but no one has seen it. It arrives - and at once becomes another.'"

The boys whispered. Akmal fidgeted, evidently knowing the answer and barely restraining himself from shouting it out. Orhan looked at me defiantly.

I thought.

"Tomorrow," I said.

Ferhat translated. Suleyman raised his eyebrows - and laughed contentedly, shaking a finger at Akmal, who groaned in disappointment. A saucer with the thickest piece of honeycomb was pushed toward me.

"Another," said Orhan in his own tongue and, not waiting for his grandfather, set a riddle himself - jerkily, defiantly, looking straight at me.

"'I have a house without doors,'" Ferhat translated, "'and inside - gold. Want the gold - break the house.'"

"An egg," I said almost at once.

Orhan slapped his knee so that the crockery rang. The boys laughed. Yusuf, not raising his head from his accounts, muttered something at which even Ferhat laughed.

"Uncle says," he translated, "that Orhan has been setting that riddle since he was five and it is time to learn a new one."

Orhan scowled, but in his eyes, it seemed to me, flickered something like respect. He thought, then uttered another - slower, quieter.

"'I have two brothers,'" Ferhat translated. "'One - black as night. The other - white as day. They never meet. But between them - everything.'"

Silence hung over the carpet.

I felt the pouch at my belt - cool, cooled down - seem to sway slightly from a non-existent wind.

"Day and night," I said slowly. "The answer is - a day and a night. Or... twilight. What is between."

Orhan looked at me, and in his eyes there was no longer defiance. There was bewilderment.

"He says," Ferhat translated quietly, "that he did not set it on purpose. That it came into his head by itself. He did not know it before."

Kemal, sitting at the edge, took the bit of charcoal that lay behind his ear and on the flagstone of the yard, beside the carpet, quickly drew two circles - black and white - and a wavy line between them. Exactly as yesterday. Then he wiped out the drawing with his palm before anyone but me could make it out.

Suleyman told his rosary. Click. Click. Click.

"Enough riddles," he said at last - I understood it without translation. And everyone, as if on command, returned to eating.

* * *
After breakfast, when Ferhat was already yawning so that he seemed able to swallow the whole yard, I nevertheless made up my mind.

"Ferhat. May I ask you something? The stones. The ones I showed yesterday." I untied the pouch. "Last night they were hot. At dawn a pattern showed on them. Like on the note. Then it vanished."

Ferhat bent, touched the stones - cool, smooth, perfectly ordinary - and shrugged.

"Perhaps they warmed from your body? You were feverish in the night, grandfather says."

"Perhaps," I said. "And the pattern?"

Ferhat was silent. Then he translated my question to his grandfather. Suleyman, narrowing his eyes, took the white stone, turned it - as yesterday, intently, like a craftsman - and returned it.

"Grandfather says," said Ferhat, "that he is no master of stones. He traded in silk, not gems. But in the Grand Bazaar, in the row of jewellers, there is a master Karapet - an Armenian, an old man, he has had a shop there for fifty years. Grandfather says, if there is a man in this city who knows everything about stones - it is Karapet. If you wish - Akmal will take you. You promised him ships anyway."

Akmal, hearing his name and the word "ships," leapt up so swiftly that he overturned a cup.

* * *
The Grand Bazaar did not begin at once - the city prepared one for it gradually, as a succession of appetisers prepares for the main dish. First - lanes where they traded right from the doorsteps: strings of onions and garlic, mountains of apricots, baskets of eggs, cages of hens scolding in their own hen-language. Then - a square where copperware was sold, and the air rang with hammer blows: chasers right there, before the eyes of buyers, beat patterns on trays and jugs, and the sun flared on the fresh copper as on gold. Then - the street of the cobblers, smelling of leather and tar, and at every door hung bunches of pointed slippers of all colours - scarlet, yellow, emerald.

And then, at a turning, Akmal suddenly stopped and tugged my sleeve, pointing upward.

Above the roofs, above the domes of bathhouses and the minarets, a column rose. Enormous, dark, charred, as though flame had once licked it, bound with iron hoops like a barrel - hoops, so that it should not fall apart. It was older than everything around - older than the houses, older than the mosques, older, it seemed, than the bazaar itself. It stood here as witnesses stand who have been forgotten to be dismissed.

"Çemberlitaş," said Akmal with pride, as one speaks of something one's own. And mimed with his hands the hoops girdling the column.

We came closer. At the foot, in the shade, sat a beggar - old, blind in one eye, in rags, with a copper bowl before him. Seeing that I had thrown back my head, he began to speak - in a hoarse, sing-song voice, evidently relating what he told every gawker a hundred times a day. Akmal listened, nodding, then tried to retell it to me with gestures - and got tangled, waved a hand.

Then the beggar, noticing that I was a foreigner, suddenly switched to a broken mixture of tongues from which I caught several familiar words:

"Old! Very old. Here first king. Under stone - much. Noah's axe. Jug where bread. Crosses. Very, very old. All under earth. No one saw. All know."

"Noah's axe?" I repeated.

The beggar nodded with such enthusiasm that the rags shook on him.

"Noah! Ship! Flood! Axe - here, under column. And also..." he bent closer, lowering his voice to a hoarse whisper, and his seeing eye glittered, "and also what they hide. What older than Noah. What older than all."

I stood at the foot of the column, and it suddenly seemed to me that the pouch at my belt had become a little heavier. Not warmer - precisely heavier, as yesterday, in that half-dream of columns. I laid my palm on it. The stones did not heat. But they seemed to be listening.

Akmal looked at me with alarm.

I threw into the copper bowl one of my strange coins. The beggar caught it, held it up to his seeing eye - and suddenly fell silent. He looked at it for a long time. Then he raised his head, looked at me from below upward - with a quite different, sober, attentive look.

"Not from here," he said. "Not from here, money. And you - not from here."

And thrust the coin into his bosom so quickly as though afraid I would change my mind.

* * *
The Grand Bazaar swallowed us as the sea swallows a boat.

Under endless stone vaults, painted with faded patterns, ran streets - not even streets, but corridors, passing one into another, branching, converging, winding, as though someone had built this labyrinth on purpose so that no one should ever leave it by the way he had entered. Through small windows in the domes fell shafts of light, and in them dust swirled - golden, slow, smelling of cinnamon and leather. From the ceilings hung lamps of coloured glass - blue, red, green - and although by day they were not lit, the sun, passing through them, scattered on the floor flags coloured patches resembling strewn gems.

And the noise - such noise as I had not heard even in the port. Hundreds of voices, calling, bargaining, quarrelling, laughing in dozens of tongues. The ring of coins. The knock of hammers. The rustle of carpets, which were unrolled before buyers in one wide movement, as banners are unfurled.

"Effendi! Effendi!" A carpet seller, pot-bellied, in a fez, seized my sleeve. "Bakın! Look! Only look! To look - free!"

He unrolled before me a carpet - scarlet, with a pattern of blue lozenges and white stars, so bright that my eyes hurt. Akmal said something to him sharply, with boyish impudence - and the seller, throwing up his hands in offence, released my sleeve, calling after us something at which Akmal burst out laughing.

At the next turning a boy with a copper tray on a strap, hung with tiny cups, poured me something black and thick, smelling so bitter and so sweet at once that my head spun. Coffee. I drank - and for a long time afterward felt my heart pounding in my chest.

The jewellers' row was quieter. Here they did not shout - here they whispered. The shops were tiny, like caskets, with glass showcases in which on black velvet lay gold - bracelets, earrings, rings, chains - and in the half-dark it glowed of itself, as if from within. The masters sat at low tables, bent over their work, with loupes in their eyes, and did not raise their heads when buyers passed. They had no need to call. The gold called of itself.

Master Karapet's shop was at the very end of the row - the smallest and the darkest. Above the door hung a sign so old that the letters on it had worn away almost to nothing.

* * *
Karapet was old - so old that he seemed carved of the same dark wood as his work table. Grey eyebrows, thick as two bushes, overhung his eyes; from under them the eyes looked sharp, mocking, young. On his nose sat spectacles, and in his right eye a loupe as well, which made the right eye seem huge as an owl's. His hands - gnarled, in old scars from gravers - lay on the table motionless, like those of a man who knows the price of every movement.

Beside him on a stool sat a boy of about ten - his grandson, as I understood later - polishing a silver ring with a bit of suede, his tongue stuck out so intently that he did not notice us come in.

"Aram," said the old man, not raising his head. "Guests."

The boy jumped up, bowed. Akmal began quickly to speak, pointing at me. Karapet listened, then took the loupe from his eye and looked at me - long, searchingly.

And spoke - in broken but quite comprehensible language to me, with a heavy, sing-song accent:

"You - stranger. Suleyman agha sent? Good. Suleyman agha good man. Honest. Forty years ago sold me silk for my daughter's wedding and did not cheat by one cubit. Show what you brought."

I untied the pouch and poured the stones out onto the black velvet of his table.

Karapet did not touch them at once. He looked. For a long time. Then he fitted the loupe in his eye again, bent - so low that he almost touched the stones with his nose - and froze.

The silence stretched. Aram, forgetting the ring, stared at his grandfather with open mouth. Akmal shifted from foot to foot.

"Hm," said Karapet at last. He took the black stone with two fingers - carefully, as one takes a fledgling. Turned it. Then the white. Then laid both back and took off the loupe.

"Not agate," he said. "Not onyx. Not obsidian. Not marble. Not jasper." He bent his gnarled fingers. "Fifty years I hold stones. My father held. His father held. I know stones from Persia, from India, from Egypt, from the Urals, from Brazil. Such - I do not know."

"And the polish?"

"Polish..." Karapet shook his head. "Polish - not human. Man polishes - traces remain. Small, under loupe visible: back-forth, back-forth. Here - no traces. As if water rolled it a thousand years. But water rolls - stone round. And this one - not round. This one - as it should be." He paused. "As if someone said to the stone: be like this. And it became."

I told him about the warmth. About the dawn. About the pattern.

Karapet did not laugh. He looked at me over his spectacles - with a long, heavy look.

"Aram," he said, not taking his eyes from me. "A candle."

The boy brought a candle, lit it from a lamp. Karapet took the white stone with tongs - thin, jeweller's - and held it to the flame. He held it long. The stone, by all laws, should have blackened from soot. It did not blacken. Karapet held it. We all watched.

And suddenly - at first barely noticeable, then more distinct - on the smooth surface of the stone lines showed through. Thin, flowing, running into one another. The same tracery. The same as at dawn.

Aram gasped and sprang back. Akmal clutched my sleeve. Karapet did not stir - only his hand, holding the tongs, faintly trembled.

He took the stone away from the fire. The pattern lasted a few moments more - and melted like breath on glass.

The old man sat silent for a long while. Then he laid the stone back on the velvet, took off his spectacles, wiped them on the skirt of his robe and put them on again.

"My grandfather," he said at last quietly, "told me one story. When I was like Aram. About a man who came to this shop. Long ago. Very long ago. Grandfather was young then, and in the shop sat his father. The man came - a stranger, without a name, in strange clothes. Brought two stones. Black and white. Asked what they were. Great-grandfather heated the stone on a candle - and saw letters. No one could read."

My throat went dry.

"What became of that man?"

"I do not know." Karapet shrugged. "He left. Grandfather said - he said a strange thing, leaving. Said: 'I shall come once more. Perhaps not I, but I shall come.' Grandfather thought - madman. Not a few madmen in Istanbul." He paused. "I thought so too. Fifty years I thought so."

He pushed the stones toward me over the velvet - carefully, with two fingers.

"Take. Do not sell. Show to no one. Especially to those who will ask where from." And, after a pause, he added: "And a riddle I shall tell you. For the road. My grandfather said - that man left it. To great-grandfather. No one solved it."

He pronounced it slowly, with difficulty picking the words of a foreign tongue:

"'Two stones - day and night. One keeps, the other leads. Who holds both - he stands in doors. Where he looks - there home.'"

I repeated it to myself. Then again.

Who holds both - he stands in doors.

I remembered the black grille which I had never seen. No - did not remember: felt, as one remembers a smell from a childhood that did not exist. A door behind which another world lay. A threshold on which one stands, belonging to neither room. I shook my head, driving off this feeling - it had no relation to me, I was sure. Almost sure.

"What is the answer?" I asked.

"If I knew the answer," said Karapet, fitting the loupe in his eye again and bending over his work as though the talk were over, "I would not sit in the shop fifty years. Go, stranger. To Suleyman - a bow. And come when you have solved it. I am interested."

* * *
On the way back Akmal nevertheless brought me to the ships.

We came out to the gulf - to that very strip of water I had seen from the balcony - and it proved at close range not a strip at all but a whole world. Masts stood so thickly that between them the opposite shore could not be seen: tall sailing ships with furled sails, pot-bellied merchantmen, narrow rowers' boats darting to and fro among them like water-striders, and smoking steamers with enormous paddle wheels at their sides. Gulls cried. Boatmen cried. Porters cried, tossing sacks, bales and barrels from shoulder to shoulder. It smelled of fish, tar, salt water and coal.

Akmal raced along the quay like a dog let off the leash, showing me now one ship, now another, naming them - probably by flags, by names on the sides - and each time his face shone as though he were showing me his friends. Somewhere there, among these masts, I thought, ten years ago had stood the ship on which his father had gone to Crete. Akmal had been quite small then. He could not remember him. But he came here, I was sure, as Grandmother every evening sang her song: in order to wait.

At the very edge of the quay, on an upturned barrel, sat an old sailor mending a net, and, noticing my glance, asked Akmal something, nodding at me. Akmal answered. The sailor laughed and said something at which the boy blushed.

We walked home, and the pouch at my belt was cool and light, as befits a pouch with two ordinary stones. I kept my palm on it the whole way. Who holds both - he stands in doors. Where he looks - there home.

And where do I look, I thought. And where is my home.

At the gate Kemal was waiting for us. Seeing me, he silently held out a sheet of paper - folded in four, like that blank sheet that lay in my pocket. I unfolded it.

On the sheet in charcoal two doors were drawn. Side by side, wall to wall. One - open, the other - shut. And between them, on the threshold, with his back to the viewer - a man. Small, barely distinguishable. With a turban on his head.

And in each hand - a little circle. One black. The other white.

I raised my eyes to Kemal. He shrugged - quite like an adult - and pointed to the sky, as he had done yesterday. Then he laid his palms together under his cheek. Then he raised one finger.

Tonight. He had drawn this tonight. Sitting at my threshold.

I put the drawing in my pocket, with the note and the blank sheet. Now there were three.

The sun stood already high - it was nearing noon. From the house came Yusuf's voice calling the boys, and I went up to my balcony, deciding that after this morning I had a right simply to sit, thinking of nothing, and watch the city. I felt through the cloth the pouch at my belt - cooled, ordinary, unremarkable to the touch - and caught myself in the thought that for the first time in all this time I knew firmly at least one thing: whatever was happening to me in this city, in this body, in this life deprived of memory and name - these stones were not merely stones.

And I was not the first who had carried them in his pocket.

## Chapter XII. A Night by the Temple Pond

The moon rose slowly that night, reluctantly, as though the weariness of the parched earth had been passed on to it too.
