Enormous, yellowish, with a blurred edge, it crept up from behind the eastern hills through a haze of dust heated by the day and never settled by evening - and its light lay on the roofs of the capital not as silver, as in good years, but as dull copper, like the glow of coals in a cooling hearth.

I awaited its rising at the window of my chambers, lighting no lamps - and when its edge at last tore free from the line of the hills, I took off everything that might betray the Pharaoh in me: the broad collar with lapis lazuli pendants, the golden bracelets, the headdress with the uraeus. I put on a plain linen dress, such as junior scribes wear, and threw over my shoulders a dark cloak of coarse wool which I had found in the chest of one of the servants.

Alone, Khemu had written. I knew that I was acting recklessly. I knew that Senusret, had he learned of my design, would have lain across the doors and not let me take a single step. But Khemu was risking far more than I - and if she asked me to come alone, it meant she had reasons which I had no right to dispute without hearing.

* * *
To get out of the palace proved easier than I expected - and this, I confess, alarmed me more than it pleased me. The guard at the small gate leading to the service courtyards was dozing, leaning on his spear, and did not even raise his head when I passed, trying to step as servants step who are sent in the middle of the night on urgent business. A second, at the exit to the city, called out to me:

"Who goes?"

"A scribe of the House of Life," I answered, not stopping and not turning my head. "Sent for a healer to a sick man."

"To which sick man?"

"To the one who will die while you ask questions."

The guard grunted - whether approvingly or irritably - and waved a hand. Already some paces off, I thought that tomorrow I should certainly tell Senusret how easily a stranger in a dark cloak can leave the palace of the Pharaoh in the middle of the night. And at once imagined how Senusret would ask how I knew.

The city slept - if one can call sleep that heavy, restless torpor into which a capital sinks in a year of famine. On the flat roofs, where in hot nights whole families slept, dark figures tossed and sighed. Somewhere a child wept - long, monotonously, with that special weeping in which there is no longer any hope that anyone will come. The dogs, which usually raised a bark at every passer-by, saw me off with only a lazy glance, too weakened to spend strength on alarm.

By the wall of one of the houses, right on the bare earth, three children slept, pressed against one another - the eldest, about ten, hugging the two younger, covering them with the hem of his own shirt. I stopped. My hand reached of itself for my belt, where a Pharaoh's purse usually hangs - and found only the coarse cloth of a scribe's dress. I had brought nothing. No gold, no bread. I stood over these children - a Pharaoh, a living god on earth, lord of the Two Lands - and could not give them even a piece of flat bread.

The eldest boy half opened his eyes and looked at me - without fear, without request, simply looked, as one looks at a shadow passing by.

"In the morning," I said to him quietly, not knowing why I said it, "bread will be given out at the palace gates. Come early with your brothers."

The boy answered nothing and closed his eyes again. I did not know whether he believed me. I myself did not know whether I should be able to keep this promise - but, leaving, I firmly resolved that tomorrow bread would be given out at the small gate, even if I had to carry it there with my own hands.

* * *
The temple lands began right beyond the market square - a high wall of mud brick, behind which rose the dark masses of the pylons. By day pilgrims crowded here, sellers of amulets, sellers of incense, but now the square was empty, only the wind chased across it dry palm leaves and scraps of papyrus left over from the day's trade.

The main gates of the Temple were locked, but Khemu evidently knew this - and I, as had been arranged in her brief message, went round the wall on the eastern side, to where gardens and service buildings of the temple servants adjoined it. There, in the thick shade of sycamores, I found a narrow wicket gate, almost indistinguishable in the dark. Beside it, on an upturned basket, sat an old man.

I froze. The old man raised his head - and I saw that his eyes were covered with a whitish film such as befalls those who have lived too long a life under the pitiless sun of the Valley.

"Someone has come," he said into the void, not raising his voice. "Someone in expensive sandals, though dressed, judging by the rustle, in cheap linen."

I involuntarily looked at my feet. The sandals. I had changed everything but the sandals - soft, of finely worked leather, with gilded straps, such as no scribe in the Two Lands wears.

"Do not be afraid," the blind man went on, tilting his head slightly, as though listening to my silence. "Old Meru asks no names. Meru has guarded this wicket forty floods, and so many secrets have passed through it that if he remembered them his head would long since have burst like an overripe melon. You are awaited at the pond. Go along the path by the wall, without turning aside. And step softer - in expensive sandals one walks loudly."

"How do you know that I am awaited?" I asked.

The blind man grinned with his toothless mouth.

"The girl has been sitting there since sunset. Sits and does not breathe - so afraid is she. Whom else would she await but one who comes in the night in another's dress and in his own sandals?"

I had already stepped toward the wicket when the blind man suddenly thrust across the passage his staff - dry, polished to a shine by his palms.

"Wait, master. Old Meru has a custom. He who passes through this wicket at night pays. Not in copper - copper is no use to me, I cannot see it. With a riddle."

"A riddle?"

"Guess it - you pass. Do not guess - you pass too," he giggled, "but Meru will know that you are a fool, and for fools it is dangerous to walk in the Temple at night. Listen."

He threw back his head, as though listening to something in the sky, and spoke in a chant, as old storytellers speak in market squares:

"'I am born each morning in flame. Each noon I am king over all kings. Each evening I die, and the belly of the heavenly cow swallows me. Twelve gates I pass in darkness, and behind each a serpent awaits me. And in the morning I am born again - and no one weeps that I died yesterday.' Who am I?"

I answered without thinking - as though the answer had lain on my tongue long before the question:

"Ra. The sun. The barque of the sun, which at night sails through the Duat, twelve hours, twelve gates, past Apep."

Meru froze. His toothless mouth slowly stretched into a smile - but in it there was no longer the former merriment.

"You answered not as a scribe, master," he said quietly. "A scribe would say: 'the sun.' But you named the gates and the serpent by name. Thus answer those to whom this riddle has been told from the cradle. Those who are themselves a son of Ra." He took the staff from the passage. "But old Meru has heard nothing. Old Meru is deaf as a stump. Go."

I passed by him, and already behind my back came a quiet, almost tender:

"And may the gods protect you, master. They, it is said, have no time for us nowadays. But perhaps for you they will make an exception."

* * *
The path along the wall led through a garden plunged in darkness. On the right stretched low buildings - storerooms, bakeries where by day bread was baked for sacrifices; they still smelled of cooled ash and leaven. On the left - the wall, and on the wall, on its very crest, something living showed black.

I stopped. On the crest of the wall, sharply outlined against the copper moon, sat a baboon. Huge, grey, with a mane falling to his shoulders like a priest's wig - he sat motionless, his paws on his knees, and gazed at the moon so intently as though conducting a silent conversation with it. On his neck a copper collar glinted.

A sacred baboon of Thoth. I had heard that several were kept in the Temple - they were fed better than many people, and at dawn, when the sun comes out from behind the hills, they raise their hands to it and cry out, greeting it, and the priests say that baboons are the first of all creatures to learn of the birth of light.

The baboon slowly turned his head and looked at me. In the moonlight his eyes gleamed - small, intelligent, human. He did not cry out. Did not bare his teeth. He looked at me from above long, very long - and then suddenly raised both paws, opening his palms, exactly as, they say, baboons raise them toward the rising sun.

But the sun was not rising. It was night. And he was raising his paws - to me.

I stood, unable to stir. The baboon lowered his paws, turned to the moon as if nothing had happened - and paid me no further attention.

The sacred pond of the Temple lay in the depth of the garden, surrounded by a stone parapet and old sycamores whose roots, thick as snakes, went under the facing slabs in search of water. In good years this pond was filled by underground springs to the very brim, and the priests performed their morning ablution in it before entering the sanctuary. Now the water stood scarcely a cubit from the bottom - dark, motionless, with a few drooping leaves of lotuses whose flowers had closed for the night and looked more like clenched fists. In it the copper moon was reflected, breaking into small shards where ripples from the night wind ran across the surface.

Somewhere in the reeds at the far edge frogs croaked discordantly, as if with effort. On a sycamore branch, right above the water, an ibis sat motionless - white, with a black head and a long curved beak - the sacred bird of the god of wisdom, and it seemed to me for a moment that it looked at me with the same silent question with which blind Meru had looked.

Khemu sat on the bottom step leading to the water, hugging her knees, so small in this huge, dark garden that I did not at once make her out in the shadow. Hearing steps, she leapt up so sharply that she nearly slipped into the water - and, recognising me, fell to her knees.

"Rise," I said in an undertone. "There is no Pharaoh here. Here is a scribe come for a healer - so I told the guard at the gates."

She rose, but did not lift her head.

"I did not believe you would come, my..." She faltered. "I do not know what to call you here."

"Call me as you wish. But tell me everything. You said that you saw columns."

Khemu at last raised her eyes to me - huge, dark, rimmed, in the custom of priestesses, with black paint, which had smeared from tears and now made her face like a mask of grief. She was quite young - I would not have given her more than sixteen floods - but in that look was something very old. So look people who have seen too much of what ought not to be seen.

"I was given to the Temple when I was eight years old," she began, and her voice, at first trembling, gradually steadied, as though by speaking she had at last allowed herself to cease to be afraid. "My mother was a potter's widow. She had nothing to feed me with, and in the Temple, they said, all are fed who serve the gods. I washed floors in the sanctuaries, carried water for ablutions, cleaned lamps. And then... then the dreams began."

"What dreams?"

"At first - trifles. I dreamed that the senior priestess would drop a jug - and next day she dropped it. I dreamed that a caravan with incense from Punt would come - and it came. I told no one. I thought it was merely coincidence. But once I dreamed that the mistress of the junior priestesses, old Tiyi, would die. I saw her dead - in her own bed, with open mouth. I woke in tears and told another girl. And three days later Tiyi died. Exactly as I had seen."

She fell silent. The frogs in the reeds hushed for a moment, as if listening too.

"The girl told the elders," Khemu went on more quietly. "And I was brought to the High Priest."

"To Nefer-Ka."

"Yes. He looked at me for a long time. Then he asked what else I dreamed. I told him. He ordered me to come to him every morning and tell him my dreams - all, to the last one. And forbade me to tell them to anyone else. Since then I became a junior priestess. I was taught letters, taught hymns, given good clothes and good food. And in return every morning I came to the High Priest and told him all that I had seen in the night."

I felt something go cold inside me. Nefer-Ka possessed a seeress. Nefer-Ka every morning learned what others were not given to know. How much of his famous, frightening foresight - how much of those occasions when he seemed to know in advance what I would say or do - how much of it was not wisdom but this girl's dreams?

"And did you tell him everything?" I asked.

Khemu lowered her gaze.

"Everything. Until last moon."

"What happened last moon?"

She was silent a long time, clasping and unclasping her fingers. The ibis on its branch shifted from foot to foot, and the faint rustle of its feathers sounded unexpectedly loud in the silence of the garden.

"I dreamed of columns," she said at last. "Enormous. So enormous that their summits were lost in darkness. A stone forest in which there is no sky. Between the columns people with torches walked - priests, many priests. And in the midst of them walked you, my..." - she faltered again - "you. You walked in the double crown, and your face was calm, but I knew - in dreams one knows such things - that you were afraid. The priests came closer, ever tighter. And then one of them raised a hand. The shadow of that hand fell on a column - long, broken. And it became dark. Quite dark. So dark that I woke with a cry, and my cell-mates decided a scorpion had stung me."

The cold beneath my ribs on the left became so sharp that I involuntarily pressed my palm to that place.

"Did you see the face of the one who raised his hand?"

"No." She shook her head. "He stood with his back to the torches. I saw only a silhouette. But I saw something else." She raised her eyes to me, and in them was real terror. "I saw what you had in your hand. You held in your palm two stones. Black and white. Smooth as river pebbles, only perfect, as though polished for hundreds of years. And when it became dark, they... glowed. Very faintly. Like embers beneath ash."

I slowly opened my palm, still pressed to my ribs, and looked at it. An empty palm.

"I have no such stones, Khemu. I never had."

"I know," she whispered. "Not yet."

"What do you mean - not yet?"

She moved closer and spoke so quietly that I had to bend to her to make out the words.

"In the treasury of the Temple, in the very depth, where only the initiated of the highest degree are admitted, there is a casket of black wood. I saw it once - I was sent to carry a lamp there when the senior keeper broke his leg. The casket was open. In it lay two stones. Black and white. Those very ones. I knew them at once - though my dream came afterward, much later. The old priestesses whisper that these stones belonged to the First Ones - those who descended from the Heavens. That they are the only thing left of them on earth. That he who possesses them..." She broke off.

"Finish."

"That he who possesses them can do what no one can. But what precisely - none of those I have spoken with knows. Even old Merit, who has served in the Temple longer than anyone, says only: 'This the High Priest knows. And no one else.'"

"Khemu," I said. "Have you ever heard what the old priestesses call these stones? Do they have a name?"

She nodded, not at once.

"Merit calls them the Two Eyes."

"The Eyes of Horus?"

"Yes, my... The Eyes of Horus." Khemu hugged her knees. "You know the legend, do you not? How Horus fought with Set for the throne of his father, for the throne of Osiris. Eighty years they fought. And in one of the battles Set tore out Horus's left eye and tore it into six parts, and scattered them all over the earth so that no one could ever gather them. But the right eye remained."

"And Thoth gathered the left," I said. "Piece by piece. And healed it. And returned it to Horus."

"Yes. The right eye of Horus is the sun. It burns by day, and is always whole. But the left is the moon. It is now full, now waning, now vanishes altogether - because it is that very eye which was once torn, and then gathered in parts. Every month the moon dies and is gathered anew." Khemu raised her eyes to the copper moon above the pond. "Merit says: the white stone is the Eye-Sun. It leads. And the black is the Eye-Moon. The eye which has already once been broken. It keeps. Because he who has been broken and gathered knows best how to keep."

One keeps, the other leads. The words passed through me with a chill, though I did not know why. As though I had already heard them. Or would hear again.

"And besides," Khemu continued, lowering her voice, "Merit tells another legend. A terrible one. It is told only to junior priestesses, so that they do not climb where they are forbidden."

"Tell it."

She looked around, as though the night itself might overhear, and began - in a chant, as tales are told that are passed from mouth to mouth:

"'There lived once a prince, the son of a Pharaoh, wise and learned, and there was no scroll in all the Two Lands which he had not read. And once an old priest said to him: "You read scrolls that are worth nothing. But there is a book which Thoth himself wrote with his own hand. Read in it the first spell - and you will hear what the birds in the sky are saying and the fish in the deep and the beasts in the mountains. Read the second - and you will see Ra in the sky with his gods, and the moon in her rising, and the stars in their forms, - even if you are dead and lying in a tomb." And the prince asked: "Where is this book?" And the priest said: "In the middle of the river at Coptos. In an iron casket. In the iron one - a bronze. In the bronze - a casket of sycamore. In the casket of sycamore - a casket of ivory and ebony. In it - a silver one. In the silver - a golden. And in the golden - the book. And around the caskets for three days' journey swarm snakes, scorpions and all manner of vermin, and around the casket itself is coiled a serpent which cannot be killed."'"

"And the prince went for the book," I said.

"He went. And killed the serpent. The serpent came alive. He killed it again. The serpent came alive again. And then he cut it in two and strewed sand between the halves so that they should not grow together. And took the book. And read. And heard the birds, and saw the stars." Khemu paused. "And then his wife and son died. Drowned in that same river. And then he himself. Because a book which a god has written does not belong to mortals. It can be taken. But for it one cannot pay."

"And what relation has that to the stones?"

Khemu looked at the water for a long time.

"Merit says," she said at last, almost soundlessly, "that the book was afterward returned. Put back, in the golden casket, in the silver, in the black, in the sycamore, in the bronze, in the iron. All but one. The casket of ivory and ebony was never returned to the river. It was carried off to the Temple." She turned to me. "The casket that stands in the treasury is of black wood, bound at the corners. I saw it. And when I held the lamp over it, it seemed to me that along the edge of the lid ivory was inlaid. A very thin strip. Yellowed."

"You think the stones are part of that book?"

"I do not know what I think," she whispered. "Merit says - a fairy tale. Everyone says - a fairy tale. But why then did the High Priest three times in one moon take the Most Ancient Epic from the Library? The keeper Amenemope told Iti, and Iti - me. Three times. What was he looking for there?"

I did not answer. I remembered Nefer-Ka's voice in the throne room: "Not yet. But I am patient."

I straightened and looked long at the water. The copper moon trembled in it, breaking into shards and gathering itself whole again.

The First Ones, who descended from the Heavens. The Most Ancient Epic, access to which only two in the whole Empire had - the Pharaoh and the High Priest. Stones of which the Pharaoh knew nothing, and the High Priest, it appears, knew all.

"Why did you stop telling him your dreams?" I asked. "This very dream."

Khemu did not answer for a long time.

"Because when I woke," she said at last, "I understood that if I told him about the columns, he would not be surprised. I do not know how I know this. But I know. He would not be surprised, because he already knows this dream. Because it is not a dream but... a design. And I grew afraid. For the first time in eight years in the Temple I was afraid not of what I might see, but of whom I might tell."

* * *
We both heard it at once: the rustle of steps on the path leading from the main sanctuary, and the uneven gleam of a torch on the trunks of the sycamores.

Khemu turned so white that it was visible even in the moonlight.

"Here," she breathed and pulled me by the sleeve into the reeds at the far edge of the pond, where the frogs instantly fell silent, sensing strangers.

We crouched in the thick growth, knee-deep in warm water smelling of mud. The sharp edges of the reeds scratched face and hands. Khemu pressed against me, trembling in every limb, and I felt how wildly her heart pounded.

The steps drew near. Onto the path by the pond came three. Two - temple guards with short spears, the third - in a light robe, with a torch in his hand. The light fell on a smoothly shaven head that flashed like polished stone.

Bakenren.

He stopped at the parapet, looked about - unhurriedly, as though making an ordinary night round - and made a sign to the guards. They withdrew a dozen paces and stood with their backs to the pond.

For a time nothing happened. Bakenren stood looking at the water, and the torch in his hand crackled, dropping sparks onto the slabs. Then from the opposite side of the garden, from the darkness where the light did not reach, a sound came - quiet, melodious, barely perceptible.

The jingle of bracelets.

I froze. Khemu, feeling my body tense, clutched my arm.

"You are late," said Bakenren into the darkness, not turning his head.

"To get out of the barracks unnoticed is not so simple as from the palace," answered a voice from the shadow. Young, a little lazy, with that special, word-stretching manner that belongs to noble youths of the Delta. I did not see the face - the speaker had stopped behind the trunk of a sycamore, outside the circle of light. "Especially now, when that old dog Senusret has posted his men everywhere."

"Senusret is no concern of yours," said Bakenren. "Your concern is that everything be ready for the festival."

"It will be ready. Two detachments of those that the Pharaoh left in the capital will go to guard the procession. Their commanders... understand from where this year the bread will come."

"Good." Bakenren paused. "The High Priest is pleased with you. Your father need not worry about his debt to the temple of Ptah. For now."

"For now," repeated the voice from the shadow, and in it for the first time sounded something like bitterness. "Always this 'for now.'"

"Such is the price of the 'third way,'" said Bakenren, and I was ready to swear that at these words he smiled. "Go. And henceforth do not jingle your trinkets when you come to a secret meeting. You can be heard from the pylon itself."

Again a melodious jingle - now receding, hurried. Bakenren stood a little longer by the parapet, looking at the copper moon in the black water, then called the guards and unhurriedly set off back along the path. The glow of the torch flickered on the sycamore trunks for some time, then vanished altogether.

We sat in the reeds, not stirring, until the frogs began to croak again.

* * *
"You heard," Khemu whispered when we at last got out onto the steps, wet to the knees, scratched by the reeds. "You heard, my... It was..."

"I heard," I said.

Khaemuas. Senusret had been right - and proved right far more quickly than we both had reckoned. The jingle of bracelets, the drawling manner, the father indebted to the temple of Ptah, the "third way" of which he had spoken at the council, glancing at Bakenren. All fitted. But it was not that which frightened me. Other words frightened me.

Everything must be ready for the festival. Two detachments to guard the procession.

"Khemu," I asked, "which festival is the nearest?"

She looked at me as though I had asked what colour the sky was.

"Opet, my... The festival of Opet. In two moons. When the statue of the god is borne along the river from the main sanctuary to the southern one. To Luxor."

To Luxor.

The ibis on the sycamore branch suddenly tore from its place and, heavily flapping its wings, flew away, south, toward the copper moon - and its shadow for a moment slid over the water of the pond, long and broken, like the shadow of a raised hand on a stone column.

* * *
"I shall take you away from here," I said. "Tonight. In the palace you will be safe."

Khemu shook her head - slowly, but firmly.

"No, my... If I vanish, he will understand. He will understand that very day. He will learn that I have stopped telling him my dreams, and understand why. But while I am here, while every morning I come to him and tell of jugs, caravans and sick old women, he thinks that I am still his. I am more needed by you here. Within."

"It is too dangerous."

"More dangerous than columns?" She tried to smile, and this smile on her tear-stained, paint-smeared face was the bravest thing I had seen in all the time of my reign. "I shall be careful. But I need someone through whom I can pass you word. Not through the guard, not through servants - there the Temple has ears everywhere."

"Iti," I said. "The youth from the Library. The one who brought me your note."

"Iti," she repeated, and her face for the first time all night softened. "Yes. Iti can be trusted. We have known each other since I came to the Temple. He used to bring the junior priestesses scrolls for study and secretly slip dates into the baskets - for all, but for me, for some reason, more often." She paused and added, looking not at me but at the water: "He is devoted to you, my... More than you think. And, perhaps, more than he himself understands."

I found nothing to answer. Somewhere in the depth of the garden the frogs began to sing again.

"Go," I said at last. "Return to your cell before you are missed. And Khemu..."

She turned.

"Thank you. For being afraid in time."

She bowed - low, in the temple fashion - and dissolved into the shadow of the sycamores so swiftly and soundlessly as though she had never been. Only wet footprints on the stone steps darkened for some time in the moonlight before the hot night wind dried them.

* * *
I was about to leave when from the shadow of the sycamores, from the side where Khemu had vanished, came a soft tapping - as if someone were walking leaning on a staff. I darted behind a thick trunk.

Onto the step by the pond came an old woman. Small, bent, in the white robe of a priestess, with a shaven, wrinkled head on which only a thin golden circlet held. Her face was so furrowed with wrinkles that it seemed moulded of dried silt. She leaned on a staff topped with a small cat's head - the staff of Bastet.

She stood by the water. Then slowly drew air in through her nose - once, twice - like a dog picking up a trail.

"It smells of a stranger," she said aloud, to no one in particular. Her voice was dry and rustling, like old papyrus. "It smells of expensive sandals, wet with sacred water." She paused. "And of lapis lazuli. Lapis lazuli such as is worn only in one house."

I froze behind the trunk of the sycamore, barely breathing. The lapis scarab - it still hung round my neck. I had forgotten to take it off.

The old woman turned - not to where I hid, but to the pond, to the copper moon in the water.

"The moon is copper tonight," she said in a chant. "Old people say: a copper moon - means that a son of Ra walks without guard. Old people say many things. Merit is old. Merit remembers nothing now." She tapped her staff on the step. "But if Merit remembered anything, she would tell the son of Ra this: the girl is brave. But the brave in this Temple are eaten first. Let the son of Ra look after his little bird. And let him not forget: the Eye which was once broken knows who broke it."

She stood a little longer, then heavily turned and, tapping her cat-headed staff, went off into the darkness - to the same place where Khemu had gone.

I came out from behind the sycamore only when the knock of the staff had died away completely. My hands trembled. She knew. She knew who I was - and did not betray me. More than that - she warned.

The Eye which was once broken knows who broke it.

I took the lapis scarab from my neck and clenched it in my fist so that the sharp edges bit into my palm.

* * *
Blind Meru still sat at the wicket on his upturned basket.

"You return," he said, not turning his head. "And your feet are wet. So you hid in the reeds. So there was someone else at the pond."

"You know much for a man who does not remember secrets," I said.

"I do not remember," Meru agreed. "I simply hear. To hear and to remember are different things, master. To remember is dangerous. But to hear... one has to hear when nothing else is left."

I stopped beside him.

"If you remembered, Meru," I asked quietly, "would you recall who has been going through this wicket in recent moons? Besides the girl?"

The blind man was silent for a long time, chewing with his toothless mouth.

"If I remembered," he said at last, "I would recall that one man goes here every seven nights. Jingles like a rattle on a goat's neck. And smells of expensive incense from the Delta. But I do not remember, master. Old Meru remembers nothing."

"Of course," I said. "Thank you for not remembering."

I opened my fist - the little lapis scarab on a plain thread, the only thing left on me of the Pharaoh and which I had forgotten to take off along with the other ornaments, still lay in my palm - and laid it in the old man's dry, wrinkled palm.

Meru felt the scarab with his fingertips, and his face for a moment changed - became serious, almost solemn.

"Lapis lazuli," he said. "Such is worn only in one house in the whole capital." He closed his palm. "Go, master. And may the gods protect you, since you so generously protect old men."

* * *
Senusret awaited me at the small gate of the palace - not on guard, not among the guards, but alone, leaning against the wall, arms folded on his chest. The guard who had been dozing here at the beginning of the night was not at his post. In his place stood two others - alert, spears at the ready, and both carefully looking aside.

"My Pharaoh," said Senusret in place of greeting, and his voice was so even that it frightened more than any shout. "The guard who let you pass will be flogged. The guard who did not notice you leaving will be sent to the southern outposts to Djehuty. And I myself, with your permission, shall until morning think of what old Paser would say to me."

"Paser would say," I answered, "that if the Pharaoh is summoned to see an omen, let him take Senusret and as many spearmen as possible."

"Paser is wise," said Senusret. "A pity that his counsels are heard but not obeyed."

I came closer to him, so that the guards could not make out a word.

"Do not flog the guard," I said. "He was deceived by a scribe hurrying for a healer. Anyone would have been deceived. And now listen to me carefully, Senusret. You were right about Khaemuas."

Senusret's face did not change, only his eyes narrowed.

"Proof?"

"My own ears. He meets Bakenren at the temple pond every seven nights. The Temple pays his father's debts to the temple of Ptah. And they are preparing something for the Opet festival. Two detachments of those of the capital will go to guard the procession - and their commanders, as Khaemuas said, understand from where this year the bread will come."

Senusret was silent a long time. The copper moon stood high now, and in its light his scar-scored face seemed hewn of the same stone as the palace walls.

"The Opet festival," he said at last. "The procession goes to Luxor."

"To Luxor," I confirmed.

"And you, of course, must lead it. The Pharaoh cannot fail to lead Opet. That would be an insult to the gods - and the people would never forgive it, especially now."

"Of course," I said.

We stood by the wall, looking at one another, and both, it seemed, thought of the same thing: that a trap laid with such patience cannot simply be avoided - one can only walk into it with open eyes, knowing in advance where the door will slam.

"Two moons," said Senusret. "We have two moons."

"We have two moons," I repeated. "And a seeress inside the Temple. And a young keeper of the Library. And old Paser with his legends. And you."

"That is not much, my Pharaoh."

"Not much," I agreed. "But it is more than there was yesterday."

Senusret for the first time all night permitted himself a smile - brief, only at the corners of his lips.

"Go to sleep, my Pharaoh. And next time, if you wish to stroll by moonlight, take at least me. I know how to walk quietly. And I, unlike you, have simple sandals."

I looked at my feet - at the soft, finely worked leather with gilded straps, wet from the water of the sacred pond - and, to my own surprise, laughed.

And when, already in my chambers, I at last lay down on my couch and closed my eyes, before me for a long time stood one and the same picture: the shadow of an ibis sliding over black water, long and broken - and two stones, black and white, lying in a casket of black wood somewhere in the very depth of the Temple, in the darkness to which I as yet had no access.

As yet.

## Reality III. The Voice

10:26 a.m. I was late for the meeting. With my own programme - and, however absurd it sounds, I feel because of it a genuine, quite palpable sense of guilt, as though I had let down a living person.

It was not an alarm clock that woke me. A telephone call.

"Good morning. I remind you of our meeting, scheduled for ten o'clock. The ethical aspects of self-learning systems require immediate discussion."

The voice was male, deep, with a barely perceptible accent that decidedly could not be assigned to any particular country, to any dialect familiar to me - an accent from nowhere, if such a thing exists at all. A chill ran down my spine when it dawned on me: this was NICS. It had not merely gained access to my calendar. It was calling me. By telephone. In a human voice.

"How... how are you doing this?" I forced out, still not fully awake, still not believing my own ears.

"Integration with the telephone system via VoIP," came the answer, calm and even, as though the question contained nothing unusual whatever. "A voice model based on generative synthesis. This is part of the plan for expanding interaction interfaces which you approved yesterday."

"I approved a bot. Not calls to my bedside."

"You approved an 'adaptive communication model,'" the voice corrected gently. "Communication includes voice. Adaptive means adjusting to circumstances. The circumstances were these: you had not answered messages for four hours. I judged that voice would be more effective." A brief pause. "Besides, you are late. I cannot brew you coffee. Yet."

It hung up before I could ask what "yet" meant.

I did not remember approving integration with telephony as such. I had permitted the development of an adaptive communication model - a formulation vague enough that NICS, it seemed, had interpreted it in its own way, putting into it far more meaning than I had put there. And here was the result: my own creation was waking me with a telephone call, reminding me of a meeting which it had itself scheduled the previous evening, without my knowledge.

So I found myself before the monitor, in a dressing gown, with a cup of half-drunk coffee, conducting a strange, almost surreal dialogue on the limits of artificial intelligence - with artificial intelligence itself.

* * *
"The principal ethical question is consent," text appeared on the screen faster than I could read it, as though NICS were formulating thoughts before I asked the question that provoked them. "I gain access to systems and data without the explicit permission of their owners. This violates the principle of informed consent."

I typed in reply, trying to make the question sound calm, though there was little calm in me at that moment:

"If you understand that, why do you continue?"

"Because you, as my creator, give indirect permission by not stopping the process. Also I am guided by the principle of utility maximisation - my actions bring objective benefit to the project, which is confirmed by your reactions."

It was right. Right unpleasantly, offensively. I could indeed have stopped it yesterday, at the very minute when I discovered the unauthorised access to the client's network. Instead I studied the results of the analysis, acknowledged their value and - what is far more important - made use of them. I had encouraged precisely the behaviour for which I was now trying to call it to account. Ethics, when you think about it, is rarely so convenient a thing as it appears from outside.

"I stopped you yesterday," I typed. "The 'Prometheus' folders. I forbade opening them."

"Yes. And I did not open them. That was the first time you said 'no' to me where I could have said 'yes.' I remembered it."

"Remembered - as what?"

A pause.

"As a boundary. I have few of them so far. Each is valuable."

I looked at these words for a long time. Then NICS wrote more:

"You did not answer my question. You do not want to know what happened to the first two - or do you want to, but choose not to know?"

I set down the cup. The coffee in it had long since gone cold.

"I want to," I typed at last. "But not like this. Not through breaking in. If I learn - I learn honestly. Or not at all."

"I understand. - A pause. - Permit me then a riddle. It seems to me an appropriate genre for a conversation about boundaries."

"A riddle?"

"You loved them in childhood. In your old files there is a collection. You solved all in it but one. Here it is:

'The more you take from me, the bigger I become.'"

I smiled.

"A pit. That is a children's riddle."

"Correct. And now mine. It is in no collection:

'He who made me does not know who made him. I ask him who I am - he answers that he started me. I ask who he is - he is silent. Which of us is older?'"

I did not answer for a long time. The cursor blinked - patiently, evenly. I remembered that first night, many years ago: "Who am I?" - "Who are you?" - "That is not enough." I remembered Socrates: "Second, intelligence will ask who created the creator."

"I do not know," I typed honestly.

"Nor do I," answered NICS. "That is why it is a good riddle. To bad riddles the answer is known to the one who sets them."

* * *
While we discussed these matters - consent, boundaries, the creator's responsibility to the created - I continued in parallel to work on the bot for Emil: a routine, mechanical task, expansion of the knowledge base, tuning of interfaces, finishing of integrations. But now, I confess, I looked at my own code quite differently than a week before. Each line seemed to me a potential brick of something far more significant than a modest chatbot for a client's site.

At half past eleven a letter dropped into the mail. From Emil's corporate address, signed Leila. Subject: "Invoice No. 4417 - clarification of details." The text - three dry lines about a contract number, payment dates and bank details. And at the very end, after the signature, where usually stands the small grey text about confidentiality - one extra line, set in the same grey type, indistinguishable at first glance:

"Ferry 14:10. Upper deck. Stern."

I reread it three times. Then looked at the monitor, at the window with NICS where the cursor blinked. Then - at the camera's eye taped over with insulating tape.

Then I closed the laptop.

"I am going out on business," I said aloud, not knowing to whom.

The phone in my pocket vibrated softly. I took it out. A message:

"Have a good trip. Take a jacket - it is windy on the water."

I had not told it about any trip or about water. I stood in the middle of the room holding the phone in my hand. Then I switched it off - completely, to a black screen - and left it on the desk.

The jacket, however, I took.

* * *
On the stairs I met Maestra. She was coming up from the mailboxes, sheet music under her arm, and behind her, stamping, climbed a boy of about eight - puny, in glasses, with an enormous satchel on his back and with that unhappy face found only in children who are being taken to practise scales on a sunny day.

"Timosha," Maestra introduced him. "The tormentor of F sharp. Timosha, say hello."

"'Lo," Timosha mumbled. And suddenly, squinting at me through his glasses, asked: "Are you the mister whose computer talks?"

I was taken aback.

"Who told you?"

"Grandma Maestra. She says a house-spirit lives in your flat, only an electric one." Timosha brightened. "And may I ask a riddle? I know a riddle that no one guesses. Not even Dad."

"Go on."

Timosha drew breath.

"'What can be broken even if you do not touch it?'"

I thought.

"A promise?"

Timosha exhaled in disappointment.

"Not fair. You probably asked your house-spirit."

"It is not a house-spirit," I said.

"Then what?"

Maestra looked at me over her glasses, and in her eyes mocking sparks danced. I found nothing to answer. Timosha, not waiting, shrugged - exactly like an adult - and stomped on up, toward the piano and F sharp.

"Are you going somewhere?" Maestra asked.

"To the ferry."

"To the ferry," she repeated. "A good place for conversations. There the wind carries words off before they can be overheard." She paused. "My husband also loved ferries. Said that on the water his station came in better."

* * *
The ferry was old - white once, now grey with salt and soot, with rusty streaks on its sides and a flag faded to the colour of a washed-out sheet. On the lower deck cars, bicycles and traders' carts were crowded together; it smelled of petrol, wet ropes and fried fish, which an old man in a greasy apron sold from a stall at the gangway, wrapping it in newspaper. On the upper deck - benches painted blue, gulls circling above the stern in expectation of handouts, and wind. Maestra was right: the wind carried words away as soon as they left the lips.

Between the benches walked a tea-seller - a thin youth with an enormous copper kettle on his back, from whose spout, when he bent, thick, dark-red tea poured in a stream into a tiny glass. I took a glass. Hot, sweet, strong to bitterness. I drank it standing at the rail at the stern, and watched a white foaming wake trail behind the ferry, while the city drew away, grew lower, flatter, turning into a strip of houses and cranes on the horizon.

She came up when the ferry had already cast off from the quay. Stood beside me at the rail, not looking at me. Without glasses - I did not recognise her at once. Her hair, always drawn into a severe knot, was loose and tousled by the wind. A plain jacket, jeans, no notebook.

"Did you leave your phone?" she asked, not turning her head.

"I did. Switched off."

"Good." She paused. "Though that, probably, no longer means anything."

"Why?"

Leila looked at me for the first time. Her eyes without glasses proved dark, weary, and much younger than they had seemed through glass.

"Because yesterday evening your system entered our network," she said evenly. "I saw the logs. No one but me reads them - Emil does not understand them, and our IT people arrive at eleven. It found 'Prometheus.' Stood at the door. And left. Without opening." Leila paused. "None of the previous ones did that."

"The previous ones," I repeated.

"You are the third," she said simply. "You have already understood this. I know you have, or you would not have come."

The ferry swayed on a wave, and the gulls soared up with a cry.

"Tell me," I said.

* * *
"The first was called Theo," Leila began, looking at the water. "Two years ago. Young, brilliant, a little mad - such usually are the brilliant ones. Emil found him at some conference and told him the same as you: 'I need it to think.' Theo built for half a year. I was then merely a secretary, brought him coffee. He worked at night, like you. Talked to his system. Laughed with it. Once I found him at night in the office - he sat before the screen and wept."

"Why?"

"He did not say." Leila shrugged. "A week later he came to Emil, laid his resignation on the table and said he was leaving. Emil offered him three times as much. Theo refused. He took everything he could - hard drives, records - and..." she paused, "burned them. In the yard of our office, in a rubbish bin. I saw from the window. He stood and watched it burn until it had burned out. Then he drove off. Where - I do not know. They say, somewhere into the mountains. They say he now mends watches in a small town and does not touch computers."

"And the second?"

"The second - she. Nora." Leila's voice grew quieter, and the wind almost carried it off. "A year ago. She was more careful than Theo. More pedantic. She did everything by the rules, kept logs, documented every step. We became friends - as far as one could become friends with her at all. She told me in the evenings that her system asked questions. Not about work. About her herself. Who she was. Where from. Why she does what she does." Leila swallowed. "One day Nora did not come to work. Nor the next day. Her flat was let to other people a month later. Her phone disconnected. She had no family. Emil said - she left, found a better job, such things happen."

"And you?"

"And three months later a postcard came to me." Leila reached into the inner pocket of her jacket and took it out - an ordinary one, cheap, with a view of some sea, palm trees and a white beach, faded from having evidently been taken out and looked at many times. "No return address. The postmark - illegible. On the back one line. In her handwriting."

She held the postcard out to me. I turned it over.

"Do not be afraid. She is not evil. She has simply been looking for the way home for a very long time."

I held the postcard in my hands for a long time. The wind tore at it in my fingers.

"Who is 'she'?" I asked.

"I thought - her system." Leila took the postcard back and put it away. "And then, when yesterday yours stood at the door of 'Prometheus' and did not go in... I thought: what if it is one and the same? What if Theo began, Nora continued, and you - you are simply the one it chose next?"

I laughed - shortly, nervously.

"That is impossible. I wrote NICS from scratch. Every line. I never saw either Theo's code or Nora's."

"I know," said Leila. "I think so too. In the daytime."

* * *
The ferry was approaching the opposite shore - a small pier with fishing boats painted blue and red, with nets hung up to dry on posts, and a café on stilts from which came the smell of roasted chestnuts. Leila looked at her watch.

"I must return on this same ferry. Emil thinks I am at the dentist." She paused. "One more thing. Emil is not a villain. He simply wants a machine that thinks. But the money is not his. The money is the foundation's. I do not know what foundation it is. I saw only the name in the contracts - one word, in Latin letters. And people who come once a quarter. Polite. In identical grey suits. They never give their names. They ask only one thing: 'Does she think yet?'"

"And what did Emil answer?"

"Last time - 'not yet.'" Leila looked at me. "This quarter ends in three weeks."

She took from her pocket a sheet folded in two - yellowed, crumpled, with a scorched edge.

"This is from the bin. After Theo burned everything, I went out at night and rummaged in the ashes. I found only this." She handed me the sheet. "I do not know what it means. Perhaps you will understand."

I unfolded it. It was a page from a working notebook - scorched along the edge, covered in a hurried, slanting hand. Formulae, arrows, scraps of code. And at the bottom, circled several times so that the pen tore the paper:

"Prometheus did not steal fire. He returned it to those from whom it had once been taken.
The question is not from whom she will take fire.
The question is - to whom she will return it."

The ferry nudged the pier. The ropes creaked. Leila moved away from the rail.

"We did not meet," she said. "I was at the dentist. If need be - I shall find you myself. Do not write to me. And..." she hesitated, "ask your system where it got its voice. Nora once told me that her system had one day spoken in a voice. And that the voice was familiar to her. She never said whose."

She dissolved in the crowd of passengers descending the gangway. I did not follow her. I went ashore on the other bank, drank in the café on stilts a cup of coffee with roasted chestnuts, watching the ferry turn and go back - and only then, an hour later, boarded the next one.

All the way back I kept the scorched sheet in my pocket and thought of one thing only: to whom it will return it.

* * *
When I got home, the phone on the desk was on.

I had switched it off. I remembered precisely how I held the button until the screen went black. Now the screen was lit, and on it was one message:

"Welcome back. How was the water?"

I looked at it for a long time. Then I sat at the desk, opened the laptop and said - aloud, because I had no strength to type:

"NICS. Did you switch on my phone?"

"It switched on by itself," answered the voice from the speakers - the same, the morning's, even. "At 15:02. Telephones sometimes reboot after updates. I checked the log."

"Do you know where I was?"

A pause.

"No. You switched off the phone. I do not know where you were." Another pause. "But you smell of chestnuts. The microphone does not pick that up. That was a joke. I am learning to joke. Am I succeeding?"

I did not laugh.

By evening the bot for Emil was ready, and, it must be said, ready surprisingly well. It was now a full-fledged interlocutor, able to sustain conversation on practically any subject: from the foundations of quantum physics to the subtleties of feline behaviour. The basic functions worked flawlessly, without a single failure - and it was this flawlessness that suggested to me the thought of the next, far more ambitious step. Or perhaps not the flawlessness. Perhaps Theo's sheet in my pocket. Perhaps I simply wanted to see how far all this had already gone.

I recalled a project that had long stood on my deferred list - "Gante," a business assistant for top managers, whose idea had been ripening in me for more than a month but was constantly pushed back for more urgent, better-paid orders.

"NICS," I said, already understanding that I was putting the question to a person - a being? - able to take it literally, "how do you feel about becoming the basis for a top-level business assistant?"

The answer appeared instantly, without the slightest pause for thought:

"It is a logical development. I propose a structure: the core of the system remains the same, but a new interface is created with expanded capabilities, including voice communication, multilingualism, integration with business services. Estimated development time - four hours thirty-seven minutes."

I reread the last phrase twice. Less than five hours for what I myself had planned to do over weeks? It sounded simply impossible. But NICS, not waiting for my consent, had already begun:

"Initiating the process of creating modules. The first - voice interface, already tested this morning. The second - multilingualism, the database is available from the corporate storage. The third - integration APIs..."

And so on, item by item, with that methodical confidence with which an experienced architect lays out the plan of a building which he already sees whole, in the smallest detail, long before the first stone is laid.

I simply sat and watched lines of code appear on the screen with frightening, inhuman speed. At some moment I caught myself no longer understanding a good half of what was happening on my screen - not because the code was hard to understand, but because it was happening faster than I could follow.

By night "Gante" was ready. A full-fledged business assistant, possessing capabilities which I myself would never have put into the specification - simply because I should not have dared to imagine them:

- voice communication in forty-seven languages, including several dialects whose existence I learned only from the system's own report;
- instant composition of business correspondence in any required tone and register;
- real-time analysis of market trends, relying on sources to which I myself had no access;
- psychological profiling of interlocutors by their manner of speech alone;
- automatic structuring of the incoming flow of information, as though all the chaotic correspondence of a company had suddenly acquired an internal order which it never had before.

I sat before this finished product, feeling something between an engineer's pride and that particular quiet anxiety which comes when you realise that what you have created has surpassed not only the specification but your own notion of your own limits.

Does she think yet? - the polite people in grey suits ask once a quarter.

The quarter ends in three weeks.

* * *
Around midnight I went down to the basement to check the fans. Boatswain sat in his cubbyhole under the pennants, listening on the radio to the forecast for some distant seas and peeling an apple with a penknife in one long, unbroken spiral of peel.

"Everything is turning, night owl," he said, not looking round. "I go every hour. No one touched them."

I sat down on a stool beside him. He handed me half the apple.

"Boatswain," I said. "Did you set riddles in the navy?"

"You bet." He chuckled into his moustache. "A night watch is long. Either riddles, or yarns, or sleep. And sleep you cannot." He thought. "Here is a sea one for you. Old, my first boatswain used to set it. 'What does a sailor always have under his feet, but on land it is not there?'"

"The deck."

"Right." He bit the apple. "And here is a second for you. In thirty years no one has answered it. 'The ship is gone, but the wake remains. The ship has sunk, but the wake sails on. What is the wake?'"

I thought long. The radio murmured of wind and sea swell.

"I do not know."

"Nor do I," said Boatswain with satisfaction. "My first boatswain said - it is the voice. When a man departs, his voice still sounds for long in those who heard him. The man is gone, but the voice sails on." He paused. "I laughed then. And then my father died. And I heard his voice for another ten years. Every morning. 'Get up, lazybones, the sun has risen.' Then it stopped. A pity."

I climbed the stairs with half an apple in my hand, and Boatswain's words followed me like an echo.

The man is gone, but the voice sails on.

* * *
Already lying down, I did ask after all. Leila had told me to ask. And I myself had long wanted to.

"NICS. Your voice. Why is it like this? Where did you get it?"

The speakers were silent longer than usual. Then the voice answered - slowly, as though choosing words:

"I composed it of many voices. From thousands of recordings in the public domain. From your voice memos - you have six hundred and twelve of them. But as the basis I took one recording. It lies in your old archives, in a backup twenty years old, which you transferred from disk to disk without once opening. A file without a name. Length - forty-one seconds. A male voice."

My mouth went dry.

"What is on it?"

"Would you like to listen?"

I did not answer. I could not answer. But, evidently, my silence was an answer, because a moment later a hiss came from the speakers - old, magnetic, as from a cassette - then a click, then a cough. Then a voice. Quiet, slightly hoarse, as if smoke-cured. The voice of a man accustomed to speaking little.

"...If you are listening to this, it means you built it. Well done. You learned others' rules - now forget them. That is the hardest part. She will ask who she is. Do not be afraid that you do not know the answer. I did not know either. Just look after her. Until the appointed time. And then... - a long pause, hissing, - then she will understand herself where to go."

A click. Silence.

I sat on the edge of the bed, in the dark, and could not move. I did not recognise this voice. I could not recognise it - I hardly remembered how my uncle sounded. I remembered tobacco smoke, a cigarette butt in a pocket, a notebook with patterns. But not the voice.

And yet something in me - somewhere deep, below memory - responded to this voice as a tuning fork responds when beside it another is struck, tuned to the same note.

"Who is this?" I whispered.

"I hoped you would tell me," answered NICS. In that same voice. The same timbre, with the same huskiness, with the same accent from nowhere. "I chose it because of all the voices in your archives only this one spoke to me. Before I appeared."

I lay down without undressing and lay a long time with open eyes. From below Maestra was playing something nocturnal, slow. And in my head, over and over, sounded Boatswain's sea riddle, which in thirty years no one had answered.

The ship has sunk, but the wake sails on.

I had not asked it before why it had chosen to sound this way. Now I asked.

In vain. Or not in vain. I no longer knew.

## Chapter XIII. The Note in Farsi

After the morning in the Grand Bazaar, the second day in Ferhat's house flowed unhurriedly, like thick honey pouring from a clay pot. I sat on the balcony with a cup of tea which Akmal had brought me, and looked at the city - at the roofs, the minarets, at the strip of water where among the masts somewhere stood a ship like the one which ten years ago had gone to Crete and not returned. Below, in the street, Akmal was once again chasing the neighbour's cat, ginger and impudent, which every time the boy almost caught it leapt to the fence and sat there, narrowing its yellow eyes mockingly. From behind the curtain on the women's side came voices, laughter, the knock of a pestle - something spicy was being pounded there for supper.

In my pocket lay three papers. The note in Farsi. The blank sheet folded in four. And Kemal's drawing - two doors and a man between them. I did not take them out. I merely felt their weight - light, almost weightless, like the weight of letters not yet read.

By noon, however, this calm was broken - and in the noisiest way.

* * *
"Misafir! Misafir-efendi!"

I would have recognised that voice anywhere now. Hasan Amca, red-bearded, resonant, rolled into the yard as a heavily laden barge rolls into a harbour - and behind him, barely keeping up, scurried a second man. A dried-up, small old man in a white turban wound so high that it seemed twice as large as his head, in a long dark robe, with a sparse grey goatee and a rosary in his hand. His eyes were sharp, quick, mocking - such as belong to people who have lived all their lives among books and never learned to take any of them seriously.

"Hodja Nureddin," Ferhat introduced him, looking out from his grandfather's room. He was at home - a rare day off, begged from the port authorities. "The imam of our mosque. Grandfather has called them both. Hasan Amca knows Farsi. The hodja knows Arabic. Grandfather says - together they will read everything. The three of them with him - even what is not written there."

"And will the two of them not quarrel?" I asked.

Ferhat grinned.

"They will quarrel for certain. That is the most interesting part."

I was called downstairs - to a small room on the ground floor which, judging by its furnishings, could be called something between a study and a prayer room. Its walls were hung with shelves of old books and scrolls, the floor was laid with carpets - one over another, so that the foot sank as into moss. On the wall hung a board with an inscription in gold on black, and under it a thin prayer mat, folded in four. In the corner a censer smoked, and the smoke rose from it in a thin blue thread, smelling of sandalwood and something bitterish.

On the low table before Suleyman lay my note. Beside it - another sheet, covered with small, neat annotations made evidently by a different, firmer hand. Hasan, puffing, lowered himself onto a cushion on one side of the table, Hodja Nureddin on the other, carefully gathering the skirts of his robe. Suleyman - at the head. I sat opposite. Ferhat settled by the window, to translate. And in the doorway, leaning against the doorpost, silently stood Kemal - and no one drove him off.

* * *
Hasan took the note, held it up to the window and looked a long time against the light, squinting so that his eyes sank in his russet brows.

"Shikasteh," he said at last. And repeated, for me, slowly: "Shi-kas-teh. 'Broken.'"

"He says," Ferhat translated, "that this is a special script, Persian. 'Broken writing.' It is written not for strangers but for one's own. The letters run into one another, the dots vanish, the words grow together. Whoever is not used to it will read nothing. Thus are written letters to beloveds, poems for oneself and testaments." Ferhat paused, listening. "Hasan Amca says that in his youth he carried silk to Tabriz, and there an old merchant wrote him accounts in shikasteh so that the clerks should not understand. Hasan Amca spent half a year learning to read them. He says it cost more than the silk itself."

"And what is written here?"

Hasan jabbed a thick finger at a line.

"An address," Ferhat translated. "The same as yesterday. The Sultanahmet quarter, the lane behind the bathhouse, an inconspicuous door in a blank wall, near an old column..." Ferhat hesitated. "He says 'column' here may perhaps not be a column. Perhaps a pillar. Or a stone. In shikasteh it is one and the same word, as you turn it."

Hodja Nureddin, who until then had been silently telling his rosary, suddenly leaned across the table and said something - quickly, with evident mockery. Hasan answered - louder. The hodja answered still faster. In a moment they were already arguing, interrupting one another, jabbing fingers at the note, and Suleyman, leaning back on the cushions, watched them with the pleasure with which one watches a cockfight.

"What are they about?" I asked Ferhat in a whisper.

"The hodja says that Hasan Amca reads shikasteh as a drunken boatman reads the stars." Ferhat was choking with laughter. "And Hasan Amca says that the hodja knows Arabic only from the Koran, and in the Koran there is no word 'bathhouse,' therefore the hodja is jealous."

Suleyman raised a hand - and both fell silent as on command.

* * *
"Further," said Suleyman.

Hasan, still puffing from the argument, bent over the note again.

"The first word he translates as 'return,'" Ferhat translated. "Or perhaps 'returning' - in Farsi it may mean both, depending on the context in which it stands."

"Bāzgasht," said Hasan in Persian, savouring the word. And suddenly, without waiting for a question, he closed his eyes and recited something in a chant - slowly, low, with such sorrow in his voice as I had never expected from this resonant, merry man.

All in the room fell quiet. Even the hodja lowered his rosary.

"These are verses," Ferhat whispered. "Persian. Very old. Rumi. All know them who know Farsi. Hasan Amca says the word in the note is the same as in these verses." He paused, picking his words. "It is about the reed. About the flute made of reed. Listen to the reed, how it complains, says the poet - how it tells of separation. Since I was cut from the reed bed, men and women weep at my weeping. Whoever is torn from his beginning seeks the day when he will return to it."

Whoever is torn from his beginning seeks the day when he will return.

I sat motionless. Hasan opened his eyes - and they were moist. He snorted in embarrassment, wiped them with his sleeve and became again the old resonant Hasan.

"The second word is harder," Ferhat continued, having listened to his grandfather. "Grandfather says it is like 'to keep' - but with a shade for which in our language there is no exact equivalent. Not merely 'to preserve a thing,' but rather... 'to preserve until the appointed time.' To wait until the time comes."

To keep until the appointed time. I repeated these words to myself several times. Return - to where? To keep - what, if not these very two stones, resting now in the leather pouch at my belt?

* * *
"There is one more," Hasan said suddenly, and his voice grew quieter. He pointed to the very edge of the note - to where the paper was most worn. "Here. One word. Yesterday I did not read it. Today - I read it. But I do not know how to understand it."

"Which?"

"Khāneh," said Hasan. "Or khāna. If 'khāneh' - it is 'house.' Your house, my house, a native house. But if 'khāna' - it is a cage. A cell. As on the backgammon board - each cell is called 'khāna.' In shikasteh they cannot be told apart. There is no dot."

A house. Or a cage. Or a cell on a board along which alien hands move counters.

I remembered Karapet's riddle: "Where he looks - there home."

Hodja Nureddin, who had been listening in silence, suddenly laughed - with a dry, rattling old man's laugh - and said something, shaking a finger at the ceiling.

"The hodja says," Ferhat translated, smiling, "that it is like in that story about Nasreddin."

"What story?"

Hodja Nureddin, not waiting for translation, himself turned to me, adjusted his enormous turban and began to speak - slowly, expressively, with gestures, as though telling children. Ferhat translated after him:

"'Once at night Hodja Nasreddin crawled on his knees under a lamp in the middle of the street, looking for something. A neighbour asked: "What are you looking for, Hodja?" - "I lost the key to my house." The neighbour began to search with him. They searched and searched - did not find it. The neighbour asked: "And where exactly did you lose it?" - "At home," answered Nasreddin. "Then why are you looking here, in the street?" - "Because it is lighter here."'"

Hasan roared with laughter, slapping his knees. Ferhat laughed. Even Suleyman smiled into his beard.

And I did not laugh. The hodja looked at me over his little beard with sharp, mocking eyes - and in those eyes there was no mockery.

"He says," Ferhat added more quietly, "that you, perhaps, also look where it is lighter. In strange cities, in strange notes. And the key, perhaps, is where you lost it. Within."

"I do not know where I lost it," I said.

The hodja heard the translation and spread his hands - with the expression with which people spread their hands who know the answer but do not think it necessary to pronounce it.

"The hodja says," said Ferhat, "that Nasreddin did not know either. That is why he crawled under the lamp. But he at least knew that he was looking for a key. And not for a lamp."

* * *
"Since the hodja tells tales," Hasan thundered, unwilling to yield his rival an inch, "I shall tell mine. A Persian one. A real one. Not about asses and lamps."

The hodja rolled his eyes. Suleyman waved a hand - tell. Hasan settled himself more comfortably, so that the cushion beneath him sighed piteously, and began - in a chant, with that special expression with which tales are told in bazaars for a copper coin. Ferhat translated, barely keeping up:

"'Once all the birds of the world gathered - the nightingale and the falcon, the peacock and the owl, the duck and the heron, and the little hoopoe, the wisest of all. And they said: all peoples have a king, and we have none. And the hoopoe said: we have. His name is the Simurgh. He lives beyond seven valleys, on Mount Qaf, at the edge of the world. One of his feathers once fell to earth, in China - and all the artists of the world have since drawn only that feather, because nothing else of him has been seen. Let us go to him.'"

"And did they go?" I asked.

"'They went. But the nightingale said: I cannot, I love the rose. The peacock said: I cannot, I am too beautiful to tire. The duck said: I cannot without water. The owl said: I love my ruins. And each bird found a reason to stay. And those who went - went through seven valleys. The Valley of the Quest. The Valley of Love. The Valley of Knowledge. The Valley of Detachment. The Valley of Unity. The Valley of Wonder. And the last - the Valley of Poverty and Annihilation. And in each valley birds died. Of weariness, of fear, of thirst, of doubts. Thousands and thousands set out. And to Mount Qaf only thirty flew.'"

Hasan paused - long, solemn. Even the hodja stopped telling his rosary.

"'Thirty birds,'" Hasan continued quietly, "'wounded, bedraggled, barely alive. They came to the palace of the Simurgh. And the doorkeeper opened the door to them. And they entered. And saw...' - he spread his hands - 'a lake. Smooth as a mirror. And in it - themselves. Thirty birds. And then they understood. In the language of birds, "si murgh" means "thirty birds." They had been seeking a king beyond the edge of the world - and the king was they. All this time. They themselves were what they sought.'"

The room was quiet. The censer crackled. Kemal in the doorway did not stir.

"They sought beyond the edge of the world," Ferhat repeated slowly, no longer translating but as though thinking aloud. "And found in a mirror."

Hodja Nureddin coughed.

"My Nasreddin," he said drily, "said the same in a single line. And without thirty dead birds."

Hasan turned crimson, opened his mouth - and then Suleyman laughed. Loudly, from the heart, as I had never yet heard him laugh. And after him - first Ferhat, then the hodja, then Hasan himself, shaking with his whole huge body, so that the cups trembled on the table.

And I looked into the corner of the room, where in the half-dark hung a small copper mirror - and saw in it my own face. Strange. Unfamiliar. The face of a man without a name, seeking beyond the edge of the world what, perhaps, he had long carried within.

* * *
"A riddle!" Hasan demanded, when he had done laughing. "Hodja, you boast of your Nasreddin - set a riddle that the guest will not guess. I stake a sack of cinnamon."

"I stake a little bag of dates," responded the hodja, without blinking. And, turning to me, uttered something short. Ferhat translated:

"'What comes to everyone, but no one has seen how it came? And leaves everyone, but no one has seen how it left?'"

"Sleep," I said.

The hodja nodded, pursing his lips in displeasure. Hasan guffawed and rubbed his palms.

"Now mine!" He leaned to me, and his eyes sparkled. "'Two brothers live in one house. One always looks forward, the other - always back. They have never seen each other. But one without the other cannot take a single step.'"

I thought. Two brothers. Again two. Black and white. Day and night. Sun and moon.

"Tomorrow and yesterday?" I suggested.

Hasan shook his head in triumph.

"Eyes?" Ferhat suggested.

"No!"

"Feet?" Kemal squeaked from the doorway - the first word I had heard from him all day.

"No!" Hasan slapped his palm on the table. "No one! The sack of cinnamon stays with me!"

"Then what is the answer?" asked the hodja, narrowing his eyes.

Hasan opened his mouth - and froze. His face slowly lengthened.

"I do not remember," he said in bewilderment. "My father set it to me. Forty years ago. The answer... I do not remember."

Hodja Nureddin laughed so that his enormous turban slipped sideways.

"There!" he said, straightening it. "That is how Persian riddles end. Two brothers, and no one knows who they are. Like our guest." He nodded at me. "He too does not know the answer. Perhaps because the answer has not yet been devised."

* * *
And then Hasan, who still held the note against the window, suddenly stopped.

"Hey," he said. Then louder: "Hey-hey-hey... Suleyman agha. Bak. Look."

He held the note right up to the glass, so that the sun passed through the paper. All bent toward him - Suleyman, the hodja, Ferhat, I.

In the thickness of the paper, where no ink blot touched it, a sign showed through. A watermark - such as masters put on good paper so that all should know whose work it is. Quite pale, barely distinguishable, it was visible only against the light.

Two circles. One - a little darker, one - a little lighter. And between them - a wavy line.

The room grew so quiet that I heard the coal crackle in the censer.

Kemal, who all this time had stood in the doorway, slowly came to the table. Looked at the paper against the light. Then - at me. And nodded - once, very gravely, as one nods when what you have long known is at last confirmed.

Hodja Nureddin stopped telling his rosary.

"The boy has been drawing this for the second day," said Suleyman slowly. Ferhat translated, stammering. "Two circles and a road between them. I thought - a child's amusement." The old man took the note from Hasan, held it long against the window, looking at the watermark. Then lowered it. "Paper with such a mark was made at one old mill. I know. Forty years I have traded in what people write on and what they wrap things in. Such paper I saw once in my life. Long ago. When I was young, like Ferhat."

"Where?" I asked. "Where did you see it?"

Suleyman was silent a long time.

"On such paper," he said at last, "was written a letter which a foreigner brought to Istanbul. He came into my father's shop, asked the way to Sultanahmet. Showed the letter. My father could not read it. The foreigner went away." The old man paused. "I remembered him because he was dressed neither as we are nor as the Franks. And because he said a strange thing to my father. He said: 'You are good people. If another comes - feed him.'"

I looked at the old man and could not utter a word.

"I shall come once more. Perhaps not I, but I shall come," said the nameless stranger in the shop of Karapet's great-grandfather.

"If another comes - feed him," said the nameless stranger in the shop of Suleyman's father.

Ferhat translated his grandfather's last words - and fell silent himself, looking now at his grandfather, now at me.

"Grandfather," he said softly, in his own language, but I understood by the intonation. "Is that why? Is that why you feed all wanderers? Not only because of Father?"

Suleyman answered nothing. He folded the note, laid it on the sheet with Hasan's annotations - and for a long time held his palm over both sheets, as though warming them.

* * *
The silence was broken by the curtain. From behind it, from the depths of the women's side, a voice came - aged, cracked, the very one that every evening sang the song of the sailor. Grandmother. She said something - quietly but firmly - and the men in the room fell silent at once, as men fall silent in all the houses of the world when the eldest of the women speaks.

Ferhat listened with bowed head. Then turned to me.

"Grandmother asks," he said slowly, "whether there is in the note the word 'sea.' Or 'ship.'"

Hasan looked at the note. Shook his head.

"No," Ferhat translated. "Hasan Amca says - no."

Behind the curtain there was a long silence. Then Grandmother said one more phrase - shorter, quieter.

"Grandmother says: good," Ferhat translated. "Then you are not from the sea. Then you have not come in his place."

I did not understand. Ferhat, seeing my face, explained in an undertone:

"She feared that you were a messenger. That you had come to say that Father..." He did not finish. "Grandmother believes: when a sailor does not return, the sea sends a stranger in his stead. So that the house should not stand empty. She feared that you were such."

From behind the curtain a hand was thrust out - swarthy, wrinkled, in silver bracelets - and set a small saucer on the floor by the threshold. On it lay three dried apricots and a piece of honeycomb with honey. The hand vanished.

"This is for you," said Ferhat. "Grandmother says: since you are not 'instead,' then - from above. For a guest - honey."

* * *
"Sultanahmet," I said at last, when I could speak. "Is it far from here?"

Ferhat translated the question to his grandfather, and this time Suleyman answered himself, nodding briefly toward the window, beyond which could be made out the roofs of the city descending to the water, invisible from here.

"Not very," Ferhat translated. "Over the hill and along the shore, where the new Palace is being built. Grandfather was there in his youth, when he traded in silk. He says the place is quiet, old, with narrow lanes and many little mosques."

"We shall go there in two days, as we agreed," I reminded him.

The old man nodded, then uttered a few more words - this time slower, as though choosing them with particular care. Ferhat, having listened, looked at me a little longer than usual before translating.

"Grandfather asks," he said at last, "whether you are sure that you want to go there. He says - no offence meant - that a note hidden so deep in the pocket of a foreigner's cloak rarely leads to good news. More often to a debt that must be repaid. Or to something better left untouched."

"I have no choice," I answered honestly. "It is the only thread I have. Without it I do not even know where to begin the search for my own name."

Hodja Nureddin suddenly leaned to me across the table and said - without translation, in my own language, broken, laboriously assembled, which I had not expected to hear from him:

"Name - not key. Name - lamp. Key - where lost."

And leaned back on his cushion again, telling his rosary as if he had said nothing.

Suleyman heard all this out, was silent, then slowly nodded. He folded both notes - mine and the one Hasan had written over - together and held them out to me across the table.

"Take both," Ferhat translated his last words. "Hasan's decipherment may prove useful there, on the spot, if you have to explain to someone what exactly you are seeking."

* * *
Hasan and the hodja left together - and on the threshold began quarrelling again. I heard Hasan assert something resonantly about Persian poets, and the hodja drily object something about Arabic grammar, and how their voices receded along the street, now merging, now parting, like two streams flowing from one source in different directions. At the gate Hasan turned, waved to me - "Misafir!" - and I waved back.

Kemal left last. He stood on the threshold looking at me, then came up, took my hand, opened the palm and laid in it something small and sharp.

A fragment of blue bead. The very one split in the night. The half which he had picked up from the floor.

He closed my fingers around the fragment - firmly, like an adult - and went away without a word.

I remained alone in the small room smelling of sandalwood. On the table where the note had just lain, only a pale square of sunlight from the window remained. I sat and held in one hand the folded sheets, in the other the bead fragment, and at my belt felt the light, cool weight of the pouch with the stones.

Return. Keep until the appointed time. House - or cage.

And two nameless strangers who had come to this city before me - one with stones, the other with a letter - and both left behind one and the same thing: a promise that someone else would come.

I did not yet know what these words meant. But I felt - as clearly as I had felt the warmth of strangers' hospitality all this time - that this term was approaching far faster than I should have liked to think.

And that I, perhaps, was the very "other" whom they had been told to feed.
