## Chapter XIV. The Salon of Artemia Aristarkhovna

"They found you by the grille," said Konstantin. "Sitting on the floor. With your back to the wall. With the candle burnt out in your hand and your eyes open. You were looking at the grille and smiling, mon cher. I swear to you - smiling. As if you had just heard the funniest joke in the world."

We stood at the window in the small drawing room while footmen arranged chairs for the evening gathering, and Konstantin spoke in an undertone, not looking at me, as though telling of the weather. Four days had passed. Four days I had lain in bed under the supervision of Doctor Strauch, who felt my pulse, shone a candle into my eyes, made me count to a hundred and back, and each time, having finished the examination, wrote something in a little black notebook which he showed to no one.

"Who found me?" I asked.

"I did," said Konstantin. "Who else. You did not cry out. But I heard you all the same." He paused. "Do not ask how. I do not know myself. I sat in the hall, Lizonka was playing her third romance, and suddenly my head began to ache. Here." He touched his temple with his fingers. "As if someone had called. I rose and went. Straight to the left wing. I did not even take a candle. I walked in the dark and knew where to go. As though someone were leading me by the hand."

"And the General?"

"The General came after." Konstantin at last turned to me, and his face was unusually grave. "He went faster than I, though he is sixty. He knew where the grille was. Knew the way better than I. And when he saw you by the wall - he was not surprised. Do you understand? Not surprised. He simply bent down, lifted you like a child, and said..." Konstantin faltered.

"What did he say?"

"'Again.'" Konstantin looked me straight in the eyes. "He said: 'Again.' Quietly. To himself. And then he saw that I was near, and did not say another word."

I was silent. Outside the window it was growing dusk; in the garden, among the rose bushes, the stooped figure of Stefan with a lantern flickered - the gardener was making the rounds of his domain before night, as the housekeeper Agafya Tikhonovna made the rounds of the locks.

"I am not asking you what was there," said Konstantin, turning back to the window. "You will tell when you wish. Or will not. I want to know only one thing." He paused. "Have you come back? Whole? Are you - you?"

The question was so strange that I laughed. But Konstantin did not laugh.

"I am," I said. "Who else."

"Good," he said quietly. And, after a pause, added in his former voice, with his former mockery: "Because your aunt has today gathered half the province, and if you faint again in the middle of the lecture, Kutasova will decide it is from love of Lizonka. And I shall have to fight a duel with you. And I, mon cher, shoot abominably."

* * *
The salon of Artemia Aristarkhovna opened at eight. By half past eight the small drawing room - which was called small only in comparison with the great ballroom, and in fact held some forty persons without any crowding - was full.

Candles burned in tall candelabra and in crystal girandoles on the walls, reflected in the dark windows and in the mirrors so that it seemed the drawing room continued beyond the glass into infinity. It smelled of wax, perfume, hot chocolate and the asters which Stefan had brought from the garden and set in Chinese vases in the corners. By the fireplace tea was being poured; at the piano someone of the young set was idly picking at the keys; in the pier between the windows a footman in white gloves held a tray of punch, and Konstantin had already twice managed to approach it.

My aunt received her guests at the doors - in dark-blue velvet, with the same unchanging string of pearls, erect, calm, with a smile which I had seen on her a thousand times and which today for some reason seemed to me a mask. Twice during the evening I caught her gaze turned on me - long, anxious - and both times she at once looked away.

The guests were mostly familiar. The General - in an armchair by the fireplace, with a cup of tea and with that impenetrable expression with which he had no doubt listened in his time to both diplomats and Turkmen elders. Evdokia Gerasimovna - beside him, in the next chair, in a silver-grey gown and a little hat on which perched a whole stuffed hummingbird with an emerald throat. Colonel Mikhail Ivanovich - already telling someone about the Caucasus. Vera Anatolievna - quiet, in lilac. Lieutenant Alexei - hovering around my aunt. Doctor Strauch - in a corner, with a cigar which he was not allowed to smoke in the drawing room and so simply held in his fingers like a talisman. Nadezhda Porfirievna Kutasova with Lizonka - of course in the front row, nearer to the General.

But there were new faces too.

"Who is that?" I whispered to Konstantin, nodding at a lady by the window.

"Ah," Konstantin winced. "That is Madame Blanchard. Joséphine. A medium. She came from Paris last winter and now turns tables in all the drawing rooms of the capital. They say that at Princess Velskaya's - no, not that one, the other - she summoned the spirit of the late husband, and he asked that it be conveyed that he had hidden the money in an old boot. The boot was found. The money - no." Konstantin snorted. "But the princess is delighted all the same."

Madame Blanchard was a lady of indeterminate age - somewhere between forty and eternity - in a black silk gown, with a high coiffure in which two heron feathers were stuck, and with so many bracelets on her wrists that at every gesture she jingled like the bell on a goat's neck. Her face was pale, powdered, her eyes heavily lined with kohl and looked so intently, so languidly, that it seemed she saw behind your back someone whom you did not see.

"And that one?" I nodded at a young man by the piano - thin, pale, with long, shoulder-length fair hair and a velvet jacket of the kind artists wear.

"A poet," sighed Konstantin. "Apollinary Treskov. Writes verses about death, the moon and unrequited love. Mainly the latter. His mother is a distant relation of Evdokia Gerasimovna, which is why he is tolerated. Tonight he will read. Prepare yourself."

"And this one?"

By a column, with a cup of chocolate, stood a lady in a lavish lilac gown, with an enormous ostrich-feather fan and with such a greedy, tenacious, all-seeing expression on her face that I involuntarily stepped back a pace.

"Oh!" whispered Konstantin with unfeigned horror. "That is Olga Kirillovna Shelestova. The most dangerous person in the province. Do not go near her. Do not look at her. Do not breathe in her direction. She knows everything about everyone - who with whom, who to whom, who how much. And what she does not know she invents, and in such a way that afterward it proves true. They say three weddings and two duels in the province in the past year were her doing."

It was too late. Olga Kirillovna had already noticed me, snapped her fan shut with a ringing click and sailed toward us like a frigate under full sail.

* * *
"Ah! There he is!" she sang out, stopping before me and running her eyes over me from head to foot as though buying a horse. "Our poor invalid! They say you fainted in the left wing? At night? Alone?" She lowered her voice to a theatrical whisper. "They say you were found by that very grille!"

"They say," I said.

"And what were you doing there, in the left wing, at midnight, eh?" She playfully poked me in the chest with her folded fan. "Ah, youth! Do not answer, do not answer, I understand everything. There, they say, the White Lady walks. Did you see her?"

"No."

"A pity!" Olga Kirillovna sighed. "And my cousin, Varvara Petrovna, stayed here in the time of Artemia Aristarkhovna's late husband and swears she saw her. In the mirror. A white dress, she says, and no face." She waved her fan. "However, Varvara Petrovna after her third glass of cordial sees even worse things."

Konstantin beside me made a strangled sound.

"And tell me," Olga Kirillovna bent to me, and her eyes suddenly became sharp as needles, "tell me, my dear, one thing. I have come to Artemia Aristarkhovna's evenings, God help my memory, for twelve years. Twelve years, every season. And, kill me, I do not remember when you appeared here. You were not - and here you are. And when, from where..." She narrowed her eyes. "You are her nephew, are you not? Son of a sister? Or of a brother? She had, I know for certain, neither sisters nor brothers..."

The world around me swayed for an instant. The candles trembled. I opened my mouth - and understood that I did not know what to answer. I truly did not know. A sister? A brother? I had never asked. My aunt had never said. When had I appeared here? I remembered this house, these corridors, this drawing room - but when had I first seen them? Yesterday? Ten years ago? Always?

"Olga Kirillovna."

My aunt's voice sounded behind my back - even, quiet, with that special velvet steel at which servants' knees gave way.

"You, my dear, forget a great deal," said Artemia Aristarkhovna, taking me by the arm. "For example, that I forbade your cousin Varvara Petrovna to appear in this house after she broke the family mirror in the hall. And that you yourself promised me at Easter to return a French novel which, if I am not mistaken, still lies with you." She smiled - dazzlingly, mercilessly. "And my nephew has been here as long as I remember myself. Is that enough?"

Olga Kirillovna crimsoned to the roots of her hair, muttered something about a novel, opened her fan and sailed off to the column.

My aunt did not release my arm. Her fingers gripped my elbow so hard that it hurt.

"Do not listen to her," she said quietly, not looking at me. "Never listen to those like her. They trade in others' secrets because they have none of their own."

"Auntie," I said just as quietly. "Is it really so that you had neither sisters nor brothers?"

The fingers on my elbow loosened.

"The lecture is beginning," said Artemia Aristarkhovna. And walked off to her chair without once looking at me.

* * *
Professor Sventsitsky proved nothing like what I had imagined.

I had expected a dry, grey, tedious scholar in a pince-nez - and onto the dais by the fireplace stepped a man of about fifty, sturdy, sunburnt, with a short, peasant-trimmed beard, in a frock coat that had clearly seen more roads than drawing rooms, and in boots polished but trodden down. His eyes were clear, light and merry, and his hands large, calloused, with an ink stain on the middle finger of the right. At his belt, under the frock coat, hung a canvas bag from which the edges of notebooks stuck out, and from time to time he slapped it with his palm as one slaps the flank of a faithful dog.

"Ladies and gentlemen," he began, and his voice was loud, sonorous, accustomed to shouting down village assemblies and fairground noise. "I thank Artemia Aristarkhovna for the invitation. I warn you at once: I do not know how to give lectures. I know how to tell. For thirty years I have walked through villages, from Arkhangelsk to Bessarabia, from the Carpathians to the Urals, and written down what old people tell me. Tales. Omens. Charms. Songs. What our learned colleagues call superstitions, and I call - the memory of the people, which it keeps longer than any archive."

"Memory or folly?" Doctor Strauch asked loudly from the corner, twirling an unlit cigar in his fingers.

A titter ran through the drawing room. Sventsitsky, not in the least abashed, smiled into his beard.

"Ah, Karl Fyodorovich! I have heard of you. You, they say, treat with cold rubdowns and Karamzin." The titter grew louder. "I shall tell you thus, Doctor: folly does not live a thousand years. Folly dies together with him who devised it. But what an old woman in the Olonets province tells her grandson word for word just as her great-grandmother told her grandmother - what has outlived the Tatars, the Time of Troubles, Peter and the French - that is no longer folly. That is something that very much wished to be preserved. The only question is - why."

"And why?" asked the General from his chair. Quietly, but all turned to him.

Sventsitsky looked at the General - attentively, a little longer than courtesy required.

"Because, Your Excellency," he said, "a people, like an individual, sometimes remembers what has not happened to it. Or what happened so long ago that it itself no longer knows whether it truly was. And this memory it hides in tales. Because in a tale one can tell the truth, and no one will call you mad."

The General slowly lowered his cup to the saucer. I saw his hand for a moment lie on the pocket of his uniform - the one where the wooden raven lay.

* * *
Sventsitsky spoke long - and no one grew bored.

He told of house-spirits, who in every province are fed differently: in one - with porridge at midnight, in another - with milk by the stove, in a third - with tobacco, because the house-spirit there, they say, smokes. Of the bath-spirit, who does not like it when people bathe after the third steaming, and may strangle for it. Of mermaids, who in Trinity week come out of the water and swing on birches - and who, as one old woman on the Volga told him, are not drowned maidens at all but "those who are not yet born and do not know whether they wish to be born." Of werewolves in Polesie. Of vampires in Bessarabia. Of "pledged dead" - those who died not their own death and cannot find the way to the other world, and so wander between.

"Between what?" asked Lizonka Kutasova. Timidly, almost in a whisper - and at once blushed, because everyone turned to her.

"An excellent question, mademoiselle!" Sventsitsky beamed. "The best question of the whole evening. Between what do they wander?"

He held a pause - long, as only good storytellers know how to hold.

"You see," he said, "among our people - not among bookmen, not among priests, but among simple folk, among whispering grannies, shepherds, healers - there is a very old notion of the world. So old that no one can any longer properly explain it. It was explained to me by one old healer near Vologda - half blind, toothless, they said she was past a hundred. She said thus: 'The world, dear sir, is not one. There is Yav - that is what is seen. Where we sit, where bread grows, where the sun rises. And there is Nav - that is what is not seen. Where the dead are, the unborn, dreams, those who were and will be. And between them - a threshold. Thin, thin. Like the film on milk. Most live on one side and know nothing of the other. But there are those who stand on the threshold. One foot here, the other - there. They are few. They were always few. It is hard for them. They do not remember where they came from, because they came from that side. And do not know where they are going, because they go to that.'"

The drawing room fell silent. So silent that I heard the candle gutter in the candelabrum nearest me.

"Two worlds," said Sventsitsky, as though summing up, as though in passing, as though it were the most ordinary phrase in the world. "Yav and Nav. And a man who stands between two worlds is neither a saint nor a madman. He is simply a man who has lost his way. Or found another."

Two worlds.

I do not know what happened to me at that moment. These words - the simplest, most ordinary words - entered me as a key enters a lock which you have never seen but which, it turns out, was all this time within you. Somewhere in the very depth something turned. Clicked. And for one brief, dazzling moment it seemed to me that I heard - not with my ears but with something beneath my ribs, on the left - the distant peal of bells. And a long-drawn call pouring from a slender tower. And the rustle of sand under someone's steps between stone columns.

I clutched the back of a chair. Konstantin beside me instantly straightened.

And at that very moment something fell in the doorway of the drawing room. Loudly, with a rustle and a thud.

All turned.

In the doorway stood Stefan. The gardener. In a coarse canvas shirt, with earth under his nails - he must have been carrying fresh flowers into the drawing room, but the basket of white roses had fallen from his hands and lay now on the parquet, spilling the flowers in a fan at his feet. He did not bend to pick them up. He stood motionless and looked - not at Sventsitsky. At me.

Long. Silently. With such an expression as I had never seen on any human face: not fear, not surprise, but something like recognition and grief at once. Thus one looks at a grave long sought and at last found.

Then he bent, gathered the roses into the basket - slowly, one by one - muttered something in his own language and left without another word.

"What is the matter with him?" Kutasova asked loudly.

"Bulgarians," the Colonel shrugged. "A superstitious people. The professor must have reminded him of something from his village."

Sventsitsky, however, did not shrug. He gazed after Stefan with lively, keen interest. And then turned his gaze to me - and in his eyes flickered something that made me uneasy.

* * *
Then there was an interval, and tea, and pastries, and conversations, and Konstantin thrusting into my hand a glass of punch with the words "drink, you are pale as the White Lady" - and, at last, the General, whom the ladies, as always, begged to tell "something interesting from his travels."

"Only not about the Caucasus!" Kutasova implored. "Mikhail Ivanovich has already told us about the Caucasus. Twice."

"Thrice," the Colonel corrected with dignity.

"About Japan, Pavel Nikolaevich!" Lizonka suddenly asked - and was herself frightened by her boldness. "They say you were in Japan. Is it true that they eat raw fish there?"

The General looked at her - and, to general surprise, smiled. Truly, warmly, without his usual icy courtesy.

"True, mademoiselle. They do. And very tasty, if one does not think what one is eating." He set down his cup. "Very well. About Japan."

He told how, as a no longer young colonel, he had been attached to the embassy which the Sovereign sent to Japan on the frigate Pallada, and afterward on the frigate Diana - to negotiate about trade and the border on Sakhalin and the Kurils. How for long, for months, they stood in Japanese harbours, and the Japanese officials - in wide silk garments, with two swords at the belt, with shaven foreheads and little tufts of hair on the crown - came every day to the frigate, bowed to the floor, drank tea, spoke civilities and decided nothing.

"A Japanese will never say 'no' to you," said the General. "He will say: 'It is very difficult.' And he will go on saying 'it is very difficult' for half a year. I knew in China a mandarin who did the same. It sometimes seems to me that they studied under one teacher."

"And the Japanese themselves - what are they like?" asked Vera Anatolievna.

"Polite, madam. Polite so that it frightens. Clean - in every village they have a bath, and they bathe every day, in very hot water, all together, men and women, and see nothing wrong in it." A shocked whisper passed through the drawing room, Kutasova covered Lizonka's ears with her fan. "Their houses are of wood and paper. Walls of paper, imagine. They slide apart. And the floors are covered with mats, and to enter a house in shoes is the same as for us to spit on an icon."

"And what happened to the Diana?" asked Konstantin. "I heard she perished."

The General's face changed.

"She perished, Lieutenant." He paused. "We stood in the harbour of Shimoda. In the morning - quiet, sun, not a cloud. And suddenly - the earth shook. Right beneath the water. The frigate rocked like a boat. And then the sea..." he fell silent, choosing words, "the sea went away. The water withdrew from the harbour as if someone had pulled out a plug. We saw the bottom. Fish thrashing on the sand. And then the water returned. A wall. Higher than the masts. It passed through the town and carried it off as a wave carries off children's sand castles. Houses, temples, boats, people. Our Diana was spun in the harbour like a chip forty-two times - I counted the turns, because I could do nothing else. Forty-two. She was smashed on the bottom, her rudder torn away, her hull stove in."

In the drawing room no one breathed.

"We lost almost no one," said the General quietly. "By a miracle. The Japanese - the very ones who for half a year had said 'it is very difficult' - pulled our sailors from the water with their bare hands. And afterward, when the Diana had sunk completely, they helped us build a new schooner. In a little village by the sea. Japanese carpenters and our sailors - without a common language, by gestures - built a ship in three months. We named it after that village. On it part of ours returned home."

"And you?" asked Evdokia Gerasimovna. So quietly that, it seems, only I and the General heard.

"And I stayed another half year, Dunya," said the General just as quietly, forgetting, it seems, that before all one must say 'Evdokia Gerasimovna.' "To sign the treaty. We signed it in a temple. A small, wooden one, on a hill above the harbour, where debris from the wave still lay about." He paused. "There was an old monk there. He watched us sign, and then came to me and gave me this."

The General reached into an inner pocket - not the one where the raven lay, but another - and took out a small paper object. A paper crane - white, worn, yellowed with time.

"He said through the interpreter: 'The Japanese believe: if one folds a thousand cranes, one wish will come true. I have folded nine hundred and ninety-nine. The last I give to you. Your wish will come true when you find one who will fold it back into a sheet.'"

"Back into a sheet?" Konstantin repeated. "How is that?"

"I do not know, Lieutenant." The General put the crane back in his pocket. "For twenty years I have carried it and do not know."

* * *
"And Australia?" asked the poet Treskov suddenly, who until then had been silent and gazing at the ceiling with the air of a man composing an elegy. "Have you been to Australia, Your Excellency? There, they say, everything is the reverse. Summer in winter. Beasts that hop. Black swans."

"I have," said the General. "Briefly. On our corvette, some ten years ago. We called at Melbourne."

And something in me quivered.

I could not have explained what. The word "Australia" - merely a word, the name of a distant, almost fabulous land at the other end of the world, where convicts are exiled and where, they say, gold is found right in the ground. I had never been there. I could not have been there. And yet at the sound of this word something in my chest contracted - sweetly and painfully, as it contracts at a smell remembered from childhood, though one does not remember the childhood itself.

"In Melbourne we were received as if nothing had happened," the General went on. "Although, as we learned afterward, there had been a panic in the city before our arrival: they thought the Russians had come to attack. English newspapers wrote for a whole week that our corvette was the first ship of an enormous fleet which was about to bombard the city." He smiled into his moustache. "And we had come for water and coal. And so that the sailors could stretch their legs."

"And what is it like there?" I asked. My voice sounded strange, hoarse.

The General looked at me - attentively, with a long look.

"It is bright there," he said slowly. "That is the first thing I remembered. The light there is different. Not as with us and not as in Asia. White, brilliant, as if the sky were higher. The sky is enormous. The stars are foreign: the Great Bear cannot be seen, but there is the Southern Cross, four stars like a kite. The city is new, as though built yesterday: wide streets, stone houses, banks with columns - gold there, gold, everyone goes mad over gold. And beyond the city - eucalyptus forests. The trees shed bark, not leaves, and stand white, bare as bones. And smell - smell so that the head spins, of honey and medicine at once. And at night in these forests a bird laughs."

"Laughs?" Lizonka repeated.

"Laughs, mademoiselle. Like a man. Loudly, rollingly, to tears. The first time I seized a pistol - I thought it a drunken vagrant. I was explained - a bird. The kookaburra. It laughs at dawn and at sunset. The natives say - it wakes the sun and sees it off."

Laughs at dawn. Wakes the sun.

The baboons of Thoth raise their hands to the rising sun. The thought came from nowhere - I did not know what the baboons of Thoth were, I had never heard of them. The thought flickered and vanished like a spark.

"And the natives?" asked Sventsitsky, leaning forward with lively interest. "I have read that the Australian savages have remarkable beliefs."

"Remarkable, Professor." The General turned to him. "I spoke with one old man. Through an interpreter - a shepherd who had lived among them twenty years. The old man was quite black, grey, almost naked, with a spear, with white stripes of paint on his chest. He told me that his people have lived on this land since the beginning of time - from that time which they call by a word which our shepherd translated as 'the Dreaming.' When the ancestors sang - and from their songs mountains, rivers, stars appeared. And that the land still remembers these songs, and if one knows how to sing, one can walk the path of the ancestors across the whole country - from sea to sea - not knowing the way, simply following the song."

"Songlines," murmured Sventsitsky, feverishly writing something in his notebook.

"And he also said..." The General fell silent.

"What, Your Excellency?"

"He looked at me and said that I was not the first white man to come to him and ask about this. That before me another had come. Long ago. Alone. Without a ship. 'He came out of a dream and went into a dream,' said the old man." The General paused. "The interpreter laughed, said the old man had lost his wits. And the old man looked at me and said: 'When he comes again - tell him that the land remembers his song.'"

In the drawing room it grew quite still.

The General was looking not at Sventsitsky, not at the ladies. He was looking at me.

"I, of course, passed on nothing of the sort to anyone," he said, looking away. "To whom should I have passed it? The old man was raving."

I sat without stirring. And in my chest everything contracted and contracted - that sweet, aching feeling, as for a home in which you have never been.

* * *
"Enough of frightening stories!" My aunt rose and clapped her hands, and her voice sounded a little louder and a little sharper than was needed. "Gentlemen, charades! We play charades. Konstantin, you set the first."

All stirred, brightened, shifted their chairs. Charades were the favourite game of my aunt's evenings - with them, it seems, all the salons in the province ended. Konstantin, not in the least abashed, came out to the middle of the drawing room, cleared his throat, thrust a hand into the lapel of his uniform like Napoleon in portraits, and declaimed:

"My first syllable is a preposition, you find it oft at the start of words where road or path is told.
My second is on bull and aurochs and all the goat-kind.
And the whole - across it one steps into the house from the porch."

"Porog - the threshold!" cried Lizonka, clapping her hands. "Po-rog!"

"Bravo, mademoiselle!" Konstantin bowed to her so low that Kutasova beamed.

"Too simple, Lieutenant," snorted the poet Treskov. "You yourself gave it away - 'from the porch.'"

"I did it on purpose," Konstantin answered imperturbably. "So that Mademoiselle Kutasova should win. She deserved it."

Lizonka blushed. Kutasova looked at Konstantin with new, appraising eyes. Konstantin, catching that look, paled and hastily retreated to me.

"I seem to have just made a fatal mistake," he whispered. "Now she will hunt me."

"Threshold," I said quietly, not knowing why.

"What?"

"Nothing."

Threshold. Thin as the film on milk. One foot here, the other there.

Next, Olga Kirillovna set one - and her charade, of course, proved spiteful, ambiguous and obviously hinting at someone in the drawing room, at which Lieutenant Alexei turned purple and went out "for air." Then the Colonel set a charade about a cannon, which no one guessed because the Colonel muddled the syllables. Then Doctor Strauch set one in German, and only Evdokia Gerasimovna guessed it.

And then Sventsitsky rose from his place.

"Permit me too," he said. "Only mine is not a charade. Mine is a riddle. A folk one. It was set to me by that same old woman near Vologda. She said that it is set only once in a life - to him who stands on the threshold." He smiled. "I, I confess, never found the answer. Perhaps one of you will."

And he pronounced it slowly, in a chant, in the old manner:

"'Two stones at the threshold lie: one - like night, the other - like snow. One holds the door, the other shows the way. Who lifts both - he will go home. Only his home is not here and not there.'"

I did not hear a cup break. I only saw: on the carpet by Artemia Aristarkhovna's chair lay shards of thin porcelain, and across the pile a dark stain of tea was slowly spreading. My aunt sat perfectly still, looking at Sventsitsky, and her face was white as paper.

The General rose from his chair.

"Professor," he said evenly, "it is late. Artemia Aristarkhovna is tired. I thank you for a splendid evening."

It was not a request. It was an order, given in the tone in which orders are given on a battlefield. And all - all forty persons in the drawing room - understood it.

* * *
The guests dispersed hurriedly and awkwardly. Kutasova led Lizonka away, glancing back at Konstantin. Olga Kirillovna left last, with so pleased a face as though she had been given a whole casket of other people's secrets. Madame Blanchard, the medium, who had been silent all evening, suddenly stopped at the very doors, turned - and looked at me with her kohl-lined eyes. Then she came up - quickly, jingling her bracelets.

"Mon petit," she said quietly, in French, so that none but I should hear. "I am a charlatan. Everyone knows it. I move tables with my foot and rap on them with my heel." She bent closer. "But in thirty years I have learned to see one thing. With some people someone always stands behind them. With you - he stands. Tall. Grey. He stood behind you all evening. And when the professor said 'two worlds,' he laid a hand on your shoulder."

She straightened, jingled her bracelets - and went off without waiting for an answer.

I stood in the middle of the emptied drawing room. Footmen were putting out the candles. Konstantin was speaking quietly with the General about something by the fireplace. My aunt had already gone to her rooms.

"Young man."

I turned. Sventsitsky stood at the door - in an overcoat, with his bag over his shoulder, a cap in his hand.

"Forgive me if I upset your aunt," he said. "I did not know. Truly, I did not know." He paused, looking at me with his clear, merry eyes which now were not merry. "Allow me to ask. Where are you from?"

I opened my mouth.

"I..."

And fell silent. Just as I had been silent today before Olga Kirillovna. Just as I had been silent four days ago before the monk in burgundy who asked what year it was.

Sventsitsky nodded - slowly, without surprise.

"You do not remember," he said. Not a question. "So I thought."

He put on his cap.

"I am staying at an inn in the district town," he said, already at the very threshold. "I shall remain until the end of the week. If you wish to talk - of Yav and Nav, of stones at the threshold, of anything - come. I, you know, have for thirty years been writing down tales. Sometimes it seems to me that it is not I who seek them." He smiled. "Sometimes it seems to me that it is they who seek one to whom to tell themselves."

He left. The door closed behind him. A footman put out the last candle at the exit.

Konstantin came up to me and silently stood beside me. We stood in the half-dark drawing room, where it smelled of wax and cooling tea, and looked at the dark window, beyond which in the garden Stefan's lantern was still flickering - he was for some reason walking round the spot where under the drawing-room windows the white roses grew. In circles. Again and again.

"He said 'two worlds,'" said Konstantin quietly, not looking at me. "You went white. Your aunt broke a cup. Stefan dropped the roses. The General drove out the professor." He paused. "Mon cher, I am, of course, a simple lieutenant. But even I see: everyone in this house knows something. Everyone but you and me."

"Perhaps we know too," I said. "Only do not remember."

Konstantin turned and looked at me - long, gravely.

"If you remember," he said, "tell me first. All right? Not your aunt. Not the General. Me."

"All right."

"Do you promise?"

I remembered a riddle that I had never heard: "What can be broken even without touching it?"

"I promise," I said.

He nodded, clapped me on the shoulder - a little longer and a little more lightly than friends clap - and went away, leaving me alone in the dark.

And outside the window, in the garden, Stefan's lantern went on circling and circling around the white roses - as though the gardener were looking for something in the dark. Or guarding something.

## Chapter XV. The Forged Scrolls

Nebamun came at dawn, when I was still sitting by the window, having never closed my eyes after the night at the temple pond - and in his hands was not his usual little box with counting tablets, but a scroll. One. Thick, tightly rolled, sealed with a clay seal bearing the impression of the sacred Eye.

"My Pharaoh," he said, bowing with that dry, unhurried precision with which he did absolutely everything. "Forgive me for troubling you at such an hour. But it seems to me that this scroll had better be read before the court wakes."

"What is it?"

"A petition, my Pharaoh. From the Temple. Delivered yesterday after sunset, by Bakenren's messenger." The keeper of the treasury laid the scroll on the little table before me, but did not take his hand from the seal, as though holding down the lid over a boiling pot. "The Temple requests from the royal granaries three thousand hekats of barley and fifteen hundred hekats of emmer. For the Opet festival. For sacrifices to the god, for the bread of the procession, for distribution to the people in Luxor."

"Three thousand hekats," I repeated. "The Temple asks grain of the throne?"

"That is precisely what troubles me, my Pharaoh," said Nebamun. "The Temple has not asked the throne for grain in forty years. The Temple itself fed half the Delta. The Temple, a moon and a half ago, was buying fields from peasants for a sack of barley. And now - it asks. And appends," he at last broke the seal and unrolled the scroll on the table, "inventories of its granaries. All empty. Or almost empty. The Temple writes that the drought has exhausted its stores too, that it has given all to the people and now, for the sake of the piety of the festival, is compelled to turn humbly to the mercy of the Pharaoh."

I looked at the even columns of signs. The names of granaries - temple ones, in Memphis, in Heliopolis, in the capital, in a dozen small towns of the Delta. Figures. The seals of scribes. All neat, clean, flawless.

"And what do you think of it, Nebamun?"

The keeper of the treasury was silent. Then said - evenly, with no expression at all, as one reads aloud the total of a column:

"I think, my Pharaoh, that in forty years I have seen many false scrolls. False scrolls are always flawless. True ones - never. In a true scroll there is always a blot, a smudge, a corrected figure, a beer stain. People who count honestly grow tired and err. People who lie take pains."

He tapped the scroll with a dry finger.

"And this scroll, my Pharaoh, has taken very, very great pains."

* * *
By the time the sun rose above the eastern hills, a strange company had gathered in my chambers.

Nebamun sat on a stool straight as a stick, with a tablet on his knees. The scribe of the council Ani - old, hard of hearing, with a reed brush behind his ear - had been summoned because he read others' handwriting better than anyone in the palace, though each line had to be repeated to him twice. And Iti - I had sent for him to the Library myself, before I had time to think why exactly I needed him. The youth came out of breath, with an ink stain on his cheek, with hair tousled from sleep - and, seeing Nebamun, froze on the threshold like a rabbit before a kite.

"Come in," I said. "Can you read the handwriting of the temple scribes?"

"I can, my Pharaoh," answered Iti, stammering slightly. "In the Library are kept copies of the temple inventories for the last twenty floods. I... I copied them. All. Last spring, when old Amenemope ordered the storeroom put in order."

"All?" Nebamun raised an eyebrow.

"All, esteemed Nebamun. Four hundred and twelve scrolls." Iti blushed. "I remember the hand of each who wrote them. Not because I tried. Simply... it sticks."

Nebamun looked at me. I looked at Nebamun. The keeper of the treasury for the first time all morning permitted himself something like a smile.

"Sit down, boy," he said. "It seems that you now stand worth more than all three thousand hekats."

Ani, tilting his head to one side, whispered loudly:

"What does he stand? Repeat for the record?"

"He is worth a great deal, esteemed Ani," Nebamun said patiently.

"Ah!" Ani nodded. "All the young are worth a great deal. Then they cheapen. In his years I myself was worth a whole bull. And now - half a jug of beer." And, pleased with his own joke, he began to scratch on his potsherd.

Iti, unable to help it, snorted into his fist - and at once looked at me in fright. I smiled at him, and he blushed still more.

* * *
We spread the Temple's scroll on the floor - it was so long that it took up half the room - and Iti knelt beside it, bending so low that he almost touched the papyrus with his nose.

For a long time he was silent. Ran a finger along the lines, not touching them. Moved his lips.

"This," he said at last, pointing to the inventory of the granaries of Memphis, "was written by Pentu. A junior scribe of the temple of Ptah. His 'k' always has a tail to the left, like a cat looking back. You see? And this - Heliopolis - also Pentu. And the capital - Pentu. And Bubastis. And Sais." Iti raised his head, bewildered. "My Pharaoh, all this was written by one man."

"Is that strange?"

"Very, my Pharaoh. Granary inventories are written on the spot. The scribe of Memphis writes in Memphis, the scribe of Heliopolis in Heliopolis. Their hands are different, I know them all. And here - one hand. Twelve granaries, twelve cities, from Memphis to Sais - and one hand. As if someone sat in one room and wrote them all in a row. In one night."

"Perhaps the Temple ordered them copied out fair?" I suggested. "For a petition to the throne."

"Perhaps," Iti agreed. "But then..."

He fell silent. Licked the tip of a finger - I had no time to stop him - and carefully touched the edge of a sign at the very bottom of the inventory.

The ink smeared.

Iti held his finger up to the light. A black smudge remained on the skin.

"Then," he said quietly, "why is the seal at the bottom old? The seal - of last flood's inventory. I have seen it. Here it is written that the inventory was drawn up on New Year's Day, on the first day of the month of Thoth, before two witnesses. That was more than two moons ago. And the ink is fresh. Ink two moons old does not smear, my Pharaoh. It eats into the papyrus. But this..." he showed his finger, "this was written the day before yesterday."

The room fell silent.

"Repeat for..." Ani began, but Nebamun laid a dry hand on his shoulder, and the old scribe fell silent.

* * *
"That is not all," said Nebamun. He was already standing over the scroll, bent, and his eyes behind narrowed lids ran along the columns of figures as fingers run over the beads of an abacus. "Boy, read me the inventory of Memphis. All of it. Aloud."

Iti read. Nebamun listened, moving his lips soundlessly.

"Stop," he said. "Again. The line about receipts."

"'On the third day of the second month of the season of Akhet,'" Iti read, "'there was delivered by river to the granary of the temple of Ptah in Memphis forty barges of barley from the Upper nomes. Twelve thousand hekats. The barley was distributed to the people within one moon, by the mercy of the High Priest.'"

"Forty barges," Nebamun repeated. "By river. On the third day of the second month of Akhet." He turned to me. "My Pharaoh, do you remember what the esteemed Merira said at the council?"

I remembered. I remembered the tattooed arms, the thunderous voice: "My barques stand in the Nile up to their bellies, like ducks on ice."

"Merira said," I answered slowly, "that cargo barges with grain would ground on the first shoal. That bread can be carried only on asses."

"Merira said that of the present season, my Pharaoh," Nebamun nodded. "And the third day of the second month of Akhet is precisely the day when the nilometer showed the lowest water in forty floods. The Keeper of the Gauge sends me a copy of his tablet every morning - I keep them all. On that day, my Pharaoh, not even a fishing boat could have passed along the Nile. And the Temple writes that forty barges with grain passed."

"So there was no grain?"

"So," said Nebamun, "there were no barges. And the grain..." He straightened. "The grain, my Pharaoh, perhaps was. Only it did not come by river, and did not go anywhere. Lay where it lay. And on papyrus it was first brought in, and then distributed to the people. So that on papyrus the granaries should be empty."

I sat looking at the endless ribbon of flawless signs spread on my floor. Twelve granaries. Twelve cities. One hand. Fresh ink under old seals. Forty barges that had passed along a river along which not even a boat could pass.

"The Temple is hiding grain," I said aloud.

"The Temple is hiding grain, my Pharaoh," Nebamun confirmed. "And now asks for more. From the royal granaries. Three thousand hekats. Which, if you give them, will empty our granaries by a third. And then by spring all will starve - except the Temple."

"And then," Iti added quietly, not raising his eyes from the scroll, "people will go not to the Pharaoh but to those who have bread."

We all looked at him. He was abashed.

"So said the nomarch Ankhtifi," he muttered. "I recorded the audience. 'If the throne cannot protect - he who has bread will protect.'"

* * *
Ani had long been nodding over his potsherd, Nebamun had gone for copies of the nilometer tablets, and Iti still sat on the floor over the Temple's scroll, running a finger along the lines - as though hoping to find something more there.

"Iti," I said. "Come here. Rest."

He rose, came over, sat on the edge of the bench - on the very edge, as though afraid to take up more room than was proper.

"You noticed what no one in the palace would have noticed," I said. "Neither Nebamun, nor Ani, nor I."

"I merely copied scrolls, my Pharaoh," he said. "Many scrolls. When you copy a great many - you begin to see. Not letters. Hands." He paused. "Every scribe writes as he breathes. Hurries - letters run. Fears - letters tremble. Lies - letters..." he sought a word, "become too beautiful. As with Pentu here. Pentu usually writes carelessly. He is lazy. And here - as if each letter were drawn for a tombstone."

"Because he was afraid," I said.

"Or because someone stood behind his back," said Iti. And at once blushed, as though he had said too much.

I looked at him. At the ink stain on his cheek. At the tousled hair. At the thin, stained fingers nervously clasped on his knees.

"May I ask, my Pharaoh?" he suddenly said, not raising his eyes. "Do you... do you know the riddles of the scribes?"

"The riddles of the scribes?"

"In the school of scribes the elders set them to the younger. " Iti brightened, and fear in his face for the first time that morning yielded to something boyish. "Our signs, you see... they are themselves like riddles. A mouth is drawn - and it reads as the sound 'r.' Water is drawn - and it reads 'n.' A beetle is drawn - and it means 'to become.' One can write a word so that only he will read it who knows how to look." He took a potsherd that lay by Ani and a reed brush. "Here. Read."

He drew three signs. An owl. A ripple of water. And a little seated man with a hand to his mouth.

I looked. Owl - "m." Water - "n." The little man at the mouth - that is the sign set at the end of words about food, about speech, about... I suddenly understood.

"Mn," I said slowly. "'Menes.'"

"Almost!" Iti beamed. "Only it is not 'Menes.' It is 'men' - 'to remain,' 'to abide.' The little man with the hand to the mouth is for words about speech, but here he stands because..." he suddenly faltered, blushed. "Because it is the name that remains when it is spoken. So we were taught: the name of the Pharaoh is what remains even when the Pharaoh himself is no more. Because it is pronounced. While the name is pronounced - the man abides."

"And if the name is pronounced by no one?" I asked.

Iti was silent.

"Then he goes into the Duat forever, my Pharaoh," he said quietly. "So the priests say. That is why names are carved in stone. That is why for enemies they are chiselled away."

I remembered myself, nameless. He who does not remember his name - no one pronounces it either.

"Set another," I said.

Iti thought, then drew: a feather. And a heart.

"Which is heavier?" he asked.

"The heart," I said. "A feather weighs nothing."

"Wrong, my Pharaoh." Iti smiled - shyly, but with evident pleasure at having caught the Pharaoh himself. "The feather of Maat weighs exactly as much as truth. And the heart - as much as a lie. If a man lived truthfully - the heart is lighter than the feather. If he lied - heavier." He looked at the scroll on the floor. "Pentu's heart now is probably heavier than a mountain."

"And the heart of the one who stood behind him?"

"I do not know, my Pharaoh," said Iti. "Perhaps he has no heart. Perhaps he left it in a jar, as is done with the dead. So that it should not be weighed."

* * *
When Nebamun returned with the nilometer tablets, Iti was again sitting over the scroll, and I was pretending to read a report from Ptahhotep. The keeper of the treasury laid the tablets on the table, spread them like dice - one to one, by day - and silently pointed to the one lying under the third day of the second month of Akhet. The figure was the lowest of all.

"Now we need one thing, my Pharaoh," he said. "To see with our own eyes at least one of these granaries. If it is empty - I am an old fool and beg the Temple's pardon. If it is full..."

"If it is full," I said, "then the Temple is a thief."

"If it is full," Nebamun corrected me with impeccable precision, "then there is an error in the Temple's inventories. Let someone else pronounce the word 'thief.' I am the keeper of the treasury. I speak only in figures."

He was gathering the tablets back into his little box, and suddenly, without raising his head, said in precisely the same tone in which he had reported figures:

"My Pharaoh. Permit an old servant a word - not about grain."

"Speak."

"At court they whisper," said Nebamun, carefully laying tablet to tablet, "that in recent days the Pharaoh sends too often for the junior keeper of the Library. That the boy carries the Pharaoh notes which no one reads. That the Pharaoh smiles when the boy enters." He closed the box. "I, of course, attach no importance to gossip. A court without gossip is like the Nile without crocodiles: both calmer and duller. But if it pleases the Pharaoh that the boy go on carrying notes which no one reads - let him carry them not by day and not through the main corridor. There the walls have ears. And some of the ears have bracelets."

I felt my ears burn. Iti, bent over the scroll two paces from us, froze - his back turned to stone, and even from the back of his head one could see how he had flushed to the roots of his hair.

"I thank you, Nebamun," I said as evenly as I could.

"Not at all, my Pharaoh." The keeper of the treasury rose, made his dry, exact bow - and already at the door added, just as imperturbably: "By the way, the boy counts splendidly. If the Library should ever grow too close for him, I have room in the treasury. There, at least, the walls are thicker."

He went. Iti did not raise his head for a long time. And when at last he raised it - he looked not at me but at the window, and said quietly, as though to himself:

"I shall go through the garden, my Pharaoh. There are no walls there."

* * *
"No," said Senusret.

"I did not ask permission," I said.

"I know, my Pharaoh. That is why I say 'no' in advance." The commander of the army stood before me, arms folded on his chest, fully armed, as though he already knew where I meant to go. "Last time you went to the temple pond in another's dress and your own sandals. The guard who let you out now stands at the southern outposts with Djehuty and, they say, thanks the gods every night that he is alive. This time you mean to go to a temple granary. At night. To Bakenren's men."

"I need to see it with my own eyes."

"Let my men see it."

"Your men the Temple knows by sight. Me - no. No one expects the Pharaoh in a granary at night."

Senusret looked at me for a long time. Then sighed heavily - as fathers sigh when they understand that their son's stubbornness is stronger than their own.

"Very well," he said. "But this time I go with you. And Inu. And Bata. And this..." he glanced at Iti standing by the doors, "this scribe, since without him no one will tell which ink is which. And sandals, my Pharaoh." He pointed to my feet. "The sandals you will put on are mine."

Senusret's sandals proved two fingers too large for me, coarse, trodden down, smelling of leather and road. Bata, seeing them on me, snorted and at once received a cuff from Inu.

* * *
The temple granary, which the inventory described as "empty after distribution to the people," stood on the northern edge of the capital, beyond a canal - where the city passed into fields, and the fields, parched and cracked, passed into desert. We went there on foot, in the dark, five of us - I, Senusret, Inu, Bata and Iti - in plain dress, as day labourers go who are returning from work. The moon was no longer copper, as on the night of the pond, but white, waning, and its light was exactly enough not to stumble.

The granary proved huge - I had not expected such. A long low building of mud brick, with a flat roof on which in a row stood dome-shaped storehouses, like gigantic beehives. On each - a round opening at the top where grain is poured in, and a small door below where it is raked out. All the doors were sealed with clay. On each seal - the sacred Eye.

At the gates, on a mat, leaning against the wall, slept a watchman. Around him stood three empty beer jugs. A fourth, half drunk, he clutched in his hand.

"Djedhor," whispered Iti. "I know him. He used to be a scribe at the Temple. They drove him out for drunkenness. Now he guards."

"And how he guards," Bata grunted.

We had almost passed him when Djedhor suddenly opened one eye.

"Who goes?" he asked in a slurred tongue. "Thieves? If thieves - come in, take, I do not care, I am drunk. If priests - I am not drunk, I am praying. Lying down. So it is nearer to the god of the earth."

Senusret stepped toward him, but I held him by the arm.

"We are day labourers, father," I said. "Looking for work. We heard that men are needed at the Temple - to load grain."

Djedhor burst out laughing - loudly, drunkenly, to tears.

"Load!" he squeezed out at last. "Load! Son, there is nothing here to load. Here all is empty. So it is written." He slapped his palm on the air, as on an invisible scroll. "Bakenren himself told me: Djedhor, if anyone asks - all is empty. All distributed. To the people. By mercy." He hiccuped. "So I say: empty."

"And in truth?" Iti asked quietly.

Djedhor turned a cloudy eye on him - and suddenly squinted.

"And I know you," he said. "You are that boy from the Library. Who copied my old inventories. You even laughed at my handwriting." He wagged a finger. "I remember everything. I am drunk, but I am not a fool." He hiccuped again and lowered his voice to a loud whisper: "Want to know what is in truth? Go and look. I saw nothing. I am asleep." And closed his eye, embracing the jug like a beloved woman.

* * *
Senusret cut the seal off the nearest door with the tip of his knife - carefully, so that afterward, if need be, it could be pressed back. Inu brought forward a lamp which until then he had hidden under his cloak. Bata pulled the door.

And from the storehouse, rustling like water, barley poured out.

It streamed to the ground, onto our feet, golden in the lamplight - dry, large, clean, smelling of summer and field. Bata leapt back. Inu swore - for the first time in all the time I had known him. Senusret stood motionless, watching a golden heap grow at his feet.

"Empty," said Bata. And laughed - nervously, almost hysterically. "Empty! Distributed to the people!"

We opened a second storehouse. Emmer. A third - barley. A fourth - wheat, select, such as there was not even in the royal granaries. A fifth, sixth, seventh. All full. To the very vault.

Iti stood in the midst of it all, holding in his palm a handful of grain, and could not utter a word.

"How much is here?" I asked hoarsely.

Iti looked at the storehouses. Counted the domes. Moved his lips soundlessly.

"If all are full alike, my Pharaoh..." He swallowed. "There is here as much as the Temple asks of you for the festival. Only three times over."

"In one granary," said Senusret.

"In one," Iti confirmed. "And in the inventory there are twelve."

And then Inu, who was going round the storehouses with the lamp, quietly called to us from the far end.

By the very wall, apart from the rest, stood sacks. Dozens of sacks, tightly tied, laid in a row as if prepared for dispatch. On each - a mark in paint. Not the sacred Eye. Another sign: a triangle, point down, and beneath it three wavy strokes.

"What is it?" I asked.

Iti bent, peered - and paled.

"It is not a temple sign, my Pharaoh," he whispered. "It is a sign... So on the maps in the Library the southern cataracts are marked. The triangle - a mountain. Three strokes - running water. It means... 'south, beyond the cataracts.'"

In the granary it became so quiet that I heard outside, at the gate, drunken Djedhor snoring.

"South," Senusret slowly repeated. "Beyond the cataracts. To where the southerners come from. To where on the prisoner a temple scarab was found."

No one answered. No one needed to answer.

* * *
We heard steps just as we were closing the last door.

Light, hurried, shuffling - and the flicker of a lamp in the doorway. Inu instantly put out his own, Senusret pushed me behind the nearest dome, Bata and Iti pressed to the wall.

Into the granary came a man. Young, thin, in the dress of a temple scribe, with a writing box under his arm and a lamp in a trembling hand. He looked about - fearfully, like a thief - passed us to a table in the corner, set down the lamp, opened the box, took out a clean scroll, an inkwell, a brush. And sat down to write.

He wrote quickly, biting his lip, glancing back at the door every now and then. Wrote, looking into another scroll - old, worn - and transferring something from it, changing, drawing each letter with that very painstakingness of which Iti had spoken - as for a tombstone.

Iti, pressed to the wall two paces from me, soundlessly moved his lips. I read one word from them.

"Pentu."

Senusret came out from behind the dome first. The scribe jerked up his head, saw an enormous dark figure in the lamplight - and dropped his brush. Ink splashed on the scroll, on the table, on his knees.

"Do not shout," said Senusret quietly. "No one means to kill you. For now."

Pentu did not shout. He slid from the bench to the floor, to his knees, and covered his face with his hands. His shoulders shook.

I came up. Crouched before him. Inu lit the lamp again, and the light fell on my face.

Pentu raised his head - and recognised me. I saw recognition pass over his face like a wave: first incomprehension, then horror, then something like relief - such as comes to people who have too long awaited being caught, and now at last are caught.

"My... my Pharaoh," he rasped and pressed his forehead to the floor.

"Rise, Pentu," I said. "And tell me who stands behind your back when you write."

* * *
He did not tell at once - first he wept, then hiccuped with fear, then Bata thrust a flask of beer at him, and he drank, his teeth chattering against the neck. And then he began to speak - quickly, disjointedly, as though afraid that if he stopped, he would no longer be able to begin.

Bakenren had summoned him three days ago. Gave him the old inventories - real, with real figures - and ordered him to rewrite them anew. All twelve. So that the granaries should be empty. To affix to each inventory the old seal - the seals Bakenren had brought himself, in a casket. To write of distributions to the people, of forty barges from the Upper nomes. The forty barges Bakenren had invented himself. Pentu had told him that by the river now not even a boat could pass. Bakenren had answered: "The Pharaoh does not look at the river. The Pharaoh looks at scrolls."

"And the sacks?" I asked. "With the southern mark?"

Pentu shook harder.

"I do not know, my Pharaoh. I swear. They are brought at night. By people I do not know. Loaded on asses and led away. Where - I do not know. I do not ask. Whoever asks - he..." He broke off.

"He what?"

"He goes to serve in the temple at the southern cataracts, my Pharaoh," Pentu whispered. "It is hot there. And scorpions. And from there no letters are written."

"Why did you agree?"

Pentu was silent for a long time.

"I have a mother, my Pharaoh," he said at last. "And three sisters. My father died in the last famine. Bakenren said: if I rewrote the inventories, my sisters would eat temple bread until the next flood. If I refused - their field..." He faltered. "We have a small field. Near Bubastis. Bakenren said it might turn up in the inventory of those bought out by the Temple. Backdated. He said: 'I know how to write backdated, Pentu. Now you do too.'"

Senusret let out a low sound - half growl, half groan.

I looked at this thin, ink-smeared youth kneeling before me in the golden barley which the Temple had "distributed to the people" - and thought of a tale I had heard once in childhood. Or had not heard - but for some reason knew.

"Pentu," I said. "Do you know the tale of the eloquent peasant?"

He raised to me tear-stained, astonished eyes.

"I know it, my Pharaoh. Everyone knows it. We were taught to write by it."

"Tell it."

He did not understand - no one understood - but began to tell. First stammering, then more evenly, as though the very familiar story calmed him.

"'There lived a peasant, and his name was Khunanup. He loaded asses with salt, reeds, leopard skins, stones and herbs from the oasis and went to the city to exchange them for bread for his wife and children. And on the road he met a man named Nemtynakht, a servant of the great steward. And Nemtynakht envied his asses. He spread his cloak on the narrow road - so that on one side was the cloak and on the other a field of barley. And said: "Do not step on my cloak." The peasant turned aside. And his ass bit off an ear of barley from the field. And Nemtynakht said: "Your ass has eaten my barley. I take your ass." And took the asses. And beat the peasant.'"

"And what did the peasant do?" Bata asked, not noticing himself how he had become absorbed.

"'He went to the great steward,'" Pentu continued. "'And began to speak. He spoke of truth. Of Maat. Of how he who holds the scales must not incline. Of how a lie comes out, as silt from water. He spoke so beautifully that the steward went to the Pharaoh and said: "There is a peasant, he speaks better than all scribes."'" Pentu sobbed. "'And the Pharaoh commanded: "Let him speak more. Do not answer him. Let him speak and you write it down." And the peasant came nine times. Nine times he spoke. And was not listened to - on purpose. And he went on speaking. And the ninth time he said: "I shall complain of you to Anubis." And went away, ready to die.'"

"And?" asked Iti, though, of course, he knew.

"'And the steward brought him back. And read him all that was written down in the nine times. And returned his asses. And gave him all the property of Nemtynakht. Because truth spoken nine times weighs more than a cloak on a road.'"

Pentu fell silent.

"Bakenren spread a cloak on the road," I said. "For you. For your sisters. For the whole Valley. And you turned aside. And your ass bit off an ear."

"Yes, my Pharaoh," whispered Pentu.

"I shall not take your ass, Pentu," I said. "And I shall not send you to the southern cataracts. You will return to the temple. In the morning. As if nothing had been. You will finish writing this inventory - as Bakenren ordered. You will give it to him. And you will go on copying all he orders, from now. Only every inventory - every one, real and false - you will copy twice. The second copy you will give to Iti. Through the garden. At night. Do you understand?"

Pentu looked at me as though I spoke a foreign tongue.

"And my sisters? And the field?"

"Your family's field from today is in the inventory of royal lands," I said. "Not temple ones. Backdated." I smiled slightly. "I too know how to write backdated, Pentu. Ask Nebamun."

Pentu covered his face with his hands and wept again - but now these were different tears.

* * *
We returned to the palace after midnight. Senusret led me to the doors of my chambers, took back his sandals from me, put them on and silently went away - only at the turn of the corridor did he look back and say:

"You let him go, my Pharaoh. He may run to Bakenren and tell all."

"He may," I agreed.

"And then?"

"And then, Senusret, I shall know that I erred in a man. That too is knowledge."

He looked at me for a long time. Then shook his head - whether in reproof or in respect - and went away.

But I did not go to sleep. I went to the Library - not knowing why. Perhaps because it was quiet there. Perhaps because Iti had gone there too, to his cubbyhole by the storeroom, and for some reason I did not wish this night to end without him.

In the Library one lamp burned. Old Amenemope sat at the table, leaning on his staff of black wood, and was reading something, moving a finger along the lines so slowly as though each word had to be not read but excavated. Iti sat opposite him on the floor, hugging his knees, and listened.

Seeing me, both leapt up. I waved a hand.

"Sit. I came to listen. What are you at?"

"The Duat, my Pharaoh," said Amenemope. "The boy asked me where those go whose names no one pronounces. And I do not know. I only read him what is written. And much is written, and various."

I sat down on the bench by the window. The night beyond the window was dark and warm; somewhere in the garden an owl cried.

"Read," I said. "I am interested too."

* * *
Amenemope read long - and not so much read as told, now and then glancing into the scroll, as if checking memory against papyrus.

He told that a man has not one soul but several. That there is the ka - the double, the force of life, which is born together with a man and stays to live in the tomb after his death, and to it must be brought bread and beer, otherwise it will starve. That there is the ba - a bird with a human head, which by day flies out of the tomb and flies over the world of the living, and by night returns to the body. That there is the akh - light, radiance, into which a righteous man is transformed when he has passed all trials. And there is the name - ren - which too is a part of a man, and the shadow - shut - which too is a part of a man, and the heart - ib - which remembers all that a man has done.

"And the heart is weighed," said Iti. "On scales, against the feather of Maat. In the Hall of Two Truths."

"Of Two Truths," I repeated. "Why two?"

Amenemope raised faded eyes to me.

"Because truth, my Pharaoh, is always double. One - that which the living see. The other - that which the gods see. And they do not always coincide. Therefore the hall is called the Hall of Two Truths. There the dead man stands before forty-two judges and says to them: 'I did not steal. I did not lie. I did not kill. I did not take bread from the hungry. I did not falsify the scales.' Forty-two oaths. And if even one is false - the heart drags down. And then it is devoured by Ammit - a beast with the head of a crocodile, the body of a lion and the hindquarters of a hippopotamus. And the man dies a second time. Now for ever."

"And if all are true?" asked Iti.

"Then he goes to the Fields of Iaru," said Amenemope. "To the Fields of Reeds. There all is as here, only better. Barley taller than a man. The river always full. No drought." He smiled. "And no Temple that hides grain."

Iti snorted. I too.

"And the stars?" I asked. "I have heard that Pharaohs after death go to the stars."

"They go, my Pharaoh. To the Imperishable Ones." Amenemope jabbed his staff at the window, at the northern part of the sky. "You see those stars that circle around one point and never set beyond the horizon? All the other stars sink in the west, die, are born again in the east. But these - never. They are ever awake. The ancients wrote that the Pharaoh after death becomes one of them. That is why in the most ancient tombs there are narrow shafts aimed straight at them - so that the soul of the Pharaoh should know where to fly."

"And that one in the south? The brightest?"

"Sopdet, my Pharaoh." The old man's voice warmed. "The star of Isis. She vanishes from the sky for seventy days - exactly as long as embalming lasts. And then returns - at dawn, just before sunrise. And when she returns - the flood begins. Every year. From the beginning of time. She is the herald. She promises that the water will come."

"Did she return this year?" I asked quietly.

Amenemope was silent for a long time.

"She returned, my Pharaoh," he said at last. "Three years in a row she has returned. On her day. In her place." He lowered his staff. "And the water - did not come."

* * *
Iti sat a long time silent, hugging his knees. Then suddenly asked - quietly, almost in a whisper, as though himself afraid of his question:

"Venerable Amenemope. Can a man return from the Duat?"

The old man looked at him.

"Ra returns every morning," he said. "Every night he passes through twelve gates, fights Apep, dies - and every morning is born again. Osiris returned - Isis gathered him in parts, and he came alive to become king of the dead. Sopdet returns every year. So - yes. The gods return."

"And men?"

"Men..." Amenemope stroked the scroll with his palm. "There is one place in the Most Ancient Epic. No one likes to read it. Because no one understands it." He paused. "It says there that the First Ones, who descended from the Heavens, did not die as we do. They went away - and returned. In another body. In another time. Not remembering themselves. And each time they had to learn anew who they were. And when they learned - they remembered everything. All the previous times."

My throat went dry.

"And what happened when they remembered?"

"That is not written there, my Pharaoh. There is only one line. Incomprehensible." The old man narrowed his eyes, as though recalling. "'And when he remembers his first name, he will return what was taken. And the two Eyes will become one.'"

The two Eyes. Merit at the pond. The white leads. The black keeps.

"Who is 'he'?" I asked.

"I do not know, my Pharaoh." Amenemope slowly rose, leaning on his staff. "I only keep scrolls. Perhaps the High Priest knows. He read that place three times in one moon." The old man moved toward the exit, shuffling. At the very door he stopped. "Boy, see the Pharaoh out. For, I see, he walks at night in another's sandals. One may lose one's way."

He went. The lamp crackled. The owl in the garden cried again.

Iti sat on the floor, still hugging his knees, and looked at me. Long. Silently.

"My Pharaoh," he said at last. "And if a man does not remember that he has already died? If he thinks that he lives for the first time? How will he know that he has returned?"

I did not know what to answer. I looked at this youth with an ink stain on his cheek, sitting in a patch of light among thousands of scrolls - and it suddenly seemed to me that I had seen him before. Not yesterday. Not at the audience. Long ago. In another place. In another light. As though we had sat so once already, and he had already asked me this, and I already had not known the answer.

"Perhaps," I said slowly, "someone will tell him. Someone who remembers for him."

Iti lowered his eyes.

"I would tell," he whispered barely audibly. "If I remembered."

The lamp flickered - and went out, burnt to the bottom. And in the darkness of the Library, smelling of cedar, dust and old papyrus, we sat a long time silent, not lighting another - a Pharaoh who did not remember his first name, and a junior keeper of scrolls who promised to remember it.

## Vision III. Oblivion

I do not know how many days this storm lasted.

That is the first thing worth saying - because the count of time, usually so simple, so self-evident, had long since lost all meaning for me in this enormous, ever-rocking iron womb. Three days? Five? Seven? The ship was flung from side to side with that monotonous, merciless regularity with which a storm flings a vessel when it has no intention of subsiding either for human weariness or for human prayer.

This ship was not merely large. It was monstrous. The largest of anything people had ever launched on the water - so the newspapers spoke of it, so its officers proudly repeated, so the passengers of the third class whispered, crossing themselves, seeing it for the first time from the quay: an iron mountain six hundred feet long, with five funnels, six masts and two paddle wheels at its sides - each as high as a three-storey house - and one more enormous screw at the stern. Four thousand people it could take aboard, they said. A city. A floating city, crossing the Atlantic from the Old World to the New.

Now this city was drowning. Not in water - not yet. In noise. In din. In the shriek of iron grinding on iron. In cries. The storm had fallen on us on the third day of the voyage, at the very edge of the Grand Banks of Newfoundland - and in the first night alone it tore off both gigantic wheels, like a child tearing the wings from a fly, broke the rudder and turned the mountain-ship into a log helplessly tumbling on waves each of which was higher than our masts.

The sailors said there had not been such a storm in a hundred years. A century storm. So it was nicknamed aboard on the second day: the century storm. As though it had been gathering for a whole century somewhere beyond the horizon and had at last waited for us.

* * *
My valet - Prokhor Ilyich, who had served me, if my own memory is to be trusted, for more than one decade - sat in the corner of the cabin on a stool bolted to the floor, imperturbable as always, though the pitching made even him grab at the wall at times. He said nothing without need. He simply was near - with that particular, unobtrusive presence of a man who has long ceased to need words to prove his devotion.

The cabin was first class - spacious, finished in mahogany and mirrors, with velvet curtains and brass lamps on gimbals which, as was intended, remained horizontal in any pitching, but because everything around them was heaving, it seemed that they were swaying while the world stood still. Across the floor, from wall to wall, at every roll my travelling trunk rolled with a crash, having torn from its fastenings yesterday. Prokhor had twice tried to tie it down. The third time he waved a hand.

"Prokhor," I called, not turning, going on looking into the dark, water-washed porthole, beyond which nothing at all could be seen but maddened, foaming blackness, "tell me honestly. Do you believe that I am in my right mind?"

He paused - whether weighing his answer or simply giving me time to rethink the question - and at last spoke, in that even, anxiety-free voice in which he always spoke, even when the world around us seemed to be falling apart:

"You ask this question for the third day running, sir. My answer has not changed since the first time."

"Then remind me of it. I seem to begin to forget even my own questions, let alone the answers to them."

"I believe that you are what you have always been," he answered. "Even if you yourself no longer believe it."

The ship heeled so that the trunk crashed into the door. Somewhere beyond the bulkhead, in the next cabin, a woman screamed - long, piercingly - and at once fell silent. Then came the sound of breaking glass, and someone swore in English.

"Let us go to the saloon, sir," said Prokhor, rising. "There are people there. When there are many people, fear is divided among all, and each gets less."

* * *
The main saloon occupied, it seemed, half the ship - an enormous hall with columns faced in mirrors, with sofas along the walls, with chandeliers which now, torn from their hooks, lay in heaps of crystal in the corners, and with a piano lashed to a column with ropes, as a raving madman is lashed. On the floor, between broken glasses and overturned tables, stood water - ankle-deep, it rolled from wall to wall with each heel, carrying off cards, gloves, someone's hat with feathers.

And people. Some forty, perhaps more. Those who could not stay in their cabins. Someone was praying. Someone was drinking. Someone, clutching a column, simply stared into emptiness with glassy eyes.

"Oh!" a piercing voice rang out. "There he is! The Russian! The one who doesn't sleep!"

Toward me, grabbing the backs of sofas, picked her way a lady - a stout Englishwoman of about fifty, in a lilac travelling dress soaked to the knees, with dishevelled greying ringlets and with a parrot in a cage which she pressed to her breast like an infant. The parrot - huge, green, with a red tail - rolled a mad yellow eye and from time to time hoarsely shouted something in Spanish.

"Mrs Aldridge," Prokhor whispered to me. "From Bristol. A judge's widow. Knows everything about everyone on this ship."

"You are a count, are you not?" Mrs Aldridge seized my sleeve, nearly dropping the cage. "The maid told me, and the laundress told her, and your steward told the laundress, that you are a Russian count. Or a prince. That you have not gone to bed for four nights. That you have..." she lowered her voice to a theatrical whisper, "scars on your back. Two. Here." She jabbed me with a finger between the shoulder blades. "The laundress saw them when she was washing your shirt - blood was showing through. Is it true? Were you wounded in a duel? Or did you escape from Siberia?"

"Ave Maria purísima!" the parrot croaked.

"Quiet, Cristóbal!" Mrs Aldridge shook the cage. "He lived with a Spanish missionary until the man died of fever. Now he prays like a nun. Perfectly insufferable bird. So is it true? About the scars?"

"Madam," I said, "if your laundress had seen everything she tells, she would have to wash the shirts of the whole Atlantic Ocean."

Mrs Aldridge was taken aback for a moment - then burst out laughing, loudly, like a man, slapping me on the shoulder.

"Witty! Very witty! I like it!" She bent closer. "But I shall find out all the same, Count. I always find out. My late husband used to say: 'Georgiana, you ought to have served at Scotland Yard instead of marrying a judge.' I said: 'Edward, I married a judge to know whom they put away.'"

The ship dropped from the crest of a wave, and all who stood fell to the floor. The parrot howled: "Dios mío!" Mrs Aldridge, sitting in the water, pressed the cage tightly to her and briskly adjusted a ringlet.

"Never mind," she said. "I have drowned three times in Bristol. In a boat, in a pond and in a bath. God does not take me. Says that with me he would have nothing but trouble."

* * *
In the far corner of the saloon, by the column with the lashed piano, stood a man in black. Tall, thin as a pole, with a narrow pale face, with long, shoulder-length grey hair, in a black frock coat buttoned to the throat, and with an enormous black book in his hands, which he held above his head like a shield. He held to nothing. He stood with legs wide apart, swaying with the ship, and shouted - in a voice that drowned even the roar of the storm:

"...and I saw a new heaven and a new earth! For the first heaven and the first earth were passed away, and there was no more sea! Repent, sinners! Repent! This is not a storm - these are the trumpets! The seventh seal is opened! He who shall fall from heaven like a star - he is here! He is among us! On this ship!"

"The Reverend Ezekiel Crow," whispered Prokhor. "From Boston. Going to preach in New York. Certain that the end of the world will come this year. Last year he was certain it would come last year."

The Reverend Crow suddenly turned - and his burning, sunken eyes stopped on me. He slowly lowered the book.

"You," he said. Not cried. Said - quietly, but I heard it across the whole saloon. "You. I saw you on deck the first night. You stood in the rain and looked at the sky. And the lightning did not strike you. It struck the mast three paces from you - and went round. I saw."

"Lightning often strikes masts, Reverend," I said. "It is iron."

"'How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!'" proclaimed the Reverend, raising the book again. "'How art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!' Who are you? Tell me your name!"

The saloon froze. Even Mrs Aldridge stopped adjusting her ringlet. Even the parrot fell silent.

I looked at this mad, burning man - and could not answer. Not because I was afraid. Because that question - tell me your name - suddenly struck me where no storm had reached. I knew what I was called in my passport. I knew what Prokhor called me. But at that moment, standing ankle-deep in water in the middle of a rocking saloon, I suddenly understood that I was not sure which of those names was the true one.

"Leave him, Reverend."

The voice sounded calm, mocking, with a soft French accent. From behind a card table, fastened immovably to the floor, rose a man - short, elegant, in an impeccable dark-blue frock coat that by some miracle remained dry in the midst of the general deluge. About forty, with a thin black moustache, with pomaded hair parted evenly, and with a pack of cards in long, deft fingers which shuffled it without stopping even when the ship heeled.

"If this gentleman were the devil," said the Frenchman, smiling, "he would long since have won all my money. And he has not even sat down at the table. What sort of devil is it that does not play cards?" He bowed to me. "Chevalier Auguste de Lambert. I travel for pleasure. And for other people's money. Would you care for a game, monsieur? Fear is best cured by gambling."

"He is a cardsharp," Prokhor whispered. "He has twice been caught. The captain wanted to put him ashore in Newfoundland, but had no time - the storm began."

The Reverend Crow muttered something about the Whore of Babylon and cards as her instrument, but turned away and began again to call upon the ceiling.

I sat down at the table.

* * *
