We played écarté. The Chevalier dealt with the ease with which one breathes, and chattered without pause - of Paris, of Monte Carlo, of the women he had beaten and the men who had beaten him. At the table, besides ourselves, sat two others: a fat, sweating American cotton trader from New Orleans, in a white waistcoat which he kept wiping with a handkerchief, and a small, dry, grey-bearded man in a black skullcap on the back of his head, with a loupe on a cord round his neck and a velvet pouch which he did not let out of his left hand for an instant.

"Mr Jacob van der Heyden," the Chevalier introduced him. "From Amsterdam. Deals in diamonds. Is carrying to New York a whole fortune - in that pouch. Is it not so, Mr van der Heyden?"

"In this pouch, Chevalier," the old man answered drily, "only my supper. Ship's biscuit. The fortune is in the captain's safe. I am not so foolish as you hope."

The cotton trader guffawed, wiping his forehead.

I played without looking at the cards. I do not know why. I simply took them, laid them down, took them again - and did not look. My thoughts were far away - somewhere under my ribs, at that point where from the very beginning of the storm a dull, aching pain had settled.

After the third game the Chevalier stopped chattering.

After the fifth - stopped smiling.

After the seventh he slowly laid the pack on the table and looked at me with a long, very attentive look.

"Monsieur," he said quietly. "For forty years I have played cards. I know every way of cheating that mankind has devised, and a dozen I devised myself. You do not cheat. I would see. " He paused. "But you do not look at the cards. And you have not lost a single trick. Not one. In seven games."

The American stopped wiping his forehead.

"Maybe just luck?" he said uncertainly.

"I too am lucky sometimes, monsieur," said the Chevalier, not taking his eyes from me. "But I am never so lucky that I do not look at the cards."

Old van der Heyden slowly took the loupe from his neck. Took my hand - without asking, with dry, cold fingers - and turned it palm up. Studied it long through the loupe. The lines. The skin.

"Interesting," he said at last. "Very interesting. You have no life line, young man."

"What?"

"A life line. Here," he drew a nail along my palm. "Everyone has one. Long, short, broken. You - none. Smooth. Like a stone that has lain long in a river." He released my hand. "For fifty years I have looked at stones through this glass. Diamond, ruby, emerald. I know how what the ages have grown looks." He paused. "Your palm is like a stone, young man. Not like a hand."

"Perhaps in Amsterdam it is the custom to pay compliments in riddles?" I asked, trying to smile.

The old man did not smile in return.

"In Amsterdam," he said, "there is an old riddle. Jewellers set it to apprentices. 'Two stones lie in one palm: one black as pitch, the other white as milk. Which is more precious?'" He looked at me over the loupe. "The apprentice always answers: the white. Or the black. And is always wrong."

"And what is the answer?"

"The one in the other palm," said the old man. And tucked the loupe under his coat.

* * *
"Charades!" Mrs Aldridge suddenly cried from some corner. "Let us play charades! My husband said: in a storm one must occupy the head, otherwise fear will occupy it!"

Someone groaned. Someone laughed. But soon, to my surprise, half the saloon - drenched, terrified, holding to columns and to one another - was already playing.

Mrs Aldridge set the first - in English, but the sense was clear without translation:

"'My first syllable is what a ship does when it sinks. My second is what we are all doing now. And the whole is what we have not got now!'"

"Sink..." the American pondered. "Sink-i... No..."

"Hope!" someone shouted.

"No!" Mrs Aldridge triumphed. "Rest! Rest - that is when a ship sinks, it... well..." She got tangled. "Never mind. My charade was bad. Who is next?"

The saloon roared with laughter - for the first time in three days. Laughed hysterically, to tears, holding to the wet columns, but laughed.

The next to volunteer, to general surprise, was the ship's cook - a huge, broad-shouldered black man in a white apron, with a gold earring in his ear, who had made his way into the saloon with a cauldron of hot broth which he ladled out to all and sundry without asking what class anyone was. His name was Samuel, but everyone called him Cook Sam.

"I don't know charades, ma'am," he said in a deep, rumbling bass. "I know a riddle. A sea one. My grandfather set it to me, and his grandfather to him, there on the islands from where we were all brought." He paused, and the saloon grew quiet. "'I walk on the sea, but I am not a ship. I burn, but I am not fire. I am seen only in a storm. What am I?'"

All were silent. The storm roared beyond the bulkheads.

"A lantern?" suggested the American.

"Lightning," said the Chevalier.

Cook Sam shook his head - slowly, solemnly. And raised a hand, pointing upward, to the ceiling of the saloon, beyond which were the deck and the masts.

"St Elmo's fire," he said. "Dead sailors. Those who drowned but found no peace. They come in a storm and sit on the masts. Glow. Watch. Look for whom to take with them." He paused. "Last night I saw them. On all six masts. At once."

No one laughed.

"And whom are they looking for, Sam?" I asked.

The cook looked at me. Long. With a heavy, calm look.

"My grandfather said, sir," he said, "St Elmo's fire never takes one who glows himself. They look for those who are in the dark." He lifted his cauldron and moved on, ladling broth. "You, sir, have nothing to fear. You are yourself like a fire on a mast. I saw."

* * *
From the crowd at the staircase leading down to the third class came a voice - thin, girlish, trembling. Someone was singing. The saloon gradually quieted, turning toward the sound.

A girl was singing. Quite young, about sixteen, red-haired, in a patched dress and an enormous man's jacket from someone else's shoulders, barefoot, wet to the skin. She stood on a step, holding the handrail, and sang - in a language I did not know - a melody that made the heart contract. Slow, drawn out, sad, with so many repetitions that it seemed the song itself did not want to end.

"Irish," Prokhor whispered. "From the third class. There are seven hundred of them there. Going to America from famine. She came to ask for a doctor for her younger brother. He has a fever."

"What is she singing?"

"I do not know, sir. But they say it is a song of a girl who waited for a sailor on the shore for seven years. And in the eighth he returned - but she did not recognise him, because the sea had changed his face."

The girl finished. The saloon was silent. Then Mrs Aldridge - loud, absurd, gossiping Mrs Aldridge - silently rose, made her way through the water to the stairs, took off her own warm shawl and laid it on the girl's shoulders.

"What is your name, child?"

"Mary, ma'am. Mary Casey."

"Lead me to your brother, Mary Casey," said Mrs Aldridge. "I was a judge's wife for thirty years. I know how to treat a fever better than any ship's doctor." And, turning to the saloon, she commanded: "Cristóbal - someone! Hold the bird! Do not let it pray - it will frighten everyone!"

And went down into the third class, holding the red-haired girl by the hand.

The cage with the parrot was for some reason thrust upon me.

The parrot Cristóbal fixed me with a mad yellow eye. Then tilted his head - and suddenly, quite distinctly, not in Spanish but in some language which I had never heard but which echoed in me with a strange, distant tremor, croaked a single word.

I did not understand it. But it was like - I was for some reason sure of this - a name.

* * *
"He repeats what he heard from the missionary," said a man who had come up to me. "Do not be frightened. Parrots are the best keepers of other people's words. They remember what people have long forgotten."

It was a no longer young, tidy German in spectacles, in a frock coat buttoned on every button, with a barometer in his hands - a real one, in a brass case - at which he glanced as one glances at a watch, awaiting a train.

"Professor Gottfried Altmann," he introduced himself with a brief bow. "Heidelberg. Meteorology. I am going to study American storms." He smiled without mirth. "As you see, the American storm decided to come to me itself, without waiting."

"What does your instrument say, Professor?"

"My instrument," said Altmann, rapping the glass with a nail, "says what cannot be. The pressure has been falling for the fourth day. It is already lower than in any storm I have ever read in records. And records, young man, have been kept on ships for more than a hundred years." He raised his eyes to me. "A century storm, the sailors say. They do not know how right they are. A hundred years. Exactly. I checked the old logs in the captain's library - at this same latitude, on these same days, exactly a hundred years ago, an English frigate vanished. Two hundred men. In a storm described only by two survivors." He paused. "Their description coincides almost word for word with what is happening now."

"A coincidence," I said.

"Naturally," agreed Professor Altmann. "I am a scientist. I believe in coincidences." He rapped the barometer again. "But here is what is curious. One of those two survivors was a Russian. A young nobleman. He travelled with his servant. The records say that he stood on deck through the whole storm and that lightning passed him by. And then, on the last night, he went to the rail - and no one saw him again. The servant was saved. Said afterward that his master had not drowned. That he had 'gone back to where he came from.'"

In the saloon the storm roared. Cristóbal in the cage in my hands was silent, head tilted.

"What was the servant's name?" I asked. My voice sounded strange to me.

"That is not recorded in the log," said the Professor. "Only initials. 'P. I.'"

I slowly turned.

Prokhor Ilyich stood by a column three paces from me. Just as imperturbable. Just as calm. And looked at me with the same long, sad look with which he had looked in the cabin.

* * *
We returned to the cabin together. The trunk was still rolling on the floor. The porthole was still black.

I went to the small mirror fastened to the wall of the cabin and peered at my own reflection, swaying in time with the ship. A face like any - tired, haggard from insomnia, but a most ordinary, human face, such as thousands may be met on any Petersburg street. Nothing in it betrayed what I, if the scraps of my own memory were to be believed - and to believe them was growing harder with every day of this accursed storm - had once been.

I unbuttoned the collar of my shirt, drew the cloth aside, baring my shoulders - and ran my fingers over two barely visible, long-healed marks under the shoulder blades, symmetrical, as though left by something that had once been attached precisely there and afterward torn or hacked out by the root. On stormy nights like this these marks ached with a dull, old pain, like wounds healed in the flesh but never healed otherwise. Tonight blood showed on the shirt again. Mrs Aldridge's laundress had not lied.

"Wings," I whispered, addressing the reflection rather than Prokhor himself. "It is not merely that I fancy they were? Or am I really going mad, inventing for myself a divine origin in order somehow to justify my own worthlessness?"

"You are not going mad, sir," answered Prokhor in the same even tone. "You have simply been a man too long. Longer than is safe for anyone born not on earth."

I turned to him sharply, feeling something inside me - whether hope or irritation or both at once - break out faster than I could master it.

"The Professor said - a hundred years ago. This same storm. A Russian nobleman and his servant. 'P. I.'" I stepped toward him. "Prokhor. Was it you?"

Prokhor was silent a long time.

"I have crossed this ocean many times, sir," he said at last. "With you. You do not remember. You never remember."

"Then tell me! Tell me who I am, if I myself am not able to remember! You remember - you said yourself just now that you remember!"

Prokhor looked at me with a long, sad look - a look with far more human compassion in it than an ordinary servant would have.

"I could tell," he said quietly. "But this truth, I fear, will not lighten your burden but only double it. You fell to this earth of your own will, many centuries ago - not as punishment, but from curiosity, from thirst to understand what had remained incomprehensible even to you yourself, for all your antiquity and all your strength. You wished to live a human life not from afar, not through the veil of divine omniscience, but from within, with every cell, every nerve, every tear and every joy. And you lived it. Many times. So many that you forgot - and that, sir, is not madness, but simply the price paid by anyone who wears another's skin too long."

"The Reverend Crow called me Lucifer," I said. "Son of the morning. The fallen."

"The Reverend Crow reads a book that men wrote, sir," said Prokhor. "And men always write of those who came down to them one of two things: that he is a god or that he is a devil. The middle they do not understand." He paused. "Do you know what your name means in the language in which it was devised? Not 'fallen.' 'Bearer of light.' The morning star. The one that rises before the sun, so that people may know: the night is ending."

I sank down on the edge of the narrow bunk, feeling the earth - or rather the water, the ever-heaving water beneath us - slip from under my feet in a far deeper, far more frightening sense than the simple pitching of a storm.

"And you?" I asked after a long silence. "Who are you, if not a simple servant?"

"I am here to remember for you what you cannot hold yourself," answered Prokhor simply, with no solemnity in his voice. "And to remind you of it when the time comes. It seems to me, sir, that the time is drawing near."

* * *
There was a knock at the cabin door - loud, insistent. Prokhor opened.

On the threshold stood Mary Casey - the red-haired Irish girl in Mrs Aldridge's shawl, barefoot, wet, with enormous frightened eyes. Behind her, holding to the wall, was Mrs Aldridge herself, dishevelled, with sleeves rolled up.

"Count," said Mrs Aldridge without preamble. "The boy is worse. The ship's doctor is drunk as a cobbler and says he can do nothing." She paused. "The boy is delirious. He keeps repeating one thing. Mary says - in Gaelic. Something like 'bring the bright gentleman.' Mary thinks this is about you. I think it is nonsense. But I am a judge's widow, Count. I know: when nothing else is left, one must check even nonsense."

I followed them down.

The third class was hell. A dark, low hold, packed with people like a barrel with herrings. Swaying lanterns. Water to the knee. Cries, weeping, prayers in a dozen languages. The smell of vomit, wet wool and fear. Seven hundred people who had fled famine for the New World - and found a storm on the way.

The boy lay on a bunk by the very bulkhead - small, about six, red-haired like his sister, with burning cheeks and dry, cracked lips. His eyes were open but looked into nothing. He was whispering something.

I knelt down beside him. Mary said something to him in Gaelic. The boy slowly turned his head - and his eyes, clouded with fever, rested on me.

He smiled.

"You have come," he said. Not in Gaelic. Not in English. In that very language in which the parrot Cristóbal had croaked his word. In a language I did not know - but which I understood. "I knew you would come. You always come when it is dark."

I took his hot hand in mine. I do not know why. I simply took it - and held it.

He closed his eyes. His breathing - hoarse, rapid - gradually grew slower. Steadier. After some time which I did not count, Mary, sobbing, touched his forehead - and cried out.

"Cold," she whispered. "Ma'am, he... he is cold... that is... the fever has broken... he is sleeping..."

Mrs Aldridge bent, felt the boy's forehead, then his neck. Straightened. Looked at me. And for the first time since I had known her, said nothing.

I rose. My hand, with which I had held the boy's, burned - as though I had held it over a fire.

As I left, through the hold behind my back, in a whisper, from mouth to mouth, in a dozen languages, ran one and the same word. I did not turn. I did not wish to know which.

* * *
The ship lurched especially hard, and somewhere above, on deck, an alarmed, straining cry was heard - whether of the boatswain giving orders or of the wind itself, which had at last found a crack through which to shout all its fury. I rose from the hold and, saying not another word to Mrs Aldridge, nor to Mary, nor to Prokhor waiting at the stairs, made my way up.

"Sir," Prokhor called after me, for the first time in all this time allowing himself something like anxiety in his voice, "one should not go on deck in such weather."

"I need air," I lied - or did not lie at all, because at that moment I did not myself know for certain what I needed more: air, an answer, or simply deliverance from the unbearable weight of my own body, alien to me.

He did not stop me - perhaps he knew that to restrain me at such a moment was useless, and perhaps he understood something which at that moment I myself did not. A hundred years ago, I thought, climbing the companionway, he probably did not stop me either.

The deck met me with a wall of water and wind that struck me with such force that I barely kept my feet, clinging to the wet, icy rail. Lightning one after another split the sky over the raging sea, snatching from the darkness the crests of waves rising higher than the funnels themselves - and in this mad, dazzling chaos there was something remotely, frighteningly like freedom. That very freedom which I perhaps had not felt for thousands of years, since the very moment when I first descended to this earth in a guise so alien to my true nature.

On the masts - on all six masts at once - fires burned. Pale, bluish, trembling, like candles in the wind which no wind could blow out. St Elmo's fire. Dead sailors, Cook Sam had said. They look for those who are in the dark.

They did not look at me. They looked at the sea. All, as one. As if awaiting something from there.

By the mainmast, clinging to a rope, stood the Reverend Crow - hatless, grey hair plastered to his skull, the black book pressed to his chest. He saw me. And did not cry out. He simply looked - long, unwaveringly - and his lips moved. I could not hear the words over the roar of the wind. But from the movement of his lips I understood: he was not cursing. He was praying. For me.

I moved along the rail, to where the deck ended, breaking off into the blackness of the raging sea - step by step, whether in search of an answer or in search of an end to all that had accumulated in me over these long, forgotten centuries of human life. What if Prokhor is mistaken? What if there is no fallen grandeur hidden under this weary, haggard human shell - but only a lonely passenger, driven mad by storm and sleeplessness, who has imagined himself something greater than a mere mortal because to admit his own unremarkable madness was simply unbearable for him?

Gone back to where he came from, said the servant a hundred years ago.

I stopped at the very rail, feeling icy spray on my face, feeling the wind tear at my clothes as if trying to strip them off together with the last remnants of the human guise to which I had clung so long and so unsuccessfully. Below, a few feet beneath me, the water roared - black, bottomless, ready to take into itself absolutely anything it was allowed, without a single question, without a single demand for explanations.

I laid my hands on the rail, preparing to throw over it a body so dubiously my own - and in that very instant the world around me froze.

Not time - time flowed on as before, I felt it with every cell of my wind-blown body - but something else, something within the storm itself. The lightning that split the sky at that moment hung for a fraction of a second longer than lightning should hang, pouring over the raging sea a light so even, so unnaturally long, that the very night for a moment seemed day. The fires on all six masts blazed up at once - and turned. All. To me. And the water beneath me, for just one short breath, ceased to obey the wind - froze in a ripple, stood in a wave that neither fell nor moved, as if the element itself held its breath, awaiting my next step with the same tense attention with which I myself awaited the answer to a question never asked aloud.

And in that frozen, glowing silence I heard behind me - very close, quite near - the hoarse, mocking voice of the parrot Cristóbal, who could not possibly have been here, on deck, in the storm. He was repeating that very word. The one. In the language I did not know.

My name.

I almost remembered it.

## Chapter XVI. A Fragment in the Archive

I had done the right thing. I knew I had done the right thing. Nebamun had said: not through the main corridor, the walls have ears, and some of those ears wear bracelets. And I had followed his advice.

But I had not expected it to be so unpleasant.

It happened at the morning audience, two days after the night in the temple granary. The hall was full - petitioners, scribes, dignitaries, guards - and at the very foot of the throne, as always, sat Bakenren, who had come to "humbly remind" me of the Temple's petition for three thousand hekats for the festival of Opet. He smiled. He bowed. He was so courteous that my jaw ached.

And in the very midst of his courteous speech the doors of the hall opened a crack, and Iti slipped through. With an ink stain on his cheek, with some scrolls under his arm, out of breath - he had evidently run from the Library on an errand for Amenemope. He bowed at the doors and froze, waiting for a sign.

I saw Bakenren's eyes slide toward him. Swiftly, fleetingly, the way a lizard's glance slides over a fly. I saw the bracelets chime by the far column - Khaemuas, who stood there among the commanders, had turned his head.

"Who allowed you to enter during an audience?" I said. Loudly. Coldly. As I had never spoken to him before. "Scribes of the Library have no business in the throne room. If Amenemope has a matter for Pharaoh, let him send a messenger. Go."

The hall fell silent. Bakenren raised his brows slightly - with interest.

Iti stood frozen in the doorway. His face - I could see it even across the whole hall - first went pale, then flared red to the very roots of his hair. He opened his mouth as if to say something. Closed it. Bowed - low, awkwardly, so that the scrolls nearly slipped from under his arm - and went out without raising his eyes.

The doors closed behind him.

"Young people these days have no notion of their place, my Pharaoh," Bakenren remarked sweetly. "In my years a scribe did not dare to breathe in the presence of a living god."

"Continue, Bakenren," I said evenly. "You were speaking of piety."

He continued. I did not hear a word. I looked at the closed doors and felt as though I had just struck a dog that had been running to me, wagging its tail.

* * *
He did not come that evening, nor the next.

The note from Pentu - the first one, with a copy of the true inventory of the granaries of Heliopolis - was brought to me not by Iti but by the boy Paney. He came into my chambers late in the evening, when I had already dismissed the servants - came in through the door to the garden, barefoot, with a bandaged hand in which a tightly rolled papyrus was clutched.

"From Iti, my Pharaoh," he said, holding out the scroll. And he added, with that directness with which only children and old men speak: "He did not come himself. He said - let Pharaoh not have to see him more than necessary. Since it is unpleasant for him."

"He said that?"

"He said exactly that, my Pharaoh." Paney hesitated, shifting his bare feet. "He said a good many other things too. Only they are not for Pharaoh."

"Tell me anyway."

Paney looked at me gravely, weighing whether he should.

"He said: 'Nebamun said - not through the main corridor. And Pharaoh, it turns out, has decided - not at all.'" The boy sniffed. "And he said that a scribe of the Library is, of course, nobody and nothing. And that he, of course, knows his place. And that his place is among the dusty scrolls where nobody goes. And that he is happy there." Paney paused. "Only he said it, my Pharaoh, the way people say things when they are not happy."

I was silent for a long time. Paney waited.

"Paney," I said at last. "You are his pupil. Tell me honestly. Was he hurt?"

Paney thought. Then he nodded - slowly, thoroughly, as Senusret nods.

"Very, my Pharaoh. He spent half the night copying the same scroll. Three times. And three times he spoiled it. Amenemope said that in twenty years he had never seen Iti spoil a scroll. And today Iti deliberately scattered all my potsherds with letters, and then gathered them up himself and apologized." The boy spread his hands. "He is like my father, my Pharaoh, when Mama was angry with him. He drops everything."

I could not help it - I smiled. Paney, seeing this, seemed to relax.

"Paney," I said. "Pass something on to him. Not a note - by word of mouth. Say: the walls have ears. The garden does not. And Pharaoh, too, sometimes walks in the garden."

Paney pondered, moving his lips, memorizing. Then he nodded.

"I will pass it on, my Pharaoh." And at the door he turned: "May I ask a riddle? Iti gave it to me and I cannot solve it. Perhaps you can?"

"Go on."

"'Who speaks without a mouth? Who remembers without a heart? Who lives a thousand years, yet dies from a single drop of water?'"

I thought.

"A scroll," I said. "Papyrus. It speaks without a mouth - by what is written. It remembers without a heart - everything that is recorded in it. It lives a thousand years in a dry storehouse - but a single drop of water washes the ink away."

Paney stared at me with admiration.

"Iti said you would solve it," he said. "He said: 'Pharaoh solves everything. Except what is right under his nose.'" And before I could ask what that meant, he darted out into the garden.

* * *
The gossip was brought the next morning by Nefret - the senior woman over the palace servants, a woman of enormous size, with a voice like a temple trumpet and a memory which, by common opinion, held more information about palace affairs than all the scrolls of the Library. She came herself - supposedly to check whether my linen garments had been properly laundered - and as she checked, she talked without pause.

"...and the keeper of the seal's wife has borne a girl again, the fifth, my Pharaoh, and now he goes about blacker than a storm cloud, says the gods are laughing at him... and the cook from the kitchen quarrelled with the baker over whose leaven is better, and now they are not speaking, and the bread, mind you, is suffering... and the nomarch Ankhtifi has sent a bearskin as a gift for the hall, and we have never had bears here, so everyone is wondering where he got it..."

I listened with half an ear, trying not to betray my impatience.

"...and another thing, my Pharaoh," Nefret lowered her trumpet voice to what she herself must have considered a whisper but which could in fact be heard in the neighbouring chambers, "they say that the junior keeper of the Library, that boy, Iti, goes to the temple garden at night. Not alone. He has been seen with a young priestess. The big-eyed one. Khemu. By the pond. Whispering, they say. Passing something to each other." She pursed her lips meaningfully. "Well, they are young. Priestesses, of course, are not supposed to. But who can hold them back when it is spring?"

I froze with the cup in my hand.

Something pricked me - somewhere under the ribs, but not on the left, where the familiar cold lived, but on the right, in a place entirely new and unknown. Swift, sharp, like the prick of a fish bone. And at once it let go.

Of course they meet by the pond. Of course they whisper and pass things - I myself had told Khemu to send word through Iti. He carries the notes. He does exactly what I asked. No spring. No "they are young."

I knew this. And yet for several moments, while Nefret, noticing nothing, went on about the bearskin, I sat motionless and listened to that strange, swift prick - trying to understand what it was.

Concern for them, I decided. If Nefret knows - then the whole court knows. Then Bakenren knows. Then Khemu is in danger. And Iti. That was what it was. Alarm. Simply alarm for two people who are helping me.

Of course.

"Nefret," I said. "And who else is talking about this?"

"Oh, my Pharaoh," she waved her plump hands, "everyone! The laundresses. The water-carriers. The gardeners. They even say that one of the men of the honourable Khaemuas asked the gardener whether the boy goes to the pond often." She giggled. "Perhaps he is jealous too."

I set down the cup.

"Nefret. When you speak with the laundresses - tell them this. The junior keeper of the Library is, by my order, collecting ancient inscriptions for the temple pond. From the garden walls. For copying. The priestess shows him where they are. That is all."

Nefret gave me a long, shrewd, not at all foolish look.

"Inscriptions," she said. "From the walls. At night." She nodded. "Of course, my Pharaoh. I shall say so. The laundresses will believe it." She gathered up the garments. "The water-carriers too. But the gardeners..." She shrugged her mighty shoulders. "The gardeners, my Pharaoh, know there are no inscriptions on the walls of the temple garden. But I shall tell them there are. The gardeners are afraid of me."

She left. I looked after her for a long time and thought that perhaps I had underestimated the palace servants.

* * *
He came to the garden on the third night.

I was waiting for him by the old fig tree at the far end of the garden, where the wall was overgrown with jasmine so thickly that a whole chariot could have been hidden behind it. The moon was thin, almost invisible, and the garden lay in darkness full of scents - jasmine, damp earth, the blooming lotus in the little pond - and of sounds: cicadas, the distant barking of a dog in the city, the rustle of the night wind in the palm leaves.

He appeared soundlessly, as he always did - I heard him only when he was already standing three paces away, at the very jasmine. In his hands was not a scroll but something wrapped in a piece of coarse linen. He pressed it to his chest with both hands, the way one holds a small child or a very fragile thing.

"My Pharaoh," he said, and bowed. Correctly. Precisely. Coldly. The way one bows not to a man but to a throne.

"Iti," I said.

He straightened and looked at me. Not in the eyes - slightly higher, at my forehead, as scribes are taught to look when they speak with exalted persons.

"You are angry with me," I said.

"A scribe of the Library does not dare to be angry with Pharaoh, my Pharaoh," he answered in an even voice, as if reading from a scroll. "Pharaoh was right. Scribes of the Library have no business in the throne room. I know my place."

"Iti."

"My place is among the scrolls, my Pharaoh. Where it is dusty and nobody goes. I am happy there."

"Iti, look at me."

He hesitated - and looked. And in the darkness, in the thin light of the almost invisible moon, I saw that his eyes were shining.

"Bakenren was in the hall," I said quietly. "Khaemuas stood by the column. They both looked at you when you came in. The way one looks at a new piece on the board - calculating where to move it. I could not allow them to see that you are to me..." I faltered. "That you are important to me. Nebamun said: the walls have ears. I made sure the ears heard that the boy from the Library is nobody. So that they would stop looking at you."

Iti was silent.

"I did not think," I said, "that you would hear it too. And believe it too."

He was silent a long while. Then he lowered his eyes - to the bundle he was pressing to his chest.

"Paney passed it on to me," he said softly, no longer like a scribe but in his own voice. "About the ears. And about the garden." He paused. "For two days I thought that you... that Pharaoh..."

"That what?"

"Nothing, my Pharaoh." He suddenly smiled - crookedly, awkwardly, as if he had forgotten how in these days. "Paney said that you solved the riddle about the scroll."

"I did."

"I set it on purpose," said Iti. "I knew you would solve it. I wanted..." He faltered. "I wanted you to think about something connected with me, at least once. Even if it was only a riddle."

I found nothing to answer. On his cheek, in the thin moonlight, a stain showed dark - ink, as always. I raised my hand, not knowing why, and wiped it away with my thumb. Simply wiped it away. The way one wipes a smudge from a younger brother's face.

Iti went utterly still. He seemed to have stopped breathing.

"You always have ink on your face," I said, lowering my hand. "How do you manage it?"

"I... rub my cheek when I think, my Pharaoh," he whispered. "With the brush. I forget it is in my hand."

"So you think a great deal."

"A great deal, my Pharaoh," said Iti. And after a pause he added, so quietly that I barely heard: "Especially these last two days."

Somewhere in the garden a night bird cried out. Iti started, as if waking, and hurriedly held out the bundle to me.

"That is not why I came, my Pharaoh. That is... not only why. Here. I found this. In the lower storehouse. Yesterday." His voice was businesslike again, quick, but his fingers, unwrapping the linen, trembled slightly. "I have shown it to no one. Not even Amenemope. Because..." He raised his eyes to me. "Because, my Pharaoh, I think it is what the High Priest is looking for."

* * *
Hardly anyone ever went down to the lower storehouse of the Library, Iti told me, while by the light of a small clay lamp, which he had taken from his bosom and lit from a flint, I examined his find. Into the lower storehouse they carried what was considered spoiled: scrolls gnawed by mice, washed out by water, scorched in some old fire, cracked tablets, shards of clay tablets with half-effaced signs. What is written may not be thrown away - that is sacrilege, the word of Thoth cannot be thrown away - so all of it was put into huge clay jars, sealed, and set in rows in an underground vault where it was dry, dark, and smelled of mice and eternity.

Over this subterranean kingdom ruled old Isiret - one of the few women scribes at court, dry as a stick, with a face like a crumpled papyrus, a tongue sharp as a reed brush, and a memory which, according to Iti, was more terrible than any archive.

"She drove me out," Iti told me while I looked at the papyrus. "On the first day. She said that the boys of the upper Library know only how to copy beautiful scrolls for Pharaoh, and do not want to do the real work - sorting what the mice have devoured. I said that I wanted to. She looked at me and said: 'Very well. Here is a jar for you. No one has been in it for three hundred years. Sort it out. If you find even one whole line, I will kiss you.'" Iti blushed. "I did not, of course, want her to kiss me. She is a hundred years old and has three teeth. But I sorted it out."

"And you found it?"

"I found it, my Pharaoh." He pointed to the papyrus in my hands. "This. At the very bottom of the jar. Wrapped in leather. The leather had almost rotted away, and the papyrus had not. As though someone had hidden it on purpose among the refuse. Where no one would look."

The papyrus was small - two palms long, one wide. Its edges were frayed, one corner was eaten away as if by mice, but the middle had survived remarkably well. And on it were signs.

Not ours.

Not hieroglyphs, not the cursive of the priests, not the counting marks of the scribes. Long, flowing, curving lines, running one into another without breaks, with no clear boundary between the signs - like water pouring over stone. Like the trace a retreating wave leaves on the sand.

I had never seen such writing. I was certain that I had never seen it.

And yet, looking at it, I felt something pass through the fingers that held the papyrus, from the fingertips to the wrist - neither warmth nor cold - something like recognition. The very feeling one has on hearing a melody known long ago, when one has forgotten where it was heard.

"My Pharaoh?" Iti asked quietly. "Can you... can you read it?"

"No," I said. "I cannot. But..."

"But?"

I did not answer. I looked at the signs, and it seemed to me - this was, of course, a trick of the lamp, of the thin, trembling flame - that the lines on the papyrus were faintly stirring. Not changing - no. Simply as if breathing. Like a sleeping beast.

* * *
"That is not all," said Iti. "Turn it over."

I turned it over.

On the reverse side, in the very corner, there was an inscription. Small, faded almost to invisibility. In our signs. Ancient, angular ones, such as were written under the very first Pharaohs - but ours.

Iti bent to the lamp beside me, so close that I could feel the warmth of his shoulder, and read aloud, slowly, moving his finger along the signs:

"'Words of the First Ones. Sent down from the Heavens together with the Two Eyes. Do not read. Do not show. Keep until the appointed time.'"

Keep until the appointed time.

I read it again. Then once more. The words were ordinary - the most ordinary words, such as are written on jars of grain and on chests of dowry. Keep until the appointed time.

But somewhere inside me - very far away, as if many days' journey down the river, or many years, or something else entirely that had no name - these words resounded as though spoken by someone I knew. Someone who held in his hand a similar scrap of paper - not papyrus but paper, thin, white, such as is not made among us. On a narrow, sun-flooded street. In a strange city smelling of the sea and of spices.

I blinked. The vision - if it was a vision - vanished.

"There is a drawing as well," said Iti. "Under the inscription. Very pale."

I brought the papyrus right up to the flame. Beneath the ancient signs there was indeed a drawing - thin, faded, almost wiped away. Two circles. One filled in. The other empty. And between them a wavy line.

"The Two Eyes," Iti whispered. "Black and white. And a road between them. Or a river."

We sat crouching under the jasmine, shoulder to shoulder, bent over a small scrap of papyrus that had lain at the bottom of a jar of refuse for three hundred years - and said nothing. The cicadas sang. The lamp crackled.

"Iti," I said at last. "Who else knows?"

"No one, my Pharaoh. Isiret saw that I had found something, but I said it was just a scrap of a prayer. She believed me." He paused. "I think she believed me."

"You think?"

"Isiret never shows whether she believes or not, my Pharaoh. She says that belief is for priests, and for scribes there is only verification."

* * *
We heard footsteps - light, quick - and both of us started. Iti blew out the lamp. I thrust the papyrus into my bosom.

From behind the fig tree came Khemu. Without a lamp, in a dark cloak over her white priestess's robes, breathless, her hair disordered.

"Iti!" she whispered, not at once making me out in the darkness. "Iti, trouble, Bakenren..." And then she saw me. She froze. She fell to her knees. "My... my Pharaoh!"

"Rise. What has happened?"

"Bakenren," Khemu gasped, getting up. "This evening he came to the Library. To Amenemope. He demanded the Most Ancient Epic. Again. The fourth time this moon. And then..." She caught her breath. "Then he asked about the lower storehouse. He asked who works there. Amenemope said - old Isiret. And the boy. Iti. Bakenren asked what the boy was looking for there. Amenemope said - sorting spoiled scrolls. Bakenren said: 'How interesting. I should like to see what he has already sorted.' And he ordered that tomorrow at dawn Isiret show him all the jars the boy has opened."

Iti turned so white that it was visible even in the dark.

"How do you know?" I asked.

"Merit heard," said Khemu. "She was in the Library - she had come for a scroll of hymns. She told me to run and warn you. She said: 'Little bird, run to the boy. The fox has gone to the henhouse.'"

"The jar," Iti whispered. "I left the jar open. And the leather the papyrus was wrapped in. It is there, at the bottom. If Bakenren sees it..."

"He will understand that something was there," I finished.

The three of us stood under the jasmine in the darkness, and no one said a word.

* * *
"Isiret," Iti said at last. "We must go to Isiret. Now."

"She will betray you," said Khemu.

"Perhaps," said Iti. "And perhaps not. I do not know whose side she is on. No one knows. But she is the only one who can make sure Bakenren finds nothing."

"I will go with you," I said.

They both stared at me.

"My Pharaoh," said Khemu. "If you are seen in the lower storehouse at night..."

"If I am seen with you in the temple garden at night, it will be worse," I said. "The palace is already whispering that you two meet by the pond." I paused. "That you, Iti, go to Khemu because of the spring."

Iti choked. Khemu snorted - nervously, briefly - and at once clapped her palm over her mouth.

"To me?" she repeated. "Him?" She looked at Iti, then at me, and something mischievous, quite girlish, flickered in her huge, kohl-rimmed eyes. "My Pharaoh, with all respect - Iti does not go to the garden for me. Iti goes to the garden..." She broke off, looked at Iti, who stood red as a crab, and finished in quite a different tone: "...for the inscriptions. From the walls. For copying."

"Nefret has already told the laundresses so," I nodded.

"Nefret?" Khemu raised her brows. "My Pharaoh, if Nefret is on your side, you have no need of an army."

Iti, still red, muttered something under his breath. I did not catch what. But it seemed to me - quite absurdly, at such a moment - that I felt lighter. There, on the right, under the ribs, where two days ago it had pricked.

* * *
The lower storehouse lay beneath the Library - a narrow stair hewn in the rock descended into the darkness, and with each step the air grew drier, cooler, and heavier with the smell of dust, mouse droppings, and old, very old papyrus. Below stretched a long corridor, and along it, in niches, stood rows of jars - huge, man-high, sealed with clay, with signs scratched on their sides: the year, the storehouse, "spoiled by water," "spoiled by fire," "spoiled by mice."

At the end of the corridor a lamp was burning. And beside it, on a low stool, sat an old woman.

Isiret was exactly as Iti had described her - only more terrible. Small, shrivelled, almost bodiless, in a dark robe, with a face so densely furrowed that it looked like a map of all the roads of the Valley, and with eyes - black, shining, alive - that in the lamplight seemed two drops of ink on old papyrus. Before her on a mat lay potsherds, and she, without raising her head, was fitting them together like a mosaic - piece to piece, sign to sign.

"You took your time, boy," she said without turning. "I thought you would come running as soon as Bakenren left. And you have, I see, brought guests besides." At last she turned her head. She looked at Khemu. At me. She held her gaze on me - long, appraising, without the slightest reverence. "Ah. Himself. A living god. In a cellar. With the mice." She snorted. "Well, then. The gods, they say, are everywhere. Even in spoiled jars."

Khemu gasped. Iti turned pale. I did not know whether to laugh or be angry - and Isiret, it seems, read this on my face, for her three teeth flashed in a smile.

"Sit down, living god," she said, nodding at the next jar. "I have no stools. Kings do not come here. Except once in three hundred years."

"Once in three hundred years?" I repeated.

"And you think you are the first?" Isiret bent again over her potsherds. "The jar the boy opened was sealed by a scribe named Hekanakht son of Pepi. I read his seal. He was keeper of this vault three hundred years ago. Under a Pharaoh whose name has been erased from half the walls of the Valley." She fitted one sherd to another. "And in the scroll of Merira son of Pepi, which lies over there in the third jar from the stair, it is written that one night Pharaoh himself came down into the storehouse. Alone. Without guards. And brought something wrapped in leather. And ordered it hidden where no one would look. 'Until the appointed time,' he said."

It grew so quiet in the vault that I could hear a mouse scratching somewhere in the darkness behind the jars.

"Which Pharaoh?" I asked.

"The one whose name was erased," said Isiret. "I told you." She raised her black, shining eyes to me. "Hekanakht son of Pepi writes that Pharaoh was young. That he came down here on the eve of a journey south. To the festival. In Luxor." She paused. "And that he did not return from the festival. Or rather - he returned. But different. He looked through people. As if he saw something else behind them."

Paser. The council of commanders. The old legend that is told in whispers.

The cold under the ribs - on the left, familiar, known - rose so swiftly that it took my breath away.

* * *
"Bakenren will come at dawn," said Isiret, returning to her potsherds. "He wants to see the jars the boy opened. Very well. I shall show him." She nodded to Iti. "Boy, go to the fifth jar from the stair. The one 'spoiled by water.' There is a scroll of grain accounts from the time of some long-forgotten Pharaoh. Of no use to anyone. Sodden. Bring it. And the leather from your jar, too."

Iti ran. He came back with the sodden scroll and a rotted piece of leather. Isiret, without looking, wrapped the scroll in the leather, tied it with a scrap of cord, and threw it into the jar from which Iti had taken the papyrus.

"There," she said. "Tomorrow Bakenren will see that the boy found in the jar, wrapped in leather, an account of grain. Sodden. Useless. In front of him I shall unwrap it, show it, grumble at the boy for wasting his time on refuse. Bakenren will laugh and leave. Priests like to laugh at scribes. It consoles them."

"Why are you helping us?" I asked.

Isiret did not answer for a long time. She fitted potsherds together.

"Do you know a riddle, living god?" she said at last. "An old one. It is asked only in this cellar. 'Which is stronger - the one who writes, or the one who erases?'"

I thought.

"The one who erases. He can destroy what is written."

"Wrong." Isiret set the last sherd in place - and the sherds on the mat suddenly came together into a whole sign. An Eye. "Stronger is the one who remembers. What is erased can be remembered. What is written can be forgotten. And the one who remembers is stronger than both. I remember everything that lies in this cellar, living god. Every jar. Every potsherd. Twenty years. And I remember that the High Priest has never come down here. Not once. Until today. And today he came down - and the first thing he asked about was the boy. So he knows there is something here that he did not find in the Epic. And if the High Priest is searching so hard for something, it is better that he not find it."

She paused.

"And besides," she added, unexpectedly gently, "the boy sorted my jar. The whole of it. In a single night. Which no one had touched for three hundred years." She looked at Iti, and her wrinkled face suddenly became almost tender. "I promised him a kiss for one whole line."

Iti stepped back a pace, turning pale.

"Do not be afraid, boy." Isiret giggled - dryly, with a rattle. "Three teeth are all I have left. I shall save the kiss for someone who needs it more." She moved her black eyes from Iti to me and back - once, swiftly, the way one shifts one's gaze from one line to another, checking that it has been copied correctly. "For someone who will wipe the ink from your cheek. Otherwise you go about like a spotted cat."

Iti turned crimson. Khemu, standing by the stair, turned to the wall - and her shoulders shook.

I looked at old Isiret and thought that in all the palace there seemed to be not a single person who did not see more than he showed.

* * *
We climbed the stair in silence. At the exit from the vault, in the darkness of the Library, Khemu touched my hand.

"My Pharaoh," she whispered. "That inscription. 'Keep until the appointed time.' I have seen it before."

"Where?"

"On a chest. The one of black wood. In the treasury. On the lid, from the inside." She swallowed. "I did not understand then what it was. I thought they were just words. And now..."

She did not finish. We both knew what she had wanted to say.

Iti walked with me as far as the garden. At the fig tree, under the jasmine, he stopped.

"My Pharaoh," he said. "The papyrus. What will you do with it?"

I touched my chest, where under my garment the bundle lay.

"Keep it," I said. "Until the appointed time."

Iti nodded. He stood a little longer. Then he said - very quietly, looking not at me but at the jasmine:

"My Pharaoh. When you said 'go' in the hall... For two days I thought I would never come again."

"And you came."

"And I came," he agreed. "Because I found the papyrus. And I thought: Pharaoh needs this. Even if Pharaoh does not need me."

"Iti," I said.

He raised his eyes to me.

I did not know what to say. I - Pharaoh, living god, lord of the Two Lands - stood under the jasmine in the darkness before the junior keeper of the Library with his perpetual ink stain on his cheek, and did not know what to say. Every word that came to my mind was either too large or too small.

"Come tomorrow," I said at last. "Through the garden. Bring me another riddle."

He smiled - truly, for the first time in these days, so that it could be seen even in the dark.

"Which one, my Pharaoh?"

"Any. One that I cannot solve."

"There is no such one," said Iti. "Paney says you solve everything."

"Paney says that you said: except what is right under my nose."

Iti froze. Then he blushed - so that it showed even in the light of the thin moon - muttered something unintelligible, bowed - awkwardly, hurriedly, not at all like a scribe - and vanished behind the jasmine so fast that it was as though all the crocodiles of the Nile were after him.

I stood alone under the fig tree, pressing to my chest the papyrus on which was written what I could not read, and words that I somehow knew. Keep until the appointed time.

And I thought not of Bakenren. Not of the High Priest. Not of the Pharaoh whose name had been erased from half the walls of the Valley and who three hundred years ago had descended into the vault on the eve of the festival at Luxor.

I thought of what exactly Iti had meant when he said: except what is right under his nose.

And of why I so wanted to solve it.

* * *
When I returned to my chambers, old Amenemope was waiting for me at the doors - for the first time in all the time I had known him, risen by himself in the night from the Library. He stood leaning on his black staff and looked at me with the same faded, all-seeing gaze with which all the old men of this palace had looked at me today.

"My Pharaoh," he said. "The boy found something below. I know. I do not ask what." He paused. "I have come to tell you a tale. An old one. It was told to me when I was like Iti. About the god Thoth and Pharaoh."

"Now? At night?"

"Tales, my Pharaoh, are better heard at night," said Amenemope. "By day they seem untrue."

I let him in. He sat on the bench by the window, laid his staff across his knees, and began to speak - slowly, quietly, the way one tells a story looking not at the listener but into one's own memory:

"'Once the god Thoth, lord of writing, came to the Pharaoh who ruled in Thebes and brought him his inventions. Number. The measuring of land. The stars. The game of senet. And writing. "Here," said Thoth, "is writing. It will make the Egyptians wiser and strengthen their memory. I have found a remedy for memory." But Pharaoh shook his head. "O most skilful Thoth," he said, "you, the father of writing, out of love for it ascribe to it a power opposite to the one it has. Writing will not strengthen memory - it will weaken it. People, having learned to write, will cease to exercise their memory. They will remember not from within, but from without - by the signs of others. You have found a remedy not for memory but for reminding."'"

Amenemope fell silent.

"And what did Thoth do?" I asked.

"The tale does not say, my Pharaoh," answered the old man. "But writing remained. And since then we keep scrolls instead of remembering." He rose, leaning on his staff. "I think of this tale each time I see a man who does not remember himself. Perhaps he need not look for the scroll on which his name is written. Perhaps he needs to remember from within."

He bowed and went to the door.

"Amenemope," I said after him. "Do you see a man who does not remember himself?"

The old man stopped in the doorway. Turned.

"Every day, my Pharaoh," he said. "Every day since you ascended the throne." And, after a pause: "Do not be afraid. The boy from the Library remembers a great deal for you. More than you think."

He left, tapping with his staff.

And I sat by the window until morning, holding on my knees the papyrus that had lain for three hundred years among the refuse, waiting for its appointed time. And when the first ray of the sun fell on its edge, it seemed to me - for only an instant - that the flowing, incomprehensible signs on it had come together into a word. One single word.

But the sun rose higher - and the word melted away like breath on glass.

## Chapter XVII. A Walk to Sultanahmet

The appointed day arrived as imperceptibly as the previous ones had slipped by - in a lazy alternation of tea, backgammon with Suleyman (I won, to my own astonishment, some five games off him, though the old man insisted that the victory had been granted me out of pure hospitality), and long hours on the balcony, where I looked at the city, which was beginning little by little to grow familiar to me, in the way any place grows familiar if one spends enough sleepless, watchful evenings in it.

Suleyman appeared on the threshold of my room early in the morning - clad not in his house robe but in a stout travelling kaftan, girded with a wide sash into which was tucked a short knife with a carved handle, more a keepsake than a weapon. On his wrist, over his prayer beads, the red thread with half of the split nazar was still wound. He nodded to me in silence, making it clear: it was time.

"He says," translated Ferhat, who had sprung up behind his back, dishevelled, with hair still wet from washing and a piece of flatbread in his hand, "that we shall go by the same way the stranger took, the one his father saw. He remembers the way. His father told him. Step by step."

"And you?" I asked. "Aren't you due on shift?"

"I am," said Ferhat with his mouth full. "But I told the harbour master that my aunt had died."

"Your aunt has died?"

"I have no aunt," Ferhat replied imperturbably. "So she can die as many times as she likes. This year she has already died three times. The harbour master sent a basket of figs to the funeral." He grinned. "God will forgive. God loves it when people help guests."

Suleyman, who had not understood a word but had evidently guessed everything from the intonation, rapped his grandson on the back of the head with his knuckles - not hard, more for form's sake - and we went out.

* * *
We left the house when the sun had barely torn itself from the edge of the sea and the air still kept the coolness of the night, that peculiar, short-lived freshness which port cities grant their inhabitants for only an hour or two before the heat enters fully into its rights. The streets, which at this hour were usually thronged with peddlers and the first customers, now seemed almost deserted - only a few figures hurried somewhere on their business in the morning dusk, and the cats, those eternal, imperturbable masters of Eastern cities, stretched lazily on steps still warm from the evening.

At the gate Kemal caught up with us. Silently, as always. He stood beside his grandfather and walked on as though it had been agreed. Suleyman looked at him, was about to say something - and did not. He only laid his palm on the boy's head, for a moment, in passing, and under that palm Kemal smiled faintly.

Akmal, of course, did not catch up with anyone - he simply flew out from around the corner, overtook all three of us and raced ahead like a dog let off its leash, turning round every so often to check that we were following.

"He will wait for us at every crossroads," Ferhat sighed. "And at every crossroads he will ask whether it is soon. Like when we were children and went to the sea."

"Did you often go to the sea?"

"Every Sunday. With our father." Ferhat paused. "He would take Akmal on his shoulders and me by the hand. Kemal did not walk yet then - Mother carried him on her back. Father used to say: 'Look at the water. The water remembers everyone who has gone out over it. If you look long enough, you can see.'" He shrugged. "Akmal still looks. Every day. He thinks I don't know."

He said it lightly, as if in passing. But I saw him turn away before he had finished.

* * *
Our way ran along the coast - first through quarters already familiar to me from short outings with Akmal, then farther, where the houses grew higher and more imposing, and the streets noticeably cleaner, as though a different, more exacting part of the city breathed the very air here. Suleyman walked unhurriedly but with assurance, in the stride of a man for whom this road had long become something habitual, though not devoid, judging by the way he glanced about from time to time, of a certain reverence for the places passed.

From time to time he stopped - at a fountain, at an old grove of plane trees, at a small mosque with a leaning minaret - and said something, pointing with his hand. Ferhat translated:

"Here the stranger drank water. Father saw it. He scooped it in his palm, drank, and laughed. He said: 'The same water as everywhere. Water is one everywhere.'" And then, at the grove: "Here he sat down in the shade and wrote something. For a long time. Father stood by a shop and watched. Then the stranger got up, and on the ground where he had sat a drawing was left, made with a stick. Two circles. Father came to look - but the wind had already wiped it away."

Kemal, hearing this, stopped at the roots of a huge plane tree. He crouched down. Ran his palm over the ground as if searching for something. Then he rose and went on, saying nothing.

We passed a hill from whose summit the whole bay opened to view - I stopped for a moment, unable to tear my eyes from the water, which reflected the morning sun with that dazzling, almost painful brightness that occurs only over the sea in a windless hour. The minarets scattered across the whole visible expanse seemed from here like thin needles stuck into the bluish haze, and the domes of the mosques like frozen drops of mercury, heavy and perfect in their roundness.

"Beautiful," I said aloud, though I was addressing, essentially, only myself.

"Grandfather says," said Ferhat, "that this view has no price. He traded for forty years and knows the price of everything. Silk, pepper, people. But not of this. He says: that is why everyone stays here. They come for a day - and stay for life. The city keeps those it likes."

"And those it does not like?"

"Those it lets go," said Ferhat. "At once. With the first ship." He smiled. "It has not let you go yet."

* * *
Descending the hill, we passed a place fenced off with scaffolding and high hoardings of fresh planks - judging by the hammering that carried from there and the calling of workmen in several languages at once, this was where the new Palace of the Sultan was being raised, of which I had heard almost from the first minute of my stay in this city. The building itself, not yet finished, already astonished by its scale - the walls, faced with pale stone, stretched along the whole shore, vanishing somewhere around the bend, and the dome of the central part, still hidden by scaffolding, could be guessed beneath it as a gigantic, half-formed shadow.

At the gate of the building site, on an overturned wheelbarrow, sat a mason - elderly, grey-moustached, with hands white from dust - smoking a long pipe and waiting until the overseer turned away. Suleyman, passing by, stopped, and they exchanged a few phrases - judging by the tone, old acquaintances. The mason burst out laughing, slapped his knees and said something, pointing with his pipe at the palace.

"What does he say?" I asked.

Ferhat was choking with laughter.

"He says he has been building this palace for eight years. And that in eight years the Sultan has changed the architect three times and the plan seven times. And that when the palace is finally finished, the Sultan will probably say he wanted something completely different and order it pulled down." Ferhat wiped his eyes. "And Grandfather answered that this is a good thing: while they are building, people have bread. Better to build for ten years than to finish in one and dismiss everyone."

"Grandfather does not like this building site," he added, lowering his voice, though there seemed to be no reason for such caution. "He says too much money goes into stone and too little into people. But it is better not to repeat that aloud."

The mason, seeing us off, suddenly called out to me - in his own tongue, but with an evident question, pointing his pipe first at me, then at the palace.

"He asks," translated Ferhat, "whether you are an architect. A new one. The fourth. He says you have the face of a man who is about to redo everything."

I laughed. The mason laughed too, waved his pipe - and at once, noticing the overseer, hid it behind his back with the air of an innocent babe.

* * *
Beyond the building site began the quarter of Sultanahmet proper - and here the city changed almost imperceptibly, yet quite definitely. The streets grew narrower, the houses older, and the stillness that reigned in this part of the city even at the height of the morning seemed somehow special, almost reverent, as if the very air here were soaked with the memory of centuries that had passed before even one of us was born.

And then the street parted - and we came out onto a huge, elongated square across which the wind roamed.

In the middle of it, one after another, stood three columns. The first was thin, tall, grey, built of rough stone blocks, as if it had been put up in haste and never been faced. The second was strange, dark, of bronze, like three snakes twisted together into a tight rope - only without heads: where the snakes should have had heads, the column broke off in uneven, broken edges. And the third...

The third was an obelisk.

Tall, slender, sharp as a needle, of rose granite, gleaming in the morning sun as if it had just been taken from the quarry. It stood on a marble pedestal, resting on it not with its base but on four small copper cubes at the corners - as though it hovered in the air, barely touching the ground. And from the very point to the base, on all four faces, it was covered with signs.

Birds. Eyes. Snakes. Beetles. Little men squatting on their haunches. Wavy lines of water. Solar discs.

I stopped. I stopped so abruptly that Kemal, who was walking behind, ran into my back.

"What is this?" I asked. My voice sounded hoarse.

"An Egyptian stone," said Ferhat. "It was brought from Egypt. Long ago. Very long ago. More than a thousand years ago, when there were still Greek kings here. They say it was twice as tall, but it broke in transport, and only the upper part was set up here." He shrugged. "Grandfather says nobody in the world can read what is written on it. Those signs have been forgotten."

I came closer. The wind stirred the skirts of my cloak. The pouch at my belt - I felt it at once - had grown heavier. Not warmer. Heavier. As at the Column of Constantine. As in that dream of the columns, on the first day.

I raised my eyes to the signs. And among the birds, snakes and suns I saw one - quite small, high up, almost at the very point. An eye. A human eye, lined with a long stroke, with a curl beneath it like a tear.

I did not know this sign. I had never seen it. But I knew - knew as firmly as I knew that my feet stood on the ground - that it was an eye which had once been torn out, torn into pieces, and then put together again.

"Misafir?" Ferhat touched my elbow. "You have gone pale."

I did not answer. Kemal stood beside me, head thrown back, looking where I was looking - at the eye by the point of the obelisk. Then he slowly raised his hand and pointed at it with a finger. Then at my belt, at the pouch. Then again at the eye.

"He says," Ferhat translated uncertainly, though Kemal had not said a word, "I don't know what he says."

Suleyman, standing a little apart, looked at the three of us - at the obelisk, at me, at his grandson with his raised hand - and told his beads. Click. Click. Click.

"Father," he said at last, quietly, and Ferhat translated after him, "used to say: the stranger also stood here. For a long time. By this stone. And wept." Suleyman paused. "Father thought - from the sun. Here there is always wind and sun. Eyes water."

I passed my palm over my face. The palm was wet.

"Here there is always wind," I said. "Eyes water."

"Yes," agreed Suleyman, and there was not a drop of doubt in his voice. "Wind."

* * *
A little farther, at the edge of the square, under the awning of a coffeehouse, a crowd was gathering. Bursts of laughter came from there, someone's piercing voices - two voices, one high and shrill, the other low and sedate - and the jingle of a tambourine.

"Karagöz!" yelled Akmal, jumping on the spot, and without waiting for permission he dived into the crowd.

"The shadow theatre," Ferhat explained, smiling. "Grandfather, may we? Just a little?"

Suleyman sighed with the air of a man who sixty years ago had himself slipped away to see Karagöz - and nodded.

Under the awning, between two posts, a white canvas was stretched, lit from behind by a lamp. And on the canvas shadows moved - two flat, coloured, translucent little figures cut from leather, with thin sticks attached to their arms and heads. One was fat, short-legged, with an enormous beard, in a turban like a pumpkin. The other was gaunt, tall, with a pointed beard and an important bearing.

"Karagöz," Ferhat whispered, pointing at the fat one. "The simpleton. Muddles everything. And Hacivat, the clever one. Knows everything. They always quarrel."

The shadows quarrelled. Fat Karagöz squealed, jumped, fell, struck gaunt Hacivat on the head, Hacivat gravely straightened his turban and replied in long, flowery phrases, and the crowd laughed till it wept. Ferhat translated to me in a low voice, breaking off with laughter:

"Hacivat says: 'O Karagöz, light of my eyes, set me a riddle that I may show you my wisdom.' Karagöz says: 'Very well. What is this: it stands on the shore, feet in the water, head in the clouds, and itself does not budge?' Hacivat thinks and thinks... 'That is, without doubt, a minaret reflected in the Bosphorus!' Karagöz: 'No! It is my uncle Mehmet, who went to catch fish and fell asleep!'" The crowd roared. "Hacivat says: 'That is a stupid riddle!' Karagöz: 'But the answer is clever! And with you it is the other way round!'"

I laughed along with everyone - without noticing how. Kemal, standing beside me, laughed soundlessly, covering his mouth with his palm. Even Suleyman, standing behind, smiled into his beard.

And then the shadows on the canvas suddenly changed. Hacivat went away. Karagöz remained alone. The lamp behind the canvas dimmed. And the invisible puppeteer - invisible, but his voice now sounded quite different, soft, without the squeal - spoke for Karagöz slowly, almost sadly.

"What does he say?" I asked in a whisper.

Ferhat stopped smiling.

"This is the end of the performance. It is always ended this way. Karagöz says..." He paused, listening. "He says: 'Do not look at our mistakes. We are only shadows on a canvas. The canvas is the world. The lamp is He who holds the light. And the shadows come, quarrel, laugh and go. And no one knows who cut them out of leather and who moves them with the sticks.'" Ferhat swallowed. "'And when the lamp goes out,' says Karagöz, 'all the shadows will become one shadow. And then it will no longer matter who was Karagöz and who was Hacivat.'"

The lamp behind the canvas went out. The crowd clapped and whistled, someone threw the puppeteer a copper coin. And I stood and looked at the empty white canvas on which two shadows had just lived, and could not move.

* * *
Then Suleyman led us past a huge cathedral with a round dome - so huge that, standing at its walls, one had to throw back one's head to see its edge - to which, at the corners, slender minarets had been added, like needles stuck in a cushion.

"This was a church," said Ferhat. "The main church of the Greek kings. A thousand years. Then our people came - and made it a mosque." He paused. "Grandfather says that inside, under the plaster, faces can still be seen. Of Greek saints. Golden ones. They were smeared over, but they show through all the same. Through the lime. A little more each year. The imam says it is damp. The old men say it is they, looking. They want not to be forgotten."

Bells. A men's choir beneath the enormous dome. Candles. People with crosses in their hands.

I had already seen this place. At night, that time when the tall guest stood by my couch and the walls of the room melted. I had seen it as it was - not a mosque but a cathedral. I had heard bells that are no longer here.

"Ferhat," I said. "Did bells once ring here?"

He looked at me in surprise.

"They did. Long ago. More than four hundred years ago. How do you know?"

"I don't," I said. "I just thought so."

Ferhat looked at me for a long time, attentively, eyes narrowed. On his cheek, I noticed suddenly, there was a dark smudge - soot, probably, from Karagöz's lamp, beside which he had stood too close. Small, uneven, almost unnoticeable. He stood before me with his head tilted slightly to one side, as he always did when he was thinking something over - and for one brief moment it suddenly seemed to me that I had already seen this face. Not Ferhat's - another. Younger. Thinner. With just such a smudge on the cheek - only not soot but ink. Bent over some scroll in the dim light of a lamp. Somewhere very far away. In a place that smelled of cedar, dust and old papyrus. And that someone, the other one, also looked at me just so - head tilted a little, as if waiting for me finally to guess something that was right under my nose.

My hand rose of its own accord - to wipe away that smudge. I stopped it halfway. Lowered it.

"You have soot on your cheek," I said.

"Eh?" Ferhat rubbed his cheek with his palm - the wrong one, smearing the stain even more. "Karagöz. I always stand too close. Since childhood. Father used to say - I want to climb behind the canvas and see who is there."

"And did you?"

"Once." Ferhat smiled. "An old man was sitting there holding the sticks. The most ordinary old man. I was so upset that I cried all the way home. Father said: 'Silly. What matters is not who holds the sticks. What matters is that the shadows are alive while the lamp burns.'" He shrugged. "I did not understand then. And I don't quite understand now."

I did not understand either. But the strange face that had flashed before me - the face with the ink smudge, bent over a scroll - did not go away for a long time. I did not know who it was. I had never seen him. And yet, whenever I closed my eyes, it appeared again - and looked at me as though it knew something about me that I did not know myself.

* * *
We passed several small mosques, each of which, despite its modest size, possessed its own unrepeatable character: one flaunted tiles of the deepest turquoise, another a plain dome, yet flawless in proportion, a third hid in the depths of a courtyard enclosed by a low stone wall, entwined with ivy so old that the wall itself seemed to be held up by its roots alone.

At the entrance to some courtyard, right on the ground, beside a dark stone well, sat an old Greek woman in black, with a rosary in her hands - not like Suleyman's, but with a cross at the end. Before her on a kerchief lay thin wax candles. Akmal, running past, almost overturned her kerchief, and the old woman burst into Greek abuse so ringing that pigeons fluttered up from the roof.

Suleyman stopped, bowed to her - the old woman, seeing him, instantly softened - and they began to talk in a mixture of Turkish and Greek. The old woman pointed a finger downward, into the well.

"She says," Ferhat translated, "that beneath us there is water. A whole underground palace of water. With columns. Hundreds of columns, she says, stand in the water under the ground, and it is dark there, and fish swim - white, blind ones. Her grandfather went down there by boat when he was a boy." Ferhat listened further. "She says that in the farthest corner two columns stand on stone heads. Women's heads. With snakes for hair. One head lies on its side, the other upside down. So that they will not look. Because whoever looks them in the eyes will turn to stone."

"Who put them there?" I asked.

The old woman, as if she had understood the question, said something with a shrug.

"No one knows," translated Ferhat. "She says: the Greeks say - the Romans. The Romans say - earlier still. And her grandfather said that those heads had always been there. That the city was built around them. That they guard the water - and what lies beneath the water."

"And what lies beneath the water?"

The old woman looked at me. Narrowed her eyes. Then she said - slowly, in Turkish, with a strong accent, so that even I almost made out the words:

"What you lost. Whoever lost it will find it."

And, turning away, she went back to telling her rosary with the cross, as though we were not there at all.

* * *
At last we turned into a narrow, winding alley, so tight that the balconies opposite almost touched overhead, leaving only a thin, broken strip for the sunlight. At the end of the alley the domes of a bathhouse could be seen - old, peeling, with grilles on the windows from which steam poured - and at its doors, on a bench, sprawled a bath attendant: enormous, bare to the waist, with a shaved head, a towel on his shoulder and such a belly that it seemed it could be used as a table.

"Suleyman Agha!" he boomed on seeing the old man. "Forty years I haven't seen you! Still dry as a dried fish! Come in, I'll steam you - you'll grow twenty years younger!"

"If I grow twenty years younger," answered Suleyman, and Ferhat translated, roaring with laughter, "I shall have to marry my wife again. And a second time I shall not survive it."

The attendant laughed so that his belly shook like jelly. Then he saw me - and stopped laughing.

"And who is this?" he asked, narrowing his eyes.

"A guest," said Suleyman.

"A guest," repeated the attendant. He looked at me for a long time. Then he said something which Ferhat did not translate at once.

"What did he say?"

"He said," Ferhat hesitated, "that some twenty years ago a similar one came to his bath. Just like you. A stranger. Without a name. He asked only for hot water and silence. He sat in the steam room for three hours and did not sweat." Ferhat shrugged. "The attendant says he then told everyone for half a year: a man came who does not sweat. No one believed him."

"And where did he go afterwards?"

The attendant listened to the question and spread his enormous hands.

"Away," translated Ferhat. "That way." The attendant pointed into the depth of the alley, where we were headed. "To where the door in the wall is."

Twenty years ago. Suleyman's father - half a century ago. Karapet's great-grandfather - earlier still. How many of them had there been, nameless, coming to this city, seeking one and the same door?

* * *
Suleyman stopped at an inconspicuous door in a blank stone wall - a door so modest that I, had I been looking for it on my own, would certainly have walked past without noticing. Beside the door, walled into the masonry, a fragment of an ancient column stuck out - grey, pitted, with traces of some carved pattern, almost worn away by time. "Near the old column. Or pillar. Or stone."

"Here," he said in his own language, and this word, simple and short, I understood without translation, to my own astonishment - whether I had involuntarily learned it in these days, or simply guessed from the intonation alone.

My heart beat faster than was fitting for the mere examination of someone else's door. I went closer, peering at the wood darkened by time, at the iron hinges covered with rust, at the stone lintel worn so smooth that the original pattern which must once have adorned it could now be read only in vague, half-effaced hints.

Ferhat knocked - at first softly, then, getting no answer, more insistently. A minute passed, another; at last slow, shuffling footsteps sounded behind the door - and mewing. A great deal of mewing. The door opened just enough to let a strip of light inside and to let out a wary glance - and three cats at once.

Her name was Hatice Hanim. I learned that later. At first I saw only a small, dry old woman in a white kerchief, with a face so densely wrinkled that it resembled a baked apple, with very lively, very cunning eyes - and around her feet, tangling in her hem, rubbing, purring, demanding attention - cats. Ginger, white, striped, black. I counted seven. Then lost count.

The conversation that followed I naturally understood only by intonation and scraps of gesture, but its general sense soon became clear even without translation: the door had been opened by a widow who had lived in this house, if her own words, relayed to me later by Ferhat, were to be believed, a good forty years, having inherited it from her husband's parents. She had neither written nor received any note. She had never before met any wanderer looking for this place. The name which I, lacking one of my own, tried to convey by gestures - pointing to myself, then spreading my hands in sign of ignorance - provoked in her not the faintest glimmer of recognition.

"And where do the cats come from?" I could not help asking.

Hatice Hanim, hearing the translation, laughed - ringingly, like a girl.

"She says," translated Ferhat, "that when her husband was dying he said: 'Do not stay alone.' She asked: 'With whom?' He said: 'With someone. Whoever comes.'" Ferhat smiled. "She says, the cats came. One, then another. Now there are eleven of them. She says - her husband probably did not mean cats. But the cats came first. And whoever comes first, you feed."

"If another comes - feed him," I said quietly, to myself.

Ferhat looked at me. He understood. Suleyman's father. The stranger with the letter.

"She says," Ferhat continued, having listened to the hostess's long, circumstantial account, "that this house had belonged to her husband's family not for the first generation. Formerly a small shop was kept here - something like a warehouse for fabrics arriving with the trade caravans. Then the shop was closed, the premises downstairs were given over as lodgings for one of the nephews, and she herself settled upstairs with her husband. She had noticed nothing unusual in the house. Except perhaps..."

He fell silent, listening to the rest of the sentence, and his brows rose slightly.
