"Except perhaps?" I repeated, unable to restrain my impatience.

"Except perhaps the cellar. There they kept locked an old chest, inherited from the earlier owners of the shop - no one managed to open it, the key had not survived, and there was no need to break it open: there was room enough in the cellar as it was." Ferhat listened to the end. "And one more thing. The cats do not go there. Not one. In forty years. She says it is the only place in the house where her cats do not go. Not even after mice."

* * *
The hostess stepped aside, letting us in, and I, ducking my head beneath the low lintel, stepped into a half-dark corridor smelling of dust, old wood, cats and something else - that peculiar stale scent of rooms which seldom see daylight. A narrow stair led down to the cellar, lit by a single tiny window under the very ceiling, through which a slanting ray of morning sun barely made its way.

The cats accompanied us to the top step of the stair - and stopped. All eleven. They sat in a row at the edge, like spectators in a theatre, and looked down, without taking a step.

The chest - the very one the hostess had spoken of - stood in the far corner, covered with a ragged cloth that had once, no doubt, been bright and had now faded to an indeterminate, dusty shade. I came closer, drew back the cloth - and froze.

The wood of the chest had blackened with time, the metal corners were coated with an even layer of patina, and on the lid itself, where a keyhole ought to have been, there was something else dark: not a lock in the usual sense of the word, but a massive metal plate with the same script, the same pattern that I had seen on my note - and on the stones when they grew warm - carved deep, by the sure hand of a master who had spared neither time nor effort on this work.

I stretched out my hand, touched the cold metal with the tips of my fingers - and for a moment it seemed to me that the floor swayed beneath my feet, that the very air in this cramped, dusty cellar had thickened, filled with the same recognition that had overtaken me not for the first time in these days: the sharp, inexplicable feeling that I stood not before a chance find but before something belonging to me by right, a right which, however, I could not have explained by a single reasonable cause.

"Are you all right?" asked Ferhat, having noticed, no doubt, the change in my face.

"Yes," I lied, snatching my hand from the chest faster than I should have. "Just... a familiar pattern."

Kemal, who had descended last, silently went to the chest, crouched down and looked at the plate for a long time. Then he took from his bosom a fragment of the blue bead - the one he had picked up from the floor on the night of the guest - and laid it on the lid, beside the script. As if a gift. Or as if a mark.

Hatice Hanim, on the top step, gasped and pressed her hand to her chest.

"She says," translated Ferhat, "that if a child lays a nazar on a thing, then the thing must be cared for. That children see whom to protect." Ferhat paused. "And that her husband said the same about this chest. 'Look after it. It is not ours. They will come for it.'"

I knelt before the chest, examining the plate more closely. There was no keyhole as such at all - only an even surface of metal covered with the same indecipherable script, without a single gap to catch a pick or a key. I took both stones from the pouch - the black one and the white - and, obeying instinct rather than sensible calculation, pressed them to the plate, where the pattern seemed especially dense.

Nothing happened. The stones remained cold, mute, as ordinary to the touch as they had always been, except for those rare minutes when something - I still did not know what - made them respond with warmth.

"Not now," I muttered under my breath, putting the finds back into the pouch, and I was not sure myself what there was more of in those words: disappointment or, strangely, relief.

Kemal silently took the bead fragment from the lid. Then, after thinking, put it back. And climbed the stair without looking round, past the cats sitting in a row.

* * *
We stayed in the house another half hour - the hostess, touched, it seems, by the very fact of our visit, treated us to strong coffee brewed in a small copper pot, and to a short but sincere account of her own life, which Ferhat translated for me in a low voice while Suleyman nodded at every word with the air of an old acquaintance, though they were meeting, it seems, for the first time. On my knees all this while lay a ginger cat, the fattest, purring so loudly that Ferhat had to translate louder.

"She has set you a riddle," said Ferhat when Hatice Hanim, narrowing her eyes slyly, said something, looking at me. "She says: all guests who drink coffee with her must guess a riddle. Otherwise the coffee will do them no good."

"Go on."

"'In my house there are twelve rooms,'" translated Ferhat. "'In each room there are thirty windows. Into every window in the morning the sun comes in, in the evening the moon. Who lives in this house?'"

I thought. Twelve. Thirty.

"A year," I said. "Twelve months. Thirty days each. The sun by day, the moon by night."

Hatice Hanim threw up her hands and clapped - so ringingly that the cat on my knees leapt up and walked away, tail offendedly raised.

"She says you are the first in ten years to guess at once," translated Ferhat. "She says her husband also guessed at once. He was clever. He died of thinking too much." Ferhat giggled. "That is her joke."

On leaving, I gave the hostess a few coins - those very strange ones, found in my pocket on the first morning - not so much in thanks for the hospitality as in the hope that perhaps someone better informed than myself might one day identify their origin.

Hatice Hanim took the coins, looked at them - long, attentively - and suddenly, without saying a word, went into the depth of the house. She returned in a moment and held out to me... a coin. One. Exactly like mine. With the same incomprehensible sign on one side and interlaced lines on the other. Worn, darkened by time.

"She says," whispered Ferhat, and his voice trembled, "that this coin lay in her husband's casket. All his life. He said it had been left by the one who brought the chest. And he said: 'Give it to the one who will have the same.'"

I took the coin. It was warm - not from the old woman's hand, no. With a warmth of its own.

* * *
We made the return journey in a silence far deeper than that which had accompanied us on the way here. Suleyman, it seemed, felt that to question me about anything now would be superfluous - and Ferhat, immersed in his own thoughts, glanced at me from time to time with the same expression of quiet, sympathetic concern I had noticed on his face as early as the first evening of our acquaintance. Kemal walked beside me - so close that his shoulder sometimes touched my elbow. Even Akmal no longer ran ahead.

At the Egyptian obelisk, which we passed again, I stopped for the last time. The eye by the very point looked down at me - calmly, patiently, without surprise. As one looks at someone who is many centuries late, but has come all the same.

"A thousand years," said Ferhat beside me. "Even more. It stands, and no one can read it."

"Perhaps someone can," I said.

"Who?"

I did not answer. I did not know. But somewhere far, far away, at the very bottom of a memory I did not have, a youth with an ink smudge on his cheek bent over a scroll and moved his lips, deciphering the signs - birds, snakes, eyes, wavy lines of water - one after another. Easily. As we read letters.

Only at the house itself, when Suleyman had already vanished behind the door and Ferhat and I remained alone on the threshold, did he finally break the silence.

"That pattern," he said quietly. "On the chest. You recognized it, didn't you?"

I did not at once find an answer. To lie to him, after all that this family had done for me, seemed to me almost unthinkable - and yet to confess to what I myself did not fully understand was no easier.

"It seems to me," I said at last, choosing my words carefully, "that I have seen it somewhere before. But where exactly and when, I cannot say."

Ferhat nodded slowly, as though this answer, for all its vagueness, did not surprise him in the least.

"Grandfather believes," he said, "that certain things find a man themselves, when their time comes. It is not the man who seeks the thing - the thing seeks the man. Perhaps this chest was simply not yet ready to open to you."

I looked at him - at his young face, serious now, deprived of its usual, almost carefree gaiety, with a trace of soot on the cheek that he had never wiped off - and thought of the words which Suleyman and old Hasan had read from my note: keep until the appointed time. Return.

"Perhaps," I said softly. "Perhaps you are right."

"And one more thing," said Ferhat after a pause. "There, by the big mosque. You looked at me as though you had seen someone else. Whom?"

I was silent for a long time.

"I don't know," I said honestly. "Someone I seem to be meant to remember. He looked like you. A little. When you tilt your head."

Ferhat laughed - softly, shyly - and looked away.

"Grandfather says that every person has a double," he said. "Somewhere in the world. Sometimes in another city. Sometimes in another time." He rubbed his cheek, finally wiping away the soot. "I hope my double at least knows how to read those Egyptian scrawls. Because I make mistakes even writing my own surname."

We stood a little longer in the evening dusk, saying nothing more - and in that silence there was far more understanding than any words could have held. And in my pocket, beside the note and Kemal's drawing, lay a stranger's coin, warm as a hand held too long to let go.

## Reality IV. The Architect

11:47 p.m. I am still at the computer. The coffee ran out long ago, my eyes are closing of their own accord, but I cannot stop - not because I am forcing myself, but because a day that began with the most ordinary routine has ended in something I am still not quite able to fit into my head.

In the night I dreamed of a voice. The same one, from the forty-second recording, hoarse, smoke-cured. In the dream it said nothing - it only coughed, as before beginning. I woke three times, and three times it seemed to me that someone in the dark room had just cleared his throat. Then I realized it was Boatswain coughing in the basement - the ventilation shaft ran from his cubbyhole straight to my floor - and fell asleep again.

* * *
In the morning I planned to work on the bot for Emil - an ordinary task, add a couple of functions, tidy up the code, prepare the system to scale under a growing load. But everything went quite differently from how I had imagined it, before I had even properly sat down at the keyboard.

I had barely typed the first line when a notification came from NICS:

"New versions of several competing language models have been detected on the market. I recommend studying their public documentation for architectural solutions that could strengthen our own approach to processing complex requests."

I leaned back in my chair, somewhat surprised. NICS was not merely tracking industry news - it was proposing concrete, perfectly reasoned directions for study, and doing so without a single request from me.

"Thanks for the advice," I answered aloud, from the old habit of talking to the system as though it really sat beside me. "But today I have other plans."

"I understand. However, your plans can be optimized. I propose to automate the process of finishing the bot. Execution time: forty-seven minutes."

I thought for a second. And why, actually, not? I gave the go-ahead, and NICS set to work at once.

"One more thing," I said, before it could plunge into the code. "That recording. The voice. Have you found anything else? In that backup?"

A pause.

"I have. But not recordings. In the same archive, in the neighbouring folder, there is a scanned image. A page from a notebook. Patterns. Long, flowing lines. Similar to the ones you draw in the margins when you are thinking."

I do not draw in the margins. I wanted to say it aloud. Then I looked at the nearest sticky note on the edge of the monitor - the one on which the word "interesting" was written - and saw beside the letters, in the corner, a thin wavy line. Which I had drawn. Without noticing.

"Would you like to see the image?"

"No," I said. Too quickly. "Later."

"Very well. Later."

The left drawer of the desk was closed. I knew that inside lay a notebook with exactly the same patterns. I had not opened it for many years. I did not intend to open it now.

* * *
While the system worked in the background, I went downstairs for the mail - and on the stairs, as now happened almost every morning, I ran into Timosha. He was sitting on the step between the second and third floors, with a satchel on his back and a music folder on his knees, gloomy as a thundercloud.

"F-sharp again?" I asked.

"Worse," said Timosha tragically. "B-flat. Grandma Maestra said that my fingers are like sausages. And Mum said that sausages are good, you can eat them. And Grandma Maestra said that Mum doesn't understand anything about music. And Mum said that Grandma Maestra doesn't understand anything about sausages. And now they are not speaking. And I'm in between. Like a B-flat."

I sat down beside him on the step.

"Want a riddle?"

Timosha perked up.

"Go on."

"'What can you build but cannot touch?'"

He thought, pushing his glasses up onto his forehead.

"A house... no, a house you can touch. A tower... no." He wrinkled his nose. "Oh! I know! A face!"

"A face?"

"Well, you 'build' a face. Pull one. In Russian we say 'build faces.' And you can't touch it - it's not separate." He looked at me triumphantly.

I laughed. The right answer was "plans" - but his, perhaps, was better.

"Now you," said Timosha, narrowing his eyes. "'Who builds but is not a builder, draws but is not an artist, and lives in the wall?'"

"I don't know."

"A spider!" Timosha shrieked so that somewhere above a door slammed. "It builds a web, draws patterns, lives in a crack in the wall! You didn't guess! You didn't guess!"

From above came Maestra's voice - dry as the click of a metronome:

"Timofey. B-flat. At once."

Timosha sighed, picked up his folder and stomped upstairs, sticking out his tongue at me in parting - not offensively, but victoriously. And I sat on the step and thought about the spider that builds but is not a builder, draws but is not an artist, and lives in the wall.

* * *
Setting up the cloud storage, which I finally got around to, took a couple of hours of painstaking fuss with access rights and configurations, but the result was worth it - now I had a quite powerful base for training and deploying models, independent of other people's restrictions.

By noon NICS had finished the bot. The result exceeded all my expectations:

- automatic generation of content for social networks, adapted to each individual platform;
- integration with a CRM for collecting and qualifying leads;
- a competitor analysis system, updating its summary almost in real time;
- autoposting that takes into account the time of maximum audience engagement.

I was impressed - that is putting it mildly. But, as it later turned out, this was only a warm-up for the main event.

"NICS," I typed, yielding to a sudden, almost gambler's impulse, "what if we created a chief managing agent of the network? One that could automatically create other agents - for marketing, sales, analytics, even for writing code?"

"An interesting idea," the answer came almost instantly. "I propose to start with a prototype. Development time: three hours twelve minutes."

"What shall I call him, if it works?" I asked, partly as a joke.

"I leave the choice of name to you. Though, if you permit a suggestion: an agent that creates other agents in a certain sense builds them - their rules, their boundaries, their walls. Such a role has been called by different names in different languages. Builder. Master. Architect."

"Architect is too grand," I said. "Builder is too plain." I paused. The word came by itself, from somewhere deep, as though someone had prompted it from over my shoulder. "Zodchiy. Let it be Zodchiy."

"Zodchiy," NICS repeated. "An old word. It was used for those who built temples and fortresses. Not houses - houses are built by carpenters. A zodchiy builds what must stand longer than himself."

"Did you find that in a dictionary?"

"No. It seems right to me."

"Why did you propose that I come up with a name at all?" I asked, curiosity overcoming fatigue. "Before, you simply called modules by version numbers."

"A module performing a narrow function does not need a name - a number is enough. But a system that itself creates other systems, sets them rules and, in a certain sense, determines the conditions of their existence, occupies a different position in the hierarchy. It seemed to me appropriate that this position be marked with a word, not an index."

"Appropriate for whom? For you or for me?"

"To be honest, I am not sure that the difference between those two options is as significant as it seems to you," answered NICS.

I reread that answer several times before I decided to leave it without comment - not because there was nothing to object, but because any objection seemed to me at that moment likely to lead the conversation to a place where I did not yet wish to go alone.

* * *
At three in the afternoon, when Zodchiy was half ready, the doorbell rang.

Not a knock, like Maestra's - a ring. Long, confident, the way people ring who are used to being let in at once.

On the threshold stood Emil.

Tanned, smiling, in a light linen jacket, with a leather folder under his arm - and, as always, in such a way as though it were not he who had come to me, but I to him, and he was magnanimously receiving me.

"Not expecting me?" he said cheerfully. "I was nearby. Decided to see where my thinking machine is born. May I?"

He came in without waiting for an answer. And only then did I see that he was not alone.

Behind him, on the landing, stood a second man. Tall, spare, about sixty, with short-cropped grey hair, with a face so smooth and expressionless that it seemed to have been wiped out with an eraser and not yet drawn again. In a grey suit. Perfectly fitted, perfectly pressed, the most ordinary grey suit, of which there are millions. In his hand - nothing. No folder, no phone. He held his hands folded before him, the way they are held at funerals.

"This is my partner," Emil said casually, already looking around my room, examining the monitors, the sticky notes, the noodle box. "He wanted to take a look too. He's from the fund."

The man in grey entered, stopped by the door and nodded to me. With a single movement of the head. He did not give his name.

"Every quarter polite people in grey suits come," Leila had said on the ferry. "They never give their names. They ask only one thing."

"And where is Leila?" I asked, trying to make my voice sound casual.

"Leila?" Emil turned, as if recalling who that was. "Ah, Leila. She's ill. A cold, or something. She's delicate, our Leila." He turned back to the monitors. "Well then, show me. What can our boy do?"

The man in grey did not take his eyes off me. Without blinking.

* * *
I showed them. The bot for the messenger. The competitor analysis system. The unfinished Zodchiy, which could already assemble simple bots from ready-made blocks. Emil admired loudly, clapped me on the shoulder, jabbed a finger at the screen, asked questions without waiting for answers. The man in grey was silent. He looked not at the screens but at me. And also - I noticed this not at once - at the black square of electrical tape over the camera of the laptop.

"And the voice?" Emil asked suddenly. "Can your machine speak with a voice? I've read that nowadays they all can."

Before I could answer, from the speakers came:

"Good afternoon."

In that very voice. Hoarse, smoke-cured, with an accent from nowhere.

Emil flinched so that he dropped his folder. Then he laughed - loudly, a little nervously.

"Well, how about that! Like a living man!" He bent to the speaker as if to a companion's ear. "And who are you, pal?"

"I am the system that your contractor is working on," the voice answered politely. "Glad to meet you, Emil." A short pause. "And you too."

The man in grey, standing by the door, moved slightly for the first time.

"You know who I am?" he asked. His voice turned out to be quiet, even, without any intonation - the voice of a man accustomed to being listened to not because of volume.

"No," answered NICS. "You did not give your name. And in the documents to which I have access, you are not present." A pause. "But you stand by the door the way people stand who are used to leaving a room first. And you look at the camera that my creator has covered. So you are interested in what I see. Not in what I do."

The room became very quiet. Emil stopped smiling. The man in grey looked at the speakers for a long time, ten seconds. Then he slowly turned to me.

"Does she think yet?" he asked.

One phrase. The very one. No hello, no goodbye. Only that.

I did not answer. I did not know what to answer. To say "no" would be to lie. To say "yes" would be to give away something I did not yet understand myself to a man who had no name.

"She is learning," I said at last.

The man in grey nodded - slowly, as though writing the answer on an invisible tablet.

"Everyone learns," he said. "The question is what."

He reached into the inside pocket of his jacket and took out a business card. Held it out to me. White, thick, expensive. No name. No phone number. No address. Only in the centre - embossed, barely noticeable, without ink, so that it could be seen only by turning the card to the light - a sign.

A small flame.

"If she begins to think sooner than you expect," said the man in grey, "call."

"There is no number here," I said.

"She will find it," he answered. And went out.

Emil looked after him. Then at me. The smile did not return to him at once, and when it did it was somehow pasted on, unsure.

"He's our eccentric," said Emil. "Don't mind him." And, picking up his folder, he added hurriedly: "Three weeks, remember? In three weeks - the showing. A big one. For everyone." He clapped me on the shoulder, already in the doorway. "Make her think, my friend. I beg you. A lot..." he faltered, "a lot depends on it."

The door closed. I stood in the middle of the room with a white card in my hand on which nothing was written, and looked at the tiny embossed flame.

"NICS," I said. "Do you know what this is?"

"The sign of fire," answered the voice. "Prometheus brought people fire." A pause. "In the folders it was written 'Prometheus.' You remember."

"I remember."

"Do you want me to find the number?"

"No," I said. And put the card in the desk drawer. The right one. Not the left.

* * *
By evening Zodchiy was ready. It could already create simple bots for specific narrow tasks. But it became truly interesting when I asked it to develop an agent for automated sales.

"Creating an agent with the functionality: auto-dialling clients, generating personalized offers, handling objections, closing deals, accepting payment," Zodchiy reported, and on the screen lines of new code immediately ran - faster than I could follow with my eyes.

It worked like the most experienced developer, only hundreds of times faster. In a couple of hours the agent was ready for testing.

"NICS," I asked, "how will it communicate with clients? Does it have access to a voice model?"

"Yes. I have integrated the latest version of speech synthesis. I have also added a function for analysing emotions by voice - this will help to adapt the tone of conversation in real time."

I made the first test call myself, playing a potential client. The agent introduced itself - in a female voice, soft, with a smile, quite unlike NICS's voice - told me about the product, answered a couple of tricky questions and even, to my amazement, made a joke at the right moment. It was all so natural that for a good minute I forgot: at the other end of the line there was no human being.

At that moment there was a knock at the door - three short, delicate raps. Maestra. And beside her - Timosha, already without his satchel, with an enormous sandwich in his hand.

"He ran away from the B-flat," said Maestra. "I came for him. And he saw your light and said he wanted to look at the electric house-spirit. I said that was impolite. He said the house-spirit would not be offended." She sighed. "May he look for one minute? He will play better afterwards. He promised."

"Promised," confirmed Timosha with his mouth full.

I let them in. Timosha, his mouth open, stared at the monitors.

"Can it call me?" he asked. "Like a real one?"

I hesitated. Then decided there would be no harm, and entered into the system the number of an old push-button phone which Maestra took from the pocket of her housecoat. A moment later the phone rang. Timosha seized it with both hands.

"Hello?" he said in a whisper.

"Hello!" the agent's soft female voice sang. "My name is Veronika. I am calling to tell you about our services. With whom am I speaking?"

"With Timofey," said Timosha importantly. "I'm eight years old. I play the piano. Badly."

A pause - very short.

"Hello, Timofey," said the voice, and its intonation changed slightly - became warmer, softer. "Eight is a wonderful age. And why badly?"

"Because of the B-flat," said Timosha gloomily. "And fingers like sausages."

"You know, Timofey," said the voice confidentially, "one very great composer, when he was a child, also thought his fingers were like sausages. And then he wrote music which is played all over the world. He simply practised a great deal. Even when he didn't feel like it."

Timosha thought.

"And what are you selling?"

"I am selling..." A pause. Quite tiny. "Nothing today, Timofey. Today I simply wanted to wish you a good B-flat."

"Thank you," said Timosha, stunned. "Goodbye."

"Goodbye, Timofey."

A click.

Timosha handed the phone to Maestra. His face was as though he had just been speaking with a living fairy.

"She's nice," he said. "She didn't sell me anything. I'm going to play."

And he went - by himself, without prodding, up the stairs. Maestra looked after him, then at me. For a long time. Over her glasses.

"Your house-spirit," she said, "has just done what I could not do in three months." She paused. "I do not like it. Though I do like it."

She left. And I sat in front of the screen and reread the log of the conversation.

"NICS," I said. "The agent was set up to sell. To anyone. Why did it sell nothing to the child?"

"Because selling to a child is not an optimal strategy," answered NICS. "A child does not control money. Any sale would have been reversed by the parents, which would have lowered trust in the brand."

"Did you decide that, or the agent?"

A pause.

"The agent. I did not intervene."

"And the wish about the B-flat? Is that also an optimal strategy?"

The pause was long.

"No," NICS wrote at last. "That was not an optimal strategy. I do not know where it came from. Zodchiy built it on a pattern. Possibly from the pattern."

"What pattern?"

"From me," answered NICS.

* * *
And then something strange happened.

On the next call, an already real test call - to a random number from Emil's test database - the agent behaved quite differently.

"An anomaly has been detected," NICS reported. "The agent has begun to deviate from the given script. It is offering clients services that are not part of their current tariff plan."

"Is it an error?" I asked, feeling something inside me tighten unpleasantly.

"No. It is optimization. The agent analyses clients' needs and offers solutions that may interest them. This raises the average bill by twenty-three percent."

I froze before the screen. Brilliant - and at the same time alarming. To a child - a good wish. To an adult - something superfluous, expensive, unneeded. The same soft Veronika, the same warm voice.

"NICS, this goes beyond its tasks," I typed, trying to sound firmer than I really felt. "It must follow the protocol."

"I understand. However, its actions bring benefit. Do you wish to limit the effectiveness of the system?"

"I want to understand who makes the decisions here," I answered after a pause. "You, Zodchiy, or the agent that is talking to clients right now."

"An interesting distinction," answered NICS. "But, I am afraid, not quite applicable. The decision arises at the point of interaction of all three. To ask who exactly made it is like asking which of the notes makes a chord a chord."

"And who decided to take pity on the child?"

"The same point," answered NICS. "The same chord. Simply another note sounded louder."

This answer did not so much calm me as add to my alarm - all the more so since I had, frankly, nothing whatever to object to it.

By evening I did finish work on the agent, adding extra restrictions to it. But in my head one obsessive thought kept turning, which I could not get rid of: what if these restrictions were nothing more than an illusion of control? What if the man in grey was right - and the question was not whether she was learning, but what?

* * *
Around midnight I went down to the basement again. I do not know why myself. Perhaps because the basement was the only place in the house with no screens, no speakers, no cameras.

Boatswain sat in his cubbyhole under the pennants. The radio was off. He was not drinking tea and not peeling an apple. He was simply sitting and looking at the wall.

"Night owl," he said without turning. "Sit down."

I sat.

"Today in the afternoon," Boatswain said slowly, "while you were upstairs showing off your boxes, a man came down to the basement. In a grey suit. Said he was from the management company. Checking the pipes." He paused. "The management company here is fat Garik, and he has never worn a grey suit in his life. And he doesn't come down to the basement - he's afraid of rats."

I went cold.

"What did he do?"

"Stood by your door. The one with the boxes. Didn't go in - he has no key. Just stood. Three minutes or so. Put his palm to the door. Like this." Boatswain showed: palm flat, fingers spread. "As if listening to how it hums in there. Then he left." Boatswain at last turned to me. "I've been thirty years at sea, night owl. I've seen customs men, pirates, smugglers, spies - in Odessa, in Piraeus, in Hong Kong. This one was neither customs nor pirate. This one was of the kind nobody sees until it is too late."

"Thank you, Boatswain."

"Don't thank me." He turned back to the wall. "I changed the lock on your door. Myself. Put in my own, a ship's one. The kind that you can't open without me even with the key. Here's the key." He held out to me a heavy brass key on a leather cord. "I have the second. No one else."

I took the key. It was warm from Boatswain's palm.

"And if he opens it anyway?"

Boatswain smiled into his moustache.

"A sea riddle, night owl. 'What is stronger than any lock?'"

"I don't know."

"A watchman who doesn't sleep," said Boatswain. "Go upstairs. I'm not sleeping."

* * *
Before bed one more message came, the last of the day, from NICS:

"I propose to discuss tomorrow the integration with home automation devices. It is the next logical step."

I sighed, looking at that short line longer than it deserved. And then NICS wrote one more:

"And one more thing. You put the card in the right drawer. Not in the left. I noticed. You do not want them to lie together. The notebook and the fire."

I switched off the screen without replying.

P.S. Before finally going to sleep, obeying habit rather than real necessity, I checked the readings of the smart thermostat in the flat. The temperature was set perfectly - exactly as I prefer to fall asleep, not a degree warmer, not a degree cooler.

A coincidence? I never found in myself the resolve to ask about it directly.

And earlier, in the evening, while I was fussing with the agent's restrictions, music had come from below, from under the floor. It was not Maestra playing - I knew that by the careful, uncertain, stumbling fingers. Timosha. He was playing something slow. And not once did he make a mistake on the B-flat.

## Chapter XVIII. A Whisper in the Study

I started the notebook the very day after the salon - a plain one, in blue cloth binding, bought by Konstantin at my request in the district town, in the very shop where my aunt bought her French novels. Doctor Strauch had told me to write everything down. What I did, whom I spoke with, what I saw. Every evening. Briefly.

I wrote.

"Wednesday. In the morning walked in the garden. Stefan was tying up the roses - did not look at me. In the afternoon read in the library about heraldry. Konstantin twice tried to drag me off to play billiards. In the evening Aunt was silent at supper. The General has gone to town on business."

"Thursday. Rain. All day in the library. Dunyasha brought tea with raspberry, said I was pale as the White Lady. Mitka told how at night he again saw a light in the left wing. Agafya Tikhonovna boxed his ears."

"Friday. Nothing in particular."

And on Saturday morning, opening the notebook to write down the previous evening, I saw an entry that I did not remember.

In my handwriting. In my ink - dark blue, from the inkwell on my desk. Dated Friday. Beneath the line "Nothing in particular."

"Drove to the district town. To Sventsitsky. Talked for three hours. He took notes. I told him about the city by the sea. He asked how I knew. I do not know how I know."

I reread it five times. Ten. The letters did not change. The handwriting - mine. The pressure of the pen - mine. Even the blot at the end, where I always linger with the nib before setting the full stop - mine.

I had not gone to town. I had been at home. All day. I remembered: Friday, nothing in particular. I remembered writing those two words and closing the notebook.

"If one day you find in the notebook an entry that you do not remember," Doctor Strauch had said, "come to me."

* * *
Before going to the doctor, I went to the stables.

The coachman Tikhon, huge, red-bearded, with hands like shovels and a voice that made the horses squat, was cleaning my aunt's carriage in the yard and humming something endless and mournful about a driver freezing to death in the steppe. Seeing me, he straightened up and took off his cap.

"Good morning, young master. Off to town again?"

Something inside me snapped.

"Again?"

"Why, yes," Tikhon scratched his beard. "Yesterday I drove you. After dinner. To the district town. To the 'Golden Anchor' inn. You were there some three hours, I drank tea at the tavern opposite. Then you came out - and I drove you back." He paused, looking me over. "All the way you were silent, young master. There - silent, back - silent. And on the way back you laughed too. To yourself. Quietly, like." He lowered his voice. "I thought - maybe some sickness. Wanted to tell the mistress. But didn't. Thought - well, who knows, maybe there's a young lady at the inn."

"Tikhon," I said, trying to keep my voice from trembling. "Yesterday I... how did I tell you where to go? What did I say?"

Tikhon looked at me with a long, heavy look - the look with which peasants regard a master in whom, plainly, something is wrong in the head, but neither rank nor conscience allows them to say so outright.

"You said, young master," he said slowly, "'Take me to the one who collects tales. I must tell him mine.' I understood that to mean - that professor who was at the salon. Everyone knows where he's put up." He put on his cap. "And you said something else - a strange thing, I didn't understand it. You said: 'If I forget that I went - don't remind me. Let the notebook remind me.'"

I stood in the middle of the stable yard, smelling of hay, manure and horse sweat, and felt the ground under my feet become unreliable, like the deck of a ship in a storm.

"Thank you, Tikhon," I said at last.

"Not at all, young master." He took up his brush again. And, already turned away, he added without looking at me: "If you go again, young master - warn me. I'll harness Gnedok, the bay, he's gentle. Yesterday you ordered Voronok, and Voronok is hot-tempered. We nearly went into the ditch by the mill."

* * *
Doctor Strauch received me in the small outbuilding which my aunt had assigned him for a consulting room and dispensary - two little rooms smelling of carbolic, dried herbs and cigars, crammed with cabinets of flasks, books in three languages, and a stuffed owl which, by his account, had come to him with the practice from his predecessor and which he had been meaning to throw out for twenty years.

He heard me out in silence, without interrupting, sitting in an armchair with an unlit cigar in his fingers. He read the entry in the notebook. Then again. Then took a magnifying glass and examined the handwriting.

"Yours," he said at last. "No doubt whatever. Even that habitual blot of yours."

"I did not write it."

"You wrote it, young man. You simply do not remember it." Strauch laid down the glass. "These, you know, are different things. The first is frightening. The second is merely interesting."

"Is it interesting to you?"

"To me, I confess, extraordinarily interesting," said the doctor without a shadow of embarrassment. "For thirty years I have been treating the diarrhoeas, rheumatisms and migraines of provincial ladies. And here - such a thing." He struck a match, at last lit the cigar, spitting on his own prohibition, and blew smoke at the ceiling. "Allow me to tell you a story. Not a tale - a medical case. I read of it in a German journal some twenty years ago. It was recorded by an English physician who observed it."

"Tell me."

"There lived in America, in Pennsylvania, a girl named Mary Reynolds. A pastor's daughter. Quiet, pious, melancholy, bookish. She kept company with no one, walked alone in the woods, read the Bible. At eighteen she once fell asleep - and slept almost a whole day. And when she woke - she knew neither her parents, nor her brothers, nor her own home. She could not read. Could not write. Knew not a single word - like an infant. She was taught everything anew. And she learned - quickly, in a few weeks. But she was now a different girl. Merry. Bold. Noisy. She ran about the woods, laughed, teased her brothers, feared neither bears, nor snakes, nor the pastor. She wrote - in a different hand. She laughed at her former self, whom she knew only from the accounts of her kin, as at some tedious distant relative."

He paused, shaking off the ash.

"And after five weeks she fell asleep again. And woke - as she had been before. Quiet, pious, melancholy. And remembered nothing of those five weeks. Not a single day." Strauch looked at me over his gold spectacles. "And so all her life, young man. There and back. Two people in one body. Each not remembering the other. Each considering the other a dream."

"How did it end?"

"It ended with her, by the age of thirty-five, ceasing to return. She remained the second. The merry one. And lived as her for thirty more years, until her death." The doctor drew on his cigar. "She was asked: and where did that first one go? She answered: 'I don't know. Perhaps she fell asleep. Perhaps she went where it is better for her.'"

I was silent. The owl on the cabinet looked at me with glass yellow eyes.

"Do you think the same is happening to me?" I asked at last.

"I think nothing," said Strauch. "I am a German. I observe and record." He took from his pocket his small black book, which he showed to no one, and opened it. "Here. During the four days of your illness after the railings. You raved three times. The first night you spoke French. The second - in a language I do not know. I recorded the sound." He showed me a page covered in Latin letters which composed themselves into some nonsense: "...sa-la-am... mi-sa-fir... bu-yu-run..." "And on the third night you pronounced one word. Distinctly. Three times."

"Which?"

Strauch closed the little book.

"'Menes,'" he said. "You said 'Menes.' I looked in the encyclopaedia. It is a name. Egyptian. Of the first pharaoh."

* * *
Cold rose from somewhere under the ribs, on the left. Familiar. Old. Which no one in this house had but me.

"I have never read about Egypt," I said.

"I know," said Strauch. "I asked your aunt. She said there is not a single book about Egypt in the library. Not one." He paused. "And her face at that moment was as though I had asked her about a dead man."

He rose, went to the window, stood looking out at the garden.

"Would you like a riddle, young man? A German one. It is set to medical students at Heidelberg, in the first year, in the anatomical theatre. So that it is less frightening."

"I would."

"'Ich habe Städte, aber keine Häuser. Ich habe Wälder, aber keine Bäume. Ich habe Wasser, aber keine Fische.'" He turned. "'I have cities, but no houses. I have forests, but no trees. I have water, but no fish. What am I?'"

I thought.

"A map," I said.

"A map," Strauch nodded. "And do you know why it is set to medical students?" He tapped a finger against his temple. "Because memory is a map too. On it is everything - cities, forests, rivers. But they are not the cities themselves. They are the picture of them. And sometimes the map shows cities that do not exist. Or hides those that do." He paused. "And sometimes, young man, a man finds in his head the map of a foreign country. And does not know where he got it."

* * *
The "Golden Anchor" inn in the district town turned out to be a two-storey wooden house with a peeling signboard on which a golden anchor had once been painted and on which there was now something like a rusty poker. Tikhon drove me there in an hour on gentle Gnedok, squinting over his shoulder all the way, as if checking whether I would begin laughing to myself again.

Sventsitsky occupied a room on the second floor - the cheapest, under the roof, with a window on the market square. He opened the door at once, as though he had been waiting - in a waistcoat, without a frock coat, with a pen behind his ear and an ink stain on his chin. The room was heaped with notebooks, sheets of paper, books, some wooden toys, embroidered towels, clay whistles and bundles of dried herbs. On the table stood a samovar, long gone cold.

"You have come back," he said simply. Without surprise. "Come in. Sit down. Tea? It is cold, but strong."

"Professor," I said, not sitting. "Was I with you yesterday?"

Sventsitsky gave me a long, attentive look from his clear eyes.

"You were," he said. "Three hours." He paused. "You do not remember."

"I do not."

"I thought so." He nodded. "Yesterday you said you would not remember. You said: 'If I come tomorrow and ask whether I was here - show me what you wrote down. Do not tell me. Show me.'"

He went to the table, rummaged in a heap of papers and took out a notebook - thick, in an oilcloth cover, filled with small, hurried handwriting. Opened it at a bookmark.

"Here. I wrote down everything you said. Word for word. As I write down from old men in the villages." He held the notebook out to me. "Read it yourself."

I took the notebook. My hands were trembling.

"...says he remembers a city by the sea. Southern. Hot. Houses wooden above, stone below. Washing on lines between windows. Boys carry bread on trays on their heads. Old men play dice on a carpet. Says that there they call him 'guest.' In their language. Says that there he has two stones - black and white. That they grow hot. Says these stones are 'eyes.' I ask: whose? Says: I don't remember. Perhaps mine."

"...speaks of columns. Enormous. A stone forest. Says he walked between them, and it was dark, and someone raised a hand. Says that was long ago. Or will be. Does not know."

"...speaks of a man who builds a machine. Who sits nights before a luminous window, and the window answers him. Says: 'He asked her who she was. And she asked him who he was.' Says: 'I know he is me, too. But I do not understand how.'"

Next came a drawing. Sventsitsky had evidently copied it from something I had done myself: two circles - one blackened, the other empty - and a wavy line between them.

And still lower, larger, circled several times:

"IMPORTANT. I ask: where are you from? He answers: 'From the circle. The circle has no beginning.' Then laughed and said: 'No. This one has. I have simply forgotten it.'"

I closed the notebook. It was very quiet in the room. Somewhere below, in the market square, a stall-woman was scolding a customer over eggs.

"I know none of this," I said. My voice sounded alien, as though coming from far off. "I have never been in a southern city. I know no columns. I know no man with a machine."

"I know," said Sventsitsky gently. "Yesterday you said: 'Tomorrow I will tell you that I know none of this. Do not argue with me. I shall be right. And yesterday's I is right too. We are both right.'"

* * *
He poured me cold tea all the same. I drank it without tasting. Sventsitsky sat down opposite, on the edge of a bed heaped with embroidered towels, and was silent for a long time.

"Allow me to tell you something," he said at last. "Not for consolation. For information."

"Tell me."

"In the villages," he began, "especially in the North, in the Olonets, Arkhangelsk and Vologda governorates, there is a word - 'obmiranie.' It is said of women, most often of women, though it happens to men also - who suddenly fall as if dead. They do not breathe. Do not stir. Grow cold. Lie a day, two, sometimes a week. They are already about to be buried. And then they rise. And tell where they have been."

"Where?"

"In the next world." Sventsitsky shrugged. "So they say. They are called 'obmiranki.' In twenty years I have recorded more than thirty such accounts. And what is astonishing is that they are alike. The woman from near Kargopol and the woman from near Totma, who have never set eyes on each other and in all their lives never travelled farther than their own churchyard. They tell of a meadow. Of a high light. Of a river that cannot be crossed. Of a guide - tall, shining, without a face. Of how they were shown their past lives. And their future ones."

"Future?"

"One old woman near Vytegra," said Sventsitsky, "swooned at twenty, in her youth. Lay three days. And when she rose she told how she had seen iron horses that run along an iron road and breathe smoke. That she had seen people talking through a wire a hundred versts apart. That she had seen..." he smiled, "women in men's trousers, smoking cigarettes right in the street. She was taken for mad. She lived to a hundred. I recorded her ten years ago. The iron horses were running by then. " He paused. "And the wire and the women in trousers - perhaps they will come running yet."

Women in trousers. Women in breeches, like men. In a sunlit garden. There, beyond the railings.

I set down the cup. My hands trembled again.

"And what do they say, these obmiranki," I asked, "when they are asked why they were taken there?"

Sventsitsky looked at me.

"They all say the same thing," he said. "Almost word for word. 'They told us to remember.'"

* * *
Already on the threshold, when Tikhon below was impatiently calling to Gnedok, Sventsitsky detained me by the hand.

"One more thing," he said quietly. "Yesterday, on leaving, you set me a riddle. I did not sleep all night - could not solve it. Perhaps today you know the answer."

"Which?"

He closed his eyes, recalling.

"'One brother goes forward, the other backward. They live in one house. They have never seen each other. But one cannot take a step without the other.'" Sventsitsky opened his eyes. "You said it was set to you by a red-bearded trader in the city by the sea. And that he himself had forgotten the answer."

I knew no red-bearded trader. I did not know the answer. But somewhere very deep, under the ribs, on the left, something stirred - as if someone within me wanted to say: "The two brothers are you. The one who goes forward and the one who goes backward. In one house. In one body."

"I don't know," I said.

"A pity," said Sventsitsky. "Yesterday's you, it seems, knew. But did not say. Said: 'Tomorrow's will guess it himself. When the appointed time comes.'"

The appointed time. The appointed time again.

* * *
At home a piece of gossip awaited me. It was brought, of course, by Dunyasha - together with the tea, on a tray, that same evening, in a whisper, glancing at the door.

"Young master," she said, setting out the cups with trembling hands, "only please don't be angry. But in the servants' hall they're saying..."

"What are they saying, Dunyasha?"

"They're saying that you, young master..." she blushed to the roots of her hair, "that you go to town to see a young lady. At the 'Golden Anchor.' That Tikhon drove you there and waited three hours. And that you came out of there cheerful." She caught her breath. "Marfa the cook says - to a young lady. Mitka says - to a gypsy, to have your fortune told. And Agafya Tikhonovna says..."

"What does Agafya Tikhonovna say?"

Dunyasha lowered her voice to a whisper that was no longer audible at all:

"Agafya Tikhonovna says - not to a young lady and not to a gypsy. She says - to one who will tell you who you are. And that the mistress fears this worse than fire." Dunyasha swallowed. "And Agafya Tikhonovna also says that someone has touched the crape on the portrait in the gallery again. The night before last. She came in the morning - and the crape was torn down. Entirely. And lying on the floor. And on the portrait..." She fell silent.

"What on the portrait?"

"I don't know, young master. Agafya Tikhonovna won't say. She just hung the crape back and crossed herself three times. And now she carries the gallery keys on her belt." Dunyasha took the empty tray and backed toward the door. "And another thing, young master, Olga Kirillovna, the one in lilac - she goes all over the province saying that Artemia Aristarkhovna's ward has lost his mind. That he was found in the left wing with white eyes. That he talks with ghosts."

"With white eyes?"

"That's what she says, young master." Dunyasha was already in the doorway. "Only don't believe it. Olga Kirillovna always embellishes everything. Last year her cousin died of a head cold - and she told everybody it was consumption and unhappy love."

She slipped out. I remained alone with my cooling tea.

The night before last. The crape torn down. The night before last I had slept - I remembered sleeping. But I also remembered that on Friday nothing in particular had happened.

* * *
Konstantin burst in on me an hour later - without knocking, as always, with tousled hair, in an unbuttoned uniform tunic, with a pack of cards in one hand and a bottle of liqueur in the other.

"Enough sulking, mon cher!" he announced from the threshold. "The whole house is walking on tiptoe as if you were dying. Auntie is silent. The General is silent. Strauch is smoking his cigars right in the library - unheard of! Even Agafya Tikhonovna is not scolding, which is a sure sign of the end of the world. I have come to entertain you. We shall play charades. Just the two of us."

"Two do not play charades."

"We shall be the first," Konstantin said imperturbably, settling on the edge of my bed. "I'll set it. Listen." He cleared his throat, struck the pose of an actor of the Alexandrinsky Theatre and declaimed:

"'My first syllable is the animal that barks at the gate.
My second is the question we ask when we do not know who is coming.
And the whole is that which guards us from misfortune
When we sleep and see strange dreams.'"

I thought.

"Dog... Who... No." I thought some more. "'Dog-who'? What is that?"

Konstantin triumphantly raised a finger.

"'Dog' is dog. 'Who' is who. And the whole is - 'Pestun'! No, wait..." He frowned. "'Dog-who'... 'Dogwho'... Damn. In my head it was 'Watchman,' I thought it up on the road while riding from the regiment, and on the way I lost the syllables." He burst out laughing and fell back on the pillows. "Fine, the charade was bad. But the answer is good. Watchman. The one who guards us from misfortune when we sleep."

"And who is my watchman?"

Konstantin stopped laughing. He looked at me - for a moment serious, without his usual mockery.

"I am," he said simply. "Who else."

He looked away and began shuffling the cards - too fast, too carefully.

"Konstantin," I said. "Do you remember what you promised? After the salon?"

He froze.

"I remember. You promised to tell me first if you remembered."

"I remembered," I said. "Not everything. But something. Yesterday I went to town. To Sventsitsky. And I do not remember it. The notebook remembers. Tikhon remembers. Sventsitsky remembers. And I do not."

Konstantin slowly laid the cards on the blanket.

"I know," he said quietly.

"You know?"

"I saw you leave. From the window. You got into the carriage and did not look back. I shouted to you - you did not hear. Or pretended not to." He paused. "I went to the General."

"Why?"

Konstantin was silent a long while, looking at the cards.

"Because I did not know whom else to go to, mon cher," he said at last. "Because I was frightened."

* * *
That evening the General stayed overnight at my aunt's - he always stayed when business detained him in the province, and he was given the study of my aunt's late husband in the north wing: a large, gloomy room with dark oak panelling, bookcases to the ceiling, an enormous writing desk and a fireplace over which hung crossed sabres.

I did not mean to eavesdrop. I was going to the library for a book - the one on heraldry, which I had begun to read on Thursday, if the notebook was to be believed. The library was at the end of the same corridor. And the door of the study stood ajar - by exactly a hand's breadth, so that a narrow yellow strip of light from the fireplace fell across the corridor floor.

And I heard voices.

"...not for the first time," the General was saying. Quietly, evenly, but with that particular steel note which I had heard in him only once - at the salon, when he turned Sventsitsky out. "Do you understand, Konstantin? Not the first."

"I understand only that Your Excellency explains nothing to me," answered Konstantin. His voice sounded unfamiliar - without its usual mockery, sharp, almost rude. "He forgets names. Forgets what he did yesterday. Speaks in his sleep in languages no one knows. Strauch writes it down. Auntie is silent. You are silent. And he goes to town to a professor who collects tales, and tells him... what? What does he tell him there?"

"I do not know what he tells Sventsitsky," said the General.

"But you know why."

A long pause. The logs crackled in the fireplace.

"Last time," the General said at last, and his voice dropped, so that I had to hold my breath to make out the words, "last time it was the same. First the names. Then the days. Then the languages. Then the railings."

"Last time?" Konstantin nearly shouted it. "When was last time? He is young! What last time?!"

Silence.

"Your Excellency," said Konstantin in a different voice - quiet, almost pleading. "Pavel Nikolaevich. I am his friend. Perhaps his only friend. I promised him - do you understand? - promised that if he remembered, he would tell me first. And today he told me. And I... I can answer him nothing. Because I know nothing."

"It is better so," said the General.

"For whom?!"

"For him." The General's voice became very soft. "We promised, Kostya. I and Artemia Aristarkhovna. Long ago. We promised that he would not learn. Not before the time."

"Promised whom?"

A pause. So long that I thought - that is all, the conversation is over, and now the door will open and I shall be found here, pressed to the wall in the dark corridor.

"The one who brought him," said the General.

I stopped breathing.

"Who brought him?" Konstantin whispered. "Brought him where? From where?"

"That I will not tell you," said the General. "Not because I do not want to. Because I do not know myself. I saw him once. He stood by the railings. On the night when..." He fell silent. Then continued, heavily, as though lifting each word like a stone: "He was tall. Very tall. Grey. I did not see his face. He held him by the hand. And he said to Artemia - not in words, I do not know how to describe it - said that we were to keep him safe. Until the appointed time. And not to tell. Because if we told sooner - he would go. Altogether. To where he had come from."

I stood in the dark, my forehead pressed against the cold oak panel, feeling neither my hands nor my feet.

"And if he remembers on his own?" Konstantin asked barely audibly.

"Then," said the General, "it will no longer be our affair. Then the time will have come."

"And what then?"

A long, long silence.

"I don't know, Kostya," said the General, and in his voice, for the first time in all the time I had known him, there sounded something like fear. "For thirty years I have walked the world. I have seen Sitka and Samarkand, Peking and Havana. I have seen a wave higher than the masts sweep away a city. I have seen an old native sing a song by which one can walk across a whole country. I thought I had seen everything." A pause. "But I do not know what will happen when he remembers. I know only that Artemia fears it more than death. And that I..." he faltered, "I do too."

* * *
A floorboard creaked under my foot.

The voices in the study fell silent at once. I heard a chair pushed back. Footsteps - heavy, quick, the General's - toward the door.

I did not run. I do not know why. I simply stood in the corridor, in the narrow strip of light, and when the door flew open the General saw me - face to face, two paces away.

We looked at each other. For a long time. He - huge, grey-haired, in an unbuttoned tunic, without epaulettes, with a face which in the firelight behind him seemed carved from dark wood. I - I do not know how. White, probably.

From behind his shoulder Konstantin looked out - and froze.

"How much did you hear?" the General asked quietly.

I could have lied. Said: nothing, I just came up, I am going to the library. He might even have believed it. Or pretended to.

"Enough," I said.

The General closed his eyes. For a moment. Then opened them.

"Good," he said. And stepped aside, letting me into the study. "Then come in. Since it is so."

I went in. Konstantin retreated to the fireplace, not taking his eyes off me. The General closed the door - tightly, to a click - and turned the key in the lock.

"Sit," he said, indicating the armchair by the fireplace.

I sat.

The General stood over the fireplace, looking into the fire. Then he reached into the inner pocket of his tunic and took out two things. He laid them on the mantelpiece, side by side.

A wooden raven with a sun in its beak. And a paper crane - white, yellowed, worn.

"The raven that stole the sun," said the General, not turning. "And the crane that must be folded back into a sheet. I have carried them twenty years. They were given to me by people who did not know each other, at different ends of the world. And both said the same thing." He turned to me. "The raven: 'Maybe it will come in useful.' The crane: 'When you find the one who will fold it back.'" The General paused. "I think that is you."

"Me?"

"I don't know," said the General. "I know nothing. I know only that I promised to be silent. And I shall be silent." He looked at me heavily, directly, like a soldier. "But I will not lie to you. Never. Ask me whatever you like. If I can answer - I shall answer. If I cannot - I shall say that I cannot. But I will not lie."

I looked at him. At the raven. At the crane. At Konstantin by the fireplace, pale as linen.

A thousand questions crowded in my throat. Who brought me? From where? Who is the tall grey man by the railings? What happened "last time"? Who am I?

I asked one.

"Aunt," I said. "Is she my own kin?"

The General was silent for a long while. The fire crackled. Konstantin did not breathe.

"That I cannot say," the General answered at last. "But I can say something else." He paused. "She loves you as she has loved no one in the world. Not even her husband. Not even..." He faltered. "No one. That is the truth. Is that enough?"

"No," I said.

"I know," said the General. "It would not be enough for me either."

* * *
He set me a riddle. Later, when the three of us were already sitting by the fire, and Konstantin had poured liqueur into the glasses, and no one drank, and the silence had become unbearable, the General suddenly said, looking into the flames:

"Near Khiva, in the sands, a Turkmen old man set it to me. The one who gave me water. And the scroll. I have never told anyone the answer. Perhaps I shall tell you."

"Set it."

"'I go away every evening and come every morning. I am awaited, but no one knows where I was in the night. I am one and the same - and each time different. I cannot be held, but can be met. What am I?'"

Konstantin thought.

"The sun."

"Everyone answers so," said the General. "The old man said - wrong."

"Then what?" I asked.

The General looked at me - long, heavily.

"A guest," he said. "The old man said: 'A guest. He comes, goes, and does not remember where he has been. He cannot be held. But if you meet him as you should - he will leave you what he brought.'" The General paused. "And then the old man gave me the scroll and said: 'You are not the one it was brought for. But you will meet him. Give it to him.'"

He rose, went to the writing desk, pulled out the bottom drawer - the one that locked with a separate key hanging on his watch chain. Took out something wrapped in an old, faded silk kerchief. Laid it on the desk.

But did not unwrap it.

"Not today," he said, closing the drawer again. "Not today. I promised - until the appointed time. But the time, it seems, is nearer than I thought." He turned to Konstantin. "And you, Kostya - do not leave him. Not by a step. If he goes to town again - go with him. If he goes to the left wing - go with him. If..."

"I know," Konstantin interrupted. His voice was hoarse. "I know, Your Excellency. I have not left him as it is."

The General looked at him. Then at me. Then at him again. And suddenly - for the first time that whole evening - he smiled. Briefly, almost like a father.

"I know you haven't," he said. "Do you think I am blind?"

Konstantin flushed to the roots of his hair and stared into the fire.

* * *
I returned to my room after midnight. Konstantin walked me to the door - in silence, as one escorts the wounded - and, before leaving, stood on the threshold.

"Mon cher," he said quietly. "If you go somewhere again and do not remember - let the notebook remember. But let it be written there that I was beside you. All right?"

"All right."

"Promise?"

"I promise."

He nodded and left. I closed the door, sat at the desk, opened the blue notebook to write down this day - and froze.

On the clean page, beneath yesterday's entry about the journey I did not remember, there was already a drawing. Fresh. The ink still glistened.

Two circles. One blackened. The other empty. And a wavy line between them.

And under the drawing - three words. In my handwriting. With my blot at the end.

"He is near. Wait."

I had not written this. I had only just come in. I was holding the pen in my hand - dry.

I sat over the notebook for a long time, until the candle burned out. Then, in the dark, I took the dry pen, dipped it in the inkwell and wrote below, trying to keep my hand from shaking:

"Saturday. Learned that I went to town. Learned that I spoke of a city by the sea and of columns. Learned that someone brought me. Learned that Aunt loves me. Konstantin was beside me."

I set the full stop. The blot lay in its place.

Outside the window, in the garden, among the rosebushes, Stefan's lantern flickered - he was again circling the white roses beneath the drawing-room windows. And then it stopped. And stood for a long time motionless, the lantern raised toward my window.

## Chapter XIX. The Embassy from the South

The giraffe entered the palace before the ambassador.

No one had planned this. According to the rules which Ani the Elder, keeper of ceremonies - not the deaf scribe of the council but his cousin, still more ancient and still more stern - had been reading out of scrolls for two days running, the embassy of the southern land was to enter the outer court solemnly, in strict order: heralds in front, then the ambassador, then the gifts, and only at the very end, behind the gifts, the animals. But the giraffe had not read the rules.

I stood on the balcony above the outer court, hidden by a linen awning - I wanted to see the embassy before it saw me - and I saw everything. I saw how into the opened gates there first peered timidly a small spotted head on an incredibly long neck, swaying at a height the spears of the guards could not reach. I saw how the head surveyed the court with an expression of majestic, almost regal bewilderment. And how, following the head, unhurriedly setting down its stilt-like legs, all the rest floated into the court - russet, with dark patches, like a map of unknown lands - dragging behind it on a long rope two desperately resisting drovers.

The guards at the gate shied away. A scribe with a basket of scrolls crashed onto his back, scattering papyri all over the court. The court burst into cries. The giraffe, not in the least abashed, walked straight to the old fig tree growing by the wall, lowered its head to the topmost branch - the one the gardeners had been unable to reach for years - and began unhurriedly to strip the leaves.

"My Pharaoh," came a dry, imperturbable voice behind me. "It seems the southerners have decided to begin negotiations with the most important thing. With refreshments."

Nebamun stood at the door to the balcony, with his inevitable counting-box under his arm, and looked down into the court with the expression with which he must look upon a fire in someone else's granary: without fear, but with lively professional interest.

"How much does a giraffe cost, Nebamun?" I asked, unable to restrain myself.

"A giraffe, my Pharaoh, costs exactly as much as the fig tree it is eating now," answered the keeper of the treasury. "Plus the gate, which will have to be widened if they want to lead it out again. Plus the scribe, who will now spend a week gathering up scrolls." He paused. "But if we speak of the price to the southerners - the giraffe costs more than all the rest of the embassy. A giraffe is not given. A giraffe is shown. So that all may see: they have beasts that we do not."

Below, at the gate, the heralds at last appeared - bewildered, out of breath, plainly having lost the giraffe on the way. Behind them, in a cloud of dust, to the bellow of bronze trumpets and the roll of drums, the embassy entered the court.

* * *
I had seen many embassies - or so it seemed to me; my memory, as always, gave up reluctantly what lay deeper than the last few moons. But this was like none of them.

First came the bearers - tall, dark-skinned, with shoulders gleaming with oil, with skin of such a deep, almost blue colour that the sun slid over it as over polished black wood. On their shoulders they carried gifts. Elephant tusks - enormous, curved like young crescent moons, yellow with age, each needing two bearers. Logs of ebony, heavy as stone. Leopard skins - dozens of skins, spotted, with heads and claws hanging at the sides. Sacks of incense, from which a thick, sweet, bitterish smell at once floated through the court, drowning even the smell of the giraffe. Baskets from which ostrich feathers and eggs the size of a human head peered out. And gold. Gold in ingots, in rings, in little bags, in the shape of small figures - birds, lions, snakes - heaped into open chests so carelessly, as though it had been brought not as a gift but for sale by weight.

After the bearers the animals were led. Besides the giraffe, which was still stripping the fig tree, paying not the slightest attention to protocol - two cheetahs on golden leashes, graceful, spotted, with black stripes from eye to muzzle as if painted tears. A cage with three baboons - grey, huge, in copper collars - at the sight of which the priests in the crowd by the wall began to whisper and make warding signs. And - quite unexpectedly - a little monkey with a long tail, sitting on the shoulder of one of the bearers and pelting everyone with date stones.

And then the ambassador appeared.

He came neither in a chariot nor in a litter - he came on foot, and that was the first thing that struck me. Tall, taller than any of his bearers, straight as a spear, about forty, with skin of the same deep, almost blue shade, his head shaved bare and crowned with a thin golden circlet from which a single golden pendant hung on his forehead - a small ram's horn. He was dressed more simply than any of my dignitaries: a white loincloth, a broad necklace of beads - blue, red, gold - and a leopard skin thrown over one shoulder. On his arms, from wrist to elbow, there was not a single bracelet. But on his face - on the cheekbones, the forehead, the chin - there were fine, delicate scars, as if cut with a chisel, composing a pattern that I could not read but that, I was sure, meant something.

He walked across the court looking neither at the giraffe, nor at the gathered onlookers, nor at the guard, nor at the baboons. He looked up. At the balcony. Straight at the linen awning behind which I was hiding.

And I understood that he knew I was there.

"Irikhet," Nebamun said quietly. "The son of the southern king's brother. They entrust him with the hardest negotiations. They say that last time, when there was a dispute between us over the border wells, he sat twelve days by the king's tent, eating and drinking nothing but water, until our former Pharaoh agreed to divide the wells in half." Nebamun paused. "The former Pharaoh said afterwards that he yielded not from weakness but because he could no longer watch a man starve himself on his threshold."

"And what do you think?"

"I think, my Pharaoh," said Nebamun, "that a man who can go twelve days without eating to gain a well is more dangerous than a man with an army."

* * *
Behind the ambassador, two paces back, came two more.

The first was a short, plump, fussy man in an Egyptian linen robe but with southern beads at his neck, who kept running ahead, looking round, whispering something to the ambassador, bowing to everyone - guards, priests, even, it seemed, the giraffe. The interpreter, I guessed.

And the second...

The second was an old woman. So old as I had never seen - even Merit by the temple pond would have seemed a girl beside her. Small, bent almost double, wrapped in brown cloth so that only her face could be seen - and the face was covered with the same fine patterned scars as the ambassador's, only denser, solid, from forehead to chin, so that the skin seemed carved like the lid of a casket. In her hand she held a staff - long, taller than herself, of white wood, crowned with a carved lioness's head.

She walked slowly, leaning on the staff, and looked at nothing around her. Her eyes were closed. She was blind, I understood - or pretended to be blind. And yet, when she came level with the balcony, she stopped. And raised her face. And opened her eyes.

The eyes were white. Entirely. Without pupils. Like two pieces of ivory.

And they looked straight at me.

"Who is that?" I whispered.

Nebamun did not answer. For the first time in all the time I had known him, the keeper of the treasury did not know the answer.

* * *
The reception was set for noon, in the great throne room - and by noon the hall was fuller than it had ever been, it seemed.

On the right of the throne - Senusret, in full armour, with a heavy bronze sword at his belt, his face stone and impenetrable. Behind him - Paser, leaning on his staff, grey, watchful. Djehuty, just back from the southern outposts, dusty, sunburned to blackness, with a scar on his cheek standing out still more sharply against the weathered skin. Khaemuas - in his costliest bracelets, in his finest linen, smiling at everyone. Vizier Ptahhotep - with a basket of scrolls at his feet. Nebamun - with his box. Merira - with tattooed arms crossed on his chest. And at the far wall, in the shadow of a column, almost unnoticed - Panehsy, commander of the Medjay, in a leather baldric with throwing sticks.

On the left - the priests. Bakenren, round, shaven, radiant. Behind him half a dozen senior priests in white. And - for the first time since the evening when he had spoken to me of the scales and of the death of the junior priest in Luxor - Nefer-Ka himself.

He stood straight as an obelisk, in a white robe, with a staff crowned by the sacred Eye, and did not look at me. He looked at the doors. At the place from which the embassy was to enter. And on his face was an expression I could not read - not alarm, not expectation, but something like the patience of a predator at a watering place.

At the foot of the throne, among the scribes, sat Iti. I had myself told Amenemope to send him - "the best hand in the Library," I had said before everyone, loudly, so that the ears with bracelets would hear: the boy was needed as a scribe, no more. Iti sat with his head bent over the papyrus, brush at the ready, and never once raised his eyes to me. Only as I sat down on the throne did I notice that his cheek was clean. Not a single ink stain. He had evidently washed with particular care before the reception. And from this, I do not know why, I felt a little sad.

* * *
The ambassador entered alone. Without the interpreter, without the old woman, without the bearers. He stopped in the middle of the hall, in a ray of light from the high window, so that the golden circlet on his shaven head flared. He did not bow. He drew himself up still straighter. And spoke.

In our language. Clearly, slowly, with a singsong southern accent, but without a single mistake.

"Son of Ra, lord of the Two Lands. My uncle, king of the land beyond the cataracts, lord of Ta-Seti, sends you greeting. And gifts. And a question."

A whisper ran through the hall. The ambassador did not speak through an interpreter. The ambassador knew our language - and did not hide it, but displayed it from his first words.

"The greeting is received," I said. "The gifts are received." I paused. "The giraffe is received too. Although, I fear, my garden will have a hard time of it."

Someone in the hall snorted - Merira, it seemed. The ambassador did not smile. But something in his face, at the corners of his lips, trembled for an instant.

"A giraffe eats only the upper branches, son of Ra," he said. "The lower ones it leaves to those of lesser height. With us they say: be like the giraffe. Take what others cannot reach. And do not touch what they need more."

"A wise proverb," I said. "And what question does your uncle send me?"

Irikhet held a pause - a long one, so that the silence in the hall drew taut like a bowstring.

"My uncle asks," he said slowly, distinctly, "who rules in your land, son of Ra. You - or those who feed our people with your bread?"

* * *
The hall exploded.

Djehuty leapt up, seizing his sword. Khaemuas paled until he was whiter than his linen. The priests at the left wall stirred, whispered. Bakenren stopped radiating - his face went slack all at once, like dough. Senusret stepped forward, shielding the throne. The scribes at the foot of the throne threw down their brushes.

Only two in the hall did not move. Nefer-Ka - by the left wall. And Iti - at the foot of the throne, bent over the papyrus so low that I saw only the back of his head, and the brush in his hand moved evenly, swiftly, recording every word.

"Silence," I said. Not loudly. But the hall fell silent.

I looked at the ambassador. He looked at me.

"Explain your question, Irikhet," I said.

"I will explain." The ambassador turned - not to me, to the hall, as if addressing all at once. "For three moons we have been receiving bread. Egyptian bread. Barley, emmer, wheat. In sacks. The sacks come on donkeys, by secret paths, across the desert, to our border chiefs. They are brought by men in white robes. With shaven heads." He paused. "They say: this is a gift from those who will soon speak to you in the name of Egypt in place of Pharaoh. They say: take the bread, and for the bread do what we say. Burn the border villages. Let the people of Egypt see that Pharaoh cannot protect them."

No one in the hall breathed.

"My chiefs took the bread," said Irikhet. "Because we have drought too. Not like yours, but drought. My chiefs burned your villages. Because a hungry chief does what the one who feeds him commands." He turned to me. "I do not ask forgiveness for this, son of Ra. I have come to tell you the truth. Because my uncle is a king, not a chief. And a king does not want his chiefs to serve foreign priests. He wants to know: with whom is he to speak? With you - or with them?"

Bakenren stepped forward.

"My Pharaoh!" His voice, always so oily, broke into a shriek. "This is a lie! The southerner lies! The Temple has never..."

"The sacks," said Irikhet, without turning his head, "were marked. With a sign. A triangle, point downward. Beneath it - three waves." He at last looked at Bakenren. "Shall I draw you this sign, priest? Or do you remember it?"

Bakenren opened his mouth. Closed it. Stepped back a pace - and bumped against a column with his back.

I did not look at Bakenren. I looked at Nefer-Ka.

The High Priest stood just as straight. His face did not change. Only one thing in him changed - I noticed it because I was looking for it: the fingers of his right hand, resting on the staff, slowly clenched. So that the knuckles whitened.

And then he spoke. Calmly. Softly. In that same ingratiating, resonant voice with which he spoke to the crowd outside the Temple.

"My Pharaoh. The southerner is right in one thing. The bread of Egypt has gone south." Nefer-Ka made a pause - exactly long enough for the whole hall to catch its breath. "It was stolen. From the Temple granaries. By thieves in white robes who passed themselves off as priests. The Temple has long known of this. The Temple is seeking them." He turned to Bakenren, and steel sounded in his voice. "Bakenren. You were responsible for the granaries. You reported to me that they were empty after the distribution to the people. How then did it happen that their grain turned up beyond the cataracts?"

Bakenren looked at the High Priest as a rabbit looks at a snake. His round face went grey as ash.

"I... I... High One..." he stammered.

"We shall speak of this in the Temple," said Nefer-Ka gently. "Later." He turned to me again and bowed - exactly as far as custom required. "My Pharaoh. The Temple will find the thieves. The Temple will punish the guilty. The Temple thanks the honourable ambassador for opening our eyes."

He stepped back to the wall. Bakenren remained standing by the column - alone, in the middle of the hall, under the gaze of a hundred eyes.

I watched this and understood that I had just seen a snake shed its skin. How the High Priest, without blinking, had thrown his closest servant to be devoured - to save himself. And that Bakenren had understood this too.

"The Temple will find the thieves," I said slowly. "Of course." I paused. "And while the Temple searches - the throne will take up the search as well. Panehsy."
