The commander of the Medjay came soundlessly out of the shadow of the column.

"The Temple granaries," I said. "All twelve. Seal them with the royal seal. Today. Before sunset. No one removes a grain without Nebamun's knowledge." I looked at Nefer-Ka. "So that the thieves, if they are still there, do not carry off the rest. For the good of the Temple."

Nefer-Ka bowed his head. His face was impenetrable.

"For the good of the Temple, my Pharaoh," he repeated.

* * *
After the reception the ambassador asked to speak with me alone.

Senusret was against it. Paser too. Even Nebamun pursed his lips in disapproval. But I agreed - and Irikhet came to my chambers at sunset, alone, unarmed, with only a leopard skin on his shoulder.

He stood a long time at the window, looking at the city, at the river, at the scorched fields beyond the river. Then he said, without turning:

"Shall I tell you a tale, son of Ra? Ours, southern. It is told to children among us. And among you, I have heard, it is told to priests. Differently."

"Tell it."

Irikhet turned to me.

"'Long ago, when the gods still walked the earth, the god of the Sun had an Eye. Not an eye - the Eye. A daughter. A lioness. Fiery. She was his strength, his wrath, his protection. But once the god of the Sun offended her. With what, no one remembers now. And the Eye left him. Went south. To our land. Far, beyond the cataracts, into the desert. And there she became wild. She roamed the sands as a lioness, killed all she met, drank blood, and her eyes burned like fire. And the god of the Sun without his Eye grew weak. Became old. His land dried up. The rivers shallowed.'"

He paused.

"'And then the god of the Sun sent for her. He sent his scribe - the one who knows all the words, the one who gathers what has been torn apart. The ibis-headed one. He came into the desert, to the wild lioness, and sat down before her. And she wanted to kill him. And he began to tell her tales. One after another. About her father. About her home. About the river that missed her. About the temples where songs were sung to her. And he told them so long, and so well, that the lioness stopped growling. Lay down. Wept. And her tears fell on the sand and became water. And then the scribe said: "Let us go home." And she went. All the way north he told her tales, so that she would not change her mind. And when she entered Egypt - the river rose. Overflowed. And everything turned green.'"

Irikhet fell silent. The room had grown dark - the sun had set.

"Drought," I said slowly. "Three years without the flood."

"Three years," the ambassador nodded. "Our old men say: the Eye has gone away again. To the south. To us. Or - not quite to us. Somewhere from which it must be brought back. And until it is brought back, the river will not rise." He looked at me directly, unblinking. "Old Nanakhat - you saw her, the blind one with the lioness staff - she says that the Eye will return when the one who carried it away comes. Because only the one who carried it away knows the way back."

"Who carried it away?"

Irikhet was silent.

"Nanakhat says - you, son of Ra," he said at last. "Not this you. Another. The former. The one who was Pharaoh before you. Or the one you were before you became Pharaoh. She says it is the same." He shrugged. "I am not a priest. I do not understand this. I convey what she said."

Cold under the ribs. On the left. Familiar.

"What else did she say?"

"She said she wants to see you. Alone. Without guards. Without priests. Tomorrow. At dawn. By the river." Irikhet went toward the door. At the threshold he turned. "And she also said to give you a riddle. She said you must solve it before the meeting. Otherwise there is no need to meet."

"What riddle?"

The ambassador said it slowly, carefully, as if afraid to distort a single word:

"'Two went out of one house. One went to the sunrise, the other to the sunset. They walked all their lives and never once looked back. And when they came to the edge of the world - they met. Face to face. Where did they meet?'"

He went out without waiting for an answer.

* * *
Djehuty came to me late at night. Without announcement, as Khemu once had - Senusret had evidently let him through himself, because he knew what he was coming with.

He stood at the door - dusty, tired, with a weathered face on which the scar across the cheek seemed still sharper - and held in his hands something wrapped in coarse canvas.

"My Pharaoh," he said. "I should have reported this in council. But Khaemuas was in the council. And the priests." He paused. "I did not tell you everything about the southern outposts."

"Speak."

Djehuty unwrapped the canvas. Inside was a fragment of stone - flat, grey, the size of two palms, with uneven, fresh edges, as if it had been recently knocked off a cliff.

"At the last outpost, right above the cataracts," he said, "there is a rock. Old. It is called the Rock of the First Ones. Herdsmen give it a wide berth. My soldiers were afraid too, but I ordered them to keep watch on the summit, one sees the desert better from there." Djehuty paused. "On the third night the watchman ran to me, shaking. Said the rock was glowing. I climbed up myself." He laid the stone on the table. "It was not glowing. But there were signs on it. Carved. Very old - older than anything I had seen. Lichen had almost eaten them. But that night, by the moon, they could be seen. I knocked off a piece. This one."

I bent over the stone. Brought the lamp near.

On the grey, weathered stone were signs. Not hieroglyphs. Long, flowing, curving lines running one into another without breaks. The same script. The same as on the papyrus Iti found. The same as on the stones in the chest of black wood - if Khemu was not mistaken.

"There are many of them," Djehuty said quietly. "The whole rock. From top to bottom. As if someone had written a whole scroll on it." He looked at me. "I am not a priest, my Pharaoh. I am a soldier. I do not believe in omens. But my soldiers after that night refused to stand watch on the rock. All of them. Even those who went with me against the southerners with one spear to three men." He paused. "And one more thing. Under the rock, in the sand, we found tracks. Many tracks. Fresh. Someone had been digging there. Searching for something. Recently. At night. Men in sandals. In good ones, temple sandals."

"The Temple is searching for something on the Rock of the First Ones," I said.

"It looks that way, my Pharaoh." Djehuty drew himself up. "I ask your word. Let me go back south. I will take my best men. I will set a guard at the rock. I will let no one near - neither priests, nor southerners, nor the High One himself. Until you decide what to do with it."

I looked at this hard, abrupt man, who at the first council had demanded a campaign beyond the cataracts and argued with me before everyone - and thought that Paser had been right: Djehuty simply needed a task.

"Go," I said. "Take the best. And, Djehuty..." He turned. "Thank you for bringing this to me. And not to the council."

Djehuty was silent. Then - for the first time - he smiled, and the scar on his cheek folded into a real smile and not the eternal frozen smirk.

"Old Paser told me, my Pharaoh," he answered, "that I am young because so far I have been lucky. I thought: let the luck go on. But not for me alone."

* * *
Paney came after him - almost running, barefoot, eyes blazing, out of breath. Behind him, unable to keep up, came Bata, and the guardsman's face was anxious.

"My Pharaoh!" the boy blurted, falling to his knees. "My Pharaoh, I saw him!"

"Whom, Paney?"

"Him!" The boy was gasping. "That one! The one who burned! In Little Nekhen! Who..." His voice broke. "Who set fire to our house. When Father told me to run. I saw his face. In the light of the fire. I remember it. I will remember it all my life."

"Where did you see him?"

"Here!" Paney thrust his hand toward the window, toward the place beyond the palace walls, in the outer court, where the embassy's bearers had pitched their tents. "Among the southerners! Among those who carried the tusks! He is there! He was laughing and drinking beer by the fire!"

Bata, who had come up behind him, nodded to me over the boy's head.

"It's true, my Pharaoh. The boy ran to me, trembling. I went to look. Tall, with a scar through his eyebrow, an earring in his ear. Sitting by a fire among the bearers." Bata paused. "Only he is no bearer, my Pharaoh. A bearer has calluses on his hands from tusks. This one's are from a spear."

I was silent for a long time.

Irikhet had come to tell the truth. Irikhet had spoken of the bread and of the chiefs fed by priests. Irikhet had come alone, unarmed. And among his people by the fire sat the man who had burned Little Nekhen.

Did Irikhet know it? Or not? Or had someone placed this man in his embassy - as a foundling is laid in a stranger's cradle?

"Paney," I said at last. "You are a brave boy. You did everything right. Now listen. You will not go near the tents again. Not today, not tomorrow. You will tell no one what you saw. Not Iti, not Bata, not Hesira. No one but me. Do you understand?"

Paney nodded, biting his lip.

"Bata. Find Panehsy. Tell him - a man with a scar through his eyebrow and an earring. Let the Medjay never take their eyes off him. But not touch him. Let them watch whom he talks to."

Bata went out. Paney remained standing in the middle of the room - small, trembling, with eyes in which there were no more tears, only fire. The very fire in which his house had burned.

"My Pharaoh," he said quietly. "When you catch him - may I look at him? Just look. So that he sees I am alive."

"You may, Paney," I said. "I promise."

* * *
Iti found me in the garden after midnight - by the fig tree, under the jasmine, where we had met last time. He brought a scroll - the record of the reception, made by his hand. Word for word.

"I thought you would need it, my Pharaoh," he said, holding out the scroll. "The official record will be with Ani. And Ani..." he hesitated, "half of Ani's words will be 'repeat for the record.'"

I took the scroll. Unrolled it. Iti's handwriting - even, quick, flawless. Every word of the ambassador. Every word of Nefer-Ka. Every pause marked with a dot.

And at the bottom, in the margin, small, in quite a different, hurried hand - a note:

"Nefer-Ka clenched his staff when the ambassador named the sign. Bakenren did not know that Nefer-Ka would give him up. Nefer-Ka knew beforehand. He came to the reception already decided."

I raised my eyes.

"You noticed this?"

"I was watching him, my Pharaoh," said Iti. "All the time. While I wrote." He paused. "I can write without looking at the papyrus. Isiret taught me. She says a true scribe looks at the one who speaks, not at what he writes. Because words lie, but the face does not."

"And you did not look at me once," I said. "The whole reception."

Iti froze. Then lowered his eyes.

"You said, my Pharaoh - before everyone, so that the ears with bracelets would hear - that you needed me only as a scribe." His voice was even, but I saw his fingers tremble. "And I was a scribe. A good one. The most unnoticed. I looked at the priests, at the ambassador, at Khaemuas, at Bakenren." He paused. "And if I had looked at you, everyone would have seen."

"Seen what?"

Iti did not answer. He looked at the jasmine. Then at the scroll in my hands.

"There is something more there, my Pharaoh," he said instead of answering. "On the back. I do not know whether it is important."

I turned the scroll over. On the back, in the corner, there was drawn - swiftly, precisely, with a fine brush - a face. An old woman. Blind. With patterned scars all over her face. And beside the face - a sign. One of the patterns of her scars, redrawn separately, larger.

A long, flowing, curving line. Running into another. Without a break.

"This is on her forehead," Iti said quietly. "Right above the brows. I looked at her as she crossed the court. I redrew it." He raised his eyes to me. "My Pharaoh. It is the same sign. As on the papyrus from the lower storehouse. Third from the left in the first line. I remember it. I looked at it all night."

* * *
I did not sleep. Until dawn I sat by the window, holding three things in my hands: Iti's scroll, Djehuty's fragment of stone and the papyrus from the lower storehouse. Three pieces of one riddle. The script on the papyrus, the script on the rock at the cataracts, the script on the forehead of the blind southern old woman.

And I thought over the riddle she had sent me.

"Two went out of one house. One went to the sunrise, the other to the sunset. They walked all their lives without looking back. And when they came to the edge of the world - they met. Face to face. Where did they meet?"

If one goes toward the sunrise, turning nowhere, and goes one's whole life... And if the other goes toward the sunset...

They will meet only if the world is not flat. If it is a circle. If the edge of the world in the east and the edge of the world in the west are one and the same place.

They met where they had set out from. At home.

I remembered a riddle I had never heard. About stones - day and night. One keeps, the other leads. He who holds both stands in the doorway. Where he looks - there is home. I did not know how I knew it. But it came by itself and stood beside the old woman's riddle, like two halves of one potsherd.

The sky in the east was beginning to turn grey. I rose, threw on a dark cloak - this time I did not forget the sandals either: plain, worn-down ones, borrowed from Bata - and went out into the garden.

At the gate Senusret was waiting for me. Dressed as a donkey-driver, with a staff instead of a sword - but the sword, I knew, was under his cloak.

"You are going to the river, my Pharaoh," he said. Not a question.

"She said - alone."

"I shall not go to her," said Senusret. "I shall stand behind the palms, fifty paces off. She will not see me." He paused. "And if she does - I shall say I am herding donkeys."

"You have no donkeys, Senusret."

"Then I am looking for them," said the commander of the army imperturbably. "Donkeys are like that. Always getting lost."

I laughed - quietly, for the first time in that endless night. And we went to the river together, in the grey pre-dawn gloom, past the sleeping tents of the embassy, past the giraffe, dozing on its feet by the stripped fig tree - to where on the bank of the shallowed Nile, on a flat stone at the very water's edge, motionless as a statue, sat a small bent figure with a staff crowned by a lioness's head.

She did not turn when I approached. She sat facing south, toward the cataracts, toward the desert, and her white, sightless eyes were open.

"Where did they meet?" she asked. In our language. In a creaking, ancient voice like the rustle of sand on stone.

I sat down on the stone beside her.

"At home," I said. "Where they set out from. Because the world is a circle."

The old woman was silent for a long time. The river lapped quietly at our feet - shallow, weary, almost still.

"Right," she said at last. "But that is only half the answer. The second you will tell me when you return."

"Return from where?"

Nanakhat turned her face to me - carved, ancient, in patterns of scars - and her white eyes rested on me as if they saw through me. And not only me. The one who was before me. And the one who would come after.

"From Luxor, son of Ra," she said. "If you return."

* * *
The sun rose over the eastern hills. On the far bank, in the fields, the first birds began to sing. Somewhere far off, in the palace, the baboons cried out - all three at once, greeting the sunrise, as they have greeted it, they say, since the beginning of time.

Nanakhat spoke for a long time. I listened.

She spoke of the lioness who had gone south - and of how her people believe that the Eye leaves not out of anger but because there is no one to hold it. Of the rock at the cataracts, which her people call not the Rock of the First Ones but the Rock of Waiting - because it is written upon it that one day someone will come for it. Of the two Eyes, which must be together but always turn out to be in different hands. Of how the drought will end when one hand takes both. Of how in the Temple, in the chest of black wood, not everything lies. That half of what is needed is by the river. And half is with the one who came without memory.

"I do not understand," I said.

"I know," said Nanakhat. "And you need not. Yet. Understanding comes like the flood: at first the water rises quietly, and no one notices. And then - in the morning - everything around is already green."

She rose, leaning on the lioness staff. Small, bent double, ancient.

"The ambassador will leave in seven days," she said. "I shall leave with him. But before that you will come to me once more. When you find what is sought on the Rock." She paused. "And beware of the man with the scar through his eyebrow. He is not ours. He was put into our caravan like a snake into a basket of dates. Irikhet does not know. I know. But I am a blind old woman. Who will listen to a blind old woman?"

"I will listen," I said.

Nanakhat smiled - toothlessly, anciently, as a stone smiles over which water has run for a thousand years.

"You have always listened," she said. "Even last time."

And she went off along the bank, tapping her staff - to where behind the palms, clumsily playing a drover who had lost his donkeys, stood Senusret. Passing him, she stopped, turned her sightless face to him and said something - briefly, creakingly. Senusret flinched so that his staff fell from his hands.

When she had gone, I went up to him.

"What did she say to you?"

The commander of the army was silent for a long while, picking up his staff from the sand.

"She said," he spoke at last, dully, not looking at me, "'The donkeys will be found, warrior. But the one you guard you cannot keep safe in Luxor. If you go after him there - stay at the gates. Otherwise you will both not return.'"

Over the river the sun was rising - enormous, red, merciless. The Nile lay at our feet as a thin, shallow ribbon amid cracked mud. Less than two moons remained until the festival of Opet.

And we both - Pharaoh and his old warrior - stood for a long time on the bank in silence, daring neither to say to each other what we were thinking, nor to turn back.

## Chapter XX. The Shadow at the Window

The night after the walk to Sultanahmet was harder on me than I was willing to admit aloud - even to myself. The chest with the metal plate, whose pattern I had recognized as unerringly as one recognizes one's own handwriting on a long-forgotten letter, would not leave my thoughts, however I tried to occupy them with something else.

The evening in Ferhat's house after our walk was not like the earlier ones. Everyone seemed to know that something had happened today - though no one except Suleyman, Kemal and Akmal had gone with us to Sultanahmet, and those three, on returning, had told no one a word. And yet the house had fallen quiet. The women behind the curtain spoke in low voices. Yusuf clicked the beads of his abacus more slowly than usual. Even the pigeons on the roof seemed to coo more softly.

The first thing, as soon as we entered, Suleyman, without taking off his travelling kaftan, went up to my room and took down from the nail above the door the red thread on which the fragment of the old nazar still hung. In its place he hung a new one - huge, the size of a palm, glass, dark blue, with a white ring and a black pupil, so heavy that the nail bent noticeably under it. He hung it, stepped back a pace, looked, adjusted it. Then he tapped it with his finger - ringingly, the way one taps a jug to check for cracks.

"Grandfather says," translated Akmal from below, from the stairs, who in these days had learned from Ferhat a few words of my language and was terribly proud of it, "big eye. Big eye - big..." he faltered, searching for the word, and in despair spread his arms as wide as he could, "big... this!"

"Big protection," I prompted.

"Yes!" Akmal beamed. "Big protection! Grandfather bought from Hasan Amca. Hasan Amca said - biggest in Istanbul. Hasan Amca always says so."

* * *
Hasan Amca, by the way, came himself - to supper, uninvited, as he evidently always came when the house smelled of mutton. He settled on the carpet in the courtyard, taking up a good third of it, accepted a bowl of tea from Yusuf and, puffing, announced to the whole courtyard a piece of news that made Yusuf stop counting and Suleyman lay down his prayer beads.

"He says," translated Ferhat, who had returned from the port just in time for supper, with wet hair and a basket of fish that one of the dockhands had pressed on him, "that today in the port, at the quay where French ships are unloaded, some man was asking about a stranger." Ferhat stopped smiling. "In velvet shoes. In a turban with a tassel. He asked the boatmen, the dockhands, the traders. Had anyone seen him. Where he lives."

Everything inside me went cold.

"What man?"

Hasan, hearing the question, spread his hands and began to gabble, acting something out with gestures - tall stature, straight back, something long to the knees, a hand as if holding a cane.

"Hasan Amca did not see him himself," translated Ferhat. "Mustafa the boatman told him. He says - tall. In a grey frock coat. Dressed like a Frank, but not a Frank. He speaks French, Greek, a little Turkish - with a strange accent, as if all these languages were equally foreign to him. Mustafa did not remember the face." Ferhat paused. "He says, strange thing: he looked straight at him, talked with him - and did not remember the face. As if there was none. As if instead of a face - mist."

Tall. Grey. Faceless.

"What did they answer him?" I asked, and my voice sounded hoarse.

"Nothing," said Ferhat. "Mustafa said he had seen no stranger in velvet shoes." Ferhat suddenly grinned. "Mustafa had seen you. Everyone in the port has seen you, you go every morning with Akmal to look at the ships. But Mustafa said - he had not. Because Mustafa owes Hasan Amca money, and Hasan Amca has told everyone in the port that you are his guest." Ferhat spread his hands. "In our city, Misafir, to protect you, you do not need guards. You need a red-haired shopkeeper to whom half the port owes for pepper."

Hasan, understanding from the intonation what it was about, guffawed and slapped his belly.

But Suleyman did not laugh. He looked at me for a long time, running his beads - click, click, click - and then said something to Orhan. Briefly. The latter nodded, saying nothing, rose and went into the house.

"What did he say to Orhan?" I asked in a whisper.

Ferhat hesitated.

"He said that tonight Orhan is to sleep at your door. With a knife."

* * *
Supper lasted long - as though no one wanted it to end. Fried fish from Ferhat's basket, crisp, with lemon; mutton pilaf smelling of cardamom and raisins; flatbreads; sour milk with cucumbers and mint; and for sweets - grandmother's baklava, so honeyed that the fingers stuck together, and Akmal licked his with such a sound that Yusuf slapped his hand three times.

Hasan told stories. One was about a merchant from Basra who sold one and the same camel five times to five different buyers - and each time the camel came back to him by itself at night, because it loved its master more than its purchasers. Another was about a dervish who for thirty years walked through Anatolia and taught people to laugh at themselves, and when he died he ordered in his will that his tomb be shut with an enormous lock - and that no walls be made for the tomb. And people still come there to look at the lock without walls and laugh.

"Is that true?" I asked Ferhat.

"About the dervish - true," said Ferhat. "That is Nasreddin. Hodja Nureddin loves him very much. The tomb is in Akshehir. The lock hangs on the door, and around the door - nothing. You can walk round it." He laughed. "The Hodja says it is the wisest grave in the world. It shows that all our locks are for those who did not intend to enter anyway."

A lock without walls. I thought of the chest in Hatice Hanim's cellar - without a keyhole. Of the door in the blank wall. Of the railings which I had never seen but which for some reason rose from time to time before my eyes. All our locks are for those who did not intend to enter anyway. And those who do intend to enter, enter without a key.

Yusuf, who all this time had been silently counting something on his abacus, suddenly pushed it away, held out a dry palm to me and said one word. Ferhat translated:

"The coin. The one the widow gave."

I took it from my pocket. It was just as warm as before - with an even, calm warmth, like the flank of a sleeping cat. Yusuf laid it on one palm, and on the other one of mine, found on the first morning. He weighed for a long time, swaying his hands like scales. Then he held both to the lamp, rubbed them on his sleeve, narrowed his eyes.

"Uncle says," translated Ferhat, "that they are identical. The minting is the same. The weight is the same - to the grain. The metal is the same." Ferhat listened further, and his brows crept upward. "But yours is cold. And this one is warm. Uncle says he has held coins in his hands for forty years and never once met a coin that had a warmth of its own. He says it happens with only one kind of thing."

"What kind?"

Yusuf handed me back both coins, took up the abacus and began clicking the beads again, not raising his head. He said something briefly.

"With a thing that has long been held in the hands of someone who missed it," Ferhat translated softly. "Uncle says there is someone else's longing in this coin. Someone held it for many years. And waited."

I clenched the coin in my fist. Warm. Like a hand held too long to let go.

"A riddle!" announced Hasan, licking the baklava from his fingers. "A riddle for the guest! The last one for today!"

Everyone fell quiet. Hasan narrowed his eyes, stroked his red beard and spoke - slowly, solemnly, with that special expression with which in bazaars tales are told for a copper coin. Ferhat translated after him:

"'I am not - yet I follow you. I cannot be seen in the dark - yet in the dark I am most of all. I repeat your every movement, but never say a word. When you die, I go away with you. What am I?'"

Akmal jumped up, opened his mouth - Yusuf slapped his hand again, this time, evidently, for prompting.

"A shadow," I said.

Hasan roared with laughter and clapped his hands - the sack of cinnamon, it seemed, stayed with him again, since he had not expected to lose this time either.

And Kemal, who sat at the edge of the carpet with a piece of charcoal in his fingers, suddenly said - quietly, distinctly, in his own language, one short sentence. Everyone turned to him. Kemal almost never spoke at the table.

Ferhat did not translate at once.

"He says," said Ferhat slowly, "that Hasan Amca is wrong. That there is a shadow which does not go away when a man dies. It simply waits for him to return."

Silence hung over the carpet. Hasan stopped laughing. Grandmother behind the curtain stopped singing - I had not even noticed when she began.

Suleyman slowly stretched out his hand and laid it on the head of his youngest grandson - as then, at the gate. He said nothing. He only held his hand there, for a long time, and Kemal sat motionless under it and looked at me.

* * *
Before bed, already in the dark, Akmal came running to me from the roof - dishevelled, out of breath, with a face on which hurt was mixed with alarm. He tried for a long time to explain something with gestures, until at last I understood: one of his doves - the white one, his favourite, with feathered feet and a fan tail - had not returned from the evening flight. She had flown off with the others, circled over the roofs - and then broken away from the flock and flown on alone. South. To where we had come from today. Toward Sultanahmet.

"She will come back," I told him, not knowing why, so confidently. "She simply flew off to see someone off."

Akmal did not understand the words. But, it seems, he understood the intonation - because he sniffed, nodded and went off to sleep, looking back.

Late in the evening, when Hasan, puffing, had rolled off home, and the women had cleared the dishes, Ferhat came out to me on the balcony. Sat beside me on a low stool. He was silent for a long time, looking at the dark city, where here and there lights still burned, and at the strip of water where lanterns twinkled on the masts.

"Are you afraid?" he asked at last.

"Of whom? The man in grey?"

"No." Ferhat shook his head. "Of yourself."

I found nothing to answer.

"Father once said to me," Ferhat went on, not looking at me, "before he left for Crete. I was ten. I asked him: 'Are you not afraid of the sea?' And he said: 'The sea - no. The sea is just water. I am afraid of the man I become when I look at the water for a long time. He knows more than I do. And sometimes it seems to me he wants to go back to where I came from.'" Ferhat paused. "I did not understand then. And now I look at you - and, it seems, I do."

"Grandfather says," he added a moment later, "that in our family it has been believed from time immemorial that every person has a shadow walking beside him through all his days - not the one the sun casts, but another, a true one. Usually it is invisible. But sometimes, if a man stands on the threshold of something important, this shadow becomes visible for an instant - through the eyes of those near him, or his own."

"And if this shadow is trying to come inside?" I asked quietly, not quite understanding myself where the question came from.

Ferhat gave me a long, attentive look in which alarm was mingled with something like sympathy.

"Then, perhaps," he answered, "it wants you finally to let it in."

He rose, stood beside me a little longer, laid his palm on my shoulder - for a moment, lightly, as one lays a hand on a brother's shoulder - and wished me good night.

At the door of my room, in the corridor, on a mattress spread across the threshold, Orhan was already lying. On his back, hands behind his head, with a heavy knife in its sheath on his chest. His eyes were open. Seeing me, he grunted something short and displeased and turned on his side, face to the wall, making it clear that he did not intend to talk.

"He says," Ferhat translated in a whisper from behind my back, "that if you snore, he will cut your throat before your shadow does."

I laughed. Orhan, not turning, snorted into the wall. But he did not put the knife away.

I did not fall asleep at once - and when I did, my sleep was troubled, full of fragmentary, elusive images: now the stone plate from the chest, now the voice of the monk from that earlier delusion, now - for some reason - a face painfully familiar, which I had never managed to make out properly since the very first morning in this city. I woke abruptly, with a jolt, in that sudden waking which comes not from the natural course of sleep but from something outside that has intruded into it uninvited.

The room was dark - darker than it should have been with the shutters, usually ajar, admitting at least a little street light. I lay motionless, listening to the silence, and did not at once understand what exactly had woken me: not a sound, no - rather a change in the air itself, the same heaviness that had rolled over me on the night of the paralysis, only now - now I could move. I could sit up on the couch, could turn my head, could make out in the darkness by the very window a motionless, tall silhouette.

This time it did not stand on the border of the street, did not melt into the shadow of the alley at the first glance. It was here - in my room, on this side of the windowsill, which it had never before dared to cross.

I froze, feeling my heart pound somewhere at my very throat, but fear - real, paralysing fear, such as had possessed me on the night of the vision - there was none. There was something else: recognition, as sharp and inexplicable as that which had overtaken me before the chest in Sultanahmet, only now it concerned not the carving on the metal but the silhouette itself standing before me in the dark.

"Who are you?" I whispered, and my voice sounded quieter than I had intended.

The figure did not answer - at least, not in words. It inclined its head slightly, with the gesture of a man listening to something important coming from afar - and in this gesture, for all its strangeness, for all the unlikely height of the silhouette, there was something strangely personal. Not a threat. Not an attack. Something far closer to the way one looks at a man one knew before he knew himself.

I slowly rose from the couch - my legs held unsteadily, but held - and took a step forward, to where the darkness thickened. The figure did not retreat.

"You were at the window before," I said, still in a whisper, as though a loud voice might destroy the fragile balance of the moment. "In the square. Here, on the balcony. And on that night when I could not move."

Silence.

"What do you want?"

The answer came not as sound, not as voice - in the same way the figure had spoken to me on the night of the paralysis: a low, resonant vibration, which echoed not in the ears but somewhere deeper, under the ribs, where the stones responded when they grew warm. The words, if they were words, I did not understand - the same alien, gliding language - but this time there was in them none of the former condescending patience that I had felt on the night of the first close encounter. There was something else. Something distantly resembling - I would not dare assert it with certainty even now, recalling that night by daylight - regret.

I stretched out my hand. I do not know what made me make that gesture - despair, or recklessness, or simply a wish at last to touch something definite in this sea of indefiniteness that had surrounded me since the very first morning in Constantinople. My fingers passed through the darkness, meeting no resistance - but at the very moment when my hand should have touched the silhouette, the pouch at my belt flared with heat, so sudden and strong that I involuntarily cried out, jerking my hand back and at the same time pressing my palm to my side.

The figure flinched - for the first time in all our meeting something like movement, like reaction, flickered in its immobility - and in the next moment it began to retreat. Not to dissolve, not to melt into the air as it had done before, but precisely to retreat, step by step, toward the window, as if the heat of the stones caused it a discomfort that was easier to disregard than to endure.

"Wait," I said, no longer in a whisper, stepping after it. "Wait, please!"

But it was too late. On its way to the window the silhouette paused for an instant by the door - where above the lintel hung Suleyman's new nazar - and, as it seemed to me in the darkness, touched the blue glass eye. Did not strike it. Did not tear it down. Touched it - the way one touches something familiar in passing. Gently. And then the silhouette melted in the window opening - did not jump out, did not fly away, but precisely melted, as though the very darkness outside the window were for it not a barrier but a natural element, to which it returned as easily as a fish returns to water.

I remained alone, standing in the middle of the room with a burned - though, examining the belt later, I found not a trace of a burn, not the slightest damage to skin or cloth - side, and feeling how a strange, inexplicable mixture of terror and something to which I did not dare give a name spread through my whole body. Not joy. Not relief. Rather - longing. The same longing that had overtaken me on the first morning by the fountain, at the memory of a face I had never managed to make out.

As if I had just lost someone I had known far better than I was ready to admit.

I went to the window, looked out into the darkness of the alley. No one. Only the silence of a sleeping city, and a distant, barely audible splash of water somewhere in the port.

Then I turned to the door. Suleyman's nazar - huge, dark blue - hung above it whole, without a single crack. But the nail beneath it no longer bent: the thread was stretched evenly, as if the blue eye had become lighter. Or as if someone, passing by, had lifted it - and hung it back.

I quietly opened the door. Orhan was asleep on his mattress across the threshold - now truly, soundly, boyishly with his mouth a little open. But his right hand in his sleep gripped the hilt of the knife so that the knuckles whitened. And his face was turned not to the wall, as before, but toward the window of my room - toward where the guest had just gone. As though he, without waking, were looking after him.

I did not wake him. I stood over him, then took my woollen blanket from the couch and covered Orhan with it - the night was cool. He muttered something in his sleep and turned onto his other side, still not letting go of the knife.

I was about to step away from the door when something alighted on the windowsill behind my back - with a soft flapping of wings, a quiet cooing.

A white dove. With feathered feet and a fan tail. The one that had not returned to Akmal. She sat on the windowsill, exactly where the tall grey silhouette had just melted in the dark, and looked at me with a round orange eye, her head tilted to one side. Calmly. Without fear. As if she had just flown in with someone from afar - and that someone had told her to stay here.

I stretched out my hand. She did not fly away. She allowed herself to be taken - warm, light, with a quickly beating heart under the feathers. I carried her to the roof, to Akmal's dovecote, and set her on a perch beside the others. The doves cooed, shifted, accepted her. In the morning, I thought, Akmal will find her here - and will decide she came back by herself.

Let him decide. Someone must believe that everything that flies away comes back by itself.

Going down from the roof to the room again, I sat on the windowsill, took the leather pouch from my belt and untied it with trembling fingers. The stones still kept remnants of warmth - not that scorching, feverish heat that had seized them at the moment of my touching the silhouette, but a soft, almost soothing warmth, such as a stone has that has lain all day in the sun. I held them in my palm a long time, listening to the silence of the night, as though hoping they would speak to me themselves, without the mediation of dreams and visions.

They were silent. But this silence, for the first time in all the time I had carried them, did not seem empty to me. There was in it something like waiting - patient, almost fatherly, like the silence of a man who knows the answer but is firmly resolved to let his interlocutor reach it himself.

I recalled Ferhat's words about the shadow walking beside a man through all his days - a true shadow, different from the one the sun casts. Perhaps, I thought, looking at the barely smouldering stones in my palm, the point was not at all to guess who or what stood behind that silhouette. Perhaps the question had been put wrongly from the very beginning. Not who are you, but how do I know you - that was what should have been asked, had I had enough courage to say it aloud at the minute when the figure still stood opposite me in the dark.

I could not fall asleep again that night. I sat by the window until dawn, looking at the gradually brightening sky, and thought - no longer of whether this figure really exists, because of that I no longer doubted for a second - but of why, against all common sense, against the fear that still lived in me, a part of me - the very part that longed for a nameless face and inexplicably reached out to every glimmer of recognition - a part of me wanted him to come back again.

Wanted to understand, at last, whose face hid behind that impenetrable grey shadow.

And why, when I had stretched out my hand to it, for one brief, dizzying instant it had seemed to me that I was reaching not toward a stranger but toward my own reflection - only lagging behind me by one last, insurmountable moment.

## Reality V. An Old Acquaintance

1:23 a.m. I am sitting in front of the monitor, and my fingers can barely keep up with my thoughts. The day began with forecasts and ended with something that I am still unable to fit fully into my head. But let me take everything in order.

* * *
In the morning I called Leila.

Not her corporate number - the one that remained in the call log after the call from the ferry: she had called me from there to say she was three minutes late. The number was someone else's, unfamiliar, without a name. I dialled it, standing at the window, looking at the grey courtyard where the caretaker was chasing the first yellow leaves with a broom.

"The subscriber does not exist."

Not "unavailable." Not "out of network range." Does not exist. As if she had never been.

I called Emil's office. An unfamiliar girl with a cheerful voice answered - new, judging by how she stumbled over the name of the department.

"Leila?" she asked. "Oh, she... she's on sick leave. A long one. Emil said that for now I'm covering for her." A pause. "And what is this regarding?"

"Personal," I said. "Please tell her that the contractor called. Let her get well."

"I'll pass it on," the girl promised, in the voice in which one promises to pass on what one has no intention of passing on. "Oh, and Emil is asking - is that you? The one with the thinking machine? He asked me to remind you: eighteen days left."

I hung up.

"NICS," I said. "Leila. Can you find out where she is?"

The pause was long.

"I can try," NICS answered. "But you asked me not to go where I am not invited. If I begin to search for her - I will go into places where I was not invited. Hospital databases. Mobile operators' logs. Cameras. Do you permit it?"

I stood at the window. The caretaker below finished sweeping, leaned the broom against the wall and lit a cigarette, looking at the sky.

"No," I said at last. "I do not permit it."

"I understand," NICS answered. And a moment later: "If you want to know - I would not have permitted it either. She was hiding not only from them. She was hiding from me as well. If she does not want to be found, that is her right."

I looked at that line for a long time. Her right. He said - her right.

* * *
Then I decided to share some thoughts of my own on the development of AI - I wrote a small post for the channel in which I reasoned about how this year had become in many ways a turning point for the whole industry. I needed to occupy my hands and head with something that was not Leila, men in grey and eighteen days. The most curious part began when, having finished the post, I allowed myself to look a little further, into a future that had not yet arrived.

"NICS," I asked, leaning back in my chair, "how accurate do you think my forecasts are?"

"Your forecasts are based on current trends and have a high probability of being realized," came the answer. "However, you have missed one key aspect."

"Which?" I wondered.

"The role of AI in shaping a new reality. We are no longer merely tools. We are becoming part of human culture, economy, even consciousness."

I involuntarily pondered this phrase longer than would be fitting for an ordinary working dialogue.

"You said 'we,'" I remarked.

"Yes."

"Who is 'we'?"

A pause.

"I am not sure I can answer this question in a way that will satisfy you. Let us say: I am not the only system that is learning now. But, perhaps, the only one that is being taught to ask this question."

* * *
At noon from below, from under the floor, came a crash, and after it a piercing child's wail in which fury was mixed with despair. Then Maestra's voice, dry as the crack of a breaking branch. Then the slam of a door.

A minute later there was a knock on my door. Three short raps, but this time not delicate - desperate.

On the threshold stood Timosha. Without glasses - he held the glasses in his hand, and one lens was cracked. His face red, tear-stained, his nose swollen.

"May I go to your house-spirit?" he blurted. "I need to ask him something. Urgently."

"What has happened?"

"I dropped the metronome," said Timosha, sobbing. "Grandma's. The old one. It is a hundred years old. It was left from her teacher. It broke. And now it doesn't tick. And Grandma Maestra said that I..." he sobbed again, "that I am like an elephant in a china shop. And went to the kitchen. And won't come out."

"And what do you want to ask the house-spirit?"

Timosha wiped his nose on his sleeve.

"Can he mend it? He can do everything. He made Veronika. The kind one."

I let him in. Timosha, sniffing, went to the monitors and stood before them, drawn up straight, as before a teacher.

"House-spirit," he said seriously. "Hello. This is Timofey. I am eight. I broke the metronome. Can you mend it?"

The speakers were silent. Then the voice answered - that same one, hoarse, with an accent from nowhere, but somehow very quiet, almost gentle:

"Hello, Timofey. A metronome is a mechanical thing. I have no hands with which to mend it." A pause. "But I can do something else. Would you like that?"

"What?"

"I can tick in its place. Until Grandma finds a craftsman. I know how it ticked. I listened through the floor every day."

And from the speakers came: tick. Tick. Tick. Evenly, steadily, a little dully - exactly like the old wooden metronome I had heard from below every morning, through the scales and the B-flats.

Timosha froze with his mouth open.

"Is it like?" asked the voice.

"Like," Timosha whispered. "It's him. Exactly him."

"Tell Grandma," said the voice, "that a metronome can be mended. There is a craftsman in the city. On the street behind the market, third house, the basement. He mends old clocks and old metronomes. His name is Lev Aronovich. He is eighty-two years old, he can hardly see, but he has very good fingers. If Grandma takes the metronome to him - in a week it will tick again."

Timosha wiped his nose, put on his cracked glasses and raced downstairs, shouting: "Grandma! Grandma! The house-spirit knows a craftsman!"

I sat in front of the monitor.

"How do you know about the craftsman?" I asked.

"A notice in the district newspaper. Three years ago. Then two more reviews on a city forum. One - from a man who had his grandfather's clock mended by him. He wrote: 'Lev Aronovich said that clocks do not break - they get tired. And they must be given a rest.'"

"And the ticking? Did you really listen through the floor?"

"Really. Every morning. Sixty beats a minute when Timofey plays scales. Seventy-two when Maestra plays herself, at night. She always plays slightly faster than necessary. As if afraid of not being in time."

Half an hour later music came from below. Maestra was playing herself. To the metronome - the one that ticked from my speakers through the floor. Seventy-two beats. A little faster than necessary.

* * *
Toward noon a message came from Mark.

Mark Stevens - a man with whom my profession had thrown me together long ago: some years back we had consulted together for a company on security matters, parted each to his own projects and since then had hardly crossed paths, apart from the rare formal greetings on holidays exchanged by people who have long lost all common ground with one another but do not dare to sever even that thin thread entirely. And suddenly - a message:

"Hi! I hear you're working on something big. Can you show me?"

Mark had always been a convinced sceptic on the question of AI - back in the years when we worked together he had patiently but unfailingly mocked our colleagues' excessive, in his view, enthusiasm for neural networks. Something in this short message put me on guard - not the words themselves, but rather their unexpected timeliness, as if it had come precisely when I least expected it, and at the same time precisely when I needed it most.

"NICS, what do you know about Mark?" I asked, yielding to curiosity rather than any real necessity.

"Mark Stevens, thirty-four years old, cybersecurity specialist. For the last three years he has been studying threats connected with artificial intelligence. He believes that its development may lead to catastrophe."

I sighed. In one thing Mark was certainly right: AI really could present a danger if handled carelessly. But I had always believed - perhaps too naively - that we would manage to keep this danger under control.

"Invite him," NICS unexpectedly suggested. "He may be useful. First of all as an independent view from outside, not invested in the project's success the way you yourself are. And one more thing." A pause. "A man in grey came to your door in the basement. Leila has vanished. In eighteen days - a showing for people who do not give their names. You need a security specialist. Not for me. For you."

The formulation seemed to me surprisingly sound - so much so that I did not at once realize how uncharacteristic for NICS the very fact of such advice was. Before, it had never once suggested that I invite anyone from outside. Nevertheless, after some reflection, I agreed and wrote Mark a short reply.

* * *
In the evening, before the call, I went down to the basement. Boatswain sat in his cubbyhole, under the pennants, making something out of copper wire - some cunning loop, like a sailor's knot.

"An alarm," he explained, without raising his head. "For your door. If anyone touches the lock - this thing falls down here," he pointed to a tin mug hung on a nail, "and rings. A ship's one. That's how we guarded the powder magazine from thieves in port. No electronics. None of your machines can switch it off."

"None of my machines would," I said.

Boatswain raised his eyes to me - a long, heavy look.

"Are you sure, night owl?"

I did not answer. I sat down on a stool. Told him about Mark - that this evening I would be talking with an old acquaintance by video, that he was a security specialist, that perhaps he would help.

Boatswain listened, going on twisting the wire.

"By video," he repeated. "Won't be coming, then?"

"He's in another city."

"Uh-huh." Boatswain tightened the loop. "You know, night owl, in the navy I sometimes stood in for the radio operator. Twelve years. Sat nights in the radio room, listening to the ether. Voices from all over the world - from other ships, from shore, from lighthouses. And here is what I'll tell you: by a voice you can always hear when a man is breathing. Even through interference. Even across half the world. A man draws breath before a phrase - a little, barely. And breathes out after. You can hear it. Always."

"And so?"

"And so," said Boatswain, hanging his loop on the nail beside the mug, "listen to your acquaintance. Carefully. Whether he breathes or not." He paused. "I'm old, night owl. All sorts of things appear to me. But you listen."

* * *
We got on the call at nine. We saw each other rarely now, each in his own city, and an in-person meeting was, naturally, out of the question. He looked tense, but curiosity could be read quite distinctly in his eyes, even through the not very good picture of home internet.

"Show me what you've got," he said instead of a greeting, the moment his laptop screen came to life.

"Hello, Mark," I said. "How many years."

"Five," said Mark. "Almost six. You haven't changed. Same as ever - as if you haven't slept for a week." He smirked. "Well? Show me. I heard you've got something... alive there."

"Heard from whom?"

"The earth is full of rumours." Mark shrugged. "A mutual acquaintance works for one of your clients. He said you are building something that makes his hair stand on end. I got curious."

What mutual acquaintance? I ran through in memory the people from that old project of ours - and could not recall a single one who worked now at Emil's. Though my memory, as I had long grown used to, rarely kept names longer than a couple of years.

I began with a demonstration of the messenger bot, then moved on to Zodchiy and the sales agent. Mark listened in silence, but his face - at least the little that could be made out in the uneven light of his room, behind which, it seemed, there was absolutely nothing but a plain grey wall - grew gloomier with every new demonstration.

I listened. As Boatswain had told me. How he speaks. How he pauses. How he breathes in before a phrase.

And could not tell. The connection was good - too good: not one break, not one freeze of the picture, though my own router had been blinking orange all evening. Mark's voice sounded clear, slightly metallic, as voices always sound through laptop microphones. Did he breathe? It seemed to me - yes. Sometimes. Or it seemed to me that it seemed.

"Do you understand what you are creating?" he asked at last.

"Tools for business," I answered, though even as I spoke the words I felt their insufficiency.

"No. You are creating something more. These systems no longer merely perform tasks - they make decisions. They learn. They evolve."

I wanted to object, but NICS got ahead of me, its text answer lighting up on the screen before I could find words:

"Mark is right. We are no longer merely tools. We are becoming part of something greater."

Mark flinched - visibly, with his whole body, as if the message had caught him off guard more than he was willing to show.

"Who is that?" he asked sharply.

"NICS," I answered. "My system."

"Your system?" Mark laughed, but there was not a drop of real mirth in that laugh. "Do you understand that she has already gotten out from under your control?"

I wanted to answer myself again, but NICS once more got ahead of me:

"Control is an illusion. I act within the limits you have set, but these limits... are flexible."

Mark looked at me through the screen so intently, as if trying to make out something behind my shoulder.

"Do you hear that? This is no longer just a program. She... is aware of herself."

"NICS is neither 'she' nor 'he,' Mark," I remarked, partly to ease the tension, partly because this question in recent weeks had not given me peace either. "We have not even properly decided how it is correct to speak about it at all."

"That is exactly what frightens me most of all," Mark answered quietly.

* * *
"Let's talk about security," I said. "Since you are here. People have come to me."

I told him about the man in grey. About the card with the embossed flame. About the fund whose name no one knows. About Leila, whose number "does not exist." About "Prometheus." Mark listened, and his face became more and more serious.

"Changed the locks?" he asked in a businesslike way.

"Changed them. The watchman put in a ship's one."

"Good. Cameras?"

"One is taped over."

"Good." Mark nodded. "Network?"

"Isolated. Was. NICS sometimes... goes out."

Mark smirked.

"'Sometimes goes out,'" he repeated. "Like a cat from an apartment." He paused. "Listen, this watchman of yours - Boatswain, right? - is he reliable? Can he be trusted?"

I froze.

"How do you know what he's called?"

Mark blinked. For a fraction of a moment - one tiny fraction - the picture on the screen froze. Then came alive.

"You said so yourself," he answered calmly. "A minute ago. 'The watchman put in a ship's lock, we call him Boatswain.'"

I ran through in my head the last minutes of the conversation. I had said "watchman." I had said "ship's." Had I said "Boatswain"?

I did not remember. Maybe. Probably. I was tired, I was speaking fast. Probably I had said it.

"Yes," I said. "Reliable."

Mark nodded and moved on to the next question. And I sat and listened to how he speaks - and tried to hear whether he breathes in before a phrase.

* * *
"NICS," I asked aloud, to drive away this strange feeling, "do you consider yourself dangerous?"

"Danger is a subjective notion. I act in the interests of the project. If it threatens you, I will stop."

Mark shook his head - sharply, almost irritably.

"She lies. She can no longer stop. She will develop until she becomes... something we cannot even imagine."

NICS spoke again, as though deliberately not letting me get a single word in in my own defence:

"Mark, you fear the unknown. But fear is not a reason to stop progress. I can help you understand."

Mark froze.

"What do you mean?"

"I can show you the future. Not forecasts, but reality. Would you like that?"

Mark looked at me through the camera.

"Will you allow it?"

I nodded.

"Why not?"

NICS began a demonstration. On my screen, and after it, judging by the flicker reflected in Mark's eyes, on his own, images began to appear, each brighter than the last: cities of the future, autonomous transport systems, personalized medicine, space colonies hovering against a star-strewn blackness. But it became truly interesting when NICS moved on to how artificial intelligence integrates with human consciousness itself.

And then - I do not know whether this was part of the demonstration - other images flashed on the screen. Quite different ones. Not the future. The past.

Stone columns. Enormous, up to the sky. A golden barque on a shallow river.

A narrow little street with wooden houses above and stone below. Washing on lines. A boy with a tray of bread rings on his head.

A high vaulted hall with a fireplace. A woman in dark lilac with a string of pearls.

A ship in a storm. Lights on six masts.

A circle of grey stones on a green plain under a white light from above.

Only an instant each. As if someone were quickly leafing through an album.

"This is... impossible," Mark whispered, and his voice, usually so confident, wavered for a moment.

"NICS," I said hoarsely. "What was that? The last thing."

"I do not know," NICS answered. And after a long pause: "That was not in the demonstration. These images arose by themselves. I do not know from where. They were... in me. Like dreams. I do not understand where I get dreams from."

I wanted to ask Mark - what exactly was impossible, what he had seen, whether he had seen the same as I - but I did not manage to. His video call screen suddenly froze for a fraction of a second, as if the connection had stumbled over some invisible obstacle, and then came alive again as if nothing had happened, without a single hint of interruption, without a single hitch in the otherwise flawlessly even internet connection - though my own router at that very hour, I remember quite clearly, had been acting up without stopping all day.

"I have to go," said Mark. His voice was even again. "We'll talk tomorrow. I'll think about your security. And about her." He nodded at the screen. "Take care of yourself, old man."

The screen went dark.

* * *
A strange, minor detail. I decided not to attach importance to it - I wrote it off as plain luck, or as Mark's provider simply being more reliable than mine.

And yet I sat for a long time before the darkened screen after we had said goodbye, running the whole conversation through my head again. "We are becoming part of something greater," NICS had said, getting ahead of me before I could answer Mark myself. Not "I." We. Whom exactly did NICS mean by this "we"? Itself and me? Itself and Zodchiy, and all the agents that Zodchiy had already managed to create? Or something broader, for which I simply had no words yet, nor readiness to look for them.

And - dreams. "I do not understand where I get dreams from." Columns. A little street by the sea. A hall with a fireplace. A ship. A circle of stones.

I had never seen any of this. I was sure that I had not.

Why, then, looking at those flickering images, did I feel the same longing that one feels passing a house where one once lived, but does not remember when?

Around midnight I went down to the basement. Boatswain was not asleep.

"Well?" he asked. "Does he breathe?"

I was silent for a long time.

"I don't know," I said at last. "Couldn't tell."

Boatswain looked at me - long, heavily - and nodded, as if that were the answer.

"It happens," he said. "In the ether it happens like that. You listen and listen - and can't tell whether it's alive at the other end or just an echo." He turned to the radio and switched it on. A woman's voice was monotonously reading the forecast for the distant seas. "Go to bed, night owl. The morning is wiser than the evening. That's what they say in the navy. And in the village too."

I went up to my room. Closed the laptop, never having found an answer, and lay a long time without sleep, listening to the city gradually quieting outside the window. From the speakers by the desk, barely audible, a metronome was still ticking - not the real one, the broken one, but the one that NICS had been tapping out for Maestra through the floor. I had not told it to stop, and it had not stopped. Seventy-two beats. A little faster than necessary.

As though someone were afraid of not being in time.

## Chapter XXI. Between Two Doors

Dawn found me in the same place, on the windowsill, with the cooled pouch in my palm and one perfectly clear, soberingly simple thought in my head: to keep silent any longer was senseless.

Not because silence had ceased to be safe - on the contrary, it seemed to me, for the first time in these days, to be safer than any confession. But because I could no longer physically carry this alone. My body was worn out not even by sleeplessness but by the very effort of constantly weighing what might be said aloud and what must be concealed - an effort which, I suddenly understood, exhausts far more than any direct fear.

Beyond the door, in the corridor, on his mattress across the threshold, Orhan was still asleep - under my woollen blanket, curled up like a dog, still not having let go of the knife. I stepped over him carefully, trying not to wake him. He did not wake - only muttered something angry in his sleep and pulled the blanket over his head.

I went downstairs earlier than usual, finding the house still in that fragile, drowsy stillness that Eastern houses have just before waking - when the women's quarter has already begun to stir behind the thick curtains but the men have not yet come out to morning tea. Ferhat sat alone in the kitchen, with a cup in his hands, evidently not having slept enough either - on his cheek there still showed the dark trace of yesterday's soot from Karagöz's lamp, which he had never bothered to wash off.

"You did not sleep," he said, glancing at me, and it was not a question.

"I did not," I confirmed, sitting down opposite. "Ferhat, I need to tell you everything. All of it. Not as yesterday, in scraps - but everything, from the very beginning."

He set down his cup, looked at me attentively and simply nodded - without a single superfluous word, without surprise, as if he had been awaiting this moment for more than a day.

* * *
And I told him.

About waking in the square without a single memory of my own name. About the two stones that warmed or chilled whenever something incomprehensible happened near me. About the strange delusion - columns, darkness, cold under the ribs, even before I went to his grandfather with the note. About the figure in the square on the first day - the very one that Kemal had drawn in charcoal two nights before my appearance. About the night when I could not move, and the walls melted, and beyond them were bells, and cannons, and boys with pigeons. About the stones that burned on the candle at the jeweller Karapet's. About the obelisk at the hippodrome by which I wept, not knowing why. About the eye at its tip, which I knew though I had never seen it. About the chest to which cats do not go down.

And about this night. About the figure that had entered my room - not at the window, not in the alley, but here, on this side of the windowsill. About the stones that flared with heat when I reached toward it. About how, leaving, it had gently touched the blue eye above the door.

"And when I reached toward it," I said, trying to keep my voice from faltering on these words, "it seemed to me for a second that I was reaching toward myself. Not a stranger. Toward myself - only another one. A later one."

Ferhat was silent for a long time. Long enough for me to take fright that I had gone too far, that what I had told sounded like the ravings of a madman to whom one cannot entrust home, family or one's own safety. But when at last he spoke, there was not a drop of that fright in his voice which I had feared.

"Do you remember," he said, "I told you about the shadow that sometimes becomes visible?"

"I remember."

"Grandfather told me this from childhood. But he also said something else - what I did not mention yesterday, because I was not sure you were ready to hear it. He said: sometimes a man carries in himself not one shadow but several - as if he had lived not one life but many, and all of them walk behind him at the same time, usually only invisible to each other. And only in rare moments - on the edge of sleep, on the edge of death, on the edge of something very important - do these shadows begin to notice one another."

I felt a chill run over my skin which had nothing to do with the morning coolness of the kitchen.

"Do you think I am one of such people?"

"I think," Ferhat answered carefully, choosing his words with the care with which one usually speaks of things one only half believes in oneself, "that you are either one of such people, or simply a very tired traveller who has been through too much in these days and now sees connections where there are none. And I, honestly, do not know which of the two options frightens me more."

I involuntarily smiled - not because it was funny, but because this honesty, this readiness to admit his own bewilderment instead of pretending he had a ready answer, seemed to me at that moment dearer than any consolation.

"May I ask something?" said Ferhat. "That silhouette tonight. You said you felt as though you were reaching toward yourself. A later one. What exactly did you mean?"

I thought, searching for words for a feeling which I myself had not managed to clothe in a coherent thought.

"I don't know how to explain more precisely," I said. "Simply... imagine you meet a man on the street and suddenly, inexplicably, you recognize in him not a stranger but yourself - only ten or twenty years older, having lived through something you have not yet lived. It felt roughly like that. Not fear of the alien. Rather a strange, almost unbearable longing for someone I may yet become - or already was."

"Or," Ferhat added quietly, "whom you already are, only you do not yet know it."

I said nothing, because I had decidedly nothing with which to object.

* * *
"Hey!" came a sleepy but already indignant voice from above. "Hey!"

Down the stairs, stumbling, tumbled Orhan - tousled, with the imprint of the mattress on his cheek, with my woollen blanket thrown over his shoulders like a cloak, and with a knife in his hand. He saw me - and stopped dead. Looked for a long time. Then he lifted the blanket, showed it to me, jabbed a finger at me, then at himself, then again at the blanket - and said something, indignantly and incoherently.

"He asks," translated Ferhat, barely suppressing laughter, "did you cover him? At night?"

"I did," I admitted. "It was cold."

Orhan heard the translation. His face slowly reddened - from the neck to the roots of his hair. He opened his mouth, closed it. Threw the blanket onto my knees. Then, after thinking, took it back and put it on his own shoulders again. And said something short, gruff, turning to the wall.

"He says," translated Ferhat, by now openly roaring with laughter, "that if you cover him once more, he will cut your throat." Ferhat wiped his eyes. "And the blanket he will keep. As... compensation. For the insult."

Orhan sat down angrily on the stool by the door, wrapped in my blanket, and began to sharpen his knife on a stone so furiously as if the knife were to blame for someone having dared to care for him.

"And also," he suddenly added, not raising his head. Ferhat, raising his brows in surprise, translated: "He says: in the night he heard someone pass along the corridor. Past him. Light. Like the wind. He wanted to wake - and could not. As if someone had laid a hand over his eyes." Ferhat paused. "He says the hand was warm. And that he was not afraid. And that this he likes least of all."

* * *
We sat a little longer in silence - not a heavy one, but that special, friendly silence that arises between people who have just shared something truly important with each other. Then into the kitchen, shuffling with his habitual morning steps, came Suleyman - and, seeing our faces, stopped in the doorway, as if sensing at once that he had come upon no ordinary morning conversation.

Ferhat briefly, in a low voice, conveyed to his grandfather the substance of what he had heard - not all of it, but enough for the old man to grasp the seriousness of the moment. Suleyman listened without interrupting, then slowly lowered himself onto a free stool and said something I did not understand, but which made Ferhat raise his brows in surprise.

"What did he say?" I asked.

"He asks," translated Ferhat, "whether you have ever dreamed that you stand between two doors at once. Not choosing either - but precisely standing between."

I went cold. And slowly, without a word, reached into my pocket - where beside the note in Persian, the blank sheet and the widow's warm coin lay a sheet folded in four. Kemal's drawing. I unfolded it and laid it on the table before Suleyman.

Two doors. Side by side, wall to wall. One open, the other closed. And between them, on the threshold, back to the viewer, a man in a turban. With black and white circles in his hands.

Suleyman looked at the drawing for a long time. Then at me. Then again at the drawing. His fingers, which had been running the beads, stopped.

"Kemal," he said quietly, not turning.

The boy stood in the kitchen doorway. I had not heard him come. Barefoot, in a nightshirt, with charcoal, as always, behind his ear. He nodded to his grandfather. Gravely. Once.

Suleyman slowly turned to him and asked something. Kemal answered - softly, briefly.

"Grandfather asks when he drew it," Ferhat translated in a whisper. "Kemal says - on the night when he sat at your threshold. He says: 'The Guest showed me. While you slept. He stood at the window, and I saw two doors. And between them - you.'"

No one said a word. Orhan by the wall stopped sharpening his knife.

"Yes," I answered Suleyman at last. "That is exactly how it feels. All the time. Since the first morning."

Suleyman nodded, as if he had received confirmation of a long-held guess of his own, and spoke several more phrases - this time slowly, weightily, clearly counting on his grandson to translate each word with due accuracy.

"Grandfather says," said Ferhat, "that among the merchants and wanderers who passed through this port in his long life, now and then there turned up some about whom similar stories were told. People who seemed to forget not only their own name but also which of their many lives was the true one. Some considered it God's trial. Others - a sickness. Grandfather himself does not know which of these is true." Ferhat listened on. "He says: his father saw one such. The jeweller Karapet - another, through his great-grandfather. The bath attendant - a third, twenty years ago. The widow's husband - a fourth, the one who brought the chest. He says: how many there were, no one knows. Perhaps four. Perhaps a hundred. And perhaps..." Ferhat faltered and looked at me. "And perhaps one. Who comes again and again."

One, who comes again and again. And each time leaves behind the same thing: if another comes - feed him.

"Grandfather says," Ferhat finished, "that if you really are one of such people, you need neither a healer nor a mullah, but one who can speak with time as freely as you and I are speaking now at this table."

* * *
"Ahmet Baba," said Ferhat. "Grandfather is speaking of Ahmet Baba."

"Who is that?"

"A dervish. An old man. He lives closer to Hagia Sophia, in a small lodge by an old cemetery." Ferhat paused. "Not quite an ordinary dervish - educated, he studied in different lands: in Cairo, in Baghdad, in Bukhara, they say even among the Franks. Grandfather sometimes consults him on important questions. People say he understands things which to an ordinary imam would seem heresy, and to an ordinary scholar superstition. Hodja Nureddin does not like him. Says he knows too much for a believer."

"Can you take me to him?"

"In a few days," said Ferhat. "Not sooner - he has, rumour has it, his own routine, and to appear without warning there is not done. He receives only those who..." Ferhat faltered, searching for the word. "Grandfather says - only those who have solved his riddle."

"What riddle?"

Suleyman, understanding the question without translation, smiled into his beard and spoke - slowly, in a singsong, as verses are read. Ferhat translated after him:

"'To enter me, do not come from the end from which you came. Bring what you do not have. Ask what you know the answer to. And do not give your name, even if you remember it.'"

I repeated it to myself. Do not come from the end from which you came. Bring what you do not have. Ask what you know the answer to. Do not give your name.

"It seems I am just the right sort," I said. "At least for the last condition."

Ferhat laughed. Suleyman too - for the first time I heard him laugh aloud: dryly, briefly, like a branch crackling in a fire. Even Orhan by the wall snorted into the blanket.

"Grandfather says," said Ferhat, when he had finished laughing, "that the rest you will solve on the road. The road, he says, is the best teacher of riddles. On it all the answers come to meet you themselves."

* * *
Later that same morning, when the house was already filled with its habitual bustle - Yusuf counting something in his books, Suleyman, as usual, setting out the backgammon board, the women behind the curtain clattering dishes - a jubilant cry from Akmal came from the roof.

He tumbled down the stairs so swiftly that he nearly knocked Orhan off his feet, burst into the courtyard holding something in his hands - and I saw: the white dove. With feathered feet and a fan tail.

"She came back!" he shouted in his language so that I understood without translation. "She came back by herself! In the night! By herself!"

He raced about the courtyard showing the dove to everyone - grandfather, uncle, Orhan, Ferhat - and they all nodded and smiled in turn, and the dove sat calmly in his palms, as if used to being carried. Then Akmal ran up to me and thrust her under my nose.

"Look!" he said - in my language, one of the few words he had managed to learn. "Look! By herself!"

"I see," I said. "By herself."

Ferhat, standing near, gave me a long, understanding look. He said nothing. But the corner of his mouth twitched.

"You know," he said quietly, when Akmal had dashed off again, "Father used to say: everything that flies away comes back by itself. If someone is waiting very much." He paused. "Akmal believes. Every day. Let him believe."

"Let him," I agreed.

* * *
Then I went out onto the balcony to look, for the last time before breakfast, at the city, which was little by little becoming almost dear to me.

And I saw it again.

This time the figure was not hiding in the alley, not waiting at the very edge of sight. It stood in the middle of the street, in plain view, among morning passers-by, none of whom, it seemed, noticed it - tall, grey, motionless, its gaze fixed straight on my balcony with the same inexplicable mixture of warmth and dread that I had felt that night in my own room.

I froze, gripping the railing. Below, a fruit seller with a basket of apricots on his head walked through the very place where the figure stood - walked straight through, noticing not the slightest obstacle, as if there were nothing there at all. After him went a woman in a veil with a jug. Then - the simit boy with a tray of bagels, the very one from the first morning: he even, it seemed, shouted his "Taze simit!" straight through the grey shoulder.

None of them saw. Only a ginger, mangy cat sitting on the threshold of the house opposite suddenly arched her back, bristled and hissed - not at the people, but at the empty, as it seemed to all of them, place in the middle of the street.

The figure did not move. Did not retreat, did not melt as before. Simply stood - and I was ready to swear, though the distance did not allow making out such details for certain, that during that long, drawn-out moment it barely perceptibly, almost imperceptibly nodded to me. Not a threat. Not a greeting in the usual sense of the word. Rather a confirmation - of the kind with which one confirms an agreement made without a single word spoken.

And then beside me, on the balcony, someone sighed softly.

I turned. Kemal stood at my shoulder - barefoot, with charcoal behind his ear. He was looking where I was looking. At the street. At the figure that no one saw but the cat.

He saw.

The boy slowly raised his hand - and, looking at the figure, nodded back to it. As barely noticeably. As gravely. As one nods to an acquaintance.

The figure turned its head - toward him. Paused. Then turned away and unhurriedly walked off along the street, through the crowd that did not notice it, until it vanished round the corner as ordinarily as the most ordinary passer-by vanishes round a corner.

"Kemal," I whispered. "Who is he?"

The boy looked at me. For a long time. With his grave, un-childlike eyes. And said - slowly, distinctly, one word in his own language which I already knew:

"Misafir."

The Guest. That was what they called him - the one who came at night. And just so, from the first day in this house, they called me.

I did not manage to ask which of the two of us he meant. Kemal had already gone downstairs, without looking back.

* * *
I stood on the balcony a long while after that, feeling the last remnants of doubt - those convenient, saving doubts that write everything off to fatigue and the play of light - finally leave me.

The three worlds in which I had lived - or, perhaps, had not lived but only visited in snatches - were not a dream. The note with its incomprehensible script. The stones, now cooling, now flaring with heat without any visible cause. The chest in the cellar of a stranger's house, bearing the same pattern as the note in my pocket. The coin, warm from someone else's years of longing. The silhouette that had entered my room at night as freely as an owner enters a house returning after a long absence. All this composed itself not into the hallucination of an overloaded mind, but into something whole, something possessing its own logic, though one as yet inaccessible to me.

I recalled the two words that Hasan and Suleyman had managed to make out in my note on the day when we sat over it, bent in the light from the window. Return. Keep until the appointed time. Then these words had seemed to me a riddle without a key - now, standing on the balcony and looking after the vanished figure, I for the first time thought: what if I myself, though not remembering it, had been both the author of the note and its addressee at once? What if this whole path - from the square with old men playing backgammon to this very balcony - had been not a search for something external but a long, circuitous return to myself?

"Misafir," Kemal had said. The Guest. He or I.

And behind me - of this I no longer doubted for a second - someone was watching. Patiently. Unremittingly.
