Since the very first morning on that sun-flooded street, and perhaps long before it - long before I had even learned to count time in hours and days rather than in something else, more spacious and far less obvious.

I did not yet know whether this was friend or foe, guardian or hunter. Did not know how he was connected with the man in the grey frock coat who had asked about me in the port. Did not know how much more truth would be revealed to me before I understood the true meaning of the words in my own note. Did not know what sort of man awaited me at Hagia Sophia, and whether he would agree to speak at all with a wanderer whose story sounded madder than any he had heard before. But one thing I now knew quite firmly, with that final clarity which comes only after long hours of doubt: the road back, to the former, cosy ignorance, was closed to me forever.

Below, in the courtyard, Suleyman clicked the pieces of the backgammon board. Yusuf called everyone to breakfast. Akmal raced about with the dove. Orhan, wrapped in my blanket, sullenly sharpened his knife. Ferhat raised his head and waved to me from the kitchen threshold. Kemal sat on a step and drew something in charcoal on a flagstone - two doors, I was sure, without seeing.

Whatever awaited me ahead - in Sultanahmet, with the old dervish, or in my own visions, coming ever more often - I had to go forward. Because the one who had been watching me from the shadows, to all appearances, had no intention of going away.

And so neither had I.

## Chapter XXII. The Rose Garden

The General took us away to his estate on the third day after the conversation in the study.

"Air," he said to my aunt at breakfast in a tone that admitted no objection. "The boy needs air. Not corridors, not the library, not railings. A garden. Roses. Horses. A week. Kostya will go with him."

My aunt was silent for a long time, looking into her cup. Then she raised her eyes to the General, and something passed between them - quick, wordless, like a signal between two sentries on different walls of one fortress.

"A week," she said at last. "And, Pavel Nikolaevich..." She faltered. "Let Stefan be near him."

The General slowly nodded. And I, sitting between them, felt as though I had just been agreed upon, in a language I did not know.

* * *
The General's estate lay forty versts from my aunt's castle, on a gentle hill above a river, and it began not with a gate but with a smell. We had not yet seen the house - only a birch avenue running uphill, and a dusty road, and the coachman Tikhon was still humming his endless song about the driver - when the wind changed, and into the carriage, through the opened windows, a fragrance poured so thick, so sweet, so unimaginable that Konstantin, who had been dozing all the way, opened his eyes and sat up straight.

"Mon Dieu," he said. "What is that?"

"Roses," I said.

"Roses don't smell like that, mon cher. Roses smell like Auntie's powder box. And this..." He drew in the air. "This smells as if someone had spilled a whole barrel of honey on the road and then set it on fire."

Tikhon on the box chuckled.

"Those are Bulgarian ones, young masters," he said over his shoulder. "The General's. Three thousand bushes here. A Bulgarian gardener looks after them like little children. Every day he talks to each bush. I've heard it myself. Talks and sings songs." Tikhon lowered his voice. "And at night, they say, he carries a lantern round the garden. In circles. The village women say he's a sorcerer. And I think - he's just homesick. For his own country."

The avenue ended, and beyond it the house opened to view - white, two-storeyed, with columns, with a broad terrace descending to the garden. And the garden...

I was not prepared for that garden.

It began right behind the terrace and went down to the river, in terraces, ledges, tiers - like an amphitheatre, like a frozen waterfall of flowers. Roses. Thousands of roses. White as snow on a mountain peak. Scarlet as blood on snow. Pink of every shade - from pale, almost transparent, like the morning dawn, to thick, dark as wine. Yellow. Tea-coloured. Cream. They twined up trellises, arches, the walls of arbours; stood in bushes as tall as a man; spread over the ground like a carpet. Between them ran paths strewn with white sand, little channels of water murmured, stone benches stood, wound with ivy.

And in the very middle, on a round lawn surrounded by a living labyrinth of clipped bushes, stood a snow-white arbour. And it was entwined from the ground to the very dome by a single rose bush - huge, ancient, gnarled, with flowers of such a deep, dark scarlet that from a distance they seemed almost black.

Under this bush, on his knees, with his back to us, in a canvas shirt, stood a man. And sang.

* * *
I did not understand the words. The language was like ours - and not like it: familiar roots, endings turned inside out, soft, singing, as if they were pronounced with a smile. The melody was slow, sad, with long drawn-out notes which now rose, now fell, like a mountain road.

The man sang, tying up a vine. Not turning round.

"Stefan," said the General. Quietly.

The singing broke off. The man slowly rose from his knees, brushed the earth from his palms and turned round.

I had seen him before - fleetingly, in my aunt's house, in the doorway of the drawing room, with a basket of white roses which he had dropped when Sventsitsky said "two worlds." I had seen him in the garden with a lantern, circling under my window. But never so close. And never by daylight.

He was fifty, perhaps more. Short, stocky, broad-shouldered, with heavy, knotted hands so densely scored by thorns that the scars on them formed a white net. His face dark, weathered, with thick black brows grown together at the bridge of the nose, and with a moustache, also black, streaked with grey, hanging to the chin. His hair short, grey at the temples. And his eyes...

His eyes were light. Unexpectedly light in that dark face. Grey, almost transparent, like water in a mountain stream.

And they looked at me.

As they had then, in the drawing room. Not in surprise. Not in fright. With an expression I had already once seen and could not forget: as though he were looking at a grave he had long sought and had at last found.

"Dobar den," he said. Quietly. To me. Not to the General.

And bowed - low, in the peasant way, pressing his hand to his chest. One bows like that not to guests. One bows like that to icons.

* * *
The General took Konstantin into the house - to show him the stables and a new English mare - and told me to "stroll about the garden, breathe." I was left alone.

No - not alone. Stefan walked after me. Ten paces behind. In silence. When I stopped at a bush he stopped too. When I walked on he walked on. He said nothing. He simply walked. As if on guard.

I endured it for some ten minutes. Then I turned round.

"Do you understand Russian?" I asked.

Stefan hesitated. Then nodded.

"Malko," he said. "A little. I speak - badly. I understand - well."

"Why are you following me?"

Stefan looked at me a long time with his light, almost transparent eyes. Then slowly, carefully choosing words, as if taking them one by one from a tight pocket, he said:

"The General said - watch. The mistress said - watch." He paused. "And I myself... I watch anyway. For a long time. Before them."

"A long time - how long?"

Stefan did not answer. He turned and went to the arbour. I followed him.

At the arbour he stopped and laid his palm on the trunk of the huge, ancient bush that entwined it. The trunk was as thick as an arm, knotted, covered with thorns, grey bark, lichen.

"This rose," said Stefan. "Do you know how old it is?"

"No."

"I brought it from the monastery. Near Tarnovo. A cutting. Small - like this." He showed two fingers. "Twenty-two years ago. The General was visiting us. In Tarnovo. I was young. I worked in the monastery garden. The General saw the roses and said: 'Will you come with me to Russia?' I said: 'I will. If I may take one rose.'" He stroked the trunk. "I took this one."

"Why this one?"

Stefan fell silent again. For a long time. Over the arbour bees droned, heavy, golden, drunk with nectar.

"Because there is a tale about it," he said at last. "At the monastery. An old one. My grandmother told it to me. And her grandmother to her."

"Tell it."

Stefan looked at me. Then at the house, at the terrace where no one was. Then at me again. And sat down on the stone bench by the arbour, patting the place beside him with his palm.

"Sit," he said. "A long tale. My Russian is short."

* * *
He told it slowly, mixing Russian words with Bulgarian, sometimes falling silent to find a word, sometimes showing with his hands what he could not find words for. But I understood. Strange - I understood nearly everything, even the Bulgarian words, as though they had been familiar to me once, long ago, and then forgotten, as the language of childhood is forgotten.

"Long ago," began Stefan. "Very long ago. When Tarnovo was still the capital. The tsar's city. When on Tsarevets - that is a hill, a fortress, big, above the river Yantra - stood the tsar's palace and the patriarch's cathedral. Before the Turks." He paused. "The Turks came. Took Tarnovo. Burned it. The Patriarch - Euthymius - they led away into exile. The kingdom ended. Five hundred years ago."

He raised his hand and pointed somewhere to the south, beyond the river, beyond the horizon.

"In the year when the Turks took Tsarevets," he continued, "a man came to the monastery. Young. A stranger. Not a Bulgarian, not a Greek, not a Turk. No one knew from where. He came at night, when the city was burning. All in dust. Without a name." Stefan looked at me. "He said to the monks: 'I do not remember who I am. I remember only that I must plant a rose here.' And took a cutting from his bosom. And planted it. By the monastery wall."

"And what happened next?"

"The monks took him in. He lived with them. A year. Worked in the garden. Did not say who he was. Did not remember." Stefan paused. "But he knew everything about roses. Everything. As if he had grown them all his life. And also - he knew languages. All of them. Spoke with Greeks - in Greek. With Turks - in Turkish. With merchants from Venice - in Venetian. And at night, in sleep, he spoke a language that no one knew."

Cold under the ribs. On the left.

"And after a year," said Stefan, "the rose bloomed. For the first time. Red. Dark. Almost black. Like this one." He touched the trunk. "And on the night it bloomed, the man left. No one saw how. In the morning - he was gone. Only by the rose, on the ground - two stones. Small. One white, one black."

I stopped breathing.

"And to the monk who was closest to him, before leaving he said..." Stefan closed his eyes, remembering. Then pronounced slowly, in Bulgarian, in a singsong, like a prayer: "'Kogato taya roza tsafne v chuzhda zemya, shte se varna.'" He opened his eyes. "'When this rose blooms in a foreign land - I shall return.'"

* * *
We were silent for a long time. Bees droned over the arbour. Somewhere by the river an oriole cried.

"And the stones?" I asked at last. My voice was alien, hoarse. "What became of the stones?"

"The monks kept them. For a long time. Two hundred years. Three hundred." Stefan shrugged. "Then - I don't know. Some say - the Turks stole them. Some say - a Russian officer took them, under Catherine, when the Russians first crossed the Danube. Some say - they went away themselves. Stones, they say, do not like to lie long in one place."

"And the rose?"

"The rose lived. Five hundred years." Stefan stroked the trunk again. "It grew old. But it bloomed. Every year. And every year the monks took cuttings and planted them in other places. In other monasteries. Near Tarnovo, at Preobrazhenski, at Kilifarevo, at Arbanasi. They said: let it grow everywhere. So that he will find it. Wherever he returns."

"And you brought a cutting here."

"I brought it here." Stefan looked at me. "Twenty-two years ago. I thought it a tale. Grandmother's tale. Just a beautiful rose." He paused. "Twenty-two years it grew here. Every year it bloomed in June. As it should."

"And?"

Stefan slowly rose from the bench. He went round to the other side of the arbour - to where the trunk of the rose went into the ground - and drew aside a leafy shoot. Under it, right at the root, was a young sprout. Thin, green, fresh. And on it - one bud. Opened. Dark scarlet, almost black.

"It is not June now," said Stefan quietly. "Now it is the end of summer. The roses have finished. All of them. In the whole garden. Only this one..." He touched the bud with the tips of his fingers, carefully, as one touches a sleeping child. "This one bloomed two weeks ago. At night. By itself. I came in the morning - and it was blooming."

"Two weeks ago," I repeated.

"Two weeks ago," said Stefan, "you were found by the railings. In the left wing." He looked at me with his light, almost transparent eyes. "I am not a clairvoyant. I am a gardener. But I can count."

* * *
From the terrace came Konstantin's voice:

"Mon cher! Where are you? The General orders everyone to dinner! There's duck with apples, and if you're late, I'll eat your portion and won't repent!"

Stefan instantly stepped away from me, lowered the leafy shoot, covering the sprout. His face became again impenetrable, peasant-like, silent.

"Go," he said. "Later. Later I will tell more."

"Stefan..."

"Later," he repeated. And, after a pause, added quite softly, in Bulgarian, as though not to me but to the rose: "Dobre doshal."

I did not know those words. But I understood them. "Welcome." Or - "welcome back."

* * *
Dinner was long and noisy - the General, contrary to his habit, was talkative, Konstantin made everyone laugh with tales of regimental pranks, and besides ourselves there were two more guests at table whom I had not expected.

The first was Father Serafim - not a Russian priest but a Bulgarian monk who had come from Tarnovo itself. Tall, thin, with a long grey beard, in a black cassock faded by the sun to the colour of dust, and with eyes lively, quick, mocking, not at all monkish. He had been travelling in Russia for half a year collecting money for a Bulgarian school at the monastery - the General, as it turned out, was his chief benefactor.

The second was a young man of about twenty, a Bulgarian, a student - Lyuben - thin, pale, in a shabby student's frock coat, with burning eyes and hair so long that the General, seeing him, winced and muttered something about nihilists. Lyuben studied in Odessa, and had come here "to visit a compatriot" - that is, Stefan. He spoke Russian almost without accent, fast, hotly, waving his hands, and kept knocking over his glass.

"Father Serafim," said the General, pouring the monk wine, "tell the young people how things are with you there now. About the Exarchate."

The monk sighed, stroked his beard.

"The Exarchate, Your Excellency, is our victory and our misfortune," he said. His voice was low, singsong, with a soft Bulgarian accent. "For forty years we fought to serve God in our own language. Greek bishops served in our churches in Greek, our books they burned, our schools they closed. Forty years! And now the Sultan has signed a firman - and we have our own church. Our own exarch. Our own books." He paused. "And the Patriarch of Constantinople has declared us schismatics. And now the Greeks curse us, the Turks laugh at us, and we..." He spread his hands. "We pray in our own language. For now."

"For now," repeated Lyuben, and his eyes flashed. "Precisely - for now, Father! A church is good. But a church is not freedom. While the Turk sits in Tarnovo, while the Turk sits in Plovdiv, in Sofia, while our girls..."

"Lyuben," said Stefan quietly. He sat at the end of the table, hardly eating and not having spoken a word all through dinner. "Not at the table."

Lyuben broke off, reddened, bent over his plate.

The General gave him a long, heavy look.

"Young man," he said slowly, "I have served the Sovereign for thirty years. I have been in Constantinople more often than you in your own bath. I know what is going on in the Balkans. I know that in Bucharest sits your committee, and that from there men cross the Danube with weapons and leaflets. And I know that two years ago in Sofia a man died on the gallows whom your people call the Apostle." Lyuben flinched. The General continued evenly: "I do not ask you to tell me anything. I ask one thing: do not bring into my house what may cost the lives of people who serve here. Stefan has been my gardener for twenty-two years. If anything happens to him because of your leaflets - I will find you. Wherever you are. Do you understand me?"

It became very quiet in the dining room. Lyuben went pale to blueness. Father Serafim lowered his eyes.

And Stefan... Stefan suddenly raised his head and looked at the General - straight, without any deference, as an equal at an equal. And said in Bulgarian something short and quiet.

The General held that look. Then slowly nodded.

"What did he say?" Konstantin asked the monk in a whisper.

Father Serafim was silent.

"He said: 'Pavel, for twenty-two years I have guarded your roses. For twenty-two years you have guarded me. Do not fear for me. Fear for the boy.'"

Konstantin looked at me. I looked at my plate.

* * *
After dinner, to clear the air, Father Serafim offered to tell "something merry." Merry, in the Bulgarian way, turned out to be a tale about Cunning Peter - a village rogue who cheated everyone: the Turkish pasha, and the greedy priest, and the rich chorbadzhi, and even the devil himself.

"Once," the monk told it, and his eyes laughed, "the pasha sent for Cunning Peter and said: 'They say you can lie so that everyone believes. Lie to me - and I will give you a horse. And if I do not believe - I will cut off your head.' Cunning Peter scratched the back of his head and said: 'Effendi, I would gladly lie. But I have no bag for lies with me. It stayed at home. Give me a horse - I will ride for the bag.' The pasha gave him a horse. Cunning Peter rode off." The monk made a pause. "And never came back. The pasha waited a week. Then understood. And laughed so that he fell off the divan. Said: 'Now that is a lie! The best! He lied to me - and I believed - and was left without a horse!'"

Konstantin laughed till he cried. The General smiled into his moustache. Even Lyuben smiled.

"And do you have riddles?" Konstantin asked when he had finished laughing. "Bulgarian ones?"

"Gatanki?" Father Serafim brightened. "We have! Many! Here is an old one. It is set to children when they are taught letters. 'Byalo pole, cherno seme. Koyto go see - toy go znae.'"

"'A white field, a black seed,'" translated Lyuben. "'Who sows it - knows it.'"

Konstantin pondered. The General smiled, clearly knowing the answer. I looked at the monk.

A white field. A black seed. A white stone and a black. A white sheet of paper and black signs on it.

"A letter," I said. "White paper, black ink. Whoever wrote it knows what is in it."

"Bravo!" Father Serafim clapped his hands. "Yes, a letter!"

"But another may read it too," objected Konstantin. "If he knows the letters."

"If he knows the letters," the monk agreed. And suddenly stopped smiling. "And if the letter is written in letters that no one knows except the one who wrote it?" He looked at me. "Then only the one who sowed knows what will come up."

I felt that in the inner pocket of my coat it suddenly became heavier - though there was nothing there but the blue notebook.

* * *
In the evening, when the heat had subsided and long blue shadows floated over the garden, Stefan called me to the greenhouse.

Konstantin went with me - the General had said "not a step," and Konstantin took the order with such seriousness that he followed me, it seemed, even to the privy. Stefan looked at him, hesitated - and nodded: let him.

The greenhouse stood at the far end of the garden, beyond the pond - a long glass building on a brick foundation, misted from within, smelling of damp earth, rotting leaves and something spicy, tropical. Inside, in the warmth, grew plants such as I had never seen: palms in tubs, lemon trees, some fleshy cacti, lianas with enormous leaves, and - in the farthest corner - a small, neat altar built of stones, on which stood a clay lamp and lay a dried wreath.

"Martenitsa," said Stefan, pointing to the wreath woven of red and white woollen threads. "Baba Marta. The first of March. We tie red-white threads on the wrist so that spring will come healthy. Later, when we see a stork or a flowering tree, we take it off and hang it on a branch." He touched the wreath. "Here are no storks. I hang it here."

"Red and white," said Konstantin.

"Red and white," nodded Stefan. "Blood and snow. Life and death. One without the other - impossible."

He went to a shelf by the wall, took from it a tin box - old, dented, with a peeling picture on which roses had once been drawn - and opened it.

Inside, on faded red velvet, lay a small glass vial - thin, narrow, with a ground stopper sealed with wax. In it a thick, almost transparent liquid glowed golden.

"Rose oil," said Stefan. "From Kazanlak. From the Valley of Roses. There - between two mountains, the Balkan and the Sredna Gora - roses grow. Fields. Versts. They are gathered at dawn, while the dew is on. By women. By hand. Every flower." He raised the vial to the light. "To make this much oil - three thousand roses are needed. Three thousand. This vial is my whole family. Mother gathered. Sister gathered. I gathered when I was a boy."

"Why are you showing it to me?" I asked.

Stefan was silent a long time. Then he put the vial back in the box and took out from under the velvet something else. Small, thin, folded in four.

Paper. Very old, yellowed, almost rotted at the folds.

He unfolded it - slowly, carefully, as one unfolds the wings of a dead butterfly. On the paper was a drawing. Faded, but still distinguishable: a dark scarlet rose. And beneath it - two small circles. One filled in. The other empty. And between them a wavy line.

And still lower - a line of writing. Not Cyrillic. Not Greek letters. Long, flowing, curving lines running one into another without breaks.

Konstantin beside me drew breath noisily.

"This is from the monastery," said Stefan quietly. "This was drawn by that man. Five hundred years ago. The monks kept it together with the stones. The stones went - the paper stayed. When I was leaving for Russia, the abbot gave it to me. Said: 'Take it with the rose. The rose will find to whom to give it.'"

He held out the paper to me.

"The rose has found," he said.

* * *
I did not take it. I stood and looked at the paper in his outstretched hand, at the flowing lines, at the two circles and the wavy stroke between them - and could not move. I did not know these signs. I was sure I had never seen them. And yet, looking at them, I felt what I had felt when Sventsitsky said "two worlds" - as though a key were entering a lock I had never seen but which had all this time been within me.

"I cannot," I said. "It is not mine."

"It is yours," said Stefan. Simply. As one speaks of the weather.

"How do you know?"

Stefan looked at me a long time. Then he laid the paper on the table, beside the box. Came up to me. Very close. And took my right hand in his - heavy, calloused, scored by thorns.

Turned it palm upward.

"That man," he said, "my grandmother said: on his palm there was no line of life. Smooth. Like a stone the water has rolled." He ran his thumb over my palm. "Twenty-two years I have looked at hands. The General's, the gentry's, the peasants'. All hands are different. All with lines." He raised his eyes to me. "Yours is the first without."

I snatched my hand away. Looked at it myself. At my own palm.

I had never looked at it so. Never. It had never occurred to me.

Smooth. Where on Konstantin - I had seen his hands a thousand times - a long curved line ran from the wrist to the fingers, on me there was nothing. Smooth skin. Like a child's. Or like a stone.

Konstantin looked at my palm. Then slowly raised his own - and looked at it. Then again at mine.

"Mon cher," he said very quietly. "I... I never noticed."

"Neither did I," I said.

* * *
We came out of the greenhouse when it was already quite dark. The paper I did take after all - Stefan put it into my hand and closed my fingers around it so firmly that refusal was impossible. Now it lay in the blue notebook, between pages, beside the drawing of two circles that I had not drawn, and the words "He is near. Wait," which I had not written.

At the pond Lyuben caught up with us - out of breath, with a stack of papers under his frock coat which he was carefully hiding.

"Stefan!" he whispered. "Bay Stefan, I need..." And, seeing us, broke off.

"Go into the greenhouse," said Stefan. "It is warm there. Hide what you carry under the martenitsa. No one will touch it." He looked at Konstantin and me. "They saw nothing."

"We saw nothing," said Konstantin gravely. And, when Lyuben had run off, added, looking at Stefan: "The General knows, though. About the greenhouse."

"The General knows," nodded Stefan. "The General knows everything. The General pretends not to know. With you Russians that is called - friendship."

"And with you?"

Stefan was silent.

"With us it is called - roses," he said. "Some people grow them, others smell them. And no one asks who watered."

* * *
At night I did not sleep. I stood at the window of my room on the second floor of the General's house and looked at the garden. The moon was almost full, and the garden lay silver under it, quiet, motionless - only the roses smelled so that one's head spun.

And in the garden below, a light was moving. A lantern. Slowly, in a circle. Round the arbour. Round the ancient, gnarled bush on which a single dark scarlet, almost black bud bloomed.

Stefan was walking round his rose. Circle after circle. Like a sentry. Like a monk round an altar.

Someone knocked softly at my door. I opened. Konstantin - in a dressing gown, with tousled hair, with a candle in his hand.

"You're not sleeping," he said. Not a question.

"I'm not sleeping."

He came in, stood beside me at the window. We silently watched the light in the garden.

"Mon cher," said Konstantin after a long time. "May I look again? At your hand?"

I held out my hand. Palm up.

He took it. Brought the candle near. Looked for a long time. Then ran his thumb over the smooth skin - slowly, from the wrist to the fingers, where on all people in the world the life line runs.

"Nothing," he said. "Nothing at all."

He did not let go of my hand. He held it in his, warm, and looked out the window at the light.

"You know," he said at last, very softly, "Strauch says that the lines on the palm are just folds of skin. That they mean nothing. That it is superstition." He paused. "I believe him. I want to believe him. But if you have no life line..." His voice wavered. "Mon cher, then I don't know how to hold you. Do you understand? If there is no line - what is there to hold on to?"

I did not know what to answer. I looked at Stefan's light in the garden, circle after circle, round the black rose that had bloomed out of season.

"Hold on to the hand," I said at last. "As long as you hold it - I am here."

Konstantin looked at me. Then at our hands. Then let go - slowly, as if reluctantly, as if his fingers would not obey. And turned to the window so that I would not see his face.

"Good night, mon cher," he said, already from the door. In an almost ordinary voice. Almost.

The door closed. The candle went away down the corridor.

And in the garden below, Stefan's light stopped by the arbour. And stood for a long time motionless. Then it rose - higher, higher - as though the gardener had lifted the lantern above his head, toward the rose itself, toward the single dark bud.

And it seemed to me - this was, of course, a trick of the moonlight - that the bud, in answer to the light, opened faintly. By one more petal.

## Chapter XXIII. The Hunt in the Papyrus Thickets

Four Years Before the Drought

The Nile came early that year and came generously.

I remember it as clearly as I seem to remember nothing else of those years - as though my memory, which gives up everything else so reluctantly, had kept that year in a separate casket wrapped in fine linen, and took it out only so that later, in the drought, there would be something to compare with. The water rose in a single night - the keeper of the nilometer, Seti, ran to the palace himself, without a messenger, in nothing but a loincloth, out of breath, barefoot, and shouted from the very gates so that the whole court heard: "Sixteen cubits! Sixteen! The barley will be fed to the donkeys!" He was four years younger then, and still knew how to run.

Sixteen cubits. A perfect flood. The kind that comes once in a generation. When the water covers all the fields but does not flood the villages. When the earth, laid bare after the ebb, becomes so black and fat that a grain thrown into it sprouts in three days.

The whole Valley was green that year. Not scorched brown, as now, not cracked, but green - lush, thick, moist, to the very horizon where the green butted against the yellow wall of the desert as the sea butts against a shore. The canals stood full to the brim. Dragonflies flew over the water - blue, green, gold. Lotuses bloomed so densely that on some channels no water could be seen. And in the Delta, in the north, where the river splits into seven branches before going out into the Great Green, there in the Delta stood thickets of papyrus taller than a man, and in them lived birds.

Millions of birds.

* * *
"Does my Pharaoh deign to shoot or to throw?" asked old Mehi, the huntsman, not raising his head from the boat he was inspecting - finger by finger, stalk by stalk.

The boat was made of papyrus - bundles of stalks tightly bound with cords of palm fibre, with the prow and stern curved upward, light as a leaf, flat as a palm. In such a boat one could pass where no wooden barge could go: through shallows, through thickets, along channels two cubits wide.

Mehi was old even then. Dry, sinewy, smoked by the sun to the colour of old leather, with hands covered with small scars from fishhooks, and with one ear - the other, as he told everyone who asked, a crocodile had bitten off when Mehi was twelve. "I found him afterward," he always added. "Thirty years later. Knew him by a tooth that was missing. My tooth. I knocked it out when he bit off the ear. We looked at each other a long time. Then he swam away. I didn't touch him. He was old already. Like me."

"Throw," I said. "Like the ancestors."

Mehi grunted contentedly and handed me a throwing stick - curved, flat, of heavy black wood, with the end carved in the shape of a snake's head. Such sticks had lain in the tombs of Pharaohs since time immemorial - with them birds were struck in the thickets, thrown so that the stick, spinning, flew over the water and brought down two or three at once.

"And the cat?" I asked.

"The cat is ready, my Pharaoh." Mehi nodded toward the stern.

In the stern, on a rolled mat, sat a cat. Huge, spotted, reddish-grey, with tufts on its ears and such green eyes that it seemed the thickets were reflected in them. His name was Mau - simply "cat," as, it seems, all hunting cats in the Delta are called. He looked at the thickets, twitching his tail, and from time to time made a quiet, throaty, impatient sound - not a mew but rather a growl.

"He knows better than I where the birds are," said Mehi proudly. "I throw - he fetches. Twenty years like that. He is my third Mau. The first was better. The second - lazy. This one - sly. Sly is better than lazy. Worse than the best."

* * *
There were many of us that day. Too many for a hunt, Mehi said, grumbling under his breath - birds take fright when there are more than three boats on the water. But I was Pharaoh, and Pharaoh did not hunt alone.

In the next boat - Senusret. Not yet commander of the whole army, then, but commander of my personal guard - younger than now by four years, with fewer wrinkles and the same stone face. He did not hunt. He sat in the stern with a spear on his knees and looked not at the birds but at the thickets around me - at every shadow, at every stirring of the reeds.

"Senusret," I said. "Throw a stick at least once. For pleasure."

"My pleasure, my Pharaoh," answered Senusret, not taking his eyes from the thickets, "lies in your returning from the hunt with the same number of ears you have now. Unlike the honourable Mehi."

Mehi giggled, not in the least offended.

In the third boat - Paser. Not yet an old man with a staff, but a sturdy, greying man, commander of the chariotry, who, the moment he stepped off a chariot, felt on water as uneasy as a fish on sand, and sat in the boat clutching its sides with both hands, with a face greenish as young papyrus.

"Paser," I called. "Are you unwell?"

"I, my Pharaoh, am always unwell where there is no ground underfoot and no horses ahead," Paser answered gloomily. "Horses at least understand where they are being led. And this bundle of reeds..." he slapped the side of the boat with disgust, "this bundle of reeds thinks only of how to drown me."

"It will not drown you, honourable one," said his oarsman, a young fisherman with white teeth. "Papyrus does not sink. It may overturn. But it will not sink."

"Comforting," muttered Paser.

And in the fourth boat, the smartest, with gilded sides and a canopy of fine linen - Khaemuas. Then he was some twenty, perhaps a little more. Young, handsome, cheerful, the son of a noble family from the Delta, who had just received his first post at court - junior charioteer - and was immeasurably proud of it. His bracelets already jingled on both arms, though not as many as now. He laughed, joked, threw his stick - clumsily, but with such zest that spray flew in all directions - and I, looking at him, thought that what the court lacked was precisely such men: light, carefree, not afraid to laugh before Pharaoh.

I could not know then what he would turn into in four years. No one could. And if someone had told me, I would not have believed it.

Though perhaps I should have. Because even then, on that sunny day, in a pause between throws, Khaemuas, laughing, said to his oarsman - loudly enough for me to hear:

"My father says we owe the temple of Ptah so much that the priests will soon take our fields. And I say - let them take them! Then I'll have a new bracelet. For a third arm!"

The oarsman laughed. Khaemuas laughed. I smiled too, then - the joke was merry.

Only now, four years later, recalling that day, I do not smile.

* * *
And in the smallest boat - narrow, old, with peeling sides - behind everyone, almost unnoticed, sat a boy.

I paid him hardly any attention that day. A boy of thirteen or fourteen, thin, dark-eyed, in a plain linen apron, with a writing board on his knees and a reed brush in his hand. A junior pupil of the scribes, sent by the senior scribe of the Library to record the hunt - how many birds, which, by whom struck - as is the custom to record all that Pharaoh does. The boy wrote with his head bent, and every so often rubbed his cheek with the brush, forgetting that the brush was inked, so that by midday his face was all black spots, like Mehi's spotted cat.

I remembered him only because at some moment - when the boats stopped in a quiet channel to wait out noon - he suddenly raised his head and looked at me. Straight. For a long time. Not as one looks at Pharaoh - with lowered eyes, with reverent fear - but as if he wanted to remember. As if he were drawing me with his gaze on that board lying on his knees.

And then he saw that I was looking at him - blushed to the roots of his hair and buried his nose in the board.

I did not know his name then. I did not ask.

* * *
The birds rose at noon.

Mau suddenly arched his back, flattened his ears, made a thin, ringing sound - and in that same instant out of the thickets, ten paces from us, with a deafening noise, with splashing, with cries, a flock burst up. Ducks, geese, herons, ibises, some small motley birds - hundreds, thousands - the sky over the channel darkened with wings.

"Throw, my Pharaoh!" cried Mehi. "Now! Throw!"

I threw. The stick left my hand - spinning, humming, snake's head foremost - and I saw it pass through the flock, saw two ducks fall into the water, tumbling. Mau leapt from the stern before they touched the water - straight into the thickets, into the reeds, into the mud - and a moment later surfaced with a duck in his teeth, wet, plastered with slime, happy.

Khaemuas threw, missed, laughed, threw again. Paser clutched the sides and shut his eyes. Senusret did not stir - he watched the thickets, where no one but the birds moved.

And the boy in the last boat wrote. Quickly, not looking at his board. He looked at the sky, at the flock, at me - and wrote.

And then happened what I afterward recalled many times.

One of the herons - huge, grey - darted right over the last boat, low, almost touching heads with its wings. The boy threw up his hand, shielding himself - the boat rocked - the board slipped from his hands - he reached for it, leaned over the side - and the light, peeling little papyrus boat overturned.

He went under without a single sound.

I do not remember how I came to be in the water. I remember only that the water was warm, muddy, full of silt, that papyrus stalks lashed my face, that somewhere behind me Senusret was shouting - "My Pharaoh! My Pharaoh!" - and that my fingers felt in the murky water a thin arm and clutched it.

I pulled him out. The boy was light as a reed. He coughed, choked, spat out water and silt, and his face, covered with ink spots, was white as linen. I held him above the water, standing chest-deep in the channel among lotuses and reeds, in clothes that cost more than his whole clan - and he looked at me with huge dark eyes.

"The board," he rasped. "My Pharaoh... the board..."

"What board?" I laughed, not knowing why myself. "You nearly drowned, and you think about a board?"

"It's written there..." He coughed again. "It's written there how many birds my Pharaoh struck. If it sinks - no one will know. As though the hunt had never been."

Senusret was already paddling up to us in his boat - white as the boy, with his spear ready. Mehi was shouting something. Khaemuas was roaring with laughter. And I stood in the water holding in my arms this absurd, ink-smeared child who, having nearly drowned, worried that my hunt would be forgotten - and suddenly felt something I could not name. As if I had held him like this once before. Long ago. In other water.

Mau, wet, plastered with slime, surfaced beside us out of the thickets. In his teeth was the board.

* * *
We saw the hippopotamus toward evening.

Mehi took us there on purpose - to a broad, deep backwater on the edge of the thickets, where the water was dark and still, and above it, like black boulders, backs protruded. Three. No, four. Huge, grey, glistening, with small ears which from time to time twitched, shaking off flies.

"They trample the fields," said Mehi, lowering his voice to a whisper. "In the last flood four villages were left without a harvest. These beasts eat in a night what a village eats in a month." He paused. "The priests say - this is Set. The evil god. He turns into a hippopotamus. When Pharaoh hunts a hippopotamus - he is like Horus striking Set. For his father. For Osiris."

"Do you believe that, Mehi?"

The old huntsman shrugged.

"I believe that a hippopotamus killed my brother, my Pharaoh. Overturned the boat and bit him in half. Whether Set was in the hippopotamus - I don't know. But my brother is gone." He held out to me a harpoon - long, with a copper head, tied to a coil of rope. "Horus struck Set for eighty years. My Pharaoh can finish in a single evening."

I took the harpoon.

I know how this was supposed to look - like on the walls of tombs: Pharaoh stands in the prow of a papyrus barge, proud, calm, with a harpoon raised over his head, and below, in the water, the vanquished beast writhes. That is how my predecessors were drawn. That, no doubt, is how I shall be drawn.

In fact it looked otherwise. The hippopotamus rose from the water right in front of our boat - suddenly, soundlessly, huge as a house - and opened its jaws. The jaws were pink. I remember that. Pink as an infant's, and in them two tusks, long, curved, yellow, each as long as my arm. The wave rocked the boat. Mehi cried out. Senusret, in the next boat, leapt up with his spear.

I threw the harpoon.

I do not remember whether it hit. I remember only that the rope pulled taut, jerked, burned my palms, that the boat was dragged, spun, that Mehi hung on the rope together with me, that the water around turned red - and that the hippopotamus, uttering a roar that shook the thickets, went into the depths and did not show itself again.

The rope went slack. At its end, when Mehi hauled it from the water, there was no harpoon.

"Gone," said Mehi. Without disappointment. Almost with relief. "Wounded, but gone." He looked at me. "My Pharaoh, this is good."

"Good?"

"The priests say: Horus strikes Set but does not kill him. Never. Eighty years he strikes - and does not kill. Because if Set dies - the world loses its balance. There will be only order, only Maat. And the world cannot live on order alone. Chaos is needed too. A little. So that order remembers why it is needed." Mehi spat into the water. "So the priests say. I say: the hippopotamus is gone, and everyone is alive. That is better than the hippopotamus dead and someone missing an ear."

* * *
We spent the night on an island in the middle of the Delta - a sandbar overgrown with palms, where servants pitched tents and lit fires.

There, by the fires, I first saw Nefer-Ka as High Priest.

The old High Priest had died half a year before that flood - quietly, in his sleep, at ninety. Nefer-Ka had received his staff only three moons earlier. He sailed to the island at sunset, on a separate barge, accompanied by junior priests - to wish Pharaoh a good hunt and to bring the blessing of the gods. He was four years younger then, but looked exactly as he does now: tall, straight as an obelisk, with an immobile face and with eyes in which nothing could be read.

"My Pharaoh," he said, bowing exactly as far as custom required. Not a finger lower. Even then. "I hear you plunged into the water to save a child."

"A scribe," I corrected.

"A scribe," Nefer-Ka agreed. "Noble." He paused. "But careless. Pharaoh is a living god. Son of Ra. Incarnation of Horus. If you had drowned in a channel saving a scribe-boy - what would the gods have said?"

"That Pharaoh saved a scribe," I answered.

Nefer-Ka gave me a long look. Then smiled - with that same smile which I afterward came to know so well: condescending, patient.

"The gods, my Pharaoh, speak in other words," he said. "But I will convey yours to them." And, already turning away, he added quietly, as if to himself: "A living god who forgets that he is a god. Curious."

He sailed away at dawn. I attached no importance then to his words.

* * *
But the main thing that night happened not by the fires, but afterward, when all had fallen asleep.

I did not sleep. I lay on a mat at the very water's edge, behind the tents, where it was quieter, and looked at the sky. The sky over the Delta that night was such as I seem never to have seen again: black, bottomless, and in it - stars. So many stars that between them there was hardly any blackness. And across the whole sky, from edge to edge, flowed a pale, shimmering, misty river.

"The Heavenly Nile," said someone beside me.

I turned. On the sand, two paces from me, sat an old man in the long white robe of a priest, with a shaven head, with some wooden rod in his hands - with a slit at one end and a plumb line on a thread. I had not heard him come.

"Seneb," he introduced himself, neither rising nor bowing, which by day would have been insolence, but at night, on the sand, by the water, somehow did not seem insolent. "Observer of the night hours from Heliopolis. I was sent with the High Priest - to watch the stars over the Delta. Here they are seen better than in the city." He raised the rod, squinted through the slit at some star. "Does my Pharaoh not sleep?"

"My Pharaoh does not sleep," I said. "Tell me about the sky, Seneb."

The old man lowered the rod. Was silent.

"The sky is Nut," he began slowly, as one begins a long-learned lesson, but his voice was warm, without any boredom. "A goddess. She stands over the earth, arched, resting her hands on the west, her feet on the east. The stars are ornaments on her body. And every evening she swallows the sun. Ra enters her mouth in the west and all night goes inside her body - through twelve hours, through the twelve gates of the Duat. And in the morning she bears him again - in the east. Red. Like an infant."

"Every day," I said.

"Every day, my Pharaoh. Since the beginning of time." Seneb raised his hand and pointed to the misty river across the sky. "And this is her milk. Or the Heavenly Nile, along which souls sail. Depending on who is telling."

He showed me three bright stars in a row - a belt - and around them several more, composing the figure of a man striding across the sky.

"Sah," said Seneb. "Osiris. The god whom his brother killed, tore into pieces, scattered across Egypt. And Isis gathered him. Piece by piece. And revived him - for one night, to conceive Horus by him. And then Osiris went away. Became king of the dead." He paused. "But every night he rises in the sky. There he is. Striding. Never stopping."

"And behind him?"

Seneb moved his hand lower, to the left, to where above the very horizon, at the edge of the earth, a star shone - brighter than all, white, shimmering, as if winking.

"Sopdet," he said softly, almost tenderly. "Isis. The wife. She always follows him. Always one step behind. Never catches up. But never lags." He paused. "Each year she vanishes from the sky for seventy days. And then returns - at dawn, just before the sun, over the eastern horizon. And on the day she returns, the flood comes." He smiled. "This year she returned right on time. And the Nile came to sixteen cubits. A good year. A very good year."

I looked at the white star by the horizon. Isis, who always walks one step behind. Never catches up. Never lags.

"Seneb," I said. "Do you believe that Pharaoh is a living god?"

The old man was silent for a long time. So long that I thought he had fallen asleep.

"My Pharaoh asks a dangerous question," he said at last. "If I say 'no' - I may be executed. If I say 'yes' - I shall lie. Because I do not know."

"Say what you think. There is no one here. Only we and Nut."

Seneb smiled.

"I think, my Pharaoh," he said, "that gods are like stars. They can be seen only when it is dark. By day, in the sun, no one looks at the sky. Everyone thinks of bread, of beer, of taxes. And at night, when it is dark, they look up and see gods." He paused. "Pharaoh is the one at whom people look when it is dark for them. When there is drought. When war. When plague. They look at Pharaoh and see a god. Because they need to see a god." He raised the rod to his eye again. "And whether there is truly a god in Pharaoh - that I do not know. Perhaps Pharaoh himself knows."

"Pharaoh does not know," I said.

Seneb lowered the rod and looked at me - for the first time in the whole conversation directly, attentively.

"Then he is a good Pharaoh," he said. "The bad ones always know."

* * *
He showed me one more thing - just before dawn, when Sah was already going down behind the horizon and the sky in the east was beginning to grey.

"Do you see, my Pharaoh?" Seneb pointed north, at stars standing high above the horizon. "These do not set. Never. All the others sink in the west, die, are born again in the east. And these - circle. Around one point. All night. All their lives. Ever wakeful."

"The Imperishable," I said.

"The Imperishable." Seneb nodded. "The ancients said: after death Pharaoh becomes one of them. That is why in the oldest tombs there are shafts directed straight at them. Narrow as a needle. So that the soul of Pharaoh knows where to fly." He paused. "But my teacher, the old observer, told me something else. He said that the Imperishable are not those who have gone. They are those who have not yet come. Who circle round the earth and wait for their hour. To descend. As the First Ones descended."

"The First Ones, who came down from the Heavens," I said.

"You know the Epic, my Pharaoh," Seneb nodded. "Of course. You are of them, after all."

I flinched.

"What does it mean - of them?"

The old man shrugged - as if he had said something self-evident.

"All Pharaohs are of them, my Pharaoh. So it is written. The blood of the First Ones. Descendants of those who descended." He paused, looking at the sky. "Though my teacher said it is not quite so. He said - not descendants. He said - the same ones. That the First Ones do not die. They go to the Imperishable - and descend again. In another body. In another time. And each time forget who they are." Seneb smiled. "My teacher was a strange man. He was afterward sent to observe the stars in the farthest temple by the southern cataracts. For heresy."

By the southern cataracts. The rock that herdsmen give a wide berth.

But then, that night, I knew nothing yet of any Rock.

* * *
The sun rose from behind the eastern edge of the Delta - huge, red, wet, as if Nut had just given birth to it. The lotuses on the channel opened their petals one after another to the light - white, blue, pink. A mist rose over the water. Somewhere in the thickets birds were crying.

Seneb had gone to his barge, never having bowed. The camp was waking. Mehi was grumbling over the boats. Khaemuas, sleepy, was laughing, splashing water on his face. Paser looked gloomily at the river, plainly calculating how many more hours he would have to spend on a bundle of reeds. Senusret - I knew without looking - stood somewhere behind my back with his spear.

And at the very water's edge, on the sand, sat the scribe boy. With the board on his knees which Mau had fished out for him. He was writing. Noticing that I was looking at him, he blushed again, but this time did not look away.

I went up to him.

"What are you writing?"

He silently held out the board to me. On it, in neat, small signs, everything was recorded: how many boats, how many birds, by whom struck. The hippopotamus who had gone with the harpoon. And at the very end - a line that did not relate to the hunt.

"Pharaoh pulled a junior scribe out of the water. The scribe promises to remember this all his life. Even if Pharaoh forgets."

I raised my eyes to the boy.

"Why 'even if he forgets'?"

The boy lowered his head.

"Because Pharaohs save many," he said quietly. "And the scribe was saved once. Pharaoh may forget. The scribe - will not."

"What is your name?"

He opened his mouth to answer.

"My Pharaoh!" Senusret's voice rang out. "The barges are ready! The High Priest has sent word - they are waiting in the capital!"

I turned to the voice. And when I turned back - the boy was already being called by the senior scribe, and he, bowing hurriedly, ran off to his peeling little boat, pressing the board to his chest.

I never learned his name. I forgot his face within a moon - among the thousands of faces that passed before the throne. I forgot him altogether.

And only now, four years later, in the drought, sitting in the dark Library beside the junior keeper of scrolls who always has ink on his cheek - only now did I suddenly remember that day. The channel. The warm muddy water. The arm, light as a reed. And the dark eyes that looked at me as if drawing me on a board so as not to forget.

"The boy from the Library remembers a great deal for you," old Amenemope had said. "More than you think."

The Nile that year came to sixteen cubits. And I did not remember. Four years - I did not remember.

But he remembered. All four years.

## Vision IV. The Circle

I do not know where I came from to that village.

That is the first thing worth saying - and, perhaps, the only thing I am sure of. I remember the road: white, chalky, dusty, leading up a gentle green slope. I remember the stagecoach that set me down at the crossroads, and the coachman who, having taken his fare, long looked after me and crossed himself. I remember the smell - of mown grass, of sheep's wool, of rain that had passed an hour ago and promised to return. But where I boarded that coach, and why, and who I was to be riding in it with one travelling bag - that I do not remember. As I did not remember at the very beginning of all my other journeys either.

The village was called Amesbury. So it was written on the peeling wooden signboard of the inn where I was given a room under the very roof - with a bed on which every spring creaked, with a window that looked out on a river, narrow, dark, unhurried, overgrown with willows, and with a view - there, beyond the river, beyond the fields, on the horizon, on the ridge of the chalk plain - of something grey, uneven, barely discernible in the haze. As though someone had set stone teeth along the edge of the world.

"The stones," said the landlady, noticing where I was looking. "Everyone looks that way. They come, they look, they go. You too, sir? For the solstice?"

"The solstice?"

The landlady - Mrs Hobbs, stout, rosy, in a frilled cap and an apron on which flour mingled with beer stains - threw up her hands so that a little white cloud fell from her.

"Lord, sir, don't you know? The day after tomorrow is the longest day of the year! The shortest dawn! The sun rises right over the Heel Stone and shines into the very middle of the circle! All the madmen of England gather to see it." She lowered her voice. "This year there are especially many. A learned man from Oxford. Gypsies. A young lady with some machine on a tripod. Our vicar goes about blacker than a thundercloud - says it's paganism. And my husband says, paganism or not, the lodgers pay promptly and drink their beer, and thank you very much."

She set a jug of water on the table, adjusted the curtain and, already in the doorway, turned back:

"Only don't go there at night, sir. Especially alone. People say you mustn't count there."

"Count?"

"Count the stones," said Mrs Hobbs in perfect earnest. "Whoever counts them twice and gets the same number will die. And whoever gets a different one will go mad. And whoever doesn't count at all never came here." She paused. "My late father-in-law counted. Three times. Different each time. Died at ninety-six, in his own bed, but to his dying day swore that the stones move from place to place at night." She tittered. "Well, he drank too. Good night, sir. Supper at seven. Kidney pie."

* * *
Downstairs, in the common room of the inn, by seven o'clock there had gathered a company that any novelist would have thought too motley to be plausible.

At a large oak table by the fireplace, heaped with papers, drawings, rulers, compasses and something resembling a brass spyglass without lenses, sat a man whom I at once christened to myself the Owl. About sixty, bald as a billiard ball, with a fringe of white down above the ears and such luxuriant grey whiskers that they reached almost to his chin. On his nose sat spectacles, over them yet another pair, and a third stuck out of the breast pocket of his tweed jacket. He was calculating something furiously, moving his lips, and from time to time exclaiming "Incredible!" or "It can't be!", each time striking the table with his fist so that the compasses leapt.

"Professor Erasmus Holloway," whispered Mrs Hobbs, setting a pie before me. "From Oxford. Came to measure the stones. Third week he's been measuring. Says the ancient people were astronomers. The vicar says the ancient people were savages. They've nearly come to blows twice already."

At the next table, straight as a pole, in a black frock coat and white collar, sat the vicar himself - the Reverend Silas Whitcombe. Thin, pale, with pursed lips and an expression as though the whole world were personally guilty before him. He ate his pie in small, reproachful bites and from time to time cast at the professor glances capable of freezing the Thames.

In the corner, by the window, on a bench, sat a young woman in a dark green travelling dress, with short, almost boyish hair sticking out from under a small hat - a thing unheard of for a respectable lady - and with hands black to the wrists, as though she had been rummaging in soot. Beside her on the floor stood a bulky wooden box on a tripod, wrapped in black cloth, and several smaller boxes from which came something sharp, apothecary-like - ether.

"Miss Ada Lovell," Mrs Hobbs went on whispering. "A photographer. From London. Alone! Without a companion! Her hands are black from those chemicals of hers - says it's silver. The vicar says it's indecent. She says what's indecent is his sermons." The landlady tittered. "I like her. She pays for her beer in advance."

And by the very fireplace, on a three-legged stool, leaning on a long shepherd's crook, sat an old man - so old, wrinkled and weathered that he seemed hewn from the same grey stone that stood on the ridge of the plain. In a rough canvas smock, in an old felt hat, with a white beard to his waist, he smoked a clay pipe and looked into the fire, paying no attention to anyone. At his feet, curled up, lay a shaggy black-and-white dog.

"And that is old Jedediah," said Mrs Hobbs, very quietly, almost with reverence. "A shepherd. All his life he's pastured sheep on the plain, right by the stones. They say he's ninety. Or a hundred. No one knows. He doesn't seem to know himself. He knows everything about the stones. Only tells no one." She paused. "And today he came himself. For the first time in ten years. Sat down by the fire and sits. As though waiting for someone."

* * *
Professor Holloway noticed me after about five minutes. He raised his head from the drawings, looked at me over two pairs of spectacles - and his eyes flashed with that particular hungry gleam with which the eyes of scholars flash on finding a fresh victim.

"You!" he exclaimed, jabbing a compass at me. "You have come for the solstice? Excellent! Excellent! Sit down! You must see this! No one in this village listens to me!"

To refuse was senseless. I moved over to him.

"Look!" He unrolled before me an enormous sheet covered with circles, lines, angles and figures. "Here is the circle. The sarsens - the big stones. Here - the bluestones, the small ones, inside. Here the horseshoe of trilithons. And here - the axis!" He drew a ruler along the plan. "The axis of the whole structure is directed exactly - exactly, sir! - at the point of sunrise on the day of the summer solstice. Through the Heel Stone. Do you understand what that means?"

"That the builders knew where the sun rises?"

"That the builders were astronomers!" cried the professor, striking the table with his fist. "Scholars! They built a calendar! A stone calendar! Four thousand years ago! When in Egypt they were only just building the pyramids!"

At the word "Egypt" something in me trembled. Columns. Sand. Heat. I blinked - and the vision went.

"Nonsense," said the Reverend Whitcombe in an icy voice from the next table, not raising his eyes from his pie. "These stones were set up by the Druids for their vile pagan sacrifices. Or by the Romans. Or - most probably - by the Evil One himself, as the tradition has it."

"Druids!" the professor turned purple. "The Druids lived two thousand years later! The Romans - three! And the Evil One, Reverend, so far as I know, is not strong in trigonometry!"

"The Evil One is strong in all that leads the soul away from God," the vicar snapped. "Including your trigonometry."

They looked at each other across the aisle like two cocks across a fence. Mrs Hobbs behind the bar rolled her eyes. Miss Lovell in the corner laughed soundlessly, covering her mouth with a palm black from silver.

"And do you know the tradition, sir?" the vicar suddenly asked, turning to me. "About the Heel Stone?"

"No."

"The Evil One," said the vicar, savouring each word, "bought these stones from an old woman in Ireland. He paid her as many coins as she could count while he carried the stones. And he carried them in an instant. The old woman managed to say only 'one.' And the Evil One set the stones here on the plain and boasted: 'No one will ever know where they came from!' And a friar hiding behind a stone cried out: 'That is what you think!' The Evil One seized the largest stone and hurled it at the friar. Hit him on the heel. Ever since, the stone has been called the Heel Stone." The vicar triumphantly sipped from his mug. "The friar, mark you, survived. Because he was under God's protection."

"And in my opinion," a ringing woman's voice suddenly came from the corner, "that story was made up by the monks. So as not to admit that they have no idea who really hauled those stones."

Miss Lovell rose, came up to our table and without the slightest embarrassment sat down on a free chair.

"There is another legend," she said, looking at me with mocking grey eyes. "About Merlin. King Arthur's wizard. That these stones once stood in Ireland, on a mountain, and were called the Giants' Dance. And the giants brought them from Africa - because there was a power of healing in the stones. If you poured water over a stone and then washed a sick man with that water - he would recover. And Merlin moved them here, to England - not with his hands but with a song. Or with machines." She winked at the professor. "Depending on who is retelling it."

"From Africa," I repeated slowly.

"From Africa," Miss Lovell nodded. "The giants - from Africa. The stones - from Ireland. The wizard - from Wales. The sun - from the sky." She shrugged. "Here everything is from somewhere. Nothing is from here. Even you, as I see."

"Me?"

"You have the face of a man who has come from everywhere at once," said Miss Lovell. "I photograph people. I know faces. Yours does not hold one expression longer than a second. As if three men lived in it by turns." She tilted her head, examining me as she must examine through the lens of her box. "May I photograph you? The day after tomorrow. At dawn. At the stones."

"Why?"

"Because," she said simply, "I am curious which of the three will come out on the plate."

* * *
Old Jedediah by the fire had not stirred all this time. But when the conversation died down - when the professor had buried himself in his drawings again, the vicar in his pie, and Miss Lovell had gone to the bar for another mug of beer - the shepherd suddenly took the pipe out of his mouth and, without turning his head, said in a low, hoarse voice like the creak of old wood:

"You. Come here."

The room went quiet. Mrs Hobbs behind the bar dropped her towel.

I went over. Crouched by the fireplace, beside the dog, which raised its head, sniffed my hand - and suddenly licked it, briefly and warmly, as one licks one's master.

"Shep knows you," said the old man, glancing sideways at the dog. "Shep licks no one. Not even me." He drew on his pipe. "Want a riddle? An old one. My grandfather set it to me. And his grandfather to him. And that one - I don't know who. Maybe the one who set up the stones."

"I do."

Jedediah let out smoke and spoke slowly, in a singsong, in the old local dialect, which I understood with difficulty, but understood:

"'Giants stand in a ring, holding hands. Above - crossbeams, below - grass. They are counted, and cannot be counted. At night they walk, by day they stand. Once a year one of them opens an eye. What does it see?'"

I thought for a long time. The fire crackled. The dog laid its muzzle on my knee.

"The sun," I said at last. "Once a year, at the solstice, the sun rises over the Heel Stone and shines into the circle. As if an eye opens."

Jedediah was silent a long while. Then slowly shook his head.

"The answer is the sun," he said. "Everyone answers so. The professor answered so. The girl with the box answered so. Everyone." He took out the pipe and jabbed it at me. "But my grandfather said: wrong. The eye opens not to see the sun. The sun it sees every day anyway. The eye opens to see the one who has come. Once a year. Or once in a hundred years. Or once in a thousand." He stuck the pipe back in his mouth. "Grandfather said: the stones were set up not for the sun. The stones were set up for the guest. So that he would know where to come."

"What guest?"

"The one who comes from above," said Jedediah simply. "And leaves from above. And each time does not remember that he has been before."

A chill ran down my back - that same one, long familiar, from under the ribs, on the left.

"Did your grandfather see him?" I asked.

"My grandfather - no." The old man paused. "But I did."

"When?"

"Seventy years ago. I was twenty. I was pasturing sheep by the stones on the night of the solstice. Alone. Shep was another one - also Shep, all our dogs are Sheps." He stroked the dog's head. "And toward morning a man came. From the side where there is no road. Young. In strange clothes. Stood in the middle of the circle. And waited. And when the sun rose - from above, right over him, a light opened. White. Not sunlight. And there was a sound - as though the very earth hummed. And heat." Jedediah closed his eyes. "And then - nothing. Sun, grass, sheep. And the man gone."

"Perhaps you dreamed it?"

"Perhaps," the old man agreed. "Only Shep - the earlier one - howled for three days after. And on the spot where the man stood, the grass did not grow for ten years. A round patch. Like this." He spread his hands. "The professor says it's chalk. The vicar says the Evil One. And I say - the guest."

He fell silent. Then, not looking at me, he added:

"He had your face, lad. I have remembered it seventy years. Yours."

* * *
That night I did not sleep. I lay on the creaking bed, listened to the willows by the river rustling outside the window, and looked at the ceiling over which moon shadows slid. Somewhere below a door banged. Somewhere a horse neighed.

Toward morning there was a soft knock at my door.

On the threshold stood a woman - short, swarthy, with jet-black hair braided in two thick plaits, twined with red ribbons and strings of small coins that jingled at every movement. She wore a motley dress, a red kerchief, copper rings on her fingers, huge earrings in her ears. She might have been forty, and might have been seventy - impossible to guess: her face was young, and her eyes ancient.

"Zora," she said before I could ask. "A gypsy. The camp is across the river. I have come to tell your fortune."

"I did not call you."

"I know." She smiled, flashing a gold tooth. "No one ever calls me. I come to those to whom I must." She held out her hand palm upward. "Give me your hand. Don't be afraid. I will take no money. From such as you, one doesn't take."

I gave her my hand. I do not know why.

She took it in hers - dry, hot, laden with rings - turned it to the light from the window and looked for a long time. Was silent. Moved a finger. Then raised her eyes to me - and in them there was neither cunning nor mockery.

"There is no life line," she said quietly.

"I have been told," I said. And was astonished myself - who told me? Where? I did not remember. But I knew that someone had.

"There is no life line," Zora repeated. "But there is something else. Here." She drew a nail across my palm, in a circle. "A ring. A line that goes round and comes to where it set out from. I have seen such once. My grandmother showed me. She told the fortune of a man who had such a ring. Long ago. Here. At the stones."

"Who was he?"

"Grandmother did not know." Zora let go of my hand. "Grandmother said to him: 'You walk in a circle, handsome. A hundred times you came, a hundred times you went. And each time you forget.' He laughed. Asked: 'And how can I stop forgetting?' Grandmother said..." Zora paused. "Grandmother told him a riddle. I will tell you the same."

She leaned toward me so close that the coins in her plaits jingled right by my ear.

"'What must one do to get out of the circle?'"

I thought. For a long time.

"Break it?"

"No," said Zora. "You break it - you will walk a new circle."

"Stop?"

"No. You stop - the circle will go on without you."

"Then I don't know."

Zora straightened. Smiled - sadly.

"Grandmother did not know the answer either," she said. "But that man told her the answer. On leaving. He said: 'One must remember where the beginning is.'" She shrugged. "Grandmother said - a circle has no beginning. So there is no getting out. And he laughed and said: 'This one has.'"

She went to the door. Stopped.

"The day after tomorrow, at dawn," she said without turning, "do not stand in the middle. Stand at the edge. By a stone. Hold on to the stone. Perhaps then they will not take you." She paused. "Or perhaps they will. As they took grandmother's."

And left, jingling her coins.

* * *
The whole of the next day I spent at the stones.

Up close they proved bigger than I could have imagined - grey, rough, eroded by the winds, overgrown with yellow and white lichen like ancient old men with beards. Some stood. Some lay, fallen, as if tired of standing. On some, at a height of three men, lay stone crossbeams - just as huge - and I could not understand how people who had neither machines nor steam nor iron had managed to raise them there.

Professor Holloway darted among the stones with rulers and plumb lines like a maddened bumblebee, shouting figures which were written down after him by a boy hired in the village - flaxen-haired, freckled, forever open-mouthed. Miss Lovell set up her box on its tripod by the Heel Stone, paced out the distance, squinted at the sky and murmured something about light. The Reverend Whitcombe stood apart, by the road, arms folded on his chest, with the air of a man who had come to make sure that the thunder of heaven would strike these heathens after all. The gypsies stood camped by the river, singing and burning fires.

And old Jedediah sat on his stool right in the middle of the circle, smoking his pipe and looking at the sky.

I decided to count the stones. I do not know why myself. Perhaps from obstinacy. Perhaps because of Mrs Hobbs and her father-in-law.

I counted slowly, touching each stone with my palm. The big ones. The small. The standing. The fallen. The crossbeams. It came to eighty-three.

I counted again. Eighty-one.

I counted a third time - still more slowly, marking each stone with a chalk stroke from a piece of chalk I had found right there in the grass. Eighty-five.

I stood in the middle of the circle holding the piece of chalk and felt a chill creep up my spine.

"Doesn't add up?" asked Jedediah, not turning.

"Doesn't add up."

"And never will," said the old man calmly. "They don't like to be counted. They're not for that." He took out the pipe. "You found chalk?"

I looked at the piece in my hand. White, soft, staining the fingers.

"I did."

"All the ground here is chalk," said Jedediah. "And in the chalk - flint. Black." He bent down, groped with his hand in the grass by his stool and held something out to me. "Here."

It was a stone. Flint. Black, smooth, almost round, with a white chalk crust at the edge, as if in a shirt.

"White and black," said the old man. "Chalk and flint. One soft, the other hard. One writes, the other strikes fire. Here they are always together. One in the other." He stuck the pipe in his mouth again. "Put them in your pocket. Both. They'll come in handy."

I put them in. A piece of chalk and a piece of flint. White and black.

They lay in my pocket side by side, as though they had always lain there.

* * *
In the evening, at the inn, for want of anything better to do - and because everyone was too excited to sleep - they played charades. English ones, real ones: not riddles in words but a performance in faces. The setter acted out a word syllable by syllable, silently, with gestures, and the others guessed.

Professor Holloway was the first to volunteer - and portrayed something so incomprehensible, leaping, flailing his arms and jabbing a finger at the ceiling, that after ten minutes everyone gave up, and it turned out to be the word "astronomy," which he had been trying to act out in parts: "astro" - a star, "no" - a refusal, "my" - no one ever understood how he intended to show "my." The room roared with laughter to tears. Even the vicar, against his will, twitched the corner of his mouth.

Then Mrs Hobbs set one - the word "pie" - and acted it so expressively, chewing the air with such relish, that it was guessed at once, and the professor's boy ran to the kitchen to check whether any pie was actually left.

Then, to everyone's amazement, the vicar rose. He stood a long time in the middle of the room, straight as a pole. Then slowly, solemnly, he portrayed - in gestures, without a single word - an angel. Arms spread like wings. Gaze upward. Then - a fall: he dropped to one knee, bowed, covered his face with his hands. Then - rose. Portrayed searching for something, looking around. Then pointed at me.

The room went quiet.

"'Fallen,'" said the professor uncertainly. "'Angel'?"

The vicar shook his head. Pointed at me again.

"'Wanderer'?" suggested Mrs Hobbs.

The vicar shook his head.

"'Guest,'" said Miss Lovell quietly.

The vicar slowly nodded. And sat down in his place without a word. And for the rest of the evening never once looked in my direction.

"What was that?" Miss Lovell whispered to me.

"I don't know," I said.

Old Jedediah, sitting by the fireplace, laughed quietly - for the first time in all that time. Dryly, as branches crackle in a fire.

"The parson saw too," he said into the fire, to no one in particular. "Seventy years ago. He was a lad then. The bell-ringer's son. Ran after me to the stones that night. He saw. He's just been pretending for forty years that he didn't." The old man drew on his pipe. "Parsons are good at pretending."

* * *
An hour before dawn we stood at the stones.

The sky in the east was barely beginning to lighten - not pink, not gold, but that grey, pearly, ghostly light with which the sky glows in the shortest night of the year, when night hardly comes at all. The grass was wet with dew. It smelled of chalk, sheep and the smoke of gypsy fires. Over the plain lay mist - low, white, knee-deep - and the stones rose out of it like islands out of the sea.

There were many of us. The professor with his rulers and the boy. Miss Lovell at her box on the tripod, under the black cloth, with a plate that she had just flooded with something from a dark flask. The Reverend Whitcombe - by the road, but nearer than yesterday. Mrs Hobbs with a basket of pies, "in case it is the end of the world - so as not to be on an empty stomach." The gypsies - in a semicircle, at a distance, in silence, without songs. Zora among them - I saw the coins in her plaits glint. And Jedediah - on his stool, in the very middle of the circle, with the dog at his feet.

"Stand here," Miss Lovell said to me, pointing to a place between two huge stones, right on the axis that led from the Heel Stone to the middle of the circle. "The light will be here. Don't move when I say. The exposure is five seconds. For my silver that is eternity."

"Do not stand in the middle," Zora had said. "Stand at the edge. Hold on to the stone."

I stood where Miss Lovell indicated. On the axis. Between two stones. But I stretched out my hand and laid my palm on the cold, rough stone, wet with dew, to my right. And did not take it away.

"It's coming!" shouted the professor. "It's coming! Look!"

Over the horizon, right over the Heel Stone, the edge of the sun appeared. Red, enormous, trembling in the morning haze. And from it through the mist, across the grass, across the whole circle, a strip of light stretched to us - long, straight, golden, like a taut string. It fell on the Heel Stone. Then farther. Nearer. Nearer still.

The professor sobbed with delight, waving his ruler. His boy stood with his mouth open. Miss Lovell dived under the black cloth.

"Don't move!" came dully from there. "One!"

The beam touched my feet.

"Two!"

And in that moment - not from the east, not from the sun - from above, right over me, a light opened.

* * *
I do not know how to describe it otherwise. It did not come - it opened. As an eye opens. White, blinding, so bright that the sun beside it seemed a dim candle-end. It poured from above, from the very middle of the sky, where the last, paling stars still remained - in a straight pillar, down, into the middle of the circle, and I stood at its edge.

There was no sound. At first. And then there was - not a sound, a hum. The earth underfoot began to hum like an enormous bell struck from inside. The hum passed through the soles, through the knees, through the spine - to the very teeth. The stones around me vibrated. I felt it with my palm - the stone under my hand trembled like a living thing, like the flank of a great beast.

And heat. Not the sun's - another. From within. As though someone had lit a fire in me, in the very middle of the chest, where people have a heart, and I - I did not know what I had there. The heat grew, rose, flooded the whole body - and in my pocket, I felt it through the cloth, the piece of chalk and the piece of flint grew hot. So hot that were they in my hand I would have dropped them.

And then the voice came.

It came from above - from the light. Not in words - in vibration, in hum, in heat, all at once. It spoke. I knew that it spoke. I felt each word - with my whole body, with every bone, every drop of blood. But I could not make out a single one. They slid into one another without pauses, without borders, like water pouring over stone, like the flowing lines of a pattern I had seen somewhere, sometime - on paper, on stone, on metal...

And through the hum, through the heat, through the dazzling whiteness I suddenly understood: this voice I had heard before. Not here. Not now. Sometime. When he stood by my bed. When he spoke to me in this same language. When he said one single word that I understood.

"Remember."

I wanted to answer. I wanted to cry out: I do not remember! I do not know what to remember! Tell me! But my throat clenched, and there was no voice.

The light above me began to narrow. The pillar grew thinner, brighter. It called. It drew. I felt my feet leaving the ground - no, not my feet, something else, something inside, as though I were being drawn out of myself, as a thread is drawn from a needle.

And only the hand - the hand that lay on the stone - held.

The stone under my palm was cold. The only cold thing in all that fire. I clung to it - with fingers, with nails, with all I had. Zora had said: hold on to the stone. And I held.

"Not now," I rasped. Or thought. "Not now. I have not remembered yet."

The light froze. For one moment - long, endless, like all my forgotten life.

And then - went out.

* * *
"...five!" Miss Lovell's muffled voice reached me from somewhere far off, from under the cloth. "That's all! You may breathe!"

I stood between two stones, on the axis, in the beam of the rising sun. An ordinary sun - red, warm, morning. The mist was melting over the grass. Somewhere sheep were bleating.
