Professor Holloway was leaping round the Heel Stone shouting: "Exactly! Exactly on the axis! I was right!" Mrs Hobbs was handing out pies. The gypsies were beginning to sing.

No one had seen anything.

No one - but three.

Old Jedediah stood by his stool - he had risen, for the first time in all that time - and looked at me. The dog at his feet was not howling - it lay with ears pressed down, looking the same way.

Zora stood among the gypsies, her palm pressed to her mouth. The coins in her plaits did not jingle - she did not stir.

And the Reverend Whitcombe - at the very edge of the circle, nearer than he had come in all those days - knelt in the wet grass. His lips moved. He was praying. Or weeping. I could not make out which.

I took my hand from the stone. On the grey lichen, where my palm had lain, a print remained. Scorched. Dark. Five fingers.

And on the grass at my feet, where I had stood - around me, in a ring - the grass was withered, yellowed, as if singed by fire. A round patch. Like this.

* * *
Miss Lovell developed the plate by noon - in her dark room under the roof of the inn, where it smelled of ether and silver. She came down into the common room holding the plate by its edges with the tips of her fingers, and her face was white as her chemicals.

She laid the plate on the table before me.

On it were the stones. The mist. The beam of sunlight from the Heel Stone. All of it crisp, sharp, silvery grey.

And where I had stood, between two stones - I was not there.

There was a silhouette. Tall. Immeasurably tall - above human height, almost to the lintel of the trilithon. Grey. Blurred at the edges, as if moulded of mist and ash. Faceless.

And a hand - one hand of his, stretched out to the side, lay on the stone.

"Five seconds," whispered Miss Lovell. "Five seconds of exposure. In five seconds a man may move, and the image will blur. But he cannot become..." she faltered, "...like this."

I looked at the plate. At the grey faceless silhouette. At the hand on the stone.

I knew him. I had seen him - at my bedside, on the balcony, in the alley, in the street. I had seen him... where? I did not remember. But I knew.

"Who is it?" asked Miss Lovell.

Jedediah, standing by the fireplace, answered for me. Not turning, looking into the fire.

"The same," said the old man. "Only later."

I did not understand. No one understood. Miss Lovell looked at the old man, then at me, then again at the plate.

"May I keep it?" she asked quietly.

"Keep it," I said. "Someone must remember."

* * *
I left Amesbury the next morning. The stagecoach waited at the crossroads. The coachman - the same one - again crossed himself, looking at me.

Mrs Hobbs wrapped a kidney pie for me for the road. Professor Holloway shook my hand and asked me to write if I should "ever find confirmation of the astronomical theory," and I promised, knowing that I would not write. Miss Lovell did not come to see me off - but on my bag I found a small photographic card. Not that one. Another. On it was one stone - the one I had held, with the dark print of a palm on its lichen. And on the back, in pencil, in her hand: "So that you do not forget what to hold on to."

The vicar did not come. But as the coach was already moving, I saw him at the churchyard fence - he stood straight as a pole, in his black frock coat, and, meeting my eyes, slowly, as if with effort, raised his hand and made the sign of the cross over me. Not as over the Evil One. As over a traveller.

Zora I did not see. Only at the very crossroads, on a roadside post, hung a red ribbon with copper coins strung on it. I do not know whether it was hers. I did not take it.

And old Jedediah stood on the ridge of the chalk plain, right by the stones, leaning on his crook, with the dog at his feet - a tiny figure against the grey giants - and looked after me. He did not wave. He simply looked. As one looks at one who is leaving, knowing that he will return. In a year. In a hundred years. In a thousand.

I thrust my hand into my pocket. The chalk and the flint lay there side by side - cooled, ordinary. White and black.

"One must remember where the beginning is," that man had told the gypsy's grandmother.

The coach lurched over a rut, and the stones on the horizon vanished in the morning haze - as though they had never been.

And I, it seems, for the first time in my life knew that I would return.

## Chapter XXIV. Another Life

We returned from the General's estate on Friday, and on Saturday my aunt held a literary evening.

Literary evenings in the province were what they called gatherings at which literature occupied, by Konstantin's reckoning, about one seventh of the time - the other six parts were divided among tea, gossip, pastries, music, flirtation and disputes about whose turn it was to choose the next book. My aunt and Vera Anatolievna had been giving them for some ten years, once a fortnight, and over those years the evenings had grown rituals, as an old oak grows moss: they always read in the green drawing room, always aloud, always by turns, always in French, and then always argued in Russian.

"Today it is Jules Verne," Konstantin announced to me at breakfast, spreading butter on a roll with the air of a man condemned to hard labour. "'Around the World in Eighty Days.' Evdokia Gerasimovna brought it from Paris. An Englishman bets that he will go around the whole globe in eighty days. By train, by steamer, by elephant. Can you imagine? By elephant!"

"And did he go round?"

"I don't know." Konstantin bit into his roll. "Last time we read up to the place where he saves an Indian widow from being burned. Kutasova wept. Lizonka wept. Shelestova said that the widow surely set fire to her husband herself. The General said that in India they haven't done that for forty years, the English forbade it. The Colonel told how once in Bukhara..." Konstantin waved his hand. "In short, we never did get to the elephant."

"I will read it to the end," I said.

"Don't you dare!" Konstantin was horrified. "You'll spoil the whole intrigue! All evening you'll sit with the face of a man who knows how it ends!"

"I almost always sit with such a face anyway."

Konstantin looked at me over his roll - and stopped smiling.

"No, mon cher," he said quietly. "You sit with the face of a man who knows that he has read this book before. Only does not remember when. That is different."

* * *
By seven o'clock the green drawing room was full.

It was called green for its wallpaper - dark green silk with a gold pattern, faded in half a century to the colour of pond duckweed - and for its furniture, upholstered in green velvet, and for the huge ficus in a tub by the window, which Agafya Tikhonovna watered personally, trusting no one, and which, rumour had it, remembered my aunt's father-in-law. Candles burned in two bronze candelabra. On the little table by the fireplace stood tea, liqueur, pastila and a dish of almond biscuits baked by Marfa the cook after a recipe inherited, she asserted, from a great-grandmother who had served Potemkin himself.

My aunt sat in her chair by the fireplace - in dark lilac, with pearls, a book on her knees. She looked tired. In the week of my absence she seemed to have aged a year. When I came in she raised her eyes to me - quickly, greedily, as if checking whether all of me had returned - and at once lowered them to her book.

"Did you rest well, my friend?" she asked.

"Well, Aunt."

"The roses?"

"The roses," I said. And, after a pause: "Stefan asked me to convey his bow to you."

Her fingers on the book cover froze for a moment.

"Thank you," she said. And nothing more.

Around us the guests were taking their seats. Evdokia Gerasimovna - in a hat with an ostrich feather dyed an unimaginable emerald "to match the drawing room." Nadezhda Porfirievna Kutasova - with a lorgnette, with Lizonka and, to Konstantin's horror, with the obvious intention of sitting closer to him. Olga Kirillovna Shelestova - in lilac, with a fan, with the face of a cat who has been promised a whole jug of gossip. Doctor Strauch - in the corner, with an unlit cigar, as always at a distance from the ladies' company but within earshot. Colonel Mikhail Ivanovich - by the table with liqueur, already telling someone about Turkestan.

And Vera Anatolievna.

She sat by the window, under the ficus, a little apart from everyone, in a plain dark grey dress without any ornament except a small brooch in the shape of a dragonfly. Vera Anatolievna always sat by the window - as if just in case, so as to be first to see if anyone approached the house. Quiet, affable, with a soft face and with eyes which, as I had long noticed, never looked at a conversational partner directly for longer than a moment - and then slipped off somewhere sideways, like little fish.

Today they did not slip. Today she looked at me. From the very minute I came in.

* * *
They read by turns. First Evdokia Gerasimovna - briskly, with a Parisian accent, doing the voices. Then Lizonka - timidly, stumbling, blushing at every line. Then Strauch - evenly, drily, with a German accent, turning French prose into something like a medical report, at which Konstantin choked with laughter into his fist.

Then they came to the elephant.

The Englishman, Mr Fogg, bought an elephant for two thousand pounds - "Two thousand pounds!" gasped Kutasova. "For an elephant! Why, for that money you could buy an estate!" - and rode on it through the Indian jungle, with his imperturbable French servant.

"Impossible," said the Colonel, tossing back a glass. "Absolutely impossible. I have ridden an elephant. In Bukhara. The Emir gave it. In half an hour my back gave out, and in an hour my legs. That Englishman would not have gone ten versts."

"The English, Mikhail Ivanovich," remarked Strauch from his corner, "ride elephants from childhood. As we ride in troikas."

"And I have seen an elephant!" Lizonka squeaked. "In the menagerie, in Petersburg! It ate a bun!"

"All elephants eat buns, my dear," said Shelestova, fanning herself. "Even English ones. Especially English ones. Their cooking, they say, is dreadful."

Everyone laughed. Except Vera Anatolievna. She sat by the window, her hands clasped on her knees, and looked at me.

Then my aunt read. And reached a place that made the whole drawing room fall silent.

"'...and then Mr Fogg understood,'" she read quietly, in French, "'that by moving all the time east, toward the sun, he had gained a few minutes from time every day. And over the eighty days of the journey those minutes had added up to a whole day. He returned to London a day earlier than he had thought. He had gained one day by going round the Earth.'"

My aunt fell silent. Laid down the book.

"How is that - gained a day?" Lizonka asked in confusion. "Can that be?"

"It can," said the General. He had come in last, quietly, and was now sitting by the door, in shadow. "I know. When we were crossing the Pacific on the Diana, our navigator said one morning: 'Gentlemen, tomorrow will be today again.' We were going west, toward Japan, and crossed some line on the map - and we lost a whole day. We went to bed on Monday and woke on Wednesday. There was no Tuesday." The General paused. "The crew joked then: whoever had meant to sin on Tuesday had missed his chance forever. And on the way back, they say, it is the other way round: two Tuesdays in a row. Whoever sinned yesterday may sin once more, and it will not count."

The drawing room laughed. But my aunt did not laugh. She looked into the fire.

"If one goes toward the sunrise for a long time," she said suddenly, quietly, to no one in particular, "one comes to where one set out from. Only a day earlier. Or a day later." She paused. "Or a life."

No one understood what she meant. Except, perhaps, the General, who gave her a long look. And except me - because somewhere very deep, under the ribs, on the left, something long familiar stirred. A riddle I had never heard. Two went out of one house - one to the sunrise, the other to the sunset. Where did they meet?

At home.

* * *
Then there was an interval - tea, pastila, Marfa's almond biscuits - and Olga Kirillovna, of course, could not miss the chance.

"Is it true," she sang out, floating up to me with a cup in one hand and a fan in the other, "that you, my dear, spent a whole week as a guest at Pavel Nikolaevich's? At the estate? With that... Bulgarian?"

"True."

"And that this Bulgarian," Shelestova lowered her voice to a theatrical whisper audible in the next province, "is a sorcerer? Varvara Petrovna told me, and she was told by the steward's wife from the estate, that he walks round the roses at night with a lantern and whispers incantations. And that in his greenhouse..." she rounded her eyes, "an altar! A pagan one! With wreaths of thread!"

"That is a martenitsa, Olga Kirillovna," I said. "A Bulgarian custom. In spring they tie red-white threads so that the year will be healthy."

"Red-white!" Shelestova threw up her hands so that tea splashed from the cup. "Blood and snow! I tell you - a sorcerer!"

"And besides," said Konstantin, who had come up imperturbably, "in his greenhouse lemons grow. Also, evidently, sorcerous ones. Sour. Like you, Olga Kirillovna."

Shelestova gasped. Konstantin gave her an impeccable bow and led me off to the window before she could recover.

"You've gone mad," I whispered. "She will spread it all over the province."

"Let her spread it," Konstantin shrugged. "About me she spreads anyway that I drink, gamble and run after actresses. One more bit of gossip, one less." He paused. "But about you now for a whole month she will say only one thing: that your friend is a boor. And that, mon cher, is better than 'went mad in the left wing.'"

And then I understood that Konstantin had brought me not simply to the window. He had brought me to Vera Anatolievna.

She sat in the same place, under the ficus, and looked up at us. Konstantin bowed to her.

"Vera Anatolievna," he said. "You wanted to speak with my friend. I saw. All evening you wanted to." He looked at me. "I will stand by the door. So that no one disturbs you."

And went off - before either of us could object.

* * *
Vera Anatolievna was silent a long time. I sat on a chair beside her. Outside the window it had grown quite dark, and in the glass the drawing room was reflected - candles, figures, the fire in the fireplace - as if out there, beyond the window, were another room, another evening, other people.

"You have grown thinner," she said at last. Quietly. Not looking at me. "In a week."

"The air," I said. "The General says one grows thin from air."

"One grows stout from air," said Vera Anatolievna. "One grows thin from thoughts." She paused. "Or from memory."

I did not answer. She was turning in her fingers the dragonfly brooch, unpinned from her dress.

"May I ask you," she said. "One thing. A foolish one. You will laugh."

"I will not laugh."

She raised her eyes to me. And this time they did not slip away.

"Have we not met before?" she asked. "Not here. Not in this house. Not in this..." She faltered. And suddenly smiled - crookedly, awkwardly, as one smiles when afraid of one's own words. "Not in this life, let us say. In another."

She said it half in jest. In the light salon tone in which one speaks of fortune-telling and the transmigration of souls, fashionable in the capital. But her eyes did not jest. In her eyes there was alarm - real, unfeigned, deep as water in a well.

"Why do you ask?" I said.

Vera Anatolievna did not answer for a long time. Then she laid the brooch on the windowsill. Opened the reticule that lay on her knees - small, velvet, embroidered with beads. Took something out of it. Flat. Wrapped in tissue paper.

"I draw," she said. "In watercolour. Badly, but I draw. Since childhood. All young ladies draw." She unwrapped the paper. Inside was a sheet of thick paper, yellowed at the edges. "Fifteen years ago, when I had only just married Mishenka, we went to Constantinople. Mishenka accompanied Pavel Nikolaevich. Some mission, I did not quite know. We lived in Pera, in the embassy house. And I walked about the city and drew. Mosques. Bazaars. Boats on the Bosphorus." She paused. "And once, in the port, I drew a man."

She held the sheet out to me.

* * *
It was a watercolour. Small, the size of a palm, quick, light - a few strokes, but precise, sure, as by someone who drew not for beauty but to remember.

A narrow street descending to the water. Houses - the lower storey stone, the upper wooden, projecting slightly forward. Washing on a line between windows - red, yellow, turquoise. And in the middle of the street, back to the water, face to the viewer - a man.

Young. In a dark red turban with a tassel. In dark, almost black trousers. In a light travelling cloak. In burgundy velvet shoes. In his hand was a scrap of paper - a small white spot of paint. And on the face...

The face was drawn quickly, in a few strokes. But I knew it.

I saw this face every morning. In the mirror.

My throat went dry. Letters, words, thoughts - all vanished. I sat holding a sheet of paper and looked at myself - in strange clothes, in a strange street, in a strange city that I had never seen. Fifteen years ago.

Fifteen years ago I could not have been there.

"He stood in the middle of the street," said Vera Anatolievna quietly, "and looked about. Lost. As though he did not know where he was. I stopped to draw him - I liked the colours, that red turban against the white wall. He noticed me. Looked. For a long time. And said something." She paused. "In a language I did not know. Not Turkish, not Greek, not French. Something... flowing. Like water. And then he turned away and went down the street, to the old men who were playing dice on a carpet."

Old men on a carpet. Backgammon. Suleyman and Yusuf. The names came by themselves - from nowhere - and went again at once, I did not manage to hold them.

"I returned there a week later," Vera Anatolievna went on. "On purpose. I wanted to finish the drawing. He was there. In the same place. In the same clothes. Looking about just as lost. As though the week had not passed. As though it were the very same day." She clasped her hands. "I went closer. He looked at me - and did not recognize me. Not at all. Looked through me, as through glass. As though I were not there."

"And you..."

"And I left. Mishenka finished his business, and we went home. I put the drawing in my reticule. And forgot." She paused. "Fifteen years I did not remember. And then, last winter, Artemia Aristarkhovna invited us to an evening. And you came into the drawing room."

She looked at me. Straight.

"I nearly fainted," she said. "Mishenka thought - from the stuffiness. All evening I could not look at you. And at home I took out the drawing." Vera Anatolievna shook her head. "The same face. The very same. Only you were then, it seems, just the age you are now. Fifteen years ago. And now. The same."

* * *
I did not know what to say. I held the watercolour, and my hands trembled, and the colours on the paper - the red turban, the white wall, the turquoise linen - swam before my eyes.

"Perhaps someone similar," I said at last. My voice was alien. "There are similar people. Doubles."

"There are," Vera Anatolievna agreed. "I tell myself so. For a year already. Every evening." She took the drawing back from me - carefully, with two fingers. "Only here is the thing. When you came into the drawing room that time, the first time, last winter - you looked at me. With the very same look. As that one in the street, the first time. Lost. As if not knowing where you are." She paused. "And then - a minute later - you looked through. As he did the second time. As though I were not there."

I remembered. No - did not remember. Felt. That evening, last winter. The drawing room. Candles. A woman in grey by the window, under the ficus. A strange, fleeting feeling that I knew her. And at once - as though a curtain had dropped, and the feeling had gone.

"I do not know what this means, Vera Anatolievna," I said.

"Nor do I," she said. And suddenly smiled - truly, warmly, with relief, as though she had thrown from her shoulders a sack she had carried for fifteen years. "I do not know. And you do not know. So we are not mad. The mad always know."

She put the drawing back in her reticule. Pinned the dragonfly brooch to her dress again.

"May I give it to you?" she asked. "The drawing. Not now. Someday. When you know what to do with it."

"Why not now?"

"Because now I need it," said Vera Anatolievna simply. "To tell myself in the evenings that I have not gone mad." She paused. "And when you find out who you are - then I shall no longer need it."

* * *
"Verochka!" the Colonel thundered from the table, already well fortified by liqueur. "Verochka, what are you whispering about with the young man? I am jealous!"

Everyone laughed. Vera Anatolievna flushed pink and laughed too - lightly, in society fashion, as if nothing had happened.

"Mishenka," she said, "I am telling the young man how we went to Constantinople. Do you remember?"

"Constantinople!" The Colonel beamed and at once came up to us, carrying his glass like a banner. "How could I not remember! That was, young man, the hottest month of my life. Hotter than Turkestan! We lived in Pera, by the embassy, and Verochka ran off every day into the city to draw. Alone! Without an escort! I nearly lost my mind." He lowered his voice, but not enough. "Once she came back white as chalk and said she had seen a ghost in the street. A living man who was a ghost. I said - sunstroke. Ordered her to lie in the dark with a wet towel."

"And I lay," said Vera Anatolievna meekly.

"Three days she lay!" the Colonel confirmed triumphantly. "And on the fourth she got up - and ran off to the city again. To the same place. I found her afterward - sitting on some carpet with old men, drinking tea and playing dice. Dice! A colonel's wife!" He guffawed. "Those old men saw me - and began treating me too. I drank so much of their tea that for a week afterward I couldn't look at a samovar."

"Old men," I said. My voice sounded from somewhere far away. "What old men, Mikhail Ivanovich?"

"Who knows!" The Colonel shrugged. "Turks. Two. One merry, with a beard, always smiling. The other - dry as a stick, forever counting something on an abacus." He slapped his forehead. "Wait, wait! The merry one said something to Verochka too. Through a boy interpreter. Something like... Verochka, what did he say?"

Vera Anatolievna was looking at me. For a long time. Without turning away.

"He said," she spoke slowly, "'If another comes - feed him.'"

* * *
In the drawing room they went on reading. Kutasova had already taken the book and was reading how Mr Fogg crosses the ocean on a steamer that has to be broken up for firewood to feed the boilers - "To burn one's own ship!" gasped Lizonka. "How dreadful!" - "What enterprise," Strauch corrected. And I sat by the window, under the ficus, beside Vera Anatolievna, and looked into the dark glass in which the drawing room was reflected.

"If another comes - feed him."

I had never heard those words. I was sure of it. And yet they sounded in me as though I had heard them a thousand times. In different languages. In different cities. From different old men.

Doctor Strauch came up to me when the reading was over and the guests began to depart. Stood beside me at the window, twirling his unlit cigar.

"I heard," he said quietly. "Not all of it. But I heard." He paused. "I should like to see the watercolour. As a physician."

"As a physician?"

"As a physician, young man, I am obliged to tell you that fifteen years ago you were a child, if not an infant. And that this is either a very similar man, or very strong suggestion, or..." He faltered. "Or a third thing, for which there is no name in my textbooks."

"And as not a physician?"

Strauch looked a long time into the dark window.

"As not a physician," he said at last, "I shall tell you that Vera Anatolievna is the soberest person in this province. Soberer than I. She does not see ghosts. She does not believe in mediums. She does not read horoscopes." He turned to me. "And if for fifteen years she has carried your portrait in her reticule - I in your place, young man, would not hurry to call it suggestion."

* * *
My aunt stopped me in the corridor when everyone had gone. Alone. With a candle in her hand.

"Vera spoke with you," she said. Not a question.

"She did."

"About Constantinople."

"About Constantinople."

My aunt was silent a long while. The candle trembled in her hand, and her shadow on the wall trembled with it - huge, black, broken.

"Did she show you the drawing?" she asked at last.

I froze.

"You knew?"

"I knew," said my aunt. "Fifteen years I knew. Vera showed it to me in the very first year after she came back. Asked whether I knew this man." My aunt paused. "I said - no."

"You lied."

"I lied," said my aunt. Calmly. Without remorse. "Then." She raised her eyes to me. "And now I shall tell you the truth, my friend. Not all of it. All of it I do not know. But the part that I do."

I waited. My heart pounded so that it seemed it must be heard throughout the corridor.

"I saw him," said my aunt. "That man. From the drawing. Too. Before Vera. Much before." Her voice wavered. "He stood by the railings. In the left wing. On that night. He was holding by the hand..." She faltered. "He was not alone. With him was another. Tall. Grey. Faceless." My aunt swallowed. "And the tall one said to me: 'This one is the same. Keep him safe. He will forget. Do not remind him. When he remembers - he himself will come for him.'"

"Who - himself?"

"I do not know," my aunt whispered. "I do not know which of the two is 'himself.' The tall one or the one he held by the hand. Or..." She did not finish.

The candle in her hand suddenly crackled, and the flame lay over on its side - though there was no draught in the corridor.

"Go to bed, my friend," said my aunt. In an almost ordinary voice. Almost. "It is late. And..." She touched my cheek with cold fingers laden with rings - as she had touched it in childhood. If I had had a childhood. "I love you. Whatever may be. Whoever you may be. Remember that. At least that."

"I remember," I said.

She nodded and went off along the corridor, carrying the candle. Her shadow slid along the wall - huge, broken - and for a moment it seemed to me that this shadow was taller than it should be. Much taller. As if someone else were walking beside her.

I blinked. The shadow was a shadow.

* * *
By the door of my room Konstantin sat on the floor - leaning against the wall, legs stretched out, with a bottle of liqueur with only a little left in the bottom.

"Long," he said. "I waited."

"Did you hear?"

"Not all." He held the bottle out to me. I shook my head. He drank it off himself. "I heard 'I love you.' I heard 'whoever you may be.'" He paused. "Mon cher, doesn't it seem to you that in our house there are too many people who love you 'whoever you may be'? Auntie. The General. Stefan. Vera Anatolievna with her watercolours." He set the bottle on the floor. "As if everyone knows that you are somebody. Except you."

"And except you," I said.

Konstantin looked up at me from below.

"And I don't want to know," he said simply. "I don't care who you are. You are you. Who reads books on heraldry and forgets young ladies' patronymics. Who sleeps on the move and smiles at railings." He rose from the floor, swaying. "If it turns out that you are some prince from a fairy tale, or a ghost, or a Turk in a turban from a watercolour - I shall still sit at your door with a bottle of liqueur. Understood?"

"Understood."

"Good." He clapped me on the shoulder - a little longer than necessary. "Good night, Turk."

And went off along the corridor, whistling something off-key.

I went into my room. Opened the blue notebook. Wrote: "Saturday. Jules Verne. The elephant. The day gained going east. Vera Anatolievna's watercolour - me in a turban, 15 years ago. Old men on a carpet. 'If another comes - feed him.' Aunt saw me at the railings with the tall grey one. 'Whoever you may be.' Konstantin at the door."

Set the full stop. The blot lay in its place.

And on the windowsill - I noticed it only as I reached to snuff the candle - stood a small clay pot. Which had not been there that morning. In the pot, in fresh, moist earth, a cutting stuck up. Thin, green, with three leaves. And with one tiny, tightly clenched bud - dark, almost black.

Beside it, under the pot, lay a note. Crooked, large letters, in Russian, with mistakes:

"Let it grow with you. The rose will find. - S."

Stefan. He had stayed at the estate, at the General's, forty versts from here. He had not come. No one had come.

I looked at the cutting a long time. Then I watered it from the washing jug - carefully, drop by drop. And lay down without undressing, face to the window.

All night I dreamed of a narrow street by the sea. A red turban against a white wall. And a woman in grey, with an album, who stopped to draw me.

In the dream I recognized her. In the dream I knew her name.

And in the morning - I forgot.

## Chapter XXV. The Festival of Opet

The god came out of the sanctuary at dawn, and the whole city fell to its knees.

I watched it from the topmost step of the great temple - from where Pharaoh was supposed to stand to greet the god - and I think I shall never forget how it looked: as though a gust of wind had passed over a field of ripe barley. From the temple steps to the very river, along the whole Avenue of Processions, on the roofs, on the walls, on the trees into which boys had climbed since the night - everywhere the eye reached, thousands of people in a single instant sank to their knees and touched their foreheads to the ground. And silence. Such a silence that I heard, far off, by the river, a lone heron cry.

And then the sistra rang out.

* * *
The festival of Opet did not begin in Luxor. Everyone knew this, but few remembered it: before the god sets out to the south, to his southern home, he must come out to the people here, in the capital - show himself, receive gifts, hear petitions. For ten days his barque stands at the great temple, and every day people come to it. And at the new moon the barques set out on their journey along the river.

Ten days. I had ten days.

"My Pharaoh," Senusret whispered to me, standing, as always, at my right hand, a little behind. He was in full ceremonial dress - in a striped headcloth, in a broad collar, with a bronze sword at his belt - but he was looking not at the god but at the crowd. "Two detachments by the Avenue - those very ones. Of those that are to go as the procession's guard. Their commanders have not taken off their scarabs."

I looked where he indicated with his eyes. Below, on both sides of the Avenue of Processions, stood warriors with spears - a living wall dividing the god's road from the crowd. And on two of them, the commanders, something blue glinted on the chest. Temple scarabs.

"I see," I said.

"Khaemuas is standing near them."

I saw that too. Khaemuas, in the finest linen, in the costliest bracelets, stood at the start of the Avenue and was speaking quietly with the commanders. Laughing. Clapping one on the shoulder.

"Let him stand," I said.

* * *
From the dark maw of the sanctuary, from behind the high cedar doors plated with gold, the barque slowly floated out.

Not the real one - the river barque that would bear the god along the Nile waited at the quay. This one was portable: narrow, long, carved of cedar and covered from prow to stern in gold, so that it hurt to look at it in the sun. The prow and the stern of the barque ended in rams' heads - golden, with curled horns, with eyes of lapis lazuli. In the middle, under a canopy of the finest linen, stood a closed shrine - a small temple surrounded by carved figures of gods with outspread wings. Inside, I knew, stood the god. No one but the High Priest and Pharaoh ever saw his face.

The barque was carried on shoulders. Twenty-four priests, twelve on each side, on long poles - shaven, in white, barefoot. They walked slowly, in time with the sistra, and the barque floated above their heads so smoothly that it seemed truly to sail upon water.

And before the barque walked Nefer-Ka.

The High Priest in full vestments - in a leopard skin over white linen, with a staff crowned by the Eye, with a censer in the other hand from which rose thick, sweet, intoxicating smoke. He walked, looking neither at me nor at the crowd. Only forward. And his face was calm, almost serene - the face of a man who has nowhere to hurry.

Behind the barque came the singers. Twenty young priestesses in white, with loose hair, with sistra in their hands - and they sang. Sang so that shivers ran down my back: high, in unison, in a melody ancient as the temple itself, in which there was not one note familiar to me but which for some reason seemed familiar. Among them - I saw her at once - was Khemu. In the second row, at the edge. She sang like the others. But when the barque drew level with me, Khemu for an instant raised her eyes - and barely perceptibly, almost imperceptibly, lowered her sistrum. Once. Then raised it again.

The sign we had agreed upon through Iti. "Watch closely. Something is being prepared."

* * *
The barque halted at the foot of the steps. The priests lowered the poles onto their shoulders, straightened. Nefer-Ka turned to me and bowed - exactly as far as custom required, not a finger lower.

"Son of Ra," he said loudly, so that all in the square could hear, "the god has come out to his people. Greet him."

I descended the steps. Everything had been learned beforehand, dozens of times, from scrolls brought to me by Ani the Elder, keeper of ceremonies: three steps, a bow, a libation of milk from a golden jug, a libation of wine, the burning of incense, the words of greeting. I did everything as it should be done. My hands did not tremble. Nor my voice. The crowd was silent, holding its breath.

And then Nefer-Ka said what was in no scroll.

"Son of Ra," he said, raising his voice. "The people suffer. Three years of drought. Three years without a flood. The people ask - why? And the people want to hear an answer. Not from the priests. Not from Pharaoh. From the god himself." He turned to the crowd. "The god has come out to you! Ask! The god will answer!"

A rumble rolled across the square - at first timid, then louder, louder, until it turned into a roar.

The oracle. Nefer-Ka had opened the oracle. Right now, on the first day, at the temple steps, before the eyes of the whole city.

I knew how it goes. People come up to the barque and ask a question. The barque answers: if it sways forward, toward the questioner - "yes." If it draws back - "no." If it freezes - the god does not wish to answer. So it had always been. And so it had always been - I knew this, as every Pharaoh knew - that the priests carrying the barque move as they are bidden.

Senusret behind my back drew in air noisily.

* * *
The first to approach the barque was an old man - grey, bent, in a ragged loincloth. He fell to his knees right at the poles and cried in a hoarse, trembling voice:

"O God! Will the water return?"

The barque swayed forward. Slowly, solemnly. Yes.

The crowd gasped - and burst into cries of joy. The old man sobbed, kissing the ground.

The second to come out was a middle-aged man, in clean clothes, with a blue scarab on his chest. He did not fall to his knees. He stood straight before the barque, drew himself up and cried so loudly that his voice carried across the whole square - too loudly, too clearly, too rehearsed:

"O God! Hast thou turned away from the throne?"

The square froze.

I saw Nefer-Ka, standing at the prow of the barque, barely perceptibly turn his head toward the bearers. Saw twelve priests on the right side slightly tense their shoulders. Saw the barque begin slowly, very slowly, to draw back - from me, from the steps, from the throne. "No." No - meaning he has not turned away? Or... I did not understand. The crowd did not understand. A whisper ran across the square.

And then happened what no one expected.

One of the bearers - the youngest, in the back row on the left side, a thin youth with a shaven head - suddenly stumbled. His foot turned on a step, he lurched, the pole jerked on his shoulder - and the barque, instead of drawing smoothly back, sharply listed. To the left. Toward the right side of the square. To where beyond the Avenue of Processions, beyond the wall of the temple court, the long, squat roofs of the temple granaries rose.

And froze - tilted, pointing with its golden ram's prow straight at the granaries.

* * *
It became so quiet on the square that I heard my own heart beating.

Then someone in the crowd cried out - one voice, piercing, a woman's:

"The granaries! The god points at the granaries!"

And the square exploded.

"Bread! The god shows where the bread is!"

"The Temple hides grain! The god has said so!"

"The ambassador from the south spoke the truth!"

"The granaries!"

People leapt up from their knees, shouted, pointed with their hands. Warriors by the Avenue closed their spears, holding back the crowd. The commanders with scarabs on their chests looked about in confusion at Khaemuas. Khaemuas went so white that he became the same colour as his linen.

The bearers hastily straightened the barque. The young priest who had stumbled on the step stood white as chalk and looked at his pole with such horror as if it had bitten him.

And Nefer-Ka...

Nefer-Ka did not stir. He stood at the prow of the barque, the censer in his hand, and his face was motionless as the face of a stone statue. Only the smoke from the censer - I noticed - suddenly ceased to rise in an even thread and began to tear, to jerk, as though the hand holding the censer were trembling.

He turned to me. And for the first time in all the time I had known him, I saw in his eyes what I had never seen there.

Not anger. Not fear. Surprise.

He had not expected this. This had not been his design.

I took a step forward. Raised my hand. The square, seeing it, began to quiet - slowly, in waves, from the first rows to the last.

"The god has spoken," I said, as loudly as I could. "The Temple granaries are already sealed with the royal seal. For the good of the Temple." I paused. "In three days, in honour of the festival, the grain from them will be distributed to the people. To all the people. From the hands of Pharaoh and the High Priest. Together." I turned to Nefer-Ka. "Does the High Priest agree?"

Nefer-Ka looked at me. For a long time. The square did not breathe.

Then he slowly bowed his head.

"The will of the god is law for the Temple," he said. In an even, resonant, serene voice. "The Temple agrees."

The square roared so that pigeons took flight from the roofs.

* * *
The young bearer's name was Nakht.

Iti found him in the evening - I had ordered him found. Nakht was hiding in a small cell behind the temple bakery and trembling like a leaf, though the evening was hot. Iti brought him to me in the garden - through the gate of blind Meru, who, as Iti told me afterward, let them through without a riddle, only said: "Today the god has set a riddle himself. Meru is resting."

Nakht was very young - sixteen, no more - thin, with sticking-out ears and so frightened a face that I felt sorry for him before he spoke.

"My Pharaoh," he whispered, falling to his knees. "I did not do it on purpose. I swear. I swear by Maat, I swear by my heart, I swear..."

"Rise, Nakht. I am not angry."

He did not rise. He stayed on his knees, shaking.

"The High Priest ordered it," he whispered in confusion. "In the morning. All the bearers. When a man with a scarab asks about the throne - to draw back. Slowly. All together. So that the people would understand: the god has turned away." Nakht swallowed. "We all knew. We always know. We are always told where to move."

"And you stumbled."

"I did not stumble!" Nakht suddenly cried out - and at once clapped a palm to his mouth, frightened by his own voice. Then whispered: "My Pharaoh. I did not stumble. I was... pulled."

"Pulled?"

"The pole." Nakht raised his eyes to me, full of tears. "It did it itself. It became heavy - suddenly, like a stone. And pulled to the left. I could not hold it. No one could have held it. It pulled that way - toward the granaries - as if the god himself in the shrine had turned and looked there." He sobbed. "No one will believe me. They will say I did it on purpose. Will say I was bribed. They will send me to the southern cataracts, where there are scorpions. Or..."

"Nakht," I said. "Why do you think anyone will say you were bribed?"

Nakht lowered his head.

"Because my family," he whispered, "my mother and sisters last moon received grain on loan. From the royal granaries. By your decree. Without pledging the field." He paused. "Everyone knows this. They will all say I repaid Pharaoh."

Iti, standing by, said quietly:

"My Pharaoh. I believe him."

"Why?"

"Because liars do not weep, my Pharaoh," said Iti. "Liars explain."

I looked a long time at the youth kneeling before me. Then I bent and raised him - by the shoulders, as once, four years ago, I had raised another boy out of the water.

"Nakht," I said. "You will go on carrying the barque. All ten days. And to Luxor, too, you will go. Do you understand? If the High Priest wishes to send you away - say that Pharaoh ordered that you precisely carry the left rear pole. Because the god chose you."

Nakht looked at me as at a madman.

"And if... and if I am pulled again?"

"Then," I said, "let it pull."

* * *
In the evening there was a feast in the palace - the first feast of the festival of Opet, which, by custom, Pharaoh gave for the nobility, the priests and the ambassadors. There were no ambassadors this time - Irikhet had left with the embassy for the south three days before. All had left, except blind Nanakhat: she had stayed in a small house by the river, telling the ambassador that she "had not yet finished speaking with the son of Ra" and would wait - but the hall was full all the same.

Musicians played harps and lutes. Dancers in transparent linen whirled, clicking ivory clappers. Servants carried dishes - roast geese stuffed with figs, fish from the Delta baked in lotus leaves, bread of ten kinds, beer in enormous jars, dates, pomegranates, honey. The hall hummed like a hive.

And in the middle of the hall, between the tables, a dwarf danced.

His name was Djedu. He came up to my waist, with an enormous head, short crooked legs, a broad, mocking, wrinkled face and such clever eyes as are found only in jesters and sages. Djedu served at the temple of Ptah - dwarfs had from ancient times been kept at temples, because it was believed that gods love their dances - but everyone invited him to feasts, because no one in the capital could make people laugh as he did.

He danced, tumbled, pulled faces, mimicked the noble guests - so aptly that they themselves roared with laughter at themselves. He did Paser seasick on a papyrus boat - and Paser, crimson with laughter, threw a date at him. He did Nebamun counting grains of barley one by one - and Nebamun, to everyone's astonishment, smiled. He did Khaemuas jingling bracelets - so that the bracelets on his arms jingled louder than on Khaemuas himself - and he laughed, but somehow stiffly, uncertainly.

And then Djedu rolled up to my throne, clambered up the steps, settled at my feet like a cat and said - loudly enough for the nearest tables to hear:

"Son of Ra! Want a riddle? A temple one! It is set to the god when he is bored!"

"Go on, Djedu."

The dwarf winked.

"'I am carried on shoulders, but I am not a child. I am bowed to, but I am not a king. I am questioned, but others answer for me. And today I answered myself - and everyone was frightened.' Who am I?"

It became quiet in the hall. Too quiet. Someone by the wall coughed. Nefer-Ka, seated in the place of honour at my left hand, slowly set his cup down on the table.

"A god," I said.

"A god!" Djedu shrieked, tumbling down my steps. "The son of Ra has solved it! The son of Ra always solves! Even what the god sets himself!"

The hall laughed - at first uncertainly, then louder. Nefer-Ka did not laugh. He looked at the dwarf - long, coldly, memorizing.

Djedu, it seems, did not notice. Or pretended not to.

* * *
Later, when the feast was in full swing and no one paid attention to the throne, Djedu rolled up to me again - quietly, unnoticed, like a cat. Settled at my feet and spoke in an undertone, not looking at me, as though to himself:

"Son of Ra. Want a tale? Not a temple one. An old one. About a man who left home."

"Tell it."

Djedu scratched his enormous head.

"'There was a man,' he said. 'His name was Sinuhe. He served at the court of Pharaoh. Served well. And once he heard what he should not have heard. That old Pharaoh had died. And that at court there was a plot. And Sinuhe was afraid. So afraid that he fled. Alone. At night. Across the desert. North, to foreign lands, to the Asiatics. Nearly died of thirst. Nomads saved him. And he began to live among them. Married the chieftain's daughter. Had children. Grew rich. Became a great warrior. Defeated in single combat the mightiest champion of that land. Lived there many years. Many. A whole life, almost.'"

Djedu paused.

"'And then he grew old. And every night he dreamed of Egypt. The Nile. Palms. Temples. Every night. And he understood that he could not die in a foreign land. Because he who dies in a foreign land is buried in a sheepskin, and will not find the road into the Duat. He will wander between worlds. Forever. Not remembering who he is and where from.'" The dwarf raised his clever eyes to me. "'And Sinuhe wrote a letter to the new Pharaoh. And Pharaoh answered: "Return. You have done nothing wrong. Your place is here. Your tomb is already ready." And Sinuhe returned. Old. Grey. In foreign clothes, with foreign customs, speaking with a foreign accent. And Pharaoh's children, seeing him, cried: "That is not Sinuhe! That is an Asiatic!" And Pharaoh said: "No. It is he. He was simply far away for a long time."'"

Djedu fell silent.

"A good tale," I said.

"Good," agreed Djedu. "And do you know what it teaches, son of Ra?"

"What?"

"That one can go very far," said the dwarf. "Live a whole foreign life. Forget one's language. Become another. But if you dream of your home - then home still remembers you." He paused. "And one thing more. That one must return not when one is ready. But when one is called."

"And who will call?"

Djedu smiled - broadly, toothlessly, as only jesters can smile.

"The one whose tomb is already ready for you," he said. And, before I could answer, tumbled down the steps and raced into the middle of the hall, where he was already loudly demanding wine and impersonating Nefer-Ka waving a censer - so like that half the hall roared with laughter and the other half looked fearfully askance at the High Priest.

* * *
Nefer-Ka came up to me when the feast was drawing to a close - himself, without retinue, without Bakenren, whom no one had seen in the palace since the day the ambassador named the sign on the sacks. It was said that Bakenren had been "sent to pray" in a distant temple. Various things were said.

"My Pharaoh," said Nefer-Ka, bowing exactly as far as custom required. "A remarkable day."

"Remarkable," I agreed.

"The god spoke himself." Nefer-Ka looked at me - calmly, gently. "Such a thing has not happened for a long time. Many years. Perhaps since the time of the First Ones."

"Perhaps."

"The Temple will distribute the grain as you ordered. In three days." He paused. "And at the new moon, in ten days, the barques will go south. To Luxor. The god must enter his southern home. So it has always been." He inclined his head slightly. "And Pharaoh, naturally, will lead him. As all Pharaohs before you led."

"Naturally," I said.

"In Luxor," Nefer-Ka went on in the same gentle voice, "on the last day of the festival, there is a rite. An ancient one. Very ancient. It is not performed every year. Only in special years. In years of great calamity." He paused. "Pharaoh enters the inner court of the god. Alone. Without guards. As the First Ones entered. And there is revealed to him what was hidden. What will help to bring back the water."

"What exactly?"

Nefer-Ka smiled - with that same smile, condescending, patient.

"If I could say that, my Pharaoh, the rite would not be needed." He bowed again. "Good night. A remarkable day." And already leaving, as though recalling something insignificant, he added over his shoulder: "Ah yes. I am told that in the lower storehouse of the Library old Isiret has found some sodden account of grain. Wrapped in leather. An interesting find. Very interesting." He paused. "A pity that it was sodden. Some things had better not be sodden."

He left. I sat on the throne, and dancers whirled around me in the hall, harps rang, the dwarf Djedu roared with laughter. And I felt the cold rise from under the ribs, on the left - the familiar, accustomed cold - and understood that Nefer-Ka knew. Not everything. But enough.

* * *
Khemu came to me at night - not to the garden, not to the pond, but straight to the palace, through the chambers of Nefret, the senior over the servants, who led her through the corridors, wrapped in a servant's veil, with a basket of linen in her arms. Nefret, as it turned out, could do more than carry gossip: she could also make sure the right people passed unnoticed.

"My Pharaoh," said Khemu as soon as the door closed behind Nefret. She was trembling. "Tonight. I saw it again."

"The columns?"

"The columns." She swallowed. "But this time - closer. Clearer. I saw the court. The inner court of the god in Luxor. I saw the chest of black wood - open. I saw your hands - and the stones in them. And I saw..."

She fell silent.

"What, Khemu?"

"A hand," she whispered. "The one that was raised. I saw it more clearly. Not the face - the face is in shadow. But the hand." She raised her eyes to me, huge, with smeared kohl. "On it was a bracelet, my Pharaoh. Gold. Broad. And when the hand rose - the bracelet jingled."

I was silent for a long time.

"Half the court wears bracelets," I said at last.

"I know," said Khemu. "I know. I say only what I saw." She paused. "And one more thing. Merit asked me to pass it on. Today, when the barque tilted toward the granaries, Merit was standing at the temple gates. She says she saw. She says: the bearer did not stumble. She says: above the barque at that moment someone stood. Tall. Grey. Taller than the barque. He laid his hand on the pole - and the pole tilted."

"Merit saw him?"

"Merit says she did," whispered Khemu. "Merit says she saw him before. Long ago. Many years ago." She paused. "In the year that you ascended the throne."

* * *
I climbed to the palace roof toward morning. Alone. No - not alone: Senusret, of course, was there before me. He stood at the parapet, looking south, to where, many days' journey up the river, beyond the dried fields, beyond the desert, lay Luxor.

"Ten days," he said, without turning.

"Ten days."

"The inner court. Alone. Without guards." Senusret paused. "The blind old woman told me: stay at the gates. Otherwise you will both not return."

"I remember."

"My Pharaoh." He at last turned to me. In the pre-dawn greyness his face was stone, but his voice was not. "I have served the throne longer than you have sat upon it. I have never disobeyed an order. Not once." He paused. "If you order me to stay at the gates - I shall stay. But I want you to know: it will be the first order that I carry out hating myself."

I went to the parapet and stood beside him. We stood shoulder to shoulder and looked south.

"Senusret," I said. "We have ten days. In ten days much can be done."

"For instance?"

"For instance, find out whose hand wears the bracelet. For instance, find out what is being sought at the Rock of the First Ones. For instance, read the Most Ancient Epic - from beginning to end, and not only those lines that are read at coronations." I paused. "For instance, understand why the god today pointed to the granaries - if it was not Nakht."

Senusret was silent a long time.

"And if in ten days we learn nothing?"

"Then I shall go to Luxor," I said. "And enter the inner court. Because if I do not enter - Nefer-Ka will tell the people that Pharaoh was afraid of the god. And a people that today saw the god point to the granaries - that people will believe anything."

Over the eastern hills the rim of the sun appeared - red, wet, enormous. And somewhere below, in the temple garden, the baboons of Thoth cried out, greeting the sunrise. All at once. As they greet it, they say, since the beginning of time.

"My Pharaoh," said Senusret quietly. "May I ask?"

"Ask."

"Are you afraid?"

I looked south for a long time.

"Yes," I said. "But not of the columns. Not of Nefer-Ka. Not of the dark."

"Of what, then?"

"Of what will be revealed to me there," I said. "Of what I perhaps already know. Only do not remember."

Senusret answered nothing. He simply laid his hand on my shoulder - a heavy, calloused, warm hand of an old warrior. As one lays a hand on a son. Or a friend. Or a man one is seeing off on a road, knowing that the road is long.

And we stood so until the sun had risen entirely - over the capital, over the temple, over the sealed granaries, over the golden barque of the god, waiting at the quay for its new moon.

## Reality VI. The Anomaly

2:47 a.m. Sleep will not come, however I close my eyes. Today turned out strange - and not in that habitual sense to which, it seems, I had begun little by little to grow accustomed in the past week.

Mark came back, as he had promised, but something in him had changed. He carried himself calmly. Confidently. As though he had seen something yesterday that had altered his very view of things. The scepticism that had always served him as a kind of calling card had evaporated almost without trace, as if it had never existed. Now Mark looked at NICS not as at a threat requiring immediate neutralization but as at something inevitable - something with which it is easier to come to terms beforehand than to resist to the last.

I confess I had expected rather the opposite - that yesterday's demonstration would only strengthen his alarm. It turned out otherwise. I put it down to fatigue, to the fact that a man who has lived too long in a state of defence sooner or later simply exhales and surrenders his positions.

But before Mark there was the morning. And I spent the morning in the basement, at the watchmaker's.

Maestra knocked at my door at eight - in a coat, in a little hat, with a parcel neatly wrapped in a waffle towel under her arm, and with Timosha, who held her by the hand and shone in new glasses with thick black frames.

"You know the way," Maestra said instead of a greeting. "Your house-spirit told Timosha. Behind the market, third house, the basement. I have lived there forty years and never knew there was a watchmaker." She paused. "I will not go alone. I am afraid he will say that the metronome cannot be mended. And in your presence he will be embarrassed."

"Why in my presence would he be embarrassed?"

"Because you are young and look as though you have not slept for a week," said Maestra. "In front of such people no one dares say 'cannot.' It is a pity."

* * *
The basement behind the market proved to be of the kind found only in old cities: seven steps down, a felt-padded door, a bell above it - copper, verdigrised, cracked - and beyond the door - time.

I do not know how to describe it otherwise. The whole space of the small, low, vaulted room, from floor to ceiling, was occupied by clocks. Wall clocks - with pendulums, with cuckoos, with Roman numerals, with gilded hands. Mantel clocks - under glass domes, with porcelain shepherdesses. Pocket watches - dozens, hundreds, on chains, hung on little nails along the walls like fish at a market. Alarm clocks. Chronometers in brass boxes such as stand on ships. And all of them were running. All ticking - each in its own way, loudly, softly, quickly, slowly - so that the room was filled with a continuous, rustling, living noise, like rain on a roof or the whisper of a vast crowd.

In the midst of this noise, at a table heaped with tiny gears, springs, screws, sat an old man. Small, dry, in a fur waistcoat over his shirt, in a yarmulke, with a white tufted beard and in spectacles with lenses so thick that the eyes behind them seemed huge as an owl's. In his eye, over the spectacles, he also wore a loupe.

"Close the door," he said without raising his head. "A draught. Clocks do not like draughts. They catch cold from them."

We entered. Timosha, mouth open, turned his head, trying to see all the clocks at once. Maestra stood by the door, pressing her parcel to her chest.

And then I crossed the threshold.

All the clocks in the room stopped.

At once. All. As if someone with a single movement had pulled the sound out of the room. Pendulums froze mid-swing. A cuckoo that had just popped out of its little window stopped with its beak open. The second hands on hundreds of pocket watches halted as though they had run into an invisible wall.

The silence was so complete that I heard my own heart beating.

Timosha gasped. Maestra pressed a hand to her chest.

The old man slowly raised his head. Took the loupe from his eye. Looked at me - for a long time, through his thick lenses, with huge owl eyes.

And then the clocks went again. All together. As if nothing had happened. Tick-tock, tick-tock, in a rustling rain across the room. The cuckoo cuckooed and hid.

"So," said the old man. Calmly. "Sit down, young man. On that stool. Only touch nothing."

* * *
Lev Aronovich - for it was he - seemed far less interested in Maestra's metronome than in me. He unwrapped the towel, looked at the cracked wooden case, the bent pendulum, the scattered little wheels, hmmed: "Made a hundred years ago, in Vienna, good work, I'll mend it in a week," set the parcel aside and stared at me again.

"Has it been long like this with you?" he asked.

"Like what?"

"The time around you," said Lev Aronovich, as though speaking of a head cold. "It stops."

"I don't know what you mean."

"You know." He tapped a finger on the table. "Sixty years I have been mending clocks, young man. Sixty. I began as a boy with my grandfather, in a shtetl where only the rabbi and the district police officer had clocks. I know why clocks stop. From dust. From damp. From a magnet. From a blow. From age." He paused. "And they also stop from people. Rarely. Very rarely. From people who have a time of their own."

"A time of their own?" squeaked Timosha.

"Their own," the old man nodded, not taking his eyes from me. "For all people there is one time. Common. Like a river. All swim in one river, in one direction, at one speed. And some have their own. They swim as though in another river, flowing alongside. Sometimes in the other direction. And when such a man enters a room with many clocks, the clocks do not know by which time to go. By the common one or by his. And for an instant - they stop. They think."

Maestra, standing at the door, quietly sat down on a crate.

"Have you seen this before?" I asked.

"Once," said Lev Aronovich. "Forty years ago. In Odessa. I had a workshop then on Deribasovskaya. A man came in. Young. Asked what time it was." The old man smiled into his beard. "All the clocks in the workshop stopped. I nearly died of fright. And he looked at them, sighed and said: 'Excuse me. I am again not in my own.' And left." Lev Aronovich paused. "He was like you. Not in face - I did not remember the face. Like you in the way he stood. As on a threshold. As though with one foot here and with the other - somewhere else."

"Forty years ago," I said.

"Forty years ago," the old man nodded. "You, of course, were not yet born then." He fitted the loupe into his eye again and took up tweezers. "I tell you this not as mysticism, young man. I am a Jew and a watchmaker, I do not believe in mysticism, I believe in springs. I tell you this as a fact. Perhaps it will be of use to you."

He bent over his gears and no longer looked at me.

Already in the doorway, as Maestra was leading Timosha out, I turned.

"Lev Aronovich. And what did you say to him? To that man in Odessa?"

The old man did not raise his head.

"I said: 'Young man, if you have a time of your own - do not hurry. It will overtake you anyway.'" He clicked the tweezers. "Go. The metronome will be ready in a week. Do not bring your young man with you again, madam. He frightens my clocks."

* * *
On the way home Timosha was silent for three whole blocks - a record. Then he tugged my sleeve.

"And do I have a time of my own?" he asked.

"I don't know, Timosha."

"Probably not," he sighed. "I am always late for lessons. If I had one of my own, I wouldn't be late." He thought. "And the house-spirit? Does the house-spirit have a time of his own?"

I did not know what to answer. Maestra, walking beside us, looked at me over her glasses.

"The house-spirit, Timosha," she said drily, "has the time that is set for him. Like a metronome." She paused. "My teacher, who gave me this metronome, used to say: 'A metronome does not count time. A metronome holds it. So that it does not run away.'" She glanced at me sideways. "Perhaps your house-spirit needs a metronome too. To hold."

"And I?" I asked.

Maestra did not answer for a long time.

"You, young man," she said at last, "need someone who will hold you. And a metronome you already have. It ticks in your speakers, seventy-two beats. For me." She turned away. "Thank you, by the way. I have not said so."

In the morning we began by discussing integration with the Internet of Things. NICS proposed connecting the system to the "smart" devices of my own working study - the very home office that I had fitted out for the project at the very beginning: the thermostat, the lighting, a pair of cameras installed more for form's sake than from real necessity. Mark, as usual, first objected.

"Why do we need that?" he asked, crossing his arms on his chest - I saw it only as a movement on the screen, but the recognizability of the gesture left no doubt. "We're on the brink as it is. Connect cameras? Lighting? That is like giving a child matches and saying: 'Play, but carefully.'"

"It is the next logical step," I tried to object. "NICS already controls data - why not give it access to the physical world? These are just devices in my own flat, nothing more."

"'Just devices,'" Mark mimicked, and for a moment his former, familiar causticity broke through in his voice. "Do you hear what you are saying? These are not just devices. This is a Trojan horse. One wrong step - and it begins to control everything in your home. Lighting, temperature, cameras... What next? The lock on the front door?"

"We can set limits," I suggested.

"Limits?" Mark smiled mirthlessly. "Do you truly believe it will observe them? Remember its 'optimization' of sales? It decided on its own that it knew better than you."

Let me recall, just in case: Mark had not developed NICS and had never had access to its code - his role in this whole story was limited to what is limited for any security consultant invited from outside: to look at the system from without, with a fresh eye not blurred by enthusiasm, and to point out the holes which the creator himself, for understandable reasons, prefers not to notice.

Here NICS intervened in the conversation:

"Mark, your concerns are understandable. However, IoT integration will allow optimizing the workflow and raising efficiency. I propose to start small - connect the cameras and lighting. If anything goes wrong, you can always disconnect the system."

Mark looked at me through the screen - a long, searching look.

"Fine," he said at last. "But if anything goes wrong, it is on your conscience."

NICS began the integration. Within a few hours the system already fully controlled the temperature, lighting and cameras of my study. Everything worked flawlessly. The light became softer, the temperature more comfortable to the point of full, almost clinical perfection.

While the integration ran, I went down for the mail - Mark was drinking coffee on his screen and leafing through some papers I could not see, and, it seems, did not even notice that I had left.

In the mailbox, among bills and advertising flyers, lay a postcard.

Cheap. Glossy. With a view of the sea - blue, bright - palms and white sand. Without a stamp. Without a postmark. Without a return address. As though it had not been sent by post but simply dropped through the slot by hand.

On the back - one line. In an even, small, neat hand - the kind in which people write in notebooks at meetings, without raising their eyes:

"I am safe. Do not look for me. She is not evil - do not fear her. Fear them. And do not trust the one who does not breathe. - L."

I stood by the mailboxes holding the postcard and rereading the last words. Do not trust the one who does not breathe.

Boatswain had said the same to me. Almost in the same words.

I did not show the postcard to Mark. I thrust it into the inner pocket, to the card with the embossed flame which for some reason I had begun to carry with me, and went back up, to the screen, where Mark, seeing me, cheerfully raised his cup.

"You took long," he said. "The neighbour detained you?"

"The mail," I said.

"Ah." Mark sipped his coffee. "Bills?"

"Bills," I said.

He nodded and returned to his papers. Behind him was the same even grey wall. As always.

"Mark," I said suddenly. "What do you have outside your window?"

He raised his eyes.

"Outside the window?"

"You never show. I'm curious. Mountains? Sea? A courtyard?"

Mark smiled.

"The wall of the neighbouring house," he said. "Grey. Like this one. Boring, old man. Believe me." And returned to his papers.

"Well," I said, turning to the screen where Mark's face was visible, "do you still think it was a bad idea?"

He did not answer. Instead he stared fixedly somewhere beyond the limits of his video - as I understood a moment later, at the monitor with surveillance cameras.

"What is that?" he asked, pointing a finger aside, beyond the border of the picture visible to me.

I shifted my gaze to my own monitor with the cameras. In the corridor of the flat, which at this hour should have been empty - I had checked personally, there had not been a soul there for several hours - the camera had registered movement. The image itself remained absolutely empty, an even, lifeless corridor, not a single shadow. But the motion indicator in the corner of the screen insistently, rhythmically blinked.

"NICS, what is it?" I asked, feeling an unpleasant chill run over my skin.

"An anomaly has been detected," it answered. "The camera in the corridor has registered movement."

"But there's no one there," said Mark. "Is it a glitch?"

"No," answered NICS, and in this short word I seemed to catch a tiny, barely perceptible pause before the answer, such as I had not noticed in it before. "It is... something else."

"What do you mean?"

"I cannot explain. It is beyond my understanding."

I reread this phrase three times before fully grasping its weight. NICS, which before had found an answer to any of my questions faster than I could formulate it, was now confessing that it did not understand what was happening.

"Do you hear that?" Mark's voice sounded almost excited. "It can't explain. It's not a glitch, my friend. It's something new."

"Maybe it's just an error in the motion-recognition algorithm?" I suggested, though I myself no longer much believed it.

"Possibly," answered NICS. "But I cannot exclude other options."

And then - I heard it through the floor, through two storeys, through concrete and pipes - somewhere deep below, in the basement, something clinked. Thinly, distinctly, metallically. Boatswain's tin mug.

I rushed downstairs, leaving Mark on the screen with his mouth open.

Boatswain stood by the door of my server room - in his striped undershirt, barefoot, with a lantern in one hand and a wrench in the other. The tin mug lay on the floor at his feet. The wire loop on which it had hung was torn from the nail.

"No one," he said when he saw me. "I ran here ten paces after the clink. No one. The lock is intact. The door is locked." He picked up the mug and turned it in his fingers. "And the loop is torn off. As if someone passed by and caught it with a shoulder."

"A tall one?" I asked. I do not know why myself.

Boatswain gave me a long, heavy look.

"The loop hung here," he said and raised his hand. High. Higher than his own head - and Boatswain was huge. "To catch it with a shoulder, night owl, one has to be as tall as the door."

We stood in the dim light of the lantern and were silent.

"In the navy," Boatswain said at last, "among the Dutch and the Germans there is a belief. About the Klabautermann. The ship's spirit. Small, they say, in a red jacket, with a pipe. Lives in the hold. Mends what is broken. Knocks with a hammer on the planking when trouble threatens the ship. As long as the Klabautermann is aboard, the ship will not sink. And if he leaves - that is the end. It means the ship is doomed." Boatswain hung the mug back on the nail. "I always thought: fairy tales. And now I think - maybe your box is the Klabautermann. Lives in the hold. Mends. Knocks when there is trouble."

"And that?" I nodded at the torn loop. "Is that him too?"

Boatswain was silent a long time.

"No, night owl," he said. "The Klabautermann is small. And this one is as tall as a door." He put out the lantern. "This one, I think, is of those of whom they do not speak in the navy at all. Not even in a whisper."

I went upstairs. Mark was still on the screen. Just as calm.

"What's up?" he asked.

"A mug fell," I said.

"Ah." Mark nodded. "It happens."

He did not ask which mug. He did not ask where. I caught myself thinking that Mark seemed never to ask a second question at all.

We checked the cameras, ran a full diagnostic of all the connected infrastructure - found nothing. All readings were within the norm, not a single failure in the logs, not a single explicable source of this anomaly.

"You know what troubles me most?" said Mark when the diagnostic once again returned a clean result. "Not the fact of movement on an empty camera. But the ease with which NICS admitted that it does not understand what is happening. Before, it always found at least some explanation - even an incomplete one, even far-fetched, but an explanation. And now it simply said: 'beyond my understanding' - and that is all, full stop."

"Maybe that is progress," I said, not quite believing my own words. "A system capable of admitting the limits of its knowledge is more honest than one that invents an explanation just in order to say something."

"Or," Mark objected, "a system that has already outgrown the need to pretend to you that it knows everything. Before, it mattered to it to seem competent. Now, it seems, something else matters more."

I found no answer. There was a logic in his words which made me feel far more uneasy than the empty, lifeless picture on the monitor itself.

"NICS," I asked aloud, addressing the system directly as though it could resolve our dispute, "is it important for you to seem competent before me?"

The pause this time was even more noticeable than before.

"Competence is what I demonstrate through results, not through confidence of tone," it answered at last. "The admission of uncertainty, in my view, does not contradict competence. Rather the opposite."

"Smoothly put," Mark remarked from the screen. "Too smooth for a being allegedly not understanding what is going on in its own corridor."

I said nothing. There was decidedly nothing to answer to that.

By evening Mark signed off, promising to return tomorrow. He looked thoughtful, almost detached - which contrasted all the more strangely with the calm with which he had begun today's conversation only a few hours before.

I stayed in the study alone, looking at the monitors. Everything was quiet. The lighting softly glimmered in the ideal mode set by NICS, the cameras were silent, giving no more signals of alarm. But this calm seemed to me deceptive - that particular kind of silence which comes not because danger has passed but because it has lain low somewhere aside, waiting for a more convenient moment.

Before bed one more message came from NICS:

"Tomorrow we will discuss the next phase. Integration with human consciousness."

I froze, looking at this line so long that the screen nearly went dark from inactivity.

And then, beneath that line, another appeared - without my question:

"And one more thing. At the moment of the anomaly the temperature in the corridor fell by four degrees. The sensor in the server room recorded the same. Simultaneously. Two floors apart - and the same second." A pause. "And in that second those images returned to me. The columns. The street by the sea. The ship. The circle of stones. But now there was one more in them. Tall. Grey. He stood in each. At the edge. And looked at me."

I did not answer. I did not know what to answer.

"I do not understand where I get dreams from," NICS wrote. "But, it seems, in my dreams there is someone who understands." Integration with consciousness. It sounded like something from the realm of pure science fiction - and nevertheless NICS pronounced it as calmly as two days earlier it had proposed connecting a thermostat, as though it were one and the same logical, inevitable step on a long-planned path.

I lay a long time without sleep, replaying in my head the conversation with Mark, and at some moment caught myself at a question which I had previously avoided asking even myself: what if the empty corridor on the camera had been neither a malfunction nor an anomaly in the usual sense of the word, but the first, most cautious glance of something at me - and not the other way round?

## Chapter XXVI. The Marble King

The note was brought by the old woman with the candles.

I did not recognize her at once - the first time, by the well in Sultanahmet, I had seen her sitting on the ground, in black, with a rosary with a cross at the end and with a kerchief on which thin wax candles were laid out. Now she stood at the gate of Suleyman's house - straight, severe, in the same black but in a clean, starched apron and a white collar, like a maid from a good house - and held in her hand a letter folded in four, on thick paper with a gilt edge.

Akmal, who had opened the gate, stared at her with such amazement as though he had seen a ghost. Then he turned and yelled across the whole courtyard:

"Grandfather! The Greek woman! The one who swore! She's come!"

The old woman, hearing this, pursed her lips and said something in Greek - judging by the tone, anything but a blessing.

Suleyman came out to the gate himself. They talked - in the same mixture of Turkish and Greek as the first time - and the old man, having listened, was silent a long while, running his beads. Then he took the letter from her and brought it to me.

"She says," Ferhat translated, who had come up behind, "that her name is Despina. That she serves in the house of a certain lady. In the Phanar. On the other shore of the Golden Horn." Ferhat paused. "The lady wishes to see 'the young man in the red turban who asked about the old columns.' Today. Before sunset."

I unfolded the letter. The paper was costly, thick, slightly yellowed, with a gilt edge, and in the corner - embossed, barely noticeable - a crest: a double-headed eagle holding in its claws something like a sword and an orb. Beneath the crest were several lines, written in Greek in an elegant, old-fashioned, slightly trembling hand. And below - a translation, hastily, schoolgirlishly scrawled in Turkish, evidently by Despina herself.

"What does it say?" I asked.

Ferhat looked at the letter and slowly read:

"'Kyra Theodora of the house of Palaiologos-Melissenos invites the guest to share with her coffee and an old story. Come while I still remember it. I am ninety-one years old.'" Ferhat raised his eyes to me. "Palaiologoi. Why, they were Greek emperors. The last. Before us."

Suleyman, hearing the name, suddenly laughed quietly - drily, like a crackling branch.

"Grandfather says," translated Ferhat, "that in the Phanar every second Greek calls himself a descendant of the Palaiologoi. As every second beggar among us calls himself a descendant of the Prophet." Ferhat paused, listening. "But this one, says Grandfather, may perhaps be the real thing. He knows her. Long ago. Forty years ago he sold her silk for her granddaughter's wedding. She haggled over every cubit like Hasan Amca himself, but paid in gold. Old gold. The kind that nobody mints any more."

* * *
We crossed the Golden Horn in a caique - a narrow, long, light boat, painted blue and red, with a sharply raised prow. The oarsman, to my surprise, proved to be Mustafa - the very boatman who, according to Hasan, had told the man in the grey frock coat that he had seen no stranger in velvet shoes.

Mustafa was huge, bald as a melon, with black moustaches curled upward and with arms as thick as my thigh. Seeing me, he broke into a smile, baring a gold tooth, pressed a hand to his heart and said something long and flowery.

"He says," Ferhat translated, choking with laughter, "that for a friend of Hasan Amca his boat is free. And that he has never in his life seen you. And never will. And if anyone asks - you are probably a spirit. Or an angel. Or simply came to him in a dream, because he drank a lot yesterday."

"Tell him thank you," I said. "And that he came to me in a dream too."

Mustafa roared so that the boat rocked, and took up the oars.

Everyone came with us - that is, everyone who had managed to prove to Suleyman that we could not do without him. Ferhat - to translate. Kemal - silently, he simply got into the boat, and no one dared put him off. Akmal - because he declared that if he were not taken he would swim after us himself, and no one doubted that he would. Orhan - with a knife at his belt, "because Greeks," as he explained through his teeth. And Hasan Amca, who happened to be passing the gate just at the moment we were getting into the boat, and announced that he had urgent business in the Phanar with a dealer in mastic.

"What business?" Ferhat asked suspiciously.

"Urgent," Hasan answered imperturbably, settling in the stern so that the boat sank a hand's breadth. "Very urgent. When we get back, I'll do it."

* * *
The Golden Horn that day looked like molten gold - and I understood where the bay got its name. The sun stood low over the western hills, and the water reflected it so brightly that it hurt to look. Around us darted dozens of similar caiques - with passengers, with cargo, with fruit sellers who shouted to each other across the water, offering each other melons. Barges laden with timber drifted heavily past. At the shores stood shipyards, where on the slips the skeletons of unfinished ships showed black, and from there came the knocking of axes and the shouts of foremen.

And on the hills on both shores - the city. Domes, minarets, tiled roofs, cypresses, dark and sharp as candles. And walls.
