I did not see them at once - ancient, enormous, half-ruined walls of thin brick and grey stone, with towers, running along the shore, along the water, here intact, there crumbled, overgrown with grass and bushes, with houses clinging to them like swallows' nests.

"The Greek walls," said Ferhat, noticing my glance. "Old. Very old. A thousand years. When Sultan Mehmed took the city, his ships could not enter the Golden Horn - the Greeks had barred the entrance with an enormous chain. Iron. From shore to shore. Then the Sultan ordered the ships hauled overland. Over the hill. On logs smeared with fat. Seventy ships in one night." Ferhat pointed to the hill on the left. "There. In the morning the Greeks woke up - and the Sultan's ships were already in the bay, behind their backs."

"And the city fell," I said.

"And the city fell," Ferhat nodded. "A month later." He paused. "Grandfather says the Greeks still cannot forgive it. Not the Turks. The chain."

Mustafa at the oars said something and roared with laughter. Hasan in the stern roared too.

"Mustafa says," translated Ferhat, "that his great-great-grandfather hauled those ships. Over the hill. All night. And ruptured his back. And ever since, all the men in their family have been oarsmen. So as never to haul ships overland again."

Kemal, sitting in the prow of the boat, had been silently looking at the ancient walls all this time. Then he suddenly turned to me and pointed - not at the walls but under the water. To where beneath the golden surface, in the dark depth, something was visible. Huge, round, black links. One after another. Going down into the depth.

"The chain," Ferhat whispered. "What is left of it. They say it was never raised. It lies on the bottom. Four hundred years."

We passed over it in silence.

* * *
The Phanar rose from the water up the hillside - in narrow, steep, cobbled lanes where, it seemed, two people could not pass without brushing shoulders. The houses here were different from Suleyman's: not wooden but stone, tall, gloomy, with narrow windows barred with grilles, with heavy oak doors bound in iron. Houses built by people who did not trust the street.

"Rich Greeks lived here," Ferhat told us as we climbed, panting, after Despina, who, in spite of her years, walked so fast that Hasan had fallen behind at the second turn. "The richest. The noblest. They served the Sultans. As translators. Dragomans. As rulers of distant lands - there, beyond the Danube, in Wallachia, in Moldavia. The Sultans appointed them hospodars. They lived there like princes. Then returned here. Built houses." He pointed to a gloomy mansion behind a grille. "Grandfather says they had a saying: 'Our grandfathers were kings. Our fathers were interpreters of kings. And we are interpreters of interpreters.'"

Orhan, striding behind with his hand on his knife, muttered something.

"He says," translated Ferhat, "that the Greeks still think the city is theirs. And that someday they will take it back."

"And do they think so?"

Ferhat shrugged.

"Ask the lady," he said. "I think we have arrived."

* * *
The house of Kyra Theodora stood at the very top of the hill, above the Golden Horn - old, stone, three-storeyed, with peeling plaster, with wooden balconies blackened by time, with a garden behind a high wall from which hung branches of fig and pomegranate. Above the gate, in a stone niche, was carved the same crest as on the paper: a double-headed eagle. One of the eagle's heads was broken off.

Despina led us through the garden - overgrown, run wild, but still beautiful: roses, lemons, huge bushes of jasmine, a marble bench almost drowned in ivy, and in the middle - a fountain. Old, marble, with a round basin into which water ran in a thin stream from a lion's mouth. Along the rim of the basin ran an inscription. In Greek letters.

By the fountain, in a deep wicker chair, wrapped in shawls, sat an old woman.

She was so old that she seemed unreal - as though carved from yellowed ivory and forgotten to be painted. Tiny, shrivelled, with a face covered by a thousand fine wrinkles, like old parchment. Grey hair, gathered in a high coiffure in the fashion of half a century ago, held with a tortoiseshell comb. On her fingers - rings too heavy for those transparent, bird-like hands: rubies, emeralds, an enormous sapphire. On her knees sat a peacock - a real one, alive, with a tail hanging to the very ground - and she stroked its blue neck as one strokes a cat.

And her eyes were young. Dark, shining, mocking. The eyes of a girl who has not yet decided whether to fall in love or to laugh.

She looked at us. At each in turn - Ferhat, Kemal, Akmal, Orhan, breathless Hasan, who at last appeared in the gateway. Then - at me. And looked for a long time.

"So," she said at last. In French. In an old-fashioned, slightly bookish French, such as was spoken half a century ago in good houses. "You have come after all. Sit down, young man. The others may drink coffee in the arbour. Despina will feed them." She looked at Orhan. "And tell your young friend with the knife that in this house the last time anyone was cut was in the year fourteen hundred and fifty-three. And it was not we who did the cutting."

* * *
I understood French. I do not know why myself - I had never thought of it, but the words came to me clearly, easily, as though I had spoken this language all my life. Ferhat, hearing me answer her, raised his brows in amazement - and withdrew to the arbour, leading the others away.

We two were left. And the peacock.

"Did Despina tell you?" asked Kyra Theodora. "How she saw you by the well?"

"No."

"She came home white as this marble. She said: 'Kyra, I saw him. The one from your story. In the red turban. By the well above the underground water. He asked what lies under the water.'" The old woman stroked the peacock. "I said to her: 'Despina, you are seventy years old and you believe in fairy tales.' And then I did not sleep for three nights." She paused. "And then a man in grey came to me."

My hands went cold.

"A man in grey?"

"A week ago. Tall. Polite. He spoke French better than I - and I, young man, have spoken French since I first spoke at all." She narrowed her eyes. "He asked about a family relic. About what has been kept in our house since that night. Since the twenty-eighth of May, fourteen hundred and fifty-three. Offered money. A great deal of money." Kyra Theodora smiled. "I told him that the Palaiologoi do not sell what does not belong to them. And what does belong to them - was sold long ago to the Genoese. He smiled and left." She paused. "Young man, for ninety-one years I have looked at people's faces. He had a face. But I did not remember it. Not a single feature. As though I had looked into water."

"The boatman Mustafa said the same," I said. "About the man who sought me in the port."

"Then he is seeking you." Kyra Theodora nodded, not in the least surprised. "And what I have. So it is connected." She raised a hand laden with rings and rang a little silver bell. "Despina! Coffee. And the casket."

* * *
The coffee was black, thick, bitter, in tiny porcelain cups painted with golden birds - so thin that light shone through the porcelain. Despina set the tray on the marble bench, beside it a small casket of dark wood inlaid with mother-of-pearl, and withdrew three paces, standing by the fountain like a sentry.

"Do you know what the Palaiologoi are, young man?" asked Kyra Theodora, sipping her coffee.

"The last rulers of this city. So Ferhat said."

"The last basileis." She set down her cup. "For two hundred years they ruled what was left of a great empire. An empire which for a thousand years was the centre of the world. When in your - wherever it may be - country people lived in dugouts and prayed to trees, here, in this city, there were a million people. Marble palaces. Libraries. A hippodrome for a hundred thousand spectators. Aqueducts. Hospitals. A university. Gold. Silk." She smiled. "And at the end there remained - one city. One set of walls. And fifty thousand people behind them. And the last emperor, Constantine. The Eleventh. Who knew that the city would fall - and did not leave."

"Why?"

"Because he was the last," said Kyra Theodora simply. "The last does not leave. The last remains so that someone will remember there was a first." She paused. "On the twenty-ninth of May, at dawn, the Turks broke through the walls at the Gate of Saint Romanus. Constantine tore off his purple boots and all the imperial insignia, so that no one would recognize him, took a sword and threw himself into the very thick. As a simple soldier. No one ever saw him again. Neither living nor dead. The body was never found."

"And what became of him?"

Kyra Theodora looked at me with her young, shining eyes.

"That, young man," she said, "is the most interesting part."

* * *
"The Greeks say," she began, lowering her voice, "that Constantine did not die. When the Turks were already near, when he was surrounded and swords were raised over him, an angel came down from heaven. Took him. And carried him under the earth. Under the Golden Gate - the oldest, the greatest gate of the city, through which emperors once entered the city in triumph. The Turks themselves walled it up, long ago - they say because they feared this legend." She paused. "The angel laid him in a cave under the gate. And turned him to marble. The Marble King. He lies there to this day. Sleeping. With a sword in his hand."

"And waits?"

"And waits," the old woman nodded. "One day the angel will return. Wake him. Give back his sword. And the Marble King will come out from under the Golden Gate - and take the city back. And drive the Turks to the Red Apple. To the very edge of the earth, from where they came."

"Do you believe it?"

Kyra Theodora laughed - drily, ringingly, as old little bells ring.

"Young man, I am ninety-one. I have outlived four Sultans, three Patriarchs and two husbands. I know how the world is made. Marble kings do not wake." She sipped her coffee. "But I know something else. There is another legend. It is told less often. About Saint Sophia."

"Tell it."

"On the night when the Turks burst into the city, a liturgy was being served in Saint Sophia. The last. The church was full - women, children, old men, all who could not fight. And the priest stood at the altar with the holy gifts in his hands." She paused. "The Turks broke down the doors. Rushed in. And then the wall behind the altar opened. By itself. And the priest entered it - with the holy gifts, not having finished the liturgy. And the wall closed behind him."

"Is he there still?"

"Still," nodded Kyra Theodora. "In the wall. Waiting. They say he will come out when the city is ours again. And finish the liturgy from the very place where he broke off. From the very word."

Two legends. A king turned to marble under a gate. A priest gone into a wall. Neither died. Both wait. Both will return.

"When this rose blooms in a foreign land - I shall return."

I did not know where these words had come to me from. What rose? What land? I had never heard them. And yet they came - and stood beside the old woman's legends like one more candle in a row.

* * *
Kyra Theodora opened the casket.

Inside, on faded purple velvet, lay three things.

A small icon - the Mother of God with the Child, dark, almost black with age, in a silver frame, bent as though it had been struck.

A ring - massive, golden, with a seal: a double-headed eagle, as on the crest above the gate.

And a coin.

One. Small, golden, worn.

With an incomprehensible sign on one side. And interlaced lines on the other.

I stopped breathing.

I knew this coin. In my pocket lay exactly such. Three - left after I gave several to Hatice Hanim. And one more - warm, her coin, which she gave me "because you have the same."

Slowly, feeling my fingers shake, I took one of mine from my pocket. Laid it beside.

Identical. To the last stroke.

Kyra Theodora looked a long while at the two coins lying side by side on the purple velvet. Then she raised her eyes to me. And in them there was no longer any mockery.

"So Despina is right," she said quietly. "And I, an old fool, did not sleep three nights for nothing."

* * *
She told me everything - slowly, in French, with long pauses, as though lifting each word from the bottom of a deep well.

Her ancestor - very distant, in the twelfth or thirteenth generation, she had lost count - had been one of those who stood on the walls on the last night. Manuel Melissenos, a relative of the emperor, commander of a detachment at the Blachernae Palace. On the night of the twenty-eighth to the twenty-ninth of May, when the whole city was praying in Saint Sophia and Turkish drums thundered beneath the walls, a man climbed up to him on the wall.

"Young," said Kyra Theodora. "A stranger. Neither Greek, nor Latin, nor Turk. In strange clothes. Without weapons. Without a name - he said so: 'I do not remember my name.' He told Manuel that the city would fall at dawn. That this could not be stopped. That so it must be." The old woman paused. "Manuel wanted to arrest him as a spy. But the man said to him: 'Do not be afraid. The city will not die. It will change its name. So it is with cities - and with people. The name changes, and the city remains. Like me.' And gave him this."

She touched the coin with the tip of a transparent finger.

"And said: 'Keep it. When another comes with the same - give him what you saw this night.'"

"What did he see?"

"That is not written in the family chronicle," said Kyra Theodora. "Manuel survived. Was taken prisoner. Ransomed. Lived another thirty years. Wrote down everything - about that night, about the wall, about the man without a name. But what he saw - he did not write. Wrote only: 'I saw how he went away. This cannot be described in words. Let the one who comes see for himself.'" She paused. "The chronicle burned in a fire in the Phanar a hundred years ago. Only that phrase remained - my great-grandfather knew it by heart. And the coin."

"And what am I to do with it?"

Kyra Theodora took her coin from the velvet. Then took my hand - with dry fingers, light as fallen leaves. Laid the coin on my palm. And closed my fingers around it.

"Take it," she said. "Five hundred years my family has kept it. Waited. My grandmothers told of it to their granddaughters, like a fairy tale. I myself told it to my granddaughter. She laughed." Her voice wavered. "She died last year. Of cholera. I have no one left to tell."

The coin in my palm was warm. Like the one that Hatice Hanim had given me.

* * *
When I was already rising to leave, Kyra Theodora stopped me - with a gesture light as the wave of a fan.

"One moment. Look at the fountain."

I looked. Along the rim of the marble basin, all round, in a circle, ran an inscription - Greek letters, weathered but still distinguishable.

"Read it," said the old woman.

"I do not read Greek."

"Try," she said with a sly smile. "It is a riddle. It was set in Saint Sophia a thousand years ago. Just such an inscription was on its fountain - where people washed before entering the church. My ancestor ordered it carved here when this house was built. I shall tell you what it says: 'Wash your sins, not only your face.'" She paused. "And now the riddle. What is special about this inscription?"

I looked at the letters. They ran in a circle. Without beginning and without end. I walked round the fountain, following them with my eyes, trying to understand where the line begins.

And suddenly understood - not knowing Greek, not knowing a single letter. Understood the way I had understood the signs on the ledger at Yusuf's.

"It reads the same," I said slowly. "From the beginning and from the end. In both directions. In a circle. One can begin anywhere - and arrive at the same place."

Kyra Theodora clapped her hands - drily, ringingly, like a child. The peacock on her knees stirred in displeasure and spread its tail - enormous, shimmering blue, green, gold, with a hundred eyes.

"Bravo!" said the old woman. "Bravo, young man! Of my guests in sixty years not one has solved it. Not one. Not even the Patriarch." She leaned toward me. "And do you know what my great-grandfather said of this inscription? He said: 'It is not a riddle. It is a description. Some people are made so. Their life reads the same from the beginning and from the end. Because it has neither beginning nor end. Only a circle.'"

* * *
We returned across the Golden Horn already at dusk. The water darkened, from gold became copper, then lilac, then black. On the shores lights were kindled. Mustafa rowed silently, powerfully, rhythmically, and the boat slid over the sunken chain as over the back of a sleeping serpent.

Everyone was silent. Even Akmal, who all evening had been feeding the peacock figs and for this had been drenched in Despina's contempt, sat quietly in the stern, looking at the water. Hasan dozed, leaning against the side - his business with the mastic dealer, it seemed, had never taken place. Orhan sharpened his knife, but without his usual fury, almost thoughtfully.

Kemal sat beside me. Then, without a word, he held out his hand palm up - and looked at me.

I understood. I took Kyra Theodora's coin from my pocket and laid it on his palm.

Kemal held it a long time. Then nodded - gravely, once - and gave it back to me.

"Warm," he said in Turkish. I understood without translation.

"Ferhat," I said, looking at the dark water. "Did you hear what she told? About the Marble King?"

"I heard," Ferhat nodded. "Despina told it in the arbour. To everyone. Three times." He paused. "Grandfather knows that legend. He says we Turks have a similar one. About the Red Apple."

"Which?"

"Kyzyl Elma. The Red Apple." Ferhat looked at the water. "It is the place we always go toward. Far away. At the edge of the world. No one knows where it is. When we took this city - we thought the Red Apple was here. Then we thought - in Rome. Then - in Vienna." He paused. "Grandfather says the Red Apple is always where one has not yet reached. And when you reach it - it turns out to be farther." Ferhat smiled. "The Greeks wait for their king to return. We seek an apple that cannot be reached. Grandfather says it is one and the same tale. Only told from two ends."

From two ends. Like the inscription on the fountain.

"And you?" I asked. "What do you believe?"

Ferhat was silent a long while.

"I believe that Father will return," he said at last. Quietly. For the first time - not merrily, not lightly. "Like the Marble King. Someday. When someone wakes him."

Mustafa at the oars suddenly began to sing - in a low, hoarse voice, something slow, drawn-out, boatmen's. Hasan woke and joined in. Akmal picked it up. Even Orhan, after hesitating, began humming the tune under his breath.

And I sat in the boat over the sunken chain, between two shores of one city that had many names, and clutched a warm coin in my pocket.

Five hundred years. Someone, five hundred years ago, climbed a wall to a man named Manuel and told him that the city would change its name but remain. "Like me."

I did not remember this. I could not remember it.

But when the caique nosed against the quay at our shore and I stepped onto the wet boards, it seemed to me for one moment that behind my back, over there, on that shore, at the top of the hill, in the dark window of an old house with a one-headed eagle over its gate, someone raised a candle.

And held it until we passed out of sight.

## Chapter XXVII. The Scroll in the Silk Kerchief

The cutting on the windowsill had put forth a second leaf.

I noticed it in the morning, drawing back the curtains: yesterday there had been three leaves and one tight, dark, clenched bud, and today there were four. The fourth was quite tiny, reddish-bronze, rolled into a tube like an infant's fist. The bud had not opened. But it seemed darker. And when I bent toward it, it seemed to me that it smelled - faintly, as a letter smells that has lain long in someone else's pocket - of honey and dust. The very smell of the General's garden.

I watered it from the jug. Drop by drop. As yesterday.

Stefan's note - "Let it grow with you. The rose will find. - S." - I had put into the blue notebook, with the other papers, of which there were more and more and which I carried about with me as one carries an amulet. The paper from the monastery near Tarnovo. The drawing of two circles which I had not drawn. The words "He is near. Wait," which I had not written.

And someone was already knocking at the door.

* * *
"Young master," said Agafya Tikhonovna as soon as I opened. "Dress. Come with me."

She stood on the threshold - small, dry, in a dark dress and white cap, with a bunch of keys at her belt that jingled with every movement like the bells of a troika. Her face was such as I had never seen it in all those years: not stern, not grumbling - bewildered.

"What has happened, Agafya Tikhonovna?"

"The crape," she said. "Again." And, after a pause, added more quietly: "Only this time, my dear sir, no one tore it down. I sat at the gallery myself in the night. On a chair. With a lamp. I did not sleep till the cocks crowed. No one passed. Not a living soul." She swallowed. "And toward morning it fell. By itself. As if someone had pushed it from within."

We walked along the corridors in silence. She ahead, I behind. The keys jingled. Portraits of ancestors looked down from the walls - ladies in powdered wigs, men in armour and uniforms, the stern great-great-grandfather whose pupils, as I had once fancied, had shifted to follow my movement.

At the entrance to the far end of the gallery stood a chair. On it - an extinguished lamp, an unfinished stocking on needles and a mug of cold tea. Agafya Tikhonovna had indeed sat here all night.

And farther on, at the very end of the gallery, on the floor, lay the crape. Black, dusty, fallen in a shapeless heap.

And the portrait looked at us.

* * *
I had already seen it - on that night, before the railings. A young man in a dark frock coat of old-fashioned cut, in a light neckcloth tied in an intricate knot - the same as I tied mine. Hands folded on his knees. In his palm - two small objects: a black one and a white one. And the face - a dark patch of cracked paint, indistinguishable, as though the canvas had been held long over a fire.

Now, in the daylight falling from the high window, I saw more.

The paint on the face had cracked into a fine net - that was true. But through the net of cracks, if one looked from the side, at an angle, features showed. Not as a whole. Separate ones. The line of a cheekbone. The curve of a brow. The corner of a mouth.

I looked, and grew colder and colder.

"Agafya Tikhonovna," I said. "Who is this?"

The old woman did not answer for a long time. She stood beside me, gripping the bunch of keys so that her knuckles whitened.

"It is forbidden, my dear sir," she said at last. "Fifty years forbidden."

"By whom?"

"By the old mistress. Not ours - the one before ours. Artemia Aristarkhovna's mother-in-law." Agafya Tikhonovna crossed herself. "I came to this house a girl, I was twelve. This portrait was already hanging under crape then. The old mistress brought me here on the very first day. Showed me. And said: 'Agafya, you will straighten this crape every morning. Until your death. And if it ever falls of itself - run to me.'" The old woman paused. "I straightened it. Fifty years. Every morning."

"And did it fall?"

"Twice," whispered Agafya Tikhonovna. "The first time - forty years ago. On that night when the key to the railings vanished. I ran to the old mistress, as I had been told. She came, looked, wept and said: 'So he has gone again.'" The old woman raised faded eyes to me. "And the second time - today."

"Who is 'he'? Who has gone?"

Agafya Tikhonovna bent, picked up the crape from the floor, shook the dust from it. And before hanging it back on the frame, for a moment she paused - looked at the portrait, then at me, then at the portrait again.

"The old mistress called him 'our guest,'" she said. "Nothing more she said. 'Our guest.'" She draped the crape over the frame, smoothing the folds with trembling hands. "And on the plaque there was a name. I remember it. Only the plaque was scraped off before my time. And the name I will not say, my dear sir. It is forbidden. The mistress took an oath of me. On the icon."

She turned and went away along the gallery, jingling her keys. At the very turning she stopped, not looking round.

"Pavel Nikolaevich will arrive today," she said. "With the professor. The mistress ordered a table laid in the study." She paused. "And ordered that you be there. For the first time in fifty years she has ordered that someone be present when they speak of this in the study."

* * *
The General arrived by dinner - in a carriage drawn by a pair of black horses, with Tikhon on the box and Sventsitsky beside him, who held on his knees his canvas bag of notebooks as though he were carrying eggs in it.

Konstantin met them on the porch - he seemed to have been on watch since morning. Seeing the professor, he bowed with exaggerated courtesy.

"Professor! So you have lingered in our parts after all? You said - till the end of the week."

"I have lingered, lieutenant," Sventsitsky said cheerfully, jumping down from the step. "Your General abducted me. Came yesterday to the inn, said he had one thing I must see - and that if I refused, he would order his coachman to take me bound." He winked at Tikhon. "Your coachman, by the way, said he would bind me tenderly. I was touched and agreed."

Tikhon on the box chuckled into his beard.

The General greeted everyone briefly, drily, as always. But I noticed that under his arm was a parcel. Small, oblong, wrapped in a faded silk kerchief - once, perhaps, blue, and now pale blue like the sky over a desert. He held it as one holds something very fragile and very heavy at once.

* * *
The study of my aunt's late husband - the very one where the General slept when he stayed, and where I had overheard a conversation not meant for my ears - was prepared as for a council. Curtains drawn. On the writing desk - six candles in two candelabra, though it was day. Armchairs arranged in a semicircle. By the fireplace, where a small fire crackled - coffee, brandy, Marfa's almond biscuits.

There were six of us. My aunt - in her chair by the fireplace, straight, pale, in dark lilac, with pearls, gripping a lace handkerchief in her hands. The General - at the desk. Sventsitsky - beside him, already spreading out his notebooks. Doctor Strauch - in the corner, with an unlit cigar, with his black little book on his knee. Konstantin - by the door, like a sentry. And I - in the armchair opposite my aunt, so that between us there was only the fire.

The General laid the parcel on the desk. Stood over it. Then turned to my aunt.

"Artemia Aristarkhovna," he said quietly. "Are you sure?"

My aunt looked long at the parcel. Then - at me.

"No, Pavel Nikolaevich," she said. "I am not sure." She paused. "But the crape fell by itself. Tonight. Agafya sat until the cocks crowed."

The General slowly nodded - as though this were precisely what he had wanted to hear. Or feared.

"Then," he said, "the time has come."

And untied the kerchief.

* * *
Inside was a scroll. Not of paper - of leather. Old, dark, almost black leather, dressed so thin that it showed through in the candlelight, rolled into a tube two palms long and tied with a faded cord of goat's wool. It smelled of dust, sand and something else - dry, bitter, steppe-like, as wormwood smells in August.

"Khiva," said the General, addressing no one, looking at the scroll. "Thirty years ago. We were going through the sands to Khiva. A detachment - a hundred and forty men. The guide fled on the second day. The water ran out on the third." He paused. "Mikhail has probably told you. How I went to the Turkmen."

"He has, Your Excellency," I said quietly. "The Colonel said you returned at dawn with a guide and with water-skins. And with a scroll."

"With a scroll." The General touched the cord with the tips of his fingers. "I did not know their language. Not a word. I came into their camp alone, unarmed, with raised hands - and expected to be cut down. I was led to an old man. Very old. Blind in one eye. He sat by a fire and told his beads. He looked at me with his one eye - for a long time. Then said something to his people. They brought water. A great deal of water. And a guide." The General paused. "And then the old man took from under his robe this. And said - I understood him, I do not know how, as one understands in dreams - 'This scroll waits for a man. For long. You are not that man. But you will meet him. Give it to him. And say: the earth remembers.'"

The earth remembers. The old aborigine in Australia: "Tell him that the earth remembers his song." The old Turkmen near Khiva: "Say: the earth remembers."

"Thirty years," said the General, "I have carried it with me. On all campaigns. On all ships. Across all oceans." He raised his eyes to me. "I thought - perhaps I shall meet him. In Samarkand. In Peking. In Cuba. In Siam. I looked at faces. All these years - I looked at faces."

"And did you meet him?" asked Sventsitsky.

The General did not answer. He was looking at me.

Then he untied the cord.

* * *
The scroll unrolled on the desk by itself - slowly, with an old, leathery rustle, as though it had grown tired in thirty years of being rolled.

It was written upon. All of it, from edge to edge. Not in letters - no, not in letters. In long, flowing, curving lines running one into another without breaks, without spaces, without beginning or end. Dark brown, almost black - not ink, I understood, but something else, something that had eaten so deep into the leather that it had become part of it.

In the study it grew so quiet that one could hear the candles gutter.

I looked at the scroll - and could not tear my eyes away. I did not know these signs. I had never seen them. And yet, looking at them, I felt what I had felt in Stefan's greenhouse when he unfolded before me the five-hundred-year-old monastery paper. As though a key were entering a lock I had never seen.

"Professor," said the General.

Sventsitsky was already leafing through his notebook - the thick one, in an oilcloth cover, in which he had written down all I had told him on that day I did not remember. His hands, usually so sure, visibly trembled. He found the page. Laid the notebook on the desk, beside the scroll.

"Here," he said dully. "Here is what he drew me then. At the inn. Himself. With my pencil. I asked: 'Show me what the signs on your note look like.' And he wrote a line. One. Without thinking. As though he had been writing all his life."

On the page of the notebook, beneath the drawing of two circles and a wavy line, in pencil, in my hand - I recognized the pressure, recognized even the habitual blot at the end, though one cannot make a blot with a pencil, but there was a thickening there, exactly the same - ran a line. Long, flowing, curving.

Sventsitsky took a candle and slowly drew it along the scroll, from line to line, checking against the notebook. We all followed the flame. A line. Another. Another.

At the seventh line from the bottom the candle stopped.

"Here," whispered Sventsitsky.

The line on the scroll. The line in the notebook.

Identical. Curve for curve. Loop for loop.

* * *
Doctor Strauch rose from his corner and came to the desk. Looked long - at the scroll, at the notebook, again at the scroll. Put on his glasses. Took them off. Put them on again. Took a magnifying glass from his pocket.

"Allow me," he said. "I assert nothing. I only observe." He bent over the scroll. "A coincidence of form. Complete. That is a fact." He straightened. "The explanations which come to my mind as a physician are the following. First: the young man once saw this scroll, memorized, forgot, and in a state of... altered consciousness reproduced it. Memory, gentlemen, keeps more than we think."

"I have never seen this scroll," I said. "The General has carried it thirty years in a locked case."

"Second," Strauch went on unperturbed, as though he had not heard. "The professor, forgive me, could have adjusted the drawing after he saw the scroll. Yesterday. At the inn. When he was 'abducted.'"

Sventsitsky turned crimson. The General raised a hand, calming.

"The professor had not seen the scroll before this minute, Karl Fyodorovich," he said. "I kept it by me. And his notebook - look at the date."

Strauch looked. Long.

"Then third," he said at last. Quietly. "For which I have no medical name."

"And do you have one, Professor?" asked my aunt. For the first time in all that while. Her voice was even, but the handkerchief in her hands was twisted into a rope.

Sventsitsky was silent a long time.

"I have, Artemia Aristarkhovna," he said. "Only it is not scientific. It was told to me by an old woman in Kargopol. An obmiranka. She said: 'There are people who write one and the same line at different ends of the earth. Not knowing each other. Not knowing the language. Because it is not they who write. It is the one who sent them who writes through them.'" He paused. "I wrote it down then and laughed. Now I do not laugh."

* * *
"Stefan's paper," I said. I do not know why I remembered it just now.

All looked at me. I took from the blue notebook the monastery paper folded in four, almost rotted at the folds - the one that Stefan had put into my hand in the greenhouse. Unfolded it. Laid it on the desk, beside the scroll and the professor's notebook.

A dark scarlet rose. Two circles, one filled, one empty. A wavy line. And a line of script beneath them.

Sventsitsky again drew the candle along. The General bent over the desk. Strauch - with his magnifying glass. My aunt rose from her chair - for the first time - and came up, leaning on the back of it.

The line on the monastery paper. Five hundred years. Tarnovo.

The line on the Turkmen scroll. Khiva.

The line in the professor's notebook. A district town. A week ago. In my hand.

One and the same.

"Three ends of the earth," said Strauch very quietly, lowering the glass. "Three centuries. One hand." He took off his glasses and polished them a long time with the skirt of his coat, though they were clean. "Gentlemen, I am a German. I believe in what can be touched." He put the glasses on. "I have touched this."

My aunt stood at the desk, looking at the three lines. Then slowly raised her hand and touched the leather scroll with the tips of her fingers - as one touches the face of a sleeping child.

"He wrote like that too," she said. Barely audible. Addressing no one. "That one. When he stood at the railings. He wrote in the dust. With a finger. This line." She closed her eyes. "For forty years I have tried to forget it."

The General turned to her. Konstantin at the door stepped forward. But my aunt had already moved away from the desk - to the fireplace, to her chair - and sat, and was again straight and pale, and the handkerchief in her hands was again just a handkerchief.

"Continue, Pavel Nikolaevich," she said evenly. "You wished to tell. Where else you have seen such signs."

* * *
The General poured himself brandy. Drank. Poured another and did not drink - simply held the glass, looking into the fire.

"In Brazil," he said. "I told you of Rio, Artemia Aristarkhovna. Of the bay, of the Sugarloaf, of the parrots. I did not tell you of another mountain."

"Which?" asked Konstantin.

"It is called Pedra da Gávea. The Rock of the Maintop - in Portuguese, from the ship's term: the maintop is a platform on a mast, and the mountain looks like one." The General paused. "An enormous granite block above the sea, south of the city. Flat on top, like a table. And on its side, on the sheer wall - signs. Huge, each the height of a man. As though someone had carved them in the granite. The locals say - Phoenicians. That the Phoenicians sailed there a thousand years before the Portuguese and left an inscription. The Brazilian learned society even sent an expedition there. Some thirty years ago." He smiled. "The scholars said - erosion. Wind and rain. No signs."

"And you?"

"And I climbed up there," said the General. "With a mulatto guide named Joaquim. Two days through jungle, over rocks, over lianas. Joaquim crossed himself the whole way and said that only madmen and Englishmen go up that mountain." The General paused. "We climbed. I looked at the signs up close. From a rope, over the abyss."

"And?"

The General glanced at the scroll on the desk.

"Erosion," he said. "Perhaps. Wind and rain. Only wind and rain, Professor," he turned to Sventsitsky, "for some reason draw the very same loop. Here." He jabbed a finger at the scroll, at the third line from the top. "The same. I remembered it. I have remembered it thirty years since."

"And Joaquim?" asked Konstantin.

"Joaquim," said the General, and in his voice for the first time a smile flickered, "when we came down, refused to take money from me. Said: 'Señor, you are the first man who looked at that mountain as though reading a letter from a relative.' And went into the jungle. I never saw him again."

* * *
"And Argentina?" asked Sventsitsky, already writing. "You surely went on south from Brazil?"

"I did," nodded the General. "On the same American steamer of Captain Hall's. To Buenos Aires." He paused. "A strange city. It stands on a river so wide it seems a sea. The water in it is the colour of coffee with milk. Ruddy. From silt. They call it the Silver River, though there is no silver in it and never was. The Spaniards named it so because they hoped. All the Spaniards in America named things for what they hoped for."

"And the city itself?"

"Low. Flat. White one-storey houses with inner courtyards, with grilles on the windows. Broad streets - straight as by a ruler. And beyond the city - the pampa." The General set down his glass. "You have seen the steppe, Professor. Near Orenburg. Near Astrakhan."

"I have."

"The pampa is a steppe stretched to the edge of the earth and forgotten to be rolled up." The General paused. "Grass above the waist. No tree. No hill. No stone. Only grass, sky and wind. You ride a day - the same. You ride a week - the same. And suddenly on the horizon - a dot. A horseman. A gaucho."

"Gaucho?" Konstantin repeated.

"Herdsmen. Mounted. Like our Cossacks - only wilder." The General, for the first time all evening, brightened genuinely. "They live in the saddle. Eat nothing but meat - roast a whole bullock on a spit over a fire. Drink maté - tea from a gourd through a silver tube, one for all, passed round the circle. In the hand - bolas: three stones on thongs. They throw - and the thongs wind round the legs of a bull or an ostrich at a gallop." He smiled. "I tried to throw. Wound them round the legs of my own horse. The gauchos laughed so that two fell out of their saddles."

Konstantin roared. Even Strauch twitched the corner of his mouth.

"I lived two weeks with them on an estancia," the General went on. "With the old owner, Don Eusebio. And one evening by the fire I saw a payada."

"A payada?"

"A duel of singers," said the General. "Two gauchos sit facing each other with guitars. And sing in turn. Compose on the spot. Set each other riddles - in verse. Whoever does not answer has lost. Sometimes the duel lasts all night." He paused. "That evening two sang. An old, grey one, named Remigio. And a young one - dark, bold, a stranger, from other parts. They sang till dawn. Neither could win. And toward morning old Remigio set a riddle that silenced the young one."

"What riddle?" I asked.

The General closed his eyes, remembering. Then slowly pronounced - first in Spanish, in a singsong, then, after a pause, in Russian, choosing the words:

"'There is a city in the pampa that is not.
All see it, but none has reached it.
It stands where you seek it,
And leaves when you approach.
Whoever lives in it does not age.
Whoever has come out of it does not remember.
What is the name of this city?'"

The study was silent.

"The young one did not answer," said the General. "Rose. Bowed to the old man. Mounted his horse and rode away - into the pampa, toward the dawn. Everyone decided he had lost, left out of shame." The General paused. "And Don Eusebio told me that all gauchos know the answer. It is the City of the Caesars. A legend. That somewhere in the south, in Patagonia, beyond the pampa, at the foot of the mountains, there is a city. Silver. Built by survivors of a wrecked Spanish ship. Or by fugitive Incas. Or by those who came before the Incas. It has been sought for three hundred years. Hundreds of expeditions. Jesuits, soldiers, gold seekers. No one has found it. Sometimes it is seen in the distance - towers, walls, lights. You ride up - it vanishes. And the people who live there, they say, do not age. And if anyone comes out of there - he forgets where he came from."

"And the young singer?" asked Sventsitsky, ceasing to write. "Did he know the answer?"

The General opened his eyes.

"Don Eusebio said," he spoke slowly, "that this young man had come to their estancia before. Forty years earlier. Just as young. Just as dark. Sang the same payada with the same Remigio, who was then young too. And left at dawn in the same way, without answering." He paused. "Old Remigio, they say, wept after that evening. And said: 'He is from that city. He cannot name it - because he does not remember. But every time I set this riddle, he rises and goes - there.'"

* * *
"Fiji," said the General suddenly.

He said it looking into the fire, as though he had remembered only now. Or had long not wished to remember.

"Fiji?" repeated my aunt. "Where is that, Pavel Nikolaevich?"

"Far, Artemia Aristarkhovna. The farthest I have been." The General paused. "Islands in the Pacific. South of the equator. Between Australia and nothing. I came there on our corvette - we were going from Kamchatka to Sydney, and the captain decided to put in at the islands for water and provisions. Some seven years ago." He smiled. "The crew did not want to. Everyone knew that on Fiji they eat people."

Lizonka Kutasova, had she been here, would have fainted. My aunt only pursed her lips.

"Eat?" asked Konstantin with lively interest.

"They did, lieutenant." The General nodded. "Then they still did. A year before our coming they had eaten an English missionary there. Together with his boots. The boots, they say, were boiled a long time - they could not chew them." He paused. "But we were received well. We were taken in on the island of Ovalau, in the town of Levuka - white traders lived there, whalers, escaped convicts from Australia, missionaries - all the scum of the Pacific. Taverns, shops, drunken brawls. And beyond the town - mountains, jungle, waterfalls. And the natives' villages."

"What are they like?" asked Sventsitsky.

"Tall. Strong. Dark skin. Hair - like this," the General spread his hands above his head, "enormous, bushy, like a cap. Their chiefs - they are called 'ratu' - wear in their hair combs of tortoiseshell and a sperm whale's tooth at the neck. They say that whoever has more whale's teeth is more important." He paused. "I was received by one such chief. Ratu Vanua. Old, huge, with scars all over his body. He invited me to a ceremony."

"What ceremony?"

"The walking on fire," said the General.

* * *
"On the small island of Beqa," he related, "lives one tribe. Only that one, among all the islands. They walk on fire." The General paused. "I saw it. With my own eyes. They dig a pit - large, several sazhens - and fill it with stones. River stones, smooth. They build a fire on the stones. Burn it all day. The stones heat white - so that one cannot approach the pit nearer than five paces, the hairs on one's arms crackle from the heat. Then the embers are raked out with long poles. And only stones remain. White. Glowing."

He paused. In the study it was quiet, only the fireplace crackled.

"And then the men come out," said the General. "Barefoot. Their priest - an old man, whom they called Tui Kai - goes in front. They walk on the stones. Slowly. Calmly. There and back." He raised his eyes to us. "I looked at their feet afterward. Not a burn. Not a blister. Not a single mark."

"Impossible," said Strauch.

"I saw it, Karl Fyodorovich," said the General. "I do not ask you to believe. I say - I saw."

"How do they explain it?" asked Sventsitsky.

"By a legend," said the General. "Long ago, they say, an ancestor of theirs, a fisherman, caught in the river a god. A little one. The god begged to be released. And in reward gave the fisherman and all his line power over fire. Fire does not burn those whom the god has released." The General paused. "But Tui Kai, the priest, told me something else. Later, at night, by the fire. Through an interpreter - a runaway Irish convict who had lived twenty years on the islands and knew all their languages."

"What did he tell?"

The General looked into the fire a long time.

"He said that fire does not burn those who themselves came from fire. That their ancestors are not fishermen. That their ancestors came down from the sky. Together with fire. And that once - long ago, in his grandfather's time - a white man came to their island. Alone. Without a ship." The General paused. "No one saw how he arrived. In the morning he was simply sitting on the shore. Young. He did not remember who he was. And when they showed him the walking on fire - he rose and walked on the stones. First. Before the priests. Himself."

"And was not burned?" whispered Konstantin.

"Tui Kai said," the General spoke slowly, "that the stones under his feet cooled. Became cold. All of them. As though he took their heat into himself." The General paused. "And then he reached the end of the pit - and went into the jungle. To the cliff at the edge of the island, from which, by their belief, the souls of the dead leap into the sea to go to the other world. And he was not seen again."

"The cliff from which souls leap," repeated Sventsitsky.

"They say," the General nodded, "that on the western edge of the largest island there is a cape. From there the soul of the dead leaps into the sea and swims to Bulu - the land of the dead, under the water. And on the way it is met by the god Degei. A huge serpent. He lives in a cave in the mountains. When he turns in his sleep, the earth shakes." The General paused. "Tui Kai said that that white man, before leaping, stood on the cape and wrote something on the rock. With a finger. On the wet stone. And that the next morning, when the water dried, the signs remained. Burned in. Like a brand."

"Did you see that cape?" I asked.

The General looked at me. For a long time.

"I did," he said. "We put in there before sailing. The captain did not want to - there are reefs - but I persuaded him." He paused. "The signs on the rock were there. Burned in. Almost effaced by the surf in half a century. But there."

He slowly set his glass on the mantelpiece. Went to the desk. Laid a finger on the Turkmen scroll - on the fifth line from the bottom.

"These," he said.

* * *
No one spoke. The candles guttered. The fire in the fireplace was dying.

Then my aunt rose. Came to the desk. Looked at the scroll, at the monastery paper, at the professor's notebook. At the three identical lines that had come from three ends of the world. And at three more places where the General had seen them - the mountain above the sea in Brazil, the cliff above the reefs on Fiji - and at one more, about which she had been silent forty years. The dust at the railings.

"Pavel," she said. Without patronymic. For the first time in all the time I had known her - before everyone. "Give it to him."

The General looked at her. Then at me.

"The old man in the sands said," he spoke slowly, "'You are not that man. But you will meet him. Give it to him.'" He paused. "For thirty years I have looked at faces. On three continents. On five seas." He carefully, tenderly rolled up the scroll, tied it with the cord of goat's wool, wrapped it in the faded blue kerchief. "I do not know whether you are that man. I know only that I have not met another."

He held the parcel out to me.

"The earth remembers," he said. "So the old man bade me say."

I took it. The parcel was light. Light as a bird. And warm - like the coin, like a stone in the sun, like a hand held too long to let go.

* * *
Then everyone dispersed. Sventsitsky - to the guest room, to write, - he said he would not sleep till he had written down everything, to the last word, and that he would leave the day after tomorrow, "if the General does not abduct me again." Strauch - to his outbuilding, where, as I learned afterward from Dunyasha, he sat till morning smoking cigar after cigar and rereading some German book. The General - to the terrace, alone. My aunt - to her rooms, saying not another word.

Konstantin walked me to my room. In silence. At the door he stopped.

"Mon cher," he said. "Brazil. Argentina. Fiji. Khiva. Tarnovo." He paused. "Everywhere there was someone. Young. Nameless. Who did not remember who he was. And everywhere left one and the same line."

"I heard."

"And everywhere went away," said Konstantin. Quietly. "Into the jungle. Into the pampa. Into the sea from a cliff." He looked at me, and in his eyes, in the uncertain candlelight, was something that made my heart contract. "Will you go too?"

I did not know what to answer.

"I don't know," I said honestly.

Konstantin nodded. As though this were exactly what he had feared.

"Then I shall sit by the door," he said. "Every night. Until you know."

"You cannot sit by the door every night."

"I can," said Konstantin. "I am a lieutenant. I know how not to sleep." He clapped me on the shoulder. "Good night, man from the City of the Caesars."

And went off without looking back.

* * *
I laid the parcel on the table. Beside the blue notebook. Beside the cutting of the black rose in its clay pot.

And saw that the bud had opened.

Not entirely. Halfway. The dark scarlet, almost black petals had parted, revealing the heart - golden, like the pollen on the legs of bees in the General's garden. From the bud came a smell. Strong. Sweet. Honey and dust. Honey and sand. Honey and something else - steppe-like, bitter, like wormwood in August.

Like the scroll.

I sat on the bed and looked a long time at the rose that had opened out of season, in a foreign land, on my windowsill.

"When this rose blooms in a foreign land - I shall return."

Somewhere far off, at the end of the corridor, in the gallery, in the moonlight, hung the portrait of a young man in a light neckcloth, with two stones in his hand. Under crape. Which Agafya Tikhonovna, I knew, had straightened again - as she had straightened it every morning for fifty years.

And I knew - not understanding how - that this crape would fall no more.

Because the one who had been awaited had already come.

## Chapter XXVIII. The Most Ancient Epic

The grain was distributed on the third day of the festival, from dawn to sunset, at the gates of the Temple granaries - and I stood there all day, from the first sack to the last, beside Nefer-Ka.

So it had been proclaimed: from the hands of Pharaoh and the High Priest. Together. And we stood together - shoulder to shoulder, on a dais by the gate, above an endless river of people flowing past us with baskets, sacks, pots, with hems of garments stretched out like bowls. Nebamun sat at the foot of the dais at a low table and counted - every sack, every measure, every handful - dry, motionless as a heron over water. Beside him Ani, the deaf scribe of the council, wrote after him, every now and then asking "Repeat for the record?" so loudly that people in the queue began to laugh and the tension on the square eased.

Nefer-Ka smiled. All day. Bowed to the people. Blessed children. Touched the brows of the old with his hand. Pronounced: "The Temple gives what is its own to the people, as the god gives his water." And the people bowed to him. Bowed to both of us. But I saw - and Nebamun, I knew, saw too - that they bowed differently. To me - quickly, respectfully, as one bows to Pharaoh. To him - slowly, long, peering into his face. As one bows to the one who decides whether you will have bread tomorrow.

"He has outplayed you, my Pharaoh," Nebamun said to me in the evening, when the gates of the granaries had closed and the last sack was recorded. "You made him give the grain. And he made sure the people will remember that it was the Temple who gave it." He folded his tablets. "Three thousand hekats. The people will be fed for two moons. And they will thank him."

"I know, Nebamun."

"You know," nodded the keeper of the treasury. "And still you stood all day." He paused. "My father used to say: there are kings who feed the people, and there are kings who feed their own glory. The first are forgotten. The second are remembered." He looked at me over his tablets. "I, my Pharaoh, prefer to serve the first. But I am too old not to fear for them."

* * *
Paney found me at the exit from the square - out of breath, barefoot, with the training spear which he now carried everywhere, as Iti had once carried his brush.

"My Pharaoh!" he blurted. "Bata told me to pass it on. From Panehsy. The man with the scar through his eyebrow. He has gone."

"Gone?"

"Last night. The Medjay were watching. He left the tent where the bearers lived - though the bearers are no longer there, they left with the ambassador - and walked across the whole city to the temple of Ptah. Knocked at the back gate. They let him in." Paney caught his breath. "Panehsy says - he has not come out. Till now. He sits in the temple."

"Who opened the gate?"

Paney shook his head.

"The Medjay did not see. It was dark. Only a hand." He hesitated. "Bata says Panehsy said - the hand jingled."

Bracelets.

"Good, Paney," I said. "Tell Panehsy: let them keep watching. Not touch. And tell Bata that you did everything right."

The boy beamed and raced off. I watched him go and thought how quickly children learn to be soldiers when around them there is a war that no one has declared.

* * *
Amenemope sent for me at dusk - not a messenger, but Iti himself.

The youth waited at the small garden gate, under the jasmine, where we now met almost every night, and, seeing me, bowed - not like a scribe but somehow anew, awkwardly and warmly at once.

"My Pharaoh," he said. "The senior keeper says: tonight. The ark is open. He has the key. The High Priest has been on the square all day and this evening will be at the feast of the nomarch of Memphis - the one in honour of the festival. Until midnight he will not be here." He paused. "The senior keeper says that you have long wished to read the Epic whole. Not only those lines that are read at coronations." Iti raised his eyes to me. "He says: tonight it is possible. Perhaps never again."

"Why never again?"

Iti hesitated.

"He did not say, my Pharaoh. He only looked at me as old men look when they know something and do not wish to speak."

* * *
The Library at night was different from the Library by day.

By day it was a place where people worked: scribes bent over scrolls, brushes scratched, papyrus rustled, someone read aloud in an undertone, someone argued over a sign. At night it was a place where things slept. Not people - scrolls. Thousands of scrolls, laid in niches along the walls, from floor to ceiling, in leather cases, in clay jars, in wooden caskets - they lay in the dark as the old sleep, quietly, motionlessly, and I, entering, involuntarily slowed my step, as though afraid to wake them.

It smelled of cedar, dust, mice and old papyrus - sweetish, slightly musty, as dried reeds smell on a riverbank. A single lamp burned in the depths, by the large table. And beside it, leaning on his staff of black wood, stood Amenemope.

On the table before him lay the ark.

I had seen it before - at the coronation, from afar, when it was carried out, opened, three lines read from it and closed again. A long casket of cedar, covered with gold, with a lid in the form of a temple roof, with guardians at the corners - little golden figures of goddesses with outspread wings, embracing the ark on all sides as though protecting it. On the lid - a sign: a winged sun disc. And beneath it - two Eyes. Right and left.

I had not noticed this before. Two Eyes.

"My Pharaoh," said Amenemope, bowing. His voice in the silence of the Library sounded like the rustle of a turning page. "I promised that I would bring it at any hour of day or night. I keep my promises." He paused. "I am old. I do not know how many more years I shall hold this key. Perhaps not many. The High Priest lately asks me whether I am tired. Whether I do not wish to retire. To a quiet temple. By the southern cataracts."

By the southern cataracts. Whence no letters come.

"You will not go to the southern cataracts, Amenemope," I said.

The old man smiled - drily, as old parchment cracks.

"My Pharaoh is kind," he said. "But Pharaoh does not always decide who goes where." He turned the key in the lock of the ark. "Sit. The night is long, and the Epic longer. The boy will read. His eyes are younger than mine. And I shall listen and correct if he errs. Though he does not err. Ever. It is even tedious."

Iti blushed.

* * *
The Epic was not one scroll. There were seven. Seven tight, heavy scrolls, each as thick as an arm, wrapped in the finest linen yellowed to the colour of ivory. Amenemope took them out one by one, carefully, as infants are lifted from a cradle, and laid them on the table in a row.

"Seven," he said. "Like the seven branches of the Nile in the Delta. Like the seven Hathors who come to every child's cradle and foretell his fate." He touched the first scroll. "This one is about the beginning. This one - about the gods. This - about the First Ones. This - about the kings. This - about how people live. This - about death and what is after. And the seventh..." He stopped. "The seventh no one has read. Because no one can."

"Why?"

"You will see, my Pharaoh."

Iti unrolled the first scroll. Bent over it - so low that the ink stain on his cheek, fresh, today's, almost touched the papyrus. And began to read. Quietly, slowly, in a chant, as ancient texts are read - with that special, solemn intonation taught in the school of scribes from the very first days.

"'In the beginning there was nothing. There was no sky. There was no earth. There was neither day nor night, neither death nor life. There were no gods, and there were no names for that which was not. There was only water. Nun. Endless, dark, motionless water, which had neither bottom nor surface nor edge. It was everything - and it was nothing. It neither slept nor woke. It waited.'"

Iti fell silent, drew breath. The lamp crackled.

"'And out of the water rose a hill. Small. The first. Benben. As the first patch of black earth rises from the flood when the water recedes. And on the hill stood He-who-created-himself. Atum. He was not born - he came into being. He said: "I am." And when he said it - he became.'"

"'I am,'" I repeated quietly. "And became."

"Yes, my Pharaoh," said Amenemope from the shadow. "The most ancient word in the world. The first thing that was said. Everything else - after."

Somewhere deep within me, under the ribs, on the left, something stirred. Two words on a luminous window, in the dark, in a room I had never seen: "Who am I?" - "Who are you?"

I blinked. The vision went.

* * *
Iti read on. How Atum, lonely on his hill, breathed out - and from his breath was born Shu, the air. And spat - and from his spittle was born Tefnut, moisture. How Shu and Tefnut were lost in the darkness of Nun, and Atum sent his Eye to seek them, and the Eye found them and brought them back, and Atum wept with joy, and from his tears people were born.

"People were born from tears?" I asked.

"From tears, my Pharaoh," confirmed Amenemope. "That is why people weep so often. It is in their blood. It is their first memory."

"And the Eye?" I asked. "The Eye that sought the lost children?"

"The Eye became independent," said the old man. "Went away from Atum. Because while it sought the children, Atum had made himself a new Eye - and set it in the place of the old. And the old one returned and saw that its place was taken. And raged." He paused. "Then Atum took the old Eye and set it on his forehead. As a serpent. As the uraeus. The very one that Pharaoh wears on his crown. So that it would always be in front. And always look where he looks."

I involuntarily touched my forehead - where by day, on the square, in the crown, I had the uraeus.

"The Eye that seeks the lost," said Iti quietly, not raising his head from the scroll. "And returns. And finds its place taken. And rages." He paused. "Like the lioness in the southern ambassador's tale. Who went to the south."

"You listened?" I asked.

"I was writing it down, my Pharaoh," said Iti. "Every word. I always write down. Even when I am not asked."

He read on. How Shu and Tefnut bore Geb and Nut - earth and sky. How Geb and Nut loved each other so greatly that they lay embracing and there was no room between them for anything. How Shu, their father, stood between them and lifted Nut up - and so she stands ever since, arched over the earth, resting her hands on the west and her feet on the east - and weeps every morning with dew, because she cannot reach Geb.

"The star-watcher Seneb told me this," I said. "Four years ago. On an island in the Delta. When..."

I broke off. Iti raised his head. Looked at me.

"When you pulled a scribe boy out of the water," he said quietly. "Yes, my Pharaoh. I remember."

We looked at each other over the ancient scroll. The lamp crackled. Amenemope in the shadow coughed - delicately, as the old cough when they wish to say "I am here" and at once "I am not here."

"Read on, Iti," I said.

"I read, my Pharaoh," he said. And bent to the scroll. But his cheeks burned.

* * *
"'But there was another account,'" Iti read, having unrolled the second scroll. "'The priests of Memphis tell it differently. In Memphis they say: the world was not made by Atum. The world was made by Ptah. Ptah, who was before Atum. Ptah conceived the world in his heart. And named it with his tongue. And all that he conceived with his heart and named with his tongue - came to be. The sky came to be because he said "sky." The earth came to be because he said "earth." The gods came to be because he called them by name.'"

Iti stopped.

"Conceived with the heart and named with the tongue," he repeated slowly. "My Pharaoh, this is... this is like us. Like scribes. We too first conceive, and then write. And what we have written remains. Even when we are gone."

"Not so, boy," said Amenemope from the shadow. "We write what already is. Ptah named what was not yet." He paused. "Though... who knows. Perhaps we too sometimes write what is not yet. And then it appears. Because it has been named."

"How - appears?" I asked.

The old man raised his staff and pointed it at the shelves going off into the dark.

"Here lie thousands of scrolls, my Pharaoh. In them are recorded names. Kings. Gods. Cities. Rivers. People. Most of these people died long ago. Most of the cities are no more." He lowered the staff. "But while a scroll lies here, while someone can read the name - they are. They are still here. Not entirely. Half. Like shadows. Like those in the Duat, between worlds." He paused. "Ptah named the world - and the world came to be. We name the world - and the world remains. Perhaps it is the same. Only from different ends."

From different ends. Like an inscription that is read in both directions.

How did I know that? I did not know.

* * *
The third scroll was about the First Ones.

Iti unrolled it - and froze.

"My Pharaoh," he whispered. "Here... here the hand is different."

I bent toward him. He was right. The first two scrolls were written in an even, solemn, ancient hand - such as was written under the very first kings. This one - also ancient, but different. More angular. More hurried. As though the writer was in haste. Or afraid he would not be in time.

"'And then,'" Iti read, running a finger along the lines without touching them, "'when the gods had gone to heaven, and people were left on earth alone, and did not know how to live, and died of hunger, and killed one another, and had neither king nor law nor Maat - then there came down from the sky the First Ones.'"

"'They came down in a barque,'" Iti read. "'Not such as ours. Their barque was made of light. It shone so that people fell on their faces and could not look. It alighted on a hill, on that very Benben where Atum had once stood. And from the barque came out the First Ones. They were tall - taller than any man. Their faces shone. They spoke a language that no one understood - and all understood.'"

Tall. Taller than any man.

"'They taught people to sow barley and emmer. To count the days by the stars. To measure the water of the Nile. To build. To write. They gave people Maat - truth, order, measure. They chose from among the people the most worthy - and set him as king. The first Pharaoh. And gave into his hands that which they had brought with them from heaven.'"

Iti raised his eyes.

"'The Two Eyes,'" he read.

I stopped breathing.

"'One Eye is light,'" Iti read on, and his voice trembled. "'It leads. It sees the path. The other is dark. It keeps. It remembers. He who holds both stands at the door between worlds. He who holds both can go and return. But cannot remain.'"

"Cannot remain," I repeated.

"'And the First Ones said to the king: "We shall go. We must. But we shall return. One of us will return. Not as now. In another body. In another time. He will not remember who he is. He will seek. When he finds - let him find the Two Eyes where they wait. And when he remembers his first name - he will return what was taken. And the two Eyes will become one."'"

Iti fell silent. In the Library it became so quiet that I heard somewhere in the dark, behind the shelves, a mouse scratching.

"You have heard this before," I said to Amenemope. Not asking.

"I have heard this for forty years, my Pharaoh," said the old man from the shadow. "From my teacher. And he from his. These lines are known by heart to all senior keepers." He paused. "And all of them asked one question. Who is 'he'? Who will return? Whom to await?"

"And who?"

"It is not written, my Pharaoh," said Amenemope. "There is no name." He paused. "But my teacher used to say: each time a new Pharaoh ascends the throne, the High Priest comes here. And rereads these lines. And looks at the new Pharaoh. Long." The old man tapped his staff on the floor. "And waits."

* * *
The fourth scroll - about the kings - Iti read quickly, hurrying; it was a long, tedious list of names, years of reign, wars, temples, floods. The fifth - about people: how to plough, how to sow, how to bury, how to judge. The sixth - about death: about the Duat, the twelve gates, the Hall of Two Truths, the forty-two judges, the feather of Maat and the beast Ammit. All this I had already heard - from Amenemope, from Seneb, from Khemu. All this was familiar.

But in the sixth scroll, at the very end, there was a place that made Iti turn pale.

"'And beyond the edge of the world,'" he read, "'beyond the deserts, beyond the seas, beyond the Great Green, beyond the land of Punt, whence incense comes, beyond the land of Keftiu, whence bulls and ships come, beyond the land of Retenu, whence cedars come - there the earth ends. And Nun begins. That same water from which everything came. It surrounds the world on all sides - above, below, at the edges. The world in it is like a bubble of air in a jar of water. Small. Fragile. And if the bubble bursts - Nun will return. And all will be as it was before the beginning. Nothing.'"

"The world - like a bubble in water," I said.

"So the ancients believed, my Pharaoh," said Amenemope. "And so they believe to this day. That is why each day the priests perform rites. So the bubble does not burst. So that Ra passes through the Duat and is born again. So that Apep - the serpent of chaos - does not swallow the solar barque." He paused. "The priests say that without them the world will end. Perhaps so. Or perhaps the world is simply very patient."

"Have you seen the edge of the world, Amenemope?" Iti suddenly asked.

The old man laughed - drily, with a rattle.

"I, boy, have never gone farther than Memphis." He paused. "But I knew a man who had seen. A sailor. He went to Punt - south, along the Red Sea, for incense. Twenty times he went. He told of people there with dark skin who build houses on piles. That trees grow there from which frankincense flows. That there are beasts there - spotted, with necks to the sky." He smiled. "We laughed at him then. A neck to the sky! And today such a beast ate the fig tree in Pharaoh's courtyard."

Iti snorted. I too.

"And farther than Punt?" I asked.

"Farther, said the sailor," said Amenemope, "the sea. Endless. And once, in a storm, their ship was carried far to the south. So far that the stars overhead became different. He said - stars appeared that no one had ever seen. Four. In a cross. Bright." The old man shook his head. "We did not believe him then. Stars are the same always and everywhere. So it is written. But he swore. He said: the world is bigger than written in scrolls. Much bigger. And at its edge - not Nun. But other people. Who look at other stars."

Four stars. In a cross. Somewhere I had heard this. Somewhere, from someone. A tall grey-haired man in strange clothes, by a fireplace, telling of a white light, eucalyptus trees and a bird that laughs at dawn...

No. I had never heard this. I blinked - and the alien voice went.

* * *
The seventh scroll Amenemope unrolled himself.

Slowly. Carefully. His hands, usually so firm, trembled.

"Here," he said. "Here is why no one has read it."

I bent over the table. Iti beside me, so close that I felt the warmth of his shoulder.

The seventh scroll was written not in hieroglyphs. All of it, from edge to edge. In long, flowing, curving lines running one into another without breaks, without spaces, without beginning or end.

The script.

The same as on the papyrus from the lower storehouse. The same as on the fragment of the Rock of the First Ones that Djehuty brought. The same as on the forehead of blind Nanakhat.

"For forty years I have looked at it," said Amenemope quietly. "And my teacher looked at it for forty years. And his teacher. No one has read a sign." He paused. "The High Priest has looked at it for thirty years. Three times in a single moon he took it. Sat right here where you sit, my Pharaoh, and looked till dawn."

Iti was not listening. He looked at the scroll - without tearing away, bent so low that he almost lay on the table. His fingers moved above the lines, not touching them - back and forth, back and forth - as though he were counting something.

"My Pharaoh," he suddenly whispered. "Look. Here. At the very beginning."

I looked. At the very beginning of the scroll, in the upper corner, the script broke off. There, in a small square window ringed with a red line, stood three lines. Not in script. In hieroglyphs. Small, ancient, faded. And beneath them - script again. One line. Short.

"Here it is written in our signs," said Iti, and his voice broke to a whisper. "'Words of the First Ones. Keep until the appointed time.' And beneath it - the script. Of the same length." He raised his eyes to me, huge, dark, shining. "My Pharaoh, it is the same. The same thing is written here - in our signs and in theirs. Side by side. Like a translation."

Amenemope, standing in the shadow, slowly came to the table. Bent. Looked long.

"Forty years," he whispered. "Forty years I looked at this corner. And thought - it is merely a heading. A keeper's note." He straightened. "And it is a key."

Iti was already taking from his bosom a rolled papyrus - the very one from the lower storehouse, found by him in the jar - and spreading it alongside. "Words of the First Ones. Sent down from the Heavens together with the Two Eyes. Do not read. Do not show. Keep until the appointed time." And beneath it - the script.

He moved his finger from one to the other. Compared. Moved his lips.

"Here," he said at last. "Here is this sign. Here - and here. The same. It stands where we have 'keep.'" The finger moved on. "And this one, with the loop - where we have 'time.'" He leaned back, pale, with burning eyes. "My Pharaoh. We know two words. Two words in the language of the First Ones. 'Keep.' 'Time.'"

"Two words," repeated Amenemope. "In forty years - two words."

"In one night," I corrected.

* * *
The door of the Library opened without a knock.

All three of us turned at once. Amenemope dropped his staff - it fell with a dull thud on the stone floor. Iti lunged - to seize the papyrus from the lower storehouse, to hide it - and froze, too late.

In the doorway stood Nefer-Ka.

Without retinue. Without torch. In a plain white robe, without the leopard skin, without the staff with the Eye. Tall, straight as an obelisk. His face - motionless, calm. He looked at the table. At the seven unrolled scrolls. At the seventh. At the small papyrus beside it.

"The feast of the nomarch of Memphis," he said quietly, "proved duller than I expected. I decided to return early." He entered, slowly, softly, treading noiselessly with bare feet on the stone slabs. "And I see I was not mistaken. It is far more interesting here."

Amenemope, trembling, bent for his staff. Nefer-Ka picked it up first - lightly, in one movement - and held it out to the old man.

"Do not trouble yourself, honoured keeper," he said gently. "At your age it is harmful to bend. One may not straighten again."

Amenemope took the staff. His hands shook.

Nefer-Ka went to the table. Stopped opposite me. Looked at the seventh scroll. Then at the little papyrus. Then at Iti.

"So this is what you found in the jar, boy," he said. "And Isiret showed me a sodden account of grain." He smiled slightly. "Old fox. I have always respected her."

Iti stood motionless. White as linen. But he did not retreat. And did not lower his eyes.

"Do not touch him, Nefer-Ka," I said.

The High Priest slowly shifted his gaze to me.

"Touch?" He raised his brows. "My Pharaoh, I do not touch scribes. Scribes are the most precious thing in the Two Lands. Without them there would be neither laws nor gods nor Epic." He looked at Iti again. "Especially such as this. Who in one night has read two words which I could not read in thirty years."

* * *
He sat. Directly opposite me, on the stool where Amenemope had just sat. Laid his palms on the table, on either side of the seventh scroll. Not touching it.

"You want to know what I seek, my Pharaoh," he said. Not asking. "You think - power. Grain. The throne. You think I want to become you."

"And do you not?"

Nefer-Ka was silent a long time. The lamp crackled. Somewhere in the dark the mouse scratched on.

"I read this Epic when I was twenty," he said at last. "In secret. My teacher, the former High Priest, gave me the key for one night - as you gave it to this boy. I read. All of it. From beginning to end. And understood one thing which before me, it seems, no one understood." He raised his eyes to me. "The First Ones return. Again and again. In another body, in another time, not remembering themselves. So it is written. You have read it."

"I have."

"And do you know what happens when they return?" His voice dropped. "I read the chronicles. All the chronicles in this Library, for all the years, for all the kings. I searched. Twenty years I searched. And found." He paused. "Every time in the chronicles a king appears who 'looks through people,' 'does not remember his name,' 'speaks in his sleep in an unknown tongue' - every time after his reign a drought comes. A great one. Three years. Five. Seven. Every time. Because he comes - and goes. And takes the Eye with him. That which holds the water. That which holds the world."

Cold under the ribs. On the left.

"Three hundred years ago," Nefer-Ka went on, "there was a Pharaoh whose name was erased from the walls. He came from nowhere. He did not remember who he was. He reigned ten years. Then he went to the festival of Opet at Luxor - and returned different. And a year later he vanished. Entirely. And for seven years there was no flood. Half of Egypt died of hunger." Nefer-Ka looked at me unblinking. "The priests erased his name. So that he would not return. But he returned. He always returns."

"And you think that is I."

"I do not think, my Pharaoh," said Nefer-Ka. "I know. I looked at you when you ascended the throne. As all High Priests looked at all Pharaohs. And I saw." He paused. "You look through people. You do not remember where you came from. You speak in your sleep. Your servants hear." He smiled slightly. "Your physician Hesira treats your headache with a clay crocodile and asks when it began. And you answer - 'it seems, always.'"

"The drought began three years ago," I said. "I have reigned longer."

"The drought does not begin when he goes, my Pharaoh," said Nefer-Ka gently. "The drought begins when he begins to remember."

* * *
Iti behind my back sighed quietly. Amenemope stood motionless, leaning on his staff.

"And what do you want, Nefer-Ka?" I asked.

The High Priest rose. Looked at the seventh scroll.

"I want him to stay this time," he said. Simply. Without a smile. "That the Eye remain here. In Egypt. By the river. That the water return - and never leave again. Never." He raised his eyes to me, and in them for the first time in all the time I had known him I saw not calculation, not condescension, not predatory patience, but something else. Weariness. Ancient, endless weariness. "For thirty years I have watched people die of hunger, my Pharaoh. I have buried children. I have seen mothers sell daughters for a sack of barley." He paused. "I do not want it to happen again. Once more. In three hundred years. In a thousand. Each time he comes and goes."

"And if he does not go? If he stays?"

"Then the circle will break," said Nefer-Ka. "And the two Eyes will never become one." He paused. "And Egypt will live. Always."

"And he?"

Nefer-Ka gave me a long, heavy look.

"And he, my Pharaoh," he said quietly, "will cease to be what he was. Will become simply a man. Like all. Who will one day die." He paused. "Is it so terrible - to become simply a man?"

I did not answer. I did not know the answer.

Nefer-Ka turned to the door. At the threshold he stopped.

"In Luxor, my Pharaoh, on the last day of the festival," he said without turning, "in the inner court, I shall reveal to you what I myself read at twenty. All that is not written here. You will be able to choose. To go - or to stay." A pause. "I hope you will choose rightly."

"And if I choose not as you wish?"

Nefer-Ka slowly turned. His face was again immobile, calm, like the face of a stone god at a temple gate.

"Then, my Pharaoh," he said, "I shall have to choose for you."

He looked at Iti. Long. Then at Amenemope. Then again at me.

"Two words," he said. "'Keep' and 'time.' In one night." He inclined his head slightly. "Boy, you are cleverer than all the senior keepers of three hundred years. Take care of yourself. The clever in this city do not live long if they do not know when to fall silent."

And went out.

* * *
We were silent a long while after the door closed behind him.
