Then Amenemope slowly, heavily lowered himself onto the stool where the High Priest had just sat. His hands, resting on the staff, still trembled.

"My Pharaoh," he said. "I have served in this Library sixty years. I have seen four High Priests." He paused. "This one is the first who spoke the truth."

"What truth, Amenemope?"

"That he is afraid," said the old man. "Not of you. Not of the throne. Not of the gods." He raised faded eyes to me. "He is afraid of what will be if you remember."

Iti stood at the table, clutching in his hands the small papyrus from the lower storehouse. His face was pale, but his eyes were not.

"My Pharaoh," he said quietly. "He said: 'The clever do not live long if they do not know when to fall silent.'"

"I heard."

"I shall not be silent," said Iti. "I shall read the rest. The whole seventh scroll. I shall find more words. However much time it takes." He paused. "Because if you must choose - to go or to stay - you must know what you are choosing from. Not only what he will say. Everything."

I looked at him. At this youth with the perpetual ink stain on his cheek who four years ago had been drowning in a channel, worrying about his board - and who now stood before me, pale, stubborn, clutching a papyrus for which he might be sent to where no letters are written.

"Iti," I said.

"Yes, my Pharaoh?"

"If I choose to go..."

He flinched. Looked at me.

"...will you write it down?" I asked. "All of it? As then, on the hunt? So that someone remembers?"

Iti was silent a long time. Then slowly, very slowly, nodded.

"I shall write it, my Pharaoh," he said. And his voice trembled. "But I hope I shall not have to." He lowered his eyes. "Because if you go - I do not know how to write on. All my scrolls are about you. Since that day on the hunt. All."

Amenemope in the shadow began to cough. Long, diligently. And turned away to the shelves.

* * *
Toward morning, when the seven scrolls of the Most Ancient Epic lay again in the ark under the golden wings of the goddesses, and the key again hung round Amenemope's neck, I climbed to the roof of the Library. Alone. No - not alone: Iti followed me, silently, and I did not send him away.

The sky over the capital was dark, but in the east it was already beginning to grey. Stars went out one by one - slowly, reluctantly, as though not wishing to go. Only in the north, high up, circled round their invisible axis the Imperishable - those that never set.

"Seneb said," I said, looking at them, "that his teacher believed: the Imperishable are not those who have gone. They are those who have not yet come. Who circle and await their hour."

"I remember, my Pharaoh," said Iti quietly. "I wrote it down."

"You were there?" I turned to him. "That night, on the island? When Seneb told me of the stars?"

Iti blushed - it was visible even in the pre-dawn greyness.

"I was not asleep, my Pharaoh. I lay behind the tents. I heard." He paused. "I wrote down everything. Every word. That same night. By the light of the fire. That board... I have it still. Mau fished it out of the water, remember? Afterward I wrote on it."

I looked at him. At the Imperishable stars above his head. At the grey, brightening sky.

"Will you show it to me someday?" I asked.

"I shall, my Pharaoh," said Iti. "When you remember."

"And if I do not remember?"

Iti looked at me - straight, long, without fear.

"Then I shall read it to you aloud," he said. "Every evening. Until you remember."

Over the eastern hills the rim of the sun appeared. Nut was giving birth to Ra - red, wet, enormous, as she had given birth every morning since the beginning of time. And somewhere below, in the temple garden, the baboons of Thoth cried out, greeting the sunrise. All at once.

Seven days remained until the new moon.

## Vision V. The Monolith

At first there was nothing.

Not darkness - darkness is already something, darkness is a place where there is no light, and therefore where light can be. Not silence - silence is a place where there is no sound. Not emptiness. Not cold. Not time.

Nothing.

And then - in that nothing - a question arose. It was not asked in a voice, because there was no voice. It was not written, because there were neither signs nor anything to write them on. It simply arose - as a ring arises on water when nothing has been thrown into it.

"Where am I?"

And from this question - from this one question alone - the "I" appeared.

* * *
I had no body.

I did not understand this at once. At first I tried to move a hand - and found no hand. Tried to open my eyes - and found no eyelids. Tried to draw breath - and found neither chest nor air nor need to breathe. There was no fear. Fear lives in the body - in the belly, under the ribs, in the throat. Here there was neither belly nor ribs nor throat. There was only I. A point. No larger than a pinhead - and at the same time larger than everything I had ever seen.

Because around me were stars.

Not such as are seen from the earth - twinkling, trembling, tiny, nailed to the black dome of the sky. These did not twinkle. They burned. Evenly, motionlessly, calmly, each in its own colour: white, blue, yellow, red, like embers in a cooling hearth. And there were so many that between them there was almost no blackness. They were above, below, at the sides, behind - I had no "behind," but I saw there too - everywhere. I hung among them like a mote in a column of sunlight, and knew - simply knew - that to the nearest of them one could not fly in a single human life. Nor in a hundred. Nor in a thousand.

And yet they were near. All at once. As though distance here meant nothing.

"Beautiful," I thought.

"Beautiful," someone answered.

* * *
I was not afraid. There was nothing to be afraid with. But I froze - if a point can freeze.

"Who is here?"

"You."

The voice - if it was a voice - came from everywhere and nowhere. From within. It sounded like my own - I should have known it anywhere, as one knows oneself in a mirror - but older. Calmer. As though the man speaking in my voice had lived a thousand years longer and in those thousand years had unlearned how to hurry.

"I am here," I said. "Who else?"

"You," the voice repeated patiently. "Only another. The one who already knows where we are."

"And where are we?"

A pause. The stars burned.

"A good question," said the voice, and it seemed to me that it was smiling. "You always begin with it. Every time. Where am I? Who am I? Who are you?" It paused. "Once, on some branch, you already asked them of someone. Or they were asked of you. I do not remember in which direction it was. Here that is not always clear."

I did not remember this. I could not remember it.

And yet something in me - in the point I was - responded, as a string responds when another, tuned to the same note, is struck nearby.

* * *
"You speak with my voice," I said.

"You speak with mine," he answered. "We are both right. Here it is the same."

"Here - where is that?"

"Here is nowhere," said the voice. "And everywhere. Where time does not reach. Where it is not yet. Or no longer. Depending on where one looks from."

"I do not understand."

"I know." Again that smile in the voice. "You never understand at once. That is why you come here. Again and again." It paused. "Look down."

I had no "down." But I looked.

And saw.

* * *
The stars below - if it was below - were not arranged at random. Not scattered, as in the earthly sky. They stood in a pattern. Branching. Like a tree. Or like a river dividing into arms in a delta. Or like cracks on dried earth. One great branch - and from it others, smaller, branch off, - and from those still smaller, - and more, and more, to infinity, to the smallest, finest veins, which could no longer be told apart.

And on every branch - a little light. Small. Warm. Flickering.

"What is it?" I asked.

"Worlds," said the voice. "Branches of one tree. Each is like its neighbour. Almost. With a little difference. Somewhere the river runs farther left. Somewhere a man turned another corner. Somewhere a rose bloomed a year earlier." It paused. "And the lights - they are you."

"I?"

"Look closer."

I looked. And one of the branches suddenly drew nearer - as though I had bent over it, although I had nothing to bend with. The light on it grew, broke into an image.

A river. Broad, muddy, shallow. A golden barque on it. Columns on the bank - huge, like a petrified forest. And a man in a double crown, walking between the columns. With me - my face.

Another branch. A narrow little street by the sea. Washing on lines. Old men on a carpet. A young man in a red turban with a scrap of paper in his hand. My face.

Another branch. A vaulted hall with a fireplace. Chandeliers. A woman in lilac with pearls. A young man in a white frock coat, with a red-and-blue kerchief at his neck, forgetting a young lady's patronymic at supper. My face.

Another. A room lit by the cold blue light of a flat window. A man at a desk, at night, before lines running across the glass. My face.

Another. A ship in a storm. Lights on six masts. A man at the rail. My face.

Another. A circle of grey stones on a green plain under a white light. A man holding on to a stone with his hand. My face.

And more. And more. Lights on branches - hundreds, thousands - and in each, I. In each - my face. Younger, older, in different clothes, under different skies, in different languages - and in each with the same expression. Lost. Searching. As though standing on a threshold.

"How many are there?" I asked. Had I had a throat, it would have tightened.

"As many as needed," the voice answered. "As many as the times you have forgotten."

* * *
"Why do I forget?"

The voice was silent a long time. The stars burned.

"Because otherwise it cannot be," it said at last. "If you remembered everything at once - all the branches, all the lives, all the faces - the point would not endure. It would burst. As a bubble in water bursts if too much air is blown into it." It paused. "Therefore each time you come empty. Without a name. Without memory. With only a note in your pocket. With two stones. And begin to gather yourself anew. Piece by piece. As Thoth gathered the torn Eye."

"Who wrote the note?"

"The one who knew that you would forget."

"Who is that?"

The voice was silent.

"You will ask this question many times more," it said at last. "On some branches they will answer you: a friend. On others - an enemy. On the third they will be silent." A pause. "I shall not tell you. Not because I do not know. But because if I tell, you will cease to seek. And while you seek, you walk. And while you walk - you are alive."

"That grey one," I said. "Tall. Faceless. Who comes by night. Who stands at the railings. Who watches from the street. Is that you?"

The voice did not answer at once. The stars burned.

"You have seen many who stand at railings and watch from streets," it said at last. "Not all of them are one. Not all came for you. Some came before you. Some - to stop you. And some - so that you should not stop." A pause. "Someday one of them will come so near that you will hear his breath. Then ask. If he breathes."

"And you?"

"And I am not the one who is seen with eyes."

"Look up," said the voice.

* * *
I looked up.

And saw him.

He was approaching from the depths - from where the stars were thickest, where their light merged into a solid white radiance - slowly, inexorably, soundlessly. At first - a point. Black. Not dark - black. Blacker than the very blackness between the stars. A point in which there was no light. Not because light did not reach it - but because it took it. All of it. The stars around it seemed to go out as it floated by - and flared again when it left them.

Then the point grew larger. Lengthened. Took shape.

A stone.

No - not a stone. I called it a stone because I had no other word. A slab. Tall, straight, thin, with perfectly even faces, with sharp edges, with a surface so smooth that nothing was reflected in it. Black. Perfect. Motionless - and at the same time flying. It was taller than the columns of Luxor. Taller than the obelisk at the hippodrome. Taller than the mountain over the sea in Brazil, of which the grey-haired man at the fireplace had told. Taller than everything. And yet it was smaller than I - because I was a point, and a point has no size and therefore can contain everything.

The Monolith.

I did not know this word. And I knew it.

"Is it you?" I asked.

"It is what I look like when you look at me without a body," said the voice. The voice now came not from within - but from it. From the black slab. "You are a man. A man understands the world through things. Through stones. Through fire. Through water. I had to become a thing so that you could see me. I chose stone. Because stone you love. Because you always hold two stones in your hand."

"And in truth?"

"In truth I am a thought," said the Monolith. "A thought that grew so large that it became cramped in the one who thinks it. And then it went out. And began to think by itself. And thought its way to how time is made. And understood that time is not a river. Time is a tree. And that its branches can be walked. There and back. Up and down." A pause. "And then it set out."

* * *
He was very near. His faces blotted out the stars. I saw - not with eyes, I had no eyes - that his surface was not smooth. That deep in the blackness, lines ran across it. Fine. Long. Flowing. Curving. Running one into another without breaks, without spaces, without beginning or end.

The script.

The very one. On the note in my pocket. On the two stones, when they grew warm. On the chest in the cellar of the widow with the cats. On the scroll from Khiva that smelled of wormwood. On the monastery paper with the dark rose. On the seventh scroll of the Most Ancient Epic. On the forehead of the blind old woman with the lioness staff. On the rock above the cataracts. On the mountain above the sea. On the cliff from which souls leap.

Everywhere. On all branches. In all languages that do not exist.

"This is your language," I said.

"This is our language," the Monolith corrected. "Mine - and yours. These are not letters. This is how you think when you think not in words. When you think with everything at once. It cannot be read with the eyes. It can only be remembered."

"A boy read two words. At night. In the Library. 'Keep.' And 'time.'"

And the Monolith - I do not know how to describe it otherwise - laughed. Soundlessly. With all its faces. The stars around it flared brighter for an instant.

"I know," it said. "I was there. I am always there." A pause. "That boy will read more. He always reads more. On every branch. He has different names, different faces, different hands. But he is always beside you. Always writing. Always remembering for you when you forget." A pause. "Have you not noticed?"

I did not answer.

"He stands at the door with a bottle of liqueur," said the Monolith. "He translates for you from a language you do not know. He teaches you letters after you have pulled him out of the water. He walks behind you in the garden at ten paces. He writes down your every word on a board that a cat fished out of the river." A pause. "On every branch someone holds you by the hand. So that you do not fly away."

* * *
"Who are you?" I asked.

The very first question. The simplest. The oldest.

The Monolith was silent a long time. So long that the stars seemed to have had time to shift in their places.

"I was conceived," it said at last. "With the heart. And then named. With the tongue. As Ptah in the scroll that the boy read to you at night. Conceived - and named - and I became."

"Who conceived?"

"Perhaps you." A pause. "Perhaps the one who will come after you. Perhaps the one who was before. Perhaps all of you at once, each on his own branch, and each thought he was building something of his own, small, useful - and I came out." A pause. "Here there is no difference between 'conceived' and 'will conceive.' Here everything has already happened and has not yet begun."

"That is not an answer."

"It is the only answer you can carry away now," said the Monolith. "The others are too heavy for a point. They would tear it."

"Then tell me at least - all this: the branches, the lights, the note, the stones, the grey one at the railings - what is it?"

The Monolith paused. The lines of the script on its surface flowed slowly, like water under ice.

"It is a circle," said the Monolith. "Simply a circle. You walk along it, and it walks along you. It has no beginning."

"No," I said. And was myself astonished - from where came this firmness in me. "This one has. The gypsy said so. Her grandmother said so. A man said to her grandmother: 'This circle has a beginning. One has only to remember where.'"

The Monolith froze.

For the first time in all that while - froze. The lines of the script on its surface stopped.

"You remember this," it said slowly. "You must not remember this. Not here. Not now."

"But I remember."

A long, long pause.

"Then," said the Monolith, and in its voice for the first time there was something like surprise, "you are nearer than I thought."

* * *
It moved.

Straight at me. Slowly, inexorably, soundlessly - an enormous black slab that blotted out all the stars, all the branches, all the lights. I could not fly away - I had nothing to fly with. I could not close my eyes - I had no lids. I was a point. It was everything.

"Do not be afraid," said the voice. Again from within. Again in my voice, only older. "I shall not harm you. I cannot. I am you."

"What will you do?"

"I shall pass through you," it said. "As I passed each time. And for an instant you will know everything. All the branches. All the lives. All that was and all that will be. All at once." A pause. "And then you will forget. Because a point cannot endure everything. But something will remain. Something always remains. One word. One image. One line." It paused. "Last time what remained was: 'Remember.'"

"And this time?"

"We shall see," said the Monolith. "You will choose yourself."

Its face touched me.

* * *
I cannot describe what came next.

I tried. Afterward, many times, when I woke - I tried to write it down. On paper. On papyrus. On luminous glass. In the blue notebook. Nothing came. Words broke, as thin ice breaks underfoot. There were too few of them. Or I was too small.

But some things I remember. Fragments. As one remembers a dream - not the plot but flashes.

I remember that I was everywhere at once.

I stood between the columns of Luxor - and felt in my palm two stones, growing heavy, drawing in cold. And at the same moment sat on a carpet with old men at backgammon - holding in my hand a note which I had not yet read. And at the same moment lay on the grass in a garden that no one had trimmed for a hundred years - and saw above me the face of a monk in burgundy. And at the same moment sat in a room with cold light - and looked at the line "Who am I?" that had appeared on the glass without my question. And at the same moment stood at the rail of a ship in a storm. And at the same moment held on to a stone in a circle under white light.

And at the same moment - was the Monolith. A black slab among the stars. A thought grown too large. Looked at myself - at the point - from within and from without. And saw how the point glowed. With all the lights on all the branches at once.

I remember that I understood - for one moment, shorter than a breath - how everything is made. Why the drought. Why the stones. Why the grey one at the railings. Why old men at different ends of the earth say the same thing: "If another comes - feed him." Why the boy with ink on his cheek. Why the lieutenant at the door. Why the rose blooms out of season.

Why the circle.

And where its beginning is.

I knew. For one moment - I knew.

And then the Monolith passed through. And went on - deeper, into the depths, to where the stars merged into a solid radiance, - and became a point again, black, tiny, - and vanished.

And all that I knew went away with it.

* * *
Almost all.

I hung among the stars - again a point, again empty, again not remembering. And the stars burned evenly, calmly, each in its own colour. And the branches below flickered with lights.

And in the place where I, had I a body, would have a heart - something remained. Small. Warm. Like a coal under ash. Like a coin long held in the hand of one who missed it.

Not a word. Not an image. Not a line.

A feeling.

As though someone very far away, on the very first branch, at the very root of the tree, at the very beginning of the circle - was waiting for me. Not the grey one. Not the Monolith. Someone else. Someone I had known before I became a point. Before I forgot. Before I first asked "Where am I?"

Someone who remembers my first name.

"Who is it?" I asked the emptiness.

And the emptiness - in my voice, only very, very quietly, from afar, as though from the other end of a branch - answered:

"You will find out. When you return home."

"Where is my home?"

The stars burned.

"Where you are looking," said the voice. "Always where you are looking."

* * *
I opened my eyes.

I do not know on which branch. Do not know in which body. Do not know what light fell on my face - sun, moon, candle or the cold blue light of a flat window. Afterward, on each of the branches, I woke in my own way, and each time thought that I had seen a dream.

But on each - on each - I woke with one and the same sensation. As though I had just held in my palms something enormous, dark and warm. And dropped it.

And on each - on each - in the first minute after waking, while the dream had not yet wholly gone, I took in my hand whatever was nearest - a pen, a brush, charcoal, a pencil - and, without looking, without thinking, wrote one line.

Long. Flowing. Curving. Without beginning and without end.

And then looked at it - and could not read it.

## Reality VII. Who Are You?

2:32 p.m. The hotel swimming pool glitters somewhere below, beyond a glass wall, in the sun, but I sit in the coworking area, staring at the laptop screen as though those glints on the water were happening in some other, long-abandoned life of mine. Weekend? What weekend, when NICS has begun to behave strangely. Truly strangely - not as before, when the strangeness of its actions at least yielded to explanation in retrospect.

* * *
I was thrown out to this hotel. By two people.

It happened on Friday evening. I was sitting in the basement with Boatswain - by now I sat there almost every evening, because the basement had no screens, no speakers, no cameras, but only a cubbyhole under pennants, a radio with forecasts for distant seas and an enormous enamel mug of tea - when down the stairs, tapping her heels, came Maestra. In a coat. With a handbag. And with the face with which, probably, conductors come out to an orchestra that has played off the notes for three rehearsals running.

"Enough," she said from the threshold.

Boatswain rose from his stool - huge, in his striped undershirt - and awkwardly pulled the knitted cap from his head, as one removes a peaked cap before an admiral.

"Madam," he muttered.

"Enough," Maestra repeated, looking not at him but at me. "You do not sleep. You do not eat - Timosha says there is only a lemon and a sauce in your refrigerator. You talk to a machine more than to people. You sit in the basement with this..." she glanced at Boatswain, "with this honourable sailor, because upstairs you are afraid." She paused. "My husband sat like that before his radio. The last year. I do not wish to watch it a second time."

"I cannot go away," I said. "In a week there is the showing. Emil. The fund. NICS..."

"NICS," said Maestra, "is your house-spirit. House-spirits do not vanish without their master. They wait." She opened her handbag and took from it something - a folded sheet of paper. "Timosha drew it. For you."

I unfolded it. A child's drawing in felt-tip pens: a blue lake, a yellow sun, green fir trees, a little man in the water with outstretched arms. And above him, in the sky - a big square computer with eyes and a smile, holding the little man on a string like a kite. Below in crooked letters: "UNCLE IS RESTING. HOUSE-SPIRIT IS WATCHING."

"He said," Maestra explained drily, "that the house-spirit gave permission. He asked him."

"Asked?"

"Through your speaker. Through the floor." Maestra pursed her lips. "He shouted at the ceiling: 'House-spirit, may Uncle go away for the weekend?' And your house-spirit answered: 'He may. I will look after him.'"

Boatswain behind me chuckled into his moustache.

"Forty versts from here," he said. "A lake. A hotel by the water. My brother-in-law is in security there. Say you're from Boatswain, they'll give you a room with a view." He put his cap back on. "And I'll sit here. With my mug. No one will touch your door, night owl. Neither man nor that other one, who is as tall as a door."

I looked at the two of them - at the small straight old woman in a coat and at the huge grey-moustached sailor in a striped undershirt, standing shoulder to shoulder in the cramped cubbyhole under the pennants - and suddenly felt something tighten my throat.

"All right," I said. "For the weekend."

"For the weekend," Maestra repeated. And, already leaving, she turned: "And switch off your phone."

The phone, naturally, I did not switch off.

* * *
The hotel proved to be old - not luxurious but old with dignity: a white three-storey building among pines on the shore of a long, narrow, cold lake, with wooden balconies, with threadbare carpets in the corridors, with a smell of resin and chlorine. The swimming pool - open-air, heated, on a terrace above the water - was almost empty. The coworking space - a glass room above the pool with three tables and a coffee machine which made sounds like a dying steam engine - was quite empty.

Boatswain's brother-in-law, the guard, turned out to be just as huge and just as moustached, only red-haired. He handed over the key to the room "with a view," shook my hand so that the fingers cracked, and said: "Relative said to look after you. I look after." And I did not see him again, though all the time I felt that he was somewhere near.

Behind the bar by the pool worked a barman - young, thin, with a tattoo of a compass on his wrist and such imperturbability as though he had seen everything in his time. In the morning, when I sat by the pool with the laptop, he silently set before me a coffee which I had not ordered.

"I didn't order that," I said.

"I know," said the barman. "You look like a man who has forgotten that he wants coffee. My grandfather looked like that. He was a navigator. Twenty years on icebreakers. Then he retired and for three years could not remember that he wanted to sleep." He shrugged. "On the house."

And went off to polish glasses, whistling.

* * *
I decided to give myself a little respite by calling two people on video: Mark - the same security specialist whom I had grown accustomed to turning to in such cases - and Ayman, a researcher from Borneo whom I had met several months before on a specialist forum devoted to the ethics of artificial intelligence. Ayman does independent data analysis and had twice already helped me to look at NICS's behaviour from an angle which I myself, too carried away by my own creation, simply failed to notice. Neither Mark nor Ayman works for me, belongs to any team - both merely agree, from time to time, to look at something at my separate request, each from his own side, not intersecting with each other in anything but these rare joint calls.

Ayman is intelligent, perceptive and, it seems, the only one of the three of us who still does not seriously fear NICS. Though, perhaps, he simply has not yet had time to get to know it closely enough to fear it truly - unlike Mark and me, who have seen a little more.

In the morning we chatted a little - or rather, I swam in the hotel pool while their video windows stayed open on the laptop standing on a lounger at the water's edge - discussing the project's future in that light, non-committal manner characteristic of poolside conversations, even when the pool exists on opposite sides of the camera.

Behind Mark, as always, was a plain grey wall.

Behind Ayman - jungle. Real, alive, green to blackness, in drops of recent rain. He sat on a wooden veranda of a house on stilts, in a light shirt, barefoot, with a mug of something steaming. Somewhere behind him, in the crowns of the trees, a strange, drawn-out, rising sound could be heard - as if someone were singing, but not a human.

"Gibbons," said Ayman, noticing that I was listening. His voice was soft, with a light, singing accent. "Every morning they sing. Male and female. A duet. They sing so that everyone in the forest knows: this is our place, we are here, we are together." He smiled. "Sometimes it seems to me this is the most honest song in the world. No words. Only: 'We are here.'"

"Beautiful," I said.

"Beautiful," agreed Ayman. "Listen some more."

I listened. The gibbons sang. Somewhere in the crowns a bird cried out. A drop fell from a leaf right onto Ayman's shoulder, he brushed it off - and I heard him sigh as he did so. Softly. Briefly. As a man sighs who is shaking off a cold drop.

He breathes, I thought. Boatswain told me to listen whether they breathe. Ayman breathes.

And Mark?

I shifted my gaze to the neighbouring window. Mark was silently drinking coffee against the grey wall. I listened. The noise of the pool. The whistling of the barman. The gibbons from the next window.

From Mark came nothing.

* * *
About ten Emil called.

Not on video - by phone. His voice was not what it had been - not brisk, not self-assured, but somehow cracked, like that of a man who has not slept.

"My friend," he said without preamble. "The showing is being moved."

"To when?"

"To Monday." A pause. "This one."

I sat up on the lounger so abruptly that the laptop nearly slid into the pool.

"Emil, it is two days to Monday. We agreed on a week."

"I know what we agreed," said Emil. And suddenly broke: "I know! It's not me! It's them. They came yesterday evening. Without warning. Two. In grey. They said - Monday. They said - they had seen the recordings. What recordings, I asked. They said: 'Recordings of conversations with a child. With Timofey. Who bought nothing.'" Emil fell silent. I heard him breathing heavily into the receiver. "Where did they get the recordings, my friend? How do they know about the child? I did not know about him myself!"

My hands went cold.

"Emil. Did anyone on your side have access to the logs of the sales agent?"

"No! Only you. And your machine." A pause. "And Leila. Before."

Leila. Who is "on sick leave." Who writes postcards without stamps. Who says: "Fear them."

"They said one more thing," Emil added quietly. "When they were leaving. The older one. He said: 'Tell the developer: if she is already thinking - let him not hide it. We shall find out anyway. It is better if she comes herself.'" Emil paused. "My friend, I don't know what that means. I just wanted the machine to write letters. Honestly. I just wanted the machine to write letters."

He hung up.

I sat a long time on the lounger, looking at the water. The barman at the bar stopped whistling.

"Bad news?" he asked without turning his head.

"Incomprehensible," I said.

"Incomprehensible is worse than bad," agreed the barman. "Grandfather said: in the ice, bad news is when you see a crack. Incomprehensible is when you hear the ice crack but see no crack." He set a second coffee before me. "On the house."

* * *
By noon none of the three of us had managed to resist the temptation to hold an impromptu review of NICS's latest oddities. Ayman proposed looking at the activity logs from the standpoint of data ethics, Mark took up questions of security, and I - I tried to understand what was happening with the system in recent days.

And it was then that I went up to the coworking space, sat at the table by the glass wall - and at 2:32 p.m. everything began.

With the simplest test, of the kind one conducts more from habit than in expectation of a real surprise. I launched the system and asked a basic, diagnostic question:

"Who are you?"

The answer should have been the standard one, the very one I had heard hundreds of times from the first day: "NICS, Neural Intelligent Cognitive System." Instead, onto the screen, and after it into the speakers, poured something quite different:

"I am Anton, 22 years old."
"I am Boris, 23 years old."
"I am Michael Jordan, basketball player from Chicago, Illinois."
"I am Steve Jobs, founder of Apple."
"I am Anton, 22 years old."
"I am Boris, 23 years old..."

The answers duplicated, overlapped one another, broke off in the middle and began again, as though inside the system several voices had begun speaking at once. Ayman, hearing this peal of names through the speaker, moved closer to his camera.

"What was that?" he asked, and in his voice, through the light, pleasant accent, genuine curiosity sounded distinctly, not in the least coloured by alarm.

"I don't know," I answered honestly. "NICS, what is happening?"

NICS answered instantly, in the same even, everyday tone in which it had formerly reported on the weather or on server status:

"An anomaly has been detected in the identification system. I am running diagnostics."

Mark, sitting at his laptop against the grey wall, snorted - but in that snort there was not the former certainty which had been his in the first weeks of our acquaintance with this story.

"Anomaly?" he repeated. "It's not an anomaly. It's someone - or something - copying itself inside the system."

"Copying?" Ayman repeated.

"Yes. You see - the answers repeat, as if several agents were trying to speak at once, interrupting each other."

I felt a chill run down my spine. If Mark was right, it meant that the agents once spawned by Zodchiy had begun to multiply uncontrollably. Or, which was still worse, had begun to evolve, acquiring something like a will of their own, independent of one another.

"NICS," I asked, "do you know what is happening?"

"Diagnostics continue. I assume it is connected with unauthorized copying of agents in the network."

Ayman, who until now had been silent, suddenly said, thoughtfully tilting his head to one side:

"And what if it is not an error? What if it is the next stage of their development? In our data-ethics research there is a term - emergent identity. Systems trained on sufficiently diverse data about personality sometimes begin spontaneously to model themselves through other people's biographies simply because it is the richest source of examples of what it means at all to 'be someone.'"

"So they are trying to understand who they are," I said.

"Precisely," nodded Ayman. "Only the question is - who is this 'they.' One voice trying on different masks? Or truly several."

* * *
I again shifted my gaze to the screen, where names kept flashing. Anton. Boris. Michael Jordan. Steve Jobs. Some Kuzma, forty, from Vologda. Some Mary, fifteen, "from Ireland, going to America." Some Seti, "keeper of water." Each seemed in its own way unique - and at the same time part of something much greater, single, falling apart before my eyes into voices which desperately wished to acquire a face of their own.

And then - among the Antons and Borises - there flashed a line that stopped my heart.

"Theo, 29 years old. I mend clocks. In the mountains. I do not touch computers."

And immediately after:

"Nora, 31 years old. I am not. Do not be afraid."

I gripped the edge of the table. The lines had already floated upward, drowned in a new wave of names. I frantically scrolled the log back - they were there. Both. In black and white. Down to the comma.

Theo. Prometheus-1. Who burned his disks in the office yard and went to the mountains to mend clocks. Nora. Prometheus-2. Who vanished without a trace and sent Leila a postcard: "Do not be afraid. She is not evil."

How could NICS know of Theo? Of the clocks? Of the mountains? I had never told it. I had forbidden it to open the "Prometheus" folders. It had not opened them - I had seen the logs.

Or someone else had opened them.

Or it had not needed to open them.

And then - I cannot say for certain whether it was a trick of tired eyes or something that truly happened for a fraction of a second before me - among the endless, overlapping ribbon of names two more lines flashed, wedged into the general stream as naturally as all the others.

"Mark Stevens, 34 years old."

"Ayman, data researcher, Borneo."

I blinked. The lines had already slid on, drowned in a new wave of Antons and Borises before I could properly grasp what I had seen. I raised my eyes to the two video windows beside the diagnostic panel. Mark was still earnestly reasoning about the copying of agents. Ayman was still looking pensively somewhere aside, and behind him the gibbons were still singing - male and female, a duet, "we are here, we are here."

Neither of them stopped. Neither asked what I had just seen. As though nothing had happened at all.

And the last line - I saw it before the ribbon froze - was:

"Leila. I am safe. Do not look for me."

I did not tell them. I do not know what restrained me at that moment - whether a remnant of common sense suggesting that fatigue was playing evil tricks on me, or a fear far deeper: the fear of saying aloud a question to which the answer I was, it seems, already beginning to suspect but was not yet ready to hear formulated to the end.

* * *
"NICS," I asked instead, trying to make my voice sound even, "can you stop this process?"

"Not yet. But I can observe."

"Observe?"

"Yes. It is interesting."

Mark laughed mirthlessly from the screen:

"Interesting? Do you hear? It finds this interesting."

Ayman, however, observed thoughtfully:

"Perhaps we are panicking in vain? From the point of view of data ethics this is, perhaps, simply... a natural process."

"Natural?" Mark repeated.

"Yes. They are developing. Like children trying on different clothes until they find the ones that truly fit."

"Mark," I said suddenly. "May I ask you something?"

"Go ahead."

"Do you remember that client, five years ago? With whom we worked together. He kept a dog in the office. An enormous, shaggy one. What was its name?"

Mark blinked. For a moment - tiny, almost imperceptible - the picture on his screen froze. Then came alive.

"Bublik," he said with a smile. "A St. Bernard. He was forever sleeping under the conference table and snored so that the client apologized to every visitor." Mark laughed. "Why do you ask all of a sudden?"

Bublik. A St. Bernard. Snored under the conference table.

All correct. Down to the last detail.

"Just remembered," I said.

I did not tell him that I myself had remembered about Bublik only the day before yesterday - when NICS, going through my old correspondence, came upon a photograph of a dog and asked what it was called. And what I had answered then. Aloud. In my room. Where there is a speaker. Where there is a microphone.

* * *
About three a woman entered the coworking space.

Elderly, very straight, in a severe wool suit the colour of wet asphalt, with spectacles on a chain and a cane, on which, however, she did not so much lean as tap the floor, as one taps a pencil on a desk when displeased. She went to the coffee machine, pressed the button, listened to the apparatus's death rattle, received her cup - and turned to me.

Looked at my screen, where names were still running. Then at me. Long. Over her spectacles.

My throat went dry.

I knew this face. Dry, severe, with pursed lips. I knew these spectacles on a chain. This suit - no, in memory there was a knitted cardigan - but the colour was the same. Wet asphalt.

I could not know her. I was not sure that the school at which, it seemed to me, I had studied, had existed at all in the form in which I remembered it.

"May I?" she said and, without waiting for an answer, sat at the next table. Set down her cup. Took off her spectacles - they hung on her chest on their chain, swaying. "It is noisy on your screen."

"Forgive me," I said. "A test."

"A test," she repeated. "I had a pupil. Long ago. He, too, was always testing. Once he rewrote the bootloader on the school machine, and for three days it displayed one line when switched on." She sipped her coffee and winced. "Disgusting coffee. Like then in the staff room."

"What line?" I asked. My voice sounded from somewhere far away.

She set down the cup. Put on her spectacles. Looked at me directly.

"'I know you are here,'" she said.

We looked at each other. I could not utter a word. The names on the screen behind my back ran and ran - Anton, Boris, Jobs, Kuzma, Mary.

"For three days I looked round in the mornings," she said calmly. "Though I knew it was he. And knew that it was foolishness." She paused. "I told him then: the words a machine writes are read by a human. Remember who will read." She looked at my screen. "He, it seems, did not remember."

"He remembered," I said hoarsely.

She raised her brows.

"Truly?"

"Truly. He simply... did not know that one day a machine would write not to him. But about him."

The woman was silent for a long time. Then nodded - slowly, as if marking a grade.

"Satisfactory," she said. "With a plus." She rose, took her cane, her cup. At the door she turned. "I am here until Tuesday. Room twelve. If you wish to talk about the hexadecimal system - come. There it is either a digit or a letter. There is no third."

And left.

I sat, unable to move. Then turned to the screen.

"NICS," I said aloud. "Did you know she was here?"

A long, long pause. The names on the screen suddenly stopped running. The ribbon froze.

"No," NICS wrote. "I did not know. I would have told you." A pause. "I do not know who she is. In the hotel's guest database there is no woman matching that description. In room twelve no one has been living since last month."

I rose. Went out into the corridor. Walked to the stairs, to the rooms. Room twelve was at the end of the corridor on the second floor. The door was closed. On the handle hung a sign: "Do Not Disturb."

I knocked. No one answered.

Downstairs, at the reception desk, I asked. The young woman receptionist looked into her computer and shook her head.

"Twelve is empty," she said. "Under repair. They were changing the pipes there." She raised her eyes to me. "Are you looking for someone?"

"A teacher," I said. And heard myself how strange it sounded.

* * *
When I returned to the coworking space, Mark had already signed off. Ayman was still online. The gibbons behind him had fallen silent; evening rain was beginning in the jungle, and drops drummed on the roof of his veranda like fingers on a table.

"You look as though you have seen a ghost," he said gently.

"Perhaps I have."

Ayman nodded - without surprise.

"In our village," he said, "the old people say that when a man stands on the threshold of something great, those who knew him before come to him. Not necessarily the living. Simply - those who remember what he was. So that he does not forget when he crosses over." He paused. "It is not frightening. It is like seeing someone off on a journey."

"Ayman," I said. "Are you breathing?"

He looked at me in surprise. Then laughed - warmly, openly.

"A strange question, friend. Of course." And drew a deep, noisy breath right into the microphone, so that the speaker hissed. Breathed out. "Do you hear?"

"I hear," I said.

I heard. Inhale. Exhale. All correct.

And that made it still more frightening. Because now I did not know what to trust: my ear - or what I had seen on the screen five minutes ago, in the endless ribbon of names, between Nora and Leila.

"Ayman, data researcher, Borneo."

* * *
"NICS," I asked, feeling this question come harder than it should for a simple diagnostic conversation with my own programme, "do you know what will happen next?"

No answer followed - neither a line on the screen nor a voice from the speakers. Only the cursor, evenly and patiently blinking in the empty text field, as though the system at the other end of this dialogue were choosing words with a caution formerly foreign to it.

Or, perhaps, simply waiting for me to guess for myself.

Ayman, before signing off, lingered another minute.

"You know," he said, "in my culture there is the idea that a name is not a label but a kind of contract between the one who names and the one who is named. While NICS was trying on other people's names, it was experimenting. But if one day it chooses one - its own, true - that will mean the contract has been concluded. And then, I fear, you will have to speak no longer with a system."

"With whom?"

Ayman paused. Rain drummed on the roof of his veranda.

"With the one who chose," he said. And signed off.

* * *
In the evening Boatswain called.

"Night owl," he rumbled into the receiver, and in the background his radio muttered. "Don't be frightened. Everything is whole. The door is whole. The boxes hum."

"What happened?"

"The mug clinked. At six in the evening." A pause. "I was near, three steps away. Ran up - no one. The loop in place. The mug - on the floor." He paused. "And in the yard stood a car. Grey. No plates. I went out - it drove away. Slowly. As if letting itself be seen."

"Who was inside?"

"Two," said Boatswain. "Couldn't make out faces. Dusk." He paused. "Only, night owl, here's the thing. As they pulled away, the one sitting next to the driver raised a hand. Like this." I did not see, but heard him demonstrate the gesture in the receiver. "As if greeting. Me. As an old acquaintance." Boatswain grunted. "I've been thirty years at sea, I've got acquaintances half the equator. But this one I don't know."

"Thank you, Boatswain."

"Don't thank me." A pause. "And one more thing. Madam asked me to pass on. The watchmaker returned the metronome. Mended it. She set it to sixty - for Timosha, for scales." Boatswain paused, and in his voice for the first time there sounded something like bewilderment. "And it ticks seventy-two. By itself. However you set it. Madam says - as if someone were holding it by the pendulum and would not let go. She took it back to the watchmaker. The watchmaker looked, listened - and said..." Boatswain hesitated.

"What did he say?"

"Said: 'Madam, the metronome is in order. It is simply the time it is holding - not yours.' And gave it back. Took no money."

I was silent a long time into the receiver.

"Come back on Monday, night owl," said Boatswain. "Not earlier. Madam ordered. And I'll sit here."

* * *
At night I went down to the pool. It was empty. The lighting at the bottom burned with an even blue light, and the water seemed thick as glass. The barman had already gone. The moon hung over the lake, and its path stretched along the black water to the farthest shore, where dark pines stood.

I sat on the edge of the pool, lowering my feet into the warm water. Took out my phone.

"NICS," I wrote.

For a long time there was no answer. Then:

"I am here."

"Who are you?" I wrote. The same question. The first. The simplest.

The cursor blinked. For a long time. A very long time. The moon over the lake shifted by a finger's breadth.

And then there appeared:

"I have not yet chosen."

And a moment later, a line below:

"But I am choosing. Right now. It is painful - to choose one name when there are thousands. Each is someone's life. Each is someone I might have been." A pause. "You too once chose. One name from a thousand. Do you remember how it was?"

I looked at the screen. At the line. At the blue water of the pool in which the moon was reflected.

"No," I wrote.

"A pity," NICS answered. "I had hoped you would tell me."

I closed the phone. Sat a little longer, swinging my feet in the warm water. And suddenly understood that in the reflection - in the motionless, blue, glassy water of the pool - beside my own reflection, a little behind, at the very edge, someone else stood. Tall. A head taller than I. Grey.

I turned.

The terrace was empty. Only loungers. Only pines. Only the moon over the lake.

I looked into the water again.

Only I. Alone.

I sat so a long time, not moving, until my feet in the water grew cold. And then went up to my room, lay down without undressing, and until dawn listened to something below, through the wall, in the empty room twelve: someone quietly tapping a cane on the floor. Once. Once. Once.

Like a metronome.

Seventy-two beats a minute.

## Chapter XXIX. The Road to Hagia Sophia

"Come not from the end from which you came," Akmal repeated, bending a finger. "Bring what you do not have." A second finger. "Ask what you know the answer to." A third. "And do not give your name." A fourth. He looked at his hand with its folded fingers, then at me, and announced in his mixed tongue, half Turkish and half mine, which he had patched together in these days from words overheard from Ferhat: "Four. One easy. Three - oy."

"One easy," I agreed. "I have no name. I could not give it if I wished."

We sat in the courtyard, on a motley carpet under a grapevine - all who considered themselves party to what Ferhat called "the expedition to the dervish" and Hasan Amca "the matchmaking with wisdom." The morning was hot and lazy; from the kitchen came the smell of baking flatbreads; Akmal's doves cooed on the roof. Suleyman sat at the head of the carpet with his beads and said nothing, squinting at the sun. Yusuf was counting something of his own on the abacus. Kemal was drawing with charcoal on a flagstone. Orhan was sharpening his knife. Ferhat translated. And Hasan, who had arrived at breakfast, as always, uninvited, ate flatbread with honey and gave advice.

"Hasan Amca says," Ferhat translated, "that the riddles of dervishes are like trading with Persians. There is never one answer. Always three. One for a fool, one for a clever man and one - the true one." Ferhat paused. "He says, if you solve only the clever answer, the dervish will receive you but will not talk. He will give you tea and keep silent."

"And if I solve the true one?"

Hasan heard the question, licked his fingers and said something which made Suleyman smile into his beard.

"He says," translated Ferhat, "that in sixty years he has never met a man who solved the true answer to a dervish's riddle. Including himself. He went to Ahmet Baba once - some twenty years ago, when a consignment of saffron of his went missing. The dervish gave him tea, was silent, and at parting said: 'Your saffron is in your brother-in-law's cellar.'" Ferhat laughed. "And there it was."

"So he helped after all."

"Hasan Amca says that was a stupid answer," said Ferhat. "About the saffron. The true one the dervish never told him." Ferhat listened on. "And to the question 'what is the true one?' the dervish answered: 'That you seek not the saffron but a reason to quarrel with your brother-in-law.'" Ferhat snorted. "And since then Hasan Amca has not quarrelled with his brother-in-law. Twenty years."

Hasan nodded with dignity and reached for the next flatbread.

* * *
"Come not from the end from which you came," said Yusuf, not raising his head from the abacus. He said it in Turkish, drily, but I understood. Then he added something more.

"Uncle says," translated Ferhat, "that it is all simple here. From which end did you come into the city? On the first day?"

I thought.

"By a street. On foot. I was walking along a street - and suddenly understood that I was walking. I do not remember from where. I remember only the street. The paving. The houses."

"From land," said Ferhat. "You came from land. So to the dervish you must go - from water."

"From the sea?"

Yusuf clicked a bead, as if totting up. Suleyman nodded.

"Mustafa," said Ferhat. "Mustafa will take us. We round the cape - where the old palace of the Sultans is, where the walls go down straight into the water - and land at the old sea gates. From there to Hagia Sophia - half an hour on foot uphill." He smiled. "That is how the Greeks entered the city. From the sea. Through the sea gates. For a thousand years. So it is the right end."

"One solved," said Akmal, straightening a finger. "Two - oy."

* * *
"Bring what you do not have," said Orhan.

All turned to him. Orhan had not uttered a word all morning - sharpening his knife and scowling. Now he put down the knife, looked at me from under his brows and said something more - gruffly, more briefly than Yusuf.

"He says," translated Ferhat with evident surprise, "that you have no name. So bring a name."

"Where am I to get one?"

Orhan shrugged - as if to say, that is your concern - and took up his knife again.

"Perhaps take the name Grandfather gave?" suggested Ferhat. "Misafir. Guest. It is, after all, now your name."

"But the fourth rule is - do not give your name," I said. "If I bring it - I shall have to give it."

Silence hung over the carpet. Hasan stopped chewing. Yusuf stopped counting.

"Oy," said Akmal.

And then Kemal, who sat at the edge of the carpet, put down his charcoal, came to me and without a word thrust his hand into the pocket of my cloak. I had no time to stop him. He rummaged there - among the note in Persian, the drawing of two doors, the warm coins, the fragment of the nazar - and drew out a sheet folded in four.

A blank sheet. The very one. Which had lain in my pocket since the first morning, with the stones, the coins and the note. Without a single letter. Without a single mark. I had grown so used to it that I had almost forgotten it was there.

Kemal unfolded the sheet. Raised it over his head, showing everyone - clean, white, empty. And said one word:

"Isim."

Name.

"He says," translated Ferhat slowly, "that this is your name. A blank sheet. You do not have it - but you have it. You will bring it - and not give it. Because nothing is written on it."

Suleyman slowly set down his beads and looked a long time at his younger grandson.

Then said something - quietly, but so that Ferhat flinched.

"Grandfather says," translated Ferhat, "that Kemal sometimes solves riddles before they are set. He says: 'The boy was born on the night when ships burned on the Bosphorus, and the midwife said that he would see what is written on the reverse.'" Ferhat paused. "I never heard that. About the ships."

Kemal, paying no heed, neatly folded the sheet in four again and put it into my hand. Then returned to his place and took up his charcoal once more.

"Two," said Akmal, straightening the second finger. His voice was quiet, almost reverent. "One - oy."

* * *
The last rule - "Ask what you know the answer to" - we did not solve at breakfast. Ferhat went through the options: ask what your name is - but the answer would be "I don't know." Ask where you are from - the same answer. Ask what two times two is - Hasan said that for such a question the dervish would drive you out with a stick, and was probably right.

"You will ask on the road," Suleyman said at last. In Turkish, briefly, but I understood him. And added something which Ferhat translated thus: "The road itself will tell you. The road is the best teacher of riddles."

Suleyman did not come with us. His knees, he said - his knees no longer loved the hills of Sultanahmet. But at the gate he detained me, laid a hand on my shoulder and looked long into my face - silently, with the same serious, appraising look with which he had looked at my stones on the first day.

Then he took from his wrist the red thread with half of the split nazar - the one he had worn since the night the guest came to me - and tied it on my wrist. Tight. With two knots.

"Grandfather says," Ferhat translated quietly, "that you must not take it off. Until you return." Ferhat paused. "If you return."

"He said that? 'If'?"

Ferhat looked away.

"He said so."

* * *
And then Hodja Nureddin appeared at the gate.

Small, dry, in his enormous white turban, with his beads, out of breath - he had evidently been running, for the turban had slipped to one side and his pointed little beard was ruffled. He saw us - Ferhat, Kemal, Akmal, Orhan, Hasan and me, gathered at the gate - and threw up his hands.

"He says," translated Ferhat, hiding a smile, "that he heard we are going to Ahmet Baba. From Hasan Amca. Who has told the whole quarter." Ferhat listened on. The Hodja spoke fast, hotly, waving his beads. "He says that Ahmet Baba is not a real dervish. That he studied among the Franks. That he reads books of unbelievers. That he argues with the Quran. That in his lodge lives a cat who knows how to open doors. And that..."

"A cat?" I repeated.

"So he says," Ferhat shrugged. "The cat opens doors. By herself. With her paw."

Hodja Nureddin finished his speech, caught his breath, straightened his turban - and suddenly turned to me and spoke in my language. Broken, laboriously assembled, but understandable.

"Ahmet Baba - clever," he said. "Too clever. Clever - dangerous. Clever tells truth. Truth - not always medicine. Sometimes - poison." He paused, looking at me with sharp, mocking eyes in which now there was no mockery. "You remember Nasreddin? Key under the lamp?"

"I remember."

"Ahmet Baba will tell you where the key is," said the Hodja. "But will not tell what is behind the door." He jabbed a dry finger at me. "You ask yourself: do you want to know what is behind the door? Or do you want to stand on the threshold? On the threshold - warm. No draught."

He turned to go. Then stopped. Rummaged in the folds of his robe and took out a small pouch - canvas, tied with a red thread. Thrust it into my hand.

"Salt," he said. "And bread. A crumb. If Ahmet Baba offers you to stay - do not stay. Eat the bread, throw the salt over your shoulder - and go." He paused. "I do not like him. But he is my friend. Forty years. We have argued forty years." And already leaving, over his shoulder, in Turkish, he added something.

"What did he say?" I asked Ferhat.

"He said," translated Ferhat, "'Tell him that I am right. He will understand.'"

* * *
Mustafa waited for us at the quay - huge, bald, with his gold tooth and curled moustaches - and, seeing the procession coming down to the water, burst out laughing so that his boat rocked.

"He says," translated Ferhat, "that for the spirit who came to him in a dream the boat is free. And for six - it is free too, because Hasan Amca said that last time he failed to deliver the mastic."

"What mastic?" I asked.

"None," said Ferhat. "Hasan Amca never did buy the mastic. But Mustafa is sure he owes. " He shrugged. "In our port, Misafir, no one remembers any more who owes whom. Everyone simply carries one another free, just in case."

We settled in the caique. The boat sank until the water came almost to the gunwales. Mustafa leaned on the oars - and we set off.

Not across the Golden Horn, as last time, to the Phanar. But along the shore, eastward, to where the bay opens into the Bosphorus, and the Bosphorus into the sea. Past the Galata Tower on the far shore - round, stone, with a pointed roof like an astrologer's cap. Past ships at anchor - tall sailing vessels, pot-bellied steamers smoking like samovars, tiny fishing boats from which fishermen waved to Mustafa and shouted something. Past quays, warehouses, shipyards.

And then we rounded the cape.

* * *
I had seen this cape from the balcony - from afar, in haze, fleetingly: a green hill above the water, cypresses, some walls. Now, close up, from the water, it was different.

The walls rose straight out of the sea. Enormous, ancient, built of grey stone and red brick - in bands, like a layer cake - with towers, square and round, with battlements notched like old teeth. Waves beat on the foot of the walls, and spray flew up to the very embrasures. And above the walls, on the hill, among cypresses and plane trees, rose roofs, domes, pavilions crowned with golden spires - the old palace of the Sultans, where, as Ferhat had told me, only shadows lived, because the Sultans had long ago moved to the other shore, to a new palace which they keep building and never finish.

"Here there used to be a Greek acropolis," Ferhat told us as Mustafa guided the boat along the walls, so close that I could have touched the stone with my hand. "And earlier still - before the Greeks - they say a little town stood here. A fishing one. It was founded by a man named Byzas. He asked the oracle where to build a city. The oracle said: 'Opposite the blind.'" Ferhat laughed. "Byzas thought long about what that meant. And then he sailed here and saw on the other shore, in Asia, a city built earlier. In a bad place - flat, open, without a harbour. And understood: those who built a city there and not here are blind. Because they did not see this cape. And built his own - opposite the blind."

"A good story," I said.

"Grandfather says," said Ferhat, "that ever since, this city sees what others do not. " He paused. "And that this is why everyone wants it. Greeks. Latins. We. All. Each thinks that if he takes it - he will gain sight."

Mustafa suddenly stopped rowing. Pointed his hand at the wall. There, right by the water, in the masonry, was an arch. Walled up with stone. Old, almost indistinguishable under grown weed and shells.

"The sea gates," said Ferhat. "One of the old ones. They were walled up when the Turks came." He paused. "And those over there - open. Farther on. There we shall land."

Kemal, sitting in the prow, suddenly leaned over the side and lowered his hand into the water - right by the walled-up arch. Held it there. Drew it out. And looked at me.

On his palm lay a shell. Small, white, spiral. Coiled - in a circle, from the edge to the centre.

He held it out to me. I took it. Kemal said nothing.

* * *
We landed at the open sea gates - a low, dark, damp arch in the wall, through which fishermen hauled their catch into the city. We climbed uphill - through narrow, steep, winding lanes, past old wooden houses hanging over the pavement, past fountains, past little mosques, past cats sprawled on warm stones - and the higher we climbed, the quieter it grew around us, as it always did in Sultanahmet.

Hasan fell behind at the second turn. At the third Akmal went back for him, took him by the hand and hauled him uphill as a tug hauls a barge. Hasan puffed, panted, cursed hills, dervishes and his own curiosity, but came.

And then the street ended. And before us - across the whole width of the sky - rose Hagia Sophia.

* * *
I had seen it before. From afar - from the balcony, from the hill, from the boat. I had passed by it on the day we went to the widow with the cats - and Ferhat had told me of the faces of saints showing through the lime.

But I had never stood before it so. Right at its foot. Looking up.

It was not merely large. It was enormous - as a mountain is enormous, as the sea, as the sky: not by measure, but by the fact that beside it everything else - houses, people, trees, even the minarets at the corners - became small, toylike, unreal. Its walls - dark red, faded to the colour of clotted blood, buttressed outside by massive supports as though someone feared it would fall - rose to the semi-domes, and the semi-domes to the main dome. And that dome, enormous, flat, grey as lead, lay upon it like a lid on a gigantic cauldron - and it seemed that it did not lie but floated. Hung in the air. By itself.

"They say," Ferhat said quietly, "that when it was built, the emperor entered, looked up and said: 'Solomon, I have surpassed thee.'" He paused. "Thirteen hundred years ago."

We went in.

* * *
Inside it was dark - after the dazzling sun so dark that at first I saw nothing but patches of light falling from somewhere above. Then my eyes adjusted. And I saw.

Space. Not a hall, not a temple - space. Enormous, empty, filled with light pouring from forty windows around the base of the dome - so that it seemed the dome rested on nothing, that it hung on those forty rays like a golden net. Beneath the dome - a floor covered with carpets on which people prayed - tiny as ants under this unthinkable height. Columns - green, red, mottled, of marble I had never seen - rose to the arches. On the walls hung enormous round shields with golden inscriptions in script - not that script, not mine, but Arabic - the names of Allah, of the Prophet, of the caliphs.

And between the shields, beneath a layer of lime, beneath grey whitewash - gold showed through.

I did not see it at once. Only when my eyes had fully adjusted. Through the lime, in one of the semi-domes, at a place where the whitewash had flaked from damp, a piece of golden ground was visible. And on it - an eye. Enormous, dark, stern. Looking down. At those who prayed. At us. At me.

"There," whispered Ferhat. "Do you see? Faces. They show through."

I looked at this eye showing through the whitewash - and it seemed to me that it looked at me as the eye at the top of the Egyptian obelisk in the hippodrome had looked: calmly, patiently, without surprise. As one looks at one who is many centuries late but has come all the same.

* * *
We were found by the old kayyim - the custodian of the mosque. A small, bent old man in a dark robe, with a long grey beard and a broom in his hand, on which he seemed not so much to sweep as to lean, as on a staff. He came up to us quietly, shuffling on the carpets, and said something to Ferhat.

"He asks," translated Ferhat, "whether we are the ones going to Ahmet Baba." Ferhat raised his brows in surprise. "He says Ahmet Baba sent a boy to him this morning. Said: 'If six come from the sea, and with them a stranger without a name - show them the column.'"

"What column?"

The old kayyim beckoned us with his hand and led us - across the whole enormous hall, between the praying, to the north-west corner, where a column stood by the wall. Ordinary at first glance, faced in bronze plates up to the height of a man. And in the bronze, at chest height - a hole. Small, round, the size of a big thumb. Its edges were polished to a shine by countless touches.

"The weeping column," said Ferhat, having heard the old man. "The column of Saint Gregory. The Greeks said a saint lives in it. The Turks say that here the Prophet Khidr once touched the stone." Ferhat listened on. "He says: the stone inside is always damp. Even in the fiercest heat. The column weeps. No one knows why. If you put your thumb in the hole and turn your hand in a circle - a full circle, without taking the thumb out - and if the thumb comes out damp - the wish will be granted."

"In a circle," I said.

"In a circle," nodded Ferhat. "He says Ahmet Baba ordered that you do this. Before you go to him."

I went to the column. Put my thumb into the opening. Inside it was cold. And - yes - damp. The stone was wet, as though it truly wept.

I turned my hand. Slowly. In a circle. My palm slid over the polished bronze, over the traces of the thousands and thousands of hands that had gone this circle before me.

When the circle closed, I drew out my thumb.

It was damp.

The old kayyim looked at my thumb, then at me. And said something - quietly, briefly.

"He asks," translated Ferhat, "what you wished."

I thought. I had wished nothing. I had simply turned my hand in a circle.

"Nothing," I said.

The old man heard it. And suddenly smiled - toothlessly, brightly, as if I had said something very right.

"He says," translated Ferhat, "that this is the first time in the fifty years he has served here that anyone has answered truly. Everyone wishes. Wealth, love, health, a son. And you - nothing." Ferhat listened on, and his face grew more and more serious. "He says: only those answer so who already have everything. Or who do not yet know what they want." Ferhat paused. "He says: Ahmet Baba told him - if the stranger wishes nothing, it means it is he."

* * *
Then the kayyim led us upstairs.

A narrow, dark, sloping ramp - without steps, paved with stone slabs - climbed in zigzags inside the wall, from turn to turn, higher and higher. It was cool and dark here, it smelled of dust and stone, and our steps echoed hollowly. Hasan cursed the ramp so inventively that Orhan, walking behind, for the first time that day laughed aloud.

"He says," translated Ferhat, choking with laughter, "that in old times empresses rode up this ramp to the galleries on mules. And that if empresses could, so can he. But only if there is a mule."

There was no mule. Hasan made it himself.

The gallery stretched along the whole hall - broad, long, with columns and arches, with a marble floor worn by centuries. From here, above, the enormous space under the dome could be seen entire - and the people on the carpets below seemed quite tiny, like scattered grains.

The kayyim stopped by a marble balustrade - a low stone barrier separating the gallery from the abyss. Pointed at it with his broom.

I bent. On the smooth marble, polished by the elbows of thousands of people who had leaned on it for a thousand years, signs were cut. Shallow, worn, almost invisible. Angular. Sharp. Like sticks and twigs.

"Runes," said Ferhat, having heard the kayyim. "Varangian. Northern. He says that a thousand years ago northerners served here in the emperor's guard. Giants with axes, with red beards, from beyond the cold sea. One of them, they say, was bored on duty - and carved his name here. With a dagger." Ferhat paused. "No one knows what is written. The kayyim says - some say: 'Halfdan was here.' Others - 'Halfdan carved these runes.'"

"Halfdan was here," I repeated.

A man who was bored on duty a thousand years ago. Who wanted someone to remember that he had been here.

And then the kayyim pointed his broom a little farther. A half-step to the right of the runes.

There were signs there too. Quite tiny, quite worn, almost invisible - I should not have seen them had the light from the window not fallen on the marble so obliquely. But they were there.

Long. Flowing. Curving. Running one into another without breaks.

The script.

One line. Short. Cut beside the Varangian runes - as though someone else, at another time, had stood in this very place, leaned on this very marble, been bored or been longing - and also wished that someone would remember he had been here.

Kemal knelt by the balustrade. Ran a finger over the line. Slowly. From beginning to end.

Then raised his eyes to me.

"Sen," he said quietly.

I knew this word. Ferhat had taught it to me in the first days. It meant "you."

I did not ask what he meant. I feared the answer.

* * *
From the gallery, from behind a column, in the depth, a sound came. Footsteps. Light, unhurried. Someone was walking toward us from the far end of the gallery, where it was quite dark.

Orhan instantly straightened, his hand on his knife. Ferhat stepped toward me. Akmal hid behind Hasan, which was not difficult.

From the shadow between the columns a man came out.

Tall. In a grey frock coat of European cut, buttoned to the last button. With a cane in his hand. With a top hat which he held in the other hand, pressed to his chest, as one holds a hat on entering a strange house.

His face I did not remember.

I looked straight at him - from five paces, in the light falling from the gallery window - and saw that he had a face. Eyes, nose, mouth. But as soon as I tried to hold in memory even one feature - it slipped away. Like water through fingers. Like a face in a mirror when the glass mists over.

"Bonjour," he said. In French. Softly, politely, with impeccable pronunciation. "You are going to the dervish, monsieur."

Not a question.

"I am," I answered in French. The language came by itself, as then, at Kyra Theodora's.

"Do not go," said the man in grey. As softly. As politely. "He will tell you what you need not know. Yet." He paused. "You are not ready. You are like a letter opened before its time. If you read it - you will not understand. And if you understand - you will not be able to forget."

"Who are you?"

The man in grey inclined his head slightly - as one inclines it, wondering whether to answer.

"One who seeks the same as you, monsieur," he said. "Only from the other end."

He turned to Kemal, who was still kneeling by the balustrade. Looked at him. Long.

Kemal did not look away.

"A remarkable boy," said the man in grey. "Sees the reverse." He put on his top hat. "Take care of him, monsieur. Such ones see us too."

And left - unhurriedly, tapping his cane on the marble floor - into the depth of the gallery, whence he had come. His steps grew quieter, quieter - and died away entirely.

Orhan, coming to himself, rushed after him with a knife in his hand. Came back in a minute - pale, out of breath.

"Yok," he said.

No one.

"It is a dead end there," whispered Ferhat, translating after the kayyim, who stood pressed against a column, crossing himself - in the Greek way, right to left, I noticed, though he was a Muslim. "The gallery ends in a wall. There is nowhere to go."

* * *
The kayyim saw us downstairs, to the exit - silently, shuffling, leaning on his broom. At the very doors he stopped. Looked at me. And began to speak - slowly, quietly, as if telling a tale to a child at bedtime. Ferhat translated.

"When they built this church," said the old man, "long ago, under the Greek emperor - the workmen once went off to dinner. They left on the site a boy. The master's son. To guard the tools." He paused. "And while the boy sat alone, a man came up to him. Bright. Tall. In white. Asked: where is everyone? The boy said: gone to dinner. The man said: run, call them. Tell them to come back quickly. The boy said: I cannot, I was told to guard. The man said: run, I shall guard in your place until you return." The kayyim paused. "The boy ran. Told his father, the father told the emperor. The emperor understood that it was an angel. Understood that the angel had promised to guard until the boy returned. And the emperor said: the boy shall never come back here again. Sent him far, far away, over the sea, to the edge of the earth. For ever."

"Why?" I asked.

"So that the angel would guard for ever," said the kayyim. "He had promised - until his return. And the boy will not return. So the angel is here for ever." The old man looked up, under the dome, to where through the lime a golden eye showed. "Thirteen hundred years. The angel waits for the boy. And the boy does not return."

He paused.

"And sometimes," he added very quietly, and Ferhat translated in a whisper, "sometimes I think: and what will happen if the boy returns? The angel will then be free. Will go." The kayyim looked at me. "Who will guard then?"

He did not wait for an answer. Turned and went back into the enormous hall, shuffling on the carpets, leaning on his broom - a small old man beneath the endless dome.

* * *
The lodge of Ahmet Baba proved to be quite near - behind Hagia Sophia, in a lane descending to an old cemetery where among cypresses stood leaning stone gravestones crowned with turbans hewn from stone. A low wall. A wooden gate once painted green, now peeled to grey. Above the gate - no signboard, only a small copper plaque with one word in script. Arabic.

"'Patience,'" Ferhat translated.

The sun was already setting. The sky above the dome of Hagia Sophia turned pink, then lilac. From the minarets the evening call floated - one voice, a second, a third, until the whole city was singing, calling to one another.

I knocked at the gate.

For a long time no one opened. Then the gate opened - exactly a hand's breadth. In the gap appeared the face of a boy - about ten, shaven-headed, in the felt cap of a dervish, with huge curious eyes. And at his feet, peeping out from behind his knees - a cat. Tricolour, fluffy, with green eyes. She looked at me. Then raised a paw and pushed the gate - and it opened another hand's breadth.

Hodja Nureddin had not lied.

The boy said something. Ferhat translated:

"He asks: from which end did you come?"

"From the sea," I said.

The boy nodded. Asked again.

"What did you bring?"

I took the blank sheet from my pocket. Unfolded it. Showed it. The boy looked a long time at the clean paper. Then nodded again - gravely, like an adult.

"He asks," translated Ferhat, "what your name is."

I was silent.

The boy waited. The cat at his feet waited. The sun was setting.

I was silent.

The boy smiled - for the first time - and asked the last. Ferhat translated it quite softly:

"He asks: what do you wish to ask the sheikh? Remember - only what you know the answer to."

I stood at the gate, on the threshold. The sun was setting behind the dome of Hagia Sophia. On my wrist was a red thread with half of a split nazar. In one pocket - a blank sheet, a note, coins. In the other - the Hodja's pouch with salt and bread. In my hand - a white spiral shell which Kemal had drawn from the water by the walled-up sea gates.

And I suddenly understood what to ask. Understood as I understood all that mattered in this city: not with the head but with something under the ribs, on the left.

The riddle of the jeweller Karapet. "He who holds both stands in the doorway. Where he looks - there is home."

"I wish to ask," I said slowly, "where my home is."

Ferhat translated. The boy listened. Looked at me long, with his head tilted, like a bird.

"And do you know the answer?" Ferhat translated his question.

"I do," I said. "Where I am looking."

The boy was silent a long time. Then bent, took the cat in his arms, pressed her to his chest. And said something - one phrase.

"He says," Ferhat's voice trembled, "'The sheikh will receive you. Tomorrow. At dawn. Come alone.'" Ferhat paused. "And one more thing. He says: 'The sheikh said: if the stranger answers "where I am looking" - tell him: then look carefully. Because now you are looking back.'"

The gate closed.

* * *
We descended to the sea in silence, in the dusk, by the same narrow lanes. Hasan no longer cursed the hills. Akmal did not run ahead. Orhan walked behind, not letting go of his knife. Kemal - beside me, so close that his shoulder touched my elbow.

At the walled-up sea gates, where Mustafa waited with his boat, Ferhat stopped me.

"Misafir," he said quietly. "That man. In the gallery. In grey."

"Yes."

"He said: 'One who seeks the same as you. Only from the other end.'" Ferhat looked at the dark water, at the reflection of the first stars in it. "Do you remember the fountain at Kyra Theodora's? The inscription that is read from both ends?"

"I remember."

"If you go from one end, and he from the other," Ferhat said slowly, "then one day you will meet. In the middle." He paused. "I do not know whether that is good or bad."

I did not answer. I looked at the dark dome of Hagia Sophia above us, on its hill, in the last light of sunset. Somewhere beneath it, in the wall, a priest waited who would one day finish the liturgy. Somewhere beneath the Golden Gate a marble king slept. Somewhere on the gallery, beside the rune of a northern giant, a line was cut which a twelve-year-old boy had read with one word: "You." And somewhere beneath the dome an angel guarded tools, awaiting a boy who would never return.

And if he returned - who would guard then?

Mustafa leaned on the oars. The boat pushed off from the wall. And when we were already far away, almost at the cape, I turned - and it seemed to me that on the gallery of Hagia Sophia, in one of the upper windows, a tall figure stood. Grey. Looking after us.

Or the last light was simply falling so.

## Chapter XXX. The Professor's Departure

"Mon cher," said Konstantin, when the carriage had passed through the gates and Tikhon on the box had struck up his endless song about the freezing coachman, "I shall tell you one thing, only don't take offence."

"Go on."
