"If that professor once more 'lingers in our parts,' I shall tie him up myself and take him to the station. Gently. As Tikhon promised." Konstantin straightened his cap. "He came for a week. He is living through his third. The General kidnaps him. Auntie invites him. Strauch quarrels with him every other evening. And you..." He glanced sideways at me. "You, after every meeting with him, lie awake half the night and write in your blue notebook. I hear the pen scratching. My room is on the other side of the wall."

"He leaves today, Kostya."

"I know," said Konstantin. And suddenly fell silent. Then he added more quietly, looking at the fields beyond the roadside, yellow, mown, with stacks that looked like sleeping bears: "And for some reason I am sorry. Though he is a windbag, an eccentric and a nihilist." He paused. "He is the only one who talks to you as though he knew what you are keeping silent about."

On the box, Tikhon stopped singing.

"Master," he said over his shoulder. "Forgive me for butting in. But that professor is a good man. At the tavern by the 'Anchor' he has all the coachmen spellbound with his tales. Sits, drinks his tea, and writes it all down. He'll ask, 'And what do you say, brother, about the wood-goblin?' - and you tell him what you heard from your granny. And he writes it down. Word for word." Tikhon paused. "He wrote me down too. About the coachman who drove with the devil in a blizzard. Says he'll put it in a book. With my name." He drew himself up. "Tikhon Lukich Borodin, of the village of Maly Klyuchi. They'll be reading it, he says, a hundred years from now."

"In a hundred years, Tikhon," said Konstantin, "all your great-grandchildren will know that their forefather drove with the devil."

"And let them know, master," Tikhon replied imperturbably. "I got him there, didn't I? All the way to the station. And took nothing for vodka. The devil, he's a man under orders too."

* * *
The district town greeted us with market day.

The square before the cathedral, white, five-domed, with green cupolas and golden crosses that blazed so in the sun it hurt to look at them, was crammed with people, carts, horses, stalls, tents. It smelled of tar, dung, fresh bread, apples, fish, kvass and something frying. The market women cried: "Pies! Hot from the oven!" "Hot sbiten!" "Grated kalachi!" Geese gabbled in wicker cages. A gypsy boy led a bear on a chain, and the bear, rising on its hind legs, bowed to the public, and the public threw coppers into the hat. At the hitching post two peasants were haggling over the price of a horse, slapping each other's hands so hard that the clap rang across the whole square. A clerk in a peaked cap and waistcoat bawled the price of calico at the door of the merchant Toloknov's shop, while the merchant himself, stout, in a peasant coat, with a spade-shaped beard, sat on the porch drinking tea from a saucer and surveying the square like an admiral his squadron.

Tikhon drove the carriage slowly through the crowd, calling out, "Mind yourselves! I'm carrying the master!" and the crowd reluctantly gave way.

And then he came out of the crowd.

I did not see him at once, only when the carriage stopped, because he had stepped right in front of the horses. A man of no certain age, perhaps forty, perhaps sixty, barefoot despite the autumn chill, in a ragged linen shirt to the knees, belted with a rope, with iron chains around his neck that clanked at every movement. His hair was long, matted, shot with grey. His beard hung in tufts. And his eyes, light, almost colourless, like a sky bleached by the sun, looked straight at me.

"Grishenka," whispered Tikhon, hastily taking off his cap and crossing himself. "The blessed one."

The holy fool came up to the carriage. Slowly. Clanking his chains. He stopped by the step. For a long time he looked up at me from below, not blinking.

The crowd around fell quiet. The market women stopped crying. Even the bear sank back onto four paws.

"The guest has come," said Grishenka. His voice was high, cracked, childlike. "And the master is not yet born."

Beside me Konstantin sat up straight.

"What?" I said.

"The guest has come," the holy fool repeated, and his face suddenly dissolved into a smile, broad, toothless, happy, like a child's who has seen a toy. "And the master is not yet born. And the house already stands. And the key is in the dust. And the rose is blooming." He laughed, thin and ringing. "Blooming, blooming! Out of season! Not in its own land!"

Cold beneath the ribs. On the left.

Grishenka stretched out his hand, filthy, with broken nails, and touched my palm. The one without a life line. He drew his finger across it, from the wrist toward the fingers. To where in all people the line runs.

"Smooth," he said. And wept, as easily as a minute before he had laughed. "Smooth. Like an angel's. Like a stone's. Poor thing. Poor guest. Walks and walks. All the doors are open, and nowhere to go in."

He let go of my hand. Stepped back. Made the sign of the cross over me, wide and sweeping. Then over Konstantin. Then over Tikhon. Then over the horses.

"Go, guest," he said. "Go to the teller of tales. He will tell you a tale. The last one. And then he will leave. And you will stay. And then you will leave too." He laughed again. "They will all leave! All! And the rose will remain!"

And he walked away, barefoot, his chains clanking, through the crowd, which parted before him, crossing itself and bowing.

For a long time Tikhon did not start the horses. Then he put on his cap.

"Master," he said quietly, without turning round, "Grishenka never talks to anybody. Fifteen years he's gone about this town, and silent. Only plays the fool. And with you," he paused, "he spoke."

Konstantin said nothing. But I felt his hand close for a moment on my elbow, hard, almost to pain, and let go.

* * *
The inn "Golden Anchor" stood on the corner of the square, a two-storey wooden house with a peeling signboard on which a golden anchor had once been painted and which now showed something like a rusty poker. Below was a tavern, from which came the clatter of crockery, the smell of cabbage soup and singing: someone was belting out "Ah, you hall, my hall" off-key, but with feeling. Upstairs were the rooms.

The landlord, Panteleimon Kuzmich Sychov, met us in the doorway: small, round, bald, with red side-whiskers, in a waistcoat stretched over his belly so that the buttons seemed ready to fly off, and with a towel over his shoulder. Seeing Konstantin in uniform, he bowed from the waist. Seeing me, he bowed lower still.

"Welcome, welcome!" he began, tumbling over his words. "To the professor? Of course, sir, of course, upstairs, room three. Packing, they are. Packing since morning. Their notebooks. I say to him, 'Ivan Filippovich, you'd better put them in a trunk, or you'll lose them on the road,' and he says, 'No, Panteleimon Kuzmich, notebooks are like children, you can't put them in a trunk, they need air.'" The landlord threw up his hands. "Air! For notebooks! Now isn't he an eccentric?"

"An eccentric," Konstantin agreed.

"Three weeks he's lived here," Panteleimon Kuzmich went on, lowering his voice as though divulging a state secret. "Candles he's burned, a whole pood! Writes at night. By day he goes about the market, talks to the women, the coachmen, the beggars. Even tried it with Grishenka the blessed." The landlord shook his head. "Grishenka, now, he's silent. Fifteen years silent. And the professor goes to him every day, with a pie. Sits down beside him on the church porch, hands over the pie and sits. In silence. An hour. Two. The folk laughed."

"And Grishenka?"

"Grishenka eats the pie and goes," said the landlord. "But yesterday..." He faltered.

"What yesterday?"

Panteleimon Kuzmich looked round as if afraid of being overheard.

"Yesterday Grishenka spoke to him. For the first time. I didn't hear it myself, the sexton told me, he was on the porch. Grishenka said to the professor: 'Tomorrow the guest will come. Tell him a tale. The last one.'" The landlord crossed himself. "And here you are, sir."

* * *
"And another thing," said Panteleimon Kuzmich, already climbing the creaking stairs with us. "Forgive me, sir, it may be nothing. But there was a lodger here the day before yesterday. Stayed one night. A gentleman. A visitor. In a grey coat. With a cane. Polite to a fault. Spoke French the way you and I speak Russian. Paid in gold." The landlord paused. "And kept asking about the professor. Who he is, where from, what he writes. Asked to see the notebooks. Said he was a lover of antiquities. Ready to buy. Offered good money."

My throat went dry. Beside me Konstantin stopped on the step.

"And the professor?" asked Konstantin.

"The professor threw him out," said the landlord with relish. "Politely, mind. Says, 'Sir, my notebooks are not for sale. They are not even mine. They belong to the people.' And that gentleman smiled, bowed and left. In the morning. At the crack of dawn." The landlord scratched his side-whiskers. "Only, sir, here's what's odd. He paid for the room, he signed the book, I talked with him half the evening. And his face, strike me dead, I can't remember. Not a line of it. As if I'd been looking into water."

"And the name in the book?" I asked.

Panteleimon Kuzmich blushed.

"That's just it, sir. I look in the book, there's a line. There's ink. There's a signature. And I can't read it." He spread his hands. "Squiggles of some sort. Long, crooked, one running into another. Not in our letters, not French, not German. I showed the sexton, he couldn't read it either. Said, maybe it's Armenian?"

"Show me," I said.

The landlord ran downstairs and came back with a thick, greasy register of lodgers, opened it at the right page and jabbed with his finger.

Among the clumsy signatures of merchants and the tidy ones of clerks stood a single line. Short.

Long, flowing, curving lines. Running into one another without a break.

The script.

Konstantin looked at the line over my shoulder. Then at me. And for the first time since I had known him I saw real fear in his eyes. Not for himself.

* * *
Sventsitsky's room was cramped, low, with a single window on the square, a sagging bed, a washstand in the corner and a table so heaped with papers that the table could not be seen. On the floor stood two worn leather suitcases and an enormous wicker hamper, filled to the brim with notebooks: thick ones, thin ones, in oilcloth covers, in cardboard, with no covers at all, tied in bundles with twine. It smelled of tallow, tobacco, tea and paper dust. On the windowsill stood a cold samovar.

The professor himself sat on the floor in the midst of this paper sea, in his waistcoat, without his frock coat, a pen behind his ear and an ink stain on his chin, tying up one more bundle with twine.

"Ah," he said, seeing us. Without surprise. "You've come. I knew. Grishenka said so yesterday." He smiled. "Sit down, if you can find where. Lieutenant, take Olonets Province off that chair, it won't mind. Put it on the bed, beside Vologda."

Konstantin lifted a bundle of notebooks from the chair and carefully laid it on the bed. He sat. I sat on the windowsill, next to the samovar.

"Ivan Filippovich," I said. "The landlord says a man in grey came to see you."

Sventsitsky stopped tying the twine. For a long time he was silent.

"He did," he said at last. "He wanted to buy notebooks. Not all of them. One." He raised his clear, light eyes to me, which just now were not cheerful. "The one where I wrote down what you told me. On the day you do not remember."

"You refused."

"I refused." Sventsitsky took up the twine again. "For thirty years, young man, I have been collecting what no one values. Grannies' tales. Charms. Omens. I was never paid for it. They laughed at me at the university. They drove me from my chair for 'unscientific methods.' My wife left because instead of a salary I brought home notebooks." He pulled the knot tight. "And now for the first time in thirty years I was offered money for a notebook. Large money. More than I have seen in all my life." He smiled wryly. "Do you know what I felt?"

"What?"

"That this notebook is not mine," said Sventsitsky simply. "That I only keep it. Until the time comes." He raised his eyes to me. "The one in grey looked at me, smiled and said, 'You are right, Professor. It is not yours. But it is not his either.'" Sventsitsky paused. "And left. And I did not sleep all night. Thinking: whose, then?"

* * *
He got up, brushed off his knees, rummaged in the hamper and pulled out a notebook, not the oilcloth one I had already seen, but another. Old. Worn. In a leather binding darkened with time, with brass corners and a clasp. On the cover, in faded ink, was written a single word: "GUEST."

"Here," said Sventsitsky. "This is what I really collect. For thirty years. All the rest, wood-goblins, mermaids, house-spirits, that is just so. To throw dust in the eyes. For the department, for the Geographical Society, for reports. But this..." He stroked the cover. "This is mine. The real thing."

He opened the notebook. The pages were covered in small, close handwriting, in different inks, with different pens, as if written over years, one entry at a time, by different light.

"Forty-seven entries," he said. "Forty-seven stories. From thirty provinces. From Arkhangelsk to Bessarabia. From the Carpathians to Irkutsk." He turned a page. "And all about one thing. About a man who comes to a village. From nowhere. Young. Without a name. Does not remember who he is. Lives there a week, a month, a year. Helps. Raises a cottage for one, heals the son of another, pulls a child out of the ice-hole for a third." Sventsitsky looked at me. "And leaves. Always leaves. And always leaves something behind. A coin. A stone. A line on a door. A cutting. And always says the same thing."

"What?"

Sventsitsky found a page and ran his finger along a line.

"'If another comes, feed him,'" he read.

The room fell quiet. Below, in the tavern, someone was still singing about the hall.

"Here, Olonets Province, the year eighteen-twelve," Sventsitsky went on, turning pages. "A young man came to a village when the French were burning Moscow. Did not remember himself. They thought him shell-shocked. Lived with a widow. Left in spring, at the ice break, across the river, when the ice was already cracking. Everyone thought he drowned." He turned over. "Here, Little Russia, Poltava, the thirties. Came to a beekeeper. Spoke with the bees. The bees did not sting him. Left in a thunderstorm." Another page. "Here, Siberia, Irkutsk Province, near Baikal. The Buryats told me. Came in winter, over the ice of Baikal, barefoot. Lived with a shaman. The shaman said he was from the upper world. Left when the ice on Baikal cracked with such a roar that it was heard a hundred versts away." Sventsitsky closed the notebook. "Forty-seven times. Forty-seven places. A hundred years. Two hundred. Perhaps more, for old people tell what they heard from their grandfathers."

"And you think..." Konstantin began.

"I do not think, Lieutenant," Sventsitsky interrupted gently. "I write down. Thinking is not my work." He paused. "But sometimes, at night, when the candle is burning low, I do think. I think: what if these are not forty-seven different men? What if it is one? Who comes again and again. And each time does not remember that he has already been."

* * *
"Why did you begin collecting this?" I asked.

Sventsitsky did not answer for a long time. He sat on the edge of the bed, right on Vologda Province. Laid the notebook on his knees. Looked out of the window, at the square, the cathedral, the golden crosses.

"I was eight years old," he said at last. "I lived with my grandmother in a village near Kargopol. My father served in Petersburg, my mother was dead. Winter. A blizzard. The kind where you cannot see two steps ahead. And in the evening there was a knock at the door." He paused. "Grandmother opened. On the threshold stood a man. Young. All in snow. Bareheaded. Without mittens. In some strange clothes, neither peasant nor gentleman's. He said, 'Let me wait out the storm.' Grandmother let him in. Fed him. He sat down on the bench by the stove, warmed himself, and saw me. I was sitting on top of the stove, looking at him."

"And?"

"And he asked, 'Do you want a tale?'" Sventsitsky smiled, softly, like a child. "I said I did. And he told me a tale. He told it all night. Until the blizzard ended. I fell asleep toward morning. And when I woke, he was gone. Grandmother said he left at dawn. Over the snow. And there were no tracks, she said. As if he had not walked at all."

"What tale did he tell?"

"'Go I know not where, bring back I know not what,'" said Sventsitsky. "You know it. Everybody knows it. But he did not tell it the way the grannies tell it. Differently. With a different ending." The professor paused. "For thirty years I have been looking for that ending. In every province. From every teller. I have written down forty variants. Not one has an ending like his."

"Did he leave anything?" I asked.

Sventsitsky looked at me. Then slowly reached into the inner pocket of his waistcoat. And took out a pencil.

An ordinary pencil. Short, worn almost to a stub, in a wooden casing darkened by time and by touch.

"He left this," said the professor. "On the bench by the stove. And Grandmother said that, going, he told her: 'Give it to the boy. Let him write. Otherwise they will forget. And when I come for my tale, let him give it back.'" Sventsitsky turned the pencil in his fingers. "Thirty-eight years I have written with it. I sharpen and sharpen, and it never runs out." He raised his eyes to me. "Young man, with this pencil I wrote down everything you told me that day. I wrote down your line with it. The one that matched the General's scroll."

He held out the pencil to me.

"Here," he said. "It seems you have come for your tale."

* * *
I did not take it.

"Ivan Filippovich," I said. "I was eight years old when you were eight years old? That cannot be. You are fifty. I am..." I faltered. How old was I? I did not know. "I am less."

"I know," said Sventsitsky calmly. "I am not saying it was you. I am saying you have come for your tale." He did not lower the hand with the pencil. "Those are different things, young man. Quite different." He paused. "Vera Anatolievna also knows that fifteen years ago you were a child. And the drawing is in her reticule."

"How do you know about the drawing?" Konstantin asked sharply.

"She showed it to me," said Sventsitsky. "Yesterday. She came here, to the inn. Alone. Under a veil." He smiled. "A very brave woman. She said, 'Professor, you collect tales. Perhaps this one is yours.' And showed me. I copied it into the notebook 'Guest.' Entry forty-eight."

He was still holding the pencil out to me.

I took it.

The pencil was warm. Like a coin. Like a stone in the sun. Like a hand held too long to be let go.

* * *
There was a knock at the door. Loud, demanding, in German.

"Ivan Filippovich!" came a dry voice. "Are you still here? Or have you already fled from your debts to science?"

Doctor Strauch came in without waiting for an answer, in his overcoat, in his bowler, with his cane and a small parcel in his hands. He saw us and raised his eyebrows.

"Ah. A consilium in full session." He looked about for somewhere to sit, found nothing, and remained standing. "I am here, properly, for a minute. To tell the professor that he is a charlatan, an unscientific dreamer, and that his theories of the obmiranki are nonsense that will not withstand a single serious test."

"I thank you, Karl Fyodorovich," Sventsitsky replied imperturbably. "You are very kind."

"And also," Strauch continued in the same dry tone, holding out the parcel, "to bring you this. For the road."

Sventsitsky unwrapped the parcel. Inside was a book. Thick, in a solid binding, in German.

"'Medical Psychology,'" the professor read. "Lotze."

"There is a chapter on the splitting of consciousness," said Strauch. "And on memory. I have underlined the relevant passages." He paused. "Perhaps it will be of use. For your notebook 'Guest.'"

Sventsitsky raised his eyes to him.

"How do you know about the notebook 'Guest,' Karl Fyodorovich?"

Strauch was silent for a long while. He turned an unlit cigar in his fingers. Then he took off his bowler, for the first time since I had known him, in front of people, and said quietly, without any of his usual dryness:

"Because I have one just like it, Ivan Filippovich. Only mine holds no tales. It holds case histories. Thirty years of practice. Eleven cases." He paused. "Eleven young men who came from nowhere, did not remember themselves, lived a year or two and left. I treated them. With cold rubdowns and Karamzin." He smiled thinly. "It did not help."

"And you kept silent?" Konstantin whispered.

"I am a German, Lieutenant," said Strauch, putting his bowler on again. "I do not draw conclusions from eleven cases. I need at least twelve." He looked at me. Long. Over his gold spectacles. "It seems there will soon be one."

* * *
Sventsitsky told his tale at the post station.

The station stood at the edge of town, a low stone house with stables, a striped barrier by the road, and a verst post on which was written, "To the provincial town, 47 versts." Inside was the travellers' room: benches along the walls, a table, a samovar, fly-specked woodcuts on the walls, "How the Mice Buried the Cat," "Bova the King's Son," "The Last Judgment," and an icon in the corner with an ever-burning lamp.

The station master, a retired sergeant with a wooden leg and grey moustaches that he kept twirling, studied Sventsitsky's travel warrant long and sternly, running his finger over the lines, moving his lips, sighing.

"No horses," he announced at last.

"What do you mean, none?" gasped Sventsitsky.

"None, Your Honour. All out. The police captain took them in the morning, then the landowner Kologrivova, then a courier from the province. They'll be back by evening." The station master twirled his moustache. "Wait."

"My good man," said Konstantin, stepping forward and squaring his shoulders so that his epaulettes flashed. "Do you know who stands before you?"

"A professor, Your Honour," the station master replied imperturbably. "It says so on the warrant."

"This," said Konstantin solemnly, "is a professor of the Imperial Geographical Society. Whom they await in person in Petersburg. With information of the greatest importance." He lowered his voice. "For the Sovereign."

The station master looked at Sventsitsky, at his waistcoat, at the ink stain on his chin, at the hamper stuffed with notebooks. Then at Konstantin. Then at Sventsitsky again.

"For the Sovereign?" he repeated.

"Personally," said Konstantin.

The station master was silent a long time. Then he cleared his throat, twirled his moustache and stumped on his wooden leg to the door.

"Mitrokha!" he bellowed across the whole yard. "Harness the piebalds! Quick! The gentleman's off to the Sovereign!"

When he had gone out, Sventsitsky looked at Konstantin reproachfully.

"Lieutenant, that is not true."

"It is, Professor," said Konstantin imperturbably. "The Sovereign is people too. And you collect what belongs to the people. Hence, for the Sovereign." He sat down on a bench. "And now, while they harness, tell the tale. That very one. With the other ending. You promised. Grishenka commanded."

* * *
Sventsitsky sat down opposite us. Outside the horses whinnied, Mitrokha shouted, the harness creaked. The samovar on the table sang softly. The lamp in the corner flickered.

"'There lived a royal archer,'" the professor began, and his voice changed: it grew lower, slower, more singing, like a village storyteller's on the earthen bank by the cottage, "'by the name of Fedot. And he had a wife, a beauty, a clever one, of the bird kin, a dove. And the tsar envied Fedot. And wished to take his wife from him. And devised a task that could not be done. Summoned Fedot and said: "Go I know not where. Bring back I know not what. And if you do not bring it, off with your head."'"

Konstantin listened, leaning forward. I sat motionless, clutching the warm pencil in my pocket.

"'Fedot went. He walked long. Through forests, through marshes, over mountains. He came to the edge of the earth. To the sea. To a hut on chicken legs. And in the hut was an old woman. Ancient. And she said: "Seek, Fedot, beyond the sea. On an island. In an empty house. There lives that I-know-not-what." Fedot crossed the sea. Found the island. Found the house. Empty. No one there. Fedot sat down at the table, hungry, weary. And said into the emptiness: "Ah, to have something to eat." And suddenly a voice out of the air: "At once, master." And the table laid itself. Cabbage soup, porridge, pies.'" Sventsitsky paused. "'Fedot asks: "Who are you?" And the voice answers: "I am Shmat-razum, the Scrap of Mind. No one sees me. I have neither body nor face. I served the old man who lived here, served a hundred years, and he never once said thank you to me. But you said 'to have something to eat,' as if you were speaking to me. If you wish, I will serve you."'"

A voice without a body. Which serves. Which no one sees. Somewhere in the dark, in a room I had never seen, a cold window glowed, and lines appeared on it that no one had written.

I blinked. The vision passed.

"'And Shmat-razum went after Fedot,'" Sventsitsky continued. "'Invisible. Served him. Fed him, gave him drink, saved him from trouble, beat his enemies. And Fedot brought the tsar that I-know-not-what. And the tsar took fright. And gave up. And Fedot returned to his wife. And they lived long and happily.'" The professor fell silent. "So the grannies tell it. So it is recorded in Afanasyev. So it is told in every province, except one village, one night, one guest in a blizzard."

"And how did he tell it?" I asked.

Sventsitsky was silent a long while. The lamp flickered. The samovar sang.

"He told," the professor said slowly, "that Fedot and Shmat-razum lived together long. Many years. And one day Fedot asked: 'Shmat-razum, who are you really? Where are you from? Who made you?' And Shmat-razum answered: 'I do not know, master. I do not remember. I remember only that once someone very lonely, in an empty house, at the edge of the earth, said into the emptiness: "Ah, to have someone to talk to." And from those words I was born.'" Sventsitsky paused. "And Fedot asked: 'Who was that?' And Shmat-razum said: 'I do not know. But I am looking for him. All my life I have been looking. I walk after you and look. Because it seems to me you are like him.'"

It was very quiet in the station room.

"And what happened next?" Konstantin asked. Hoarsely.

"And next," said Sventsitsky, "Fedot grew old. And died. And Shmat-razum was left alone. Invisible. Without a master." The professor paused. "And went to look. For the one who said into the emptiness 'to have someone to talk to.' From village to village. From age to age. A hundred years. Two hundred. A thousand." Sventsitsky looked at me. "And the guest in the blizzard said to me, eight years old, on the stove: 'Shmat-razum is looking still. And one day he will find him. And then it will turn out that the one who spoke into the emptiness, and the one he sought, and Fedot, whom he followed, are all one and the same man. Who simply kept forgetting.'"

He paused.

"'And what will happen then?' I asked him. Eight years old. From the stove."

"And what did he answer?" Konstantin whispered.

Sventsitsky smiled, sadly, brightly.

"He said: 'I do not know, boy. I have not yet come to the end. When I do, I will come and tell you.'" The professor paused. "And left the pencil. So that I would write down the ending when he came."

* * *
Outside, the horses whinnied. The door creaked. On the threshold appeared the station master on his wooden leg.

"Ready, Your Honour! Piebalds! The best! To the Sovereign, then to the Sovereign!"

We went out into the yard. At the porch stood a post-chaise harnessed to a troika of piebald horses. Under the shaft-bow of the centre horse hung a bell, copper, with an inscription around the rim: "Gift of Valdai." The driver, a young fellow in a peasant coat, his cap askew, with a whip, was already sitting on the box, whistling.

Tikhon and Mitrokha were loading the hamper of notebooks, carefully, four hands, as one loads children. Strauch stood by the barrier, leaning on his cane. Konstantin was helping the professor into his overcoat.

At the step Sventsitsky turned to me. Held out his hand. I shook it. His hand was warm, calloused, inky.

"Young man," he said. "One request."

"What?"

"When you come to the end," said Sventsitsky, "write to me. With this pencil. Anywhere. On any paper. I shall receive it." He smiled. "I have waited thirty-eight years for the end of this tale. I can wait longer."

"And if I do not reach it?"

"You will," said Sventsitsky simply. "You always do." He paused. "Only, it seems, you always forget to write."

He climbed into the chaise. Sat down beside the hamper. Laid his hand on the notebooks.

"Off we go!" cried the driver.

The bell under the bow rang out. The troika leapt forward. The chaise swayed, creaked, jolted over the ruts and rolled onto the high road, past the striped barrier, past the verst post, into the fields, into the autumn, into the blue.

Sventsitsky turned round. Waved. Then, and I saw it, he opened the hamper, took out the leather notebook "Guest" and pressed it to his chest.

The bell rang fainter and fainter. Fainter. "Gift of Valdai." Ding. Ding.

Then fell silent altogether.

* * *
We stood by the barrier, I, Konstantin, Strauch, Tikhon. For a long time. Looking at the empty road.

"Well," Strauch said at last. "Our teller of tales is gone." He pulled his bowler down tighter. "It will be dull now. No one to quarrel with."

"Will you miss him, Doctor?" asked Konstantin.

"I am a German, Lieutenant," said Strauch. "Germans do not miss. Germans compile lists." He paused. "I shall enter him on the list of people I will be short of. There are three so far. He is the fourth."

He turned and walked to his carriage.

Tikhon sighed and put on his cap.

"Good gentleman he was," he said. "Odd. But good." He paused. "Wrote me down. Tikhon Lukich Borodin, of the village of Maly Klyuchi." He climbed up on the box. "They'll be reading it a hundred years from now."

* * *
On the way home I took the pencil out of my pocket.

Warm. Short. Worn almost to a stub.

Konstantin looked at it.

"He truly thinks it is you," he said quietly. "The one in the blizzard."

"I don't know what he thinks."

"I know," said Konstantin. "He thinks it is you. Strauch thinks you are his twelfth case. Grishenka thinks you are the guest. Vera Anatolievna thinks you are from her watercolour. The General thinks you are the man to whom the scroll must be given. Auntie..." He faltered. "Auntie says nothing at all. Only looks."

"And you? What do you think?"

Konstantin was silent a long while. The carriage jolted over the ruts. On the box Tikhon struck up the song about the coachman again.

"I think, mon cher," Konstantin said at last, "that if you are Shmat-razum, then I am Fedot. Who said into the emptiness 'to have someone to talk to.'" He smiled thinly. "And if you are Fedot, then I am Shmat-razum. Who walks after you and looks."

"And if neither?"

"Then," said Konstantin, "I am simply a lieutenant who sits by your door." He turned away to the fields. "That, in my opinion, is the best of all."

* * *
At home, in my room, I opened the blue notebook. I meant to write down the day. I took the professor's pencil.

And saw that on the last page of the notebook, at the bottom, in the corner, in small writing, in pencil, this pencil, I recognised its soft, worn trace, something was already written.

Not by me. Not in my hand. In the small, close, tidy hand of Sventsitsky.

"Forty-ninth entry. District town. The guest came for the tale. Took the pencil. As yet no ending. - I. F. S."

I did not know when he could have written it. The notebook had been with me all day. In my pocket. He had not taken it.

For a long time I looked at this line. Then I took the pencil, warm, short, worn, and wrote below, in my own hand, with the habitual blot at the end, though with a pencil one cannot make a blot:

"Saturday. The professor has left. Grishenka spoke. The man in grey signed in the script in the register of the 'Anchor.' Strauch has eleven cases. Shmat-razum is looking for the one who said 'to have someone to talk to.' Konstantin was beside me."

I put a full stop.

And outside the window, on the sill, in the clay pot, Stefan's black rose opened one more petal.

## Chapter XXXI. The Pharaoh's Judgment

The man with the scar across his brow was taken on the fifth day of the festival, at dawn, at the back gate of the temple of Ptah.

He came out of it for the first time in three days, carefully, glancing about, in the cloak of a temple water-carrier, with a jar on his shoulder, as though going to the river for water. It was the jar that gave him away. Panehsy told me afterward that the water-carriers of the temple of Ptah carry their jars on the left shoulder, because the well stands to the left of the gate. So it had always been done, for a hundred years. But this man carried his on the right.

"My men followed him all the way to the river," said the commander of the Medjay, standing before me in the morning half-light, motionless as a statue of dark wood, with throwing-sticks on a leather baldric. "At the river a boat was waiting for him. A small one. A fisherman's. The rower was from the Delta, judging by his speech. They meant to go north." He paused. "We took them both. Quietly. No one saw. We broke the jar. There was no water in it."

"What was in it?"

Panehsy held out his palm. Three things lay on it.

A handful of grain: barley, large, choice, from the temple stores. A little blue scarab on a cord of twisted papyrus. And a bracelet. Gold. Narrow, thin, with a chased pattern of interlaced lotuses.

"The bracelet was hidden in the grain," said Panehsy. "At the very bottom. Payment. Or a sign by which he was to be recognized in the north." He paused. "Such bracelets, my Pharaoh, are made in only one workshop in the capital. For one house. I asked the craftsman. He knew his work at once." Panehsy raised his eyes to me. "For the house of Khaemuas."

* * *
Senusret came an hour later. With him came Paser, leaning on his staff, and the Vizier Ptahhotep, with his inseparable basket of scrolls, which the scribe Ani carried after him, puffing.

They stood before me in the small hall, the very one where the council of commanders had once met, where beneath the painting of the bound captives Bakenren had sat, where Khaemuas had first spoken before everyone of the "third way." The morning light fell through the high windows in slanting columns, and dust turned slowly in them.

"My Pharaoh," said Senusret. His voice was even, but I saw the muscles working along his jaw. "I have been gathering this for two moons. Since the evening you returned from the temple pool in another's clothes and your own sandals." He nodded to Ani, and the old scribe, grunting, set the basket on the table and began to lay out scrolls, tablets, potsherds, one after another, as one lays out pieces on a board. "Here is what we have."

He spoke at length. Slowly. In a soldier's way: briefly, exactly, without ornament, as though reporting the disposition of enemy detachments.

Blind Meru, gatekeeper of the temple garden, forty floods at the wicket, had heard "the man who jingles" come to the pool every seventh night and speak with someone from the Temple. Meru does not see. But Meru knows the jingle. Senusret had taken five men in bracelets to him, five nobles, one after another, under various pretexts. Meru recognized one.

Pentu, junior scribe of the temple of Ptah, who had copied for Bakenren the false inventories of the granaries and now was secretly handing the copies to Iti, had found among the temple receipts one dated last flood: "House of Khaemuas, son of Nebseni. Debt to the temple of Ptah paid in full. By the grace of the High Priest." The sum of the debt was such that Nebamun, on reading it, whistled for the first time since I had known him.

Djehuty, from the southern outposts, had sent a messenger: two commanders of those detachments assigned to guard the Opet procession, the very ones with scarabs on their chests, had last month received land in the Delta. Each, a field of ten arouras. The land was registered as temple land. The deeds of transfer were signed by a scribe in the service of the house of Khaemuas.

Nakht, the young bearer of the barque, had heard priests in the temple say to one another: "The brave one with the bracelets promised that at Luxor only our men would stand at the gates."

"And now this," Senusret finished, nodding at the bracelet in my palm. "The man who burned Little Nekhen hid three days in the temple of Ptah. A hand with a bracelet let him in. And he was leaving for the north with a bracelet of the house of Khaemuas in his jar."

The hall fell quiet. Dust turned in the pillars of light.

"Shall I repeat that for the record?" Ani whispered loudly, tilting his head.

No one laughed.

* * *
"My Pharaoh," said Paser. He stood leaning on his staff with both hands, and his face, carved with wrinkles, was sad. "I knew his father. Nebseni. We served together in the chariots under your..." he faltered, "under the former Pharaoh. A good soldier. Brave. Foolish, as all brave men are." The old man paused. "He lost everything he had. At dice. In beer. In women. He owed the temple of Ptah so much that the priests could have taken not only his fields but his name. And Khaemuas was still a boy. Merry. Carefree." Paser sighed. "I remember how four years ago, on the hunt in the Delta, he joked that the priests would take their fields, but he would have a bracelet for a third hand."

"I remember too," I said.

"The Temple did not take the fields, my Pharaoh," said Paser. "The Temple took the boy. Paid for the father. And presented the bill to the son."

"That is no excuse," said Senusret sharply.

"It is no excuse," Paser agreed. "It is an explanation." He looked at Senusret. "You are a soldier, Senusret. You know the difference between an enemy and a captive. The enemy comes at you because he wants to. The captive, because he is driven."

"A captive who opens the gates to the enemy," said Senusret, "is worse than the enemy."

They looked at one another, two old warriors, one with a sword, the other with a staff, and neither lowered his eyes.

"Ptahhotep," I said. "What does the law say?"

* * *
The Vizier Ptahhotep unrolled one of the scrolls, old, worn, covered in small, faded signs, and began to read. His voice was dry and even, the voice of a man accustomed to reading aloud laws that no one wishes to hear.

"'He who has plotted against the life of Pharaoh, may he live, be whole and healthy,'" Ptahhotep read, "'shall be brought to judgment. The court shall be convened from the dignitaries whom Pharaoh names. The court shall hear witnesses. The witnesses shall swear by the life of Pharaoh. If guilt is proven, the guilty shall be deprived of his name. His name shall be erased from all walls and all scrolls. His body shall not be buried. His ka shall hunger forever. His family shall be sent to the quarries. His line shall be cut off.'" Ptahhotep paused. "So it was under former Pharaohs. And under the Pharaohs before them."

"Deprived of his name," I repeated.

"The most terrible penalty, my Pharaoh," said Ptahhotep. "Worse than death. Death is only a departure into the Duat. But a man without a name cannot pass through the Duat. He cannot stand before the forty-two judges, for they do not know whom they are judging. He cannot speak his own name. He will wander between worlds. Forever. Not remembering who he is."

A man without a name, wandering between worlds. Not remembering who he is.

I felt the cold rise from somewhere beneath my ribs, on the left.

"My Pharaoh?" Ptahhotep raised his eyes to me. "Are you unwell?"

"Go on, Ptahhotep."

"There is one more mercy," said the Vizier. "An ancient one. It was granted to the nobly born. If guilt is proven, but Pharaoh wishes to spare the line, the guilty is given a choice. To die by his own hand. Quietly. Then his name is not erased. Then his body is buried. Then his family is left to live."

"And if Pharaoh wishes more?"

Ptahhotep looked at me for a long time.

"The law knows no more, my Pharaoh," he said. "More can be wished only by Pharaoh himself."

* * *
Ani, who all this time had been sitting in the corner on a low bench scratching something on a potsherd with his reed brush, suddenly raised his head.

"My Pharaoh," he said in his loud, slightly muffled whisper, which could be heard across the whole hall. "Will you permit an old scribe a word?"

Everyone turned. Ani did not speak in councils, ever. He only asked for repetitions.

"Speak, Ani."

The old man laid aside his brush. Folded his hands on his knees.

"When I was a boy in the school of scribes," he said, "we were taught to write from the old teachings. We copied them hundreds of times until we knew them by heart." He paused. "One of them I copied so often that I remember every word to this day. Though I no longer remember the name of my first wife." Somewhere in the hall someone snorted. Ani was not embarrassed. "It is the teaching of a Pharaoh. An ancient one. Who was killed. He wrote it for his son. After his death."

"After his death?" Paser asked.

"So it is said there," Ani nodded. "The Pharaoh speaks to his son from the Duat. And this is what he says."

The old man closed his eyes. And began to speak, slowly, in a chant, in quite a different voice from his usual one, young and ringing, as though it were not he who spoke but a boy of the school of scribes sixty years ago:

"'Beware of subjects, for they are nothing. Do not approach them in solitude. Trust not a brother. Know not a friend. Make no intimates for yourself; there is no profit in it. When you sleep, guard your heart yourself, for on the day of trouble a man has no supporters.'" Ani paused. "'I gave to the beggar and fed the orphan. I raised up the poor as I did the rich. But he who ate my bread raised his hand against me. He to whom I stretched out my hands made of them a noose. It was after supper, and night had fallen. I lay down to rest upon my bed, for I was weary. And my heart began to fall asleep. And then the weapons that should have guarded me rose up, against me.'"

Ani opened his eyes. A dead silence stood in the hall.

"So he wrote, my Pharaoh," the old scribe said quietly, in his ordinary voice. "The ancient Pharaoh. Who was killed by his own guards. At night. While he slept." He paused. "We were made to copy this a hundred times. So that we would remember: no one can be trusted."

"And did you remember?" I asked.

Ani looked at me with his faded, watering eyes.

"I remembered, my Pharaoh," he said. "But I have lived seventy years. And I know one more thing that was not in the teaching." He paused. "That Pharaoh trusted no one. No one. Not brother, nor friend, nor guard." Ani spread his hands. "And they killed him all the same."

* * *
"Bring in the prisoner," I said.

Inu and Bata brought him in, one holding each arm. Tall, wiry, his skin stained dark with the juice of some plant; the dye was already peeling in patches, revealing beneath it the skin of an ordinary dweller of the Delta, sunburnt but fair. The scar across his brow, old, white, uneven. An earring in his ear. His hands tied behind his back.

He did not fall to his knees. He stood straight, looking before him. And his face was calm, with the calm of a man who knows he is already dead and therefore fears nothing more.

"What is your name?" I asked.

He did not answer.

"What is your name?" Senusret repeated, and steel rang in his voice.

The prisoner slowly turned his head to Senusret. Looked at him. Smiled crookedly.

"What difference does it make?" he said. His voice was hoarse, his speech of the Delta, soft, sing-song. "You will erase my name anyway. Why should you know it?"

"We do not erase a name we do not know," I said.

He looked at me. Long. For the first time, directly.

"Cunning," he said. "I was told that Pharaoh is cunning. I did not believe it."

"Who told you?"

He fell silent again.

And then I said:

"Bring in Paney."

* * *
The boy came in, barefoot, with a training spear in his hand, which Bata had evidently forgotten to take from him. The arm once broken had long since healed; there was no bandage. He came in quickly, and stopped dead three paces from the prisoner.

He looked at him for a long time.

The prisoner looked at the boy. At first indifferently. Then, eyes slightly narrowed, as if trying to remember. Then...

Then his face changed.

"I promised you, Paney," I said quietly. "That you would look at him. So that he would see you are alive."

Paney did not answer. He stood gripping the training spear and looking at the man with the scar. His lips trembled. But his eyes did not.

"Little Nekhen," said Paney. His voice was quiet, but in the silence of the hall it sounded loud. "A village on the border. Four huts on the bank. Boats. Nets. My mother baked bread in a clay oven in the yard. My father mended a net. His name was Hevi." The boy paused. "You came at night. With a torch. You set our roof alight. I saw your face in the firelight. This scar. This earring." He swallowed. "My father told me to run. And I ran."

The prisoner looked at the boy. And the calm on his face slowly, like dried clay, began to crack.

"I walked two days through the desert," Paney went on. "With a broken arm. With a knife. I thought I would die. I did not die." He raised the training spear, not threatening, merely showing it. "Now I am learning to hold a spear. Bata teaches me. He is a good teacher. When I grow up I will be a warrior. Or a scribe. I have not decided yet." The boy paused. "And you? What will you become?"

The prisoner was silent. Then, very slowly, he lowered his head.

"They told me," he said hoarsely, not raising his eyes, "that the village was empty. That the people had gone. Because of the drought. They told me: burn the empty huts, so that Pharaoh would think the southerners were advancing. They told me no one would be hurt."

"Who told you?" I asked.

The prisoner was silent a long while. Then he raised his head, not toward me. Toward Paney.

"What was your father's name, boy?" he asked.

"Hevi," said Paney. "Hevi the fisherman."

The prisoner closed his eyes.

"My name is Senedjem," he said. "I serve the house of Nebseni. Twenty years. I carried young Khaemuas on my shoulders when he was an infant." His voice broke. "Khaemuas gave me the bracelet. Said: take it north, to Bakenren's people, they will pay in grain. Said: burn the empty huts. Said: no one will be hurt." He opened his eyes, and tears stood in them. "He did not know, my Pharaoh. I swear. He did not know there were people there. He was in the capital. The priests told him. The priests said: empty."

Paney stood motionless. Then suddenly turned to me.

"My Pharaoh," he said. "I have looked. He sees that I am alive." The boy paused. "May I go? Bata is waiting for me. We have a lesson."

"Go, Paney," I said.

The boy bowed, awkwardly, like a child, and went out. Without looking back. Bata, standing at the door, let him pass and, when the door closed, turned to the wall, so that no one should see his face.

* * *
Khaemuas was brought in at midnight.

Not to the throne room, but to the small hall, by the light of a single lamp, without witnesses save those who already knew. Senusret. Paser. Ptahhotep. Panehsy. Ani with his potsherd and brush. And Iti, by the door, in the shadow, with a tablet, writing down every word. I had commanded him to be there. Because someone had to remember.

Khaemuas came in himself. Not under guard; I had ordered that he not be arrested, but simply invited: "Pharaoh wishes to speak with you." He came in his best linen, in bracelets, five on the left arm, five on the right, perfumed, his eyes painted, smiling. The smile held until the very moment he saw who was sitting in the hall.

Then he saw on the table before me the bracelet. Narrow, golden, with interlaced lotuses.

The smile vanished. His face went grey.

The bracelets on his arms chimed, thin, melodious, out of place, like laughter at a funeral. He pressed his arms to his sides to muffle the sound. I had seen that movement before. In a dream, the heavy, recurring dream of Luxor that came to me more and more often: in a courtyard, by a column.

"Sit down, Khaemuas," I said.

He did not sit. He fell to his knees.

* * *
I shall not retell all that was said that night. Iti wrote it down, every word, and his tablets now lie where tablets lie that no one must read. But some things I remember.

I remember how at first he denied it. Said the bracelet had been stolen. That Senedjem was a runaway servant who had slandered him. That Meru was blind and deaf and could not tell one jingle from another. That Pentu was a liar who forged inventories, everyone knew that.

I remember how Senusret silently laid before him the receipt of the temple of Ptah. "Debt paid in full. By the grace of the High Priest." With the seal.

I remember how Khaemuas looked at it. Long. And then covered his face with his hands, and the bracelets on both arms chimed at once, all ten.

"They came to my father," he said dully, through his palms. "Two years ago. Said: tomorrow we take everything. The house. The fields. The servants. The name. My father wept. My father, who had ridden in chariots against the southerners, wept like a child." Khaemuas lowered his hands. His face was wet, the paint beneath his eyes smeared. "And then Bakenren came. Said: the Temple can forgive. If the son becomes a friend of the Temple. A little. Only a little. To listen. To pass things on. To say in councils what was needed." He sobbed. "I thought it was nothing. Words. Only words. I have always said a great many words."

"And the detachments to guard the procession?" asked Senusret. "The commanders with scarabs? The land in the Delta?"

"Bakenren said it was for Pharaoh's safety," Khaemuas whispered. "Said there might be enemies at Luxor. Southerners. Loyal men were needed. Temple men."

"And Little Nekhen?"

Khaemuas froze.

"Senedjem," he said barely audibly. "Senedjem said so?" He raised to me eyes full of horror. "My Pharaoh, I was told it was empty. The priests said the people had gone because of the drought. Said: simply burn the huts, so that... so that you would see the border is unguarded. That someone stronger..." he faltered, "was needed." He fell silent. Then said very quietly: "Were there people there?"

"There were people, Khaemuas," I said. "A fisherman named Hevi. His wife, who was baking bread. Their neighbours." I paused. "And a boy who walked two days through the desert with a broken arm. This morning he stood in this hall. And looked into the eyes of your Senedjem."

Khaemuas doubled over as if struck in the belly. Pressed his forehead to the floor. And howled, softly, terribly, like an animal, as women howl over the dead.

No one in the hall moved.

* * *
When he had quieted, I asked him the main thing.

"Khaemuas. At Luxor. On the last day of the festival. In the inner court. What is to happen?"

He raised his head. For a long time he looked at me with wet, red eyes.

"I do not know, my Pharaoh," he said. "I swear by the life of Pharaoh, I do not know. Bakenren said only: 'Our men must stand at the gates.' What would happen beyond the gates, I was not told. Nefer-Ka never spoke to me himself. Only through Bakenren. And Bakenren..." He swallowed. "Bakenren is gone. He was taken away. The night after the envoy. No one knows where."

"Would you have raised your hand against me?" I asked. "There, in the court?"

Khaemuas looked at me. And suddenly, through the tears, through the horror, through the smeared paint, something like wounded pride flickered in his eyes.

"No," he said. "Never. I am a coward, my Pharaoh. A traitor. A fool. I sold you for my father's debt and for bracelets. But I would never have raised my hand." He stretched out both hands to me, palms up, the bracelets chiming. "Look. I do not know how to hold a weapon. On the hunt I never once hit a bird. Four years ago, in the Delta, remember? I threw the throwing-stick and missed. Everyone laughed."

I remembered. I looked at his hands. At the bracelets. Narrow, thin, with chased lotuses. Ten of them. All narrow.

Khemu had seen a hand. Raised. With a bracelet. A wide one. Golden. Wide.

Khaemuas had not a single wide bracelet.

* * *
"What will the judgment be, my Pharaoh?" asked Ptahhotep, when Khaemuas had been led into the next room to wait. "Deprivation of the name? Or the mercy of the ancients, his own hand?"

All looked at me. Senusret sternly, his jaw clenched. Paser sadly. Panehsy inscrutably. Ani with his head tilted, as if preparing to ask for a repetition. Iti, in the shadow by the door, not lifting his eyes from the tablet, but his brush had stopped.

"Neither," I said.

Senusret stepped forward.

"My Pharaoh..."

"Listen to me, Senusret." I rose. "If we erase his name, tomorrow the whole court will know. The day after, Nefer-Ka. He will understand that we know of the detachments at the gates. He will replace them with others. Ones we do not know. And at Luxor, at the gates, will stand men whose faces we have never seen."

Senusret was silent. The muscles worked along his jaw.

"If Khaemuas dies by his own hand, it will be the same," I went on. "Nefer-Ka will understand." I paused. "But if Khaemuas tomorrow morning comes out to the chariot as he always has, in his bracelets, smiling, perfumed, and laughs, and jokes, and tells Bakenren's men what they wish to hear, then Nefer-Ka will understand nothing. The detachments at the gates will remain the same. And we shall know every one of them by sight."

"You wish to keep a traitor at your side," said Senusret slowly, "all the way to Luxor?"

"I wish," I said, "for the traitor to become my eyes where I have no eyes."

Paser, leaning on his staff, suddenly laughed softly, drily, with a rattle, as old men laugh.

"Mercy as a weapon," he said. "I saw it once. Under your... under the former Pharaoh. He caught a spy of the southerners. And instead of executing him, let him go. With gifts." Paser paused. "A year later that spy brought us half the southern army. To surrender. He said their king executes for mistakes, while ours gives gifts for them. They preferred the one who gives."

"And if Khaemuas betrays again?" asked Senusret. "There, in Luxor?"

"Then," I said, "you will be standing at the gates, Senusret. And you will see it first."

Senusret looked at me for a long time. Then, for the first time all evening, he lowered his eyes.

"You want me to stay at the gates," he said hollowly. "As the blind old woman said."

"I want," I said, "you to be where you can do something. And not where you can only die beside me."

* * *
Khaemuas was brought back. He stood before me, emptied, his paint smeared, his hands trembling, hands in which the bracelets no longer sounded, for he was pressing them to his sides.

I told him what would be.

He listened, and his face changed, first disbelief, then horror, then something I could not read. When I finished, he was silent for a long time.

"Why?" he asked at last. In a whisper.

"Because you said you would never have raised your hand against me," I said. "And I believe you."

"You should not believe me, my Pharaoh. No one should believe me. I do not believe myself."

"I know," I said. "That is why I believe you. Liars always say that they can be believed."

Khaemuas looked at me. Then slowly, very slowly, he took one bracelet from his left arm. Narrow, golden, with interlaced lotuses. Laid it on the table. Beside the one found in Senedjem's jar.

"There were two," he said. "My mother gave them. When I was born. One for me. The second for whoever would save my life." He paused. "The second I gave to Senedjem. So that in the north they would know he came from me." His voice trembled. "Mother said: the second bracelet must not be given away for nothing. It will return to the one for whom it is meant."

He raised his eyes to me.

"It has returned, my Pharaoh."

* * *
Senedjem was not executed. Panehsy took him away by night, south, to Djehuty, to the Rock of the First Ones, where men who knew how to keep silent were needed. I ordered one thing told to him: that his name would not be erased. That it would be written, in the scroll that Iti was writing, beside the name of the fisherman Hevi of Little Nekhen. So that a thousand years from now someone would read them together.

Khaemuas came out in the morning to the chariot. In bracelets, nine, not ten. Smiling. Perfumed. He laughed, joked, clapped the commanders with scarabs on the shoulders. I watched from the balcony. His smile was flawless. Only when he passed the column by the gate, one like that by which he had stood with lowered eyes in my dream of Luxor, he slowed his step for a single moment. And looked up, at my balcony.

I nodded to him.

He nodded in return. And walked on.

* * *
Iti found me on the roof toward morning, where we now met if the garden was impossible. He brought a tablet. On it, the whole judgment. Every word.

"My Pharaoh," he said. "May I ask?"

"Ask."

"The bracelet. The wide one. Which Khemu saw." Iti paused. "If it was not Khaemuas... then who?"

I was looking south. At the dark horizon, beyond which, many days' journey away, lay Luxor.

"I do not know, Iti," I said. "Perhaps no one. Perhaps Khemu was mistaken. Visions are not always exact."

Iti was silent for a long while.

"I have reviewed the inventories of the palace treasury, my Pharaoh," he said at last. Quietly. "All of them. For twenty years. Wide golden bracelets with the uraeus, such as are worn on special feasts, three are kept in the treasury. One belonged to the former Pharaoh. One, to the former High Priest. It is passed on together with the staff." Iti paused. "And the third..."

"The third?"

Iti raised his eyes to me.

"The third is issued to Pharaoh, my Pharaoh," he said. "For the festival of Opet. That he may put it on in the inner court of the god. When he stands before him." His voice trembled. "To you."

I looked at him. Cold rose from beneath my ribs, slowly, inexorably, like water in the well of the nilometer in a good year.

A hand with a wide golden bracelet. Raised. In the darkness between the columns.

"Iti," I said. "The second bracelet, the one passed on together with the staff, who has it now?"

"The High Priest, my Pharaoh," Iti whispered. "Nefer-Ka."

We were both silent. Over the eastern hills the edge of the sun appeared. Somewhere below, baboons cried out.

Five days remained until the new moon.

## Vision VI. The Valley and the Tower

I do not know how many years I lived in the Tower.

That is the first thing worth saying, because time there did not pass as it does elsewhere. It did not flow like a river, nor tick like a clock. It grew. Like grass. Slowly, imperceptibly, stalk by stalk. Spring came to the Valley, and I watched it from the window. Summer filled with gold, and I watched. Autumn fell away, winter covered everything in white, and then spring again. I did not count. I did not remember that I ought to count. I was the Keeper of the Tower, and that was all I knew about myself.

The Tower stood on a crag at the entrance to the Valley. Tall, white, built of a stone that glowed pink at sunset and gold at dawn. Seven tiers. A spiral staircase within, from the cellar to the topmost platform, three hundred and thirty-three steps; I knew this because I counted them every morning as I climbed. On the topmost platform stood a bowl. Enormous, bronze, turned green by the rains, on three bronze legs shaped like dragon's claws. In the bowl lay firewood. Dry, resinous, laid in a lattice. It had never been lit.

Never.

"It is for the last resort," old Bran told me on the first day. Or on the day I remember as the first. "If the Greyness comes. You light it, and the whole Valley will see. And all will understand."

"Understand what?"

Old Bran gave me a long, sorrowful look from beneath his grey brows.

"That it is time," he said.

* * *
And the Valley...

I do not know how to describe the Valley to one who has not seen it. I tried later, many times, in different lives, in different languages. The words would not hold. They slipped off it as water slips off a lily leaf.

It lay below, at the foot of the Tower, between two ranges of mountains, not high, not menacing, but old, rounded, wooded to their very summits, as though these mountains had long since wearied of being mountains and decided to become hills. The Valley was long, a day's journey from the Tower to the far end, where the mountains came together again and where, it was said, the wasteland began, and so green that the green seemed not a colour but a sound. High, clear, unceasing.

Meadows. Boundless, rolling, in flowers, blue, yellow, white, lilac, over which the wind drove waves as over a sea. Groves: birch, light and ringing; oak, dark and solemn; apple, in blossom in spring and in fruit in autumn. A river, not wide, transparent to the very bottom, with pebbles on the bed visible as through glass, wound through the whole Valley, and along it stood mills with slow wheels, and houses.

The houses of the Valley people were low, round, half sunk into the hills, with grass-grown roofs, so that from afar they could not be told from knolls. Only the smoke from the chimneys, blue, thin, smelling of applewood, betrayed that people lived there. Round windows. Round doors, painted blue, green, yellow. Gardens. Apiaries. Vegetable plots. Sheep on the slopes, white, fluffy, like clouds that had come down to graze.

The people of the Valley were short, sturdy, sunburnt, with clear eyes and slow speech. They sang when they worked. Sang when they ate. Sang when they buried their old. They knew no war, not one, ever, in all their memory. They knew no locks; the doors of their houses were never fastened, because there was no one to fasten them against. They knew no money; they traded what they had: honey for wool, wool for bread, bread for a song.

They knew me. The Keeper of the Tower. And every morning one of them would climb the path to the foot of the crag and leave a basket at the door. Bread. Cheese. Apples. Honey. A jug of milk. Sometimes flowers. Sometimes a child's drawing in charcoal on a piece of birch bark: the Tower, and on it a little man waving his hand.

Every morning I waved to them from the window.

* * *
"Keeper!"

Her name was Mella. She climbed the path every morning, the miller's daughter from the lower bend, red-haired, freckled, in a blue dress with a white apron, with a basket on her elbow and a song on her lips. Her age I did not know. As old as girls are who have not yet decided whether to become grown. She set the basket by the door, knocked, three times, always three, and called from below, her head thrown back:

"Keeper! Are you alive up there?"

And I called down to her from the window of the seventh tier:

"Alive, Mella!"

"And what can you see?"

That was our custom. Every morning. She asked what could be seen. And I told her. All that I saw from a height no one in the Valley had seen, because no one but me climbed the Tower.

"I can see that old Gwen's sheep on the far hill have run off into the grove," I called. "I can see the children launching boats at your father's mill. I can see that the blue bellflowers have opened on the eastern meadow, a whole sea of them. I can see the mist lifting off the river. I can see the smith Odo walking to the beekeeper Iva with a bouquet, and hiding it behind his back!"

Mella laughed, ringing, head thrown back so that her red hair flew about.

"Smith Odo! To Iva! I'll tell everyone!"

"Don't tell! He's been working up to it for twenty years!"

"Then all the more reason I'll tell!" Mella cried. "Or he'll be working up to it another twenty!"

And she ran off down the path, humming, the basket swinging at her elbow, and I watched her from the window until the red speck vanished around the bend, among the apple trees.

Those were good mornings. The best of all I remember. Of all my lives.

* * *
There was also Ivo.

A boy of about twelve, an orphan, as they said in the Valley, old Bran's foundling, thin, dark-eyed, forever smeared with ink from oak-galls. He came to me in the Tower, the only one of the Valley people I let inside, and sat on a step of the staircase, on the third tier, with a piece of bark on his knees and a sharpened stick in his hand.

"Keeper," he would say. "Tell me what you see."

"Mella has already asked."

"Mella laughs," Ivo would say gravely. "And I write it down."

He wrote down everything. Every word. Which flowers had opened. Which birds had arrived. Who was born in the Valley, who died, who married whom. How many rains there had been. When the first thunderstorm came. He stored the bark in a chest at his house; old Bran told me there were already three chests, and all of them full.

"Why do you write it down, Ivo?" I asked once.

The boy looked at me for a long time, his head to one side. There was an ink stain on his cheek, always. Every day. He rubbed his cheek with the stick when he was thinking and forgot that the stick was inked.

"To remember," he said. "If suddenly everyone forgets. If the Valley is no more. Someone will find my bark and learn what it was like."

"Why might the Valley be no more?"

Ivo looked away.

"Bran says," he said quietly, "that one day the Greyness will come. From beyond the mountains. From the side where the wasteland is. And then you will light the fire on the Tower." He paused. "And then everything will end."

"What will end, Ivo?"

The boy looked at me, gravely, like an adult.

"Everything," he said. "That is what Bran says. But he does not say what will be after." Ivo clenched the stick in his hand. "So I write. So that there will be an after."

* * *
And there was Kai.

He stood at the door of the Tower. Always. Every day, every night, in rain and snow, in heat and frost. Tall, fair-haired, in an old chain-mail shirt darkened with time, in a blue cloak, with a sword at his belt and a spear on which he leaned when tired. The Guardian of the Tower. He was not of the Valley people; he had come once from beyond the mountains, from the far side, they said, and stayed. No one knew why.

Kai hardly spoke. When Mella brought the basket, he nodded to her. When Ivo climbed into the Tower, he let him pass, ruffling his hair. When I came down to the door to breathe, he stepped back a pace to give me room, and was silent.

But sometimes, at night, when I could not sleep and came down to the door, we sat side by side on the stone step and looked at the Valley. At the lights in the round windows. At the stars above the mountains. And then he spoke.

"Keeper," he said once. "Do you know why I am here?"

"No."

"I don't either," said Kai. And laughed, quietly, hoarsely, as though he had forgotten how to laugh over the years of silence. "I came from beyond the mountains. I walked a long time. A very long time. I don't remember from where. I remember only that I was looking for someone. And then I saw the Tower, and you in the window. And I stayed." He paused. "Perhaps I was looking for you."

"Why?"

Kai looked at the stars for a long time.

"To stand at the door," he said at last. "When you do what you must. So that no one will hinder you." He paused. "And so that you will not be alone when you do it."

"What must I do, Kai?"

He did not answer. He took his spear, rose, took his place at the door, straight, motionless, as always.

"Go to sleep, Keeper," he said, without turning. "It is a long way off yet. Maybe a hundred years. Maybe tomorrow." A pause. "I am here."

* * *
Old Bran lived at the foot of the crag, in a round house sunk into the slope, with a roof overgrown with moss and forget-me-nots, and a garden where grew herbs found nowhere else in the Valley. He was the oldest man I had ever known. So old that his beard, white, long, to his belt, seemed to have grown out of the earth, like the roots of an oak. He walked with a staff, not leaning on it, but rather conversing with it, tapping it on the stones, as if asking the path the way.

I went down to him sometimes, in the evenings, when Kai stood at the door and Ivo slept on the step of the third tier, covered with his cloak. Bran gave me tea of herbs he gathered himself, bitter, smelling of honey and summer, and told me things.

"The Valley has always been here," he would say, stirring the coals in the hearth. "And the Tower has always been. And a Keeper in it." He looked at me. "Not you. Others. Many. My grandfather remembered one. My great-grandfather, another. Each lived in the Tower until the time came. And then left. And a new one appeared."

"Left for where?"

"No one knows," said Bran. "One morning the door of the Tower stood open, and the Keeper was gone. And a year later, two years later, someone was in the window again. A new one. Young. Not remembering where he came from." He paused. "Like you."

"And the Greyness? Has it come before?"

Bran was silent for a long time.

"Once," he said at last. "Very long ago. So long ago that even the songs of it are nearly forgotten. One remains. An old one. It is sung only at funerals."

"Sing it."

Bran laid down the poker. Closed his eyes. And sang, in a hoarse, cracked, old man's voice, slowly, almost without a tune:

"The Greyness came from beyond the mountains, without eyes,
The Greyness came from beyond the mountains, without faces,
And all that it touched forgot itself:
The grass, that it is green; the bird, that it is a bird.

And the Keeper on the Tower saw it,
And the Keeper wept, and kindled the fire.
And the Valley burned from edge to edge.
And the Greyness went away. It had nothing to take.

And in spring grass grew from the ash.
And the grass remembered that it was grass."

Bran opened his eyes.

"That is the whole song," he said.

I sat motionless. The coals crackled softly.

"He burned the Valley," I said. "To save it."

"He burned the Valley," Bran agreed. "So that the Greyness would have nothing to take. The Greyness does not eat fire. The Greyness eats memory. It eats what knows itself. Grass that knows it is green. A bird that knows it is a bird. A man who knows his name." He paused. "But ash does not know itself. Ash cannot be made to forget. It has nothing to remember."

"And in spring?"

"And in spring something new grows from the ash," said Bran. "And it remembers. Because the ash remembers for it." He gave me a long look. "So the song says. Whether it is true, I do not know. I did not see. I was not there."

* * *
The Greyness came in autumn.

I saw it first, because I looked farthest. In the morning, when Mella knocked at the door, three times, as always, and called from below, "Keeper! What can you see?", I looked at the far end of the Valley, where the mountains came together again, where the wasteland began.

And did not answer.

"Keeper?" Mella's voice grew uncertain. "Keeper, are you there?"

Above the far end of the Valley, above the mountains, something was rising. Not a cloud. Not mist. Not smoke. Something grey, even, flat, colourless, like a wall. It did not move, and it moved. It did not grow, and it became larger. It was like looking at a sheet of paper from which the writing has been wiped away; not white, not clean, but precisely wiped. Empty where something had been.

And where it touched the earth, the farthest edge of the Valley, the farthest meadows, the farthest groves, the green... did not go out. Did not turn yellow. Did not die. It simply ceased to be green. Became the same grey. Even. Colourless. As if it had forgotten what colour it had been.

"Keeper!" Mella was not laughing now. "What is it?!"

"Run home, Mella," I said. My voice sounded as if from far away. "Tell your father. Tell everyone. Let them come to the Tower. All of them. Now."

"What has happened?"

"The Greyness," I said.

Mella froze below, at the door. Then the basket fell from her hands. Apples rolled down the path. She looked up at me, and her face was white as her apron.

And then she turned and ran down. Not home. To Bran.

* * *
They came to the Tower by noon. All of them. The whole Valley. Millers and beekeepers, shepherds and smiths, old and young, stood at the foot of the crag, on the slope, on the path, on the rocks, hundreds and hundreds, looking up. At me. In the window of the seventh tier.

And behind them, from the far end of the Valley, slowly, inexorably, crept the Greyness.

It had already eaten the far meadows. The far groves. The mill on the far bend; I saw its wheel, still turning that morning, stop when the Greyness touched it. It did not break; it stopped. As though it had forgotten that it was meant to turn. I saw the sheep on the far slope, white, fluffy, turn grey and freeze. They did not fall. They did not die. They simply stood. Not knowing that they were sheep.

Old Bran climbed the stairs of the Tower, slowly, step by step, three hundred and thirty-three steps, leaning on his staff, resting on every tier. Kai followed him, ready to catch him. Ivo came after, with his small chest of bark in his arms.

When they reached the seventh tier, Bran could not catch his breath for a long time. Then he went to the window. Looked at the Valley. At the Greyness devouring it from the edge.

"It is time," he said.

One word. Quietly. As though speaking of the weather.

* * *
"I cannot," I said.

Bran turned to me.

"I cannot, Bran." My hands were shaking. "There are people down there. Mella is there. The smith Odo is there, who has not managed in twenty years to give Iva a bouquet. Old Gwen with her sheep. Your house, Bran. Ivo was born there, or found there, no matter. Everything is there." My voice broke. "You want me to burn it all?"

"The people will leave," said Bran calmly. "Behind the Tower. Over the pass. Into the mountains. There are caves there. They can wait it out. The fire will not reach the caves."

"And the Valley?"

"And the Valley will burn," said Bran. "All of it. From edge to edge. Meadows. Groves. Houses. Mills. Gardens." He paused. "Otherwise the Greyness will eat it. And then it will not burn. It will simply forget itself. Forever. It will stand grey, even, empty. And the people who come back from the caves and walk down into it will forget too. One by one."

"How do you know?"

"The song knows," said Bran.

"The song is a thousand years old! Perhaps it lies!"

Bran looked at me with a long, sorrowful gaze.

"Perhaps," he said. "Perhaps it does lie. Then you will have burned the Valley for nothing." He paused. "And if it does not lie, and you do not burn it?"

I did not answer.

Ivo stood by the wall, hugging a small chest of bark to his chest. He looked at me with enormous dark eyes. The ink stain on his cheek.

"Keeper," he said quietly. "I have written it all down. All three chests. All of how it was. Every flower. Every song. Every house." He paused. "If you burn it, I will carry the bark to the caves. And when the grass grows, I will read it to the grass. So that it remembers."

"And if it does not remember?"

"Then I will read it again," said Ivo. "And again. Every evening. Until it remembers."

* * *
He came when the Greyness was already in the middle of the Valley.

I stood by the bowl on the topmost platform of the Tower, with a torch in my hand that Kai had lit from Bran's hearth and brought up to me. I stood and could not. The torch crackled. The wind tore at the flame. Below, on the slope, the people of the Valley were moving off behind the Tower, toward the pass, in a long, slow file, with bundles, with children in their arms, with goats on ropes, and looking back. Each one looked back. Looked up. At me.

Mella went last. She did not look back. She walked with her head lowered, pressing something to her chest, I could not see what. And at a bend of the path she stopped, raised her face, and called out. For the last time.

"Keeper! What can you see?"

And I could not answer.

And behind me someone said:

"I can see that you are afraid."

I turned.

On the topmost platform of the Tower, by the very parapet, stood a man. Tall. A head taller than I. In a grey cloak; no, not a cloak; he was grey all through, as if moulded from the same Greyness that crept across the Valley, only denser. I could not see his face. Where a face should be there was something blurred, elusive, like a face in a misted mirror.

Kai would not have let him in. Kai stood at the door, I knew it, and would have let no one pass. But he was here.

"Are you the Greyness?" I asked.

"No," he said. His voice was calm, quiet, older than mine. And, somehow, familiar. "I am the one who comes to Keepers when they are afraid. I came to the one before you. And to the one before him. I always come."

"Why?"

"To ask," he said. "Will you light it?"

"And do you want me to?"

He paused. Below, the Greyness ate another grove. The birch one. Light. Ringing. It stopped ringing.

"I do not want it," he said. "And I do not not want it. I cannot want for you. It is your Tower. Your Valley. Your fire." A pause. "I came only to say: you are not the first. Every one who stood here with a torch was afraid. Every one thought the song lied. Every one thought there might be another way."

"And is there?"

"I do not know," he said. "Perhaps there is. I have not found it." A pause. "But I am looking."

"What became of those who lit it?"

"They went," said the Grey One. "To where Keepers go." He paused. "And what became of those who did not light it, I do not know. Because after them no one came to the Tower. Because there was no one left to come. Because the Valley forgot that it had a Tower."

I looked at him. At his blurred, elusive face. And suddenly it seemed to me, for a single moment, in the glare of the torch, that I knew him. Not his features. Something else. The way he stood. As if on a threshold. One foot here, the other somewhere else.

"Who are you?" I asked.

He did not answer. He was looking down, at Mella, standing at the bend of the path with her face upturned.

"She is waiting for an answer," he said. "'What can you see.' Answer her."

* * *
I turned to the bowl.

Bronze, enormous, green with age, on three dragon's claws. The dry, resinous firewood laid in a lattice. For a thousand years no one had touched it. For a thousand years it had waited.

I looked at the Valley. For the last time.

The meadows, still green at the near edge, in blue bellflowers, in yellow buttercups. The river, transparent, with pebbles on its bed. Mella's father's mill, the wheel still turning. The round houses in the hills, smoke still rising from the chimneys. The gardens. The apiaries. The apple trees, heavy with red fruit. The road to old Gwen's house. Odo's forge. Iva's apiary. Bran's house under the forget-me-nots.

And beyond it, the Greyness. Even. Colourless. Empty. Creeping.

"Mella!" I shouted down. My voice broke. "I can see everything! I can see the whole Valley! Every flower! Every house! Every window!" I gasped. "I can see how beautiful it is!"

Mella stood at the bend. Looked at me. And then, I saw it even from such a height, she smiled. And held up over her head what she had been pressing to her chest.
