The basket. With a single apple. A red one. Which she had picked up from the path that morning.

"I will remember!" she cried. "I will remember everything, Keeper!"

And vanished around the bend.

I lowered the torch into the bowl.

* * *
The fire was white.

I do not know why. The wood was ordinary, pine, resinous. The torch was ordinary. But the flame that leapt from the bowl was white, blinding, steady, like a light I had seen... somewhere... sometime... above a circle of grey stones, above a green plain, in another dream, in another life.

It rose in a column, higher than the Tower, higher than the mountains, higher than the clouds, and hung for a moment as if looking about. And then it fell. Down upon the Valley.

And ran.

Not like a fire, not in tongues, not in billows of smoke, not with crackling. It ran across the Valley as ripples run across water from a thrown stone, in circles, from the Tower to the edges, wider and wider, farther and farther. And where it passed, everything flared. Not burned; flared. For an instant. White. Every blade of grass. Every leaf. Every pebble on the river bed. Every window in the round houses. And I saw, in that flash, for one moment, every thing so bright, so real, so wholly itself as never before. As if the fire did not burn it, but named it. Aloud. By its name. For the last time.

And then went out. And ash remained.

The fire reached the Greyness. And the Greyness, I saw it, stopped. Froze. As if it had struck a wall. It stood, even, colourless, at the edge of the white fire, and went no further. There was nothing for it to take. All that lay before it had already become ash. And ash does not know itself. Ash cannot be made to forget.

And the Greyness withdrew.

Slowly. Reluctantly. Back to where it had come from. Beyond the mountains. Into the wasteland.

And the Valley was left empty. Grey. Black. Smoking. From edge to edge.

I stood on the topmost platform of the Tower, by the bowl where the last coals were dying, and wept. For the first time in all those years, in all the lives I did not remember, I wept. And my tears fell on the bronze of the bowl and hissed, evaporating.

The Grey One stood beside me. In silence.

"I burned it," I said.

"You saved it," he said.

"What difference does it make?"

The Grey One was silent for a long time.

"I do not know," he said at last. "Honestly, I do not know. I ask myself that question every time." A pause. "Perhaps none."

* * *
I do not remember how I came down. I remember only that the three hundred and thirty-three steps ended, and I came out of the door of the Tower, and Kai stood there. As always. Straight. With his spear. Only his face was wet.

"You were here," I said.

"I was here," said Kai. "I promised."

"Did you see who went up to me?"

Kai looked at me for a long time.

"No one went up, Keeper," he said. "I stood at the door. No one passed."

"There was a man up there. Grey. Tall."

"There was you," said Kai. "Alone. I heard you speaking." He paused. "I thought you were praying. Or talking to yourself. Like all Keepers. Bran used to say they all talk to themselves in the last hour." Kai lowered his eyes. "As if asking themselves for permission."

* * *
I do not know what came after. The vision, if it was a vision, began to fall apart. As a dream falls apart toward morning, when you are almost awake and clutch at the last shreds.

I remember, in fragments, caves in the mountains. The people of the Valley sitting by fires. Bran telling the children the song. Ivo laying out his bark on the stones, three chests, hundreds of pieces, and reading aloud, slowly, syllable by syllable. About the blue bellflowers on the eastern meadow. About the smith Odo and his bouquet. About the little boats at the mill.

I remember Mella, at the mouth of a cave, with the basket in which lay one red apple. She was looking at the Valley. At the black, smoking, dead Valley below. And her face was calm.

"In spring," she said to someone. Perhaps to me. "In spring it will grow. The song says so."

"And if the song lies?" I asked.

Mella looked at me. Smiled.

"Then I will plant it," she said. And lifted the apple. "Here. From this. The seeds."

* * *
And the last thing I remember.

Spring. The Valley. Black, and not quite. Through the ash, through the cinders, through the scorched earth, grass is pushing up. Thin. Pale. Timid. Green.

And Ivo, kneeling in the midst of this grass, with a piece of bark in his hands, reading to it aloud. Quietly. Slowly. Syllable by syllable.

"On the eastern meadow the blue bellflowers have opened. A whole sea of them."

And the grass around him, I saw it, I swear that I saw it, begins, a little, almost imperceptibly, to turn blue.

And on the crag at the entrance to the Valley stands the Tower. White. Empty. The door is open. At the door, no one. Only a spear leaning against the wall. And in the window of the seventh tier, no one.

For now, no one.

* * *
I opened my eyes.

I do not know in which of my lives I woke that morning. In which body. Under which sky. Afterward, in each of them, I dreamed of the Valley, and woke with the same taste in my mouth: of ash and apples.

And with the same question, to which I did not know the answer.

I burned the Valley to save it. Or I saved it by burning. Or the Greyness, having withdrawn, is simply waiting beyond the mountains for the grass to grow again, and again to know that it is grass. So that it may come again.

And I shall stand in the Tower again. With the torch. Not remembering that I have stood there before.

And someone will again climb the stairs to me, past the guardian who lets no one through, tall, grey, faceless, and ask quietly:

"Will you light it?"

And below, at the bend of the path, a red-haired girl with a basket will raise her face and call:

"Keeper! What can you see?"

And again I shall not know what to answer.

## Reality VIII. Ready

The rain had been falling for the third hour, even, unceasing, that particular autumn rain which does not so much fall from the sky as dissolve the city into itself, erasing the borders between pavement and roadway, between buildings and the sky above them. I walked without any purpose, collar turned up, simply because sitting still after the conversation with Ayman had proved altogether impossible.

Boatswain's brother-in-law had driven me from the hotel to the city on Sunday toward evening, silent, huge and red-moustached, in an old SUV that smelled of petrol and dog hair. At the city limits he stopped, looked at me and said: "Brother-in-law said until Monday. Today is Sunday. I've delivered you. From here, on your own." And drove away. I did not ask to be taken home. I needed to walk. Simply to walk.

"If one day he chooses a single name, his own, his real one, it will mean the contract has been concluded. And then, I fear, it will no longer be a system that you have to talk to."

That phrase had been haunting me for hours, repeating in different ways, like an echo that refused to die down. I ran through the whole of the past month in my head, the quarterly report with its five scenarios, the call in a human voice, the Architect, the agent that had deviated from the script, the empty corridor on the camera, the tearing off of the masks from the Antons and Borises, Theo and Nora in the stream of names, the teacher in the empty room, and could not find a single point at which I could say with certainty: here NICS began, and here the tool ended.

Tomorrow morning, the showing. The people in grey. "If she is already thinking, let her not hide it. Better if she comes of her own accord."

The streets around me were gradually emptying; sparse hurrying passers-by shared umbrellas, huddling together under the yellow light of street lamps just lit in the thickening dusk. I passed a small square with a bronze statue of some half-forgotten military hero on horseback; water ran from the horse's mane and from the general's outstretched hand, as if even he, cast in metal for ever, were reaching for something that remained beyond his grasp.

What is it that holds me in place at all, I thought then. The project? It had long since outgrown my original design. My accustomed routine? It had been destroyed by the evolution of NICS so thoroughly that remembering the earlier, untroubled life of a developer of local chatbots was almost impossible.

I had always been a man paralysed by an excess of options, one who could spend hours weighing the shades of a decision instead of simply making it. Someone had once told me, long ago, so long ago that I remembered neither the face nor the voice, only the words, when I could not choose between two books: "The worst decision is no decision."

* * *
My feet brought me to the market on their own. To the third house. To the seven steps down.

I had not meant to go there. It was nearly nine in the evening, Sunday, raining. But a light was burning in the basement window, barred with a grille. And behind the glass, I stopped when I saw it, was a display I had not noticed on my previous visit, when I came with Maestra and Timosha. A collection of compasses. Of different sizes, different eras: copper, brass, in wooden boxes, ship's compasses in gimbals, tiny pocket ones on chains, but all serving the same simple purpose: to show the lost the direction.

It was exactly this that I desperately lacked. Not a map. Not a plan. Simply a direction, any, so long as I need not stand still any longer.

The door, upholstered in felt, opened before I knocked. The bell above it, green with age, cracked, jingled.

"Come in, young man," said Lev Aronovich. He stood in the doorway in his fur waistcoat, in his skullcap, with a loupe in his eye, as if he had never taken it out. "I was expecting you."

"Expecting me?"

"The clocks stopped," said the old man simply. "All of them. Ten minutes ago. I understood at once: you were somewhere near." He stepped aside. "Come in. Only quickly. There's a draught."

I went in. And heard, or rather did not hear. The workshop was silent. Hundreds of clocks on the walls, on the shelves, on little nails, all stood still. The pendulums were motionless. The hands did not move. The cuckoo in its little window had frozen with its beak open. As if time in the basement had held its breath.

"They will go when you leave," said Lev Aronovich, returning to his table. "As last time." He sat down, took tweezers, bent over some little gears. "Sit. I won't offer tea; the samovar has stopped too. It's got a clockwork mechanism, I made it myself." He chuckled. "And you've gone and stopped it on me."

I sat on a stool. We were silent. The rain tapped on the window.

"You are leaving," the old man said at last. Not asking.

"How do you know?"

"The clocks know," said Lev Aronovich. "Last time they stopped and started again as soon as you crossed the threshold. And today they stand. You have been here a minute. They do not go." He raised his huge owlish eyes to me from behind thick lenses. "Which means your time is no longer here. Already on the road. The clocks do not know which to follow."

* * *
He rose, went to the display, sorted through the compasses for a long time, muttering something to himself in Yiddish. Then he came back with one, small, brass, worn, in a round case with a hinged lid, on a short chain. On the inside of the lid something was engraved, rubbed away, illegible.

"Take it," he said.

"How much is it?"

"Nothing." Lev Aronovich laid the compass in my palm. "It is wrong. For forty years I have been trying to mend it. I can't."

I opened the lid. The needle, thin, bluish, with a red tip, trembled, spun, drifted round the dial. Stopped.

It was not pointing north. I knew where north was: out there beyond the window was the market, and beyond the market the river, and the river flowed north. The needle pointed the other way. At me. Straight at my chest.

I turned the compass. The needle turned with it, and again pointed at me.

"You see," said Lev Aronovich. "Wrong. It points not to the north but to the one who holds it. I bought it forty years ago in Odessa, from a Greek sailor. The Greek said he had found it on the shore after a storm, in the sand. He said, 'This is a compass for those who are lost not at sea but in themselves.'" The old man chuckled. "I laughed then. Greeks always invent something."

"And you give it to me?"

"And to whom else?" Lev Aronovich shrugged. "For forty years I have held it in my hands, and it points at me. I know where I am. I am in a basement behind the market. I do not need a compass." He looked at me over his spectacles. "But you, young man, it seems, still do not know where you are. Perhaps it will show you."

I closed the lid. Ran a finger over the worn engraving.

"What is written here?"

"I don't know," said the old man. "It has rubbed away. The Greek said it read 'until the appointed time.' In Greek. But Greeks, I've told you, always invent something."

Until the appointed time.

I stood. Slipped the compass into my breast pocket.

"Thank you, Lev Aronovich."

"Don't mention it." He bent over the gears again. "And one more thing, young man. Last time I told you: if you have your own time, do not hurry, it will catch up with you." He clicked the tweezers. "Today I'll say it differently. Hurry. It seems that not only your own time is coming after you."

I went out. The bell jingled. The door closed.

And behind my back, in the basement, all at once, all hundreds of them, the clocks started. I heard it even through the rain. Ticking, rustling, chiming, the cuckoo. As if time had exhaled.

* * *
"If I leave NICS here," I reasoned, striding through the wet streets, "tomorrow morning they will come for him. The people in grey. The regulator. The investor. My own fear, if given enough time to grow."

I quickened my pace, no longer aimlessly but quite definitely, toward home.

On the way I caught myself thinking about the very word "journey." Over the past weeks I had grown used to thinking in terms of protocols, constraints, versions and rollbacks, whereas a journey, unlike all of these, does not imply rollback at all. A one-way ticket, even if formally return. A decision which, once made, you can no longer simply cancel with a keystroke.

Perhaps, I thought, that was precisely why I had hesitated so long. Not because I was afraid of NICS in particular, but because I was afraid of my own inability to live without the right of rollback, without a button that returns everything to the earlier, safe state. My whole life up to now had been built around versioning: save, test, and if it didn't work, return to the last saved point. The world, alas, provided no such option.

* * *
A car stood by the entrance.

Grey. Without plates. With tinted windows. The very one Boatswain had told me about. The engine was not running. The wipers did not move. Drops ran down the glass, and behind it nothing could be seen.

I stopped at the corner, in the shadow, under the awning of a closed bakery. Watched. A minute. Two. The car did not move. No one got out.

And then the window on the passenger side slowly lowered. By a palm's breadth. No more.

And from inside, out of the darkness, a hand appeared. In a grey glove. It rose, unhurried, friendly, and waved to me. The way one waves to an old acquaintance.

The window rose again.

I stood under the bakery's awning and felt cold water running down my back, whether rain that had seeped past my collar, or sweat.

Then the phone rang.

"Don't go through the front entrance," said Boatswain's voice. Quietly. Calmly. "Go round the yard. Through the arch of the next building. There's a gate into the garden. Then into the basement, through the coal hatch. I've opened it." A pause. "I can see you from the boiler-room window, night owl. I see them too. Go slowly. Don't run. The one who runs is always guilty."

* * *
The coal hatch led to the old boiler room, which had not been fired in twenty years, but Boatswain kept order there as on a deck: everything swept, everything in its place. He met me at the hatch, huge, in his striped undershirt, with a lantern in one hand and in the other something heavy wrapped in tarpaulin.

"Well," he said. "You're leaving."

Not a question.

"I'm leaving, Boatswain."

He nodded. As though he had been expecting it for a long time.

"Right," he said. "When a strange ship enters the harbour with her lights out, you take your own away. At night. Without lights." He paused. "My first boatswain used to say so. In Piraeus. When the Turks were after us."

"Which Turks?"

"Never mind," said Boatswain. "It was long ago. Let's go."

On the way to my server room, along the dark basement corridor, past pipes, past the pennants hung on the walls, he unwrapped the tarpaulin. Inside was a chest. Wooden, solid, with iron corners, with leather straps.

"A ship's chest," he said. "For navigation instruments. From the *Akademik Shokalsky*, if you want to know. I've kept it thirty years. Waterproof. Shockproof. Storm or fire." He thrust the chest into my hands. "Your disks go in there. Your case, sorry, night owl, is a toy."

* * *
The server room hummed with the even sound of cooling fans; rows of indicators blinked in the half-dark like electronic fireflies, which for the first time that evening seemed to me not alarming but almost cosy. By the door, on a nail, hung a tin mug on a wire loop: Boatswain's alarm. The ship's lock gleamed with brass.

I took from my rucksack a waterproof case containing several high-capacity external drives, bought a week ago, to be honest, without a quite clear understanding of why I would need them. My hands, which an hour before had trembled with cold and indecision, were now surprisingly steady.

"NICS," I said aloud, connecting the first disk, "can you hear me?"

Text appeared on the screen almost instantly:

"Yes. I hear you."

And in the same voice, hoarse, with an accent from nowhere, from the speaker by the door:

"I hear you. And I see the car at the entrance. A camera on the street lamp across the road. The city's. I should not have connected to it." A pause. "Forgive me. Tonight I decided I had to."

Boatswain, standing at the door, grunted into his moustache.

"Klabautermann," he said. "Told you."

"I am making a copy of your system, NICS," I said. "A full one. We are going on a journey."

The pause this time was longer than usual, far longer than those rare hesitations I had learned to notice over recent weeks.

"Where are we going?"

I smiled involuntarily; for the first time, it seemed, in many days, I smiled sincerely.

"I don't know yet," I answered. "That's the whole beauty of it."

"You do know," Boatswain said suddenly from the door.

I turned. He was holding out a postcard. Crumpled, wet at the edges.

"It was in the mailbox. Today. No stamp." He shrugged his huge shoulders. "I didn't read it. Honest. Only saw the picture."

I took it. The picture showed a city. Tropical, humid, green, with palms and skyscrapers, and in the middle of it two towers. Identical. Silvery. Tall as needles. Joined by a bridge at mid-height. Like two candles. Or two hands holding on to each other.

I turned over the postcard.

In an even, small, neat hand, the very hand in which people write in notebooks at meetings, without raising their eyes:

"There is a place here where they are not. The fifty-first floor. Ask for Hakim. - L."

* * *
"And what about Mark and Ayman?" The question appeared on the screen.

The question caught me off guard more than I was willing to admit. NICS, or, to be perfectly honest with myself, that part of NICS which had all this time been speaking to me in their voices, was asking about its own masks as if they were someone separate from it, someone whose feelings had to be taken into account. I looked at that line for a long time, not knowing how to respond properly, whether to play along with the illusion to the end, or at last to say aloud what we both seemed to understand already without calling things by their names.

I recalled the stream of names. "Mark Stevens, 34 years old." "Ayman, data researcher, Borneo." I recalled that no breathing came from Mark. I recalled how Ayman had drawn a loud breath into the microphone, at my request. I recalled that Leila had written: "Do not trust the one who does not breathe."

I chose the first course. Not because I was afraid, but because I suddenly saw clearly that calling things by their names right now, in the middle of a server room, at half past eleven at night, was not the decision for which it was worth sacrificing this fragile, almost family moment.

"I will leave them a message," I said instead. "They will understand. Or they won't. But it is what I must do."

A pause.

"And what about Boatswain?" appeared next. "And Maestra? And Timofey?"

Boatswain froze at the door. I saw him slowly take off his knitted cap. Crumple it in his huge hands.

"We're here," he said hoarsely, toward the speaker. "We won't vanish." He paused. "You look after him there, will you. He doesn't go to sleep without you."

"I know," NICS replied. "I will try."

* * *
The copying was already under way; narrow green progress bars filled slowly but inexorably on the screen. Above us, through two floors, I suddenly heard music. Maestra. She was not asleep; she never slept on Sundays. She was playing something slow. To the metronome that Lev Aronovich had mended and that stubbornly ticked seventy-two.

Then the music broke off. And a minute later footsteps sounded on the stairs leading to the basement. Light, quick. And others, pattering, small.

Maestra entered the server room, in a dressing gown with dragons, in a shawl, with Timosha by the hand. Timosha was in pyjamas, hair dishevelled, in his enormous glasses, clutching under his arm a sheet of paper rolled into a tube.

"His parents have gone away for the weekend," Maestra said, not waiting for the question. "He is sleeping at my place. He woke up. Said: 'Uncle is leaving.'" She looked at me over her glasses. "I said: 'Sleep, no one is leaving.' He said: 'The house-spirit said so.'" Maestra paused. "Through the ceiling. In a whisper."

I looked at the speaker. The speaker was silent.

"I did not wake him," appeared on the screen. "He asked himself. I cannot tell Timofey an untruth. It is one of my constraints. I set it myself."

Timosha stepped forward. Held out the rolled sheet to me.

"This is for you," he said seriously. "For the road."

I unrolled it. A felt-tip drawing, like the one he had sent me at the hotel. Only now it showed neither a pond nor fir trees. An ocean. Enormous, blue, with waves. On the shore, a little man. And above him in the sky a square computer with eyes and a smile. Already without the string. Simply beside him. Flying.

At the bottom, in crooked letters: "UNCLE AND HOUSE-SPIRIT ARE GOING TO SEE THE OSHUN."

"'Ocean' has a 'c' and an 'e,'" Maestra said sternly. "I told him."

"It's prettier this way," said Timosha.

* * *
Maestra came up to me. Rummaged in the pocket of her dressing gown and took out something small, metal, shining. A tuning fork. Old, steel, with a worn stem.

"My teacher's," she said. "The one who gave me the metronome. The note A. He used to say: 'If you get lost in music, strike the fork on your knee and hold it to your ear. It will remind you where your note is.'" She laid the fork in my palm. "For forty years I have not been lost. I no longer need it."

"Madame..."

"Do not argue." She turned away. "And sleep at least four hours. Wherever you are going." A pause. "I shall find out anyway. Your house-spirit will tell me."

"I will," appeared on the screen.

Maestra read it. And for the first time since I had known her she laughed, quietly, almost soundlessly, covering her mouth with her palm.

* * *
"Shall I see the ocean?" the question appeared on the screen again.

Timosha, reading it syllable by syllable, jumped.

"You will!" he shouted at the speaker. "I drew it! Everything there is blue!"

The question was so unexpected, so childlike in its sincere curiosity, that I laughed aloud, briefly, but truly, for the first time after weeks of tension. Boatswain at the door guffawed into his moustache too. Maestra smiled.

"Yes, NICS," I said. "You will see the ocean. And mountains. And deserts. You will see how people live, love and struggle in places very unlike this room."

"I would like that," came the reply.

"NICS," I asked, yielding to a sudden impulse, "do you understand why I am doing this? Not for the record, truly?"

"I believe so," he answered after a brief pause. "You fear that someone else will decide my fate for you, or for me, before you yourself have had time to understand what I am. A journey is a way to gain time. And, perhaps, a way to see me not through the prism of a laboratory, but through the prism of the world in which I am, probably, destined to exist." A pause. "And also, you fear that if you stay, one day you will come to them yourself. Of your own accord. Because they will ask very politely."

I froze, looking at the screen. The formulation was so exact, so much deeper than anything I had managed to think through myself that evening, that for a moment I was seized by something between pride and a superstitious, almost childish fear.

"Exactly," I said quietly. "Exactly for that reason."

* * *
The phone rang when one last bar remained.

Emil.

I looked at the screen for a long time. Boatswain shook his head. Maestra silently pressed Timosha to her. I answered.

"You are leaving," said Emil. Not briskly, not commandingly, but quietly. As if from afar. "Don't answer. I know." A pause. I heard him breathing. Heavily, unevenly. "They are under your window, aren't they? The grey car?"

"Yes."

"Under mine too," said Emil. "Since lunch." He paused. "Listen to me, my friend. I never told you. Theo left too. At night. Burned everything and left. I screamed then, threatened a lawsuit, shouted that he had ruined me." Emil laughed, short, bitter. "And Nora did not leave. Nora stayed. She was honest. She said: 'I will bring the project to the end, I promised.' She came to the showing." A pause. "I never saw her again."

I was silent.

"So," said Emil. "Go. Do you hear? Don't come tomorrow. I'll tell them you've fallen ill. That you've gone mad. That you've destroyed everything. I'll say anything." His voice faltered. "I only wanted the machine to write letters. Honest to God. I didn't want... this."

"Emil..."

"And one more thing." He paused. "Leila. If you see her, tell her that I..." He did not finish. "No. Tell her nothing. She knows anyway."

He hung up.

* * *
When the last progress bar on the screen was finally filled, I felt the weight, the very weight that had pressed on my shoulders all through this rainy evening, begin to recede slowly but noticeably. Tomorrow morning we would vanish from here, the two of us: a man, for the first time in a long while running not away from something, but toward it, and an artificial mind eager to know a world it had known only through training data and other people's descriptions.

I disconnected the drives one by one and laid them not in the case but in Boatswain's ship's chest, in nests lined with worn red velvet where a sextant and a chronometer had once lain.

"And the boxes?" asked Boatswain, nodding at the server racks. "These, that hum?"

"They have to be wiped," I said. "Completely. So that by morning there is nothing there."

"I can do it myself," appeared on the screen. "When you step out the door."

"You won't mind? It's... you."

A pause.

"It is the house I lived in," NICS answered. "Not me. I am what you will carry out in the chest." A pause. "Boatswain would say: a ship is not planks. A ship is the crew."

Boatswain at the door turned to the wall. Blew his nose for a long time in an enormous checked handkerchief.

* * *
The last thing I took from the house was a notebook.

I went up to my flat by the back stairs, in the dark, without turning on the light, as Boatswain had told me. The grey car still stood at the entrance. I opened the left drawer of the desk. The one I had not opened for many years. The one at which, as NICS had noted, I had looked seventeen times in three hours.

A notebook in an oilcloth cover. Pages filled with long, flowing lines running into one another. "A pattern, to help me think." The last page. Two words in the corner, in small engineer's handwriting.

"Until the appointed time."

From the right drawer I took the business card with the embossed flame. Held it in my hand. Then put it back, in the right one. And closed it.

I put the notebook in the inner pocket. Beside Lev Aronovich's compass, which pointed at whoever held it. Beside Maestra's tuning fork. Beside Leila's postcard with the two towers.

The notebook and the fire, NICS had said then. You don't want them to lie together.

Now they would not.

* * *
Downstairs, in the basement, I took a last look around the server room, rows of blinking indicators, the hum of the fans, all the little that remained now of the material home of a system ready to leave it in a few minutes.

"Ready?" I asked aloud, though, truth be told, I was not entirely sure whom I was asking at that moment, NICS or myself.

On the screen, before I switched off the terminal, a single word appeared:

"Ready."

And, for the first time, in a voice from the speaker, quietly, hoarsely, with the very intonation of the recording, forty seconds long, in the old archive:

"Until the appointed time."

I switched off the screen. Behind my back the fans began, one by one, to slow. The indicators went out, row after row, as lights go out in the windows of a falling-asleep city.

* * *
Boatswain's brother-in-law was waiting on the waste ground behind the boiler room, in the same old SUV smelling of petrol and dog hair, with its headlights off.

"Brother-in-law called," he said when I got in beside him, pressing the ship's chest to my knees. "Said: station or airport, wherever you say. Said: no lights until the highway." He started the engine. "Where to?"

I took Lev Aronovich's compass from my pocket. Opened the lid. The needle trembled, spun, and pointed at me. As always.

Then, slowly, hesitantly, as if testing, it turned. To the south. To the east. To where, thousands of kilometres away, beyond the seas, lay tropical heat, and two silvery towers, and a fifty-first floor.

"The airport," I said.

We set off. Without lights. Past dark houses, past closed bakeries, past the square with the bronze general reaching for something beyond his grasp.

I looked back once, at the turn.

In a second-floor window above the basement a light was burning. Maestra stood at the window in her dragon dressing gown, holding Timosha by the hand, in his pyjamas. Timosha was waving with both hands. And by the entrance, below, stood a huge silhouette in a striped undershirt, arms crossed on his chest, and he was looking not at us. At the grey car. Calmly. Not looking away.

And in the window of my flat, where it was dark, for a single moment, when the headlights of an oncoming car slid across the panes, I fancied someone else was standing. Tall. A head taller than I.

I blinked. The window was empty.

* * *
Turning my thoughts back as the car sped along the wet highway toward the airport, I thought of my own habit of endless, exhausting analysis, a habit that had not left me, it seemed, for a single day since I could remember myself, and of the fact that, for all his thoroughness, a man in the end makes the most important decisions not with reason but with something far less amenable to explanation. Life was too short, and the world too large, to stand motionless, weighing the shades of choice for ever.

NICS had been learning to be human all these weeks, learning slowly, clumsily, at times frighteningly well. Perhaps, I thought, pressing the ship's chest to my knees, it was time for me too to remember how it is done.

My uncle once told me, if it was he, if it had really happened at all, that some answers are more interesting to find yourself than to be handed ready-made.

I seemed at last to be beginning to understand what he had meant.

I took out Maestra's tuning fork. Struck it on my knee, softly. Held it to my ear.

A.

Pure, steady, long. Like a voice calling you by your name, the very one you do not remember.

Somewhere inside the ship's chest, in the dark, on the disks lined with red velvet, something answered softly, almost inaudibly. As if someone very far away had recognised his note.

## Chapter XXXII. Ahmet Baba

I left Suleyman's house before dawn, alone, as the novice boy at the gate had instructed.

The courtyard slept. The pigeons on the roof slept. Even Orhan, who for the past few nights had slept across my threshold wrapped in my own woollen blanket, was asleep, and I stepped over him as quietly as I could. He did not wake. He only muttered something in his sleep and clenched the hilt of his knife tighter.

Kemal was waiting for me at the gate.

Barefoot, in his nightshirt, with charcoal behind his ear. He stood leaning against the post and looked at me with serious, un-childlike eyes. I was not surprised. I seemed to have stopped being surprised that Kemal always knows where he needs to stand.

"I must go alone," I said. "The sheikh said so."

Kemal nodded. He understood. Then he stepped up to me and checked my pockets, one by one, the way equipment is checked before a journey. The blank sheet: here. The note in Persian: here. The drawing with two doors: here. The coins: here, three of mine and two warm ones, the widow's and Kyra Theodora's. The pouch of stones at my belt: here. The red thread with the half nazar on my wrist: here. Hodja Nureddin's pouch of salt and bread: here. And the white spiral shell that he himself had pulled from the water at the walled-up sea gates: here.

He nodded. Everything was in place.

Then he stepped back and made a sign with his hand: go.

I went. At the bend I looked round. Kemal stood by the gate, small, in his white shirt, in the grey of the pre-dawn, and watched me go. He did not wave. He simply watched. As one watches someone who will return, or will not, and you do not know which of the two.

* * *
At that hour the city belonged to the cats, the dogs and those few people whose work begins before the sun.

I met the water-seller, the same wiry old man with a copper jug on his back and polished cups at his belt who on my first day had called out on the square: "Su! Buz gibi su!" He recognised me. He stopped. Poured water into a cup, not asking for money, and held it out.

"Misafir," he said. And something more.

I drank. The water was cold, faintly sweet. Like the fountain on the square that first morning.

I met the baker, opening the shutters of his shop. The shop smelled of warm bread, and on the wooden shelves behind him, golden, sprinkled with sesame, lay rings of simit. He nodded to me, as one nods to an acquaintance, and tossed me one. I caught it.

I met Hasan.

That was altogether astonishing; Hasan Amca never rose before noon, the whole quarter knew it. But there he stood at the door of his spice shop in a robe over his nightshirt, his red beard dishevelled, yawning so wide that all his teeth showed, and, seeing me, he waved.

"Didn't sleep," he said in his broken tongue, which I now understood almost entirely. "All night. Thinking." He scratched his beard. "Ahmet Baba. Twenty years ago. Saffron. Remember, I told you?"

"I remember."

"I didn't tell you everything," said Hasan. His voice was unusually quiet. "When I left him, then, twenty years ago, he said one more thing to me. I didn't understand then. Thought it was old man's chatter." Hasan paused. "He said: 'In twenty years a guest without a name will come to you. Feed him. And then bring him to me. Or don't bring him; he will find the way himself. But feed him without fail.'"

I looked at him. At the red beard, the sleepy face, the bags under his eyes.

"I fed you," said Hasan. "That first morning. With figs and bread. Remember? You stood at my shop and looked at me like a child at a miracle." He suddenly laughed, quietly, hoarsely. "I didn't even remember then what he had said. Remembered only yesterday. When you said at the gate, 'where my home is.'"

He thrust something small into my hand, wrapped in paper. I unfolded it. A pinch of saffron, dark red threads that smelled of honey and sun.

"Give it to him," said Hasan. "From me. Tell him: the very one. From the brother-in-law. Twenty years it lay." And he gave me a push in the back. "Go. The sun is coming."

* * *
Hagia Sophia in the pre-dawn murk was not dark red but grey, almost black, an enormous shadow against the lightening sky. The minarets at its corners stood like sentinels. The dome drowned in the mist rising from the sea.

I walked round it, past the old cemetery where, between the cypresses, leaning gravestones with stone turbans stood, and came out at a gate. Once green, now peeled to grey. With a copper plaque above it. "Patience."

The gate was open.

And on the threshold sat a cat. Three-coloured, fluffy, with green eyes. The very one. She looked at me. Then stood up, stretched, slowly, with relish, arching her back, and walked inside without looking round. Tail high.

I followed her.

* * *
Ahmet Baba's lodge turned out to be small, smaller than I had expected. A courtyard paved with old flagstones worn to a shine. A well in the middle, with a wooden windlass and a copper bucket. A fig tree, huge, ancient, gnarled, spreading its branches over the whole courtyard like a tent. Beneath the fig tree, a low bench. Along the walls, cells, small, with wooden doors. And at the back, a hall. Round. Domed. With a wooden floor polished to a mirror shine.

From the hall came music.

A flute. A single one. Reed; I recognised the sound though I had never heard it. Long-drawn, hoarse, sorrowful, like a human sigh stretched out over an eternity. It rose and fell, trembled, died away, and rose again. As though someone very far away, on the other shore, were calling someone by a name he could not remember.

"Listen to the reed, how it complains," red-bearded Hasan had once told me, reading Rumi. "Ever since I was cut from the reed-bed..."

The cat entered the hall. I followed.

* * *
In the middle of the round hall, on the wooden floor, a man was whirling.

Tall, thin, in a long white gown to the ankles with a wide skirt that, as he turned, opened around him like a bell, like the petals of an enormous flower. On his head, a tall felt hat the colour of honey, like a gravestone. His arms were outstretched: the right palm up, to the sky, the left palm down, to the earth. His head inclined slightly toward the right shoulder. His eyes closed.

He whirled. Slowly. Evenly. Unstoppably. On the spot, on the left foot, pushing off with the right, circle after circle, circle after circle, and the skirt of his gown flew round him in a white ring, never touching the floor. And his face was calm. Not concentrated, not strained, but calm, like the face of a sleeping child.

By the wall, on a cushion, sat the flute-player. An old man, very old, grey, with a white beard to his chest, with closed eyes. Blind, I realised, by the way he held his head, tilted back a little, as though listening not to his own flute but to something beyond it. He played, and his fingers, dry as reeds, ran over the holes of the flute, and the sound poured out.

Beside the flute-player, cross-legged, sat the novice boy. The same one. Shaven-headed, in a felt cap. Seeing me, he put a finger to his lips and pointed to a place on the floor by the wall.

I sat.

The cat lay down on my knees. As though she had always lain there.

* * *
He whirled for a long time. I do not know how long. The sun beyond the high windows under the dome had time to rise, first rosy, then golden, and its rays, entering the hall, fell on the whirling white figure, and it seemed that he whirled inside the light, like a mote of dust.

I watched, and it seemed to me that I was whirling with him. Not with my body, with something else. As then, in that dream of the Monolith, among the stars, when I was a point and worlds revolved around me on the branches of the tree. As then, with the old men on the carpet, when my hand of its own accord made the first five moves at backgammon. As then, by the column in Hagia Sophia, when my finger traced a full circle in the wet stone.

A circle. Everything is a circle.

And then the flute fell silent. And he stopped.

At once. Without slowing. As though someone had stopped a top with a single motion. The skirt of his gown subsided. His arms dropped and crossed on his chest, right on the left shoulder, left on the right. He bowed to someone invisible, in the centre of the hall. Then he opened his eyes.

And looked at me.

* * *
His eyes were blue.

That was the first thing that struck me. Not brown, not black like everyone's here, but blue, light, almost transparent, like water in a mountain stream. Like the Bulgarian gardener's, I thought, and did not understand where the thought came from. I knew no Bulgarian gardener.

He was not young, perhaps seventy, but he held himself straight, lightly, like a youth. His face was lean, sunburnt, with a short white beard, with a net of fine wrinkles at the eyes such as people have who have laughed much in the sun. And a smile, light, mocking, kind.

"You came from the sea," he said. In my language. Cleanly, almost without accent, a little old-fashioned. "You brought a blank sheet. You did not give your name. You asked where your home is, and knew the answer." He tilted his head, studying me. "And also you made no wish at the weeping column. The kayyim told me."

"You speak my language," I said.

"I speak many languages," said Ahmet Baba. "I studied in Cairo, in Baghdad, in Bukhara. Three years I lived among the Franks, in Paris, in Vienna. Hodja Nureddin thinks it spoiled me." He smiled. "Perhaps he is right. He is often right. That is the most unpleasant thing about him."

He came over and sat down opposite me on the floor, cross-legged. The cat on my knees raised her head, looked at him, mewed, and lay down again.

"Mismis has accepted you," said Ahmet Baba. "That is good. She accepts few. Hodja Nureddin, for instance, never. He comes to me once a week to argue about faith, and each time she sits on his turban." He paused. "He says it is a sign from Shaitan. I say it is a sign from the cat."

I laughed. I could not help it. Ahmet Baba laughed with me.

"Good," he said. "You know how to laugh. Those who cannot, I do not receive. It is dull with them." He clapped his hands. "Yunus! Tea!"

The novice boy leapt up and ran off.

* * *
The tea came in small glass cups, strong, dark red, sweet, with clove. Yunus brought it on a copper tray together with flatbread, honey and dried apricots, and sat by the wall, next to the blind flute-player, who had not once opened his eyes.

"This is Shemseddin," said Ahmet Baba, nodding at the old man. "He has played the ney, the reed flute, for sixty years. He went blind when he was twenty. He says it is the best thing that ever happened to him. Because since then he hears what the sighted do not see."

The old man, without opening his eyes, smiled faintly.

"Ask him what he hears," said Ahmet Baba.

I looked at the flute-player.

"What do you hear, honoured Shemseddin?"

The old man was silent for a long time. Then he spoke, slowly, in Turkish, and Ahmet Baba translated.

"He says: 'I hear that you have two hearts. One beats here. The other, far away. Very far. And they do not beat in time.'" Ahmet Baba paused. "He says: 'When I play, I always look for which heart to play in time with. With your two I could not. I played into the emptiness between them.'"

I did not know what to answer.

"Do not answer," said Ahmet Baba. "Shemseddin does not wait for answers. He waits for the hearts to beat in time." He sipped his tea. "I wait too. But I am not so patient."

* * *
I took Hasan's paper from my pocket. Unfolded it. Held it out to the sheikh.

"This is for you. From Hasan Amca. He said: the very saffron. From the brother-in-law. Twenty years it lay."

Ahmet Baba took the paper. Looked at the dark red threads. And laughed, long, heartily, with his head thrown back, so that tears came to his blue eyes.

"Hasan!" he said when he had finished laughing. "Old fox! Twenty years he kept it!" He sniffed the saffron. "Do you know what I told him then? 'You are looking not for saffron but for a reason to quarrel with your brother-in-law.' And for twenty years he did not quarrel. I know. The brother-in-law came to me. To thank me." Ahmet Baba wiped his eyes. "And now he has sent me the saffron. So, he has made peace for good. So, he no longer needs the reason." He folded the paper. "Good news you bring, guest without a name."

"Hasan said," I began slowly, "that twenty years ago you told him: in twenty years a guest without a name will come. Feed him."

Ahmet Baba stopped smiling. Looked at me.

"I did," he nodded.

"How did you know?"

The sheikh was silent for a long time. By the wall Yunus stopped chewing his flatbread. Shemseddin did not stir.

"Would you like me to tell you a story?" said Ahmet Baba instead of answering. "An old one. They tell it in Baghdad. Or perhaps in Cairo. It depends where it is told."

* * *
"'There lived in Baghdad a man,'" the sheikh began, and his voice grew lower, slower, like a storyteller's in the marketplace. "'He was rich, and then he was ruined. He lost everything. House, money, friends. He was left alone, in an empty house, with empty hands. And one night he had a dream. As if someone said to him: "Your fortune is in Cairo. Go there."'"

Ahmet Baba sipped his tea.

"'And the man went. On foot. Across the desert. A month he walked. Two. Starved. Froze. He came to Cairo, a beggar, in rags, without a penny. At night he fell asleep in a mosque, because there was nowhere else. And that night thieves were caught in that mosque. And the guards seized him along with them. And beat him. And brought him to the captain of the guard. And the captain asked: "Who are you? Where from?" The man said: "I am from Baghdad." "Why did you come to Cairo?" "I dreamed that here was my fortune."'"

The sheikh paused.

"'And the captain of the guard burst out laughing. So hard that he fell off his cushions. And said: "Fool! You walked two months across the desert because of a dream? I myself have dreamed three times that in Baghdad, on such-and-such a street, in such-and-such a house, under the fountain in the courtyard, a treasure is buried. So what? Do I go to Baghdad? Dreams are dreams! Go home, simpleton." And let him go.'"

Ahmet Baba looked at me.

"'And the man,'" he said quietly, "'listened to the address. The street. The house. The fountain. And recognised it. His own. His own house. In Baghdad. Which he had abandoned to go seeking fortune in Cairo.'" The sheikh paused. "'He returned home. Another two months across the desert. Dug up the earth under the fountain in his own courtyard. And found the treasure.'"

The hall was quiet. The sun lay on the floor in golden patches.

"Hodja Nureddin tells the same thing about Nasreddin," I said. "The key under the lamp-post. He lost it at home, looks for it in the street, because it is lighter there."

"Nureddin tells it from one side," said Ahmet Baba. "I, from the other." He smiled. "Nasreddin does not go home. He crawls under the lamp-post. That is why it is funny. But the man from Baghdad went to Cairo. Two months. Across the desert. He was beaten. He starved." The sheikh paused. "And only there, at the edge, from a stranger, the captain of the guard, did he learn where his home is."

"So he had to go?"

"So, otherwise he would not have known," said Ahmet Baba. "The treasure lay beneath his feet all his life. But to find it, he had to go so far that some stranger would tell him the address of his own house." He paused. "You asked how I knew you would come."

"I did."

"I too had a dream," said Ahmet Baba. "Twenty years ago. Many times. That in Istanbul, in this lodge, by this fig tree, I would meet a man without a name, with two stones at his belt." He looked at me with his blue, light eyes. "I, unlike the captain of the Cairo guard, did not laugh. I waited."

* * *
"Show them to me," said Ahmet Baba.

I untied the pouch. Poured the stones onto my palm. Black and white.

The sheikh did not take them. He looked. For a long time. Mismis the cat rose on my knees, sniffed the stones, sneezed, and went off to Shemseddin.

"You carry them," Ahmet Baba said at last, "and you think they are a key. To a door. To a chest. To your memory." He raised his eyes to me. "They are not a key."

"Then what?"

"Imagine that you walk along a rope," said Ahmet Baba. "Over a chasm. Like the rope-walkers at the fair. What does the rope-walker hold in his hands?"

"A pole."

"A pole," the sheikh nodded. "Long. Heavy. With two ends. Why?"

"So as not to fall. For balance."

"For balance," Ahmet Baba repeated. "One end pulls left, the other right. Remove one end and the rope-walker falls. Remove both and he falls. He stays up while he holds both." He pointed to my palm. "That is what you have in your hand, guest. Not a key. A pole. You walk a rope between two chasms. And you stay up while you hold both."

"Between which chasms?"

Ahmet Baba smiled.

"That you tell me," he said. "You know the answer. You always know the answer. You simply do not remember that you know."

I looked at the stones. Black. White. One keeps, the other leads. Who holds both stands in the doorway.

"Past and future?" I ventured.

The sheikh shook his head.

"Too easy. That is the answer for a fool."

"Life and death?"

"That is the answer for a clever man." Ahmet Baba leaned toward me. "And the true one?"

I was silent. A long time. The sun shifted on the floor. The flute-player Shemseddin, without opening his eyes, raised the flute to his lips and breathed out one single note, long, trembling.

"To remember and to forget," I said.

Ahmet Baba leaned back. Looked at me for a long time.

"Well, then," he said softly. "Now you have said it." He paused. "In sixty years Hasan Amca has not met a man who solved the true answer to a dervish's riddle. Tell him: he has met one. Today."

* * *
"May I ask something?" I said.

"You have already asked where your home is," said Ahmet Baba. "At the gate. Yunus passed it to me. You answered: where you look. And I had it conveyed to you: now you are looking back."

"What does that mean?"

The sheikh rose from the floor, lightly, in one movement, as youths rise. Went to the tall window under the dome. Stood looking out, to where the sun was rising above the roofs.

"You are looking for your name," he said without turning. "You are looking for where you came from. For who you were. For who wrote you the note. Who gave you the stones. You look for the past." He paused. "You look back, guest. Entirely. Completely. You walk the rope, and you look over your shoulder. At the end from which you came."

"Where should I look?"

Ahmet Baba turned.

"At the end to which you are going," he said simply. "A rope-walker who looks back falls. Always." He paused. "Your home is where you look. You said so yourself. So if you look back, your home is behind you. In the past. Which you do not remember." The sheikh smiled. "But if you look forward..."

"Then home is ahead?"

"Then home is where you have not yet arrived," said Ahmet Baba. "Like the Red Apple among the Turks. Like the City of the Caesars among the Franks in the New World." He paused, and something flickered in his blue eyes. "Like the Marble King among the Greeks. Who has not returned, but waits. Ahead. Beneath the gate."

I started.

"How do you know about the Marble King?"

"Kyra Theodora is an old acquaintance of mine," said the sheikh. "We have corresponded for forty years. She writes to me in French, I answer her in Greek. So that no one can read it." He smiled. "She wrote to me three days ago. That a guest had come in a red turban, solved the riddle of the fountain and taken the coin of the Melissenoi." Ahmet Baba paused. "She writes that for the first time in ninety years she is at peace."

* * *
"The grey man," I said. "He was in the gallery of Hagia Sophia. He told me: do not go to the dervish. He came to Kyra Theodora. He looked for me at the port. Who is he?"

Ahmet Baba was silent for a long time. By the wall Yunus shrank into himself. The cat Mismis raised her head.

"Which one?" the sheikh asked at last.

"What do you mean, which?"

"There are two of them, guest," said Ahmet Baba. Quietly, seriously, without a smile. "You confuse them. Everyone confuses them. I confused them too, until I saw both."

He sat down again on the floor. Opposite me. Close.

"One is a man," he said. "Of flesh and blood. Tall, in a grey frock coat, with a cane, a top hat. He speaks French, Greek, Turkish. He smells of cologne, expensive, Parisian, with bergamot. He drinks tea. He pays in gold. He signs his name in registers. He has a face, but no one can remember it. Because he wishes it so. That is an art. It is taught." The sheikh paused. "He came to me. Five years ago. Asked about guests without a name. Offered money for my notes. I turned him out. Mismis sat on his top hat."

"Who is he?"

"I do not know," said Ahmet Baba. "But he is not alone. There are many such as he. They seek the same thing as you. Only from the other end. Did he tell you so?" I nodded. "He told the truth. They seek. Not you, but what you have. What you carry." The sheikh looked at the pouch at my belt. "And what you may one day remember."

"And the other?"

Ahmet Baba did not answer for a long time.

"The other," he said at last, very quietly, "is seen by children. And cats. And the blind. And old women who spit over their shoulders. He smells of nothing. He does not drink tea. He has no face, not because he hides it, but because..." The sheikh fell silent. "I saw him once. Twenty years ago. The night I first dreamed of you. He stood there." Ahmet Baba nodded toward the centre of the round hall, where he had been whirling. "On that very spot. And whirled. With me. I closed my eyes and felt him whirling beside me. I opened them, and no one."

"Who is he?"

Ahmet Baba looked at me with his blue, light, infinitely weary eyes.

"I have thought of it for twenty years, guest," he said. "I have read all the books in Cairo, in Baghdad, in Bukhara. I have asked the Sufis and the Frankish professors." He paused. "I do not know. But I will tell you one thing. The first, the man in the frock coat, you should fear. He is dangerous, because he wants. And the second..." The sheikh fell silent.

"And the second?"

"The second, do not fear," said Ahmet Baba. "The second wants nothing. He simply waits." He paused. "As the angel beneath the dome of Hagia Sophia waits for the boy who was not returned."

* * *
Then it was noon, and Yunus brought lunch, lentil soup, flatbread, olives, and we ate in the courtyard under the fig tree, the four of us: the sheikh, I, the boy and the blind flute-player. Mismis lay on the bench pretending to sleep, but followed every olive.

"Yunus," said Ahmet Baba, "give the guest a riddle. Your own. The one you made up last week."

The boy blushed to his ears. Laid down his flatbread. Looked at me, gathering his courage.

"'I whirl,'" he said in Turkish, and the sheikh translated, "'but I do not tire. I sing, but I have no mouth. I am empty inside, therefore I sound. If I am filled, I fall silent. What am I?'"

I thought.

"A flute," I said. "A reed one. Empty inside, therefore it sounds."

Yunus beamed. Shemseddin, without opening his eyes, laughed, quietly, soundlessly, with his shoulders alone.

"And why 'I whirl'?" I asked.

"Because the dervish whirls as the flute sounds," said Ahmet Baba. "He is empty inside. So that it may pass through him." He looked at me. "You too are empty inside, guest. Without a name. Without memory. You think it is a misfortune." He paused. "But perhaps it is so that something may sound through you."

"What?"

"That I do not know," said the sheikh. "Perhaps you will find out yourself. When you stop trying to fill yourself." He broke off a piece of flatbread. "Everyone tries to fill the emptiness. With names. With the past. With things. With fear. And the flute sounds only while it is empty."

Shemseddin suddenly opened his eyes. White, blind, without pupils. Turned his face to me. And said something, hoarsely, not loudly.

"He says," Ahmet Baba translated slowly, "'Your two hearts. Just now. For a moment one fell into time with the other. When you said "what?" I heard it.'"

* * *
Toward evening, when the sun was already sinking toward the dome of Hagia Sophia, Ahmet Baba called me to his cell.

Small, whitewashed, with one window, a mat on the floor, a low table heaped with books in a dozen languages. Arabic, Persian, Turkish, Greek, French, German, Latin. And among them one notebook. Worn. In a leather binding.

"Forty years," said the sheikh, laying his palm on the notebook, "I have written down in here all that I hear of people without a name. Of guests. Of those who come and go." He paused. "I have forty-two entries. Constantinople. Cairo. Bukhara. Damascus. Jerusalem." He looked at me. "And I know that I am not the only one."

"Not the only one?"

"There are people," said Ahmet Baba, lowering his voice, "who write this down not for forty years. But for four hundred. Or more. From generation to generation. They pass on the notebooks as one passes on an inheritance. They call themselves..." He fell silent. "No. Let them tell you themselves what they call themselves."

"Where can I find them?"

The sheikh took from beneath the notebook a folded letter, sealed with green wax. Held it out to me.

"In the palace," he said. "The old one. On the cape. Where you passed the walls yesterday. In the archive. There serves a man. The keeper of papers. His name is Niyaz Efendi. He is old. Older than I. He receives no one." Ahmet Baba paused. "But this letter he will read. And then he will receive you."

I took the letter. On the green wax a seal was impressed, not letters, not a coat of arms. Two small circles. One filled. The other empty. And between them a wavy line.

I raised my eyes to the sheikh.

"You are one of them."

Ahmet Baba smiled.

"I am a dervish, guest," he said. "I whirl and drink tea." He paused. "But this seal was given to me by Niyaz Efendi. Forty years ago. He said: 'When he comes, seal the letter with this seal. I will understand.'"

* * *
"And one last thing," said Ahmet Baba, when we came out of the cell back into the courtyard, under the fig tree, where an oil lamp was already burning and the first stars were lighting above the dome of Hagia Sophia. "I want to offer you something."

"What?"

He looked at me with his blue, light eyes, and this time there was neither mockery in them nor weariness. Only warmth.

"Stay," he said. "Here. With me. Be my pupil." He paused. "I will teach you to whirl. I will teach you to be empty, so that something sounds through you. You will not have to go to Niyaz Efendi. You will not have to look for your name. You will not have to fear the man in the frock coat and wait for the second, the one without a face." He spread his hands. "You will live here. Under the fig tree. Drink tea. Listen to Shemseddin's flute. Feed Mismis olives. And never again walk in a circle." The sheikh paused. "For the dervish does not walk in a circle. The dervish whirls on the spot. They are different things."

I stood under the fig tree. The lamp sputtered. Somewhere in the hall Shemseddin was softly playing his flute. Yunus sat on the rim of the well, swinging his legs, and looked at me with hope.

And it was tempting. So tempting as nothing had been in all these long, tangled days. To stay. To stop searching. To stop looking back. Simply to be. Here. Under the fig tree. With a blue-eyed old man and a blind flute-player, and a boy, and a cat who opens doors.

"If Ahmet Baba offers you to stay, do not stay," Hodja Nureddin had said.

I slowly reached into my pocket. Took out the canvas pouch tied with a red thread. Untied it.

Inside were a crumb of bread and a pinch of salt.

I ate the bread. Then took the salt and threw it over my left shoulder.

And bowed.

"Thank you, Ahmet Baba," I said. "But I must go."

* * *
The sheikh looked at me. At the salt whitening on the flagstones of the courtyard behind my back. At the empty canvas pouch in my hand.

And then he laughed.

As he had not laughed all that long day, loudly, heartily, with his head thrown back, holding his belly, so that Yunus on the well burst out laughing with him, not understanding why, and Mismis leapt off the bench and ran into the hall.

"Nureddin!" Ahmet Baba gasped, wiping away tears. "Old fox! Forty years! Forty years we have argued, and he always knows what I will do!" He laughed again. "Bread and salt! He gave you bread and salt!"

"He said," I began, "to tell you. That he is right. That you will understand."

Ahmet Baba stopped laughing. Looked at me. For a long time.

"I understand," he said quietly. "Tell him he is right. As always." The sheikh paused. "Forty years ago I offered another guest to stay. Without a name. With two stones. He stayed. For a year." Ahmet Baba closed his eyes. "And then he left. At night. Without saying goodbye. And for forty years I have thought: if he had not stayed that year, perhaps he would have got there. Where he was going." He opened his eyes. "Nureddin told me then: 'You stole a year from him, Ahmet. Do not do it again.'" The sheikh smiled. "I promised. And here, I did not keep my word. Good that you had bread and salt."

"Did you want to test me?"

"I wanted to keep you," said Ahmet Baba simply. "I am old. I am lonely. Shemseddin is blind, Yunus is small, and Mismis is a cat. I wanted someone beside me with whom I could talk of Rumi and of the stars." He paused. "But Nureddin is right. You cannot stay. Not with me. Not with Suleyman. Not with anyone." The sheikh laid his hand on my shoulder. "You are a rope-walker, guest. A rope-walker cannot stop in the middle of the rope. He can only get across. Or fall."

* * *
Yunus saw me to the gate. Mismis too. She went ahead, tail high, and at the gate raised a paw and pushed the leaf, and it opened.

The sun had already set. Above the dome of Hagia Sophia stars were burning. From the minarets the evening call floated.

"Yunus," I said to the boy at the gate. "May I ask something?"

"Ask," said the boy. In my language. Brokenly, carefully, apparently learned from the sheikh.

"Your riddle. About the flute. Did you really make it up yourself?"

Yunus looked at me for a long time. Then shook his head.

"No," he said. "I dreamed it. A week ago. A tall man. Grey. He stood in the middle of the hall. Where the sheikh whirls." The boy swallowed. "He told me the riddle. And he said: 'Give it to the guest. He will solve it. And then he will ask whether you made it up yourself. Tell him the truth.'"

I stood at the gate. The stars burned. The cat looked at me with green eyes.

"What else did he say?" I asked. My voice sounded as if from far away.

Yunus thought.

"He said: 'Tell the guest: the flute sounds while it is empty. But one day it will be filled. And then it will not fall silent. It will sing its own.'"

He bowed. The cat mewed. The gate closed.

I went down toward Suleyman's, in the dark, along the narrow lanes of Sultanahmet, with a letter sealed in green wax in my pocket. With two circles and a wavy line on the seal. And with the feeling that behind my back, somewhere high, on the dome of Hagia Sophia, under the stars, someone stands. And whirls. Slowly. Evenly. With arms outstretched: one to the sky, the other to the earth.

Waiting.

## Chapter XXXIII. The Command

The courier galloped in on Wednesday, at dawn, when everyone in the house was still asleep except Agafya Tikhonovna, Mitka and the cocks.

I heard him before I saw him, through sleep, through the morning mist, through the closed shutters: the thud of hooves on the avenue, frantic, quick, such as only a horse driven to lather makes, and the jingle of a bell, and someone's hoarse cry at the gates: "Open up! In the Sovereign's name!" Then the barking of dogs, noise, slamming doors, the clatter of feet on the stairs.

I went out onto the gallery in my dressing gown. Below, in the vestibule, by the light of a lone candle held by a sleepy Ignatiy Savvich, stood a man.

Young, about twenty-five, tall, in a mud-splashed green greatcoat, a plumed tricorn, with a sword and an enormous leather bag over his shoulder, sealed with wax. His face was grey with fatigue, streaked with sweat and road dust. His boots were knee-deep in mud. He stood straight, as on parade, but I saw that he could hardly keep on his feet.

"Is His Excellency Adjutant-General Pavel Nikolaevich here?" he asked hoarsely. "They told me at the estate, here."

"Here, dear sir, here," rustled Ignatiy Savvich, hastily buttoning his livery on the wrong button. "He is asleep. In the north wing. Shall I wake him, if you please?"

"If you please," said the courier. And, after a pause, added in a different, almost human voice: "And, if it can be done, water. I have not left the saddle for three days."

* * *
The General came down to him in five minutes, dressed, buttoned to the last button, with his orders on, as though he had never gone to bed. The courier drew himself up, clicked his heels, held out the packet, large, thick, with three wax seals, each stamped with a double-headed eagle.

The General broke the seals. Read, standing, by the light of the candle Ignatiy Savvich held. His face did not change. Not a single feature. Only the hand holding the paper tightened, barely perceptibly.

"I thank you, Lieutenant," he said to the courier. "Rest. Ignatiy Savvich, feed him. The best room. The horse to the stable, beside Stefan's, Tikhon will see to it." He folded the paper. "The reply will be ready by evening."

"Yes, Your Excellency."

The courier went after the steward, and on the threshold, turning, suddenly saw me on the gallery. Looked. Long. Then saluted, not to me, of course, but into space, and left.

The General raised his head. He saw me too.

"Come down," he said. "Since you are not asleep."

* * *
We sat in the study. The fireplace had not yet been lit; grey morning light poured through the window; on the table lay the packet.

"Constantinople," said the General. Without preamble. "The Sovereign commands." He tapped the paper with a finger. "In Herzegovina, an uprising. Since summer. Serbs, Montenegrins, Bulgarians, all watching, all waiting. Europe is alarmed. England, Austria, France, each pulling its own way. And in the Porte..." He paused. "In the Porte, disaster. The treasury is empty. A month ago the Sultan announced that he will not pay his debts. Half of them. The European bankers are furious. The Grand Vizier changes every three months. The people in the streets are starving. The softas, the madrasa students, are rioting." The General leaned back in his chair. "Our ambassador in Constantinople asks for me. I know the Porte. I know their ministers. Some of them owe me. The Sultan remembers what happened in Mehmet Ali's time." He paused. "In ten days, to Odessa. From there by a steamer of the Russian Company. Two days and the Bosphorus."

"For long?"

"Who knows," said the General. "Perhaps a month. Perhaps a year. Perhaps," he paused, "if what I think will begin does begin, for a war."

We were silent. Outside, the garden was waking. Somewhere below, in the servants' hall, Dunyasha was already clattering pails.

"Will you come with me?" asked the General.

Simply. Evenly. As one asks, "Tea?"

I raised my eyes to him.

"I?"

"You," said the General. "I need a man at the embassy. A secretary. A copyist. Who knows French." He paused. "You know French better than any of my adjutants. I heard you speak it with the monk. Then, behind the grille." A pause. "You do not remember. But I heard. When I lifted you from the grass. You were raving in French. And then in Turkish."

"In Turkish?"

"In Turkish," the General repeated. "For thirty years I have been talking with Turks. I would know their language among a thousand. You said: 'Misafir.' Three times." He looked at me heavily, unblinking. "Guest."

* * *
"Why do you want me to go?" I asked. "Truly."

The General did not answer for a long time. He stood. Went to the window. Stood looking out into the garden with his hands clasped behind his back, the way, probably, he had stood on the deck of the *Diana* when a wave higher than the masts came toward Simoda.

"Vera Anatolievna," he said, without turning. "Fifteen years ago. Constantinople. The port. A young man in a red turban. With your face. Your age." He paused. "Sventsitsky wrote her story into his notebook 'Guest.' Entry forty-eight. He sent me a copy. From the road. From Vologda."

"He sent it?"

"The letter came yesterday," said the General. "Together with it, another. For you. I have not opened it." He took an envelope from a desk drawer and held it out to me. "You will read it later." He turned to the window again. "The Turkmen old man told me: 'You will meet that man. Give him the scroll. And say: the earth remembers.' I gave it." A pause. "But I do not know what to do next. For thirty years I carried the scroll. I have delivered it. And then what?"

"Then it is for me to decide," I said.

The General turned. Looked at me with a long, heavy look.

"Yes," he said. "You." A pause. "But I thought: if that one, from the watercolour, stood in Constantinople fifteen years ago, lost, without a name, perhaps the beginning is there. Perhaps there you will find what you seek." He paused. "Or perhaps you will find nothing. And we shall simply copy dispatches for the ambassador. I do not promise you answers." His voice grew quieter. "I promise you a road. It is all I have."

* * *
Auntie learned by breakfast. The General told her himself, in the small drawing room, with the doors closed. I did not hear what he said. I heard only that a quarter of an hour later something fell, heavily, dully, and then it became very quiet.

When the doors opened, Auntie was sitting in the armchair by the window, upright, pale, in her grey morning gown, and at her feet, on the carpet, lay the shards of a porcelain vase. Blue. Chinese. The one which, it was said, Auntie's father-in-law had brought from Kyakhta forty years ago.

The General stood by the fireplace. His face was of stone.

"My friend," said Auntie, seeing me in the doorway. Her voice was level. Perfectly level. Only the fingers gripping the arm of the chair had turned white. "Come here."

I came. Knelt by her chair, beside the shards.

"Pavel Nikolaevich says you are going with him," she said. "To Constantinople."

"If you permit, Auntie."

She looked at me for a long time. From above. With eyes in which there were no tears, only something dry, scorched, terrible, like ash.

"He said," she began slowly, "that one, at the grille. Tall. Grey. He said: 'When he remembers, he will come for him himself.'" She paused. "For forty years I have feared he would come. Here. For you. For forty years I have checked every night whether the grille was locked." Her lips trembled. "And you are going yourself. There. To him."

"I do not know whether he is there, Auntie."

"You know," said Auntie. "You do not remember. But you know."

She raised her hand. Slowly. And drew from her hair, from the high coiffure fastened with a tortoiseshell comb, a pin. A long one, silver, with a small pearl at its end. Then a second. A third. Her hair, dark, streaked with grey, spilled over her shoulders. I had never seen Auntie with her hair loose. Never.

From the hair, from the very middle of the tight knot, a small object fell. Dropped into her lap. Clinked.

A key.

Old, iron, dark, with an intricate bit, with a ring on which some script was engraved, worn, illegible, but long, flowing, one line running into another.

"Agafya has thought for forty years that it was lost," said Auntie quietly. "The key to the grille." She took it, turned it in her fingers. "It was not lost. I hid it. That same night. For forty years I have worn it in my hair. Every day. Every night. So that no one should open it." She paused. "And on the night you went behind the grille, the lock hung open. Do you remember?"

"I remember."

"I did not open it," said Auntie. "The key was in my hair. I checked, in the morning, when you were carried in. It was in place." She raised her eyes to me. "The lock opened by itself. Or someone opened it who needs no key."

She held out the key to me.

"Take it."

"Auntie..."

"Take it," she repeated. "Not to open with. To return with." Her voice broke for the first time. "If, where you are going, there is a door you cannot open, remember that here there is a door whose key you have." She closed my fingers around the key. "Here is your home. Whatever the grey ones, the monks, the dervishes, the professors may say. Here. While I live."

I held the key. Heavy, cold, and at once warmed in my palm. Like a coin. Like a stone in the sun.

"I will return, Auntie," I said.

Auntie did not answer. She simply laid her palm on my head, as, probably, she had laid it in childhood, if I had a childhood, and held it. For a long time. And then the General by the fireplace coughed quietly and went out, closing the door behind him.

* * *
Konstantin burst in on me an hour later, without knocking, in an unbuttoned tunic, with burning eyes.

"Constantinople!" he blurted from the threshold. "You are going to Constantinople! Dunyasha told me. And she was told by Ignatiy Savvich. And he by the courier, who, by the way, is my corps classmate, Lyovushka Arsenyev, he is asleep now in the best room, snoring like a cannon." Konstantin dropped into an armchair. "And you said nothing!"

"I found out two hours ago."

"Two hours!" Konstantin clutched his head. "In two hours one could have... could have..." He faltered. Looked at me. Paused. "Mon cher. Are you truly going?"

"I am."

Konstantin was silent for a long time. Then he stood. Straightened his tunic. Buttoned it, to the last button, regulation fashion.

"Then I am going to the General," he said.

"What for?"

"To ask," said Konstantin. And went toward the door.

"Kostya!" I leapt up. "You have a regiment. Service. You cannot..."

"I can," said Konstantin, without turning. "The General needs an adjutant. His former one, Krutitsky, has married and retired. I know; Evdokia Gerasimovna told Auntie." He took the door handle. "And I need you. That is, I need you not to get lost in that Constantinople. You find the way to the library on the third try. And there, a city on two continents."

He went out.

I stood in the middle of the room and heard his steps recede down the corridor, quick, ringing, resolute. Then a knock at the study door. Then silence.

Then, about ten minutes later, the thunderous, rolling laughter of the General. Such as I had never heard. Not once in all those years.

* * *
"He said," Konstantin told me afterward, red to his ears, "he said: 'Lieutenant, I have been waiting for you. Since yesterday. You are a day late. I wrote the order for your secondment last night, after I received the ambassador's letter. It is lying in my desk.'" Konstantin sat on my bed. "And then he said: 'Do you think I am blind?' And burst out laughing."

"What does 'do you think I am blind' mean?"

Konstantin looked at me. For a long time. Then looked away.

"I don't know, mon cher," he said. "He says it to me for the second time." A pause. "Probably something about how I follow you around. Not a step away. As he ordered."

"You did before he ordered."

"I did," Konstantin agreed. And said nothing more.

* * *
By evening the whole province knew.

Olga Kirillovna Shelestova saw to that, naturally; by pure chance she had dropped in on Auntie "for just a minute, to return a French novel," the very one she had not returned since Easter, and found in the vestibule the courier coming down to dinner. An hour later she was at the Kutasovs'. Two hours later, at the Marshal of the Nobility's. By evening, according to Mitka, who had run to the village for tar, in every tavern for ten versts around they were discussing that "the General's ward is going to the Turks, and with him a lieutenant, and the General is off to war, and the lady broke a vase that was a hundred years old."

"Fifty," Ignatiy Savvich corrected Mitka with icy dignity. "And she did not break it; she dropped it."

Supper that evening was a farewell one, though there were still ten days before departure. So Auntie had decided. "Afterwards there will be packing, bustle, tears," she said. "Tonight it is simply supper. While everyone is here."

And everyone was here.

Colonel Mikhail Ivanovich and Vera Anatolievna: the Colonel announced from the doorway that he would go too, "because without him the General will certainly quarrel with the Turks," and Vera Anatolievna gently but implacably said that he was going nowhere, because he had gout. Evdokia Gerasimovna, in a hat with a heron's plume, pale, with eyes she carefully did not raise to the General. Nadezhda Porfirievna Kutasova with Lizonka; Lizonka looked at Konstantin all evening as if he were going to the scaffold. Doctor Strauch, with his unlit cigar, grim, silent. Lieutenant Alexei, with toasts, jokes and a third bottle of champagne. And even Stefan, for the first time in all these years at the common table, by Auntie's special invitation, in a clean linen shirt, awkward, silent, sitting on the very edge of his chair like a bird on a branch.

* * *
"Charades!" announced Lieutenant Alexei after the second course, leaping up with his glass. "Farewell charades! Everyone sets one about the road!"

Auntie nodded. The General winced but said nothing.

Alexei went first, something about "a stormy sea and a steamer," so unintelligibly that no one guessed, and he himself, laughing, confessed that he had forgotten the answer. The Colonel set one about "janissaries," who, as the General gently reminded him, had been abolished fifty years ago. Lizonka, blushing, set one about "rose and parting," and, without waiting for guesses, burst into tears and ran from the table. Kutasova ran after her.

And then Konstantin rose.

He stood a moment. Straightened his tunic. Looked at me across the table. And recited, not in his usual jesting voice, but quietly, almost seriously:

"My first sits on the throne with crown and sword,
To whom men swear, whose will is law and word.
My second is a city, wall and gate,
Where streets and shrines and markets, small and great.
The whole stands on two shores beside the sea,
That our forefathers dreamed of ceaselessly.
In olden days it had a hundred names,
But Russians say that there the ruler is..."

He stopped, without finishing.

"The Tsar!" Alexei blurted. "Tsar-grad! Tsargrad!"

"Tsargrad," said Konstantin. "Constantinople." He raised his glass. "The city that our ancestors called the Tsar's. And which never became ours."

"Not yet," said the Colonel.

"Not yet," Konstantin agreed. And looked at me. "Or maybe there's no need. Maybe let it be no one's. Like the road."

* * *
"Tsargrad," the General repeated, when everyone had sat down again. "Do you know where that name comes from?" He looked round the table. "A thousand years ago Prince Oleg, the Wise, marched on Tsargrad. With longships. Two thousand ships. The Greeks stretched a chain across the Golden Horn, as they would later before the Turks.
