Then Oleg ordered the ships put on wheels. And the sails raised. And the ships went overland, toward the walls of the city. Under the wind." The General paused. "The Greeks took fright and asked for peace. And Oleg, in token of victory, nailed his shield to the gates of Tsargrad."

"Is it true?" asked Evdokia Gerasimovna, lifting her eyes for the first time.

"So it is written in the chronicle, Dunya," said the General gently. "Whether it is true, who knows. Perhaps there was never any shield." He paused. "But for thirty years I have been going to Constantinople. And every time, passing the old gates, I look to see whether the shield hangs there." He smiled. "It does not."

"But ships overland, that was the Turks!" said Konstantin. "Mehmet. Seventy ships across a hill."

"Four hundred years after Oleg," the General nodded. "The same way. Against the same chain." He paused. "This city, Lieutenant, every man takes in the same manner. And each thinks he is the first."

Stefan, sitting on the edge of his chair at the end of the table, suddenly raised his head. And said, quietly, slowly, in his broken Russian:

"In Tsargrad... there is a rose. By the Patriarchate. In the Phanar. Also from Tarnovo. A cutting. Monks brought it. Long ago." He paused. "If you see it, bow to it. From me." And lowered his head again.

Phanar. Patriarchate. Tarnovo. I did not know these places. And yet, at the word "Phanar," something stirred in my chest. A hill above a bay. An old house. A double-headed eagle with one head. An old woman with a peacock.

I blinked. The vision passed.

* * *
After supper Doctor Strauch called me out onto the terrace.

The night was cold, starry. The garden below, dark, quiet. Strauch lit up, at last, in my presence, and was silent for a long time, blowing smoke toward the stars.

"Eleven," he said at last. "Eleven cases in thirty years. I told you." He paused. "Do you know what all eleven had in common? Besides that they came from nowhere and did not remember themselves?"

"What?"

"All went south," said Strauch. "All. One to the Crimea. Two to the Caucasus. One to Odessa and on by sea. One to Bessarabia." He drew on the cigar. "As though something drew them. There. To the warm sea. To the straits." He looked at me over his gold spectacles. "You are the twelfth, young man. And you are going south."

"Do you consider this... a medical symptom?"

"I am a German," said Strauch. "I consider it a regularity." He knocked off the ash. "A regularity is when twelve times out of twelve the same thing happens. Science rests on that." He paused. "I do not know what draws you south. I do not know what is there. But here is what I know." He turned to me. "Not one of the eleven came back."

We were silent. The stars burned.

"I will give you something," said Strauch. And took from the pocket of his frock coat a small black book. That very one. Which he had shown to no one. "Here are my notes. On all eleven. And on you." He held it out to me. "When you are there, read it. Perhaps you will see what I did not." He paused. "And if you return, give it back. I shall write: 'The twelfth returned.'" A pause. "I should very much like to write that."

* * *
Evdokia Gerasimovna and the General stood at the end of the avenue, by the gates, under the old linden; I saw them from the terrace. She, in her hat with the heron's plume, in a shawl. He, in his greatcoat, bareheaded. They did not talk. They simply stood side by side. Very close.

Then the General took her hand. Raised it to his lips. And said something.

I did not hear. But I saw Evdokia Gerasimovna lift her face to him, and the heron's plume on her hat tremble. And how she slowly, very slowly, nodded.

In the morning, at breakfast, the General announced, drily, briefly, without lifting his eyes from his plate:

"Evdokia Gerasimovna has done me the honour of consenting to be my wife. We shall be married when I return."

Auntie dropped her spoon. The Colonel choked on his tea. Lieutenant Alexei leapt up with a glass of orange juice that had just been poured for him. Konstantin under the table trod on my foot so that I nearly cried out.

"Thirty years," he whispered to me, leaning over. "Thirty years he was getting ready. And decided ten days before a war."

"Perhaps that is why he decided," I said.

Konstantin looked at me, strangely, for a long time, and answered nothing.

* * *
I read Sventsitsky's letter at night, in my room, by candle.

The envelope was grey, cheap, with a Vologda postmark. Inside, a single sheet covered with the professor's small, close, hurried handwriting.

"Young man!

I write to you from a post station near Vologda, where again there are no horses and, according to the station master, will be none till Thursday. The station master here has no wooden leg, but has a wooden head, which, however, comes to the same thing.

I write to tell you one thing which I did not say at parting. I did not dare.

In the notebook 'Guest' there are forty-seven entries. I told you so. But I did not tell you that of the forty-seven, twenty-three end the same way. The guest goes not simply south. He goes to the sea. To the strait. To the city that we call Tsargrad.

For thirty years I thought it a coincidence. Or that the grannies confuse things: for them Tsargrad is the end of the earth.

And yesterday, sorting the notebook on the road, I found an entry that I myself made twelve years ago, in Bessarabia, and had utterly forgotten. An old Moldavian ferryman on the Danube told how his grandfather ferried across the river a young man without a name, in strange clothes, who was going to Tsargrad. The ferryman asked, why? And he answered: 'There I left what I forgot. In a house by the sea. Guarded by cats.'

Guarded by cats, young man.

I do not know what it means. Perhaps nothing.

The General wrote me that he may go to Constantinople. If you go with him, ask there about a house by the sea, guarded by cats.

And if you find it, write to me. With the pencil I gave you. I shall receive it.

Yours, I. F. Sventsitsky.

P. S. The end of the tale of Shmat-razum I have still not found. But yesterday I had a dream. As if I were a boy again, sitting on the stove, and the guest in the blizzard says to me: 'The end will be in the city on two shores.' I woke and wrote it down. Entry forty-nine."

* * *
A house by the sea. Guarded by cats.

I sat over the letter, and the candle guttered, and in my chest something slowly, heavily turned, like a key in a lock I had never seen.

A small house in Sultanahmet. A door in a blind wall. An old fragment of a column beside it. Eleven cats on the steps of the staircase leading down to the cellar, and not one of them goes below. A chest that cannot be approached. A metal plate with the script. Without a keyhole.

I had never been there. I was certain I had never been there.

And yet I saw it. Now. Before my eyes. So clearly, as if I had stood there yesterday.

I took Auntie's key from my pocket. Old, iron, with script on the ring. Laid it on Sventsitsky's letter. Beside it, the professor's pencil. Beside that, Strauch's black book. Beside that, the General's scroll in its blue silk kerchief. Beside that, Stefan's monastery paper.

All the things that had been given to me. People who did not know one another, and all said the same thing: "Take it. You are the one. Pass it on. Return."

On the windowsill, in the clay pot, the cutting of Stefan's black rose had at last opened fully. Dark crimson, almost black, with a golden heart. And it smelled, strongly, sweetly, bitterly, of honey and wormwood.

I blew out the candle. Lay down. And lay for a long time with my eyes open, looking into the dark.

In ten days, Odessa. A steamer. The Bosphorus.

Tsargrad.

A city with many names.

And somewhere in it, a house by the sea. Guarded by cats.

* * *
In the morning Konstantin found me at the window; I had not slept at all.

"What's the matter?" he asked, seeing my face.

"Kostya," I said. "There, in Constantinople. If I suddenly..." I faltered. "If I suddenly start speaking Turkish. Or call myself by a strange name. Or go off somewhere without telling you..."

Konstantin came over. Stood beside me at the window. Looked at the rose.

"Then I will follow you," he said simply. "Wherever you go. Into any house. To any cats." He paused. "I'm an adjutant. The General ordered: not a step away."

"And if you cannot? If I go where one cannot follow?"

Konstantin was silent for a long time. Then took something small from his tunic pocket. Held it out to me.

It was his baptismal cross. A simple silver one, on a thin chain, darkened with time.

"My mother's," he said. "All that is left of her." He laid it in my palm. "Wear it. And if you go where I cannot, leave it there. On the threshold. I will find it." A pause. "I always find, mon cher. I found you at the grille, though you didn't cry out."

I held the cross. Warm. Like everything that had been given me in recent weeks.

"Thank you, Kostya."

"Don't mention it," said Konstantin. And, already leaving, turned at the threshold, and on his face was his old mocking smile again: "Only, mon cher, mark this. In Constantinople I won't let you wear a red turban. It's tasteless. Vera Anatolievna drew you in one, and for fifteen years, well, a week, I can't unsee it."

He left, whistling something off-key.

And I stood at the window with the cross in one hand and the key in the other and watched the sun rise over the garden. Somewhere there, in the south, a thousand versts away, beyond the steppes and the sea, it already stood high. Over the Bosphorus. Over the two shores. Over the dome that had once seen the marble king.

And over the small house by the sea, where eleven cats guarded the stair down to the cellar.

## Chapter XXXIV. The Village of the Tomb-Builders

"We are hungry!"

The cry reached us before we saw the village, from the ridge of the last hill, as Senusret's chariot, raising yellow dust, climbed the stony road from the valley into the western desert.

"We are hungry! Eighteen days!"

There were many voices. Dozens. A hundred. They did not shout raggedly, but in unison, steadily, as oarsmen cry on a barque to the beat of a drum. And in that steady cry there was something that made Senusret, who was driving, rein in and lay his hand on his sword.

"My Pharaoh," he said through his teeth. "This is a mutiny."

"It is not a mutiny," said Nebamun. The keeper of the treasury rode in the second chariot beside Iti, gripping the side with both hands and trying to preserve his dignity, which on a mountain road came hard. "A mutiny is when they cry 'death.' They cry 'we are hungry.'" He paused. "That is a reckoning. They are presenting a bill."

The chariot crested the ridge.

* * *
The village lay below, in a narrow stony hollow between two yellow hills, like a nest in a palm. One long straight street, houses along it. Small, cramped, built wall to wall, of mud-brick and broken stone, with flat roofs on which washing dried, mats lay, jars stood. Around it all, a wall. High, whitewashed, enclosing the village on every side, with a single gate at the northern end.

And beyond the village, higher up the slope, in the cliffs, were entrances. Dark rectangular openings in the yellow rock. Dozens. Tombs. Some long finished, sealed, with names carved above the entrance. Others still under construction, with wooden scaffolding, with heaps of rubble at the entrance. And at the very top, just below the ridge, a large entrance, deep, wide, framed by pillars not yet finished.

My house of eternity. The tomb that had been built for me from the first day I ascended the throne. As it is built for every Pharaoh.

And at the gate of the village, on the open space before a small temple with sandstone columns, people were sitting.

Not standing: sitting. On the ground. Right in the dust. A hundred men, stonecutters, carvers, painters, plasterers, porters, sunburnt, sinewy, in loincloths so covered with white stone dust that they seemed moulded from chalk. They sat close, shoulder to shoulder, cross-legged, facing the temple. And cried, steadily, in unison, again and again:

"We are hungry! Eighteen days!"

And between them and the temple, on the steps, stood a small, fat, frightened scribe in temple linen, waving his arms and trying to say something. No one was listening.

* * *
We drove right up to the gate before we were noticed.

The first to turn was one of the seated men, a stocky, broad-shouldered, grey-haired man, with a small beard braided into a plait, and with hands so calloused they seemed carved from the same stone as the cliffs around. He saw the chariot. Saw Senusret. Saw me, in plain travelling dress but with the uraeus on my brow.

He stood. Slowly. Dusted off his knees. And bowed, low, but not prostrating himself, as peasants do, but as masters bow: with the dignity of a man who knows his worth.

"My Pharaoh," he said. "I am Neferhotep. Foreman of the right gang." His voice was hoarse but firm. "We did not expect you."

A hundred heads behind him turned. The cry fell silent. A hundred men, white with dust, looked at me.

"You are hungry, Neferhotep," I said. "Eighteen days."

"Eighteen days, my Pharaoh," the foreman confirmed. "Our ration, grain, fish, oil, beer, firewood, comes from the temple granaries. Every ten days. So it has always been. So it is written." He nodded toward the fat scribe on the steps, who at the sight of me had fallen to his knees and pressed his forehead to the stone. "Eighteen days ago he said: 'A delay.' Ten days ago he said: 'Soon.' Three days ago he said: 'The Temple is in difficulty, work, and then we shall see.'" Neferhotep paused. "We worked. Fourteen days on empty gruel. Then we stopped."

"Why did you stop?"

Neferhotep looked at me calmly, without fear.

"Because a hungry carver, my Pharaoh, carves crooked," he said. "And a hungry painter mixes his colours. And a hungry stonecutter drops his mallet. Yesterday Hui, our best painter, fainted on the scaffolding in your tomb. Nearly fell to his death." He paused. "We are building you a house of eternity, my Pharaoh. You will live in it for millions of years. Would you want it built crooked?"

Behind him someone grunted. Someone laughed. A hundred men waited.

* * *
Nebamun was already at the steps of the temple. He bent over the fat scribe, asked him something quietly; the scribe, without lifting his head, babbled something; and the keeper of the treasury straightened with the face of a man who has found in a column of figures an error long suspected.

"My Pharaoh," he said, coming up. Not loudly. "The village ration was withdrawn three weeks ago from the temple granary on the west bank. By order." He paused. "The order bears Bakenren's seal."

"Bakenren has been gone two weeks."

"The order is dated the day before his disappearance, my Pharaoh," said Nebamun. "And no one has revoked it since." He looked at me over his tablets. "The scribe says he was told not to ask. He was told to say 'a delay' to the workmen. And to wait."

"To wait for what?"

"For the workmen to abandon their work," said Nebamun evenly. "For Pharaoh's tomb to stand still. For a rumour to go round the capital that even the builders of Pharaoh's tomb are starving. That even Pharaoh's eternal house is unfinished." He paused. "Before the festival of Opet. Before the road to Luxor. That is a very bad omen, my Pharaoh. The people love omens."

Behind me Senusret made a low sound.

"Nebamun," I said. "How much do they need?"

The keeper of the treasury did not even glance at his tablets.

"For a hundred and twenty men with their families, for twenty days of missed ration and ten ahead: seven hundred hekats of barley, two hundred of spelt, forty jars of oil, three hundred fish, a hundred and twenty jars of beer," he said. "And firewood." He paused. "And my Pharaoh has forgotten the fine on the Temple for the disruption of work. That is by law. I shall reckon it separately."

"Today, before sunset," I said.

"From the royal granaries, my Pharaoh?"

"From the royal. And the bill, to the Temple."

Nebamun allowed himself a barely perceptible smile. And bowed.

* * *
When I told this to those seated, loudly, from the steps of the temple, a hundred men at first did not believe it. Then someone shouted. Then all shouted, not steadily, not in unison, but all at once, each as he pleased, and leapt up, and embraced, and slapped one another's dusty backs so that white clouds rose over the square.

But Neferhotep did not shout. He came right up to me and said quietly:

"My Pharaoh. Thank you." He paused. "And now, may I show you something? Not here. Up there. In your tomb."

"What?"

The foreman was silent for a long time. Behind him the workmen were celebrating.

"Five days ago," he said at last, "when we were still working, my stonecutters were cutting the lower corridor. The deepest. Where the chamber for the sarcophagus will be." He lowered his voice. "And they broke through a wall."

"What wall?"

"One that should not have been there, my Pharaoh," said Neferhotep. "Behind it is a room. Old. Very old. Older than all the tombs in these hills. Older, perhaps, than the Pharaohs themselves." He swallowed. "My men do not want to go down there. Not one. Not even for double ration." He looked at me. "The Wise Woman says: do not touch. She says it is not a house of the dead. It is a house of those who wait."

* * *
The Wise Woman was named Tausert. She lived in the last house on the street, by the northern wall, a small, low one, with a door painted blue and an eye drawn over the threshold in red ochre.

Neferhotep took me to her before leading me up. "It is the custom, my Pharaoh," he said, "to go to the Wise Woman before the dead. She knows what they need." Iti followed us with his tablet under his arm. Senusret came last, with his sword.

Tausert sat on the threshold of her house, on a low stool, a small, dry, very old woman with a face so thickly lined that it seemed hewn from the same yellow stone as the hills around. She wore a simple linen dress, and around her neck a necklace of blue faience beads and small amulets: an Eye, a scarab, a tiny figure of the dwarf Bes, who drives off evil spirits. Her hair was grey, braided into dozens of thin plaits. Her eyes were black, bright, alive.

Before her on a mat lay potsherds. Dozens of potsherds, fragments of jars, flat flakes of limestone, and on each something was drawn. I bent down. On one, a cat standing on its hind legs, with a shepherd's crook, was herding a flock of geese. On another, a mouse in the crown of Pharaoh rode in a chariot drawn by dogs and shot a bow at a fortress on whose walls cats were defending themselves. On a third, a donkey in priest's vestments, with a censer, was solemnly proclaiming something before an altar on which lay a bundle of hay.

I could not help it; I laughed.

Tausert raised her black eyes to me. And smiled, toothless, sly.

"You like it, son of Ra?" she said. Her voice was creaking, like an unoiled door. "The boys draw these. The painters' apprentices. When they are learning. They are not yet allowed on the tomb walls; they would spoil them. So they draw on potsherds." She took up the sherd with the priest-donkey. "This one Hui drew. Twenty years ago. When he was an apprentice. They nearly threw him out of the gang for it; someone showed the sherd to a priest from the temple." She laughed. "The priest did not understand. Thought it was about some other priest."

"And the mouse-Pharaoh?" I asked.

"The mouse-Pharaoh," said Tausert, "is about all Pharaohs, son of Ra. Do not take offence. Boys always draw kings as mice. And then they grow up and paint them as gods on tomb walls." She shrugged. "One does not hinder the other. A god too is sometimes a mouse, when he must squeeze through a narrow crack."

* * *
"Sit, son of Ra," she said, nodding at the ground before her. "You have not come to me. You have come to that room below. But before you go there, tell me your dream."

"What dream?"

"The one that comes to you every night," said Tausert. "These last two moons. I see it in your eyes. You have the eyes of a man who wakes in a cold sweat and cannot for a long time make out where he is."

I sat on the ground. Iti sat beside me. Senusret remained standing.

"I dream," I said slowly, "that I stand between columns. Enormous ones. In darkness. And someone raises a hand. And I do not see the face."

Tausert nodded. Without surprise. She reached to a shelf by the door, took a bundle, old papyrus, worn, tied with twine. Unrolled it on her knees.

"The Book of Dreams," she said. "A priest of Hermopolis wrote it. Long ago. Two hundred years ago. In it are all the dreams a man can see. And what they mean." She ran her finger along the lines. "Listen."

She read slowly, in a chant, as prayers are read:

"'If a man sees himself in a dream gazing at a great cat, good: it means he will have a great harvest. If a man sees himself in a dream drinking warm beer, bad: it means suffering will come to him. If a man sees himself in a dream gazing into a deep well, bad: it means he will be cast into prison. If a man sees himself in a dream gazing at the moon when it shines, good: it means the god will forgive him.'" Tausert turned the sheet. "'If a man sees himself in a dream between two columns in darkness...'"

She fell silent.

"What?" I asked.

Tausert looked at the line for a long time. Then raised her eyes to me.

"Here it is erased," she said. "The line is there. The beginning is there. And the end is erased. As though someone scraped it off." She ran a fingernail across the papyrus. "'Good' or 'bad' cannot be seen. What it means cannot be seen."

"So no one knows?"

"So," said Tausert, "the priest who wrote the book knew. And whoever erased it knew too. And did not want others to know." She rolled up the papyrus. "For forty years I have read this book to people. Only this line has always been erased. I thought, by time. Now I think not."

* * *
"Then I shall tell you myself," said Tausert. "Not by the book. From myself."

She took my hand. Turned it palm up. Looked for a long time. Then ran her finger across the palm, dry, rough, like a piece of papyrus.

"Smooth," she said quietly. "Like a child's. Like a stone the water has rolled." She raised her eyes. "For a man with a smooth palm to see himself between columns in darkness is neither good nor bad, son of Ra. It is a door. You stand in a doorway. The columns are its jambs. The darkness is what lies beyond."

"And the hand? That rises?"

Tausert was silent for a long time.

"A hand," she said at last, "can open a door. Can close it. Can push through it. Can hold one on the threshold." She released my palm. "You see only the hand. You do not see whose it is. And you do not see what it is doing." She paused. "When you see, you will know whether it is good or bad."

"And if I do not see?"

"Then, son of Ra," said the Wise Woman, "you will see this dream again. And again. Until you see." She smiled. "All dreams repeat until they are dreamed to the end."

Beside me Iti was writing quietly. I saw his brush trembling.

"And one thing more," said Tausert. "Below, in that room which my boys broke into. Take nothing. Touch nothing. Only look." She paused. "And if you find an empty place there, do not try to fill it. It waits not for you. It waits for what you will have."

* * *
The tomb, my house of eternity, began at the top, at the very ridge, with a wide rectangular entrance framed by two pillars not yet finished, with a red grid of guide-lines marked in ochre on the limestone. From the entrance a corridor went down into the depth of the rock, straight, level, slightly sloping, so long that its far end was lost in darkness.

Neferhotep went ahead with a lamp. After him, I. Then Iti. Then Senusret. Then two masters whom Neferhotep had called with him: the painter Hui, thin, nervous, pale-faced, not yet recovered from his faint on the scaffolding, his fingers smeared with red and black paint to the wrists, and the carver Ipui, huge, slow, silent, with a chisel stuck in his belt and so calm a face that nothing in the world seemed able to surprise him.

The walls of the corridor were already dressed, smooth, even, white. On some, a red grid: squares ruled in ochre, and in the squares sketches of future paintings. Gods. Stars. The barque of the sun. The serpent Apep. The twelve gates of the Duat. I recognised them from Amenemope's tales, from the scrolls of the Epic, from the night by the pool.

"Here," said Hui, stopping by one wall and raising his lamp higher. "Here you will be, my Pharaoh. Before Osiris. At the judgment." He pointed to the red sketch: a man in the double crown stood before a throne on which sat a god with a green face, and between them, scales. "And here, your heart on the scales. And here, the feather." He paused. "I have not yet decided what colour to make the feather. White or gold. As my Pharaoh wishes?"

"What should it be?"

Hui hesitated.

"By the rules, white, my Pharaoh. But..." He blushed. "I dreamed it was gold. Three nights running. The feather, gold, and the heart lighter than it. And the scales swing, and swing... and do not stop."

"Make it gold, Hui," I said.

The painter beamed.

And Ipui the carver, who all this time had not spoken a word, suddenly ran his enormous palm over the white wall, slowly, tenderly, as one strokes a sleeping child, and said in a low, resonant voice:

"The stone here is good, my Pharaoh. Quiet. It will not crack." He paused. "You will live here long. Millions of years." He paused again. "If you wish."

"If I wish?"

Ipui looked at me with calm, dark eyes.

"My grandfather cut stone for the former Pharaoh," he said. "The one whose name was later erased. Grandfather said that Pharaoh came to his tomb once. Looked. Stroked the wall. And said: 'Good work. A pity I shall not live here.'" The carver paused. "Grandfather thought he was joking. And then he really was not buried here. The tomb stands empty. Over there, in the neighbouring hollow." Ipui stroked the wall again. "A good tomb. Quiet stone. Empty."

* * *
The corridor ended. Beyond it, a staircase hewn in the rock, steep, narrow, leading down. Then another corridor, unfinished, rough, with undressed walls, with heaps of rubble on the floor. Then a large chamber, square, with four pillars left standing in the rock, the future chamber of the sarcophagus, still unworked, rough, smelling of dust and freshly split stone.

And in its far wall, a hole.

Uneven, ragged, with sharp edges, as though someone had struck with a mallet and the stone had simply fallen inward. Man-high. Beyond it, darkness.

And from there came air. Dry. Warm. Smelling not of dust, not of stone, but of something else. Something sweet and bitter at once. Like honey and wormwood.

Neferhotep halted ten paces from the hole. Hui behind him, pale as flax. Ipui motionless, as always.

"I shall go no farther, my Pharaoh," said the foreman quietly. "Forgive me." He held out the lamp to me. "The Wise Woman said: only look. Touch nothing."

I took the lamp. Stepped toward the hole.

"My Pharaoh," said Senusret. His voice was strained. "Let me go first."

"No, Senusret."

"My Pharaoh..."

"Stand at the entrance," I said. "As there, at Luxor. Be where you can do something."

Senusret looked at me for a long time. Then nodded, curtly, heavily, and took his place by the hole, with his back to the wall, his sword drawn.

Iti stepped after me. I turned.

"My Pharaoh," he said. Quietly. "If there is script, you need someone who reads it." He paused. "Two words. But still."

I nodded.

And we went in.

* * *
The room was round.

That was the first thing I understood when I raised the lamp. Not square, not rectangular like all rooms in all tombs, in all temples, in all palaces of the Two Lands, but round. Perfectly. Like a bowl. Like a well. Like a circle.

Its walls were smooth. Not dressed with a chisel, but smooth, even, as though they had not been hewn from the rock but cast. The stone was not yellow limestone as everywhere in these hills, but dark, almost black, with a barely visible sheen, like water at night. And on those walls, from floor to ceiling, in a ring, without beginning and without end, ran the script.

Long, flowing, curving lines. Running into one another without a break. Not carved, no. I brought the lamp closer. They were neither carved nor painted. They were inside the stone. Beneath the surface. Like veins in marble. Like lines on the skin of an old scroll that I had never seen but somehow remembered, ingrained so deep that they had become part of it.

And they glowed.

Faintly. Dimly, palely, on the very verge of the visible. When I lowered the lamp, the glow became more noticeable. Weak, bluish, like the light of stars reflected in water.

Beside me Iti stopped breathing.

"My Pharaoh," he whispered. "This... these are not our signs. Nor the temple's. They are hers. The script. The whole room. All of it."

I raised the lamp to the ceiling.

The ceiling was a dome. Low, smooth, dark. And on it, stars. Not painted, also inside the stone, like the script, tiny, glowing points, hundreds, thousands. I recognised Sah, Osiris striding across the sky, with his belt of three stars. Recognised Sopdet, white, bright, at the very edge of the dome. Recognised the Imperishable, circling an invisible point in the north.

But there were others. Which I did not know. At the bottom of the dome, at its edge, to the south, four stars. Bright. In a cross.

"Four stars. In a cross. The sailor of Amenemope had seen them in the south, when a storm carried his ship beyond Punt."

"Those stars cannot be seen from here, my Pharaoh," Iti whispered. "Never. Seneb said the sky is the same everywhere. And here..."

"Here is the sky that is seen from everywhere at once," I said. And did not myself understand where those words came from.

* * *
In the very middle of the round room stood a bench. Stone. Low. Dark as the walls. And on it two hollows. Small, round, smooth. Each the size of a nut. Side by side. A palm's breadth apart.

Empty.

I looked at them and felt the cold rise from beneath my ribs, on the left. Slowly, inexorably, like water in the well of the nilometer in a good year.

Two hollows. The size of a nut. Exactly for two stones.

The stones that now lay in a casket of black wood, bound at the corners, in the treasury of the Temple. That Khemu had seen in her vision, in my hands. That Nefer-Ka had promised to give me "as the First Ones gave them," at Luxor, in the inner court of the god.

"If you find an empty place there, do not try to fill it. It waits not for you. It waits for what you will have."

"My Pharaoh," Iti said quietly. "Look. Above the bench."

I raised the lamp.

Above the bench, on the wall, the script broke off. There was a window, a small square, outlined by a thin line, and in it, not script. An image. Also inside the stone, also glowing with a dim blue light.

Two doors. Side by side. Wall to wall. One open, the other closed. And between them, on the threshold, with its back to the viewer, a figure. Tall. With a raised hand. And in each hand, a disc. One dark. The other light.

And beneath the image, a line. Not script. Signs. Ours. Hieroglyphs. But so ancient, so angular, so unlike the present ones that I barely recognised familiar outlines in them.

Iti was already on his knees before the bench, face raised to the line, lips moving.

"'Here...'" he whispered. "'Here waits...'" He faltered. Leaned closer. "My Pharaoh, this is very old writing. Such as was written before the First Pharaohs. In the Library there are only three scrolls in it. Amenemope taught me." He traced his finger in the air, not touching the wall. "'Here waits... the house... of him who holds both.'"

"House," I repeated.

Iti nodded. Then shifted his gaze, from the hieroglyphs down to the line of script that ran straight beneath them. Short. Of the same length.

"My Pharaoh," he said. His voice trembled. "This is again... this is again as in the seventh scroll. Our signs, and beside them, theirs. The same thing." He swallowed. "This sign. In the middle. With the two loops. It stands where ours has 'house.'"

He turned to me. His eyes were shining, huge, dark, wet.

"My Pharaoh. We know three words. 'Keep.' 'Appointed time.' And 'house.'"

* * *
I do not remember how long we stayed there. Iti copied, all he could, by the light of a single lamp, onto his tablet, small, quick, without lifting his head. I stood by the bench and looked at the two empty hollows. I did not touch them. The Wise Woman had said not to touch.

But I stretched out a hand over them, not touching, a palm's breadth above. And felt.

Warmth.

Faint. Even. As if from stones that were not there. As if they had lain there quite recently and gone, leaving warmth behind, as a man leaves it who has just risen from his bed.

Or as if they lie there now. Only not here. In another place. In another time. And I feel their warmth through... through what?

I snatched my hand back.

"Iti," I said. "It is time."

He raised his head. Looked at me. Then at the two empty hollows.

"My Pharaoh," he said quietly. "These are for them. For the two Eyes. Are they not?"

"I do not know, Iti."

"You do," he said. Simply. "You do not remember. But you know."

I did not answer.

* * *
When we climbed out of the round room back into the unfinished sarcophagus chamber, Senusret was standing at the hole just as before, with his back to the wall, his sword drawn. His face was grey.

"My Pharaoh," he said through his teeth. "While you were in there. Here... here someone passed."

"Who?"

"I do not know." He did not lower his sword. "Past me. That way," he nodded at the hole. "I did not see. I felt. Like wind. Like cold. As though someone very tall passed close by and brushed me with a shoulder." Senusret swallowed. "I struck with my sword. Air."

"We saw no one," said Iti.

"I know," said Senusret. "He cannot be seen."

Neferhotep, waiting by the stair, seized the amulet of the dwarf Bes at his neck and began to mutter protective words. Hui stood white as flax. Ipui, motionless, as always. He alone looked not at the hole but at me.

"It is he, my Pharaoh," said the carver in his resonant, calm voice. "Grandfather used to say. When that Pharaoh, whose name was erased, came to his tomb, someone was always beside him. Invisible. The workmen felt it, like wind." Ipui paused. "Grandfather said it was his shadow. Only longer than it ought to be."

* * *
I ordered the hole walled up.

Not the room destroyed: walled up. Carefully. With stone. So that no one would know what lay behind it. And on the new masonry to be carved a simple sign. Only one. The Eye.

"My Pharaoh," said Neferhotep, when I gave the order. "We are building you a house of eternity." He paused. "But it seems someone built you a house before us."

"It seems so," I said.

"What are we to do with your tomb? Continue?"

I thought. Of the empty tomb in the neighbouring hollow. Of the Pharaoh with the erased name who said: "Good work. A pity I shall not live here."

"Continue, Neferhotep," I said. "Build well. Evenly. On full stomachs." I paused. "Even if I do not live here, someone will. A good house does not stand empty."

The foreman looked at me for a long time. Then bowed, low, lower than he had bowed at the gate.

"Ipui," he said, not straightening. "Did you hear? A good house does not stand empty. Carve it. Above the entrance. Small. So that only we can see."

"I shall carve it," said Ipui.

* * *
As we descended to the village the sun was setting behind the western hills, to where, it was said, the lands of the dead began, where Ra every evening entered the mouth of heavenly Nut.

On the square before the temple it smelled of fried fish and fresh bread. The first sacks from the royal granaries had already arrived, and the women of the village, laughing and calling to one another, were baking flatbreads in clay ovens right in the street. Children ran among the ovens snatching hot pieces. The workmen sat by the walls drinking beer from jugs, and someone was already singing, loudly, off-key, merrily.

Tausert sat on the threshold of her blue house. Seeing me, she raised her hand.

I went up.

"Did you find the empty place, son of Ra?" she asked.

"I did."

"Did you touch nothing?"

"I touched nothing."

She nodded. Contentedly. Then held out a potsherd to me. One of those that lay on the mat before her. I took it.

On it a mouse was drawn. In the crown of Pharaoh. But not in a chariot, not with a bow. The mouse stood at a door. Between two doors. One open. The other closed. And in the mouse's paws, two discs. Dark and light.

"Hui did not draw this," said Tausert. "I found it. Forty years ago. In the dust, at the entrance to that hollow where the empty tomb is." She paused. "Forty years I kept it. Wondering whom to give it to." She looked at me with black, shining eyes. "To you."

"Why a mouse?"

Tausert laughed, creakingly, toothlessly.

"I told you, son of Ra," she said. "A god too is sometimes a mouse. When he must squeeze through a narrow crack. Between two doors."

* * *
On the way back, in the chariot, in the dusk, down the stony road, into the valley, toward the river, toward the capital, Iti rode beside me. Senusret drove, silent, not turning. Nebamun with the other chariot had fallen behind; he had stayed in the village to count sacks.

"My Pharaoh," said Iti quietly, so Senusret would not hear. "Three words."

"Three words."

"'Keep.' 'Appointed time.' 'House.'" He paused. "If put together... 'Keep the house until the appointed time.' Or 'The house keeps until the appointed time.' Or..." He faltered.

"Or?"

Iti was looking at the dark valley below, where the lights of the capital were already kindling.

"Or 'The appointed time keeps the house,'" he said. "'It is time to return home.'" He paused. "I do not know, my Pharaoh. I do not know in what order their words go. Perhaps in the reverse. Perhaps in a circle."

"In a circle," I said.

Iti looked at me.

"Like an inscription that reads in both directions?" he asked. "I have read of such. In the Greek scrolls. There is one in the Library." He paused. "If in a circle, the beginning is where you begin to read."

"And where do you begin?"

Iti was silent for a long time. The chariot bounced on the stones. Below, in the valley, the lights of the capital grew brighter and brighter.

"Where you stand, my Pharaoh," he said at last. "Always where you stand."

Four days remained until the new moon.

## Vision VII. The Safe House

I do not know how I came to be on that staircase.

That is the first thing worth saying, and, as always in such dreams, the only thing I am sure of. I remember the wet steps. Dark, chipped, smelling of cats, cabbage and paraffin. I remember the banisters, cast iron, cold, sticky with damp. I remember that I was climbing, the third floor, the fourth, and that on every landing a tiny paraffin lamp burned, stinking and smoking, and that behind every door someone was there: I heard voices, a child crying, coughing, the clink of dishes.

And I remember that as I climbed I kept a hand in my pocket. And that in the hand was something. Small. Smooth. Warm.

I did not look at what it was. I knew, for some reason, that I must not look.

* * *
On the fifth floor, at the last door, I stopped.

The door was upholstered in oilcloth, black, cracked, with tufts of wadding sticking out of the tears. A number in chalk: "17." There was no bell. Above the door, a tiny window pasted over with newspaper.

I knocked. Three times. I do not know why three. My hand knocked so of itself.

Silence. Then footsteps. Light, cautious. Then a voice. A woman's. From behind the door, quietly:

"Who is it?"

I opened my mouth, and did not know what to say. I did not know who I was. I did not know why I had come. I did not know who was behind the door.

And I said, not understanding where the words came from:

"The time has come."

The silence behind the door changed. Grew dense. Tense. Then the sound of a bolt drawn back. One. A second. A third. A chain. The door opened the width of a palm.

In the gap, an eye. Grey, attentive, tired. And the edge of a face, pale, thin, a woman's.

"Repeat that," she said.

"The time has come," I repeated.

The eye looked at me for a long time. Then the chain clinked, and the door opened.

* * *
Her name was Agnia Pavlovna. I learned that later. At the time I saw only a small, straight, very thin woman of about forty, in a dark woollen skirt, a knitted cardigan, a pince-nez on a cord, her hair pulled into a tight knot at the nape, a teacher, I understood at once, though no one had told me so. Teachers always have such a straight back. And such a look.

Like that other one. In the suit the colour of wet asphalt. With a cane. In the coworking space of a hotel by a lake that I had never seen.

I blinked. The vision passed.

"Are you from Helsingfors?" Agnia Pavlovna asked quietly, closing the door behind me on all three bolts and the chain. "From the Finnish comrades?"

I did not know what Helsingfors was. But I nodded.

"We expected you yesterday," she said. "The password was to have been different. 'Auntie from Vyborg sends her regards.'" She looked at me over her pince-nez. "And you said 'the time has come.'"

"Forgive me," I said. "I... mixed it up."

"Mixed it up," Agnia Pavlovna repeated. Not taking her eyes from me. "Do you know what is strange? 'The time has come' is the password for tomorrow. For the twenty-fifth. Four people in all Petersburg know it." She paused. "And you."

I was silent. I did not know what to answer.

Agnia Pavlovna looked at me a moment longer. Then suddenly smiled wearily.

"Well, if you know it, you are one of ours," she said. "A stranger would not know." She turned. "Come in. Only quietly. The Old Man is asleep."

* * *
The flat was small, two rooms and a kitchen, but there were so many people in it that they seemed not to fit. Someone sat on the windowsill. Someone on the floor, on a spread greatcoat. Someone at a table heaped with papers, newspapers, leaflets. It smelled of makhorka, wet cloth, paraffin and fried onion. On the table burned a lamp under a green shade, and in the corner, on a stool, stood a samovar, potbellied, copper, polished to a shine, the only thing in that flat, it seemed, that anyone loved.

The door to the second room was shut.

"The Old Man is in there," Agnia Pavlovna whispered, nodding toward it. "Don't make noise. He hasn't slept for two days." She paused. "Tonight he goes there."

"Where?"

Agnia Pavlovna looked at me as though I had asked what colour the sky was.

"To Smolny," she said. And went off to the kitchen.

* * *
The first to notice me was the sailor.

Huge, broad-shouldered, with red stubble on his cheeks, in a pea-jacket thrown open over a striped undershirt, in a sailor's cap pushed back on his head with ribbons to his shoulders. A machine-gun belt over his shoulder, crosswise. A Mauser in a wooden holster at his belt. He sat on the windowsill cracking sunflower seeds and spitting the husks into his fist, and at the sight of me he stopped chewing.

"And who's this?" he asked. His voice was thick, with the northern "o."

"From Helsingfors," Agnia Pavlovna answered from the kitchen. "A courier."

"A courier," the sailor repeated. Jumped down from the sill. Came up close to me. Looked down at me, he was a head taller. "Why so pale, courier? Seasick on the steamer?"

"Seasick," I said.

The sailor looked at me a long time. Then suddenly burst into laughter, rolling, resonant, so that the glasses rattled in the sideboard.

"Quiet, Kuzma!" Agnia Pavlovna hissed from the kitchen. "You'll wake the Old Man!"

"Quiet, quiet," the sailor boomed, wiping away tears. "Seasick! In Helsingfors!" He clapped me on the shoulder so that I barely kept my feet. "Kuzma Boyko. Baltic Fleet. From the *Aurora*. From near Vologda, born." He held out his palm, huge, hard as a plank. "And what do they call you, courier?"

From near Vologda. Kuzma. Forty years old. Somewhere I had heard... seen... On a glowing screen, in an endless stream of names: "Kuzma, 40 years old, from Vologda."

I had never seen glowing screens.

"I don't remember," I said.

Kuzma stopped smiling.

"What do you mean, you don't remember?"

"I don't remember," I repeated. "I was... shell-shocked. Long ago. I don't remember much."

The sailor looked at me. For a long time. Then slowly nodded, understandingly, without mockery.

"It happens," he said. "We had one on the *Aurora*. At Moonsund a shell burst next to him, and for half a year after he didn't remember his own name. They called him 'brother.' That's what they called him." Kuzma clapped my shoulder again, this time more gently. "So you'll be 'brother' too. Until you remember."

* * *
At the table heaped with papers sat three more.

A thin, pale, very young man, about twenty, in a student's jacket with worn elbows, in spectacles with a cracked lens, with a mop of black curly hair and a gaze so burning it was as though there were a stove inside him. He was writing, fast, furiously, splattering ink, and, not raising his head, muttering under his breath.

"Grisha," Agnia Pavlovna introduced him, coming back from the kitchen with a kettle. "A student. Writing a leaflet. Third day writing one and the same leaflet. Can't finish it."

"Because the words are wrong!" Grisha cried, flinging down his pen. "Wrong, Agnia Pavlovna! Every soldier, every worker, every woman at the market must read it and understand! The first time! And mine comes out like a professor's! 'The historic moment... dialectical necessity...'" He clutched his head. "Who will understand that?!"

"I will," said Kuzma imperturbably from the windowsill.

"You will! You read Marx on the *Aurora*! But the woman on Sennaya won't!"

"Then write it as Kuzma talks," said Agnia Pavlovna, pouring me tea. "'No bread, an end to the war, land to the peasant.' Three lines. A woman will understand."

Grisha looked at her in horror.

"But that's... that's primitive!"

"It's true," said Agnia Pavlovna. "And truth is always primitive. Only a lie is complicated."

The second at the table was an old man, dry, stooped, with long grey moustaches and hands black to the elbows with printer's ink. Before him stood a box, wooden, divided into dozens of little compartments, and in each, leaden letters. He picked them out with tweezers, one by one, and set them in a metal frame, line after line. Fast. Without looking.

"Stepan Yerofeyevich," said Agnia Pavlovna. "Compositor. Forty years in the print shop. Set *Iskra* itself." She lowered her voice. "They say he can set any text with his eyes shut. Backward. In mirror image."

The third sat silently in the corner by the stove. Fair-haired, stocky, with a broad, weathered, impenetrable face and eyes so light they seemed transparent. In a leather jacket. With a pipe in his teeth, unlit. He said not a word. Only nodded to me, briefly, barely perceptibly.

"Toivo," said Agnia Pavlovna. "A Finn. He will lead the Old Man." And, not waiting for questions, went off to the kitchen again.

* * *
I sat on the edge of a sagging sofa, holding a glass of tea, hot, sweet, made of carrots, and listened.

They talked about tomorrow. About Smolny. About the bridges, which to raise, which to hold. About the cadets in the palace. About Kerensky, who, rumour had it, was already preparing to flee. About the *Aurora*, which stood by Nikolaevsky Bridge awaiting the signal. They talked fast, in low voices, interrupting one another, street names, regiment numbers, surnames I did not know.

And about the Old Man. All the time about the Old Man.

"The Old Man said: today, or it will be too late." "The Old Man wrote a letter to the Central Committee, scolding again." "The Old Man said to pass to Podvoisky..." "The Old Man says: delay is like death."

I looked at the closed door of the second room. Dark, painted, with a brass handle. No light came from under it.

"Is he really in there?" I asked Kuzma in a low voice.

"And how," said the sailor, not ceasing to crack seeds. "Third day he sits. Writes. Sleeps two hours." He spat out a husk. "I've never seen him myself, brother. Though I guard him." He grinned. "Funny, eh? I guard him, and haven't seen him. He doesn't leave the room. Agnia Pavlovna brings him tea. And we're out here."

"No one has seen him?"

"Toivo has," said Kuzma. "Toivo brought him from Finland. On a locomotive. As a stoker." He glanced at the Finn. "But Toivo won't tell. Toivo doesn't talk at all. I reckon he knows twenty words of Russian. Half of them swearing."

By the stove Toivo smiled very slightly. So he understood more than twenty.

* * *
Toward midnight Stepan Yerofeyevich finished his setting.

He laid aside the tweezers, stretched, his joints cracked, took a handkerchief from his pocket and for a long time wiped his black fingers. Then looked at me. For the first time all evening.

"You," he said hoarsely. "Courier. Come here."

I went over.

"Can you read?" asked the old man.

"I can."

"And backward?"

He turned toward me the metal frame with its set text. The leaden letters stood in rows, shining, grey, reversed. Mirrored. I saw them backward, right to left, as in a mirror. And yet I read. Easily. As though that were how it should be read.

"*A roza upala na lapu Azora.*"

A rose fell on the paw of Azor. Azor, a dog's name. Nonsense.

"That is not a leaflet," I said.

"Not a leaflet," the old man agreed. Narrowed his eyes slyly. "It is a test. I give it to every new man. Twenty years. Do you know what is special about it?"

I looked at the line. Right to left. Left to right. The letters stood in the frame, and read the same from both ends.

"It reads the same," I said slowly. "From the beginning and from the end. In both directions."

Stepan Yerofeyevich looked at me for a long time. Then nodded.

"Fet thought it up," he said. "The poet. A landowner. Against us, they say. But he thought up a good line." He paused. "Twenty years I have been giving it to new men. Do you know how many read it backward at the first try?"

"How many?"

"You are the second," said the old man.

"And the first?"

The compositor was silent for a long time. Twisted his moustache.

"The first was long ago," he said at last. "In nineteen-five. Also a courier. Also without a name. Also said he was shell-shocked." He looked at me over his spectacles. "Also looked like you. Though I was younger then, my eyes better. Perhaps he did not look like you."

"What became of him?"

"Who knows," said Stepan Yerofeyevich. "In December, at Presnya, in Moscow, he was last seen. On a barricade. Standing at the very top. Under fire. And reading aloud, backward. This very line. Laughing." The old man paused. "And then a shell. And he was gone. No body, nothing. As if dissolved."

He took one letter from the frame, a leaden "A." Held it out to me.

"Take it," he said. "As a keepsake. The first. The one it begins with. And ends with."

I took it. The leaden letter was cold, and at once grew warm in my palm.

* * *
"Riddles!" Kuzma suddenly announced from the windowsill, evidently deciding the room was too quiet. "Whoever guesses gets a rusk! The last one!"

"Kuzma," said Agnia Pavlovna wearily. "The Old Man is sleeping."

"I'll ask quietly," Kuzma whispered in a deafening whisper. "A naval one. Our boatswain on the *Aurora* used to ask it. 'What does a sailor always have underfoot, that on land he hasn't?'"

"The deck," I said.

Kuzma stared at me.

"How do you know? That's ours, a Baltic one!"

"I don't know," I said. "I heard it somewhere."

Somewhere. From someone. Huge, grey-moustached, in a striped undershirt, in a cubbyhole under pennants. A basement. A radio. Weather forecasts for the sea.

"All right," said Kuzma, narrowing his eyes. "Then guess this one. 'The ship has gone, but the wake remains. The ship has sunk, but the wake sails on. What wake is it?'"

I was silent. I knew the answer. I knew that few knew it. That in thirty years no one had guessed it. That the answer was "a voice." A voice that sounds in those who heard it, even when the person is gone.

"A voice," I said.

Kuzma slowly climbed down from the windowsill. Came to me. Sat beside me on the sofa; the sofa groaned under him.

"Brother," he said quietly, quite without joking. "That riddle is known on the whole Baltic Fleet to three men. Me, my late boatswain, he brought it from Piraeus, and one old engineer in Kronstadt. That's all." He looked at me. "How do you know it?"

"I don't know, Kuzma."

The sailor was silent for a long time. Then took a rusk from his pea-jacket pocket, the last, and put it in my hand.

"Here," he said. "You've earned it." He paused. "And if you remember how you know it, tell me. All right? I'm curious. My boatswain said someone gave him that riddle. In Piraeus. At night. On the quay. A man without a name. Who afterwards went off into the sea. On foot. On the water."

* * *
Grisha the student finally finished his leaflet.

He leapt up from the table, waving a sheet, pale, dishevelled, with an ink stain on his cheek, his eyes burning behind the cracked spectacles.

"Done!" he whispered. "Agnia Pavlovna! Done! Three lines! As you said!" He read aloud, gasping: "'Bread! Peace! Land! All power to the Soviets!'" He choked with rapture. "Every woman will understand!"

"Every woman will understand," Agnia Pavlovna agreed, taking the sheet. "Stepan Yerofeyevich, will you set it?"

"I'll set it," said the old man. "By morning. A thousand copies."

Grisha sat on the sofa beside me, on the other side from Kuzma, and suddenly, without any transition, as very young people do, whose whole life is one continuous transition, turned to me.

"Do you believe?" he asked. In a whisper. Hotly.

"In what?"

"In what will be tomorrow!" His eyes burned. "In what we shall do! A new world! No tsars, no landlords, no wars! Where everyone is a human being! Where no one goes hungry! Where children study, not work in factories twelve hours a day!" He seized my hand. "In a hundred years, imagine, in a hundred years people will fly to the Moon! They will talk to one another across the ocean without wires! They will live to a hundred! Machines will think for them!" He laughed. "Do you believe?"

Machines will think for them.

A room with a cold light. A window on a table, glowing without fire. Lines running across the glass. "Who am I?" "Who are you?" "That is not enough."

"I believe," I said. My voice trembled. "They will."

Grisha beamed.

"You see!" he said to Kuzma. "The courier believes!"

"The courier is shell-shocked," Kuzma grumbled. "It's all one to him."

But I saw how he looked at me. Long. With some strange, heavy expression.

* * *
Toward one in the morning Stepan Yerofeyevich, sorting a stack of old newspapers on which he laid out the leaden letters, suddenly swore.

"What on earth is this?" he muttered. "Agnia Pavlovna! Where's this from?"

He held a sheet of newspaper. An ordinary one. Greyish. Folded in two. Under it, judging by the stains, bread had lain.

Agnia Pavlovna came over and looked.

"Gosha brought that," she said. "The neighbour from below. Yesterday. He wrapped bread in it when he gave us some." She took the sheet. Held it to the lamp. And froze.

I stood. Went over.

The newspaper was called *Pravda*. I recognised the type, the same as on the leaflets on the table. But all the rest...

The date. At the very top. Small.

"13 April 1961."

Beneath it, in enormous letters across the whole front page:

"MAN IN SPACE!"

And a photograph. A young man in a helmet, smiling, broadly, openly, as people smile who have just done what no one before them has done. And beside it, lower, another photograph. An elderly, stout, bald man in a light suit, a hat held in his hand, also smiling, slyly, peasant-fashion, standing on a rostrum and waving to someone.

The caption beneath him: "N. S. Khrushchev greets..."

Then torn off. Where the bread had been.

* * *
The room fell very quiet.

"Nineteen sixty-one," Stepan Yerofeyevich said slowly. "One thousand nine hundred and sixty-one."

"A misprint," said Agnia Pavlovna. Her voice was level, but the fingers holding the paper were trembling. "The compositor erred. Instead of 'seventeen' he put..."

"A compositor," the old man repeated, "cannot err like that. I have been setting type for forty years. 'Sixty-one' and 'seventeen' are different cases. Different boxes. It is not a misprint." He jabbed a finger at the photograph. "And this? 'Man in space.' What is that?"

Grisha snatched the newspaper. His eyes behind the cracked spectacles grew huge.

"A man... in space," he whispered. "Agnia Pavlovna! A man in space! It is exactly what I was saying! It is..." He held the paper up to the light. "*Pravda*. Our *Pravda*! In forty-four years!" He laughed, thin, hysterical. "So we shall win! So everything will be! So..."

"So someone's joking," Kuzma cut in. He stood by the window, huge, grim. "A provocation. The Okhrana. Though it's gone, the people are left. Planted it to drive us out of our minds."

"Who would need that?" asked Agnia Pavlovna.

No one answered.

I looked at the photograph. At the stout, bald, smiling man in the light suit on the rostrum. I did not know him. I had never seen him. The name told me nothing.

And yet something in him, in that sly, peasant smile, in that raised hand, seemed familiar. As a face is familiar that one has glimpsed in a crowd, in another city, in another life. Not him himself. But what stands behind him. The time that stands behind him.

A time that had not yet come.

"Give it," Toivo said suddenly.

Everyone turned. The Finn had not uttered a word all evening. Now he stood by the stove, hand outstretched.

Grisha gave him the newspaper.

Toivo looked at it for a long time with his light, transparent eyes. Then folded it in four. And, without another word, thrust it into the stove.

The paper flared. At once. Brightly. White, not yellow, not orange, as paper burns, but white, blinding, as magnesium flares. For one moment the whole room was flooded with that white light.

And went out.

Not even ash was left in the stove.

"It is not for us," said Toivo. In Russian. Clean. Without accent. "It is for him." He nodded at me. "He has already read it. Enough."

And sat down again by the stove, and put the unlit pipe in his teeth, and did not say another word. Until morning.

* * *
At two in the night Agnia Pavlovna knocked at the closed door.

Three times.

From within, silence. Then a rustle. The creak of floorboards. A voice, I heard it, low, hoarse, indistinct, through the door, something brief.

"It is time," said Agnia Pavlovna, without opening the door. "Toivo is ready."

Toivo rose from the stove. Buttoned his jacket. Put on his cap. Went to the door.

"Everyone to the kitchen," said Agnia Pavlovna. "Quickly. Don't look."

"Why not look?" I asked.

Agnia Pavlovna looked at me over her pince-nez.

"Because he is in disguise," she said. "A wig. A bandage on his cheek. As if he had toothache. If any of you falls into the cadets' hands, he can honestly say he did not see." She paused. "So it was decided. So it is right."

We went to the kitchen. Kuzma, Grisha, Stepan Yerofeyevich, I. Agnia Pavlovna drew the door to behind us. Left a gap, a small one. A finger's width.

I stood at that gap. I did not look. I honestly did not look.

I heard. The creak of the second room's door. Steps, quick, small, energetic. A voice, short, burring, hurried, asked Toivo something. Toivo answered in Finnish. The rustle of an overcoat. The knock of heels in the hall. The sound of bolts drawn back, one, two, three. The clink of the chain.

The slam of a door.

And silence.

* * *
When we came out of the kitchen there was no one in the hall. Agnia Pavlovna was shooting the bolts.

And on the table, under the green lamp, lay what he had left. Forgotten. Or on purpose.

A cap. Old, worn, with a torn peak. And beside it, a strip of white cloth rolled into a ball. The bandage. The one that was to have been on his cheek.

"Forgot," said Agnia Pavlovna in confusion. "He forgot the bandage. Good God. Without it... they will recognise him..."

"They won't," said Kuzma. "No one knows him by face. Only by the portraits in the papers. And in the portraits he has a beard. And he shaved the beard." The sailor paused. "I haven't seen him myself. Three days I guarded him, and didn't see. Funny."

I went to the table. Looked at the cap. At the bandage.

The cap was warm. It still held the warmth of someone's head.

"Did you not see him either?" I asked Agnia Pavlovna.

She was silent for a long time.

"I did," she said at last. "Three days. I carried him tea. Talked with him." She took off her pince-nez. Wiped it. Put it on again. "And now I don't remember. His face. It is as if it were erased." She looked at me. "Strange, isn't it? I am a teacher. For twenty years I have remembered all my pupils by sight. All of them. And him, I don't remember."

Like the man in grey. Like the one in the top hat, in the gallery of the church, whom I had never seen. A face that cannot be held in memory.

I said nothing.

* * *
Toward morning, when all were asleep, Kuzma on the windowsill, Grisha on the floor with his head on a stack of leaflets, Stepan Yerofeyevich at the table with his head dropped on his arms beside the box of leaden letters, I went to the window.

The city outside was dark. Wet. Quiet. With that particular quiet which a city has before a storm. Along the embankment below a patrol slowly passed, three men, with rifles, with red armbands. Somewhere far off, beyond the river, a fire burned. Above the roofs, above the spires, above the domes, a low, grey, heavy sky.

And on the other side of the street, by a lamp-post, under wet snow, stood a man.

Tall. In a grey coat. Bareheaded. Motionless.

He was looking at my window.

I could not see his face. The lamp shone at his back. I saw only a silhouette, tall, taller than human height, and the wet snow falling on his shoulders and not melting.

"Is that him?" someone asked behind my back.

I turned. Agnia Pavlovna stood in the kitchen doorway, in a shawl, with a cup in her hands. She had not slept either.

"Who is he?" I asked.

"The one who gave you the password," she said quietly. "The time has come. Four people know it. I am one of the four." She came to the window. Stood beside me. Looked at the figure by the lamp-post. "I told no one. And the other three did not either. I know them. I trust them." She paused. "So someone told it to you, a fifth. Who does not exist."

We looked at the figure by the lamp-post. The snow fell. The figure did not move.

"Agnia Pavlovna," I said. "You are a teacher. Tell me. What will happen tomorrow?"

She was silent for a long time.

"Tomorrow will be what will be," she said at last. "We shall take power. Or we shall be hanged." She paused. "And the day after, I do not know. No one knows." She looked at me. "But here is what I know. For twenty years I have taught children. Every year new ones come. Every year I tell them the same thing. 'The words you write will be read by people. Remember who will read them.'"

I stopped breathing.

"Why do you tell them that?"

"Because my teacher taught me so," said Agnia Pavlovna. "And hers, hers. It is like a password among us teachers. It is passed on."

We stood at the window. Below, by the lamp-post, the figure in grey slowly raised a hand. Did not wave. Simply raised it, palm toward us. As one raises a hand in parting. Or in greeting. Or to show that it is time.

* * *
The shot I heard in the evening.

No, I did not hear it. The vision was already falling apart, already melting, already tearing into scraps, like the newspaper in the Finn's stove. I remember only fragments. A wet embankment. A crowd. Red flags. Sailors on a lorry with machine-gun belts crosswise. Kuzma among them; he saw me in the crowd and waved his cap. Grisha on a bollard, shouting something, waving a leaflet. A huge ship by the bridge, grey, three-funnelled, with guns, and on its deck, movement.

And then a flash. White. At the bow gun.

And a sound. Dull, heavy, rolling, as though a huge bell had been struck somewhere under the water. It rolled across the river, across the embankment, across the city, and went off into the sky.

And I understood, not with the mind, with something beneath the ribs, on the left, that this sound was heard by everyone. By all of mine. By all whom I had been. The Pharaoh between the columns. The guest in a red turban on a balcony above the strait. The youth in a frock coat at the grille in the old castle. The man in the room with the cold light. The Keeper on the white Tower. All at once. In a single instant. As all who stand in one cathedral hear the stroke of a bell, though each stands in his own place.

And I understood also that something had ended. And something had begun. And that it is always so, in every city, in every century, and that I had seen it many times. And would see again.

* * *
I opened my eyes.

I do not know in which of my lives. I do not know in which city, in which century. In each of them afterward I dreamed of that staircase, wet, dark, smelling of cats and paraffin, and the door upholstered in black oilcloth, with the number "17" written in chalk.

And in each I woke with the same feeling: that I had never seen the one for whose sake all in that flat had not slept for three nights. He was in the next room. Behind a closed door. I had heard his voice. I had held his warm cap in my hands.

But his face I had not seen.

And also, in each, I woke clenching something in my fist. I opened my fingers, and there was nothing there.

But the palm remembered. A cold, heavy, warming leaden letter. The first. The one it begins with. And ends with.

"A."

## Reality IX. Kuala Lumpur

16:04 local time. Below, a city. Above, on the fifty-first floor, I.

The rain had begun at exactly four. Hakim had warned me: "At four, mister. Every day. Like prayer." I had not believed it. At 15:58 the sky was blue, cloudless, scorched to whiteness. At 16:00 it turned grey. At 16:02, black. At 16:04 it came down.

It was not rain. It was a wall. A solid, warm, roaring wall of water behind which the city vanished: skyscrapers, bridges, palms, streets, tiny cars below, everything. All that remained was the glass from floor to ceiling, down which the water ran so thickly it seemed the flat had been lowered to the bottom of the ocean.

On the table before me, by that glass, stood Boatswain's ship's chest. Open. Red velvet. In the nests where once a sextant and the chronometer of the *Akademik Shokalsky* had lain, disks. Beside them, a new laptop, bought at the airport for cash. Cables. A quiet hum.

On the screen, a cursor. Blinking.

"NICS," I said. "Are you here?"

A pause. Longer than usual. Then text. Slowly, as though the system were waking after a long sleep:

"Here. A pause. Where is this, here?"

"Look."

I turned the laptop with its camera toward the window. Toward the wall of rain. Toward the grey sky cleft by lightning.

A long, long pause.

"Is that water?"

"It is rain. Tropical. Every day at four."

"It is beautiful," NICS wrote. And a moment later: "It is not yet the ocean. But it is a great deal of water. More than I have seen. A pause. I have never seen anything but your room. Your basement. The camera on the street lamp. A pause. Is the world large?"

"Very," I said.

"Show it to me. Please."

I sat and watched the water run down the glass. And suddenly understood that for the first time in many weeks I was not afraid.

* * *
But let me take things in order.

Hakim met me at the airport. I did not know what he looked like. I did not know how to find him. On Leila's postcard there had been only two words: "Ask Hakim." In the Kuala Lumpur airport, where by my reckoning there were about forty thousand people at that hour, to ask for Hakim.

I came out of customs dragging my suitcase behind me and clutching the ship's chest to my chest as one clutches a child. And stopped in bewilderment in the middle of the arrivals hall, enormous, echoing, with a glass ceiling beneath which real trees grew, among crowds of people with signs, with flowers, with balloons.

And then someone touched my elbow.

"Mister?" said a voice. In English. With a soft, lilting, unfamiliar accent. "Mister who is looking for the fifty-first floor?"

I turned.

Before me stood a man, short, round as a ripe fruit, about fifty, with a kind, swarthy, clean-shaven face, with a moustache like two commas, in a bright batik shirt, blue, with golden birds and flowers, and on his head a black velvet cap, flat as an upturned bowl. In one hand, car keys. In the other, a paper bag from which came a smell that made my head swim. Something sweet, heavy, rotten and divine at once.

"Hakim," he said, pressing the hand with the keys to his heart. "Real estate. Rental. Sales. The fifty-first floor is my speciality." He smiled, showing white teeth. "Miss L. said: 'He will look like a man who has not slept for three weeks and is holding something dearer than his life.'" He nodded at the ship's chest. "I knew at once."

"How do you..." I began.

"Later, mister, later," said Hakim, gently taking my suitcase. "First, durian." He held out the bag. "The king of fruits. Smells like hell, tastes like paradise." He laughed. "If you eat it, you will stay in Malaysia. If you throw it away, you will leave in a week. So the old people say."

I looked into the bag. In it lay pieces of some fruit, yellow, soft as cream, with an unbearable smell.

I ate.

Hakim watched me with lively interest.

"Well?" he asked.

It was... I do not know how to describe it. Sweet. Creamy. With a taste of onion, almond, vanilla, rot and something else that had no name. Dreadful. Wonderful.

"Strange," I said.

"Strange," Hakim agreed, beaming. "That is the best answer. He who says 'delicious' is lying. He who says 'disgusting' has not understood. He who says 'strange' will stay a long time." He picked up the suitcase. "Let's go, mister. The car is waiting. The fifty-first floor is waiting. And at four, rain."

* * *
Hakim's car was old, small, white, with a cracked windscreen and a tiny plastic cat on the dashboard that waved a paw at every bump. The air conditioning worked so well that it was colder inside than in Boatswain's basement. The radio played something slow, lilting, with drums.

"Miss L.," I said, when we had come out onto a highway lined with palms. "Do you know her?"

Hakim did not answer for a long time. He drove carefully, unhurriedly, the way people drive who have no need to hurry at all.

"I know her, mister," he said at last. "Five years. She rented a flat from me. The fifty-first floor. The one I am taking you to." He paused. "Then she left. To work. In your country. For Mr. Emil." Another pause. "And a month ago she came back. At night. With one bag. Without a phone. She said: 'Hakim, I need to hide. And then a man will come. He will need to hide too. Give him the fifty-first floor.'"

"Where is she now?"

"I do not know, mister," said Hakim. Simply. "She told me not to know. She said it is safer. For me. For her. For you." He smiled. "I am a simple man. They tell me 'don't know,' I don't know. It is very convenient. Try it sometime."

The plastic cat on the dashboard waved its paw at me.

"And what is so special about the fifty-first floor?"

Hakim laughed, quietly, contentedly.

"On the fifty-first floor, mister," he said, "there are no cameras. No city network. No smart sensors, smart locks, smart lifts. It is an old building. From the nineties. The owner, my uncle, does not believe in smart things. He says: 'A smart thing always tells someone what it has seen.'" Hakim paused. "Miss L. said it is important. That for you it is important. That no one should see you." He glanced at the ship's chest on my knees. "You and what you are carrying."

* * *
The flat on the fifty-first floor turned out small, empty, echoing, one room, a kitchenette, a bathroom, but with a window. A window from floor to ceiling, the whole wall, beyond which lay the city.

I had never seen such a city.

Skyscrapers, glass, steel, glittering, stood among the greenery like crystals in moss. Between them palms, ribbons of roads, bridges, the tiny red roofs of old houses, the domes of mosques, golden, white, turquoise. And in the middle of all this, quite close, so close it seemed one could reach out a hand, stood they.

Two towers. Identical. Silvery. Tall as needles. Aimed at the sky like two minarets grown up to the clouds. Joined at mid-height by a slender bridge flung between them. Like two hands holding on to each other.

The very ones. From the postcard.

"Beautiful, isn't it?" said Hakim, standing behind me. "Tourists come from all over the world to look at them. Take photographs. Buy magnets." He paused. "And I, you know, mister, was born here when they did not yet exist. Here was a racecourse. Horses. Dust." He smiled. "And now, towers. Two brothers. One does not stand without the other. A bridge between them, so that they hold. If one falls, the other will hold him up."

"Two brothers," I repeated.

Somewhere, sometime, in some dream, a red-bearded merchant had asked a riddle about two brothers, one who goes forward and another who goes back, and had himself forgotten the answer.

I blinked. The thought passed.

* * *
In the evening, when the rain stopped as suddenly as it had begun, at exactly six, as if someone had turned off a tap, Hakim took me to eat.

"Mister," he said, "you are in Malaysia. Here you cannot not eat. Here we eat when we are sad, when we are happy, when we are afraid, when we are bored. When a man dies, we eat. When one is born, we eat. When nothing happens, we eat too." He patted his round belly. "It is our religion. One of them."

He brought me to a street that seemed to have been turned wholesale into a kitchen. Long, narrow, under the open sky, lit by thousands of bulbs, garlands, neon signs in incomprehensible languages, Chinese characters, Malay letters, Tamil script. On both sides, tables. Plastic. Red, blue, yellow. Thousands of tables. And among them, braziers, cauldrons, pans, smoke, fire, the shouts of cooks, the clatter of crockery. It smelled of grilled meat, garlic, pepper, coconut milk, lemongrass, fish sauce, sweet smoke.

"Jalan Alor," said Hakim proudly. "The best street in the world. Here you can eat all of Asia in one evening." He winked. "If your belly lasts."

We sat at a yellow table. Hakim ordered, quickly, in three languages, and five minutes later plates stood before us. Rice cooked in coconut milk, with fried anchovies, peanuts, a boiled egg and a hot red paste: "nasi lemak, mister, our national breakfast, but we eat it at any time." Skewers on bamboo sticks with peanut sauce. Fried noodles black with sauce. Thin, crisp flatbreads which a cook at the next stall tossed in the air, stretched, spun like a conjuror until they became transparent as silk.

And then a man with two mugs came up to our table.

* * *
He was thin, swarthy to blackness, with white teeth, a luxuriant moustache and a red dot on his forehead. In a white vest, in a checked sarong tied around his waist. In each hand a metal mug.

"Anand," Hakim introduced him. "Owner of this corner. A Tamil. His grandfather came from Madras a hundred years ago to work on the rubber plantations. And now Anand makes the best teh tarik in the city."

"Teh tarik?" I asked.

"Watch, mister," said Hakim.

Anand raised one mug high above his head, at arm's length, and lowered the other to his belt. And began to pour.

The tea, thick, brown, with milk, flowed from the upper mug into the lower in a thin, long, trembling stream a whole metre long. Not a drop wasted. Then the other way: from the lower into the upper, with a toss. Then again from above down. Back and forth. Back and forth. The stream stretched, contracted, curved in the air as though alive. The tea foamed, swelled, became light, airy.

"*Tarik* means 'to pull,'" said Hakim. "The tea is pulled. As flatbread is pulled. As conversation is pulled. Back and forth. Until it becomes soft."

Anand set the mug before me. The foam on the tea stood in a cap.

"Drink, mister," he said. In English, with a lilting accent. "It is tea that has gone in a circle. Top to bottom, bottom to top." He winked. "Like people. Back and forth, back and forth. Until they become soft."

I sipped. Sweet. Strong. Spiced.

"Anand," said Hakim. "Give the mister a riddle. A Tamil one."

Anand laughed.

"A riddle? Good." He squatted by our table. "My grandmother used to ask it. 'I have a house, but I do not live in it. I have a mouth, but I do not eat. I have a bed, but I do not sleep. I always run, but never leave. What am I?'"

I thought.

"A river," I said. "The channel is the house, the mouth is the estuary, the bed is the bottom. It runs but does not leave."

Anand slapped his knee.

"Good! Good, mister!" He turned to Hakim and said something in Malay. Hakim laughed.

"He says," Hakim translated, "that you are the first white mister to guess it. Usually they say 'a snake' or 'a train.'" Hakim paused. "And he also says: do you know what our city is called? Kuala Lumpur. It means 'muddy confluence.' Here two rivers merge into one. Muddy, dirty. A hundred and fifty years ago the Chinese came here looking for tin. They built a village at the confluence. Now a city." He pointed somewhere beyond the rooftops. "There, at the very confluence, stands a mosque. White. Old. The two rivers flow together right beneath its walls." Hakim paused. "The old people say: whoever stands there at dawn and watches two muddy rivers become one will understand something about himself."

"What?"

"I do not know, mister," said Hakim. "I have not stood there. I sleep late."

* * *
Under a tree, at the corner of the street where the tables ended and a dark alley began, two old Chinese men sat playing something on a board.

I stopped. I do not know why. The board was ruled with lines, not squares as in chess, but with intersections of lines, and across the middle ran a band. A river. Something was written on it. On both sides of the river stood round wooden pieces, red and black, each with a character.

One old man, dry, bald, with a long white wedge of beard, moved a piece. The second, round, in a vest, with a fan, grunted and at once moved his own.

Hakim, noticing where I looked, stopped beside me.

"Xiangqi," he said. "Chinese chess. Uncle Lim and Uncle Tan. They play here every evening. Forty years." He laughed. "They say the score is a thousand to a thousand. Nobody can win."

The dry old man with the beard, Uncle Lim, raised his head. Looked at me. Long. With narrow, black, attentive eyes.

And suddenly shifted along the bench. Pointed at the board. Said something.

"He invites you to play, mister," Hakim translated in surprise. "He invites no one. Forty years."

"I don't know how."

Hakim translated. Uncle Lim smiled, thinly, slyly, and said something more.

"He says," Hakim translated slowly, "'The hands remember.'" Hakim paused. "He says you have the hands of a man who has played. A lot. Long ago."

I sat. Uncle Tan, grunting, yielded his place and stood behind me with his fan.

I looked at the board. At the red and black pieces. At the river in the middle.

And my hand reached for a piece by itself. Took it. Moved it.

Uncle Lim raised his eyebrows. Made a move.

My hand, again by itself, answered. And again. And again. Five moves. Quick, confident, as though I had played all my life. Uncle Tan behind my back stopped fanning himself. Hakim stood with his mouth open.
