Vera Anatolievna stood by the steps. In grey. With the dragonfly brooch. She did not come up. She only raised a gloved hand and held it raised a long time.

Doctor Strauch stood by a column. With his unlit cigar. He came to the second carriage. Held out his hand to me.

"Twelfth," he said. "Come back. I should so like to write it in."

"I shall try, Karl Fyodorovich."

"Germans do not try," said Strauch. "Germans do." And stepped away.

Stefan stood by a rose bush at the start of the avenue. He did not come up. He was looking not at me but at the pot with the rose at my feet. His lips moved. He was speaking to her. In Bulgarian. Quietly. I could not hear the words.

And Auntie...

Auntie stood on the top step of the porch. Straight. In a dark dress. With her braid thrown over her shoulder. With a string of pearls. She did not weep. She looked at me, long, unwaveringly, as if she wished to memorise every feature, and I understood that she would not come down. That if she came down she would not be able to let me go.

I climbed up to her myself.

"Auntie."

She said nothing. She took my face in her hands, cold, ringed, and held it. A long time. Then kissed my forehead.

"Have you the key?" she asked.

"I have."

"Good." She released me. "Go."

And turned away. Before I could answer.

* * *
Agafya Tikhonovna stood at the step of the second carriage. Small, dry, in her cap, with the bunch of keys at her belt. As I climbed in she bent to me, so close that I smelled incense and wax, and whispered.

One word.

A name.

I did not ask again. I could not ask again. My voice was gone.

It was not my name. Not the one by which I was called in that house. Another. Strange. Ancient. Which I had never heard.

And which I knew.

Not with the mind. With something deeper. As one knows a melody heard before birth. As one knows the smell of a house in which one has not lived. As one knows a face never seen, but which comes in dreams.

Agafya Tikhonovna straightened. Crossed me. Stepped back.

"Off we go!" cried Tikhon.

The carriages started.

I looked back. The house. The porch. Auntie on the top step, with her back to us. The General's betrothed by the column. Vera Anatolievna with her hand raised. Strauch with his cigar. Stefan by the rose bush. Dunyasha. Marfa. Ignatiy Savvich. Mitka on the roof waving with both hands.

And the gallery window. At the end of the left wing. Tall, narrow. Where the portrait hung, without crape. Without a face.

In that window, for a single moment, as the carriage turned into the avenue, someone stood. Tall. Grey. Motionless.

And watched me go.

* * *
The train to Odessa took two days.

I had never travelled by locomotive, or did not remember having done so, and for the first hours I sat at the window like Timosha at... like a child at a confectioner's window. Fields. Forests. Villages with crooked huts. Churches with green domes. Stations, stone, wooden, with bells, with buffets, with ring-rolls and tea from a samovar, and at every station the locomotive puffed, whistled, let off steam, and passengers poured out onto the platform to stretch their legs, and crammed back into the carriages.

In our carriage, first class, blue, with velvet sofas, travelled strange people.

A Greek merchant from Taganrog, stout, moustached, in gold rings, who all the way ate olives from a jar and told Konstantin that in Constantinople he had three shops, and in each a wife. "Not the Turkish way, no!" he assured. "The Greek way! Each thinks she is the only one!"

A Polish nun, small, severe, in black, with a rosary, who was going to Odessa and from there to Jerusalem, to the Holy Sepulchre, on foot, "if God grants." She spoke to no one but me. And only once. On the second day, at a station near Kiev, when everyone had got out, she came up to me and said in Polish, quietly, and I understood: "You are like the one I saw in a dream at Czestochowa. Before the icon. He stood between two doors." And crossed me. And did not approach again.

And a blind old kobzar, bearded, grey, in a white svita, with a bandura on his back and a boy guide, who was travelling third class but at one of the stations near Vinnytsia entered our carriage; the boy had mistaken the door. The General would not allow him to be turned out. Bade him sit. Poured him tea. And asked him to play.

* * *
The kobzar sang for a long time.

Not a song, a duma. Long, slow, sorrowful, almost on a single note, with runs on the bandura like the lapping of water. I did not understand all the words, the Little Russian accent, the archaic turns, but I understood the main thing.

About captives. Cossacks taken prisoner by the Turks. Chained. Sitting on galleys, on Turkish ships where men row, shackled to the benches, day and night, for years. In the middle of the Black Sea. On the way to Tsargrad.

"Oh, hey, on the Black Sea, on a little white stone..."

They row and look north. Where home is. Where the steppe is, the Dnieper, the native cottage, mother on the threshold. They cannot return. They are chained. But they look. Every day. And pray to God, not for freedom. That at least a wind from the native side might blow in their faces. Once.

"Oh, strike, God, upon the sea, the quiet, the Black..."

The kobzar sang with his blind eyes closed. The boy guide sat at his feet and wept without a sound. The Greek merchant stopped eating olives. The Polish nun prayed. Konstantin turned to the window.

And the General sat motionless, clutching in his fist Evdokia Gerasimovna's ring.

When the duma ended, the kobzar opened his white, sightless eyes. Turned them to me. Straight at me, though no one had told him where I sat.

And said, in Little Russian, slowly:

"You, lad, row too. I sense it. Chained. Between two shores." He paused. "Only you do not look north. You look back." A pause. "And you need to look forward."

"Now you are looking back," the boy at the dervish's gate had said.

I had never seen that boy. Had never heard those words.

But they were. In me. Like the kobzar's duma.

* * *
Odessa greeted us with sun.

A white city on a high shore. Broad, straight streets lined with acacias. Houses light, stone, with balconies, with columns, with stucco, as if brought from Italy. Noise. Shouting. Laughter. Dozens of languages, Russian, Greek, Italian, Yiddish, Armenian, Turkish, Bulgarian, all mingled, at every corner. The smell of the sea. Of salt. Of fish. Of coal. Of acacia.

And the staircase.

Enormous, from the boulevard on the shore down to the port, stone, broad, endless, two hundred steps, said the General. From above, only the landings are visible. From below, only the steps. The builder's trick. A deception of the eye.

"Like life," said Konstantin, standing on the top landing and looking down at the port, at the masts, at the smoking funnels. "From above it seems all stops. From below, all steps. And in fact, both."

"Lieutenant," said the General, "you are becoming a philosopher. It is dangerous in an adjutant."

* * *
The steamer was to leave in the evening. Until the evening there was time.

The General went to the office of the Russian Company to see to papers. Konstantin with him. I was left alone. With the pot of the rose in my arms, Stefan had told me not to leave her for a minute, and with the letter in my pocket. The letter for Preobrazhenskaya. For the Bulgarian house.

I found it quickly. Two-storeyed, with green shutters, with a sign above the door, in Bulgarian, in Cyrillic, "School." I knocked. A young man opened, swarthy, black-moustached, with burning eyes, very like Lyuben whom I had seen at Stefan's.

"From Stefan of Tarnovo," I said.

The young man turned pale. Looked about. Pulled me inside. Took the letter. Unfolded it. Read. Raised eyes to me, wet.

"Do you know what is here?" he asked in Russian.

"I do."

"And you brought it."

"I brought it."

He looked at me for a long time. Then at the pot with the rose in my hands. Then again at me.

"Is this from Tarnovo?" he asked quietly. "The rose?"

"From Tarnovo."

The young Bulgarian slowly sank to his knees. Right on the floor. And kissed a leaf of the rose.

"Five hundred years," he said. "Five hundred years." He raised his face to me. "My grandmother said: when a rose from Tarnovo goes south, it means soon. It means they will come. Will free us." He laughed through tears. "You are the one who carries the rose. Do you know what that means?"

I did not know. I knew nothing.

But I nodded.

* * *
On the way back, on Deribasovskaya, noisy, crowded, with cafés, shops, cabmen, street vendors, I stopped at a shop window.

A clockmaker's workshop. Small. Below, in a half-basement, seven steps down. Behind the glass, clocks. Dozens. Hundreds. On the walls, on shelves, in the window. With pendulums. With cuckoos. Pocket watches on chains. And all were ticking.

I do not know why I went down. My feet went by themselves.

The door was upholstered in felt. Above it a copper bell. New. Shining. Without a crack.

I pushed the door. The bell jingled.

And all the clocks in the workshop, all at once, all the hundreds, stopped.

The silence was so complete that I heard my own heart beating. The pendulums stood still. The cuckoo froze in its window with its beak open.

At a table by the window sat an old clockmaker. Grey, in a skullcap, with a loupe in his eye. He raised his head. Looked at me. His face went white.

And beside him, on a stool, sat a boy. About ten. Thin, curly, in large, too large for his face, spectacles with thick lenses, behind which his eyes seemed huge, like an owl's. With tweezers in his hand. An apprentice.

The boy looked at me. Without blinking. With his huge owlish eyes.

I opened my mouth. And said, not knowing where the words came from:

"Excuse me. I am off again."

And went out.

The bell jingled. The door closed.

And behind my back, in the basement, all at once, all the hundreds, the clocks started.

I stood on Deribasovskaya among the crowd, with a pot of rose in my arms. And through the noise of the street, through the cabmen's shouts, through the laughter, through the jingle of harness bells, I heard below, in the workshop, the boy in the huge spectacles ask the old man:

"Grandfather, who was that?"

And the old man answered, quietly, hoarsely:

"I do not know, Lyovushka. Remember him. Perhaps you will meet him again."

* * *
The steamer was called the *Grand Duke Konstantin*.

"It is a sign," announced Konstantin, seeing the name on the hull. "This is my steamer. I was named after it. Or it after me. No matter." He patted the iron rail of the gangway. "It will carry us."

She was large, two-funnelled, with enormous paddle wheels on her sides, with masts on which furled sails hung, white, with a red stripe. On deck, bustle. Sailors. Porters. Passengers. Greeks, Armenians, Turks, Jews, Russians. Pilgrims, to Jerusalem, through Constantinople. Merchants. Officers. Ladies with lapdogs. Ship's boys.

I went up the gangway with the pot of the rose in my arms. The General ahead. Konstantin behind.

And on the upper deck, at the very rail, leaning on it, stood a man.

Tall. In a grey coat, cut in the European fashion. In a top hat. With a cane. He was smoking a thin cigar and looking at Odessa, the white city on the high shore, the staircase, the acacias.

He did not turn as we passed.

But Konstantin, walking behind me, suddenly stopped. Sniffed.

"Mon cher," he said softly. "Do you smell it?"

"What?"

"Bergamot," said Konstantin. "Cologne. Expensive. Parisian." He looked at the man in grey. "I have smelled him before. Today. On the stairs. When you went to the Bulgarian house and the General and I went to the office." He paused. "This man followed you. All the way to Preobrazhenskaya."

The man in grey did not turn. He finished his cigar. Threw the stub into the water. And slowly, unhurriedly, tapping his cane on the deck, went off into the first-class saloon.

"General," said Konstantin. "Who is that?"

The General looked after the man in grey for a long time. His face was stone.

"I do not know, Lieutenant," he said. "But in the steamer's passenger register his name, I saw it when I was arranging the papers, is written in letters I could not read." A pause. "Long ones. Crooked. One into another."

* * *
The steamer cast off at dusk.

Odessa receded, slowly, reluctantly, a white city on a high shore, the lights on the boulevard, the lights on the staircase, the lights in the windows. Then only the lighthouse. Then only the sea.

The Black Sea. Nocturnal. Dark as ink. With white crests of waves flaring in the glow of the side lights. With the wind fresh, salt, cold.

I stood at the rail. With the pot of the rose. The General beside me. Konstantin on the other side.

"Two days," said the General. "The day after tomorrow in the morning, the Bosphorus."

"General," I said. "That monk. In Siam. He said: 'You simply do not remember that you yourself called him into this world.'" I paused. "Called whom?"

The General looked at the dark sea for a long time.

"I thought I knew," he said at last. "Thirty years I thought so. I thought it was about God. That I was seeking God." He paused. "And now I think it is about you."

"About me?"

"For thirty years I looked at faces," said the General. "In Samarkand, in Peking, in Havana, in Sitka, in Melbourne. I thought I was seeking someone." He turned to me. "But perhaps it was not I who sought. Perhaps it was you who called me. Through all this. Through all these lands. So that I should bring you the scroll. So that I should bring you to where you must come." He paused. "Perhaps that is what the monk meant. That I called you, and you called me. And no one remembers who was first."

"A circle," I said.

"A circle," the General agreed. "It has no beginning." A pause. "So the monk said."

"And the gypsy woman at the stones," I said, not knowing where the words came from, "said: 'This one has one.'"

The General looked at me. Long. Very long.

"What gypsy woman?"

"I do not know," I said. "I have never seen a gypsy woman at stones."

* * *
At night I did not sleep.

I stood at the rail holding the pot with the rose. Konstantin slept in the cabin; I could hear his breathing through the open door. The General too. The deck was empty. Only the watch sailor on the bridge. And the wind. And the sea.

And the name.

The name that Agafya Tikhonovna had whispered to me at the step of the carriage.

I repeated it to myself. Over and over. I did not utter it aloud; I could not. I only thought it. Word by word. Sound by sound.

It was old. It was strange. It was mine.

And the longer I repeated it, the more clearly I understood that it was not the only one. Behind it stood others. As behind one reflection in a mirror, others, endless, receding into depth. Other names. In other languages. In other cities. In other centuries. An Egyptian one, short, guttural, sounding like a blow on bronze. A Turkish one, "Misafir," guest. Another, simple, modern, which I could not recall but which someone wrote to me on a glowing screen and I did not respond. And more. And more.

And in the very depth, behind them all, behind all the reflections, one. The very first. The most ancient.

Which I could not hear. Could not remember. Only sensed, as one senses warmth from a stone that is not in the hand.

The rose in the pot in my hands stirred in the wind. One of the three buds, dark crimson, almost black, slowly opened. Right here, at night, on the deck, in the middle of the Black Sea.

And one petal tore away. Flew. Down. Into the dark water.

I watched it fall. Watched it vanish in the white foam astern.

"When I return, the rose will go with me. To where I came from. And there it will bloom again. For the third time."

In the east, above the edge of the sea, the sky began to grey.

In a day, the Bosphorus.

## Chapter XXXVII. The New Moon

There was no moon.

I went out onto the palace roof an hour before dawn, for the last time, as I thought, before the long road south should take me from these roofs, these palms, this city, and looked at the sky. The stars burned as brightly as they burn only on moonless nights: Sah strode in the west, lowering his belt toward the horizon, the Imperishable circled in the north, and above the eastern hills, low, almost touching them, shone Sopdet, white, shimmering, winking. The star of Isis. The one that always walks a step behind.

But there was no moon. None at all. Only darkness in the place where it should be, as though someone had taken it from the sky as an eye is taken out.

The new moon. The Eye that was once shattered had gone to gather itself anew. So the priests said. So Amenemope said. So Merit said by the pool.

"My Pharaoh," said a voice behind me.

Senusret. Of course. He was always at my back: on the roof, at the wicket, at the gates, at the hole in the tomb. I had ceased to be surprised.

"Seti has sent a messenger," he said. "In the night. He bade me tell you as soon as you wake."

"I have not slept."

"I know, my Pharaoh. That is why I came now." Senusret paused. "Seti says: the water has risen."

I turned.

"Risen?"

"By a finger," said Senusret. "One finger. Overnight." He paused. "For the first time in three years. Seti says he went down to the nilometer three times with a lamp. Three times he measured. A finger above yesterday." The old warrior looked at me, and in his stony face there was something I had never seen there before. Hope. "Seti bade me add: 'Tell the son of Ra, the river heard that he is leaving. And awoke to see him off.'"

* * *
The nilometer stood at the very edge of the water, at the southern tip of the island opposite the palace, a stone well going down to the river, with a stair winding along the wall and with marks on the wall, notches, signs, numbers. For forty floods Seti had descended this stair each morning. For forty floods he had recorded how far the water had risen.

He waited for me below, by the water itself, small, stooped, withered, with a lamp in his hand, and, seeing me on the steps, did not bow, but only raised the lamp, lighting the wall.

"Here, my Pharaoh," he said. His voice shook. "Look."

On the wet stone, a little above the dark, motionless water, was a fresh scratch. Seti had scored it in the night with a knife. And a finger's breadth below, yesterday's.

"A finger," the old man whispered. "Only a finger." He looked at me, and I saw that his eyes were wet. "My Pharaoh, do you know what a finger is, after three years of nothing? Three years I came down here and saw the same thing. Every morning. The same." He swallowed. "And today, a finger."

"It is not yet the flood, Seti."

"Not the flood," the old man agreed. "Not even the beginning of the flood. It is..." He searched for the word. "It is as if a sleeper in his dream had moved a finger. Not yet awake. But no longer dead."

He lowered the lamp over the water. Dark, heavy, motionless. The lamp's reflection trembled on it in a yellow patch.

"Nefer-Ka came last evening," Seti said suddenly. Quietly. Not raising his eyes. "As at the beginning of the drought. Before your messenger. Asked what the nilometer shows. I said, nothing." The old man paused. "That was yesterday. Yesterday it was nothing." He raised his eyes to me. "And today he did not come. Today I shall tell him nothing. Today, only you."

"Why, Seti?"

The keeper of the nilometer was silent for a long time.

"Because for forty floods, my Pharaoh," he said at last, "I have recorded what the river does. And never, not once, has the river risen at the new moon. Never. The water comes when Sopdet rises. Not before." He paused. "And today it rose. By itself. Without Sopdet. On the night when there is no moon. On the night when you leave for the south." The old man set the lamp on a step. "The High Priest will say: it is a sign that the god is pleased. That the festival is welcome. That we must sail." He looked at me. "But I am an old man who has measured water for forty years. And I think: a river does not see one off. A river warns."

* * *
Djehuty's messenger arrived when the sun was already above the hills.

He came on foot from the southern outpost, forty days' journey, because his horse had fallen at Abydos and boats did not run on the shallowed river. He was so thin he seemed a skeleton covered with sunburnt skin. He fell on his knees at my feet in the courtyard, by the very steps, and could not speak; he only held out to me something wrapped in dirty cloth.

Senusret caught him, Bata thrust a flask at him. The messenger drank long, choking. Then gasped:

"The Rock... of the First... Djehuty bade... only you... into your hands..."

I unwrapped the cloth.

A little box. Clay, small, palm-sized, sealed with ancient clay, so ancient that the seal crumbled at my touch. Dark, fired, with signs scratched on its sides. The script.

"We found it under the rock," the messenger wheezed. "Where the men in temple sandals were digging. Djehuty set a guard. At night the temple men came again. We drove them off. And in the morning..." He swallowed. "In the morning we found a pit. Deep. They had almost dug through. One night more and they would have reached it. Djehuty himself went down. Took this. Bade me run. Day and night." The messenger closed his eyes. "I ran."

I opened the box.

Inside was a sheet. Not papyrus. Something thinner, smoother, whiter; I had never seen such material. Folded in two. I unfolded it.

On the sheet, two lines. The upper, the script. Long, flowing, running together. The lower, signs. Ours. Ancient, angular, the same as above the bench in the round room beneath the tomb.

"Iti," I said. Without turning.

He was already standing beside me. As always when he was needed. He bent over the sheet. His lips began to move.

"'He who holds both,'" he read slowly, in a whisper, "'let him not enter with them...'" He faltered. Leaned closer. "'...into the southern house. Until there comes...'" He raised his eyes to me. "The rest is erased, my Pharaoh. The clay has crumbled. One word." He pointed. "The last sign. I do not know it. It looks like... like a man. Seated. With a raised hand."

"'Let him not enter with them into the southern house,'" I repeated. "Luxor. The southern house of the god."

"Yes, my Pharaoh," Iti whispered. "'Until there comes...'" He gazed at the last sign. "Who?"

No one answered.

* * *
"Nefer-Ka will give you the stones at Luxor," said Paser.

The council had gathered in the small hall, for the last time before the sailing. Paser with his staff. Ptahhotep with his basket of scrolls. Nebamun with his tablets. Merira with tattooed arms folded on his chest. Panehsy by the wall. Senusret by the door. Iti in the shadow, with his brush. Deaf Ani on the bench in the corner. And Khaemuas.

Khaemuas sat among the commanders, in his bracelets, nine, not ten, perfumed, with painted eyes, but he did not smile. He was looking at the floor. When I entered he raised his eyes to me, quickly, anxiously, and lowered them again.

"The casket of black wood," Paser continued, "has already been loaded onto the High Priest's barque. I saw it. Yesterday evening. Four priests carried it. On a litter. Under a cover." The old man paused. "At Luxor, on the last day, in the inner court, he will open the casket and hand you the Two Eyes. 'As the First Ones gave them.' So he said at the banquet. Before all."

"And the letter from the Rock says, do not enter the southern house with them," said Senusret.

"The letter from the Rock says, until someone comes," Paser corrected. "Who, is erased."

"Then we must wait," said Merira in his thunderous voice. "Not enter. Until he comes. My barques can sail slowly, my Pharaoh. Very slowly. The river is shallow. We can run aground. Once. Twice. Ten times." He grinned. "For thirty years I have been running barques aground. I can do it so that no one will understand whether it is on purpose or not."

"Shall I repeat that for the record?" Ani whispered loudly.

"Merira knows how to run barques aground, honoured Ani," Ptahhotep said patiently.

"Ah!" Ani nodded and scratched with his brush. "Wise. Very wise. I can too. In my youth I ran aground a beauty from Bubastis so thoroughly that to this day she cannot understand how she came to marry me."

Merira roared with laughter. Paser smiled into his beard. Even Nebamun allowed himself a dry smile.

And Khaemuas, Khaemuas suddenly raised his head.

"My Pharaoh," he said. His voice trembled. "Permit me."

All fell silent.

"Last night," said Khaemuas, looking at me, "Bakenren's man came to me. In secret. As he always came." He swallowed. "He passed word: Bakenren is alive. He is in Luxor. Already three weeks. He waits."

"For what does he wait?"

"He did not say, my Pharaoh." Khaemuas clasped his hands so hard that the bracelets chimed. "He said only: 'Our men must stand at the gates. Inside, all is ready. The masons have done what was needed.'" Khaemuas paused. "I asked, what masons? He laughed and said: 'Those who know how to lay stone so that no one finds the door.'"

In the hall it became very quiet.

"Masons," Nebamun repeated slowly. "My Pharaoh. Two moons ago six masons vanished from the royal workshops in Memphis. Masters. The best. Those who set secret passages in tombs." The keeper of the treasury looked at his tablets. "I thought they had run away from hunger. I struck their ration from the books." He raised his eyes. "Now I think they did not run away."

* * *
Pentu came after the council. Through the garden, at night, no, by day, but through the garden, as bidden, past blind Meru, who, they say, let him pass without a riddle and only said: "Today the riddle is at the river."

He was pale as flax. In his hands, a scroll. A copy. The last.

"My Pharaoh," he whispered, falling to his knees. "This is an inventory. Not of granaries. Of works." He unrolled the scroll with trembling hands. "The temple of Luxor. Works paid for by the Temple in the last three moons." He stabbed a finger at a line. "Here. 'The inner court of the god. The eastern wall. A secret niche. Six masters from Memphis. Stone from the old quarry. Payment, one hundred hekats of barley.'" Pentu raised his eyes to me. "My Pharaoh, this is not a repair. This is a niche. In the wall. Behind the columns."

"For what?"

"It is not written, my Pharaoh." Pentu's voice broke. "But at the end there is a note. In Bakenren's hand. I know his writing. 'To close it, when he enters.'"

I looked at that line for a long time. "To close it, when he enters."

Columns. Darkness. A hand rising in the dark. And then nothing. Darkness. As though someone had shut a door.

Or walled it up with stone.

"Thank you, Pentu," I said. "Go. And do not come again. It is dangerous."

"My Pharaoh," Pentu whispered, not rising from his knees. "My sisters. The field near Bubastis. You said it was transferred to the royal lands." He swallowed. "Is that true?"

"It is true, Pentu."

The young man covered his face with his hands. His shoulders shook.

"Then I shall go with you," he said through his palms. "To Luxor. As a scribe. A temple one. They take me, Bakenren ordered it, before he vanished." He raised his face, wet with tears. "I shall be near the niche, my Pharaoh. I shall see what they do." A pause. "I owe you. For the field. For my sisters. I owe."

* * *
Nanakhat was waiting for me by the river. In the same place as last time. On a flat stone at the very edge of the water. Facing south.

I came alone. Senusret stayed behind the palms, "looking for donkeys," as he said to Bata with a stone face. Bata snorted and got a clout on the back of the head.

The blind old woman did not turn when I approached. She sat leaning on her staff of white wood crowned with a lioness's head, and her white, sightless eyes were turned to the river.

"The water has risen," she said. Not asking.

"By a finger."

"By a finger," Nanakhat repeated. "The Eye has stirred. In its sleep." She paused. "Did you find what they sought on the Rock?"

"I found it." I sat beside her on the stone. Held out to her the sheet from the clay box. She did not take it. She could not see. But she passed her fingers through the air above it, slowly, tenderly, as one strokes a sleeping beast.

"'Let him not enter with them into the southern house,'" she said. Not reading. Knowing. "'Until there comes...'" She fell silent.

"Who, Nanakhat? The last word is erased."

The old woman was silent for a long time. The river lapped softly at our feet, shallow, dark, a finger higher than yesterday.

"Last time you asked me where two met," she said at last. "One walking to the sunrise, the other to the sunset. You answered, at home. Because the world is a circle." She turned to me her carved, ancient face. "I said: that is half the answer. The second you will speak when you return from Luxor."

"I remember."

"Here is the second half," said Nanakhat. "Those two are one." She paused. "The one who left, and the one who returned. The one who holds both Eyes, and the one who brought them. The one who will enter the southern house, and the one who must come before he enters." She stretched out a hand and touched my face with dry, hot, rough fingers. "The last word on the sheet is you. Not this you. Another. The one who will come."

"I do not understand."

"I know," said Nanakhat. "And you will not understand. Until you meet him." She lowered her hand. "At Luxor. Or after. Or in another place where there is no Luxor. It does not matter. What matters is not to enter the southern house with the Eyes before he has come."

"And if Nefer-Ka compels it?"

The old woman laughed, drily, toothlessly, as stone cracks in the sun.

"Nefer-Ka cannot compel anyone, son of Ra," she said. "He can only ask. Very courteously. Very beautifully. So that one cannot refuse." She paused. "Therefore, refuse."

* * *
She took something from her neck, a cord of goat's wool on which hung a little figure. A lioness. Of black stone. Polished to a shine by thousands of touches.

"Take it," she said. "It is from me. And from her." She nodded toward the south. "From her who went away once and came back. Let her go with you. If it is dark for you, she will see."

I took it. The figure was warm.

"And you, Nanakhat? Will you sail with us?"

"No," said the old woman. "I shall go home. South. On foot. Along the river." She rose, leaning on her staff. "I am a hundred years old, son of Ra. I wish to die at home." She paused. "We shall meet again. Not in this life. In another. You will be in another body. I too. But you will know me." She smiled. "By the staff."

And she walked away along the bank, tapping with her lioness staff, south, small, bent, ancient, past the palms behind which stood Senusret, "looking for donkeys."

Drawing level with him, she stopped again. Again turned her blind face to him. And said something.

This time Senusret did not drop his staff. He listened. Bowed his head. And stood so a long time, motionless, after she had gone.

"What did she say?" I asked, coming up.

The commander of the army raised his eyes to me.

"She said," he answered dully, "'You will remain at the gates. So it must be. But when the gates are shut, do not break them. Go to the river. The river will show where the other door is.'"

* * *
Iti I found in the Library.

He sat at the great table where we had read the Epic, alone, by lamplight, copying something. Fast. Not raising his head. Beside him a heap of scrolls. Tablets. Potsherds.

Seeing me he leapt up. Overturned the inkpot. The ink spread across the table in a black pool.

"My Pharaoh... I did not expect..."

"Iti," I said. "You are staying."

He froze. In mid-movement, with a rag in his hand with which he had been trying to wipe the ink.

"Staying?" he repeated.

"Here. In the capital. In the Library." I came closer. "You are needed here. The seventh scroll. The bilingual texts. Three words: keep, appointed time, house. You must find more. While I am gone." I paused. "And if I do not return, someone must know what is written there."

Iti looked at me. The rag in his hand was black with ink. Ink dripped on the floor.

"You will return," he said. Quietly. Not a question.

"I do not know, Iti."

"You will return," he repeated. Stubbornly. And his voice shook. "You pulled me out of the water. Four years ago. You said: 'You almost drowned, and you are thinking of a tablet.'" He swallowed. "I remember every word. You do not. So you owe me."

"Owe you?"

"You owe it to return," said Iti. "To remember." He threw the rag on the table. Reached into his bosom. Took out something small, flat, wooden, darkened with time, with chipped edges. "Here."

A tablet. That one. From the hunt. The one the cat Mau fished out of the channel.

"I promised to show it when you remembered," said Iti. "But you are leaving. And I..." He faltered. "Take it. Read it there. At Luxor. If it is dark, read it." He laid it in my hands. "Everything is there. The hunt. The birds. The hippopotamus. The night on the island. Seneb. The stars." A pause. "And what I wrote at the end. Then. As a boy."

I looked at the tablet. Small, neat, childish signs. How many boats. How many birds. The hippopotamus that went off with the harpoon. The Imperishable stars.

And at the very end, a line. Which I had already seen. Then, on the sand, at dawn.

"Pharaoh pulled the junior scribe from the water. The scribe promises to remember this all his life. Even if Pharaoh forgets."

And beneath it, another line. Which had not been there then. Fresh. The ink still glistened.

"The scribe remembers. The scribe waits. Pharaoh will return."

I raised my eyes. Iti stood before me, with an ink stain on his cheek, of course, a fresh one, and looked straight. Without fear. Without shame. Without reverence.

I did not know what to say. I, Pharaoh, a living god, lord of the Two Lands, stood in the Library before a junior keeper of scrolls, holding in my hands a child's tablet, and could not find a single word.

I stretched out a hand. And wiped the ink stain from his cheek. With my thumb. Slowly.

Iti did not move. He only closed his eyes.

"I shall return, Iti," I said.

"I know, my Pharaoh," he whispered, not opening his eyes. "I have written it down."

* * *
Amenemope caught up with me at the Library exit, shuffling, leaning on his black staff, out of breath.

"My Pharaoh. One moment." He thrust into my hand something, a small scroll, tightly rolled, sealed with wax. "A copy. Of the window from the seventh scroll. Where our signs stand beside theirs. And also what the boy found in the round room. All that we know." The old man paused. "If at Luxor they show you something written in the script, compare. Perhaps you will find a fourth word."

"Thank you, Amenemope."

"Do not thank me, my Pharaoh." The old man looked at me with faded eyes. "The High Priest asked me again yesterday whether I was not tired. Whether I did not wish for rest." He smiled. "I answered that I shall be tired when you return. He smiled." Amenemope paused. "My Pharaoh. When you sail, I shall hide the boy. Isiret will help. In the lower storehouse, among the jars, there are places no one will find." He paused. "Because when you sail, it will be dangerous for the boy here. He knows too many words."

* * *
The barques of the god left at noon.

The whole capital came out onto the bank. From the palace to the temple, from the temple to the river, along the whole embankment, on roofs, on trees, on walls, thousands, tens of thousands of people. In white, in festive dress. With flowers. With palm fronds. With sistra and tambourines. They shouted, sang, wept.

At the quay stood the barque of the god, not the portable one but the river barque, huge, long, gilded from stem to stern, with rams' heads at bow and stern, with a canopy amidships under which stood the shrine. It was called Userhat, "Mighty of Brow." Thirty years ago, they said, it had sailed to Luxor on a full river under sail, and all Egypt came out to watch. Now the sail was furled. The river was shallow. The barque was towed.

On the bank, along the water, stood the haulers. Hundreds. Men stripped to the waist, with ropes on their shoulders, thick, tarred, long, fastened to the bow of the barque. They stood in a row, knee-deep in water, and waited.

Merira, on the prow of the barque, with tattooed arms, with a voice that overtopped the roar of the crowd, gave the commands.

"Haul-l-l!" he thundered.

The haulers began to sing. Low, steady, in one voice, an old song which, they said, had been sung on the river since the time of the First Ones. And leaned into the ropes. And the barque of the god, huge, golden, heavy, slowly, reluctantly, with a creak, moved from its place. And sailed. South.

* * *
Behind the barque of the god came the barque of the High Priest, a little smaller but equally gilded, with the casket of black wood under a cover at the stern. Nefer-Ka stood at the rail, in a leopard skin, with a staff crowned with the Eye, and looked at the crowd. When his barque came level with mine, he turned his head. And bowed, exactly as far as custom required.

"A good journey, my Pharaoh," he said. Not loudly. But I heard. "Luxor awaits you."

"I know, Nefer-Ka."

"The water has risen," he said. "By a finger. Have you heard?"

"I have heard."

"The gods are pleased," said Nefer-Ka. And smiled. "The gods are waiting for you to come to their southern house. As they have always waited."

And his barque passed on.

And behind it, mine. The royal one. With Senusret at the rail. With Paser, clutching the handrails with a green face. With Nebamun, drily counting the jars of beer for the haulers. With Khaemuas, at the stern, not raising his eyes. With Bata and Inu at my feet. With the dwarf Djedu, on the cabin roof, pulling faces at the crowd and shouting: "The son of Ra sails south! The son of Ra! Look! Whoever does not see will regret it!"

And behind mine, the barques of the singers. Khemu among them, in white, with a sistrum. When our barques drew level she raised the sistrum and lowered it. Once. A sign: "I am here."

And behind them the barques of the nobles, the barques of the priests, the barques of the warriors. Dozens. Hundreds. A flotilla stretched along the river so far that from the first barque the last could not be seen. Merira called it "the slowest fleet in the history of Egypt."

"We shall take forty days to Luxor, my Pharaoh," he told me that evening, grinning. "Perhaps fifty. If I try, sixty." He winked. "Shoals, my Pharaoh. Shoals are my best friends."

* * *
Nakht, the young bearer of the god's barque, with his protruding ears, found me at sunset.

He rowed up to my barque in a small boat, secretly, while the priests on his barque were at prayer, and clambered aboard, wet, trembling.

"My Pharaoh," he whispered. "Today. When the barque was being loaded. The shrine." He swallowed. "It was light."

"Light?"

"Usually it is heavy, my Pharaoh. There are twenty-four of us, and still it is heavy." Nakht looked at me with huge, frightened eyes. "And today, as if empty. As if the god is not there."

Cold beneath the ribs. On the left.

"Have you told anyone?"

"No, my Pharaoh. No one." Nakht paused. "But the other bearers felt it too. I saw it in their faces. All are silent." He swallowed. "The chief bearer said: 'The god has gone ahead. To wait for us at Luxor.'"

* * *
At night I did not sleep.

I stood at the rail of my barque, at the stern. The flotilla had halted for the night at the bank, the barques tied to palms, the haulers asleep on the sand by their fires. Silence. Only the lapping of water. Only the crackle of the fires. Only the cry of a night bird somewhere in the reeds.

There was no moon. The new moon. Darkness.

In my hands I held Iti's tablet. Nanakhat's lioness. Amenemope's scroll. The sheet from the Rock of the First Ones. Tausert's potsherd, the mouse in the crown between two doors.

All that had been given me. People who did not know one another, and all said one thing: "Take it. You are the one. Remember. Return."

Senusret stood beside me. Silent.

"Senusret," I said. "What else did Nanakhat tell you? You did not pass on all of it."

The commander of the army was silent for a long time.

"She said," he said at last, "'When he enters and the gates are shut, he will not die. He will go away. These are different things. You will not understand. But remember.'" Senusret paused. "And also: 'In a thousand years he will come again. In another city. Where two rivers flow into one. And you will be there. In another body. With another sword. Standing at other gates.'" He turned to me. "My Pharaoh, I am a soldier. I do not understand these words. I understand only one thing." His voice grew dull. "I shall stand at the gates. Here. And there. As long as needed."

I did not answer. I laid my hand on his shoulder. As he had laid his on mine.

We stood so for a long time.

* * *
And then Bata, dozing on the deck at my feet, suddenly cried out in his sleep, and woke. Sat up. Looked round. His face was white.

"My Pharaoh," he whispered. "The water."

I looked at the river.

Dark. Motionless. Without the moon, without reflections. Only the lights of the fires on the bank trembled on it in yellow patches.

And the reflection of our barque. Dark, inverted. The side. The mast. The cabin. The figures at the stern, mine, Senusret's, Bata's, seated on the deck.

And one more.

Tall. A head taller than any of us. Standing at the very rail, beside me. Motionless. Faceless.

I turned.

The deck. Senusret. Bata. I. No one else.

I looked into the water again.

The reflection was in place. Four figures. Senusret. Bata. I.

And he. Beside me. Very close. As if he had laid a hand on my shoulder, as I had just laid mine on Senusret's.

"My Pharaoh," Senusret whispered. He too was looking into the water. His hand fell on his sword. "There..."

"I see," I said.

We looked. For a long time. The reflection did not move.

And then, slowly, very slowly, the tall figure in the water raised a hand. Not to me. To the south. To where, forty days' journey away, beyond shoals and sands, beyond palms and villages, lay Luxor.

And lowered it.

And the reflection smoothed. Became only water. Dark. Motionless. A finger higher than yesterday.

* * *
Bata sat a long time on the deck, hugging his knees. Then said, quietly, hoarsely, looking at the water:

"My mother used to say, my Pharaoh. When the god of the river wishes to warn, he shows in the water what is not there." He paused. "I threw her scarab into a ditch then. Thought it all a deception." He swallowed. "And now I think, perhaps not all."

"What did he mean, Bata?"

The young guardsman looked at me.

"I do not know, my Pharaoh," he said. "Perhaps: go." A pause. "And perhaps: wait."

Above the eastern hills, low, at the very horizon, a white star flared. Sopdet. The star of Isis. The one that always walks a step behind.

And there was no moon.

The new moon.

To Luxor, forty days. If Merira tried, sixty.

And somewhere there, in the southern house of the god, behind the columns, in the eastern wall of the inner court, six vanished masons from Memphis had already built the niche. "To close it, when he enters."

## Vision VIII. Chicory

The water was so still that the boat seemed to hang in the air.

That is the first thing I remember. Not how I came to be in the boat, that I never remember, in any of these dreams, but the water. Transparent to the very bottom, to the white sand, to dark stones overgrown with weed, to the fish that hung in the depths motionless, as if suspended on threads, and only now and then, lazily, stirred their tails. The sun pierced this water through and through, and on the sand below a golden net trembled, the shadow of the light ripple on the surface.

The boat was small. A fisherman's. Old, with blue paint peeling on its sides, with patches on the bottom, with a smell of fish, tar and wet wood. On the bow an eye was painted, large, black, with long lashes, as they paint on every boat in these waters, so that the boat may see where it is going.

There were two of us. I at the stern, with oars. And he at the bow, also with oars, his back to me.

Young. Twenty at most. Tall, thin, wiry, tanned to blackness, in a white shirt with sleeves rolled up, in white sailor's trousers, barefoot. Bareheaded; his hair, dark, cropped short, had been bleached by the sun to a russet. On his neck a thin chain, and on it something glinted. He rowed evenly, steadily, strongly, as they row who were taught to row from childhood, and whistled something under his breath, some song that I knew. From somewhere.

"Pavel," I said.

The name came of itself. I did not know from where.

He turned. His face was young, open, with the first, barely sprouting moustache, with a stubborn chin and with eyes, grey, attentive, mocking, which I knew. Which I had seen many times. Older. Beneath grey brows. By a fireplace. Over a scroll in a silk kerchief.

"What?" he asked. "Tired? Say so, we'll swap. I don't mind which end I row from."

"No," I said. "It's only... Where are we sailing?"

Pavel laughed. Merrily, ringingly, with his whole throat, the way people laugh only at twenty.

"Have you had too much sun?" he said. "We are looking for chicory."

* * *
The bottle was found by old Yannis.

That was three days ago, I remembered now, suddenly, as if someone had switched on a light in a dark room, in a small harbour on the island where our frigate had put in for repairs after the battle. The big battle. In the bay off the coast of the Morea, where our ships, the English and the French burned the whole Turkish-Egyptian fleet in a single day. October. The twentieth. Pavel said afterwards that the fire had been seen twenty miles away, and the smoke hung over the bay for three days.

Our frigate had suffered. A hole at the waterline. The mizzen shot away. The captain brought her to this island, small, white, rocky, with one village on the slope and one harbour, to mend. A week, said the carpenter. Perhaps two.

Pavel, a midshipman, the youngest of the young, out of boredom on the second day went into the village. And came back with Yannis.

Yannis was a fisherman. Old, so old that his face, brown, weathered, furrowed with wrinkles, seemed carved from an olive root. Grey moustaches, enormous, curled, took up half his face. On his head a black fez, pushed to one side. A broad sash. Bare feet, hard as hooves. And eyes, blue, pale, faded by sea and sun, which looked as though they saw not you but the horizon behind you.

He came to our camp on the beach carrying a fish in his arms. An enormous one. A tunny, half a man's height. He laid it on the sand at Pavel's feet. And said something in Greek, which Pavel, who knew Greek from school, translated:

"He says he caught it this morning. And that inside there is a gift for the Russians."

"What gift?"

Yannis drew a knife. Slit the tunny's belly in one motion. And pulled out a bottle.

Green. Thick-walled. With a long neck sealed with red wax. Cloudy, caked with slime and tiny shells.

"The tunny swallowed it," Pavel translated, not believing his own words. "Yannis says tunny swallow anything that glitters. He once found a silver spoon in a tunny. With a coat of arms. And in another, a wedding ring." Pavel laughed. "He says he gave it back to a widow. She wept and said her husband had drowned twenty years before, and the tunny must have been carrying the ring all that time, to give it back."

Yannis nodded gravely. He understood no Russian, but seemed to understand the intonation.

"And why is the bottle for the Russians?" I asked.

Pavel translated. Yannis answered.

"He says," Pavel said slowly, "that inside there is a note. He can see it. Through the glass. And one word on it is in our tongue. In Russian letters." Pavel looked at me. "He cannot read. But he knows Russian letters. Says his grandfather traded with Odessa."

* * *
We broke the bottle on a rock. Carefully; Pavel wrapped it in his shirt so the shards should not fly.

Inside was a note. Rolled in a tube. The paper, thick, good, yellowed, was soaked. Salt water had seeped through the wax, and most of the lines had blurred, run into blue stains, as if someone had wept over them.

But something remained.

The note was in three languages. The same one, three times. At the top, in Greek. In the middle, in French. At the bottom, in Russian. And in each, gaps. Blurred places. Lost words. Different in each line.

Pavel spread it on a flat stone by the fire. Bent over it. And read aloud, slowly, in pieces, now in Greek, now in French, now in Russian.

"In Greek: '...by two rocks... a cave... waits...'" He jabbed a finger at a gap. "Lost here. Then: '...blue... flower...'" Another gap. "'...does not leave...'"

"In French?"

"'...grotte... à l'est... chicorée... attend depuis...'" Pavel raised his eyes. "'Grotto... in the east... chicory... has waited since...' And again a gap. '...ne partira pas...' 'Will not leave.'"

"And in Russian?"

Pavel bent lower. The Russian line was the most blurred of all. Only scraps remained.

"'...chicory...'" he read. "'...at the entrance... find... waits...'" He fell silent. Was silent a long time. "And at the very end, almost whole: '...home.'"

We looked at the note. Three languages. Three scraps. One story.

"Someone is waiting," I said. "In a cave. In the east. By two rocks. Where the chicory is."

"And will not leave," said Pavel. "Until he is found." He straightened. His eyes blazed. "A man, you see? Shipwrecked. Or a prisoner. Sits in a cave. Waits. Threw a bottle into the sea, who knows, someone may find it." He seized my shoulder. "And we found it! The tunny swallowed, Yannis caught, and we found it! It is... it is fate!"

"Pavel," I said. "We do not know when it was thrown."

"We do!" Pavel jabbed at the note. "'Has waited since...' A gap here. But the paper is good. Not old. A year. Perhaps two. The man is still alive!"

"And if not?"

Pavel looked at me. Long. And in his grey eyes, twenty years old, blazing, there was something that I saw in him later, old, forty years on, when he told of the Turkmen old man in the sands.

"Then at least we shall find where he waited," he said. "So that someone should know."

* * *
Yannis gave us a boat.

His own. Blue, with an eye on the bow. He said, take it, Russian, my hands are no longer what they were, the tunny have grown stronger than I. Then he looked at me, long, with his faded blue eyes, and said something more. Pavel translated, laughing:

"He says you look like one who lives in caves. Says on their island there are such. The Nereids carry them off when they are little, and then release them, grown, without memory." Pavel winked at me. "Says they can be recognised: they are not afraid of the dark and always know where the water is deepest."

Yannis nodded. Gravely. And held out to me, not to Pavel, to me, something small. A bit of bread. And a pinch of salt in a scrap of paper.

"What is this for?" I asked.

Pavel translated. Yannis answered.

"He says, if in the cave they offer you to stay," Pavel translated, no longer laughing, "eat the bread, throw the salt over your shoulder, and go." Pavel paused. "Says that is what they do. So that the Nereids do not take one."

Bread and salt. Over the shoulder.

Somewhere, sometime, in a city on two shores, a small, dry little old man in an enormous white turban had pushed into my hand a canvas pouch, and said the same. Word for word.

I had never seen that little old man.

I took the bread and salt.

* * *
The Frenchman attached himself to us on the second day.

His name was Monsieur Anselin, Auguste-Marie Anselin, a member of the Paris Society of Naturalists, a botanist attached to the French squadron "for the study of the flora of the Levant." He was not young, about fifty, round-faced, bald, short-sighted, in enormous spectacles, in a straw hat with a wide brim and in a frock coat whose pockets were stuffed with herbaria, lenses, test tubes, penknives and rusks. He had learned of the note from Yannis (Yannis, it seemed, had told the whole island) and came to our beach at dawn, panting, with a tin plant-case over his shoulder.

"Messieurs!" he cried, seeing us at the boat. "Messieurs, you cannot! You cannot look for Cichorium intybus in a cave!"

"Why?" asked Pavel.

"Because Cichorium intybus," Monsieur Anselin raised a finger, "grows in the sun! On roadsides! On waste ground! On dry meadows! It needs light! A great deal of light! In a cave chicory cannot grow! It contradicts all the laws of botany!"

"But the note says, at the entrance," I said. "Not inside. At the entrance."

Monsieur Anselin froze. Adjusted his spectacles.

"At the entrance," he repeated. "At the entrance... that is... hm. At the entrance, possibly. If the entrance faces south. Or east. If there is a cleft where the sun comes in..." He suddenly came to life. "Messieurs! That changes things! I must see it! Chicory at the entrance of a sea grotto! On limestone! In salt spray! It will be a sensation! I shall write a paper for the *Annales*!"

"Monsieur," said Pavel patiently, "the boat has two seats."

"I shall sit in the middle!" cried the botanist. "I am small! I shall take up no room! I shall hold the case on my knees!"

He was not small. But he sat in the middle. Three days. With the case on his knees. And with a lens in his hand, with which he examined every bush, every blade of grass, every lichen on the rocks we sailed past.

* * *
"And do you know, messieurs," said Monsieur Anselin on the second day, as we sailed along the white cliffs of the island's eastern shore, "do you know what they tell of chicory in Germany?"

"No," said Pavel, bending to his oar.

"Oh!" The botanist beamed. Adjusted his spectacles. Cleared his throat. "In Germany it is called Wegwarte. That means 'she who waits by the road.' Or 'the guardian of the road.'" He paused, looking at the cliffs. "There is a legend. Old. Rustic." He took off his hat, as if before something holy. "There was a girl. Beautiful. Kind. And she had a betrothed. A knight. Or a soldier. Or a sailor, every village tells it differently. And one day he went away. To war. Or to sea. Or on a crusade. And said to her: 'Wait for me. I shall return.'"

Pavel stopped rowing. Turned round.

"And she waited," Monsieur Anselin went on. "Every day. She went out onto the road by which he had gone, and gazed into the distance. With blue eyes. A day. A month. A year. Ten years. He did not return. And she stood. And stood. And stood." The botanist paused. "And one day God took pity on her. And turned her into a flower. Blue. Like her eyes. And so she remained standing by the road. For ever. And every morning she opens her blue petals and looks at the road, is he not coming. And by noon she closes them. Tired of waiting." Monsieur Anselin put on his hat. "It is true, messieurs. Botanical truth. The flowers of chicory open at dawn and close by noon. Every day. I have observed it. Twenty years."

We were silent. The boat drifted slowly along the cliffs. Water lapped at the side.

"And did he return?" asked Pavel. Quietly. Quite unlike the way he usually asked.

Monsieur Anselin looked at him over his spectacles.

"In the legend, no, young man," he said. "In the legend, never." He paused. "Otherwise it would not be a legend. But simply a story of how a man came home. There are thousands of such stories. No one tells them."

Pavel turned away. Took up his oar. Rowed, hard, sharply, long, without looking round.

And I looked at the chain on his neck. At what glinted on it. A small silver medallion. Oval. With a tiny clasp.

* * *
In the evening, by a fire on a little beach under the cliffs where we stopped for the night, Monsieur Anselin was already snoring, covered with his frock coat and hugging his plant-case, Pavel opened the medallion.

Not for me. For himself. He sat by the fire looking inside, and I saw his face in the glow of the flames, young, tanned, stubborn, and something in it that I had not seen by day. Longing.

"Who is it?" I asked.

He started. Snapped the medallion shut. Then, slowly, opened it again. Held it out to me.

Inside was a portrait. Tiny, on ivory, in a fine brush. A girl. About sixteen. Fair hair, dressed in a simple style. A thin face. Serious eyes. Blue. Like chicory.

"Dunya," said Pavel. "Evdokia." He paused. "A neighbour. On the estate. We have, since childhood..." He faltered. "I went to the navy two years ago. She came out onto the road to see me off. And said: 'I shall wait, Pavlusha.' I was eighteen. She sixteen." He swallowed. "I said: 'I shall return in a year.' And now it is two. And war. And another war will come, with the Turks, they say, in spring. And after, who knows."

I looked at the portrait. At the serious girl's face. At the blue eyes.

I knew this face. Older. Much older. Beneath a hat with a heron's plume. In a silvery-grey dress. Straightening the collar of a general's uniform late in the evening in an empty drawing room, thinking no one saw.

"I have waited for you since you were twenty, Pavel. What are five more years to me?"

"She will wait," I said.

Pavel looked at me.

"How do you know?"

"I know," I said. I could not explain. "Long. Very long. Longer than you think."

Pavel looked at me for a long time across the fire. Then slowly closed the medallion. Tucked it under his shirt.

"You are strange," he said. Without mockery. "I have known you all my life. We were in the Corps together. We came to the frigate together." He paused. "And sometimes I look at you and do not know you. As if you were not from here. As if you knew what has not yet been."

I did not answer. I did not know whether I had been with him in the Corps. I remembered no Corps. I remembered only the boat, the water, the cliffs, and his face, which I knew old.

* * *
On the third day we found the two rocks.

They rose from the water at the island's eastern tip, two enormous white limestone blocks, eaten by wind and waves, standing so close to each other that our boat could barely pass between them. Like two pillars. Like the two jambs of a door. And behind them, in the sheer wall of the island, a dark opening. Low, wide, semicircular. A grotto.

"Les deux rochers!" shrieked Monsieur Anselin, leaping up so abruptly that the boat nearly capsized. "Two rocks! Messieurs! It is they! It is they!"

"Sit down, monsieur," said Pavel through his teeth, steadying the boat with an oar. "Or we shall bathe before our time."

The botanist sat. But went on bouncing on the thwart like a child.

We guided the boat between the rocks. Slowly. Carefully. The water here was dark, deep, almost black, and somewhere below us, in the depths, great shadows moved. Tunny, said Pavel. Or not.

The mouth of the grotto was low; we had to duck, almost lie on the bottom of the boat, to pass under the overhanging rock. The stone overhead was wet, cold, fringed with weed. It smelled of salt, iodine, damp, and of something else. Bitterish. Herbal. Like wormwood.

And at the very entrance, on a ledge of rock above the water, where through a narrow crack in the vault fell a ray of sunlight, a single one, thin as a string, a plant grew.

Low. Stiff. With thin, wire-like stems. With narrow leaves. And with flowers.

Blue. Like the eyes of the girl in the portrait. Like the sky at noon. Like water over white sand.

Chicory.

Monsieur Anselin uttered a sound such as, probably, only botanists make who have found what cannot be. Seized his lens. Leaned over the ledge so that he nearly fell into the water. Pavel caught him by the frock coat.

"Impossible," the botanist whispered. "Impossible. Cichorium intybus. In a sea grotto. On bare limestone. In salt spray. With one ray of sun a day." He raised to us eyes wet behind his spectacles. "Messieurs, this is impossible. This cannot be. But, here it is."

"It is waiting," I said.

The botanist looked at me.

"What?"

"Chicory," I said. "She who waits by the road. It waits."

* * *
We sailed into the grotto.

It was large, larger than it seemed from outside. A high vault going up into darkness. Water, motionless, black as ink, reflecting the faint light from the entrance. Walls, white, wet, shining. And silence. Such a silence as does not exist on earth. Only drops falling from the vault. Drip. Drip. Drip. Slowly. Evenly. Like a metronome. Like a clock. Seventy-two beats.

How did I know, seventy-two?

At the far end of the grotto, by the farthest wall, was a ledge. A flat stone shelf above the water. And on it, something.

Pavel steered the boat there. Slowly. Monsieur Anselin held a lantern, a small tin one which, it turned out, he also carried in one of his bottomless pockets.

The light fell on the ledge.

No one was there.

No man. No skeleton. No traces. Only a flat stone. Smooth. Dry, the only dry place in the whole grotto. And on it, two things.

An empty bottle. Green. Thick-walled. With a long neck. Just like the one Yannis took from the tunny. Not yet sealed. And beside it, a stub of pencil.

And on the wall above the ledge, an inscription. Long. Carved in the stone, or no, not carved, as if dissolved in it, in long, flowing, curving lines. Running into one another.

And beneath it, three words. In familiar letters. In Russian.

"Go home, Pavel."

* * *
Pavel looked at the inscription. For a long time. Without moving. The lantern in Monsieur Anselin's hand shook, and shadows danced on the wall.

"What is there?" the botanist whispered. He did not read Russian. "What is written?"

Pavel did not answer.

He looked at the inscription. At his own name. At the three words. Then slowly, very slowly, turned to me.

"That is your handwriting," he said.

"What?"

"That is your handwriting," Pavel repeated. His voice was level, perfectly level, but I saw the knuckles whiten on the hand gripping the oar. "I would know your hand among a thousand. In the Corps we kept one notebook between us. For navigation. You always put a blot at the end." He pointed at the wall. After the word "Pavel," a small thickening. As if the pen had been held back. "There it is."

I looked at the wall. At the three words. At the blot.

"I did not write this, Pavel."

"I know," said Pavel. "You were with me. All three days. You could not. But it is your hand."

Monsieur Anselin, understanding nothing, looked from one to the other.

"Messieurs," he said fearfully. "Messieurs, what has happened? What is written there? Who waited in the grotto?"

Pavel was silent for a long time.

"No one, monsieur," he said at last. "No one waited." He turned away from the wall. "It is only written here where to go."

* * *
We sailed out of the grotto. Into the sun. Into the light. The chicory at the entrance, on the ledge, still glowed blue in its single ray. But, I noticed, passing, its petals were beginning to close. Slowly. One by one. It was noon.

She who waits by the road was tired of waiting.

Pavel, passing the ledge, stretched out a hand and, before Monsieur Anselin could protest, plucked one flower. The smallest. Opened the medallion. Laid it inside, beside the portrait. And closed it.

"Barbarian!" groaned the botanist. "The only specimen!"

"Not the only one, monsieur," said Pavel, not turning. "There are more there. Let them wait."

Monsieur Anselin sat in the middle of the boat hugging his tin case, and was silent. For the first time in three days, silent. Only now and then he moved his lips as if talking to himself in Latin.

And Pavel rowed. Hard. Sharply. Without looking round. And only when the two white rocks were far behind, when the island had grown small and our frigate in the harbour visible, did he suddenly drop the oar.

"I shall return," he said. Not to me. To the sea. "In spring. After the war. I shall return."

"You will return," I said.

He turned.

"You know that I shall not return," he said. "In spring there will be war. With the Turks. Then another. Then an embassy. Then more." He looked at me with grey, twenty-year-old, suddenly aged eyes. "You know. I see it in your face. You know that I shall go away and away. And not return. For long."

I was silent.

"How long?" asked Pavel. "How long will she wait?"

"Long," I said. "Very long."

"How long?"

I did not know how I knew it. But I knew.

"Almost half a century," I said.

Pavel looked at me for a long time. Then laughed. Briefly. Bitterly. As if he had been struck.

"Half a century," he repeated. "And she will wait?"

"She will."

"Like chicory by the road."

"Like chicory."

Pavel turned away. Looked at the island, small, white, receding. At the two rocks by the eastern shore, barely visible from here. Then took the chain from his neck. Opened the medallion. Looked at the portrait. A long time.

"And I?" he asked quietly. "Shall I return? Ever?"

"You will return," I said. "In half a century. Under the linden by the gates. You will take her hand. And she will say 'yes.'"

Pavel closed the medallion. Put the chain back on. Took the oar.

"Then it is well," he said. "Then I too will wait."

* * *
Yannis was waiting for us on the shore.

He sat on an upturned boat, another, old, without an eye, smoking a pipe and looking at the sea with his faded blue eyes. Seeing us, he did not rise. Only took the pipe from his mouth.

Pavel steered the boat to the shore. Leapt into the water. Hauled it onto the sand. Monsieur Anselin climbed out after, hugging his case. And I...

I remained in the boat.

I do not know why. I wanted to stand, and could not. My legs would not obey. My hands lay on the oars. The boat rocked on the shallow wave at the very shore.

"Well?" Yannis asked in Greek. Pavel translated, not turning:

"He asks, did you find the one who waited?"

"We did," said Pavel. "Not the one who waited. The one who is waited for."

Yannis looked at him a long time. Then slowly nodded, as though that were the very answer he expected. Then shifted his gaze to me. To the boat. To my hands on the oars.

And said something. Quietly. Pavel froze.

"What did he say?" I asked.

Pavel turned to me. His face was white beneath the tan.

"He said," Pavel said slowly, "'And this one is already leaving. The Nereids have called.'" Pavel looked at me. "What does that mean?"

I looked at my hands. At the oars. They were... transparent. Not quite. A little. Like water over white sand. Through my fingers I saw the wood of the oars.

"Pavel," I said.

"What?" He stepped toward me. Into the water. Knee-deep. "What is wrong with you?"

"Remember the note? Three languages. 'Waits... will not leave... home.'"

"I remember."

"I wrote it," I said. I did not know whether it was true. But the words came of themselves. "Not now. Later. In half a century. Or sooner. Or before. I do not know." The boat rocked. Water showed through my knees. "I wrote it to you. So that you should find it. So that you should remember. That you are awaited."

"Why?" Pavel stood waist-deep, gripping the boat's side. "Why in half a century?"

"Because in half a century," I said, "you will have something to do. For me." I looked at him. "You will have to give me a scroll. And bring me to the city on two shores." I paused. "And you will do it, Pavel. Because you remember that you are awaited. And that I wrote to you, 'go home.'"

Pavel looked at me. Waist-deep in water. With the medallion on his neck. Twenty. With grey eyes which would one day become the eyes of an old general by a fireplace.

"Who are you?" he asked.

I opened my mouth.

And could not answer. Not because I did not know. But because the boat, with me, suddenly became light. Quite light. Like a leaf. Like a feather. And it was borne away, not by wave, not by wind, by something else. Away from the shore. Away from Pavel. Away from the island.

"Stop!" cried Pavel. Lunged after. The water came to his chest. "Stop! Tell me! Who are you?!"

"You will know!" I cried. My voice sounded far off, as though through water. "In half a century! You will look at faces! All your life! On all continents! And one day you will see!"

The boat drifted away. The island grew smaller. Pavel too. A little dark figure in a white shirt, standing chest-deep in the transparent water, with a raised hand.

And beside him, on the shore, old Yannis, who had taken the pipe from his mouth. And Monsieur Anselin hugging his tin case, in which, I knew, lay a pressed blue flower plucked at the entrance of the grotto. Impossible. Botanically impossible.

And through the noise of the water, through the distance, through everything, I heard the last thing Pavel cried:

"I will find you! Do you hear?! I will search! All my life!"

* * *
I opened my eyes.

I do not know in which of my lives. In which body. Under which sky. Afterward, in each of them, I dreamed of this boat, blue, with an eye on the bow, and the still water over white sand, and the two white rocks like the jambs of a door, and a blue flower in a single ray of sun.

And in each I woke with the same feeling. As if I had just, very long ago, sent a letter. The most important letter of my life. In a bottle. To the sea. Not knowing who would find it. Not knowing when.

And as if that letter had been found.

And as if someone, young, with grey eyes, with a medallion on his neck, had read in it three words. And for half a century had carried them within him. Over the sands of Khiva and the steppes of Mongolia. Along the streets of Peking and Havana. On the decks of ships in the Pacific. Through the eucalyptus forests of Australia. On the slopes of Sitka in the rain. In the temples of Siam. Through halls and drawing rooms, embassies and wars.

Half a century, looking at faces.

Until one day, late in the evening, by an old castle, on the grass by a black grille, he bent over a young man without memory, lying with open eyes and smiling, and said quietly, to himself:

"Again."

And in the breast pocket of his uniform, beside the wooden raven that stole the sun, and the paper crane that must be folded back into a sheet, all this time, half a century, lay an old silver medallion. And in it, beside the faded portrait of a girl with blue eyes, a small, dried, blue, botanically impossible flower.

Chicory.

She who waits by the road.

## Reality X. The Ocean

06:11. I am sitting on black sand. The laptop on my knees, its camera turned to the water. Boatswain's ship's chest beside me on the sand, open, like a pirate's coffer. The sun has not yet risen. The sky in the east is pink-grey, like the inside of a shell. The sea is still dark, almost black, quiet, breathing.

NICS has been silent for nine minutes.

I time it by the clock on the screen. Nine minutes. Not a line. Not a sound. Only the cursor blinking in the empty field. Evenly. Patiently. Like a metronome.

I do not hurry him.

* * *
But let me take things in order.

We arrived on Langkawi yesterday evening, by ferry from Kuala Perlis, overcrowded, thundering, smelling of diesel, fried noodles and children's sick. Hakim came with us. "Mister," he said, "you cannot manage on the island without me. They speak the Kedah dialect there. Even I understand it only every other word. And you not a single one."

He sat beside me on the ferry, in his batik shirt with the golden birds, in his velvet songkok, and ate rambutans from a bag, red, hairy, like little sea urchins, peeling them with one motion of a fingernail and tossing the peel overboard.

"Langkawi, mister," he said, chewing, "means 'red eagle.' Or 'russet eagle.' *Lang* is eagle, *kawi* is reddish-brown. Like clay. Eagles live here. Hundreds. You will see." He spat out a stone. "And some say 'Langkawi' means 'necklace of beads.' Because the islands, there are a hundred here, a hundred and four, lie in the sea like beads on a thread." He thought. "And my uncle says that 'Langkawi' means 'the place where my uncle once lost a sandal.' But my uncle translates everything so."

The ferry lurched. Hakim imperturbably caught a rambutan that rolled off his knee.

"And is it true that the island was cursed?" I asked.

Hakim stopped chewing.

"Mahsuri," he said. "Yes. Two hundred years ago. Seven generations." He looked at the sea. "Mister, on the island they will tell you. There is her grave. And there lives an old woman who says she is the great-great-granddaughter of Mahsuri's granddaughter." He smiled. "On the island there are many such old women. Each a great-great-granddaughter. But this one, they say, is real."

* * *
The taxi driver who met us at the quay was called Pak Dol. He was small, dry, wrinkled, with one gold tooth and a tattoo on his forearm, a blue anchor, exactly like Boatswain's.

I stared at the anchor.

Pak Dol noticed my look. Grinned. Said something.

"He says," Hakim translated, "that for twenty years he sailed on merchant ships. Singapore, Hong Kong, Busan, Rotterdam." Hakim listened on. "Says in Rotterdam they gave him this anchor. A drunken tattooist. He wanted a dragon. Got an anchor." Hakim laughed. "Says, good that it was not a mermaid."

"Tell him," I said, "that I have a friend. Also a sailor. With the same anchor."

Hakim translated. Pak Dol turned to me, the car swerved on the road, looked at me closely and said slowly, in English, with a heavy accent:

"Friend, with anchor? On left arm?"

"On the left."

"Thirty years at sea?"

"Thirty."

"Boatswain?"

I froze.

Pak Dol looked at me in the rear-view mirror for a long time. Then suddenly laughed, high, with a rasp, and slapped the wheel.

"All boatswains have anchor on left arm!" he said. "All! All over the world! It is law!" He roared again. "You think I know your friend? I know all your friends! They are all the same! They drink, they swear, they listen to weather forecast on radio and guard other people's things!" He winked. "Right?"

"Right," I said.

"Tell him from me," said Pak Dol, "that old Dol of Langkawi sends greetings. He does not know me. But he will understand. All boatswains understand each other."

* * *
The guesthouse to which Pak Dol brought us stood on stilts above a mangrove swamp, in the shade of enormous trees whose roots, like spiders' legs, stuck out of the water. The hostess was a woman of about sixty, round, laughing, in a flowered sarong and headscarf, named Mak Cha. She met us on the veranda with a tray bearing two glasses of something bright green.

"Pandan juice," said Hakim. "With coconut. Drink, mister. Mak Cha will be offended if you don't. And when Mak Cha is offended, it stops raining on the island."

Mak Cha laughed and said something.

"She says," Hakim translated, "that it is true. Three years ago she was offended with her husband. For a week. And for a week there was no rain on the island." Hakim paused. "And then the husband brought her a durian. And the rain came." He shrugged. "On the island everyone believes it. The husbands too."

I drank the green juice, sweet, smelling of vanilla and grass. Mak Cha watched me closely. Then looked at Boatswain's chest, which I did not let out of my hands.

And said something, quietly, seriously.

"She asks," Hakim translated, "what you have in the chest. She says the chest smells. Of sea. But not this sea. Cold. Northern." Hakim was himself surprised. "Says she can sense it."

"Tell her," I said, "there is a friend in it. Who wants to see the ocean."

Hakim translated. Mak Cha looked at the chest for a long time. Then came up. Laid her palm on the lid. Held it there. As though testing whether it was warm.

And said:

"Bawa dia ke Pantai Pasir Hitam. Waktu subuh."

"Take him to the Beach of Black Sand," Hakim translated slowly. "At dawn."

"Why black?"

Mak Cha answered, at length, in a sing-song, as though telling a tale.

"She says," Hakim translated, "that the sand there is black because it is ash. Two hundred years ago, when the Siamese attacked the island, the people burned their stores of rice so that the enemy should get none. The rice burned for three days. And the rain washed the ash onto this beach." Hakim listened on. "She says, it is rice that burned so that the island might live." He paused. "And that at dawn the sea speaks there. If one knows how to listen."

* * *
The grave of Mahsuri stood in the midst of rice fields, in the shade of mango trees, beneath a white marble canopy. A simple stone. White. With an inscription in Arabic script, Hakim read it aloud to me. Around it, a garden. Flowers. Quiet. There were no tourists; it was evening, and the sun was setting behind the hills, flooding the fields with russet, copper, warm light.

By the grave, on a low bench, sat an old woman.

Very old. Small. In white. With a face brown and wrinkled like the sun-dried rind of a mangosteen, with eyes dark, deep, astonishingly clear. She was running through her fingers a string of beads, wooden, dark, polished. And humming something.

"Nene Sari," Hakim whispered. "The very one. The great-great-granddaughter. She is, they say, a hundred and two."

A hundred and two. Like Niyaz Efendi, I thought. And did not understand where that name came from. Niyaz Efendi. A hundred and two years. Two pairs of spectacles. A round room with shelves.

I had never seen such a man.

The old woman stopped singing. Raised her eyes to me. Looked. A long time. Then said something, quietly, in Malay.

"She asks," Hakim translated, "where you are from."

I opened my mouth. And closed it.

"I do not know," I said.

Hakim hesitated, then translated.

Nene Sari was not surprised. She nodded, slowly, as though she had awaited precisely that answer. And patted the bench beside her.

I sat.

* * *
"Mahsuri was beautiful," Nene Sari told, and Hakim translated, under his breath, so as not to break her rhythm. "The most beautiful on the island. Her husband went to war, with the Siamese. And in her house a wanderer stopped. Young. A poet. A singer. Without a name. He came from nowhere." The old woman ran the beads through her fingers. "He sang her songs when she missed her husband. Nothing more. Only songs. But wicked people said she had been unfaithful. The chieftain's wife envied her beauty. Mahsuri was seized. Tied to a post. They meant to stab her with a dagger." Nene Sari paused. "The dagger would not take her. Seven times they struck, it would not take. Then she herself said: 'Take my father's dagger. It hangs in my house.' They brought it. Struck." The old woman looked at the grave. "And from the wound flowed blood. White. Like milk."

"White blood," I repeated.

"A sign that she was innocent," said Nene Sari. "And then Mahsuri cursed the island. 'For seven generations,' she said, 'there will be neither peace nor harvest here.' And died." The old woman paused. "And indeed, for two hundred years the island was poor. The Siamese came. Pirates came. Rice did not grow." She passed her hand over the beads. "And then seven generations passed. And the island revived. Tourists. Hotels." She smiled toothlessly. "Mahsuri, I think, is glad."

"And the wanderer?" I asked. "The poet without a name? What became of him?"

Nene Sari was silent for a long time.

"We do not tell that to tourists," she said at last. "Only to our own." She looked at me. "You are not ours. But you do not know where you are from. So perhaps you are ours."

She leaned toward me. Hakim leaned too, to hear and translate.

"The wanderer went into the sea," the old woman whispered. "On the night Mahsuri died. Straight into the water. From the beach that is now black sand. Walked and walked until the water closed over his head." She paused. "The fishermen said he did not drown. They said the water glowed around him. Blue. And he walked on the glowing water. And sang. And went away to where the sea meets the sky." Nene Sari straightened. "And before leaving he said to her little son: 'In seven generations I shall return. To see how you live without the curse.'"

Hakim translated the last phrase and fell silent. Looked at me.
