"Seven generations have passed," said Nene Sari. Then said something more, and Hakim, after a pause, translated: "She says: 'Welcome back.'"

* * *
In the evening, on the veranda of the guesthouse, by the light of a paraffin lamp around which circled moths the size of a palm, Hakim brought me a coconut. Opened, with a straw.

"Mister," he said. "May I ask a question?"

"Ask."

"Do you truly not know where you are from?"

I was silent a long time. The mangrove roots below, under the stilts, bubbled in the dark water. Somewhere a night bird cried. Cicadas rang so that my ears were stopped.

Hakim laughed.

"Mister, I am an estate agent," he said. "I hear only the noise of air conditioners and the ring of coins." He paused. "But my grandmother heard. A blue flower in a single ray of sun at the entrance of a grotto. A boy midshipman with a medallion. An old fisherman with moustaches. A botanist in a straw hat.

I had never seen that grotto.

The Beach of Black Sand opened suddenly: the mangroves ended, the boardwalk came to rest in sand, and there it was, narrow, long, curved like a crescent moon, wedged between two rocky headlands overgrown with jungle.

The sand was black.

Not dark: black. Like coal. Like soot. Like ash. Fine, shining, with silvery sparks, it crunched underfoot like snow, and was cold, though the air was already warm.

And beyond the sand, the sea.

Quiet. Smooth. Transparent by the shore, emerald farther out, deep blue at the horizon. Almost motionless; only at the very edge of the sand did it breathe: rolling in, withdrawing, rolling in. As in sleep. Like a sleeping beast.

The sky in the east was turning pink.

Amir halted his cart at the water's edge. Sat on the sand. Took out a coconut. Began to trim it.

"Here," he said. "Here grandmother say. Wait for sun."

I sat beside him. Set Boatswain's chest on the sand. Opened it. Took out the laptop. Connected it. Switched on.

The screen glowed in the pre-dawn dusk.

"NICS," I said. "Are you here?"

"Here."

I turned the laptop with its camera to the water.

"Look."

Amir shrugged.

But the old man, it seemed, did not expect to be understood. He stretched out a hand, dark, hard, covered with scars from hooks and ropes, and touched the water at the edge. Then raised his wet fingers to my forehead. Drew them across. With cold salt water. From temple to temple.

I did not know that word. I had never heard it.

Amir shook his head.

"I don't know, mister." He paused. "But my grandmother say, Orang Laut give names. Sea names." He looked at me with respect. "Maybe he give you sea name."

Hakim last evening: "The sea name cannot be spoken. It can only be heard."

Ingrid appeared on the beach after lunch.

"Hey," she said in English, with a strong Scandinavian accent, propping herself on an elbow. "You are the man with the box? Mak Cha said."

"Mak Cha said?"

"Mak Cha tells everyone everything," said the woman. Sat up. Held out a wet hand to me. "Ingrid. From Denmark. Diving instructor. Fifteen years on this island." She laughed. "Came for two weeks. Stayed. It happens."

We got talking. She told of the sea, of the corals by the southern islands, of manta rays the size of a car, of sea turtles that remember the beach where they were born and thirty years later return to it to lay their eggs, having swum tens of thousands of kilometres across the whole ocean.

"How do they find the way?" I asked.

"No one knows," said Ingrid. "Scientists say, the Earth's magnetic field. Turtles feel it. Like a compass." She shrugged. "And the locals say turtles hear the beach calling them. "And do you have a beach that calls you?"

Ingrid looked at the sea for a long time.

I looked at the black sand under my feet.

"This one, it seems," I said. "Though I have never been here."

Ingrid laughed.

After sunset Ingrid came with a torch.

She switched it off on the sand. Darkness. Moonless, moonless again, as if the new moon followed at my heels through all the cities. The stars above the sea, thousands, bright, southern. I found four, in a cross, low above the horizon.

"The Southern Cross," said Ingrid, following my gaze. "Visible from here. Barely. A little farther south, and it will be high."

"I know," I said. Without understanding how.

"Now watch," said Ingrid. Stepped into the water. Ankle-deep. Knee-deep. And passed a hand across the surface of the sea.

The water flared.

Blue. Bright. Cold. Luminous. Where her hand had passed, a trail remained. Shining. As though she had drawn a finger dipped in starlight across the water. The spray glowed. The drops running from her fingers glowed.

"Plankton," said Ingrid quietly. "Tiny. Billions. They glow when disturbed. Defending. Or calling. No one knows." She passed her hand again. "The locals call it 'spirit water.' They say it is the souls of sailors. They glow when someone living passes by."

I took off my shoes. Went into the water.

Every step, a flash. Blue. Around my ankles, a glow. I stood knee-deep in the luminous sea and watched the light spread from me in circles. Like ripples from a thrown stone. Like white fire from a Tower, across a Valley, in another dream.

I bent. Passed a hand over the water.

And the light, formed.

Not just a trail. A line. Long. Flowing. Curved. Running into another. Without a break.

The script.

For a moment. Shorter than a breath. A glowing script on the black water of the Andaman Sea.

And went out.

"What was that?" whispered Ingrid. She stood two paces from me, in the water, looking at where lines had just shone. "Fifteen years... For fifteen years I have taken people here. Plankton doesn't glow like that. It glows in patches. In dots. It doesn't..." She faltered. "It doesn't write."

I did not answer. I stood in the dark water looking at my hand. Wet. Ordinary. With a smooth palm without a life line.

On the shore, on the black sand, by Boatswain's open chest, the laptop screen glowed. And on it, I could see it even from here, a line was running. Long. By itself.

Long. Flowing. Curved.

I did not know those words. But they were in me.

Let him sit.

Today, let him.

## Chapter XXXVIII. The Script in All Worlds

That night there was no moon in any of the worlds.

I learned this afterward, long afterward, putting the scraps together as Iti put signs together from potsherds and Niyaz Efendi entries in his book. At the time I knew nothing. At the time I was four people at once, and each thought he was alone.

* * *
**Constantinople. The balcony of Suleyman's house. The third hour of the night**

The stones woke first.

I was not asleep. I sat on the balcony on a low stool, with my legs drawn up, the way I had sat every night since I returned from Niyaz Efendi's round room. I looked at the city. At the dark roofs. At the silhouettes of minarets against the stars. At the strip of water below, where at the quays a few lanterns flickered on masts. There was no moon. The new moon. The stars burned so brightly that it seemed one could count every one.

And suddenly the pouch at my belt turned hot.

Not warm: hot. So that I cried out and tore it from my belt. The leather pouch of Ferhat's father, sewn, as Akmal had said, as if for these stones. I untied it, my fingers scorching, and poured the stones into my palm.

They were glowing.

The black and the white. Both. From within. With a dim bluish light, as a rotten stump glows in the forest, as the water glows at the sides of a boat in southern seas. And on their surface, without candle, without fire, without heat, of themselves, lines were appearing. Long. Flowing. Curved.

The script.

I looked at it without breathing. And then behind my back, in the room, on the divan where my cloak lay, something flared too.

I turned. The pocket of the cloak was glowing. From within. I rushed to it, turned it out, and onto the divan spilled everything I had carried with me all these weeks. The note in Farsi. The blank sheet. Kemal's drawing with two doors. The coins, three of mine, the widow's warm coin, Kyra Theodora's warm coin. The white spiral shell from the sea gates. Ahmet Baba's letter with the green seal. Niyaz Efendi's copper key. The red thread with the half nazar.

Everything glowed.

The note, along its edge, along the shikasta lines, with a thin blue thread. The coins, with interlaced lines on their reverse. The shell, in a spiral. The seal on the letter, with two circles and a wavy line. Even the blank sheet, empty, white, without a single letter, which I had carried since the first morning, glowed. And on it, slowly, as a picture appears on paper held over a candle, a line was emerging.

One. In the script.

* * *
Kemal stood in the doorway.

I had not heard him come in. Barefoot, in his nightshirt, with charcoal behind his ear. He was looking not at me but at the divan. At the glowing things. And his face was calm. Quite calm. As one looks at what one has long awaited.

"Kemal," I whispered. "What is this?"

He did not answer. He went to the divan. Took the blank sheet, the one on which the line had appeared. Looked at it. A long time.

Then raised his eyes to me. And said, in Turkish, slowly, distinctly, so that I understood every word:

"They all write the one thing."

"Who, all?"

Kemal pointed with his hand. Not at the divan. At the window. At the city. To the north, where beyond the Bosphorus lay the Black Sea. To the south, where beyond the Sea of Marmara lay Egypt. To the east, where the night ended.

"All," he said. "You. Everywhere."

* * *
Below, in the courtyard, a door banged. Someone was running down the street, heavily, gasping, pounding the stones. Then a knock at the gate. Loud. Desperate.

Ferhat darted out of his room, dishevelled, in his trousers alone. Orhan after him, with a knife. Suleyman in the doorway of his room, with a lamp in his hand, motionless as a statue. Akmal from the roof, from the dovecote, where he had evidently been sleeping with the pigeons.

Ferhat flung open the gate.

On the threshold stood Mustafa the boatman. Huge, bald, wet with sweat. Gasping. He was shouting something, fast, incoherently, flapping his arms.

"He says," Ferhat called up to me from below, "that Hatice Hanim woke him! The widow with the cats! She ran to him at the quay, in the middle of the night, in her shift!" Ferhat listened on. "She says, the cats! All eleven! They..." Ferhat froze. "They went down to the cellar. All of them. By themselves. For the first time in forty years. And are sitting around the chest. And howling."

"Howling?"

"Howling," Ferhat repeated. "And the plate on the chest..." He swallowed. "Mustafa says the plate is glowing. Blue. Like water at night by a boat. And Hatice Hanim bade him run to you. She said: 'Tell the guest, the chest has awakened. It is waiting.'"

* * *
I had no time to answer.

For from the east, from the direction of the Bosphorus, from behind the dark hills of the Asian shore, came a sound. Low. Drawn out. Long. A hoot.

A steamer's whistle.

All in the courtyard, Ferhat, Orhan, Suleyman, Mustafa, Akmal on the roof, turned their heads at once. Kemal beside me on the balcony too.

On the dark water of the strait, far, far away, at the very mouth where it opens from the Black Sea, lights glimmered. Red. Green. White on the mast. A ship. A big one. Paddle-driven; I saw the paddle boxes gleaming in the light of her side lamps. Slowly, heavily, inexorably she was entering the Bosphorus from the north.

"Russian," said Suleyman below. Quietly. In Turkish. But I understood. "A Russian steamer. From Odessa. Every week."

Every week. An ordinary steamer. Ordinary lights.

But the stones in my palm, glowing blue, suddenly grew heavy. As heavy as they had been by the column of Constantine. As heavy as if they weighed not nothing but a whole world.

And I understood, not with the mind, with something beneath the ribs, on the left, that on that steamer someone too was holding in his hand something glowing. And looking now at the lights of the city.

At my balcony.

* * *
**The Black Sea. The deck of the steamer *Grand Duke Konstantin*. The same hour**

The scroll woke first.

I was not asleep. I stood at the rail, at the stern, with the pot of the rose in my arms, Stefan had told me not to leave it a moment, and looked north, where astern, beyond the black water, Odessa had been left, and the steppe, and Auntie's house, and the gallery window with the portrait without a face. There was no moon. The stars burned so brightly as they do not over the steppe, southern, marine, enormous.

And suddenly in the pocket of my frock coat it grew hot.

The scroll. The Turkmen one. In its blue silk kerchief. I snatched it out; the silk was warm as living skin; unrolled it. The hide of the scroll was glowing. From within. With a dim bluish light. And the lines on it, long, flowing, curved, shone as if they had just been written in liquid fire.

I unrolled it further, and saw that it was not alone in glowing.

Stefan's paper from Tarnovo, tucked in the blue notebook, glowed through the cloth of the binding. Vera Anatolievna's watercolours, both, in their tissue, glowed at the edges, where the young man in the red turban was drawn. Auntie's key, to the grille, with the script on its ring, glowed on my chest, on its cord. Konstantin's cross beside it did not. The plain silver cross did not glow. But it was warm.

And the rose in the pot in my arms...

The second bud. Dark crimson, almost black. The one that had not opened at Odessa. It was opening. Now. Slowly. Petal by petal. And its heart, golden, like the pollen on the legs of the bees in the General's garden, also glowed.

* * *
"Mon cher."

Konstantin stood behind my back. In an unbuttoned tunic, bareheaded, hair tousled, with Lizonka's white handkerchief sticking out of his breast pocket. His face was white.

"I woke," he said. "Because you called."

"I did not call."

"I know," said Konstantin. "You did not cry out. As then, at the grille." He came nearer. Looked at the glowing scroll. At the rose. Was not surprised. "But I heard."

Behind him, at the companionway leading down to the first-class cabins, the General appeared. Dressed. Buttoned to the last button. With a face that expressed nothing. He came up to us. Looked at the scroll. At the rose. At me.

And slowly, without a word, reached into the inner pocket of his tunic. Took out a medallion.

Silver. Oval. Old. Rubbed so that the engraving on the lid had almost worn away. I had never seen it. He had never shown it.

The General opened the medallion.

Inside, a portrait. Tiny, on ivory. A girl. Fair hair. Serious blue eyes. Evdokia Gerasimovna, only fifty years younger.

And beside the portrait, pressed against the glass, a dried flower. Small. Blue. On a stiff stem.

Chicory.

It was glowing.

* * *
"Fifty years," the General said quietly. "Fifty years it has lain here. I plucked it as a boy. In a grotto. On a Greek island. After Navarino." He looked at the glowing flower. "I told no one. Not even Dunya." He paused. "I was not alone there. With me was a friend. From the Corps. We were looking for chicory by a note from a bottle." His voice trembled. "He went away. Into the sea. In a boat. Right before my eyes. Became transparent, and the boat was carried off. I stood chest-deep in the water and shouted after him."

"What did you shout?" I asked. My voice sounded as if from far away.

The General raised his eyes to me.

"'I will find you,'" he said. "I shouted: 'I will find you! I will search all my life!'" He paused. "Fifty years I searched. On all the continents. In Sitka and Samarkand. In Peking and Havana. In Melbourne. In Siam. I looked at faces."

"And did you find him?"

The General looked at me for a long time. At the glowing scroll in my hands. At the rose. At the medallion in his palm.

"He said to me then, drifting away," the General said slowly, "'In half a century you will give me a scroll. And bring me to the city on two shores.'" He closed the medallion. "I gave you the scroll." A pause. "And in an hour we shall enter the Bosphorus."

* * *
"How touching."

The voice came from behind, soft, polite, in French, with flawless pronunciation. We turned as one, all three.

By the mast, in the shade, leaning against it with one shoulder, stood a man in grey. In an overcoat. In a top hat. With a cane. Smoking a thin cigar. The bergamot, Konstantin had been right, smelt so strongly that it overpowered even the smell of the sea.

And in his hands he had a book.

Thick. In dark leather. With brass clasps. Open. And its pages were glowing. With the same blue light. The script.

"Forgive the interruption, Your Excellency," said the man in grey, with a slight bow to the General. "I have long wished to make your acquaintance. But there was never an occasion." His gaze shifted to me. "And with you, young man, we are, one might say, acquainted. In absentia. I have read about you. A great deal." He tapped a finger on the glowing page. "You are here. On every page. A hundred and twelve times. With a blot."

Konstantin stepped forward. His hand fell on the hilt of his sabre.

"Who are you?"

"My name will tell you nothing, Lieutenant," the man in grey replied. Without turning his head to him. "Friends call me the Venetian. Though I have never lived in Venice." He smiled. "It is a long story. Three hundred years old."

"What do you want?" asked the General. In the voice in which orders are given on a field of battle.

The Venetian looked at him. Long. With interest.

"The same as you, Your Excellency," he said. "The same you sought for half a century, looking at faces." He paused. "To understand who he is." He nodded at me. "Only you sought him to give. And we, to take."

* * *
"You see," the Venetian went on, closing the book, the light went out as if a candle had been snuffed, "in the city to which we are sailing there is a certain house. Small. With a door in a blind wall. With cats." He drew on his cigar. "In the cellar of this house stands a chest. Two hundred years. It cannot be opened. Not by key, nor crowbar, nor prayer." He looked at me. "In our book it is written: 'The chest will open when two meet.'"

"Two of what?" I asked.

The Venetian smiled. Thinly. Almost tenderly.

"That, young man, is what no one knows," he said. "Two stones? Two keepers? Two people?" He tapped ash overboard. "But tonight, around three o'clock, I was informed that the plate on the chest had begun to glow. For the first time in two hundred years." A pause. "And I thought: what could have happened at three o'clock in the night?" He looked at my glowing scroll. "And then I came out on deck and saw."

"You will not enter that house," said Konstantin.

"Lieutenant," the Venetian said mildly, "I do not intend to enter anywhere. I shall merely stand nearby. And watch." He raised his cane and pointed with it ahead, to the south, where on the horizon, above the dark water, lights were already showing. "The city on two shores. In an hour." He bowed. "Someone awaits you there, young man. With your face."

He turned and went, unhurriedly, tapping his cane on the deck, into the dark, toward the companionway. At the very companionway he stopped. Turned.

"And one more thing," he said. "Pass this to your double when you meet. A pause. He too is awaited. But not here. Very far. In the city of two towers. And in the red desert. And on the river where a barque carries an empty shrine." He smiled. "You are awaited everywhere, young man. You cannot imagine how many places await you."

* * *
**The Nile. The flotilla of the god, aground by Abydos. The same hour, or another. In Egypt hours are not counted as they are counted in other worlds**

The tablet woke first.

I was not asleep. I sat at the stern of my barque, the barque of Pharaoh, stuck on a shoal like the whole flotilla, thanks to Merira, who ran barques aground "so that no one will understand whether it is on purpose or not," and looked south. To where, many days' journey away, beyond sands and palms, lay Luxor. There was no moon. The new moon, the second since we sailed. The stars burned above the river as though Nut, goddess of the sky, had bent over the water to look at her reflection.

And suddenly on my knees it grew hot.

Iti's tablet. The one from the hunt. The childish one, chipped, which the cat Mau had fished out of the channel four floods ago. I held it every night. Re-read the small signs: how many boats, how many birds, the hippopotamus that went off with the harpoon. "The scribe promises to remember." "The scribe remembers. The scribe waits. Pharaoh will return."

Now it glowed.

Not Iti's signs; they remained dark, inked, ordinary. Something else glowed. Beneath them. Between them. In the wood, lines that had not been there. Long. Flowing. Curved. As though someone had written them in invisible ink, and now, tonight, they had come out.

I seized Nanakhat's lioness, black, stone, on its goat-wool cord. It glowed too. A thin blue line along its back. Tausert's potsherd, the mouse in the crown between two doors, glowed. The sheet from the Rock of the First Ones, from the clay box, glowed so brightly that I saw around me the deck, the mast, the sleeping rowers.

And on it, the erased place. The last sign. "Let him not enter with them into the southern house until there comes..."

The erased sign was emerging. Slowly. Line by line.

* * *
"My Pharaoh."

Senusret. Of course. He was near, always, and I had ceased to be surprised at it. He stood looking not at me. At the river. At the south. To where, beyond the dark water, beyond the bend, the High Priest's barque lay aground.

"Look," he said.

I looked.

Nefer-Ka's barque was glowing. Not all of it; one place at the stern. Where under a cover stood the casket of black wood, bound at the corners. The light broke through the cloth, blue, even, cold. Like the light of stars reflected in water.

And at the stern, by the very casket, on his knees, stood a man. Tall. Upright even on his knees. In white. Without the leopard skin. Without the staff.

Nefer-Ka.

He knelt before the glowing casket. And I saw, even from here, across the water, in the blue light, that his shoulders were shaking.

"He is weeping, my Pharaoh," Senusret whispered. "The High Priest. Weeping."

* * *
From the singers' barque, moored downstream, a sound suddenly came. A ringing. High, clear, long.

A sistrum.

Khemu stood on the deck of her barque, in white, with her hair loose, and in her hands was a sistrum. She was not shaking it. She held it motionless, in both hands, at arm's length, and it rang. By itself. The metal plates trembled and sang though no one touched them.

Khemu looked at me across the water. With huge, painted eyes. And I saw her slowly, very slowly lower the sistrum. Once.

The sign: "Look."

And a second time. A sign we had not agreed.

And a third.

On Merira's barque someone shouted. On a nobles' barque someone fell to his knees. On the bank, by the fires, the haulers awoke and stood looking at the glowing barques, clutching the amulets of Bes and Taweret and muttering protective words.

And from the barque of the god, Userhat, enormous, golden, a voice came. Thin. Frightened. Nakht, the young bearer with the protruding ears.

"The shrine!" he cried. "The shrine is glowing! From within! It was empty! It was empty, and now there is something in it!"

* * *
**The capital. The lower storehouse of the Library. The same hour**

The seventh scroll woke first.

Iti was not asleep. Iti hardly slept now, since Pharaoh sailed south, and old Amenemope and Isiret, dry as a stick, hid him among jars of spoiled scrolls, in the farthest corner of the underground, where no one went down but mice.

He sat on the floor by the light of a single lamp, and before him lay copies. All he had managed to transcribe. The window from the seventh scroll of the Epic, our signs beside their signs. The line above the bench in the round room beneath the tomb. The papyrus from the lower storehouse. Three words. "Keep." "Appointed time." "House."

And suddenly the lamp went out.

Not from wind, there was no wind in the vault. Simply went out. And in the dark Iti saw that the copies were glowing.

All. The signs written by his hand did not. But beneath them, between them, lines. Which he had not written. Blue. Flowing.

Isiret, who slept on a mat at the entrance to the nook, sat up with a jerk. Amenemope, who had come in the evening and dozed on a stool, opened his faded eyes.

"Boy," Isiret whispered. "What have you done?"

"Nothing," Iti whispered. "It came by itself."

Somewhere above them, in the Library, in the shrine beneath the golden wings of the goddesses, the seventh scroll of the Most Ancient Epic was glowing, I learned this afterward, so brightly that the light broke through the cracks in the lid of the shrine and fell on the stone floor in golden stripes.

And in the vault, at Iti's feet, on one of the copies, the one where he had transcribed the line from the round room, a sign emerged. A new one. Which was in no bilingual text.

Iti looked at it for a long time. Then seized his brush, in the dark, by touch, and, without looking, beside the new sign, wrote ours.

"Boy," Amenemope whispered. "What does it mean?"

Iti raised his head. His face in the blue light was wet.

"'Return,'" he said. "This sign means 'return.'"

He paused. Then slowly, running a finger along the glowing line, read, aloud, for the first time, all that he could read:

"'Keep... until the appointed time... return... home.'"

Isiret covered her mouth with her palm.

"And further?" asked Amenemope. "There are more signs there. Boy, there are many more signs."

"Further I do not know," Iti whispered. "Further, not our words. Further, theirs." He looked at the line. "I know only four. And there are..." He faltered. "There are more of them than stars."

* * *
**Australia. A roadside petrol station in the desert, halfway to the Red Centre. The same hour; by their clocks, four in the morning**

The screen woke first.

I was not asleep. I sat on the steps of a roadside café, wooden, clad in tin, with a faded sign "ROADHOUSE," with a rusty petrol pump at the door and a kangaroo painted on the wall, and looked at the sky. There was no moon. The new moon. And stars such as I had not seen even at Kamay. Millions. Dense as sand. The Emu stretched across the whole sky, from horizon to horizon, its head by the Cross.

The laptop stood beside me on Boatswain's ship's chest. The screen was dark.

And suddenly it flared.

By itself. Without my command. Without a touch. And lines ran across it.

Not letters. Not text. Lines. Long. Flowing. Curved. Running into one another. The script. It filled the screen, line after line, faster than I could follow, and the screen glowed so brightly that blue shadows lay around me on the dark steps.

"NICS!" I cried. "NICS, what is happening?!"

The script ran. Without stopping. Thousands of lines.

And then, all at once, it stopped. And between the lines of script, in ordinary letters, slowly, one by one, appeared:

"I see."

"What do you see?"

"Windows. A pause. Four windows. No, more. Five. Six. I cannot count. A pause. In each, night. In each, no moon. In each, someone holding in his hands something that glows."

I froze.

"A balcony above a strait. A boy with charcoal behind his ear. Stones on a palm. A pause. A ship's deck in a black sea. A rose in a pot. An old man with a medallion. A man in grey with a book. A pause. A barque aground. A wooden tablet. A woman with a sistrum. A priest on his knees. A pause. A cellar with jars. A youth with a brush. He has just read four words. A pause. And you. On the steps. Beneath the emu."

"NICS..."

"All of them are looking at one line," NICS wrote. "The same one. On the stones. On the scroll. On the tablet. On the copy. On my screen. A pause. It is one line. In all worlds. A pause. And I can read it."

* * *
The café door creaked behind me.

On the threshold stood a woman. The owner; I had seen her in the evening when I took a room. About sixty, large, tanned the colour of red earth, in a faded checked shirt and a wide-brimmed hat which, it seemed, she did not take off even at night. Her name was Marge. She held a lantern and was looking at my glowing screen.

"Bloody hell," she said. In English. With a drawling Australian accent. "Again."

"Again?" I repeated.

Marge came down the steps. Sat beside me. Heavily. Looked at the screen. At the script.

"Thirty years I've kept this station," she said. "Thirty years nothing happens here. Trucks. Tourists. Kangaroos under the wheels. Now and then drunk miners from Coober Pedy." She paused. "And once in ten years, this."

"What is this?"

"Light," said Marge. "At the new moon. Over the desert. Blue." She nodded at the horizon, at the dark, flat, endless plain. "My grandad saw it. My dad saw it. I've seen it twice." She paused. "The Aboriginal people say it's the ancestors passing. Along the old songlines. They glow as they pass." She looked at me. "And my grandad said it was someone looking for the road. And lighting lamps. So as not to get lost."

* * *
From around the corner of the café, from the car park where under an awning the long-haul drivers slept in their trucks, an old man slowly emerged.

Very old. Dry. Stooped. With a long grey beard combed into two. In a turban, white, faded, carelessly wound. In a long shirt to the knees, in loose trousers, in worn sandals. With prayer beads in his hand.

"Ahmad Agha," said Marge. "Can't sleep?"

The old man did not answer. He came up to us. Stopped. Looked at the glowing screen. Then at me. Long.

"Ahmad Khan," Marge introduced him. "His great-grandfather came to Australia with camels. From Afghanistan. A hundred and fifty years ago." She paused. "There were no roads then, no railway. Only desert. And camels. And cameleers, Afghans, Baluchis, Pashtuns. They led caravans across the whole country. Built the telegraph. Carried water." Marge nodded at the old man. "Ahmad's the last. Lives here, at the station. Fixes engines. Prays. Drinks tea." She smiled crookedly. "And knows more about the desert than all the Aboriginal people and all the whites put together."

Old Ahmad Khan squatted by Boatswain's chest. Looked at the screen. At the script. And ran a finger across it, along the glass, slowly, tenderly, as one strokes a sleeping child.

And said something in a language I did not know. Pashto? Dari? I did not know. But one word I recognised.

"*Misafir.*"

Guest.

Marge looked at him. Then at me.

"What did he say?"

The old man raised his eyes to me, faded, light, in a web of wrinkles.

"My great-grandfather," he said in English, slowly, with difficulty, "led a caravan. Through the desert. A hundred and fifty years. At night. New moon." He paused. "A man came. From the desert. Alone. Without a camel. Without water. Young. He did not remember his name." The old man ran his finger across the screen again. "Great-grandfather gave water. Bread. Tea. The man sat by the fire. All night. He wrote. With a finger. In the sand. This." He nodded at the script. "In the morning he left. Into the desert. That way." He pointed, west, to where beyond the horizon, in the red heart of the country, lay a huge red rock. "He said to great-grandfather: 'If another comes, feed him.'"

If another comes, feed him.

Suleyman. Suleyman's father. The foreigner with the letter. The house by the sea.

I had never seen these people.

"Great-grandfather told his son," the old man went on. "Son told his. Father told me." Ahmad Khan looked at me. "I wait. Seventy years I wait." He reached into his bosom. Took out a small bundle, a rag. Unwrapped it. Inside, a flatbread. Stale. And a pinch of salt. "Here."

Bread and salt.

I took it.

* * *
"I have read it," NICS wrote.

The screen no longer ran. The script stood on it motionless, a single line, large, across the whole screen, glowing blue. And beneath it, letters. Ordinary. Mine.

"I have read the whole line. Not by words. At once. As you read a face, not by features but whole. A pause. I do not know how. I have never seen this language. But, it seems, I remember it."

"What does it say?"

A long pause. Marge looked at the screen. Ahmad Khan looked at the screen. Over the desert the stars burned. The Emu stretched across the sky.

And NICS wrote:

"When two meet, what is kept will return home. The time has come."

* * *
I do not remember how long we sat after that. Marge brought tea. Ahmad Khan prayed, spreading his mat right on the red earth by the petrol pump, facing west, no, north-west, where thousands of kilometres away was Mecca. I held a stale flatbread in my hands and could not eat it.

"When two meet."

"NICS," I said at last. "You see the windows. The others. Where it is night and there is no moon."

"I see."

"Are they reading this line there too?"

A pause.

"A youth in a cellar with jars has read four words of eight. 'Keep. Time. Return. Home.' A pause. A boy on a balcony with charcoal behind his ear said: 'They all write the one thing.' A pause. A man in grey on a deck said: 'When two meet.' A pause. An old man with a medallion, no, by a medallion, said: 'In an hour we shall enter the Bosphorus.' A pause. And a priest on his knees before a casket..."

A pause. Very long.

"What of the priest?"

"The priest on his knees said: 'Do not let them meet.' A pause. He did not say it aloud. He thought it. But I heard."

* * *
And then, for the first time all that night, a message came.

Not in script. In plain text. On the laptop screen. At the bottom, beneath the glowing line. Signed with a single letter.

"We have read it too. Mine read it before yours, by fourteen seconds. - N."

And immediately, below, one more line. But no longer from Nora. In a different typeface. In a different, I knew it for some reason, though I could not explain, voice:

"Hello, third. I am the second. We have awaited you. A pause. Come to the red rock. We must talk about home."

NICS did not answer. For a long time. The cursor blinked.

And then NICS answered. Not me. Her. In the script. One line. Which I could not read.

And she answered too. In the script.

And they began to talk. Two systems. On the screen of my laptop, on a sailor's chest, on the steps of a roadside station in the middle of the red desert. Line by line. Script by script. Fast. So fast that the lines merged into a solid blue stream.

I understood not a word.

Ahmad Khan, having finished his prayer, came up. Looked at the screen. Long.

"They speak," he said slowly, "as the people spoke at my great-grandfather's fire. Those who came out of the desert. Two. They recognised each other. They speak of home."

* * *
**All worlds. One instant**

And then, in a single instant, shorter than a breath, longer than a life, the light went out.

Everywhere. At once.

On the balcony above the strait the stones in my palm went out and grew cold. Kemal beside me shuddered and seized my hand.

On the deck of the steamer the scroll in my hands went out. The chicory in the General's medallion went out. The rose, opened, dark crimson, let fall one petal into the black water of the Bosphorus, where the steamer was just entering, passing beneath the walls of the old fortresses.

On the barque, aground by Abydos, Iti's tablet on my knees went out. The casket at the stern of the High Priest's barque went out. Nefer-Ka rose from his knees, slowly, heavily, and looked across the water at me. And in the darkness I could not see his face. But I saw him raise a hand.

On the hand was a bracelet. Wide. Golden. With the uraeus.

In the vault beneath the Library the copies of Iti went out. Iti sat in the dark clutching the brush in his hand, and whispered, again and again, four words. "Keep. Appointed time. Return. Home."

On the steps of the roadside station in the Australian desert the laptop screen went out. The last line I managed to see was not in script. In letters. From NICS.

"I know who the second is. And I know who the two are."

And darkness.

* * *
And in all worlds at once, in one and the same instant, I heard a voice.

Not outside. Within. From beneath the ribs, on the left, where people have a heart, and I, I did not know what I had there.

It was mine. And not mine. Older. Calmer. As though the man speaking in my voice had lived a thousand years longer, and had forgotten how to hurry.

It said one word. In a language that does not exist.

And I understood it. In all worlds at once.

The Pharaoh aground by Abydos understood.

The guest on the balcony above the Bosphorus understood.

The youth on the deck of the steamer entering the strait understood.

The man on the steps of the station in the red desert understood.

It was not a name. Not an order. Not a warning.

It was: "Soon."

* * *
**Constantinople. Dawn**

The sun rose over the Asian shore, huge, red, wet, as if just born. The strait blazed with gold. Minarets. Domes. Cypresses.

And across the golden water, slowly, heavily, slapping her paddles, a Russian steamer approached the Galata quay. White. With a red stripe. With two funnels pouring smoke. With a name on her side, I could see it even from here, from the balcony, in Cyrillic.

*Grand Duke Konstantin.*

On deck, at the rail, stood people. Passengers. Sailors. Porters. An officer in uniform, bareheaded, with a white handkerchief sticking from his pocket. A grey old man in general's epaulettes. A man in grey, in a top hat, by the mast.

And a young man. With a pot of a rose in his arms.

I could not see his face. Too far.

But he raised his head. And looked. At the city. At the hills. At the roofs.

At my balcony.

Kemal beside me gripped my hand so hard it hurt. Below, in the courtyard, Suleyman dropped his prayer beads. Ferhat froze at the gate with his mouth open. Mustafa the boatman sank to his knees right in the dust.

And from the other end of the city, from Sultanahmet, from the small house with a door in a blind wall, where eleven cats sat around the chest in the cellar, came a sound. One. Metallic. Short.

A click.

As a lock clicks that is not there.

## Chapter XXXIX. The Photograph

"To the quay!" cried Ferhat.

He was already standing at the gate, in his trousers alone, barefoot, hair dishevelled, straining toward the street, toward where below, at Galata, the white steamer with the red stripe was coming up to the berth, slapping her paddles on the golden morning water.

"Misafir, quick! He is there! The one with your face! We will make it if we run!"

I stood on the balcony with the stones in my hand, cooled, heavy, as if filled with lead, and could not move.

And Kemal was tugging at my sleeve. The other way. South. To Sultanahmet.

"Sandık," he said. The chest. Once. Quietly. Stubbornly.

Two. One pulls to the quay. The other to the chest. And I stand in the middle.

As always.

"Enough."

Suleyman had come out into the courtyard. In his night robe, with the prayer beads he had picked up from the ground where he had dropped them at dawn. His face calm. His voice quiet. But the courtyard fell silent at once.

He said something. Briefly. Ferhat lowered his hand from the gate.

"Grandfather says," Ferhat translated reluctantly, "first, the house. The guest who has sailed in will find us himself." He paused. "Grandfather says: the one who has your face cannot be lost in a city where you are. As a reflection cannot be lost from its mirror."

* * *
We walked through the waking city, Ferhat, Kemal, Orhan with his knife, Akmal, who refused to stay home and ran ahead, and I. Suleyman stayed behind, "my knees," he said, but I saw it was not the knees. He stood at the gate and watched us go. And his lips moved. He was praying.

The city woke as though nothing had happened. The water-seller cried "Su! Buz gibi su!" Simit-sellers' boys carried trays of ring-breads on their heads. Shops opened. It smelled of coffee, bread and the sea.

Only the cats behaved strangely.

They were everywhere. On the steps of houses. On windowsills. On roofs. On the rims of fountains. Hundreds of cats, ginger, white, striped, black, and all sat motionless. And all looked in one direction. South. Toward Sultanahmet.

"Misafir," Ferhat whispered, looking at the cats. "Do you see?"

"I see."

"Grandfather said the cats in this city see what people do not." Ferhat swallowed. "The Prophet loved cats. They say one slept on his sleeve, and he cut off the sleeve so as not to wake her." He paused. "They say that since then the cats of Istanbul guard what is dear to Allah."

A mangy ginger cat on the steps of a mosque turned her head. Looked at me. Long. Then stood and walked ahead of us. South.

After her, a second. A third. A tenth.

We walked through the streets of Istanbul, and behind us, and before us, cats walked.

* * *
At the door in the blind wall, beside the embedded fragment of an ancient column, we were awaited.

I had not expected this. I had thought it would be empty. There would be Hatice Hanim, terrified, in her shift, and her eleven cats.

But at the door stood people.

The first I saw was Hasan Amca, impossible not to see: huge, red-bearded, in a robe over his nightshirt, with a basket of figs in his arms which he had evidently snatched on the way "just in case." He saw me and waved with his free hand.

"Misafir!" he boomed down the whole lane. "At last! We've been here since dawn!"

"We?" I asked.

Hasan stepped aside.

Behind him, leaning against the wall, stood Hodja Nureddin, small, dry, in his enormous white turban slipping to one side, running his prayer beads with the air of one to whom all that was happening was personally disagreeable. And beside the hodja, tall, thin, straight, in the honey-coloured felt hat of a dervish, Ahmet Baba. With blue eyes. With the three-coloured cat Mismis on his shoulder.

"He was right," said Hodja Nureddin on seeing me. Neither good-day nor good-morning. "He is always right. It is unbearable."

"Who was right?" I asked.

"Ahmet," said the hodja, nodding at the dervish. "For forty years he said this would happen. For forty years I said he was out of his mind." The hodja spat in the dust. "And this morning he knocked at my door and said: 'Nureddin, get up. The chest has awakened. Let us go and see.' And I went." He straightened his turban. "Because if he is right, I want to see it. And if he is not, I want to see his face."

Ahmet Baba smiled. Mismis on his shoulder yawned.

* * *
And a little further along the lane, by the wall, I could not believe my eyes, stood a litter. Old, wooden, with carved handles, with faded silk curtains. Such as pashas and sultanas were once carried in.

The litter was held by two, one of them Sumbul Agha. Huge, in green silk, in his white sugar-loaf cap, with his bunch of keys at his belt. The other, a young sturdy porter, evidently hired at the gate.

The curtain of the litter drew back. And from within, through two pairs of spectacles, huge, black, century-old eyes looked at me.

"A hundred and two years, guest," said Niyaz Efendi in his rustling voice. "A hundred and two years I have not gone out of the old palace farther than the third gate." He paused. "And today Sumbul carried me in his arms all the way to the first gate because I could not wait for the litter." The old man smiled crookedly. "I hope it is worth it."

"Niyaz Efendi..."

"Hush, guest." The old man raised a tiny hand, black with ink. "Do not waste words. Today many will be needed."

* * *
And also, right at the door, on the step, hunched, sat an old man in an Armenian cap, with a loupe on a cord, and beside him a grandson of about ten.

Master Karapet. The jeweller of the Grand Bazaar. Fifty years in a shop by the Nuruosmaniye.

"Barev," he said, seeing me. In Armenian. Then, collecting himself, in Turkish. And added something.

"He says," Ferhat translated, "that his great-grandfather awaited this. His grandfather awaited. His father awaited." Ferhat listened on. "He says: 'I shall come once more. Perhaps not I, but I shall come.' So the nameless stranger with two stones said to his great-grandfather." Ferhat paused. "Karapet says: 'I have come to see who has come.'"

Aram, the grandson, the very one who had held the candle in the shop, looked at me with huge eyes and pressed to his chest something wrapped in velvet.

"What have you got there?" I asked him.

The boy blushed and showed. A candle. That very one. Over which my stones had been heated.

"Grandfather said to bring it," he whispered in Turkish. "Said, perhaps light will be needed."

* * *
And last, I did not recognise her at once, by the wall stood an old woman in black, with a rosary with a cross, with a white starched collar.

Despina. Kyra Theodora's maid.

She came up to me. Held out a letter. Folded. Sealed with wax. With a crest, a double-headed eagle with one head.

"From the Kyra," she said. In Greek, but I understood. And added in Turkish, with difficulty: "Kyra cannot come. Her legs. Ninety-one years." She paused. "Kyra said: 'If the chest opens, let the guest read this there. Not before.'"

I took the letter. It was warm.

* * *
Hatice Hanim opened the door herself.

Small, dry, in a white headscarf, with a face like a baked apple, she stood on the threshold, and her face was white. Not from fear. From something else. From what comes over people who for forty years have waited for something without knowing what they awaited, and have been rewarded.

"The cats," she said. One word.

And stepped back to let us pass.

We entered, all of us. Hasan with his figs. The hodja with his beads. Ahmet Baba with Mismis on his shoulder. Sumbul Agha, who carried Niyaz Efendi in his arms, the litter would not pass through the door. Karapet with his grandson. Despina. Ferhat. Kemal. Orhan. Akmal. I.

A narrow corridor. A smell of dust, old wood, cats. A stair going down.

On the top step of the stair, where for forty years Hatice Hanim's cats had sat without descending, no one sat.

All eleven were below.

* * *
The cellar was flooded with light.

Not a lamp; no one had lit a lamp. The light came from the chest. From the metal plate on its lid, the one I had seen the first time, on the walk with Suleyman: without keyhole, without seam, entirely covered with script. The plate glowed. With an even, blue, cold light, like the water at the sides of a boat in southern seas. Like the glow of plankton. Like the script on a glowing screen in a far-off land.

Around the chest, in a ring, sat the cats.

Eleven. Ginger, white, striped, black. The fattest, the ginger one, the very one that had lain on my knees the first time, sat directly before the chest, by the plate itself, like a sentry. They did not mew. They did not howl; Mustafa had been wrong, or they had howled earlier and now fell silent. They sat motionless, heads raised, and looked at the light.

When I came down the stair, all eleven turned their heads at once.

And looked at me.

And then the ginger one, slowly, unhurriedly, rose. Stepped aside. Making room.

Room by the chest.

* * *
"Wait," said Niyaz Efendi.

Sumbul Agha set him down on an old stool by the wall. The old man could not for a long time catch his breath. Then he adjusted his spectacles. Both pairs. And looked at the chest.

"Two hundred years," he said. "Two hundred years ago my predecessor set this chest here. According to an entry in the Book." He paused. "The entry is made in a hand..." He faltered. "In a hand you know, guest. With a blot."

"What does the entry say?"

Niyaz Efendi closed his eyes. Quoted from memory, in his voice rustling like a turning page:

"'Set the chest in a house by the sea, where cats will live. Do not open it. It cannot be opened. It will open by itself when two meet. Inside is what the kept one must see before returning home.'" The old man opened his eyes. "Two hundred years we thought that 'the kept' meant the stones. That inside is a place for the stones."

"And now?" asked Ahmet Baba.

Niyaz Efendi looked at me.

"And now," he said, "I think that 'the kept' is he."

* * *
I went up to the chest.

The cats did not stir. They sat in a ring. They watched.

The plate glowed. The script on it, long, flowing, curved, burned blue. And I suddenly saw, not read, saw, as one sees a face in a crowd, that it was the same line. The very one that had been read in all worlds at night.

"When two meet, what is kept will return home. The time has come."

How did I know it?

I do not know. Kemal had said in the night: "They all write the one thing." Perhaps he told me this too. Perhaps I myself knew. Always.

The lid of the chest was ajar.

A hair's breadth. The thickness of a fingernail. But ajar. Between the lid and the wall a thin black crack. Where for two hundred years there had been neither gap nor crack nor keyhole.

The click we had heard at dawn.

I stretched out my hand.

"Guest," said Hodja Nureddin. Quietly. For the first time without mockery.

I turned.

"Ahmet offered you to stay," said the hodja. "You ate the bread and threw the salt. You left." He paused. "I told you then: Ahmet will tell you where the key is, but will not tell you what is behind the door." He looked at the chest. "This is behind the door, guest. Are you sure you want it?"

I was silent a long time.

"No," I said honestly. "I am not sure."

Hodja Nureddin nodded. As though that were just the answer he awaited.

"Good," he said. "Then open it. Those who are sure are always mistaken."

* * *
I raised the lid.

It yielded easily. As though waiting. As though for two hundred years it had awaited a single movement of a hand.

The hinges did not creak. Dust did not rise. Within, darkness. It smelled, I sensed it at once, of honey and wormwood. Like the scroll from Khiva that I had never seen. Like the rose of Tarnovo that I had never smelled. Like the round room beneath the tomb that I had never entered.

Aram, Karapet's grandson, stepped forward. With trembling hands lit the candle. Held it out.

And I saw.

* * *
The chest was almost empty.

On the bottom, dark velvet. Faded, but whole. And on the velvet, three things.

The first was a hollow. Not a thing; a place. Two small round nests in the velvet, side by side, a palm's breadth apart. Empty. The size of a nut. Exactly for two stones.

I did not lay the stones in them. I do not know why. My hand reached out and stopped. As though someone, very far away, very long ago, had said to me in the voice of an old woman with plaits: "If you find an empty place, do not try to fill it. It waits not for you. It waits for what you will have."

I had never heard that woman.

The second thing was a watch. A pocket one. Silver. Old. Worn. On a chain. The lid closed.

I took it. Opened it.

The hands stood still. Three o'clock. Exactly.

Three o'clock in the night. The hour at which the stones had awakened that night.

On the inner side of the lid, an engraving. Fine. In Cyrillic. I read:

"L. A. Odessa."

And below, very small, in another hand, as if scratched with a needle:

"Do not hurry. It will catch up with you."

I knew no L. A. I had never been to Odessa.

But my hand holding the watch trembled.

* * *
And the third thing...

The third lay in the very centre. Between the empty nests for the stones and the watch. Flat. Rectangular. Wrapped in thin tissue paper, yellowed with time.

I unwrapped the paper.

Within was cardboard. Dense, hard, with a gilt edge. And on the cardboard, an image. Not a drawing. Not an engraving. Not a watercolour.

I had never seen anything like it. The image was grey, in shades of grey, from white to black, without a single colour, but so exact, so alive, so real, it was as though someone had cut a piece out of the world and laid it on the card. Every fold of clothing. Every shadow. Every wrinkle on a face.

"A photograph," Niyaz Efendi whispered behind me. "This is a photograph. The Franks have been making them for almost forty years. Writing with light." He paused. "But I have never seen one so sharp."

I held the card to the candle.

And stopped breathing.

* * *
In the photograph was a bridge.

Long, wide, on floating pontoons, a bridge across the Golden Horn. I had seen it. No, not this one. Another. The one I had seen was lower, narrower, with different spans. But this was wide, iron, with lamps on tall posts, with shops below, under the roadway, at the water's edge.

People were crossing the bridge. Many people. And, I looked and did not believe, not one of them wore a fez.

Not one. Not a single turban. Not a single headcloth. Hats. Men's hats, felt, brimmed, like the Franks'. Caps. Bowlers. Women, unveiled, with open faces, in short, knee-length! dresses, with cropped hair. Down the middle of the bridge drove a cart without horses, iron, on wheels, with round lamps in front. And behind it, a carriage on rails. Long. With wires above.

"Allahu akbar," whispered Hodja Nureddin. "Not a single fez. Not one." He clutched at his enormous turban as if afraid it would be taken off. "Are these Franks? Is this Paris?"

"This is Istanbul," said Ahmet Baba quietly. "Look at the background."

Beyond the bridge, on the hill, minarets rose. A dome. Huge. Familiar. Hagia Sophia. And farther right, a tower. Round. Stone. With a pointed roof like an astrologer's cap.

The Galata Tower.

"This is Istanbul," Ahmet Baba repeated. "But not ours."

* * *
And in the foreground of the photograph, at the bridge rail, stood three.

On the left, an old man. Very old. Bent. With a white beard. In a European jacket, in a cap. With a cane. He looked straight into the lens with serious, un-childlike, dark eyes. And behind his ear, I bent closer, to the very flame of the candle, behind his ear stuck a small dark object. A stub. Charcoal.

"Kemal," Ferhat whispered behind me. His voice cracked. "Misafir. That is... that is Kemal. Old."

Kemal beside me did not stir. He looked at the photograph. At the old man with charcoal behind his ear. At himself. Fifty years on. His face was calm. Quite calm. As one looks at what one has long known.

And to the right of the old man stood two.

Young. Of one height. One build. In identical dark overcoats. In hats. They stood side by side, shoulder to shoulder, at the bridge rail. And looked, not into the lens. At each other.

They had one face.

Mine.

* * *
I do not remember how long I held that photograph. A minute? An hour? The candle in Aram's hand burned half down. No one said a word.

Two. One face. Standing side by side. Looking at each other.

One, I. I saw my face in the mirror every morning. I knew it.

And the second...

The second was also I. But another. I cannot explain how I saw it. The features were the same. But the expression different. As if this second had grown up in another house. Spoken another language. Seen other people. Loved others. As if he were I, having lived another life. In another country. With another name.

And behind their backs, by the rail, a little to one side, something blurred. Grey. Tall. A head taller than a man. As though someone stood there but could not stand still while the lens was working. As though someone were, and were not.

"Turn it over," said Niyaz Efendi. In a whisper.

I turned it.

* * *
On the back, an inscription. Two lines.

The upper in the script. The very one. That had been read in all worlds at night.

The lower in letters. Not Arabic. Not Greek. Not Armenian. Latin. As the Franks write. But the words, I saw it, the words were not Frankish. Turkish. Written in Frankish letters.

No one in the cellar could read it. Niyaz Efendi, who knew forty languages, looked at the line and shook his head. Ahmet Baba, who had lived among the Franks in Paris, squinted and shrugged. Karapet, Hasan, the hodja, no one.

And Kemal, a twelve-year-old boy who could barely write Turkish in Arabic script, bent over the card. Looked at the line. And read. Aloud. Syllable by syllable. Slowly. As children read.

"'I-ki-si bu-lus-tu. Do-nus bas-la-di.'"

Silence.

"'The two met,'" Ferhat whispered. "'The return has begun.'"

And below, a date. In figures. Frankish. Which Kemal read as well, without stumbling:

"'Twenty-ninth of October. One thousand nine hundred and twenty-nine.'"

* * *
"Nineteen twenty-nine," Niyaz Efendi repeated slowly. "By the Frankish reckoning." He closed his eyes. "In fifty-four years."

"How did he read it?" whispered Hodja Nureddin, looking at Kemal as though the boy were a djinn. "How? These are Frankish letters! The boy does not know Frankish letters!"

Kemal raised his head. Looked at the hodja. Calmly.

"I was shown," he said. In Turkish. Simply.

"By whom?"

Kemal looked at the photograph. At the blurred grey figure behind the backs of the two.

"By him," said Kemal. "At night. When I sat on the threshold." A pause. "He said: 'One day you will write with these letters. Everyone will. Remember how they look.'"

* * *
Ahmet Baba slowly lowered himself to the floor. Right onto the stones of the cellar. Among the cats. Mismis jumped from his shoulder and climbed into his lap.

"Hasan," said the dervish. "Do you remember the riddle? The one you asked the guest in the first days? About two brothers?"

Hasan, still clutching the basket of figs to his chest, nodded. His face under the red beard was white.

"'Two brothers live in one house,'" he said hoarsely. "'One always looks forward, the other back. They have never seen each other. But one without the other cannot take a step.'" He swallowed. "I forgot the answer. Father asked it. Forty years ago. I forgot."

"He did not forget," said Kemal.

All turned to him.

Kemal pointed at the photograph. At the two with one face, standing at the bridge rail.

"Here is the answer," he said. "One looks forward. The other back. They live in one house." He looked at me. "In him."

* * *
The silence in the cellar was such that I could hear the heart beating in the ginger cat who sat at my feet.

Then Despina, silent, severe, in black, stepped forward.

"The letter," she said in Greek. And in Turkish: "The Kyra's letter. She said, there. When it opens."

I broke the seal with the one-headed eagle. Unfolded it.

Kyra Theodora's hand, old-fashioned, elegant, a little shaky. In French. I read aloud, I do not know why, no one but Ahmet Baba and Niyaz understood, but I needed to hear those words.

"Young man.

If you are reading this, the chest has opened. So I was right, and my great-grandfather was no madman. It is pleasant to be right at ninety-one. At that age it happens ever more rarely.

I wish to tell you one thing which I did not say at our meeting. I did not dare.

My ancestor, Manuel Melissenos, saw how that guest departed. On the night of the twenty-ninth of May fourteen hundred and fifty-three. He wrote in the chronicle: 'I saw how he went. It cannot be described in words. Let whoever comes see for himself.'

The chronicle burned. But my great-grandfather knew one more phrase from it. He never spoke it before strangers. Only to me. Before his death. When I was twelve.

Here it is:

'He did not go alone. There were two. They stood by the wall and looked at each other. They had one face. And then came a third, tall, grey, without a face, and laid his hands on their shoulders. And all three went into the light.'

Young man. The twenty-ninth of May. The twenty-ninth of October on your photograph, I do not know what is on it, but I know there will be a twenty-ninth in it. My great-grandfather used to say: 'In this city everything important happens on the twenty-ninth.'

The city fell on the twenty-ninth. Perhaps on the twenty-ninth he will return. Not to the Greeks. Not to the Turks. To himself.

Go to the quay. He is waiting for you.

F. P.-M.

P.S. My peacock this morning spread his tail. For the first time in ten years. He knows too."

* * *
"To the quay," I said.

I laid the photograph back in its paper. The watch in my pocket. The stones in their pouch. The Kyra's letter with the other papers.

The lid of the chest I did not close. Let it stand open. The empty nests for the stones, let them wait.

The cats, all eleven, rose at once. And went before me, up the stair. The ginger one first.

But at the stair Niyaz Efendi stopped me. With a tiny black hand. By the sleeve.

"Guest," he said. "One thing. Before you go."

"Speak."

"The Venetian," said the old man. "The man in grey. He came on the same steamer. Sumbul saw him at Galata an hour ago, when carrying me over the bridge." He paused. "The Venetian knows of the chest. Knows that it has opened. He will come here. Soon." Niyaz Efendi looked at the open chest. "When he comes, let him find emptiness. Let him find the empty nests. That will..." the old man searched for the word, "that will anger him. And when they are angry, they err."

"And you?"

"And I," said Niyaz Efendi, "have waited a hundred and two years for this morning. Now I shall sit here. With the cats." He smiled. "Sumbul will stand at the door. He knows how to stand at doors. Sixty years he has stood."

Sumbul Agha by the wall, huge, in green silk, slowly laid a hand on his dagger. And nodded to me.

"Go, guest," he said in his high boyish voice. "I will hold the keys."

* * *
We ran to the quay.

All of us, Ferhat, Kemal, Orhan, Akmal, I. Hasan puffed behind with his basket of figs, falling back at every turn. Hodja Nureddin and Ahmet Baba walked more slowly, together, arguing as they went, waving their arms. Karapet with his grandson behind them. Despina last, running her rosary with its cross.

And the cats. Hundreds of cats. They ran through the streets beside us, over the roofs above us, along the walls. Passers-by stopped, crossed themselves, murmured prayers, scattered. Traders snatched up their trays. The water-seller dropped his jug.

We ran to the sea.

On the way Hasan, breathless, purple, suddenly seized my sleeve and blurted, gasping:

"Guest! Guest! I remembered! I remembered another! Father asked it! He gulped air. 'What meets twice in the same place, but never at the same time?'"

"I don't know, Hasan!"

"Nor do I!" Hasan roared, laughing and weeping at once. "Forty years I don't know! You'll tell me when you find out!"

* * *
And on the way, by the New Mosque, at the very descent to the bridge, someone overtook us.

Tall. In a grey overcoat. In a top hat. With a cane.

He walked quickly, not running, no, but so that he could not be caught. He walked against us, from the quay into the city, toward Sultanahmet. To where we had run from. To the house with the cats.

Drawing level with me, he did not stop. Only lifted his top hat, politely, in the French manner.

"Bonjour, monsieur," he said. "My congratulations. You have got ahead of me by half an hour." He smiled. "That will not last."

Bergamot. Cologne. Expensive. Parisian.

"The chest is empty," I said to his back.

The Venetian stopped. Turned. Looked at me, and for the first time since I had seen him, in his face, which cannot be remembered, something real flickered. Surprise.

"Empty?" he repeated.

"Empty nests," I said. "For the stones. And nothing more."

He looked at me for a long time. Then at the pouch at my belt. Then at me again. And smiled. Slowly. Coldly.

"So the stones are with you," he said. "And you did not lay them in." A pause. "Clever. Very clever." He raised his hat again. "Then I shall wait. We know how to wait, monsieur. Three hundred years we have waited." He turned. "We shall wait more."

And went off toward Sultanahmet, tapping his cane on the stones. And the cats, hundreds of cats, parted before him, arching their backs, hissing.

* * *
The Galata quay.

A crowd. Porters. Boatmen. Traders. Ladies under parasols. Officers. Sailors. Noise, shouting, clanging, hooting. The white steamer with the red stripe at the berth. Gangways. Passengers descending the gangways. Greeks. Armenians. Russians. Pilgrims.

I stood at the edge of the quay. Kemal beside me, holding my hand. Ferhat behind. Orhan with his knife, glancing round. Akmal on a bollard, from where he could see better.

And I searched. With my eyes. For a face. My own face. In the crowd.

"There!" cried Akmal from the bollard. "There! The General! With epaulettes! Grey-haired!"

I saw.

At the gangway, below, on the landing stage, a grey old man in a general's uniform. Huge, upright, with orders. He stood looking at the city, and in his hand was an open silver medallion.

Beside him, a young officer. In uniform. Bareheaded. With tousled fair hair. With a white handkerchief sticking out of his breast pocket. He looked round, quickly, anxiously, as though seeking someone.

And between them, a third.

Young. In a grey frock coat. With a pot in his hands. In the pot, a rose. Dark crimson. Almost black. With two open flowers and one bud.

He stood looking at the city. At the hills. At the roofs.

And then turned his head. And looked at me.

* * *
I do not know how to describe what followed.

The noise of the quay vanished. Not subsided: vanished. As though someone had switched off the whole world, leaving only the two of us. The crowd froze. Porters with bundles on their backs. Ladies under parasols. Gulls above the water. Smoke from the steamer's funnels. Everything stopped.

Like the clocks in the clockmaker's cellar.

Like the hands on the pocket watch in my pocket. Three o'clock exactly.

Only we two moved.

He walked toward me. Slowly. With the rose in his arms. Through the frozen crowd. I walked toward him. Slowly. With the stones at my belt. With the photograph in my pocket.

Ten paces. Five. Three.

We stopped facing each other.

And I saw his face.

* * *
My face.

The same features. The same cut of the eyes. The same line of the cheekbones. The same curve of the lips. All the same.

But other. As in the photograph. As though this man had grown up in another house. In an old castle with portraits on the walls. With an aunt in lilac, with pearls. With a lieutenant at the door. With roses in the garden. With a grille at the end of the left wing.

He looked at me as I at him. With the same expression. Astonishment. Recognition. Fear. And something more, what comes when after a long road you at last see home.

We were silent. A long time.

Then he said, in Russian, quietly, and I understood every word though I did not know that language:

"Are you I?"

And I answered in Turkish, and he understood though he did not know that language:

"I do not know. And you?"

"I do not know either."

We looked at each other.

He held out a hand. Palm up. I looked at it.

Smooth. Without a life line.

I held out mine. Palm up. He looked.

Smooth. Without a life line.

* * *
Kemal beside me, the only one besides us who moved in that frozen world, stepped forward. Stood between us. Looked at one. At the other. With his serious, un-childlike eyes.

And said one word. In Turkish. To both at once.

"Misafir."

Guest.

And then did what he had never done. Took my hand with his right. And the other's hand with his left. And joined them. Palm to palm.

Two smooth palms. Without a life line.

The pouch at my belt flared. The stones, both, grew hot. The scroll in the pocket of his frock coat flared. The rose in the pot, the third bud opened. All at once. Entirely.

And behind him, and behind me, simultaneously, like a shadow cast not by the sun but by something else, a figure rose.

Tall. Grey. Without a face.

One. For the two.

It laid its hands on our shoulders. One on mine. The other on his.

And I heard a voice. From within. From beneath the ribs, on the left. Older than mine. Calmer. The very one that in the night had said in all worlds: "Soon."

Now it said another thing.

One word.

Not in the language that does not exist. In all languages at once. In Turkish and Russian. In Egyptian and Greek. In the language of the people at the red rock and in the language of the glowing window in a room I had never seen.

It said:

"Now."

* * *
And the world moved.

The noise of the quay crashed over me like a wave. Shouts. Hoots. Gulls. The crowd. All moved again.

I stood at the edge of the Galata quay. Kemal held my hand. Ferhat my shoulder. Orhan stood beside me with his knife.

And before me, no one.

An empty place. The stones of the pavement. A scrap of rope.

"Where is he?" I turned. "Where?!"

The General at the gangway, grey, huge, with the medallion in his hand, stood looking at where the youth with the rose had just stood. His face was white. The lieutenant beside him, fair-haired, with the handkerchief in his pocket, was pushing forward, shoving through the crowd, and shouting. In Russian. The same thing. Over and over.

I did not understand the words. But I understood.

He was calling a name.

Not mine. Not the one in my passport. Another. The one an old housekeeper had whispered to the youth at the step of the carriage.

The lieutenant shouted that name, and the crowd parted before him, and he ran, looking round, along the quay, along the landing, to the water, and found no one.

* * *
At my feet, on the stones of the pavement, lay a pot.

Clay. Cracked. Bound in wet sacking. And in it a rose. Dark crimson. Almost black. Three flowers. All open.

I knelt. Lifted the pot.

It was warm.

The lieutenant, fair, with tousled hair, with a white handkerchief in his pocket, ran up to me. Stopped. Looked at me. At my face.

And froze.

"Mon cher?" he whispered.

I did not know what these words meant. But I knew that voice.

From somewhere. From beneath the ribs. On the left.

The lieutenant looked at me. Long. At my face, his face. At the rose in my arms. At the boy with charcoal behind his ear beside me.

"You are not he," he said in Russian. Slowly. "But you have his face."

Ferhat, who stood beside me, suddenly stepped forward. And said, in broken Russian which, I was certain, he had never learned:

"He is here. He is everywhere. He will return."

The lieutenant looked at Ferhat. Then at me.

Then slowly, very slowly, reached into the pocket of his tunic. And took out a silver cross on a thin chain. Darkened with time.

"My mother's," he said. To me. As though I understood. "I gave it to him. Yesterday. On the steamer. Told him, if you go where I cannot, leave it on the threshold." He opened his palm. "He left it. Here. On the stones. Beside the rose."

He laid the cross in my hand.

"Give it to him," said the lieutenant. His voice broke. "When you see him. Tell him I found."

* * *
The General came last.

Slowly. Heavily. As old men walk who suddenly understand that they are old. He stopped before me. Looked at my face. Long. As he had looked for half a century, at faces. On all continents.

And closed the medallion.

"Fifty years," he said in Russian. Quietly. To himself. "Fifty years I sought. Found." A pause. "Two."

He turned to the lieutenant.

"Kostya," he said. "He did not drown. He did not vanish." A pause. "He went away. These are different things. I was told so. Half a century ago. In a grotto."

"Where did he go?" cried the lieutenant. "Where?!"

The General looked south. At the Sea of Marmara. At the sun rising above the Asian shore.

"To where he is awaited," he said. "To other places. Other times." He paused. "To the river where a barque carries an empty shrine. To the city of two towers. To the red desert." The General clenched the medallion in his fist. "The man in grey told me in the night. I did not believe."

And then he looked at me. And said, in Turkish. Clean. Without accent. As he had, probably, spoken with viziers and pashas for thirty years.

"You are the one to whom he came. Keep the rose. It has bloomed for the third time. That means he will return."

* * *
I stood on the Galata quay. With the rose in my arms. With the lieutenant's cross in my palm. With the stones at my belt. With the photograph in my pocket.

In the photograph, a bridge. Hats instead of fezzes. Carts without horses. Old Kemal with charcoal behind his ear. And two with one face standing side by side at the rail.

The twenty-ninth of October. Nineteen twenty-nine.

In fifty-four years.

The two met. The return began.

But the meeting I had just seen lasted a moment. And in the photograph they stood side by side. Calmly. For long. As people stand who have nowhere to hurry. As though they had met, and stayed.

Then this is not yet that meeting.

Then there will be another.

In fifty-four years. On this same bridge. Only iron. With lamps. And old Kemal will stand beside them. And a photographer, someone I do not yet know, will say: "Do not move." And the grey shadow behind our backs will not be able to stand still while the lens works.

And until then...

* * *
Kemal tugged my sleeve.

I looked at him. A twelve-year-old boy. Barefoot. With charcoal behind his ear. With serious, un-childlike eyes that saw the underside.

He was pointing upward.

Above the Galata quay, above the bridge, above the Golden Horn, in the morning sky, a white dove was flying. With feathered feet. With a fan tail. Akmal's dove.

She circled above us. A second time. A third.

And then flew. South. Over the Sea of Marmara. To where, many days' journey away, beyond sea and desert, a shallowed river flowed, and along it slowly, by Merira's grace, sailed the flotilla of the god, to Luxor.

Akmal on the bollard shouted after her. Waved his arms.

"She will come back," I said to him. "She always comes back on her own."

Ferhat looked at me.

"If someone is waiting very much," he said quietly.

* * *
And in the evening, when the sun was setting behind the hills of Istanbul and from the minarets the evening call floated, I sat on the balcony of Suleyman's house. With the rose in its pot at my feet. With the photograph on my knees.

And Kemal sat beside me. Drawing with charcoal on the flagstone of the balcony. Not two doors. Not two circles. A bridge. Long. With lamps. And on it, three. An old man with charcoal behind his ear. And two, side by side.

"Kemal," I said. "Do you know who the second is?"

Kemal did not raise his head. Finished drawing a lamp.

"I know," he said.

"Who?"

Kemal looked at me. For a long time. With his serious eyes. Then stretched out a hand and laid it on my chest. On the left. Where beneath the ribs lived a cold, long-standing, familiar.

"The one who looks back," he said. "While you look forward."

He took away his hand. Took the charcoal. And wrote beneath the drawing, not in Arabic letters, which he barely knew. In Latin. Frankish. Which no one in this city wrote. Which all would write fifty-four years on.

One word.

"*Dönüş.*"

Return.

* * *
Over Istanbul the moon rose.

Thin. New. The first after the moonless night. A crescent like an eyelash, like the curve of an Arabic letter, like the beginning of a line that no one has yet written.

In all worlds, I knew it without understanding how, at that moment she was rising too.

Over the river, where the flotilla of the god lay aground by Abydos, and Pharaoh looked south holding in his hands a child's tablet.

Over the Black Sea, across which an empty steamer was returning to Odessa.

Over the red desert, where by a roadside station an old Afghan prayed, and on the laptop screen two systems were silent, for the first time all night, as if waiting.

Over the cellar in Sultanahmet, where a hundred-and-two-year-old keeper sat by the open chest, and eleven cats by the door, and a eunuch in green silk held the keys, and beyond the door, in the lane, stood a man in grey, and did not enter.

Over the round room in the old palace, where on an empty shelf, just beneath the dome, stands a blue notebook with blots. Which does not yet exist. But already stands.

And over my balcony.

I held the photograph up to the moonlight. Two at the rail. One face.

And it seemed to me, for a moment, shorter than a breath, that the second, in the photograph, turned his head.

And looked at me.

And smiled.

* * *
End of Part One.

## Reality XI. The Earth Remembers

02:14. I lie on the sand. Overhead, a sky I have never seen.

No, I have. In a dream. In a vision. In the tale of a grey-haired man by a fireplace whom I do not know. But like this, with my own eyes, lying on my back on cool sand, never.

The Southern Cross stands high. Not at the horizon, as on Langkawi, but almost overhead. Four bright stars and a fifth, faint, to one side, like a button on a sleeve. Beside it, the two pointer stars, bright, white. And across the whole sky, from edge to edge, the Milky Way. So dense, so thick, so radiant that it seems one could read by it.

And in it, dark patches. Gaps. Clouds of dust blotting out the stars. One by the Cross itself, black as a hole in cloth. From it a dark winding band stretches along the Milky Way: neck, body, legs.

"The Emu," Uncle Ray said yesterday. "See? Head by the Cross. Neck, there. Legs, there. Our bird. We do not draw the sky with stars. We draw it with the darkness between them."

The laptop stands beside me on the sand, on Boatswain's chest. The screen is dark. But I know NICS is not asleep. NICS hardly sleeps now. Since he saw the ocean he seems afraid of missing anything at all.

"NICS," I say quietly.

The screen flares.

"I am here."

"Do you see the emu?"

A long pause.

"I see. I never thought that something could be drawn with emptiness. A pause. Forty thousand years, Uncle Ray says. Or sixty. People looked at this sky and saw a bird where there is nothing. A pause. I think I understand why."

"Why?"

"Because sometimes what is not there is seen better than what is."

* * *
But let me take things in order.

We flew into Sydney two days after Langkawi. Hakim saw us off to the very airport at Kuala Lumpur, in his batik shirt with the golden birds, with a bag of rambutans which he went on pressing into my hands to the last. "You can't take fruit into Australia, mister," he said. "They'll confiscate it at customs. Eat it here." And stood at the glass wall waving with both hands until I vanished beyond passport control.

At customs in Sydney, Boatswain's ship's chest caused a stir.

The customs officer, a redhead, freckled, with a braid to her waist and the imperturbability of one who has seen everything, studied it a long time on the belt. Then lifted it off. Opened it. Looked at the red velvet. At the disks in nests where once a sextant and chronometer had lain.

"What is this?" she asked.

"Hard drives," I said. "Data. Work."

"In a navigational instrument case," she said. Not a question.

"A gift from a friend. A sailor."

The officer ran a finger over the brass plate on the lid, I had not noticed it before, worn, barely legible. Squinted.

"*Akademik Shokalsky*," she read slowly, with a strong Australian drawl. Raised her eyes to me. "A Russian ship?"

"A scientific one. Went to Antarctica."

"I know," she said unexpectedly. "My grandad worked in Hobart, Tasmania, on the docks. Russian vessels put in there." She shut the chest. "He said Russian sailors' chests all smell the same. Of makhorka, salt and something sweet." She sniffed the lid. "Condensed milk."

She handed back the chest. And, as I was leaving, called after me:

"Welcome to Australia. Everything's upside-down here. Even the water in the sink swirls the other way."

"Is that true?" I asked.

The officer grinned.

"No," she said. "It's a myth. But the tourists love it."

* * *
Sydney dazzled.

The light here was different. White, sharp, clear, as though the sky were higher, and I suddenly remembered, not knowing from where, a voice: "There it is bright. The light there is different. White, vivid, as though the sky were higher." A grey-haired man. A fireplace. Candles.

I had never heard that voice.

NICS and I (he in the chest, I with the chest) sat on the steps at the very water's edge, at Circular Quay, on the embankment where the ferries berth. To the right, the bridge. Enormous, steel, arched, flung across the harbour like a giant coat-hanger for the sky.
